title: Hittite Deportation and Resettlement of Conquered Populations
actors: Hittite kings from Hattusili I and Mursili I to Suppiluliuma I and Mursili II moved captured civilian populations from Syria, Anatolia and the Aegean fringe to the Hittite homeland as agricultural and temple labour
peopleRange: No reliable total. Hittite royal annals count deportees by the Sumerogram NAM.RA (Hittite arnuwala-, 'transportee'), a legal category distinct from prisoners of war, and individual campaign entries in the annals of Mursili II run from a few hundred to figures in the tens of thousands; the largest single claims exceed 60,000. These are the king's own campaign records, composed for the gods and for posterity, and Hittitologists treat the larger figures as rhetorical. No independent or administrative check exists.

flows.label: Aleppo and northern Syria → Hattusa and the Hittite homeland
Western Anatolia (Arzawa lands) → Hittite core territory

summary: Deportation was an institutionalised instrument of Hittite statecraft from the Old Kingdom to the collapse of the empire around 1180 BCE. The Telipinu Proclamation records that Mursili I carried the deportees and goods of Aleppo, and then of Babylon, back to Hattusa; the annals of Suppiluliuma I and Mursili II record the transfer of populations from Arzawa and other western Anatolian lands to the Hittite core. Transportees were designated NAM.RA / arnuwala-, a defined legal status rather than simple captivity, and were assigned to royal and temple estates, to depopulated farmland and to military settlements, with their labour serving to repair the chronic manpower shortage of the Hittite heartland. The numbers survive only in royal campaign narratives written to display the king's success; scholars accept the practice as systematic and large-scale while treating the specific totals, especially those above ten thousand, as unverifiable.
contested: The scale is disputed: the annals' deportee counts are the king's own claims, and Hittitologists disagree over whether the large figures reflect real transfers or the conventions of royal self-presentation.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: The Hittites
University of Texas Linguistics Research Center: The Annals of Mursili (Hittite text with NAM.RA terminology)
Britannica: Hittite

deathsNote: No death toll can be given. Hittite annals describe the destruction of towns and the killing of defenders but were principally concerned with the living population carried off, whose value lay in their labour; mortality in transit is not recorded.
violenceNote: The assignment of NAM.RA transportees to royal, temple and agricultural labour is documented in the Hittite royal annals and summarised in the general literature on the Hittites.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: the deportations spanned four centuries and the whole of Anatolia, Syria and the Aegean fringe, none of it enumerated
baselineNote: Hittite royal annals record captives, the NAM.RA, by campaign rather than by population: Mursili II's ten-year annals alone claim tens of thousands from single campaigns, and Bronze Age Hatti's own population is guessed at roughly one to two million from settlement survey. There is no register, tax list or archaeological base from which the population of the conquered territories over 1600-1180 BCE could be reconstructed, so any percentage would be invented.

title: Egyptian Conquest and Colonisation of Nubia
actors: Successive Egyptian New Kingdom pharaohs destroyed the Kushite kingdom of Kerma, annexed Nubia as far as the Fourth Cataract, planted Egyptian temple towns and garrisons, and removed Nubian elite children to Egypt
peopleRange: No figure is defensible. Egyptian inscriptions record captives taken in Nubian campaigns in the hundreds and low thousands and record Nubians settled in Egypt, but these are royal texts without an accounting purpose. The lasting demographic change was produced by garrisons, administrators and settlers moving south and by Nubians moving north over roughly five centuries, a process reconstructed from archaeology and cemetery evidence rather than counted.
territoryDesc: Nubia from the First to the Fourth Cataract, roughly 1,000 km of the Nile valley in present-day southern Egypt and northern Sudan, administered as an Egyptian province under a viceroy titled King's Son of Kush.

flows.label: Nubia → Egypt (captives, tribute-bearers, elite children)
Egypt → Nubia (garrisons, officials, temple-town settlers)

summary: Beginning with Ahmose I and completed under Thutmose I and Thutmose III, Egypt destroyed the Kushite capital at Kerma and annexed Nubia as far upstream as the Fourth Cataract, holding it as a colony for roughly five hundred years. Rule was exercised through a viceroy, garrisons and a network of new temple towns — Soleb, Sesebi, Amara, Sedeinga and above all the Amun sanctuary at Gebel Barkal — which drew in Egyptian settlers and reorganised local society around Egyptian gods and Egyptian administration. Nubians were taken to Egypt as captives and labourers, and the children of Nubian chiefs were brought to the Egyptian court to be educated and returned as loyal local rulers, the same device applied in Canaan. Archaeologists differ over how much of the resulting 'Egyptianisation' reflects coercion, elite emulation or the gradual blending of populations, and no reliable figures exist for how many people were moved in either direction.
contested: Whether the cultural transformation of Nubia reflects coerced population change and settler colonisation or largely voluntary adoption of Egyptian practice by Nubian elites is actively debated among Nubiologists.

sources.title: Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, University of Chicago: Nubia — New Kingdom
J. Budka, 'The Egyptian "re-conquest of Nubia" in the New Kingdom' (Propylaeum, Heidelberg University)

deathsNote: There is no basis for a death toll. Egyptian texts record the killing of Nubian rulers and fighters in individual campaigns, but the five-century colonial period is documented mainly by administrative and religious monuments rather than by accounts of mass violence.
violenceNote: Egyptian royal inscriptions and the Egyptological literature summarised by ISAC and Budka document captive labour and the removal of Nubian chiefs' children to the Egyptian court.
baselineWhat: The population of Lower and Upper Nubia under Egyptian New Kingdom rule
baselineNote: No denominator can be reconstructed for a programme spanning nearly five centuries. Egyptological settlement survey — much of it salvage work before the flooding of Lower Nubia by the Aswan High Dam — indicates populations in the tens of thousands for Lower Nubia and a substantial urban centre at Kerma, but there is no census, and the depopulation of Lower Nubia in the later New Kingdom is itself debated between demographic collapse, migration and changes in Nile hydrology.

title: Expulsion of the Hyksos from Egypt
actors: The Theban rulers Kamose and Ahmose I made war on the West Asian ('Hyksos') Fifteenth Dynasty ruling the eastern Nile Delta from Avaris, and later Egyptian tradition recorded the expulsion of its population
peopleRange: No defensible figure. Manetho, preserved in Josephus a millennium and a half later, speaks of 240,000 people leaving Avaris under treaty; that number is a late literary construct with no support in contemporary evidence. The contemporary Egyptian sources — the Kamose stelae and the tomb autobiography of Ahmose son of Ibana — are royal propaganda that boast of plunder and captives without totals. Excavation at Tell el-Dab'a (ancient Avaris) has found no destruction layer for the period and shows a West Asian population continuing to live on the site into the New Kingdom, so the scale of any forced removal is unknown and may have been small.
territoryDesc: The eastern Nile Delta and the Hyksos-controlled territory of Lower Egypt were absorbed into a reunified Egyptian state under the Eighteenth Dynasty.
summary: Around 1550 BCE the Theban Seventeenth and early Eighteenth Dynasty kings, Kamose and then Ahmose I, ended the rule of the West Asian Fifteenth Dynasty that had governed the eastern Nile Delta from Avaris for roughly a century, and pursued its forces into southern Canaan at Sharuhen. New Kingdom Egyptian texts present this as the violent expulsion of foreign occupiers, and Manetho's much later account gives a treaty departure of 240,000 people. Archaeology at Tell el-Dab'a, however, indicates that the Hyksos rulers emerged from a West Asian community that had been settling the Delta gradually for centuries rather than from an invasion, that no destruction horizon marks the transition, and that people of West Asian material culture went on living at the site afterwards. The episode is included here because a state ended a rival polity and Egyptian sources describe a forced removal, but the scale of any actual population transfer is not established, and the 'expulsion' narrative served the legitimising purposes of the New Kingdom monarchy.
contested: Whether there was any mass expulsion at all is disputed: New Kingdom royal texts and Manetho describe one, while excavation at Tell el-Dab'a shows neither a destruction layer nor the disappearance of the West Asian population.

sources.title: American Research Center in Egypt: The Hyksos
Biblical Archaeology Society: The Expulsion of the Hyksos
Archaeology Magazine: The Rulers of Foreign Lands (Tell el-Dab'a excavations)

deathsNote: No usable death toll exists. Egyptian royal texts describe fighting and captives at Avaris and Sharuhen but give no figures, and excavation has produced no evidence of mass violence at Avaris in this period.
baselineWhat: The population of Egypt at the end of the Second Intermediate Period
baselineNote: There is no census. Karl Butzer's reconstruction from cultivated floodplain area and settlement density in Early Hydraulic Civilization in Egypt gives roughly 2.9 million for early New Kingdom Egypt, against about 1.6-2 million for the Middle Kingdom. The population of the Hyksos-ruled eastern Delta is not separately reconstructible, though excavation at Tell el-Dab'a suggests Avaris itself held on the order of 25,000-30,000 people.
shareCaveat: The denominator is all of Egypt while the events acted on the eastern Delta and the Levantine campaigns that followed; no figure exists for the population actually expelled or killed.

title: Egyptian New Kingdom Deportations from Canaan and Syria
actors: Thutmose III and his New Kingdom successors campaigned annually in Canaan and Syria, deporting captives to Egypt as temple and estate labour and removing the sons of local rulers to be raised at the Egyptian court
peopleRange: The Annals of Thutmose III, carved on the walls of the temple of Amun at Karnak, list captives campaign by campaign in figures of hundreds to a few thousand at a time; cumulative totals for the reign run into the tens of thousands, but the annals are a dedicatory royal record designed to display the god's gifts and were not compiled as a census. There is no independent check on the numbers, and Egyptologists treat individual entries as plausible in order of magnitude while regarding the genre as celebratory rather than statistical.

flows.label: Canaan and Syria → Thebes and Egyptian temple estates

summary: From the campaign that ended at Megiddo in about 1457 BCE, Thutmose III conducted some seventeen campaigns into Canaan and Syria and instituted a durable imperial system there. Captives were carried to Egypt and assigned to temple estates, royal workshops and agricultural labour, and the annals inscribed at Karnak record them alongside cattle, chariots and metal as part of the spoils dedicated to Amun. A distinct and systematic element was the removal of the sons of Syro-Canaanite rulers to Egypt, where they were raised at court and later returned to govern their inheritances as Egyptianised vassals; Egyptologists read this both as hostage-taking and as a device for producing a loyal client elite. The scale of the transfers is known only from Egyptian royal inscriptions, which enumerate captives in the hundreds and low thousands per campaign but were composed to glorify the king and the god rather than to record numbers accurately.
contested: Whether the captive figures in the Karnak annals are administrative records or celebratory approximations is unresolved, and the total number moved to Egypt over the period cannot be established.

sources.title: Britannica: Thutmose III
World History Encyclopedia: Thutmose III at the Battle of Megiddo

deathsNote: No death toll can be given. The Egyptian annals record enemy dead in the low hundreds for individual engagements and emphasise captives taken alive, since living captives were the object of the campaigns; mortality among deportees in transit and in temple labour is undocumented.
violenceNote: Forced labour of captives and the removal of the sons of vassal rulers to the Egyptian court are both described in the Karnak annals and in the Egyptological literature summarised by Britannica.
baselineWhat: The population of Late Bronze Age Canaan, the region from which New Kingdom Egypt deported captives
baselineNote: Magen Broshi and Ram Gophna's archaeological survey, which estimates population from excavated settlement area and density coefficients, puts Late Bronze Age Canaan west of the Jordan at roughly 140,000 people, sharply down from the Middle Bronze Age. Egyptian campaign records give captive tallies — the annals of Thutmose III list a few thousand per campaign — that are internally consistent with a region of this size.

title: The Neo-Assyrian Mass Deportation Programme
actors: Neo-Assyrian kings from Tiglath-pileser III through Sargon II, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal systematically uprooted conquered populations across the Near East and resettled them in distant provinces of the empire
peopleRange: About 4.5 million people over roughly three centuries is the figure commonly cited in the field, derived from Bustenay Oded's catalogue of the deportation notices in the Assyrian royal inscriptions (Mass Deportations and Deportees in the Neo-Assyrian Empire, 1979); roughly 4 million of that total falls in the reigns of Tiglath-pileser III, Sargon II and Sennacherib. The figure is an aggregation of the kings' own inscribed claims, not an independent count, and individual entries range from precise-looking numbers such as 27,290 or 200,150 to round rhetorical totals. Archaeological survey supports large-scale depopulation in some conquered regions and large-scale resettlement in others, so most scholars accept the order of magnitude while treating the aggregate as an upper bound built from propagandistic sources.

flows.label: Levant → the Habur region and Assyrian heartland
Elam (Susa) → Assyria
Assyrian core → the Zagros and Median frontier

summary: From the accession of Tiglath-pileser III in 744 BCE the Assyrian state made two-way mass deportation a standing instrument of rule, moving whole communities out of conquered or rebellious territories and settling other deported groups in their place. The purposes recorded in the inscriptions and reconstructed by modern scholarship were to break political cohesion in annexed provinces, to supply skilled craftsmen, scribes and soldiers to the imperial centre, to repopulate the Assyrian heartland and its new capitals, and to bring marginal land under cultivation. Deportees were normally moved as family units under military escort, given land and obligations at their destination, and absorbed into the imperial population; palace reliefs at Nineveh and Nimrud depict them travelling with carts, animals and children. The commonly quoted total of some 4.5 million derives from Oded's compilation of the royal inscriptions themselves, which are victory texts, and the practice is better documented than any of its individual numbers.
contested: The aggregate total of roughly 4.5 million rests entirely on numbers the Assyrian kings themselves inscribed on their monuments, and scholars disagree over how far those figures were literal.

sources.title: Assyrian Empire Builders (University College London / Oracc, Penn Museum): Mass deportation — the Assyrian resettlement policy
A. Faust, 'The Impact of the Assyrian Conquests on Judahite Society', Religions 16 (2025) — cites Oded's c. 4.5 million total
I. Koch (Tel Aviv University), 'Assyrian Deportation and Resettlement: The Story of Samaria'

deathsNote: No aggregate death toll is recoverable. Assyrian campaigns involved sieges, massacres of defenders and exemplary executions recorded in the inscriptions and shown on the palace reliefs, but the deportation programme itself was designed to preserve populations for labour and settlement; mortality on the marches is undocumented.
violenceNote: The Assyrian royal inscriptions and palace reliefs, catalogued by Oded and summarised in the Oracc Assyrian Empire Builders project, document the destruction of settlements and the assignment of deportees to imperial labour and military service.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: the empire's conquered territories changed with every reign across 120 years and were never enumerated
baselineNote: Bustenay Oded's standard study counts about 157 recorded deportations in the royal inscriptions and sums the stated totals to roughly 4.5 million people between the ninth and seventh centuries, a figure many Assyriologists regard as inflated by royal rhetoric and double-counting. There is no census, tax roll or settlement survey that would give the population of the conquered lands over the programme's span: broad estimates put the whole Near East from Egypt to Iran at somewhere between 10 and 20 million in 700 BCE, but the empire's boundaries and the areas actually raided shifted constantly, so a percentage would be arbitrary.

baselineSources.title: Resettlement policy of the Neo-Assyrian Empire — Wikipedia

title: Assyrian Destruction of the Kingdom of Israel and Deportation from Samaria
actors: Shalmaneser V besieged and Sargon II claimed the capture of Samaria, ending the northern Israelite kingdom, deporting its population eastwards and settling deportees from Babylonia and Syria in its place
peopleRange: 27,290 is Sargon II's own figure, inscribed in his annals at Khorsabad ('I besieged and conquered Samaria and led away as booty 27,290 inhabitants of it'); some copies give 27,280. It is a royal victory claim and applies to the city and its immediate district in a single operation, not to the kingdom as a whole. Archaeological survey shows that settlement in the Samarian highlands contracted sharply but did not cease, and scholars including Israel Finkelstein and Ido Koch conclude that most Israelites remained on the land while an elite and skilled stratum was removed. Earlier deportations by Tiglath-pileser III from Galilee and Gilead (c. 733–732) added an unquantified further number.
territoryDesc: The northern kingdom of Israel was annexed and reorganised as the Assyrian province of Samerina.

flows.label: Samaria → Halah and the Habur river region
Babylonia, Cuthah, Hamath → resettlement in Samerina

summary: After a siege begun under Shalmaneser V, Samaria fell in about 722 BCE and the northern Israelite kingdom was annexed as the Assyrian province of Samerina. Sargon II's annals at Khorsabad claim the deportation of 27,290 of its inhabitants, the incorporation of fifty of their chariots into his army, and the resettlement of the province with populations brought from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim — a two-way exchange typical of Assyrian imperial practice and echoed in 2 Kings 17. Which king actually took the city is disputed, since the biblical account credits Shalmaneser V and the Assyrian annals credit Sargon II, who may have been claiming his predecessor's success or suppressing a later revolt in 720. Archaeological survey of the Samarian hills indicates severe but partial depopulation, and excavations at sites such as Tel Hadid have identified communities of deportees brought in from Mesopotamia. The later tradition of 'ten lost tribes' overstates what the evidence shows: a substantial Israelite population remained in place under Assyrian administration.
contested: Whether Shalmaneser V or Sargon II captured Samaria, and whether the 27,290 figure represents the city alone or a wider region, remain unresolved.

sources.title: Center for Online Judaic Studies: The Annals of Sargon II (Khorsabad text)
I. Koch (Tel Aviv University), 'Assyrian Deportation and Resettlement: The Story of Samaria'
Livius.org: Samaria
World History Encyclopedia: Sargon II

deathsNote: No death toll is recorded. The Assyrian and biblical accounts describe a siege, a capture and a deportation rather than a massacre, and the deportees' value to the empire lay in their survival; siege mortality at Samaria is unquantified.
violenceNote: The Assyrian annals record the conscription of Samarian deportees into royal service and the dissolution of the kingdom into an Assyrian province, a policy of deliberate destruction of political identity described in the Assyriological literature.
baselineWhat: The population of the northern kingdom of Israel in the second half of the eighth century BCE
baselineNote: There is no census. The figure rests on archaeological settlement survey: Broshi and Finkelstein calculated built-up area across excavated and surveyed sites and applied a density coefficient, giving roughly 350,000 for the kingdom of Israel against about 110,000 for Judah. Alternative coefficients yield figures between about 220,000 and 400,000.
shareCaveat: The 27,290 figure is Sargon II's own inscriptional claim for deportees from Samaria and its district, not a count of everyone removed from the kingdom, and Assyrian royal inscriptions routinely round and inflate.

title: Sennacherib's Campaign in Judah
actors: Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah, stormed Lachish and other fortified towns, deported their populations and stripped Hezekiah of most of his territory
peopleRange: Sennacherib's annals, preserved on the Taylor Prism in the British Museum and its duplicates, claim the capture of 46 fortified cities and the driving out of '200,150 people, young and old, male and female'. This is the king's own commemorative record. The number is widely regarded as implausible against modern demographic estimates for late-eighth-century Judah, whose total population is generally reckoned in the low hundreds of thousands; some scholars read it as an inflated round claim, others as including livestock or as counting all persons brought under Assyrian control rather than physically deported. The Lachish reliefs at Nineveh show columns of deportees leaving the city, so substantial deportation is not in doubt, only its magnitude.
territoryDesc: Sennacherib records detaching the Shephelah and much of Judah's western territory and transferring it to the Philistine kings of Ashdod, Ekron and Gaza, leaving Hezekiah a rump kingdom around Jerusalem.

flows.label: Lachish and the Judaean Shephelah → Assyria

summary: In 701 BCE Sennacherib campaigned in the Levant against a coalition that included Hezekiah of Judah, storming the fortified town of Lachish and reducing the Judaean lowlands before blockading Jerusalem, which he did not take. His annals claim 46 conquered cities and 200,150 people driven out, together with the transfer of Judaean territory to neighbouring Philistine rulers and a heavy tribute from Hezekiah. The campaign is exceptionally well documented for an ancient event: the Assyrian prisms, the biblical narrative in 2 Kings 18–19, and the great relief cycle Sennacherib installed in his palace at Nineveh showing the siege of Lachish and the deportation of its inhabitants. Excavation at Lachish has confirmed the siege ramp, the destruction layer and mass burials. The 200,150 figure is the king's own and sits awkwardly with modern estimates of Judah's total population; the scale of the deportation is therefore disputed even though the fact of it is not.
contested: The figure of 200,150 deportees comes from Sennacherib's own annals and is regarded by many scholars as inflated or as counting something other than people physically removed.

sources.title: British Museum: the Taylor Prism (hexagonal clay prism of Sennacherib, 691 BC)
Metropolitan Museum of Art: Sennacherib and Jerusalem (Ira Spar)
A. Faust, 'The Impact of the Assyrian Conquests on Judahite Society', Religions 16 (2025)

deathsNote: No figure can be given. Excavation at Lachish has produced a destruction layer and a mass grave containing the remains of at least 1,500 people, but the burial cannot be securely dated to the 701 BCE assault alone, and no source records deaths across the campaign as a whole.
violenceNote: The siege and storming of Lachish and the destruction of Judaean towns are documented by Sennacherib's own palace reliefs at Nineveh and by the excavated destruction layer at Tel Lachish.
baselineWhat: The population of the kingdom of Judah at the time of Sennacherib's invasion
baselineNote: The figure comes from archaeological settlement survey rather than any text: Magen Broshi and Israel Finkelstein, working from excavated site areas and population-density coefficients, put Judah at roughly 110,000 in the late eighth century BCE, with the Shephelah — the region Sennacherib devastated — holding a large share of it. Sennacherib's own annals claim 200,150 people carried off from forty-six walled towns, a figure that exceeds most modern estimates of the entire kingdom's population and is generally read as royal propaganda.

baselineSources.title: Sennacherib's campaign in the Levant — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The Assyrian deportation claim of 200,150 exceeds the archaeological estimate of Judah's whole population, so any percentage built from the annals will exceed 100 per cent and should be treated as a propaganda figure rather than a count.

title: The Spartan Helot System
actors: The Spartan state held the conquered populations of Laconia and Messenia as helots — unfree agricultural labourers bound to the land and owned collectively by the community rather than by individuals
peopleRange: No census figures exist. Ancient authors imply that helots vastly outnumbered Spartan citizens, with a ratio of roughly seven to one commonly inferred from Herodotus's account of the Persian War muster; modern estimates of the helot population of Laconia and Messenia at its height run from about 100,000 to over 200,000, all reconstructed from carrying-capacity and army-size arguments rather than from records. Ancient Greek writers on Sparta wrote from outside and often with an agenda, and Messenian traditions were reconstructed after liberation in 369 BCE, so both the numbers and the details of helot conditions are inference.
territoryDesc: Laconia and, from the Messenian Wars of the eighth and seventh centuries BCE, the whole of Messenia in the southwestern Peloponnese were held as Spartan territory worked by helots.
summary: Sparta's conquest of neighbouring Laconia and then of Messenia reduced their populations to the status of helots: unfree cultivators tied to allotments, obliged to hand over a fixed share of their produce to Spartan citizen landholders, and owned by the state rather than by private masters. Unlike chattel slaves elsewhere in Greece, helots lived in their own families and communities and retained a collective identity, which is why Messenian helots could be constituted as a free polity when Thebes liberated Messenia in 369 BCE and founded the city of Messene. Ancient sources report that the Spartan ephors declared war on the helots every year so that killing one carried no religious pollution, and that a body of young Spartans, the krypteia, was sent into the countryside to intimidate and kill helots judged dangerous; Thucydides records the disappearance of some 2,000 helots who had been invited to claim their freedom. The system is included here as a case of a population held in place by state coercion over centuries rather than moved, and almost everything known about it comes from non-Spartan Greek authors.
contested: The size of the helot population, the reliability of the reports of the krypteia and the annual declaration of war, and how far Messenian identity survived continuously under Spartan rule are all debated among historians of Sparta.

sources.title: Livius.org: Helot
Britannica: Krypteia

deathsNote: No range can be given for the deaths caused over three centuries. The single best-attested incident is Thucydides' report that about 2,000 helots who had been promised freedom were made to disappear; systematic mortality from the krypteia and from suppression of helot revolts is undocumented.
violenceNote: Compulsory agricultural labour, confinement to allotted land, and the killing of helots by the krypteia and the disappearance of 2,000 helots are reported by Thucydides, Plutarch and other Greek authors as summarised by Livius.org and Britannica.
baselineWhat: The helot population of Laconia and Messenia at the height of the Spartan system in the fifth century BCE
baselineNote: No count survives. Estimates are reconstructed from the size of the Spartiate citizen body, land-allotment arithmetic and Herodotus' claim of seven helots per Spartiate at Plataea; Figueira's modelling gives roughly 170,000-224,000 helots, while more cautious readings put the figure nearer 140,000. Messenians were the larger part.

title: The Babylonian Exile of Judah
actors: Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon deposed the Judaean monarchy in successive campaigns, destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, and deported the kingdom's ruling, priestly and artisan classes to Babylonia
peopleRange: The biblical figures conflict: 2 Kings 24:14–16 gives 10,000 and separately 8,000 taken in 597 BCE, while Jeremiah 52:28–30 gives a much lower and more administrative-looking total of 4,600 across three deportations in 597, 586 and 582. Modern reconstructions of the numbers deported range from roughly 4,600 to about 20,000, with the higher figures assuming that the counts record adult men only. Archaeological survey shows the population of Judah falling steeply — estimates of the decline run from about half to as much as two-thirds — but that reflects death, flight to Egypt and the surrounding regions, and settlement collapse as well as deportation. The 15,000 central figure here is a mid-range reading of the deported total and should be treated as an order of magnitude.
territoryDesc: The kingdom of Judah was abolished and its territory administered from Mizpah as a Babylonian province.

flows.label: Jerusalem and Judah → Babylonia (Babylon, Nippur, Al-Yahudu)
Return from Babylonia under Persian rule, from 538 BCE

summary: Nebuchadnezzar II took Jerusalem in 597 BCE and deported King Jehoiachin with the court, military and skilled classes; after a revolt he returned in 587/586, destroyed the city and the temple, and carried off a second group, with a third deportation following in 582. Those removed were settled in the Babylonian countryside, especially around Nippur, in villages named for their places of origin — the cuneiform archives from Al-Yahudu, 'the town of Judah', show deportee families holding land in exchange for taxes, labour and military service over some 160 years. A substantial population remained in Judah under a Babylonian-appointed administration at Mizpah, and others fled to Egypt. After Cyrus II took Babylon in 539 BCE, Persian policy permitted return and the rebuilding of the temple, and part of the community went back while a large and permanent Jewish population remained in Mesopotamia. The numbers are contested because the two biblical tallies disagree by a factor of three or more, and archaeology measures overall population collapse rather than deportation specifically.
contested: How many were actually deported is disputed — Jeremiah's 4,600 and Kings' 10,000-plus cannot be reconciled — as is how much of Judah's archaeologically visible population collapse is attributable to deportation rather than to war deaths, flight and economic breakdown.

sources.title: Biblical Archaeology Society: How Bad Was the Babylonian Exile?
T. Alstola, 'Everyday Life in Exile: Judean Deportees in Babylonian Texts', ANE Today (ASOR)

deathsNote: No usable range exists. The siege and sack of Jerusalem in 586 BCE caused deaths from fighting, starvation and executions of officials described in 2 Kings and Jeremiah, but no source gives numbers and the archaeological record cannot separate war deaths from emigration in the region's population decline.
violenceNote: The siege of Jerusalem, the burning of the temple and city, and the land-for-service obligations imposed on deportees in Babylonia are documented in the biblical narrative and in the Al-Yahudu cuneiform archive discussed by Alstola.
baselineWhat: The population of the kingdom of Judah on the eve of the Babylonian conquest
baselineNote: The estimate is archaeological rather than textual: Magen Broshi and Israel Finkelstein's settlement surveys, which calculate population from built-up area and density coefficients, put late Iron Age Judah at roughly 110,000, with other reconstructions ranging from about 75,000 to 150,000. The biblical figures for the deportations (2 Kings 24 gives 10,000, Jeremiah 52 gives 4,600) are not consistent with each other, and most scholars treat the total deported across the campaigns of 597, 587 and 582 BCE as something in the range 10,000-20,000, drawn disproportionately from the Jerusalem elite.
shareCaveat: The deportations targeted the royal court, priesthood, officials and craftsmen rather than a cross-section, so the modest percentage understates how completely the kingdom's governing and literate class was removed.

title: Achaemenid Persian Deportations of Conquered Cities
actors: Achaemenid kings from Cambyses to Darius I deported the populations of defeated cities — Barca in Cyrenaica, Miletus in Ionia, Eretria in Euboea and groups of Egyptians — and resettled them in the Iranian and Central Asian interior
peopleRange: The numbers come almost entirely from Herodotus, writing decades later from Greek informants. He records 6,000 Egyptians deported with their king by Cambyses, the transfer of the surviving Milesians to Ampe on the Tigris after 494 BCE, the settlement of the Barcaeans in a village in Bactria, and the removal of the Eretrians to Ardericca in Elam in 490 BCE. Only the Egyptian figure is numerical; the others are described as 'the survivors' or 'those enslaved'. Encyclopaedia Iranica treats the practice as securely attested and the individual counts as approximate. Persian administrative texts from Persepolis independently show foreign work-gangs (kurtaš) of many ethnicities, corroborating the practice without confirming Herodotus's numbers.

flows.label: Miletus → Ampe at the mouth of the Tigris (494 BCE)
Eretria → Ardericca in Elam (490 BCE)
Barca (Cyrenaica) → Bactria

summary: The Achaemenid empire used deportation selectively, as a punishment for rebellion and a means of placing useful populations where the crown wanted them. Herodotus records that after crushing the Ionian revolt in 494 BCE the Persians killed or enslaved the Milesians and settled the survivors at Ampe near the mouth of the Tigris; that in 490 BCE the Eretrians, who had aided the revolt, were carried off to Ardericca in Elam, where a distinct community was still recognisable centuries later; that the Barcaeans of Cyrenaica were resettled in a Bactrian village; and that Cambyses removed 6,000 Egyptians with their king and many artisans to Susa. Encyclopaedia Iranica notes that Achaemenid deportees were given land, kept their languages and religions, and were subject to taxation and restrictions on movement rather than being enslaved outright. The Persepolis administrative tablets record large multi-ethnic labour forces in the imperial heartland, consistent with the practice, though the Greek narrative sources remain the only origin for the individual episodes and figures.
contested: All the individual episodes derive from Herodotus, a hostile Greek source writing after the events, and the numbers he gives are not independently corroborated.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: DEPORTATIONS
Livius.org: Eretria
Livius.org: Miletus

deathsNote: No usable range. Herodotus reports the killing of most Milesian men and the burning of the city and its temple in 494 BCE, and the burning of Eretria in 490, but gives no counts; the deportations themselves were intended to preserve the population for resettlement.
violenceNote: Herodotus records the burning of Miletus and its sanctuary at Didyma and the destruction of Eretria's temples before the deportations, as summarised on Livius.org.
baselineWhat: The populations of the cities the Achaemenid kings deported — Barca, Miletus, Eretria and others
baselineNote: There is no census basis for a total. The affected communities were single cities, each plausibly holding a few thousand to some tens of thousands of people on archaeological and textual grounds — Herodotus is the main source and his numbers are rhetorical rather than statistical — and the deportations were scattered across three decades and several satrapies, so no defensible aggregate denominator can be reconstructed.

title: Athenian Destruction of Melos
actors: Athens besieged the neutral island city of Melos, executed the adult male population, sold the women and children into slavery and planted 500 Athenian colonists on the island
peopleRange: Thucydides gives no totals, stating only that the Athenians 'put to death all the grown men whom they took, and sold the women and children for slaves, and subsequently sent out five hundred colonists'. Modern estimates for the adult male population killed cluster around 1,000–1,500, extrapolated from the island's size and from the size of the Melian contribution recorded in Athenian tribute assessments; those enslaved would have been of comparable or greater number. Thucydides is a near-contemporary Athenian source, generally regarded as the most reliable narrative for the period, but the figures are modern reconstructions rather than his.
territoryDesc: The Cycladic island of Melos, roughly 151 km², was cleared of its population and settled by Athenian colonists until they were expelled by Lysander in 405 BCE.

flows.label: Athens → Melos (500 colonists)

summary: In 416 BCE, during the Peloponnesian War, Athens demanded the submission of Melos, a Dorian island that had stayed neutral, and besieged it when the Melians refused. Thucydides frames the episode with the Melian Dialogue, in which the Athenian envoys argue that 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must', and then records the outcome in a single sentence: on surrender the Athenians killed every adult man they captured, sold the women and children into slavery, and sent out 500 settlers of their own. The population was not merely subjugated but eliminated as a community and replaced. Melian survivors were restored to the island by the Spartan commander Lysander after Athens's defeat in 405 BCE. The event is treated in the modern literature as one of the clearest ancient cases in which killing and enslavement were the deliberate instrument of policy rather than an accompaniment to conquest, though whether the modern term genocide is appropriate is debated.
contested: Whether the destruction of Melos meets a modern definition of genocide is disputed; some scholars apply the term because of the evident intent to destroy the community, others hold that the category cannot usefully be retrofitted to classical warfare.

sources.title: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.84–116 (the Melian Dialogue), The Latin Library
World History Encyclopedia: Genocide in the Ancient World

deathsNote: Thucydides records that all captured adult males were executed but gives no number. The range reflects modern reconstructions from the island's population and its recorded tribute, with the upper end around 1,500 used in general reference works and the lower end reflecting the fact that an unknown number escaped or were not captured.
violenceNote: Thucydides, a contemporary Athenian historian, records the execution of the captured adult male population and the enslavement of the women and children.
baselineWhat: The free population of the island city of Melos at the time of the Athenian siege
baselineNote: No count survives. The estimate is reconstructed backwards from Thucydides, who reports that Athens killed the adult males and enslaved the women and children, then sent 500 colonists to occupy the island. Modern estimates of the Melian citizen body run to roughly 500-1,000 adult males, implying a total free population of about 2,500-4,000, plus an unknown number of slaves.

title: Alexander's Destruction of Thebes
actors: Alexander III of Macedon stormed Thebes after its revolt, and the allied Greek council he chaired voted to raze the city, kill its defenders and sell the surviving population into slavery
peopleRange: Diodorus Siculus states that 'over six thousand Thebans perished, more than thirty thousand were captured'; Plutarch and Arrian give broadly similar orders of magnitude, with Plutarch reporting 6,000 killed and 30,000 sold. These are Hellenistic and Roman-era historians writing two to four centuries later from the lost contemporary accounts of Alexander's campaign. Historians treat the figures as conventional round numbers, and 30,000 would be a very high share of a city whose total population is usually estimated in the tens of thousands, but the enslavement of most survivors is not in doubt.
territoryDesc: The city of Thebes was demolished apart from its temples and the house of Pindar, and its territory was divided among neighbouring Boeotian cities until Cassander refounded it in 316 BCE.

flows.label: Thebes → slave markets of Greece and the Aegean

summary: When Thebes revolted on a rumour of Alexander's death in 335 BCE, he marched south, took the city by assault, and referred its fate to the council of his Greek allies, which voted for destruction. Diodorus records more than 6,000 Thebans killed and more than 30,000 taken and sold into slavery; the city was demolished except for its sanctuaries and, by tradition, the house of the poet Pindar, and its land was distributed to neighbouring Boeotian communities. The decision was framed as a collective Greek judgement on Thebes for medism and treachery, which allowed Alexander to present the annihilation of a major Greek city as lawful punishment rather than Macedonian terror, and contemporaries understood it as a deterrent that secured Greece for the duration of the Asian campaign. Thebes was refounded in 316 BCE by Cassander, with surviving Thebans and their descendants returning. The numbers come from historians writing long after the event and using now-lost sources.
contested: The figures of 6,000 killed and 30,000 enslaved come from Diodorus and Plutarch, writing centuries later, and are generally regarded as round rather than exact; responsibility for the decision — Alexander's or the allied Greek council's — was already disputed in antiquity.

sources.title: Diodorus Siculus on the sack of Thebes (Livius.org)

deathsNote: Diodorus gives 'over six thousand' Theban dead in the storming of the city and Plutarch gives 6,000; both are later literary figures with no independent corroboration, and the range is presented as a single reported value rather than a scholarly estimate.
violenceNote: Diodorus, Plutarch and Arrian record the killing of the population during the storming of the city and its subsequent demolition.
baselineWhat: The population of Thebes and its immediate territory in Boeotia
baselineNote: No count survives. Reconstruction rests on the ancient narrative sources - Diodorus and Plutarch report about 6,000 killed and 30,000 sold into slavery - together with estimates of the walled area and of Boeotian manpower from the fourth-century campaigns. Modern estimates of the city's population range from about 25,000 to 50,000.
shareCaveat: The numerator and the denominator derive from the same ancient figures, so the ratio is close to tautological rather than an independent measurement.

title: Alexander's Sieges of Tyre and Gaza
actors: Alexander III of Macedon took the island city of Tyre after a seven-month siege and then Gaza, killing and enslaving their populations and repopulating the sites
peopleRange: The figures come from Arrian, Diodorus and Curtius Rufus, writing three to five centuries later: about 6,000 Tyrians killed in the storming, 2,000 crucified along the shore, and about 30,000 sold into slavery; at Gaza the ancient accounts describe the killing of the male defenders and the enslavement of the women and children without a figure. These are literary numbers drawn from the lost contemporary historians of the campaign, and 30,000 is likely a round order-of-magnitude claim for a city of Tyre's size rather than a count.
territoryDesc: Tyre was repopulated with settlers and made a Macedonian possession; the causeway Alexander built to reach the island permanently joined it to the mainland.

flows.label: Tyre → slave markets of the eastern Mediterranean

summary: Tyre refused Alexander entry in 332 BCE and he besieged it for roughly seven months, building a causeway from the mainland to the island city. When it fell, the ancient historians record about 6,000 defenders killed in the assault, some 2,000 men crucified along the shore as an exemplary punishment, and about 30,000 of the remaining inhabitants and resident foreigners sold into slavery, with those who had taken refuge in the temple of Heracles spared. Gaza, which also resisted, was stormed shortly afterwards; its male population was killed and the women and children enslaved, and the site was resettled with people from the surrounding country. Both cities were repopulated and continued to function, so the outcome was the replacement rather than the permanent erasure of an urban population. All the figures derive from Roman-era authors using earlier campaign histories that no longer survive.
contested: The casualty and enslavement figures are transmitted only by Arrian, Diodorus and Curtius, writing centuries later, and the round number of 30,000 enslaved is treated by historians as an approximation.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: Alexander's Siege of Tyre, 332 BCE

deathsNote: The range combines the roughly 6,000 Tyrians reported killed in the storming with the 2,000 reported crucified afterwards. Both figures come from Roman-era historians rather than from any contemporary record, and deaths at Gaza are unquantified.
violenceNote: Arrian, Diodorus and Curtius Rufus describe the seven-month blockade, the killing of the population at the storming and the mass crucifixion of some 2,000 survivors.
baselineWhat: The combined population of Tyre and Gaza at the time of the sieges
baselineNote: The ancient sources - Arrian, Diodorus and Curtius - report about 8,000 killed and 30,000 sold into slavery at Tyre and 10,000 killed at Gaza, with the women and children sold. Modern estimates of Tyre's population, from its island area and its role as a Phoenician metropolis, run 30,000-40,000, and Gaza's around 10,000.
shareCaveat: Numerator and denominator both derive from the same ancient round numbers reported by partisan sources, so the ratio is near-tautological.

title: Hellenistic City Foundations and Forced Transplantation of Populations
actors: Alexander's successors, above all the Seleucid kings, founded and repopulated cities across the Near East by compulsory synoecism of existing communities and by transplanting settler groups from one part of the empire to another
peopleRange: No aggregate figure is possible. The best-documented single transfer is Antiochus III's order, preserved as a letter to his viceroy Zeuxis in Josephus, Antiquities 12.147–153, to move 2,000 Jewish families with their households from Mesopotamia and Babylonia into fortress settlements in Lydia and Phrygia, with grants of land and ten years' tax exemption. Other transfers are known only qualitatively: the concentration of the population of Babylon and other old cities into new royal foundations such as Seleucia-on-the-Tigris and Antioch, and the resettlement of Macedonians, Greeks, Jews, Thracians and others as military colonists. The documents are royal letters and later literary reports, and the totals moved are unknown.

flows.label: Babylon → Seleucia-on-the-Tigris (compulsory transfer of population)
Mesopotamia and Babylonia → Lydia and Phrygia (2,000 Jewish military-colonist families under Antiochus III)

summary: The Hellenistic kingdoms that succeeded Alexander built their power on new cities, and populating those cities frequently meant moving people who had no choice in the matter. Seleucus I's foundation of Seleucia-on-the-Tigris drew off much of the population of Babylon, and Antioch, Apamea, Laodicea and dozens of other foundations absorbed existing villages and towns by synoecism, the compulsory merging of communities into a single new civic centre. Settler groups were also transplanted deliberately across the empire for security reasons: Josephus preserves a letter of Antiochus III instructing his viceroy Zeuxis to move 2,000 Jewish families from Mesopotamia and Babylonia to garrison points in Lydia and Phrygia, granting them land, their own laws and a decade's tax relief in return for holding disturbed territory. The policy reshaped the demography of the Near East and created the Greek-speaking urban networks of the region, but it was executed by royal command and the numbers involved are almost never recorded.
contested: How coercive these transfers were is debated: royal letters present them as grants of privilege to settlers, while the effect on the communities absorbed or moved is largely undocumented.

sources.title: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 12.147–153 (Antiochus III's letter to Zeuxis), Lexundria
Encyclopaedia Iranica: DEPORTATIONS (on Seleucid and successor practice)

deathsNote: There was no significant death toll attached to the transplantation policy itself. These were state-organised transfers of populations intended to be productive at their destination, and the sources record grants of land and tax relief rather than killing.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The Seleucid realm at its height stretched from the Aegean to the Iranian plateau and was never enumerated; modern estimates of its population differ by more than a factor of two, from roughly 14 million to 25 million or more in the reconstructions of Aperghis and others, and the compulsory synoecisms that founded cities such as Antioch and Seleucia acted on individual localities whose sizes are unrecorded.

title: Alexander's Campaign and Colonisation in Bactria and Sogdiana
actors: Alexander III of Macedon suppressed the Bactrian–Sogdian revolt with mass killings and enforced resettlement, and planted garrison cities settled with Greek and Macedonian troops and local populations
peopleRange: No dependable numbers. Curtius Rufus and Diodorus report the destruction of whole districts and figures such as 120,000 Bactrians and Sogdians killed over the campaign, and Alexander is said to have destroyed the Branchidae community and settled Greek troops in new foundations including Alexandria Eschate; these are Roman-era literary figures with no corroboration and are regarded as unreliable. What is archaeologically clear is that new fortified Greek settlements appeared in the region and that populations were concentrated into them. The size of the Greek settler population is indicated only by Diodorus's report that some 23,000 settlers in the upper satrapies attempted to march home after Alexander's death.
territoryDesc: Bactria and Sogdiana, roughly present-day northern Afghanistan, southern Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, were incorporated into the Macedonian empire and garrisoned with new colonial foundations.

flows.label: Greece and Macedon → garrison colonies in Bactria–Sogdiana

summary: Alexander's two-year campaign in Bactria and Sogdiana was the most destructive phase of his eastern conquest. The ancient accounts describe the systematic devastation of rebel districts, the storming of fortified rocks with the crucifixion of leaders and enslavement of the population, and the annihilation of the Branchidae, a community of Greek descent accused of an ancestral sacrilege. Alexander then concentrated populations in new fortified foundations, the best known being Alexandria Eschate on the Jaxartes, settling them with Greek and Macedonian veterans, mercenaries and local inhabitants — a policy of forced urban synoecism intended to hold the country. The settlers themselves regarded the posting as a form of exile: Greek colonists in the upper satrapies revolted around 326 BCE and, after Alexander's death, some 23,000 of them attempted to march back west. The reported casualty figures come from Curtius and Diodorus, writing centuries later, and are widely doubted; the pattern of destruction and forced settlement, by contrast, is supported by the archaeology of Hellenistic Central Asia.
contested: The ancient casualty figures for the Bactrian–Sogdian campaign are regarded as unreliable, and archaeologists now attribute some foundations once credited to Alexander, such as Ai Khanoum, to the Seleucid period instead.

sources.title: McGill University, Department of History and Classical Studies: The Failure of Alexander's Conquest and Administration of Bactria-Sogdiana
S. Vacante, 'Alexander the Great and the Defeat of the Sogdianian Revolt', Ancient History Bulletin 26 (2012)

deathsNote: No defensible range. Roman-era accounts give figures such as 120,000 killed across the campaign, which modern scholarship treats as rhetorical; there is no independent basis for a total.
violenceNote: Curtius Rufus, Diodorus and Arrian record the devastation of rebel districts, the crucifixion of captured leaders and the destruction of the Branchidae settlement, as discussed in the modern scholarship on the Sogdian revolt.
baselineWhat: No defensible figure exists for the population of Bactria and Sogdiana in 329 BCE
baselineNote: The only evidence is Greek and Roman narrative accounts of the campaign, which give army and captive numbers rather than populations, and archaeological survey of irrigation systems along the Oxus and Zarafshan, which establishes intensive settlement without supporting a headcount. Published guesses for the two satrapies vary by an order of magnitude.

title: Mass Enslavement as a Consequence of Roman Conquest
actors: The Roman state and its commanders systematically enslaved the populations of conquered and rebellious communities across the Mediterranean and moved them to Italy and the provinces
peopleRange: No total is recoverable. Individual operations are recorded in six-figure numbers — 150,000 in Epirus in 167 BCE, roughly 50,000 at Carthage in 146, 53,000 Aduatuci in Gaul in 57 — and the enslaved population of the empire in the first century CE is generally estimated at 10–20 per cent of perhaps 50 million people, that is five to ten million, a figure the British Museum gives as the scholarly consensus range. Crucially, Walter Scheidel's demographic modelling in the Journal of Roman Studies concludes that natural reproduction among the enslaved contributed more to the Roman slave supply than child exposure, warfare and the slave trade combined, so war captives, though spectacular, were not the main source of the enslaved population over the long run.

flows.label: Greece and the Balkans → Italy
Gaul → Italy
Judaea → Italy and the provinces

summary: From the First Punic War to the high empire, enslavement of defeated populations was a standing and legally normal outcome of Roman warfare: commanders sold captives on the spot through dealers who followed the armies, and the proceeds went to the soldiers and the treasury. Named operations give the scale — 150,000 Epirotes in 167 BCE, some 50,000 survivors of Carthage in 146, 53,000 Aduatuci in Gaul, tens of thousands from Judaea after 70 CE, and captives from Dacia after 106 — and the aggregate enslaved population of the early empire is usually estimated at five to ten million, or 10 to 20 per cent of the total. Modern demographic work has changed how this is understood: Scheidel argues that reproduction within the enslaved population, not conquest, was the dominant source of supply, which means that mass enslavement should be read as a recurrent catastrophe for specific conquered communities rather than as the engine of Roman slavery overall. It is treated here as a single systemic entry because the individual episodes are scattered across the record and no aggregate count exists.
contested: The relative contribution of war captives, natural reproduction and the slave trade to the Roman enslaved population is disputed; Scheidel's demographic argument that reproduction dominated has revised earlier views that conquest was the principal source.

sources.title: British Museum: Slavery in ancient Rome
W. Scheidel, 'Quantifying the Sources of Slaves in the Early Roman Empire', Journal of Roman Studies (Cambridge Core)

deathsNote: No death toll can be attached to enslavement as a practice. Deaths occurred in the sieges and campaigns that produced captives, and in transport and labour afterwards, but neither ancient sources nor modern demography provide a basis for quantifying them.
violenceNote: Roman legal and literary sources, summarised by the British Museum, document that enslaved people were compelled to labour and had no legal capacity to refuse sexual demands from those who owned them.
baselineNote: No single denominator exists for a practice spanning four and a half centuries and the whole Mediterranean world. Modern estimates give a sense of scale rather than a base: Walter Scheidel and others reckon the Roman world absorbed on the order of 100,000 new slaves a year at the height of expansion, with the slave population of Italy alone put at 1-1.5 million against a Roman empire of roughly 45-60 million in the first century CE.

baselineSources.title: Demography of the Roman Empire — Wikipedia

title: The Mauryan Conquest of Kalinga
actors: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered and annexed the eastern Indian kingdom of Kalinga, and his own inscriptions record the deportation of 150,000 people
peopleRange: 150,000 deported and 100,000 killed, 'and many more died', are Ashoka's own figures, carved in his Major Rock Edict 13 and repeated at Kalsi, Girnar, Shahbazgarhi and other sites. They are unusual among ancient royal numbers in that they appear in a text of remorse rather than of boasting, which some historians take as a reason to credit them and others as a reason to read them as rhetorically heightened for religious effect. No independent source records the war, there is no corroborating archaeology, and no census or administrative record survives against which to test the figures. They should be treated as the ruler's own claim about his own war.
territoryDesc: Kalinga, corresponding broadly to coastal Odisha and northern Andhra Pradesh, was annexed to the Mauryan empire and administered from Tosali and Samapa.

flows.label: Kalinga → the Mauryan interior

summary: In about 261 BCE, eight years into his reign, Ashoka conquered Kalinga, the last major independent kingdom on the eastern seaboard of the subcontinent. His Major Rock Edict 13 states that 150,000 people were deported, 100,000 were killed and many times that number died of other causes, and presents the emperor's remorse at this suffering as the turning point that led him to renounce conquest by arms in favour of 'conquest by dharma'. The edict is the earliest surviving self-reported deportation figure in South Asian history and one of the very few ancient texts in which a ruler records the human cost of his own campaign as a reproach to himself. Because the numbers exist only in Ashoka's own inscriptions and no other account of the war survives, they cannot be verified; historians differ over whether the remorseful framing makes them more credible than a typical victory monument or simply gives them a different rhetorical purpose. Kalinga remained part of the Mauryan empire, and Ashoka's separate Kalinga edicts address the administration of the conquered province.
contested: The figures of 150,000 deported and 100,000 killed are known only from Ashoka's own edicts; historians disagree over whether the penitential framing makes them more or less likely to be literal.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: The Edicts of Ashoka the Great (text of Major Rock Edict 13)
Britannica: Ashoka

deathsNote: The figure of 100,000 killed, with unspecified further deaths from associated causes, is Ashoka's own statement in Major Rock Edict 13 and has no independent corroboration; it is reported here as a single claimed value rather than as a scholarly range.
violenceNote: Ashoka's Major Rock Edict 13 is itself the source documenting the killing and deportation carried out in his campaign.
baselineWhat: The population of the kingdom of Kalinga at the time of Ashoka's conquest
baselineNote: There is no basis for a figure. Ashoka's Thirteenth Major Rock Edict — the only quantitative source — states that 100,000 were killed, 150,000 deported and many times that number died afterwards, but there is no census, tax register or settlement survey against which to set those claims, and estimates of Mauryan India's total population (on the order of 100 million by some reconstructions, far less by others) cannot be disaggregated to Kalinga.
shareCaveat: The deportation figure comes from the conqueror's own inscription and cannot be checked against any independent source.

title: Qin Unification: Forced Resettlement of Elites and Frontier Colonisation
actors: The Qin state, having conquered the warring kingdoms, deported the wealthy and aristocratic households of the eastern states to the capital region and drove convicts, conscripts and settlers to the northern and southern frontiers
peopleRange: The Shiji records 120,000 wealthy and powerful households transferred to Xianyang in 221 BCE, which at conventional household sizes implies roughly half a million people; further movements of convicts, amnestied criminals, manumitted slaves and conscripted labourers to the Ordos loop and to Lingnan in the south are recorded without consistent totals. These figures come from Han-dynasty historiography written a century later, partly to characterise Qin rule as tyrannical, and the household count in particular is a suspiciously round administrative figure. Modern scholarship, including work by Oxford-based historians and archaeologists on state-induced migration in the early Chinese empires, accepts the practice as real and enormous while noting that the fiscal cost implied by the recorded numbers strains credibility.

flows.label: Conquered eastern states (Qi, Chu and others) → Xianyang and the Guanzhong metropolitan region
Interior → military-agricultural colonies in the Ordos loop
Interior → Lingnan garrison colonies after the Baiyue campaigns

summary: Immediately after unifying China in 221 BCE, the First Emperor moved the aristocratic and wealthy households of the conquered eastern kingdoms — 120,000 households according to the Shiji — to the new imperial capital region around Xianyang, disarming them and melting their weapons into bronze statues. The purpose was to sever the old elites from their regional power bases and to concentrate wealth and manpower where the throne could control them. In parallel, the Qin drove convicts, conscripted commoners and other coerced settlers north into the Ordos loop taken from the Xiongnu and south into Lingnan after the campaigns against the Baiyue, founding garrison colonies that were to hold newly annexed frontiers and feed the armies there. Recent scholarship prefers the term 'state-induced migration' because these flows mixed outright coercion with land grants, tax incentives and subsequent voluntary movement, but the largest transfers were compulsory. The figures are those of Han historians writing later and hostile to the Qin.
contested: The Shiji's figures, including the 120,000 households moved to Xianyang, come from Han-dynasty historiography written to condemn Qin rule, and their literal accuracy is questioned; modern analysis suggests the recorded transfers would have consumed an implausible share of state grain reserves.

sources.title: 'State-Induced Migration and the Creation of State Spaces in Early Chinese Empires' (Oxford University Research Archive)
ChinaKnowledge.de: Emperor Qin Shihuang

deathsNote: No defensible range. Han sources report heavy mortality among the conscripted labourers driven to the northern frontier for wall and road construction, but give no figures beyond the formulaic claim that thousands died, and deaths in the resettlement transfers themselves are unrecorded.
violenceNote: The use of convicts, conscripts and amnestied criminals as forced settlers and labourers on the Qin frontier is documented in the Shiji and analysed in the modern scholarship on state-induced migration in early China.
baselineWhat: The population of the Qin empire after the unification of 221 BCE
baselineNote: The first surviving Chinese census is the Han register of 2 CE, which counted 57.7 million people in a larger territory. Working back from it, historical demographers place the Qin empire at roughly 20 million, with published estimates ranging from about 15 million to 40 million. The 600,000 figure is derived from the Shiji's statement that 120,000 wealthy households were moved to Xianyang, at an assumed five persons per household.

baselineSources.title: Censuses of Han China / Han dynasty

shareCaveat: The numerator is a household count multiplied by an assumed household size, not a count of people, and it excludes the separate frontier colonisation drafts.

title: Roman Deportation and Colonisation within Italy
actors: The Roman Republic uprooted whole peoples within Italy — most notably the Ligurian Apuani in 180 BCE — and repeatedly confiscated the land of Italian communities to settle citizen colonists and discharged soldiers
peopleRange: Livy gives 40,000 Apuani Ligurians deported from the Apennines to Samnium by the consuls of 180 BCE, with a further 7,000 the following year — the largest deportation of a free population recorded within Italy. Livy was writing about 150 years later from annalistic sources, but the figures are of the administrative kind his sources preserved and are broadly accepted; the deportees' descendants are attested in the second century CE by the alimentary tablet of the Ligures Baebiani, a community in Samnium named for the consul who moved them, which confirms both the transfer and its permanence. The much larger land confiscations of the civil wars, particularly the triumviral proscriptions and settlements of 41 BCE that dispossessed the population of some eighteen Italian towns, are not quantified in the sources.
territoryDesc: Ligurian mountain territory in the northern Apennines was cleared and annexed; over the following century the land of numerous Italian communities was confiscated for veteran colonies, most extensively in the settlements of the 80s and of 41 BCE.

flows.label: Apuani Ligurians of the Apennines → Samnium (180–179 BCE)

summary: Rome's consolidation of Italy involved both the removal of populations and the implantation of new ones. In 180 BCE the consuls Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus removed the Apuani Ligurians from their mountain territory and transported some 40,000 of them, with a further 7,000 the next year, to public land in Samnium several hundred kilometres to the south, where they were resettled at state expense — an operation Livy describes in the language of an administrative undertaking and which left a community known for centuries afterwards as the Ligures Baebiani. Confiscation and redistribution of Italian land for citizen colonies and, from Sulla onward, for discharged soldiers, dispossessed many further communities; the triumviral settlements of 41 BCE stripped the territory of around eighteen Italian towns to provide farms for veterans, an episode remembered in the poetry of Virgil and Propertius. The Ligurian figures come from Livy and are corroborated by the later attestation of the resettled community; the civil-war confiscations are described qualitatively rather than counted.
contested: Livy's figure of 40,000 Apuani is a single literary source, though its administrative character and the survival of the Ligures Baebiani community in Samnium support it; the scale of the later civil-war confiscations is not quantified in any source.

sources.title: '180 BCE: Mass Deportation and the Order of Roman Italy', Acta Classica 67 (Newcastle University ePrints)

deathsNote: There was no significant death toll attached to the Ligurian deportation itself: Livy describes a state-funded transfer in which the deportees were given land and money at their destination. Deaths in the preceding Ligurian wars and in the civil-war proscriptions belong to those events rather than to the resettlement.
violenceNote: Livy records the clearing of Ligurian settlements before the transfer, and the confiscation of Italian civic territory for veteran settlement is described by Appian and reflected in contemporary Latin poetry.
baselineWhat: The population of peninsular Italy in the mid-second century BCE
baselineNote: Italian population figures for the Republic are the subject of the long-running 'low count / high count' dispute. Brunt's low count, built from the census figures of adult male citizens, gives roughly 4-5 million free inhabitants of Italy plus one to two million slaves in the second century BCE; Lo Cascio's high count, reading the census figures differently, implies 12-14 million. The baseline follows the low count, and would be nearly three times larger on the high count.

baselineSources.title: Demography of the Roman Empire — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The affected figure counts documented deportations such as the 47,000 Ligurian Apuani moved to Samnium in 180 BCE, and omits the far larger and unquantified dispossessions of the triumviral land confiscations of 41 BCE.

title: Xiongnu Expulsion of the Yuezhi
actors: The Xiongnu confederation under Modu Chanyu and his successors defeated the Yuezhi of the Gansu corridor and drove them west, setting off a chain of displacements that ended with the Yuezhi conquest of Bactria
peopleRange: No figures exist. The whole episode is known from Chinese sources — the Shiji's account of Zhang Qian's embassy and Modu Chanyu's letter to the Han court — which describe the defeat of the Yuezhi, the killing of their king and the making of his skull into a drinking cup, and the flight of the main body westward, without any population count. Modern estimates of steppe confederation sizes are inferential. This entry is included because the movement was compelled by military defeat at the hands of an organised steppe state, not because any number can be attached to it.

flows.label: Gansu corridor → Ili valley and Dzungaria
Ili valley → Sogdiana and Bactria, after displacement by the Wusun

summary: The Yuezhi, a pastoral confederation occupying the Gansu corridor, were defeated by the Xiongnu under Modu Chanyu around 176 BCE and again under his successor, who according to the Chinese sources killed their king and made his skull into a drinking vessel. The main body fled west into Dzungaria and the Ili valley, displacing the Sai (Saka) peoples in their turn; then, pushed again by the Wusun with Xiongnu backing, they moved south to the Syr Darya and by about 130 BCE crossed into Bactria, where they overthrew the Greco-Bactrian kingdom and eventually gave rise to the Kushan empire. A remnant, the 'Lesser Yuezhi', stayed behind and was absorbed. The episode is the best-documented ancient instance of a steppe state driving an entire people across a continent, and it is known almost entirely from Han Chinese records made because the Han were seeking the Yuezhi as allies against the Xiongnu; no numbers of any kind survive.
contested: The identification of the Yuezhi with later peoples and the exact chronology of their westward stages are debated, and the entire narrative depends on Han Chinese sources with no independent corroboration.

sources.title: ChinaKnowledge.de: Yuezhi
Encyclopaedia Iranica: XIONGNU

deathsNote: No death toll is recorded. Chinese sources note the killing of the Yuezhi king and the defeat of their armies but give no casualty figures, and losses during the long westward migration are entirely undocumented.
baselineWhat: The Yuezhi confederation of the Gansu corridor before its expulsion
baselineNote: No count exists. The Shiji credits the Yuezhi with 100,000-200,000 archers, which if taken at face value would imply several hundred thousand people, but Han figures for steppe confederations are conventional and are not treated by historians as demographic data; there is no archaeological settlement basis for a pastoral population of this kind.

title: Roman Enslavement of Epirus
actors: On the Senate's instruction, Lucius Aemilius Paullus sacked seventy towns of the Molossians in Epirus in a single coordinated operation and enslaved their inhabitants
peopleRange: 150,000 enslaved from seventy towns is the figure given by Polybius and repeated by Livy and Strabo, and it is accepted in the modern literature — Adam Ziolkowski's study in the Papers of the British School at Rome calls it 'the largest manhunt in the history of Rome'. Polybius was a contemporary Greek eyewitness of the period and a hostage in Rome at the time, which makes his testimony better than most, but the number is still a literary one and is very large in relation to the likely population of Epirus. Some scholars regard it as an upper bound or as including the whole of the Epirote population brought under Roman control rather than those physically shipped out.
territoryDesc: The Molossian territory of Epirus in northwestern Greece was stripped of population and its towns destroyed; the region did not recover its urban life for generations.

flows.label: Epirus → the slave markets and estates of Italy via Brundisium and Tarentum

summary: After the defeat of Macedon at Pydna, the Roman Senate ordered the punishment of the Molossians of Epirus, who had sided with King Perseus. Lucius Aemilius Paullus placed garrisons in seventy towns on a single day and gave the signal for a simultaneous sack, enslaving their populations — 150,000 people according to Polybius, Livy and Strabo. The operation was conducted with the machinery of a state, not as opportunistic plunder: the towns were secured in advance, the timing was coordinated to prevent flight, and the captives were moved to the Adriatic ports on the army's route home. Ziolkowski's study argues that the primary motive was economic, to replenish an Italian slave supply depleted by the plague of 175–174 BCE, rather than punitive. Archaeological survey in Epirus shows a long collapse of settlement afterwards, consistent with severe depopulation. The 150,000 figure is a literary one, but it comes from a contemporary and is generally accepted in outline.
contested: Whether 150,000 is a literal count or a round contemporary estimate is debated, as is whether the operation was primarily punitive or driven by Italy's demand for enslaved labour.

sources.title: A. Ziolkowski, 'The Plundering of Epirus in 167 B.C.: Economic Considerations', Papers of the British School at Rome (Cambridge Core)

deathsNote: No death toll is recorded and none is implied by the sources: the operation was designed to capture people alive for sale, and the ancient accounts emphasise enslavement rather than killing. Mortality during transport and sale is undocumented.
violenceNote: Polybius, Livy and Strabo record the simultaneous sacking and demolition of seventy Molossian towns, discussed in Ziolkowski's study.
baselineWhat: The population of Epirus, and principally of the Molossian territory sacked in 167 BCE
baselineNote: No enumeration survives. Modern estimates built from settlement archaeology and army sizes (Beloch's classical demography, Hammond's study of Epirus) put the whole of Epirus at roughly 200,000-300,000 in the Hellenistic period. Several scholars regard Livy's figure of 150,000 enslaved as implausibly large for Molossia alone and treat it as a rhetorical or inflated total.
shareCaveat: Both numerator and denominator are ancient-literary and modern-reconstructed respectively; the resulting share is an order-of-magnitude statement about the scale of the sack, not a measured percentage.

title: The Roman Destruction of Carthage
actors: Rome besieged Carthage for three years under Scipio Aemilianus, destroyed the city, killed most of its population and sold the survivors into slavery, annexing its territory as the province of Africa
peopleRange: Ancient and modern figures differ widely. Appian reports 70,000 killed in a single phase of the final assault, a number Ben Kiernan regards as exaggerated, and gives 50,000 survivors sold into slavery; Polybius, who was present with Scipio, says only that the dead were 'incredibly many'. Kiernan works from a pre-siege population of 200,000–400,000 and concludes that at least 150,000 died and that some 55,000 survivors, including 25,000 women, were enslaved; other reference treatments give a survivor figure of 30,000–50,000 from a population of 100,000–200,000. All the underlying counts derive from Roman-era literary sources, and the pre-siege population itself is a modern estimate from the excavated area of the city.
territoryDesc: Carthaginian territory in what is now northern Tunisia was annexed as the Roman province of Africa; the city site was cursed and left largely unoccupied until Rome refounded a colony there a century later.

flows.label: Carthage → the slave markets of Italy and the Mediterranean

summary: The Third Punic War began with Roman demands that Carthage abandon and destroy its city; when the Carthaginians refused, Rome besieged it from 149 to 146 BCE. The final assault involved days of street fighting through the residential quarters, and the city was burned and systematically demolished on the Senate's instruction. Ancient accounts report tens of thousands killed and roughly 50,000 survivors sold into slavery; the territory became the Roman province of Africa. Because the object was explicitly the elimination of the city rather than its subjugation — Cato's repeated demand that Carthage must be destroyed, and the Senate's decree of demolition — the historian Ben Kiernan, writing for the Yale Genocide Studies Program, argues that the episode meets the terms of the 1948 Genocide Convention while acknowledging it was neither a racial extermination nor a war on Carthaginian culture as such. Other historians reject applying the modern category. The story that Rome sowed the site with salt is a nineteenth-century invention with no ancient authority.
