contested: Whether the destruction of Carthage constitutes genocide is disputed: Ben Kiernan argues that it does, while other classicists hold that the modern legal category cannot be applied to a Hellenistic-era siege; the casualty and enslavement figures from Appian are also widely regarded as inflated.

sources.title: B. Kiernan, 'The First Genocide: Carthage, 146 BC', Diogenes 203 (Yale Genocide Studies Program)
World History Encyclopedia: Genocide in the Ancient World
Britannica: Battle of Carthage, 146 BCE

deathsNote: The lower figure is Appian's report of 70,000 killed in the final assault, which Kiernan considers exaggerated for that phase; the upper figure is Kiernan's own estimate of total deaths across the three-year siege, derived from a pre-siege population of 200,000–400,000 against roughly 50,000 recorded survivors. The disagreement is driven by the unknown size of the city's population and by the fact that every ancient count comes from Roman-era authors.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Polybius, who was present, and Appian describe the three-year blockade and famine, the killing during the final assault and the systematic demolition and burning of the city, as analysed by Kiernan.
baselineWhat: The population of Carthage at the start of the Third Punic War
baselineNote: Strabo reports 700,000 inhabitants at the siege, a figure modern historians treat as rhetorical. Estimates from the walled area and from the city's known military manpower put Carthage at roughly 200,000-400,000 in 149 BCE, making it one of the largest cities in the Mediterranean. Appian says 50,000 survivors surrendered and were sold into slavery.
shareCaveat: The 50,000 counts the survivors enslaved, not the affected population: the great majority of the city's inhabitants died in the siege and the final street fighting, so a low share here means a higher death toll, not a lighter one.

title: The Roman Destruction of Corinth
actors: Lucius Mummius sacked Corinth at the end of the Achaean War, killed its male citizens, sold the women and children into slavery and confiscated its territory for the Roman state
peopleRange: No figures survive. Pausanias and other later Greek and Roman authors state that the male citizens were killed and the women, children and freed slaves sold, without numbers; Corinth's pre-war population is a modern estimate in the tens of thousands. Excavation by the American School and the Corinth Computer Project indicates that the physical destruction of buildings was partial and selective rather than total, and that people continued to live among the ruins during the century before the Roman refoundation, which qualifies the literary picture of complete annihilation.
territoryDesc: Corinthian territory was confiscated as Roman public land, surveyed and partly leased out, then centuriated and distributed to settlers when Julius Caesar founded a Roman colony on the site in 44 BCE.

flows.label: Corinth → slave markets and Italy
Rome → Caesarian colonists at Corinth, 44 BCE

summary: In the same year as the destruction of Carthage, Rome ended the Achaean War by storming Corinth, the league's leading city. The later sources record that Mummius had the male citizens killed and the women, children and freed slaves sold into slavery, that the city's art and treasure were shipped to Italy, and that the site was left desolate; Greece was brought under Roman supervision. Archaeological work has complicated that account: the destruction of buildings appears to have been partial and selective, occupation continued among the ruins, and an inscription of 111 BCE shows Roman officials measuring and selling Corinthian public land in the interval. Julius Caesar refounded Corinth as a Roman colony in 44 BCE, laying out the confiscated territory in a centuriated grid for settlers, and the city became the administrative capital of Roman Greece. No population figures survive for either the destruction or the refoundation.
contested: Whether Corinth was genuinely left desolate for a century, as the literary sources claim, is contradicted by archaeological evidence of continued occupation and Roman land administration on the site.

sources.title: Corinth Computer Project, University of Pennsylvania: Roman Landscape 146–44 BC
World History Encyclopedia: Corinth

deathsNote: No figures exist. Pausanias states that the male citizens were killed but gives no number, and no archaeological evidence of mass burial or general destruction has been identified.
violenceNote: Pausanias and later Roman authors record the killing of Corinth's male citizens and the sacking of the city; the extent of physical destruction is qualified by the excavation record.
baselineWhat: The population of Corinth and its territory at the time of the sack
baselineNote: No count survives. Modern estimates rest on walled area multiplied by assumed density and on the size of the citizen body implied by Corinth's military contributions; they range from about 40,000 to 90,000 for the city in its classical prime, and Corinth in 146 BCE was smaller than at its fifth-century peak. Beloch's calculations and the more recent 'shotgun' area estimates of Hansen differ by a factor of two, so 50,000 should be read as an order of magnitude.

title: Han Frontier Colonisation and the Xiongnu Wars
actors: Emperor Wu of Han drove the Xiongnu from the Ordos and the Hexi corridor and settled hundreds of thousands of state-directed migrants, convicts and garrison farmers in the newly annexed frontier commanderies
peopleRange: The Hanshu and Shiji record specific state resettlement operations: over 700,000 people moved after the Yellow River dyke breaches from 132 BCE, 725,000 directed toward the frontier in 119 BCE, and 400,000 in 107 BCE, alongside continuous military-agricultural colonisation (tuntian) in the Hexi corridor and the Juyan basin. These are figures from the imperial histories, drawn in part from genuine administrative records — Han census and military documents on wooden slips have survived from the Juyan garrisons — which makes them better grounded than most ancient numbers, though still transmitted through court historiography. The displaced Xiongnu and other steppe populations pushed out of the Ordos and Hexi are not quantified at all.
territoryDesc: The Ordos loop and the Hexi corridor were annexed and organised into the frontier commanderies of Wuwei, Zhangye, Jiuquan and Dunhuang, extending Han control roughly 1,000 km northwest toward the Tarim basin.

flows.label: North China plain → Hexi corridor colonies
Xiongnu and allied groups displaced from the Ordos and Hexi northward

summary: From 133 BCE Emperor Wu abandoned the Han policy of appeasing the Xiongnu and launched decades of offensive campaigns that took the Ordos loop and then the Hexi corridor, expelling the Xiongnu and their subordinate confederations from pasture they had held for generations. The conquered ground was held by settlement: the imperial histories record repeated state operations moving hundreds of thousands of people — disaster refugees, convicts, amnestied criminals, freed slaves and poor peasants — into new frontier commanderies, supported by military-agricultural colonies whose settlers depended on the state for land, tools, seed grain and protection. Han administrative documents recovered from the Juyan and Dunhuang garrisons give an unusually direct picture of these colonies. The result was a permanent demographic transformation of the northwest, the opening of the corridor toward Central Asia, and the displacement of steppe populations whose numbers no source records. The Chinese figures are better grounded than most ancient numbers because they derive partly from real fiscal and census administration, but they still reach us through court historiography.
contested: The settler figures come from the imperial histories and cannot be checked directly, and the number of Xiongnu and other steppe people displaced from the Ordos and Hexi is entirely unrecorded.

sources.title: 'State-Induced Migration and the Creation of State Spaces in Early Chinese Empires' (Oxford University Research Archive)
'Resettlement strategies and Han imperial expansion', Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2019)

deathsNote: No range can be given. The Han–Xiongnu wars involved large campaign armies and heavy losses on both sides recorded episodically in the Shiji and Hanshu, but there is no basis for a total, and mortality among the resettled colonists is undocumented.
violenceNote: The compulsory movement of convicts, conscripts and state-directed settlers into frontier military-agricultural colonies is documented in the Han histories and in the surviving Juyan garrison documents analysed in the modern scholarship.
baselineWhat: The registered population of the Han empire during Emperor Wu's frontier wars
baselineNote: The only hard datum is the census of 2 CE, which registered 57,671,400 people in 12,233,062 households — one of the earliest reliable state censuses anywhere. Working back from it, historians of Han demography put the population at the height of Emperor Wu's campaigns at roughly 40-50 million, allowing for growth over the intervening century and for the wars' own losses.
shareCaveat: The 725,000 are state-directed settlers, convicts and garrison households moved onto the newly conquered frontier, so the ratio measures the scale of a resettlement programme against the whole empire, not the share of any population that was displaced from its home by force.

title: Han Conquest and Annexation of Nanyue
actors: Emperor Wu of Han destroyed the kingdom of Nanyue and annexed its territory, dividing it into commanderies and opening the region to Chinese settlement
peopleRange: No figure. The Chinese histories record the campaign and the division of the kingdom into commanderies but give no population transfer numbers. What followed was a long, state-encouraged flow of settlers, officials and garrison troops from the north, visible in Han census returns for the southern commanderies and in the archaeology of the region, rather than a single measurable displacement.
territoryDesc: The kingdom of Nanyue — present-day Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam — was annexed and reorganised into Han commanderies including Nanhai, Cangwu, Jiaozhi, Jiuzhen and Rinan.

flows.label: Han interior → officials, garrisons and settlers in the southern commanderies

summary: Nanyue, founded by a former Qin commander after the collapse of the Qin, ruled the far south and northern Vietnam for about a century until Emperor Wu of Han sent an expedition that took its capital at Panyu in 111 BCE and abolished the kingdom. Its territory was divided into commanderies under direct imperial administration, and the region became a target for sustained Chinese settlement, which over the following centuries brought the sinicisation of Guangdong and Guangxi and introduced Chinese administration and culture into northern Vietnam, beginning a period of northern rule that Vietnamese historiography treats as the first era of Chinese domination. The conquest is recorded as a territorial annexation rather than a mass deportation; the demographic consequences accumulated over generations through settlement, garrisoning and the imposition of Han administration, and no contemporary source quantifies them.
contested: Vietnamese and Chinese historiographies differ over whether Nanyue should be treated as a Vietnamese state extinguished by foreign conquest or as a Chinese regional kingdom reincorporated into the empire.

sources.title: Britannica: Nam Viet
'Resettlement strategies and Han imperial expansion', Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2019)

deathsNote: No significant recorded death toll beyond the fighting of a short campaign. The Chinese histories describe the capture of the capital and the execution of the Nanyue leadership rather than mass killing of the population.
baselineWhat: The registered population of the Lingnan and Red River commanderies created out of Nanyue
baselineNote: The only usable count is the Han census of 2 CE, preserved in the Book of Han, which registers roughly 1.3-1.4 million people across the commanderies carved from Nanyue - Nanhai, Cangwu, Yulin, Hepu, Jiaozhi, Jiuzhen and Rinan. It postdates the conquest by more than a century, counts taxpaying registered households, and almost certainly omits much of the upland non-Han population.
shareCaveat: The denominator is a fiscal register taken 113 years after the annexation, not a population count at the time of the conquest.

title: Han Conquest of Gojoseon and the Four Commanderies
actors: Emperor Wu of Han destroyed Wiman Joseon in northern Korea and replaced it with four directly administered Chinese commanderies
peopleRange: No figure. The Chinese sources record an invasion force of some 50,000 troops with a naval contingent of 7,000, the siege and capture of the capital Wanggeom, and the establishment of commanderies, but no population transfer count. Korean and Chinese accounts note that refugees from the destroyed kingdom moved south into the Korean peninsula, carrying Gojoseon material culture with them; that movement is visible archaeologically but has never been quantified.
territoryDesc: Northern Korea and part of Liaodong were organised into four Han commanderies — Lelang, Lintun, Xuantu and Zhenfan — of which Lelang, centred near modern Pyongyang, endured until 313 CE.

flows.label: Refugees from Wiman Joseon → the southern Korean peninsula

summary: Emperor Wu, having secured his northern and western frontiers, sent an army and fleet against Wiman Joseon in 109 BCE; after a siege the capital Wanggeom fell in 108 BCE and the kingdom was abolished. Four commanderies were established in its place, the most durable being Lelang near modern Pyongyang, which functioned as a Chinese administrative and commercial enclave on the peninsula for four centuries and left a rich archaeological record of Han-style tombs and artefacts. The Han motive recorded in the sources was strategic and economic — removing a state that obstructed contact with the peoples further south, and gaining access to iron and salt. Displaced elites and commoners from the destroyed kingdom moved south, contributing to the formation of the later Korean polities. The extent of Chinese settlement, and how far Lelang was a colony of immigrants rather than an administration imposed on a local population, remain matters of scholarly and nationalist dispute.
contested: The location, character and extent of the Han commanderies — and particularly whether Lelang was a Chinese settler colony or a thin administrative overlay on a Korean population — are disputed between Chinese, Korean and Japanese scholarship, with a strong nationalist charge.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: Gojoseon

deathsNote: No usable figures. The sources describe a year-long campaign with a siege and internal assassination of the Joseon king rather than mass killing of the population, and give no casualty totals.
baselineWhat: The registered population of the Han commanderies established in the former territory of Wiman Joseon, as recorded in the Han census of 2 CE
baselineNote: The Book of Han's census of 2 CE records 406,748 people in 62,812 households in Lelang commandery and about 221,845 in Xuantu, the two surviving commanderies of the four founded in 108 BCE. The count is a tax register taken a century after the conquest and covers registered households only, so it is a floor rather than a full population.

title: Caesar's Conquest of Gaul
actors: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul over eight campaigning seasons, annexing it to Rome and enslaving or killing large parts of several Gallic and Germanic peoples
peopleRange: Plutarch, writing about 150 years later, states that Caesar killed one million Gauls and enslaved a million more; Velleius and Appian give comparable round millions. Caesar's own Commentaries give figures for individual episodes — 53,000 Aduatuci sold in a single sale, the population of Avaricum massacred, the Veneti council executed and the people sold, the survivors of Alesia distributed as slaves to his soldiers — but he was writing as a participant with a keen eye to his own political self-presentation. Modern assessments, including the case study by the University of New England, conclude that the figures 'may be doubted', that recorded mass enslavements were in fact occasional and exemplary rather than routine, and that Caesar's own numbers for enemy populations are inflated: he claims, for instance, to have found a census tablet showing 368,000 Helvetii of whom 110,000 returned home.
territoryDesc: Gaul between the Rhine, the Alps, the Pyrenees and the Atlantic — roughly 500,000 km² — was annexed to the Roman empire.

flows.label: Gaul → the slave markets of Italy
Attempted Helvetian migration turned back by Caesar in 58 BCE

summary: Caesar's eight campaigns from 58 to 50 BCE brought all of Gaul under Roman rule and made his political career. His own account records the forcible return of the migrating Helvetii to their homeland, the destruction of the Usipetes and Tencteri at the Rhine, the sale of 53,000 Aduatuci in one transaction, the massacre at Avaricum, the execution of the Veneti leadership and the sale of their people, and the distribution of the captives of Alesia to his soldiers. Later Roman writers summarised the war as a million killed and a million enslaved, figures that have shaped the modern debate over whether the conquest amounted to genocide. Recent scholarship treats those totals as unreliable and argues that mass enslavement, while real and devastating where it occurred, was used selectively as an exemplary punishment rather than as a routine practice, and that Caesar's Commentaries are a work of self-justification rather than a record. What is not in dispute is that a large territory was annexed, that several peoples were destroyed as political communities, and that captives from Gaul entered the Roman slave supply in very large numbers.
contested: Whether Caesar's Gallic war constituted genocide, and whether the ancient totals of a million killed and a million enslaved bear any relation to reality, are both actively disputed; recent scholarship regards the figures as doubtful and mass enslavement as exemplary rather than systematic.

sources.title: 'Mass-Enslavement in Caesar's Gallic Conquest: A Case Study' (University of New England research repository)
British Museum: Slavery in ancient Rome (on war captives as a source of enslaved people)

deathsNote: The upper bound of one million killed comes from Plutarch and other Roman-era summarisers and is treated by modern scholarship as an unverifiable round figure. No lower bound can be defended: Caesar's own episode-by-episode counts are self-reported and inflated, and there is no independent demographic or archaeological basis for a Gallic death toll.
violenceNote: Caesar's own Commentaries record the massacre at Avaricum, the destruction of the Usipetes and Tencteri, the blockade and starvation of Alesia and the burning of Gallic settlements.
baselineWhat: The population of Gaul on the eve of Caesar's campaigns
baselineNote: There was no census of independent Gaul. Beloch's classic estimate and McEvedy and Jones' regional series put the population of what is now France at roughly 5-6 million in the mid-first century BCE; other reconstructions from settlement archaeology and later provincial tax rolls run as high as 12 million. Caesar's own figures - the Helvetian tablets, a million dead and a million enslaved reported by Plutarch and Appian - are propaganda arithmetic and are not used here.

title: The First Jewish–Roman War and the Destruction of Jerusalem
actors: Roman armies under Vespasian and Titus suppressed the Judaean revolt, destroyed Jerusalem and the Second Temple, and enslaved and dispersed large numbers of the population
peopleRange: 97,000 taken prisoner across the war and 1,100,000 dead in the siege of Jerusalem are the figures of Flavius Josephus, who commanded in Galilee, defected to the Romans and wrote his account under Flavian patronage; he also reports a defector's count of 115,880 corpses carried out of one gate. Tacitus gives 600,000 besieged. Both are literary figures from authors with reasons to magnify the scale — Josephus to exalt the achievement of his patrons and to dramatise the catastrophe, Tacitus at second hand. Modern estimates of Jerusalem's ordinary population range from about 20,000 to 80,000, swollen by refugees and pilgrims at the time of the siege, so the death figure in particular is generally regarded as impossible; the captive figure of 97,000 is treated as high but nearer the plausible range.
territoryDesc: Judaea was placed under a permanent legionary garrison and imperial governor, temple land was made imperial property, and the Temple tax was converted into the fiscus Judaicus payable to Jupiter Capitolinus.

flows.label: Judaean captives → Rome, the Egyptian mines and the provinces

summary: The revolt that began in Judaea in 66 CE was suppressed over seven years, culminating in Titus's five-month siege of Jerusalem in 70, the burning of the Second Temple and the demolition of most of the city, with the final reduction of Masada in 73. Josephus, the principal source and an eyewitness to much of the war, gives 1,100,000 dead in the siege and 97,000 prisoners taken over the whole conflict, distributed to the arena, the Egyptian mines and provincial slave markets; the temple treasures paraded in Titus's triumph are depicted on the Arch of Titus in Rome. The Roman state converted the annual Temple tax into a poll tax on Jews throughout the empire, the fiscus Judaicus. Josephus's numbers cannot be reconciled with modern estimates of Jerusalem's population and are treated as rhetorical, but the destruction of the temple, the ending of the sacrificial cult, and the enslavement and dispersal of a large part of the Judaean population are not in question. The war did not by itself produce a general exile: Jewish settlement continued in Judaea and especially in Galilee.
contested: Josephus's death toll of 1,100,000 is rejected by modern historians as far exceeding any plausible population of Jerusalem, and the extent to which the war produced a general dispersal of Jews from Judaea is disputed, since substantial Jewish settlement continued afterwards.

sources.title: Livius.org: Titus' Siege of Jerusalem
Livius.org: Jewish War (66–70)
Livius.org: Fiscus Judaicus

deathsNote: The upper bound of 1,100,000 is Josephus's own figure for the siege of Jerusalem and is rejected by modern historians as incompatible with the size of the city; Tacitus's 600,000 besieged is similarly a literary figure. No defensible lower bound exists, because there is no independent evidence — documentary, demographic or archaeological — from which to reconstruct the toll of the siege and the wider war.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Josephus, a participant and eyewitness, records the famine during the blockade, mass crucifixions outside the walls, the burning of the Temple and the city, and the assignment of captives to the mines and the arena.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of Roman Judaea and Galilee on the eve of the revolt
baselineNote: Broshi's estimate from agricultural carrying capacity and settlement survey puts the population of Roman Palestine at roughly 1 million around 66 CE, of whom the great majority were Jews; other reconstructions run to 2-2.5 million. Josephus' figures - 1.1 million dead and 97,000 enslaved at Jerusalem alone - are regarded by most historians as heavily inflated.
shareCaveat: The 97,000 enslaved is Josephus' figure and is not independently corroborated; the denominator is itself a modelled estimate, so the percentage rests on two soft numbers.

title: Trajan's Conquest and Colonisation of Dacia
actors: The emperor Trajan destroyed the Dacian kingdom in two wars, annexed its core as a Roman province, and repopulated it with colonists brought in from across the empire
peopleRange: No reliable figures. A lost passage of Trajan's physician Criton, cited at second hand, has been read as giving 500,000 Dacian captives, a number modern historians reject; the surviving epitomes record captives, deportations and Dacian recruits drafted into auxiliary units serving in Britain and the east, without totals. For the settlement side, Eutropius states that Trajan 'brought in huge masses of people from the four corners of the empire to settle in towns and rural areas, for Decebalus's long war had left Dacia short of men' — an explicit ancient statement of colonisation but not a count. Modern estimates rest on epigraphy showing settlers from Pannonia, Noricum, Dalmatia, Syria, Asia Minor and Thrace.
territoryDesc: The core of the Dacian kingdom — much of present-day Transylvania, Oltenia and the Banat — was annexed as the province of Dacia, held until Aurelian's withdrawal in the 270s.

flows.label: Dacian captives → Italy and the empire
Pannonia, Noricum, Dalmatia and the eastern provinces → colonists in Dacia

summary: Trajan fought two wars against Decebalus, in 101–102 and 105–106, ending with the storming of the Dacian capital Sarmizegetusa Regia, the king's suicide and the annexation of the Dacian heartland. The conquest is commemorated in the reliefs of Trajan's Column in Rome, which show fighting, the deportation of Dacian families and the burning of settlements. Ancient sources describe a country left short of people — through deaths, enslavement, flight beyond the new frontier and the drafting of Dacian men into auxiliary regiments posted far away — and Eutropius records that Trajan deliberately imported settlers from across the empire to repopulate it. Epigraphy confirms a colonist population of very mixed origin: Italians, Pannonians, Dalmatians, Thracians, Syrians and Galatians. The scale of the Dacian losses is the subject of a long and politically charged argument in Romanian historiography about continuity of population, and the ancient figures, including the reported 500,000 captives, are not credible as counts.
contested: The extent of Dacian depopulation, and whether the province's later Latin-speaking population descended from surviving Dacians or from imported colonists, is a long-running and nationally charged historiographical dispute; the reported captive figures are rejected as unreliable.

sources.title: History of Transylvania (Hungarian Academy of Sciences / MEK): The Population — Dacians and Settlers
Britannica: Dacia

deathsNote: No usable range. The wars were large and destructive and the sources describe mass suicide among the Dacian nobility and heavy losses, but the only numbers transmitted are late, indirect and rejected by modern historians.
violenceNote: Trajan's Column depicts the burning of Dacian settlements and the removal of the population, and the ancient sources record Dacian captives sold and Dacian men drafted into distant auxiliary service.
baselineWhat: No defensible figure exists for the population of the Dacian kingdom in 101 CE
baselineNote: Estimates rest entirely on archaeological survey of hillforts and settlement density in the Transylvanian core and on inference from later provincial taxation; published figures span well under 500,000 to over 2 million, a spread too wide to support a percentage. Ancient claims of 500,000 Dacians enslaved derive from a lost passage of Crito preserved only in a Byzantine excerpt and are not usable as demography.

title: The Bar Kokhba Revolt and Its Aftermath
actors: Roman forces under Hadrian crushed the Judaean revolt led by Simon bar Kosiba, depopulated much of Judaea, barred Jews from Jerusalem and renamed the province
peopleRange: Cassius Dio, writing roughly a century later, reports 50 fortresses and 985 villages destroyed and 580,000 men killed in the fighting, with more dying of famine, disease and fire. There is no captive or deportation figure; rabbinic tradition describes slave markets glutted with Judaean captives at Hebron and Gaza, in terms the modern literature treats as partly legendary. Dio's numbers are of the conventional round-literary kind and are far above any plausible population for Judaea, but archaeological survey does show a sharp and lasting drop in Jewish settlement in Judaea proper, with the centre of Jewish life shifting to Galilee — so the depopulation was real even though the figures are not measurements.
territoryDesc: The province of Judaea was renamed Syria Palaestina, Jerusalem was refounded as the colony of Aelia Capitolina with a temple to Jupiter on the temple mount, and Jews were forbidden to enter it.

flows.label: Judaea → Galilee (surviving Jewish population)
Judaean captives → slave markets at Gaza and Hebron

summary: The revolt led by Simon bar Kosiba from 132 to 136 CE briefly established an independent administration in Judaea, documented by its own coinage and by letters recovered from caves in the Judaean desert. Rome committed a very large force and reduced the rebels stronghold by stronghold, ending at Betar. Cassius Dio records the destruction of 985 villages and 50 fortified places and 580,000 killed in action, with many more dead from famine and disease. Afterwards Hadrian refounded Jerusalem as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina, barred Jews from entering it, and renamed the province Syria Palaestina; observance of Jewish law was restricted for a period. Archaeological survey confirms that Jewish settlement in Judaea proper collapsed and did not recover, while Galilee became the centre of Jewish life and of rabbinic activity. Dio's figures are literary and cannot be verified, and the general expulsion of Jews from the whole land often attached to this event in later tradition is not supported by the evidence.
contested: Dio's figure of 580,000 killed is a later literary number regarded as inflated; the extent of the ban on Jews — whether it covered Jerusalem alone or a wider area, and how consistently it was enforced — is also disputed.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: The Bar-Kochba Revolt
Britannica: Bar Kokhba
Posen Library: The Bar Kokhba Revolt and Its Aftermath

deathsNote: The upper bound of 580,000 killed in the fighting is Cassius Dio's figure, written about a century after the events and widely regarded as far exceeding Judaea's population; Dio adds an unquantified further toll from famine, disease and fire. No lower bound can be defended, since no independent record of casualties survives, though archaeological survey confirms severe and permanent settlement loss in Judaea.
violenceNote: Cassius Dio records the razing of villages and fortresses and mass killing; the refoundation of Jerusalem as a pagan colony, the exclusion of Jews from the city and the renaming of the province are recorded in Roman sources and confirmed by the coinage and inscriptions of Aelia Capitolina.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of Judaea on the eve of the Bar Kokhba revolt
baselineNote: Estimates rest on carrying-capacity and settlement-survey work rather than records. Magen Broshi argued that Roman Palestine as a whole could not have exceeded about one million people, of whom Judaea proper held perhaps 500,000-700,000. Cassius Dio's report of 580,000 killed and 985 villages destroyed is close to or above the whole plausible population and is treated by most historians as inflated, though excavation of the refuge caves confirms devastation and depopulation across the Judaean hills.
shareCaveat: Dio's casualty figures approach the entire estimated population of the region, so ratios drawn from them are not meaningful.

title: Sasanian Deportation of Roman Populations to Iran
actors: Sasanian kings, above all Shapur I and later Shapur II, carried off the populations of captured Roman cities in Syria, Cilicia and Cappadocia and settled them in new and existing cities of the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia
peopleRange: No dependable numbers survive. Shapur I's own trilingual inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam, the Res Gestae Divi Saporis, states that 'men of the Roman Empire, of non-Iranians, we deported. We settled them in the Empire of Iran, in Persis, Parthia, Khuzistan, in Babylonia and in other lands', and lists dozens of captured cities without giving totals. Later Syriac and Arabic sources describe the resettlement of the population of Antioch and other cities and the founding of Gundeshapur and Bishapur with Roman labour, and give figures for individual later episodes; Encyclopaedia Iranica treats the practice as well attested and the counts as unreliable. Modern estimates of the total moved over the period run into the tens of thousands but have no documentary base.

flows.label: Antioch and Syria → Gundeshapur and Khuzistan
Cappadocia and Cilicia → Bishapur and Persis

summary: Sasanian Persia used deportation as a standing instrument of imperial development. Shapur I's campaigns against Rome — culminating in the capture of Antioch and the defeat and capture of the emperor Valerian in 260 CE — produced very large numbers of prisoners and civilians whom he settled across his empire, as his own inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam records. Roman captives were used to build and populate new royal foundations, including Bishapur in Fars and Gundeshapur in Khuzistan, and to construct bridges and dams; deportees were given agricultural land and housing, kept their Christianity, and formed the nucleus of the Christian communities of Sasanian Iran, a point stressed in the Syriac Chronicle of Seert. Shapur II continued the practice in the fourth century. Iranian policy resembled the Assyrian and Achaemenid pattern in aiming at productive resettlement rather than destruction, and the deportees' skills — masonry, engineering, weaving — were the point. No source gives usable totals.
contested: The numbers deported are unrecorded, and later Syriac and Arabic accounts of particular transfers vary widely and are sometimes conflated across reigns.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: DEPORTATIONS
The Inscription of Shapur I at Naqsh-e Rustam (Sasanika, University of California, Irvine)

deathsNote: No death toll is recoverable, and none is implied by the policy: deportees were valued as builders, craftsmen and farmers and were settled with land and housing. Deaths occurred in the sack of cities such as Antioch, but no source quantifies them.
violenceNote: Shapur I's own inscription and the Syriac and Arabic sources summarised by Encyclopaedia Iranica record the use of deported Roman captives to build cities, bridges and dams in Iran.
baselineWhat: The populations of the Roman cities of Syria, Cilicia and Cappadocia captured by Sasanian armies
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The deportations spanned nearly a century and a half and many separate campaigns, and the affected cities — Antioch, Dura-Europos, Amida, and the towns of Cilicia and Cappadocia — have no agreed populations; estimates for Antioch alone range from about 100,000 to 300,000. The evidence is Shapur I's Res Gestae Divi Saporis inscription, later Syriac and Greek chronicles, and the archaeology of the Iranian foundation cities such as Gundeshapur, none of which supports an aggregate.

title: The Hunnic Invasions and the Displacement of Peoples in Europe
actors: The Huns conquered and subordinated the peoples of the Pontic steppe and central Europe, driving Alans, Goths and others into and across the Roman frontier, and under Attila destroyed cities and carried off captives from the Balkans and Gaul
peopleRange: No figures exist for any stage. Ammianus Marcellinus describes the Huns falling on the Alans, the Alans on the Goths and the Goths on the Taifali and Sarmatians in a cascade of displacement, but neither he nor Priscus, who visited Attila's court and is the other main source, gives population numbers. Later fifth-century sources record ransom payments for Roman captives and the return of prisoners under treaty, implying large numbers taken, without totals. Everything quantitative about Hunnic-era population movement is modern inference.
territoryDesc: At its height the Hunnic hegemony extended from the Pontic steppe across the Carpathian basin into central Europe, ruling a mosaic of subject Germanic and Iranian-speaking peoples; it fragmented within two decades of Attila's death in 453.

flows.label: Pontic steppe → Carpathian basin (Huns and subject peoples)
Peoples displaced across the Danube into the Roman Balkans
Balkan captives carried to the Hunnic heartland

summary: The arrival of the Huns on the western steppe around 370 CE set off the chain of movements that historians call the Migration Period: the Alans were defeated and partly absorbed, the Goths were pushed onto the Danube and into the Roman empire, and further groups were driven west and south. Under Attila from the 440s the Huns extracted enormous tribute from Constantinople, destroyed Balkan cities including Naissus — which Priscus found still littered with bones years later — and campaigned into Gaul and Italy before Attila's death in 453 and the rapid collapse of his empire. Captives were a central object of Hunnic warfare: prisoners were incorporated into Hunnic forces and households, and treaties with Rome specified ransom rates and the surrender of fugitives. The Huns are included here because an organised steppe power displaced whole peoples and carried off populations, but no ancient source gives numbers, and the extent to which the Huns caused rather than accelerated the movements of the period is debated.
contested: How far the Huns actually caused the Migration Period displacements, as against accelerating movements already under way, is debated, and no ancient source quantifies either the peoples displaced or the captives taken.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: Huns
Britannica: Hun

deathsNote: No range can be defended. Priscus and other contemporaries describe the destruction of Balkan cities and the killing of their inhabitants, and Priscus reports finding the ground at Naissus still covered with human bones, but no numbers were recorded and no archaeological estimate exists.
violenceNote: Priscus, who travelled to Attila's court, and other fifth-century writers record the sacking and depopulation of Balkan cities such as Naissus and the carrying off of their inhabitants.
baselineWhat: The peoples of the Pontic steppe and central Europe subordinated or displaced by the Huns
baselineNote: No denominator can be reconstructed. The groups involved — Alans, Greuthungi, Tervingi, Gepids, Sciri, Rugii and others — were mobile confederations with no registers, and the Roman sources that describe their movement give only rhetorical multitudes. Modern estimates for individual groups run to tens of thousands of people, but summing them across eighty years and a shifting set of peoples would be invention.

title: The Gothic Crossing of the Danube and the Gothic War
actors: Tervingi and Greuthungi Goths, displaced by the Hunnic advance, crossed the Danube into the Roman empire and, after exploitation and starvation at the hands of Roman officials, revolted and devastated the Balkan provinces
peopleRange: Eunapius gives 200,000 fighting men crossing the Danube, a figure historians reject; Ammianus Marcellinus, the best contemporary source, says only that the numbers were beyond counting. Modern estimates of the Tervingi and Greuthungi who entered the empire in 376 CE range from about 15,000 to 20,000 warriors — implying perhaps 60,000 to 100,000 people in total including families — with Peter Heather and others arguing for the higher end of that band. No census or administrative record exists, and the estimates are derived from army sizes and logistics.
territoryDesc: By the treaty of 382 the Goths were settled inside the empire in Thrace and Lower Moesia as federates under their own leaders, the first such settlement of an intact barbarian people on Roman soil.

flows.label: Gothic lands north of the Danube → Roman Thrace and Moesia (376 CE)

summary: In 376 CE Gothic groups pressed westward by the Huns appeared on the north bank of the lower Danube asking for admission to the Roman empire. The Tervingi were permitted to cross and settle as federates; the Greuthungi were refused and crossed anyway. The Roman officials responsible for provisioning them exploited the refugees severely — Ammianus records famine conditions and the sale of food at ruinous prices, including the reported exchange of children for dogmeat — and in 377 the Goths rose in revolt. The war culminated at Adrianople on 9 August 378, where the eastern field army was destroyed and the emperor Valens killed, with losses conventionally put at around two-thirds of the army present. Six further years of fighting and devastation across the Balkans ended in the treaty of 382, under which the Goths were settled inside the empire as a coherent group under their own leadership. The numbers who crossed are not recorded; Eunapius's 200,000 is rejected, and modern reconstructions are inferences from military logistics.
contested: The number of Goths who crossed in 376 is disputed, with the ancient figure of 200,000 rejected and modern estimates ranging from roughly 60,000 to 100,000 people; whether the settlement of 382 amounted to a Gothic state within the empire is also debated.

sources.title: Britannica: Battle of Adrianople (378)
World History Encyclopedia: The Goths

deathsNote: Roman military losses at Adrianople are conventionally estimated at up to 40,000, about two-thirds of the field army present, from Ammianus's account. Civilian deaths among the Gothic refugees from starvation in 376–377, and among the Balkan provincial population during six years of warfare, are described by Ammianus but not quantified in any source.
violenceNote: Ammianus Marcellinus, a contemporary and a former officer, records the deliberate starvation and extortion of the Gothic refugees by Roman officials, including the taking of children in exchange for food, and the devastation of the Balkan provinces in the war that followed.
baselineWhat: The Tervingi and Greuthungi Gothic groups who crossed the Danube in 376
baselineNote: Ammianus Marcellinus speaks only of innumerable multitudes. Modern reconstruction, principally Peter Heather's, works back from an estimated 10,000-20,000 warriors to a total group including women, children and dependants of perhaps 100,000; other historians argue for figures half that size. The number is a scholarly inference from army sizes, not a count.

title: The Vandal Conquest of Roman Africa
actors: Gaiseric led the Vandals and Alans from Spain into Roman North Africa, seized Carthage and the richest African provinces, expropriated the Roman landowning class and exiled Catholic clergy
peopleRange: 80,000 is the number given by Victor of Vita for the Vandals and Alans who crossed from Spain to Africa in 429 CE; it is a total for the whole people including women, children and dependants, not a fighting force. Victor was a hostile Catholic African writing some fifty years later, and historians differ over whether the figure derives from a real muster or is a literary round number, though it is generally treated as being of the right order. On the receiving side, the expropriation of Roman landowners across northern Tunisia is well attested in law and in Victor's account, but the number dispossessed is unrecorded; the imperial government's reduction of the African tax assessment by seven-eighths for the devastated districts is the clearest surviving measure of the disruption.
territoryDesc: Africa Proconsularis, Byzacena and part of Numidia — the grain-producing heart of the western empire, in present-day Tunisia and eastern Algeria — passed to the Vandal kingdom, recognised by treaty in 442.

flows.label: Baetica (southern Spain) → North Africa, 429 CE
Expropriated Roman landowners and exiled clergy driven from the Proconsular province

summary: In 429 CE Gaiseric moved the Vandals and Alans across the strait from Spain to Africa — 80,000 people according to Victor of Vita — and over the next decade took the western African provinces, capturing Hippo Regius after a siege during which Augustine died and seizing Carthage in 439. A treaty in 442 recognised Vandal possession of the richest provinces. The conquest was followed by systematic expropriation: across much of northern Tunisia Roman landowners were driven off and their estates handed to Vandal settlers as sortes Vandalorum, and imperial legislation cutting the African tax assessment to an eighth for the affected districts registers the scale of the disruption. As Arian Christians ruling a strongly Nicene population, the Vandal kings exiled and imprisoned Catholic bishops and clergy and confiscated churches; the extent of this persecution is disputed because the fullest account, Victor of Vita's History of the Vandal Persecution, was written to denounce it. The loss of the African grain supply was a decisive blow to the western Roman state.
contested: The 80,000 figure is a single hostile source's number; the severity of the religious persecution of Nicene Christians is disputed because it is known mainly from Victor of Vita's polemic, and modern historians consider it exaggerated though not invented.

sources.title: Britannica: North Africa — The Vandal conquest

deathsNote: No figures survive. The conquest involved sieges at Hippo Regius and Carthage and reported devastation of the countryside, and Victor of Vita describes killings and deaths in exile among the Nicene clergy, but no source gives totals and modern historians treat his account as polemical.
violenceNote: The expulsion of Roman landowners from their estates, the confiscation of Nicene churches and the exile and imprisonment of Catholic clergy are recorded by Victor of Vita and in imperial legislation, as summarised by Britannica.
baselineWhat: The population of the Roman provinces of North Africa
baselineNote: Estimates for Africa Proconsularis, Byzacena, Numidia and the Mauretanias in late antiquity range from about 3 to 6.5 million, derived from urban density, the extent of olive and cereal cultivation and the size of the annona grain levy to Rome. Four million is a conservative mid-point.
shareCaveat: The 80,000 figure is the number Victor of Vita and other sources give for the Vandal and Alan host that crossed from Spain - the incoming population, not the number displaced - so dividing it by the provincial population measures settlement, not expulsion.

title: Justinian's Gothic War and the Depopulation of Italy
actors: East Roman armies under Belisarius and Narses and Ostrogothic forces under Witigis and Totila fought a twenty-year war across Italy, repeatedly besieging, sacking and emptying its cities
peopleRange: No defensible total exists. The narrative rests almost entirely on Procopius, an eyewitness secretary to Belisarius whose figures are rhetorical: he writes that Rome was reduced at one point to a few hundred inhabitants after Totila expelled the population in 546, and in the Secret History claims Italy lost 'no less than fifteen millions' — a number modern historians reject outright, since Italy's total population was probably 4-7 million. Archaeological and settlement surveys show sharp urban contraction and abandonment of villa estates across the peninsula in the mid-sixth century, but cannot separate war from the plague of 541-543 or from longer-run late-antique decline.
territoryDesc: Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and Dalmatia passed from the Ostrogothic kingdom to East Roman rule; the Lombard invasion of 568 undid most of the conquest within a generation.

flows.label: Roman senatorial families and captives to Constantinople

summary: Between 535 and 554 the East Roman emperor Justinian sought to reconquer Italy from the Ostrogothic kingdom, producing a war that ran for two decades over the whole peninsula. Cities changed hands repeatedly: Milan was destroyed in 539 with its male population reportedly killed and its women handed to Burgundian allies; Rome was besieged and taken four times, and in 546 Totila expelled its inhabitants entirely, leaving the city briefly empty. The fighting coincided with the plague pandemic of 541-543 and with famines described by Procopius in Picenum and Aemilia, so mortality cannot be attributed to the war alone. The conquest was completed in 554 but collapsed almost immediately when the Lombards invaded in 568. The episode fills a long silence in the atlas between the Hunnic invasions and the Umayyad conquest of Iberia, and is the clearest case of state-directed urban emptying in early medieval western Europe.
contested: Whether the demographic collapse of sixth-century Italy was caused mainly by the war, by the plague of 541-543, or by longer-run late-antique decline; and whether Procopius's figures reflect anything countable.

sources.title: Gothic War (535-554) — Wikipedia
Gothic War — World History Encyclopedia
Totila — Wikipedia

deathsNote: No credible total. Procopius's claim of fifteen million dead in Italy is rhetorical and is rejected by modern historians; there are no censuses, tax registers or burial series for the period that would support a reconstruction. Deaths arose from sieges, massacres of captured city populations, famine and the concurrent plague in proportions that cannot be separated.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Procopius, an eyewitness to the campaign, describes the sieges and famine of Picenum and Aemilia, the sack of Milan in 539 and the emptying of Rome in 546.
baselineWhat: The population of the Italian peninsula at the start of the Gothic War
baselineNote: There is no sixth-century count. Atlas-scale reconstructions, chiefly McEvedy and Jones, put Italy at roughly 4 million around 500 CE, down from perhaps 7 million at the height of the Roman empire; other estimates for the early sixth century range from about 3.5 to 7 million. The war overlapped with the Justinianic plague from 541, whose mortality is itself heavily disputed, so the population during the conflict was falling for reasons the war alone does not explain.

title: Slav and Avar Settlement of the Balkans
actors: Avar khaganate armies and Slavic groups raided, occupied and settled the Roman Balkan provinces while imperial administration and much of the provincial population withdrew to coastal cities and fortified sites
peopleRange: No defensible figure exists. The evidence is Byzantine narrative — Procopius, Menander, Theophylact Simocatta, the Miracles of St Demetrius and the Chronicle of Monemvasia — supplemented by coin-hoard sequences, the abandonment of Danubian forts and hilltop refuge sites, and the disappearance of episcopal sees. These texts describe cities sacked and inhabitants carried off but give no totals, and their numbers where present are rhetorical. Florin Curta has argued that 'the Slavs' were substantially formed as an identity on the Danube frontier rather than arriving as a single migrating people, which further undercuts any attempt at a migration count.
territoryDesc: Most of the Roman Balkan interior between the Danube and the Peloponnese passed out of imperial control; Byzantine authority contracted to Thessalonica, the Aegean and Adriatic coasts and a few fortified enclaves, and was only rebuilt piecemeal from the ninth century.

flows.label: Danube frontier → Macedonia and Greece
Provincial populations → fortified coastal cities

summary: Between roughly 580 and 630 the Roman Balkan provinces ceased to function as an imperial space. Avar and Slavic raiding, the collapse of the Danube frontier after 602, and the withdrawal of field armies to the eastern front left the interior open to permanent settlement by Slavic-speaking groups, while surviving provincial populations concentrated in coastal cities, offshore islands and mountain refuges. Byzantine writers describe sacked cities, mass captive-taking and depopulation; archaeology shows the abandonment of Danubian forts and a break in urban life across the interior. The scale is unquantifiable: the chronicles give no reliable totals, and modern scholarship is divided between models of large-scale folk migration and models in which a smaller intrusive population catalysed a change of identity among people already there. The episode is included because the collapse of imperial control was accompanied by documented forcible movement of populations, not because a mass expulsion can be demonstrated.
contested: Whether this was a mass migration that replaced the Balkan population or a smaller military and political takeover under which existing populations adopted a new identity is actively disputed, with Florin Curta's 'Making of the Slavs' the best-known statement of the second position; the argument carries a strong modern nationalist charge in the region.

sources.title: The Balkans and the Danube limes during the sixth and seventh centuries (Curta, The Making of the Slavs, CUP)
Slavs and Bulgars (The New Cambridge Medieval History)
World History Encyclopedia: Slavs

deathsNote: No usable figures. Byzantine sources describe massacres and enslavement during raids but give no totals, and there is no demographic reconstruction that can separate deaths from flight, captivity or the ordinary mortality of a disrupted period.
violenceNote: The destruction and abandonment of Danubian forts and Balkan towns is documented archaeologically and in the Miracles of St Demetrius and Theophylact Simocatta; other forms alleged in the chronicles cannot be tied to specific documented episodes.
baselineWhat: The provincial Roman population of the Balkan provinces around 580 CE
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The late Roman Balkans have no surviving register, and any figure for 580 would have to reckon with the Justinianic plague of 541 onwards, whose demographic effect is itself one of the most contested questions in late antique history — estimates of mortality run from a few per cent to a third. McEvedy and Jones and other atlas-scale reconstructions give the peninsula figures in the low millions, but these are extrapolations from later medieval data rather than evidence for the sixth century.

title: Expulsion and Killing of the Jewish Tribes of Medina
actors: The early Muslim community under Muhammad expelled the Banu Qaynuqa and Banu Nadir from Medina and, after the Battle of the Trench, executed the adult males of the Banu Qurayza and enslaved their women and children
peopleRange: No reliable figure. The sira tradition — Ibn Ishaq as transmitted by Ibn Hisham, with al-Waqidi and al-Tabari — gives the Banu Qaynuqa some 700 fighting men and describes the Banu Nadir leaving Medina with their movable property on camels for Khaybar and Syria. These are the numbers of a genre written a century and a half or more after the events, in a form that regularly uses round figures; they cannot be treated as counts. The total displaced would have been on the order of a few thousand people across the three tribes.
territoryDesc: The date palms, fortresses and lands of the three tribes in and around Medina passed to the Muslim community; the Nadir's estates became the basis of important early property settlements.

flows.label: Banu Nadir → Khaybar
Banu Qaynuqa → Syria

summary: Between 624 and 627 the three principal Jewish tribes of Medina were removed from the settlement. The Banu Qaynuqa were besieged and expelled in 624, the Banu Nadir besieged and expelled in 625 with permission to take movable goods, and after the siege of Medina in 627 the Banu Qurayza surrendered and were judged by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who sentenced the adult males to death and the women and children to enslavement. Ibn Ishaq's account, the fullest, gives the executed as between 600 and 900. The episode rests entirely on the Muslim biographical tradition recorded well over a century later; W. N. Arafat argued in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society in 1976 that the Qurayza massacre account is a late accretion of doubtful reliability, while M. J. Kister and most subsequent specialists have defended the tradition's substance while treating the numbers as conventional. There is no independent documentary or archaeological evidence either way.
contested: Whether the mass execution of the Banu Qurayza happened as described is disputed: Arafat (1976) argued the account is unreliable late tradition, while Kister and most later scholarship accept the core of the episode but not the precise figures.

sources.title: Britannica: Banū Qurayẓah
W. N. Arafat, 'New Light on the Story of Banū Qurayẓa and the Jews of Medina', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (1976)
Brill, Encyclopaedia of Jews in the Islamic World: Banū Qurayẓa

deathsNote: The range brackets the figures given in the sira tradition for the Banu Qurayza executions — most often 600 to 900, occasionally as low as 400. Every figure derives from the same body of later Muslim biographical writing; there is no independent check, and Arafat's 1976 article disputes the episode's historicity altogether.
violenceNote: The executions of the Banu Qurayza men are documented in Ibn Ishaq's sira as transmitted by Ibn Hisham and in al-Tabari; their reliability is disputed.
baselineNote: No enumeration exists for seventh-century Yathrib. The sira literature is the only source and gives orders of magnitude rather than counts: the Banu Qaynuqa are said to have been able to field some 700 fighters, the Banu Nadir a smaller number, and between 400 and 900 men of the Banu Qurayza are reported to have been executed in 627. Modern historians treat these figures as approximations from a tradition written down more than a century later.

title: The Arab Conquests and the Dhimmi Settlement Regime
actors: Rashidun and Umayyad armies conquered Sasanian Iran, the Byzantine Levant, Egypt and North Africa, founded garrison towns for Arab settlers, and placed conquered non-Muslims under a tributary 'dhimma' regime
peopleRange: No aggregate figure, and the conquests are notable for how little mass population transfer they involved. The documented movements are of the conquerors rather than the conquered: Arab tribal groups were settled in new garrison towns (amsar) at Kufa, Basra, Fustat and Kairouan, and later in Khurasan, under state direction. Departures of Byzantine officials, soldiers and some Chalcedonian clergy from Syria and Egypt are recorded in the chronicles without numbers. The evidence is Arabic conquest narratives compiled a century or more later, Greek and Syriac chronicles, Egyptian papyri and the archaeology of the new towns; the papyri in particular show administrative continuity rather than upheaval.
territoryDesc: Within roughly a century the caliphate absorbed the entire Sasanian empire and the Byzantine provinces of Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa, together with Transoxiana, Sind and most of the Iberian peninsula.

flows.label: Arabian tribal settlers → the garrison town of Kufa
Arabian tribal settlers → Fustat

summary: Between the 630s and the 740s Arab-Muslim armies destroyed the Sasanian empire and stripped Byzantium of its southern provinces, creating a single polity from the Atlantic to Central Asia. The characteristic instrument of rule was not expulsion but the dhimma: Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians and later others retained their communities, law and worship in exchange for tribute, principally the jizya poll tax, together with legal subordination that hardened into formal disabilities from the eighth century onward. Conquering forces were settled in purpose-built garrison towns rather than dispersed among the conquered, which limited displacement but created a durable structure of separate and unequal populations. Later Islamic tradition also records the removal of Christians and Jews from the Hijaz under Umar I. The demographic effect was gradual: conversion and Arabisation took centuries, and Egypt and Syria retained Christian majorities long after the conquest. The entry records a change of sovereignty and a legal regime of subordination, not a mass deportation.
contested: The scale of violence and disruption in the conquests is debated: the Arabic conquest narratives were written down long afterwards and are shaped by later concerns, while papyri and archaeology suggest greater administrative and settlement continuity than the narratives imply.

sources.title: Britannica: dhimmah
World History Encyclopedia: Rashidun Government
Archaeology and New Urban Settlement in Early Islamic Syria and Iraq (The Byzantine and Early Islamic Near East, CUP)

deathsNote: No defensible figures. The conquests involved pitched battles, sieges and the sack of some cities, but no source or modern reconstruction supports an aggregate death toll, and much of the territory changed hands by capitulation treaty rather than storm.
baselineWhat: The population of the lands conquered between 633 and 750: Sasanian Iraq and Iran, Byzantine Syria, Palestine and Egypt, and North Africa
baselineNote: There is no census for the seventh century. McEvedy and Jones's regional estimates give roughly 12 million for Iran and Iraq, 3-4 million for Syria and Palestine, 4 million for Egypt and 3-4 million for North Africa around 600-650 CE, giving an order of magnitude of 25-30 million. Later Islamic tax registers (the jizya rolls) count dhimmi households in particular provinces but cannot be aggregated backwards. Conversion was slow: Bulliet's curve from onomastic evidence suggests majorities of Muslims were reached only in the ninth to tenth centuries.

title: The Trans-Saharan Slave Trade, 7th–15th Centuries
actors: Merchants and states on both sides of the Sahara — the Maghribi and Egyptian markets, and the Sahelian polities of Ghana, Mali, Kanem-Bornu and the Hausa states — moved enslaved Africans northward across the desert over eight centuries
peopleRange: Roughly 3 to 5 million people over eight centuries, on the standard modern reconstructions. There is no register of the trade; the figure is an extrapolation built by Ralph Austen from scattered Arabic geographical and commercial references, caravan sizes and later nineteenth-century observations, and adopted with modifications by Paul Lovejoy, whose census puts the total for 650–1600 at roughly 4.3 to 4.8 million. Britannica's summary of the same evidence gives a rate that 'could rarely if ever have transported more than 6,000 or 7,000 slaves a year'. These are order-of-magnitude estimates from fragmentary evidence, not counts, and John Wright and others have criticised the precision they imply.

flows.label: Central Sudan → Tripoli and the Fezzan
Western Sudan → Morocco
Darfur and Kanem → Egypt via the Forty Days Road

summary: From the Arab conquest of North Africa onward, an organised long-distance trade carried enslaved Africans north across the Sahara to markets in the Maghrib, Egypt and the wider Islamic world, where they were used as domestic servants, concubines, soldiers, miners and agricultural labourers. The trade was sustained by Sahelian states that raided their southern neighbours and by caravan networks tied to the gold and salt trades. Nothing resembling a register survives; the volume is reconstructed by extrapolation, principally by Ralph Austen, whose census gives an average of a few thousand a year and totals in the low millions for the medieval centuries, with Paul Lovejoy putting the whole period 650–1600 at roughly 4.3 to 4.8 million. Mortality on the desert crossings was high and is not separately measurable. Because most of those taken were women and children, and because male captives were frequently castrated for the eunuch trade with very high death rates, the demographic effect on source regions is thought to have been severe, but it too cannot be quantified.
contested: The volume estimates are extrapolations from fragmentary evidence rather than counts; John Wright and other specialists have criticised the confidence placed in Austen's census, and no independent check on the medieval figures exists.

sources.title: Britannica: western Africa — Pre-European slave trading
Regional study: trans-Saharan trade (The Cambridge World History, vol. 5)
'The slave trade across the Sahara' — review of John Wright, The Trans-Saharan Slave Trade, Journal of African History

deathsNote: No defensible figures. Deaths in raiding, on the desert crossing and in the castration of boys for the eunuch trade are attested qualitatively in Arabic sources and are believed to have been very high, but there is no basis for a total.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Enslavement for labour, military service and domestic and sexual servitude across the Sahara is documented in the Arabic geographical and legal literature and reconstructed in Austen's and Lovejoy's censuses of the trade.
baselineWhat: The populations of the Sahelian and sub-Saharan regions that supplied captives to the trans-Saharan trade
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists, for the same reason as the Atlantic trade: the traffic ran for eight centuries across dozens of polities from the Senegal to the Nile, and there is no population reconstruction for medieval West and Central Africa that could serve as a base. The volume figure itself is an estimate — Ralph Austen's reconstruction from Arabic geographical and commercial sources, later revised by Austen himself and challenged by others — with margins of error that some scholars put at 50 per cent or more.

title: Byzantine Population Transfers: Slavs to Anatolia, Armenians and Syrians to Thrace
actors: Byzantine emperors — notably Justinian II, Constantine V and their successors — moved whole populations across the empire to garrison frontiers, repopulate devastated provinces and break up communities judged unreliable
peopleRange: No cumulative figure. Theophanes the Confessor states that Justinian II, after campaigning in Macedonia in 688-689, resettled large numbers of Slavs in the Opsikion theme in Bithynia and raised from them a corps of 30,000 men, of whom some 20,000 later deserted to the Arabs at Sebastopolis in 692; those are the only quantities in the tradition and are round numbers. Peter Charanis's survey of the practice catalogues dozens of transfers — Slavs into Anatolia, Armenians and Syrians into Thrace under Constantine V in the 750s, Anatolians into the Balkans — almost none of them numbered. The evidence is Byzantine chronicles and saints' lives; seals and later provincial toponymy confirm the settlements existed.

flows.label: Slavs from Macedonia → the Opsikion theme, Bithynia
Armenians and Syrians → Thrace under Constantine V

summary: From the late seventh century the Byzantine state used compulsory population transfer as a standing instrument of policy. Justinian II moved Slavic groups from Macedonia into Bithynia in Asia Minor, forming from them a military corps that Theophanes numbers at 30,000; when much of it defected to the Arabs in 692 the emperor is said to have had the settlers' families killed. Constantine V moved Armenians and Syrians from the eastern frontier into depopulated Thrace in the 750s and moved others in the reverse direction, using transfer at once to repopulate, to garrison and to dilute communities regarded as religiously or politically suspect. Peter Charanis's 1961 study established transfer as a continuous policy rather than a set of emergencies. The figures are almost entirely absent, and where present are round chronicle numbers; the practice is nonetheless securely documented across two centuries.
contested: The single quantified case, Justinian II's 30,000-strong Slav corps, is a round chronicle figure, and Theophanes' report that the settlers' families were massacred after the desertion at Sebastopolis is not independently corroborated.

sources.title: Peter Charanis, 'The Transfer of Population as a Policy in the Byzantine Empire', Comparative Studies in Society and History (1961)
Ethnic and Religious Violence in Byzantium (The Cambridge World History of Violence)

deathsNote: No usable figures. Transfer was intended to move populations rather than destroy them; the one killing reported in this context, the massacre of the deserters' families in 692, is given without numbers by Theophanes and is not corroborated.
baselineWhat: The population of the Byzantine Empire during the period of the transfers
baselineNote: Warren Treadgold's reconstruction from army pay, fiscal and thematic records puts the empire at roughly 7 million around 780, down from perhaps 19 million in the sixth century before plague and territorial loss. No register of the transferred populations survives; the individual transfers are known only from chronicle notices that give round numbers or none.

baselineSources.title: Byzantine Empire under the Isaurian dynasty

shareCaveat: The programme spans nearly 150 years and many separate operations, while the denominator is a single-date estimate for an empire whose borders moved substantially over that time.

title: The Red Sea and Indian Ocean Slave Trades, 7th–15th Centuries
actors: Merchants operating from the Swahili coast, the Horn and the Red Sea ports carried enslaved East Africans and Ethiopians to Arabia, the Persian Gulf, Iraq and India, in a trade organised through Islamic commercial networks
peopleRange: On the order of 1 to 3 million over roughly seven centuries. As with the Saharan trade there is no register: the figure derives from Ralph Austen's separate censuses of the Red Sea and Indian Ocean routes and from Paul Lovejoy's synthesis, built from port references in Arabic and Persian geographers, later observed volumes and assumptions about continuity. Specialists working on the Swahili coast regard the medieval leg as the least securely quantified of all the slave trades, and the estimate should be read as an order of magnitude.

flows.label: Swahili coast → the Persian Gulf and Basra
Red Sea ports → the Hijaz and Arabia
East Africa → western India

summary: Alongside the Saharan routes, a maritime trade carried enslaved people from the East African coast, the Horn and the Nilotic Sudan across the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean into Arabia, the Gulf, Iraq and India, where they served as domestic and agricultural labour, concubines and soldiers. The trade is visible in Arabic and Persian geographies, in the presence of East Africans in Abbasid Iraq — the Zanj of the ninth-century revolt were its product — and in the African-descended Habshi and Siddi communities that later held political power in parts of India. Estimates of volume for the medieval centuries are extrapolations rather than counts; the commonly cited totals of one to three million rest on Austen's censuses and Lovejoy's synthesis and are acknowledged by their authors to be provisional. The trade continued and expanded into the nineteenth century, so figures quoted for 'the Indian Ocean slave trade' often cover a far longer span than the medieval period treated here.
contested: The medieval volume of this trade is the least well evidenced of the major slave trades; the figures are extrapolations from later observed volumes and scattered references, and different specialists produce estimates differing by a factor of two or more.

sources.title: Slavery in the Islamic Middle East (c. 600–1000 CE) (The Cambridge World History of Slavery)
Gwyn Campbell, Africa and the Indian Ocean World from Early Times to Circa 1900 (CUP)
Britannica: Zanj rebellion

deathsNote: No defensible figures. Mortality in capture, on the coastal march and on the sea crossing is attested qualitatively but never counted for the medieval period.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Enslavement and transport for labour and domestic and sexual servitude is documented in the Arabic and Persian geographical literature and reconstructed in the Cambridge World History of Slavery and in Austen's and Lovejoy's censuses.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The trade drew captives over seven and a half centuries from the Horn, the Ethiopian highlands, the Swahili hinterland and, later, the Great Lakes - societies for which no contemporary counts exist and whose populations changed enormously across the period. The volume estimates themselves, by Ralph Austen and Paul Lovejoy among others, are reconstructions from port records, tariff yields and traveller accounts, with wide margins.
shareCaveat: The figure is a cumulative total across 750 years and cannot meaningfully be set against any single population.

title: Umayyad Conquest and Settlement of Iberia
actors: An Umayyad army of largely Berber troops under Tariq ibn Ziyad, followed by Musa ibn Nusayr, destroyed the Visigothic kingdom and settled Arab and Berber groups across the peninsula under a tributary regime for Christians and Jews
peopleRange: No defensible figure. The conquering forces are given as roughly 7,000 to 12,000 men in the Arabic chronicles, with later Syrian contingents; these are the only quantities in the sources and are conventional. Movement of the conquered population is undocumented in numbers: the Visigothic aristocracy was partly destroyed, partly absorbed by treaty — the Pact of Tudmir of 713 preserved a local lord's lands and his subjects' religion in exchange for tribute — and an unmeasured flow of Christians moved into the northern mountains, where the Asturian kingdom formed. The evidence is late Arabic chronicles, the Latin Chronicle of 754, and archaeology of settlement continuity.
territoryDesc: Almost the whole Iberian peninsula was absorbed into the Umayyad caliphate as al-Andalus, later an independent emirate at Córdoba; Christian polities survived only in the Cantabrian mountains and the Pyrenees.

flows.label: Berber and Arab forces → the Guadalquivir valley
Christian flight → the Cantabrian north

summary: In 711 a force crossing from North Africa under Tariq ibn Ziyad defeated the Visigothic king Roderic, and within a decade most of the Iberian peninsula was under Umayyad rule. Conquest was accomplished as much by treaty as by battle: local lords who submitted kept their lands and their subjects kept their religion under tribute, as the surviving Pact of Tudmir shows. Arab and, in far greater numbers, Berber groups settled across the peninsula in a hierarchy that placed Arabs above Berbers above native converts, and the resulting tensions produced the Berber revolt of 740. Native Christians and Jews continued under dhimmi status, and conversion to Islam proceeded gradually over more than two centuries rather than as an immediate consequence of conquest. There is no evidence of mass expulsion of the indigenous population; the measurable displacement is the movement of some Christians into the northern mountains, which cannot be quantified.
contested: The Arabic narrative sources for 711 are late and legendary in parts, and the size of the incoming Arab and Berber population — and thus how far the conquest changed the peninsula's demography as opposed to its rulers — remains debated.

sources.title: Britannica: Spain — Muslim Spain
The Iberian Peninsula and North Africa (The New Cambridge History of Islam)
Britannica: al-Andalus

deathsNote: No usable figures. The conquest turned on a small number of engagements and many negotiated surrenders; neither the Arabic chronicles nor the Latin Chronicle of 754 supplies casualty totals, and no modern reconstruction attempts one.
baselineWhat: The population of the Iberian peninsula under the Visigothic kingdom
baselineNote: There is no census. McEvedy and Jones's Atlas of World Population History puts Iberia at about 4 million around 700, back-projected from later Islamic fiscal records and Christian land surveys; other reconstructions run from 3 to 6 million. The number of Arab and Berber settlers is separately estimated at only tens of thousands.

title: The An Lushan Rebellion and the Tang Census Collapse
actors: The rebel armies of An Lushan and Shi Siming, Tang loyalist forces and their Uyghur and Central Asian auxiliaries fought across the Tang heartland, sacking both capitals and destroying the empire's household registration
peopleRange: No count. The rebellion set off a large and lasting migration from the North China Plain to the Yangtze basin and the far south, visible in the shift of registered households southward across the eighth and ninth centuries, but the registers that would measure it are precisely what the war destroyed. The evidentiary basis is the Tang household and population registers preserved in the dynastic histories, which are tax documents recording households the state could reach, not a census in the modern sense.

flows.label: North China Plain → the Yangtze basin and the south

summary: An Lushan's revolt in 755 broke the Tang state's control of its own territory for eight years, saw Chang'an and Luoyang sacked more than once, and left the northeast in the hands of semi-independent military governors. Its most cited consequence is demographic: the registers give about 52.9 million people in some 9 million households in 754 and about 16.9 million in fewer than 3 million households in 764, a gap of roughly 36 million that has been repeated in popular accounts as a death toll and used to rank the rebellion among the deadliest events in history. Specialists reject that reading. The Tang registers counted taxable households the government could reach; the war destroyed the registration apparatus, put whole provinces beyond central control, and gave both households and provincial governors strong reasons not to be counted. Denis Twitchett and the Cambridge History of China, and demographic work going back to John Durand, attribute most of the gap to administrative collapse and tax evasion rather than mortality, while accepting that deaths from fighting, famine and epidemic were severe and are not separately recoverable.
contested: Whether the 36 million shortfall between the 754 and 764 registers represents deaths or the collapse of household registration is the central dispute; specialists in Tang history hold the second view, while the first continues to circulate in popular and cross-historical mortality rankings.

sources.title: Britannica: An Lushan
Population Change (The Cambridge Economic History of China)
ChinaKnowledge: An Lushan Rebellion 安史之亂
Economic transformation in the Tang–Song transition (The Economic History of China, CUP)
