Actual excess mortality from fighting, famine and epidemic was certainly heavy but has never been reliably estimated; no defensible lower bound exists.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
baselineWhat: The registered population of Tang China in the census immediately before the rebellion
baselineNote: The registers of 754 recorded 9,069,154 households and 52,919,309 individuals; the census of 764 recorded only 16.9 million. Historical demographers, including Durand and Bielenstein, treat the collapse as largely a failure of registration as the state lost control of tax rolls rather than a record of deaths, and put the actual population of the empire in 755 nearer 60-70 million.
shareCaveat: The 36 million fall in registered population that is often quoted as a death toll is an artefact of the tax registers; deaths and displacement were severe but are not measurable from it.

title: Charlemagne's Saxon Wars, Forced Conversion and Deportations
actors: Charlemagne's Frankish armies conquered the Saxon lands between the Rhine and the Elbe, imposed Christianity by capital law, and deported Saxon populations into Francia while settling others in their place
peopleRange: No reliable total. The Royal Frankish Annals and the Annales qui dicuntur Einhardi record repeated deportations — hostages taken by the thousand, whole districts removed, and in 804 the transfer of the Saxons living beyond the Elbe together with their wives and children into Francia, with Abodrite Slavs settled on the vacated land. The annals' figures, such as the 'every third man' formula and the 4,500 executed at Verden in 782, are conventional round numbers produced by the court's own historians; historians treat them as indicative of policy rather than as counts.
territoryDesc: Saxony between the lower Rhine, the Elbe and the Eider was annexed to the Frankish realm, organised into counties and bishoprics, and its pagan cult sites suppressed.

flows.label: Deported Saxons → Frankish interior
Abodrite Slavs settled on vacated Saxon land

summary: From 772 to 804 Charlemagne fought a series of campaigns to subjugate the Saxons, combining military conquest with the forcible imposition of Christianity. The Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae prescribed death for refusing baptism, for cremating the dead in pagan fashion and for eating meat in Lent; the pagan sanctuary at the Irminsul was destroyed in 772. The Royal Frankish Annals record the beheading of 4,500 Saxons at Verden in 782 after a revolt, and repeated deportations of Saxon populations into Francia, culminating in 804 with the removal of the Saxons beyond the Elbe and the settlement of Abodrite Slavs in their place. All the figures come from Frankish court annals written to justify the conquest; the Verden number in particular has been questioned, including an argument that the manuscript verb meant 'deported' rather than 'beheaded', which most specialists now reject while still doubting the round figure. What is not in doubt is that deportation and forced conversion were declared policy.
contested: The 4,500 executions at Verden are attested only by the Frankish annals; the number is widely regarded as unreliable, and an older philological argument that the text meant deportation rather than execution is now generally rejected but still cited.

sources.title: Britannica: Charlemagne — Military campaigns
The Saxon Wars (Conquest and Christianization, CUP)
World History Encyclopedia: Saxon Wars

deathsNote: The only specific figure is the 4,500 said by the Royal Frankish Annals to have been beheaded at Verden in 782; it is a court-produced number and is not independently corroborated. No total for the thirty-three years of campaigning exists, and deaths from the campaigns as a whole cannot be estimated.
violenceNote: The Royal Frankish Annals record the Verden executions and the destruction of the Irminsul, and the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae prescribes death for pagan practice.
baselineNote: No enumeration exists for eighth-century Saxony, and modern estimates for the lands between Rhine and Elbe vary by a factor of several depending on assumptions about settlement density; McEvedy and Jones put all of Germany at roughly 3.5 million around 800 CE, but the Saxon share cannot be isolated with confidence. The Frankish annals give episodic figures — 10,000 Saxons deported in 804, 4,500 executed at Verden — that cannot be converted into a share of the population.

title: Viking Slave Raiding and the Northern Slave Trade
actors: Scandinavian raiders and traders took captives from Ireland, Britain, Francia and the Slavic east and sold them through Dublin, Hedeby and the Volga route into Byzantium and the Islamic world
peopleRange: No total exists. Irish annals record individual raids carrying off captives — the Annals of Ulster note raids in which 'a great booty of women' was taken — and Anglo-Saxon and Frankish sources record ransoming and manumission of captives, but there was no register and no port record. The evidence is annalistic entries, law codes on slave status, Arabic accounts of the Rus slave traders on the Volga such as Ibn Fadlan's, and the silver-hoard record that tracks the trade's proceeds. Any aggregate is guesswork.

flows.label: Ireland → Iceland and the Norse North Atlantic
Eastern Europe → Constantinople via the Rus river routes
Hedeby and the Baltic → al-Andalus

summary: Slave-taking was a structural feature of Viking-age raiding rather than a by-product of it. Captives seized in Ireland, Britain, Frankia and the Slavic lands were held for ransom, kept as thralls in Scandinavia and the North Atlantic colonies, or sold on: Dublin functioned as one of Europe's principal slave markets, and the Rus river routes carried captives to Constantinople and the Islamic markets, where the silver that flows back into Scandinavian hoards is the trade's clearest surviving trace. Genetic and place-name evidence from Iceland indicates a substantial proportion of the founding female population came from Ireland and Britain. No total can be reconstructed: the annals record particular raids and not aggregates, and the trade left no registers. The practice declined in the eleventh and twelfth centuries with Christianisation and with church campaigns against the sale of Christians.
contested: The scale of Viking slave-taking is debated: some scholars treat it as the central economic driver of the raids, others as one activity among several, and there is no evidentiary basis for resolving the question numerically.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: The Vikings in Ireland
'Slave raiding and slave trading in early England', Anglo-Saxon England (CUP)
Castrating Monks: Vikings, the Slave Trade, and the Value of Eunuchs (Castration and Culture in the Middle Ages, CUP)

deathsNote: No usable figures. Raids killed, and mortality among captives in transit was presumably significant, but neither is recorded in any quantified form.
violenceNote: Captive-taking for thraldom and sale is documented in the Irish annals, Anglo-Saxon law and charter material, and the Arabic accounts of Rus traders, and is analysed in the Cambridge scholarship cited.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: the raids and the trade ran for three centuries across Ireland, Britain, Francia, the Baltic and the Slavic east
baselineNote: There is no register of captives and no single population acted upon. Estimates of the scale rest on chronicle notices of individual raids, on Irish and Frankish annals, on the Dublin and Hedeby slave markets, and on the volume of Islamic silver reaching Scandinavia, from which some historians infer tens of thousands of captives moved east across the ninth and tenth centuries. The populations concerned - Ireland at perhaps half a million, England at one to two million, the Slavic lands unenumerated - were never a single unit and changed greatly over 793-1100.

title: The Saqaliba Trade: Slavic Captives to al-Andalus and the Islamic World
actors: Frankish, Ottonian and Jewish long-distance merchants bought captives taken in wars on the Slavic frontier and sold them through Prague, Verdun and Mediterranean ports into al-Andalus, North Africa and the eastern Islamic world
peopleRange: No total. Ibn Hawqal and other Arabic geographers describe the trade and the eunuch workshops on the route, and Umayyad Córdoba's saqaliba are numerous enough in the tenth century to form a political faction and, on some accounts, thousands of palace servants and guards; but there is no register and the Arabic figures for palace establishments are court estimates. Marek Jankowiak's work on the silver-hoard evidence has been used to argue for a large-scale trade, while others treat the quantities as unrecoverable.

flows.label: Slavic frontier → the Prague market
Prague → Verdun, a centre of castration and transit
Verdun → Córdoba and al-Andalus

summary: Between the ninth and eleventh centuries a long-distance trade moved captives from the Slavic-speaking lands of central and eastern Europe into the Islamic Mediterranean, where they were known collectively as saqaliba. Captives taken in Ottonian and Frankish wars on the eastern frontier, and by Slavic rulers on each other, were bought by merchants and moved west and south through Prague and Verdun — the latter notorious in the Arabic and Latin sources as a place where boys were castrated for the eunuch market, an operation with very high mortality — and thence to al-Andalus, Ifriqiya and the eastern caliphate. In Umayyad Córdoba the saqaliba became a distinct military and administrative corps and, after 1009, a political force in the taifa period. The trade declined as the Slavic lands Christianised and their rulers stopped selling co-religionists. No quantities can be recovered; the evidence is Arabic geography, Latin toll records and the distribution of Islamic silver in northern hoards.
contested: The scale of the trade is disputed: arguments from Islamic silver hoards for a very large traffic are contested by scholars who hold that the hoard evidence cannot be tied specifically to slave sales.

sources.title: Britannica: Ṣaqālibah
'What Does the Slave Trade in the Saqaliba Tell Us about Early Islamic Slavery?', International Journal of Middle East Studies (CUP)
Eastern European Slave Trade (Slaves from the North, Brill)

deathsNote: No figures. Mortality from castration and from the long overland transit is described qualitatively in the Arabic sources as very high but was never counted.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Enslavement and transport of Slavic captives for military, domestic and sexual servitude is documented by Ibn Hawqal and other Arabic geographers and analysed in the Brill and IJMES scholarship cited.
baselineWhat: No single population can serve as a denominator for three centuries of captive-taking across the Slavic frontier

title: Byzantine Persecution and Deportation of the Paulicians
actors: Byzantine emperors suppressed the Paulician communities of eastern Anatolia by persecution and campaign, destroyed their state at Tephrike in 872, and transplanted surviving Paulicians to Thrace as frontier settlers
peopleRange: No reliable figure. Byzantine chronicles record deportations of Paulicians to Thrace under Constantine V in the eighth century and, on a larger scale, under John I Tzimiskes in the 970s, who settled them around Philippopolis to hold the Bulgarian frontier; the sources give no counts. The one quantity attached to the episode is the claim in the chronicle tradition that around 100,000 Paulicians died in the persecution under the empress Theodora in the 840s — a figure produced by hostile Byzantine writers and not a count.
territoryDesc: The independent Paulician principality centred on Tephrike in eastern Anatolia was destroyed in 872 and its territory reabsorbed into the empire.

flows.label: Paulicians → Thrace and the Philippopolis frontier

summary: The Paulicians were a dualist Christian movement on the Byzantine eastern frontier whom the imperial church treated as heretics. Persecution under the empress Theodora in the 840s drove survivors into Arab-held territory, where they built an armed principality at Tephrike that raided deep into Anatolia until Basil I destroyed it in 872. Alongside repression the empire used transplantation: Paulician communities were moved to Thrace, in the eighth century under Constantine V and most substantially in the 970s under John Tzimiskes, who settled them near Philippopolis as a military frontier population, where their descendants remained for centuries. The chronicle figure of about 100,000 killed under Theodora is a hostile estimate with no evidentiary support; Carl Dixon's recent study of the movement treats the Byzantine accounts as polemical constructions that need to be read against their purpose. What is well established is that the imperial state combined killing, confiscation and forced resettlement against a religious minority over more than a century.
contested: The 100,000 death figure for the persecution under Theodora comes from hostile Byzantine chronicles and is not accepted as a count; recent scholarship also questions how coherent a 'Paulician church' the sources describe as opposed to a polemical category.

sources.title: Britannica: Paulicians
Carl Dixon, The Paulicians: Heresy, Persecution and Warfare on the Byzantine Frontier, c.750–880 (Brill, 2022)
Peter Charanis, 'The Transfer of Population as a Policy in the Byzantine Empire', CSSH (1961)

deathsNote: The upper bound is the figure given in the Byzantine chronicle tradition for those killed in the persecution under Theodora in the 840s. It is a hostile, unverified estimate of a kind these chronicles produce routinely; no lower bound can be established, and modern specialists including Carl Dixon treat the number as rhetorical.
violenceNote: Byzantine chronicles and the imperial anti-heretical legislation document the suppression of Paulician worship and communities; the killing figures they attach are not treated as reliable.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Byzantine sources give no count of the Paulician communities of eastern Anatolia, and the chronicle figure of 100,000 killed under the empress Theodora is a literary topos rather than an enumeration; the Paulician state at Tephrike is known only from narrative sources and its subject population cannot be reconstructed.

title: Zanj Enslavement in the Iraqi Salt Marshes and the Zanj Revolt
actors: Abbasid-era landowners imported East African ('Zanj') enslaved labourers to clear the salt flats of lower Iraq; the labourers rose in 869 under Ali ibn Muhammad and held the region for fourteen years before Abbasid forces crushed them
peopleRange: No count exists for the number of East Africans transported to lower Iraq. Al-Tabari, the main source, describes the enslaved being organised in work gangs which Britannica summarises as numbering from 500 to 5,000 men each, without stating how many gangs there were; the aggregate is unknown. Figures in the tens of thousands that circulate are inferences from the size of the rebel armies, not from any record of the trade.
territoryDesc: At its height the revolt controlled much of lower Iraq and Khuzestan from a capital at al-Mukhtara, taking Basra in 871 and threatening Baghdad's food supply.

flows.label: East African coast → the salt marshes of lower Iraq

summary: Landowners in ninth-century lower Iraq used enslaved East Africans, known collectively as Zanj, to strip the salt crust from the marshland flats south of Basra so the land could be cultivated — heavy gang labour under harsh conditions. In 869 a preacher, Ali ibn Muhammad, mobilised these work gangs into a revolt that captured Basra in 871, established a capital at al-Mukhtara, and controlled much of lower Iraq and Khuzestan until the Abbasid regent al-Muwaffaq destroyed it in 883. Al-Tabari's history is the principal source and gives the movement's course in detail while attaching enormous casualty claims to it, running from hundreds of thousands to well over a million. Alexandre Popovic's study, the standard modern treatment, regards these as impossible. The revolt was not a general slave rebellion — the rebels themselves took captives and slaves — and modern historians debate how far it was defined by servile status as against regional and religious grievance.
contested: The death figures given by al-Tabari and later Arabic writers, which run from several hundred thousand to more than a million, are rejected as impossible by Popovic and subsequent scholarship; the composition of the rebel movement and how far it was a 'slave revolt' are also debated.

sources.title: Britannica: Zanj rebellion
Alexandre Popovic, The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq in the 3rd/9th Century (Markus Wiener)
Slavery in the Islamic Middle East (c. 600–1000 CE) (The Cambridge World History of Slavery)

deathsNote: Arabic chronicles give figures for the war ranging from around 300,000 to as high as 1.5 or 2.5 million; the upper bound shown here is a conservative reading of that tradition and is still far beyond what the region could support. Popovic and later specialists treat all of these as rhetorical. No lower bound can be established, and the fourteen-year war certainly killed heavily on both sides.
violenceNote: The use of imported enslaved East Africans in gang labour on the salt flats is documented by al-Tabari and set out in Popovic's study and in Britannica's account.
baselineWhat: No defensible figure exists for the number of enslaved East Africans held in the salt flats of lower Iraq
baselineNote: Abbasid sources describe gangs of 50 to 500 labourers clearing the sabkha but give no total, and modern estimates of the enslaved workforce range from a few tens of thousands to several hundred thousand. Al-Tabari's account of the revolt supplies army sizes, not a population, so neither the enslaved workforce nor the East African source populations can be quantified.

title: Mahmud of Ghazni's Raids into Northern India and the Ghaznavid Slave Trade
actors: Ghaznavid armies raided the Punjab, the Ganges plain and Gujarat, carrying captives and plunder back to Afghanistan
peopleRange: Court chroniclers writing for the Ghaznavids - al-Utbi, Farrukhi Sistani, and later Baihaqi - report captives in the tens and hundreds of thousands from single campaigns and say that slave prices in Ghazna and Khurasan collapsed because of the glut. These are panegyric figures, produced to magnify a patron, and cannot be treated as counts. Modern historians, notably Andre Wink and Mohammad Habib, accept that the raids produced enslavement on a large scale and fed a Central Asian and Middle Eastern slave market, while rejecting the specific numbers; no independent evidence permits a total.
territoryDesc: The Punjab annexed to the Ghaznavid empire with Lahore as its Indian capital; the rest of the raided territory was plundered rather than held

flows.label: Captives from the Punjab and Ganges plain to Ghazna

summary: Between about 1000 and 1027 Mahmud of Ghazni led some seventeen campaigns into northern India, sacking Kannauj, Mathura, Thanesar and the temple of Somnath, and annexing the Punjab, where Lahore became the Ghaznavid Indian capital. Ghaznavid court chronicles present the campaigns as jihad and record enormous quantities of plunder and enormous numbers of captives, describing slave markets in Ghazna, Khurasan and beyond glutted with Indian captives; the numbers are conventional and propagandistic, and modern historians treat them as unusable while accepting that enslavement occurred at scale. Temples were destroyed at several of the sacked cities, an element that has since become central to competing modern Indian narratives about the period. The raids did not attempt to hold most of the territory they crossed, but the annexation of the Punjab established a permanent Muslim political presence in northern India and the routes and precedents used by the later Ghurid conquest and Delhi Sultanate. Assessment of the campaigns is politically charged in South Asia, with Hindu nationalist historiography treating them as a foundational trauma and other historians emphasising plunder economics over religious motive.
contested: All contemporary figures for captives and plunder are panegyric; the relative weight of religious and economic motives, and the modern political meaning of the temple destructions, are strongly disputed.

sources.title: Mahmud of Ghazni
Ghaznavid dynasty
Somnath temple and the raid of 1026

deathsNote: No defensible range. The chronicles claim great slaughter at Somnath and elsewhere in the conventional language of victory narratives, and there is no independent evidence against which to test them.
violenceNote: Ghaznavid court chronicles themselves record the destruction of temples and the marching of captives into slavery, which is the only documentation available.
baselineWhat: The population of the Punjab, the Ganges plain and Gujarat raided by Ghaznavid armies
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Eleventh-century northern India has no census or fiscal register that survives in usable form; atlas-scale reconstructions give figures for the subcontinent as a whole but cannot be apportioned to the raided regions. The captive numbers in the Persian court chronicles — Utbi, Baihaqi, and the later Firishta — are rhetorical set-pieces meant to magnify the sultan's holy war, ranging from 5,000 to 500,000 for single campaigns, and modern historians treat them as unusable as counts.

title: The Harrying of the North
actors: William I's Norman army systematically destroyed settlements, crops, livestock and food stores across Yorkshire and the north of England to suppress rebellion and Danish intervention
peopleRange: No count of those displaced. The nearest measurable trace is the Domesday survey of 1086, which records a very high proportion of manors in Yorkshire and adjoining shires as 'waste' or of sharply reduced value seventeen years later, and refugee movement southward and into Scotland is recorded in the chronicles without numbers. The interpretation of the Domesday 'waste' entries is itself disputed: they may record destruction, or fiscal exemption, or the collapse of the tenurial records the commissioners were using.
territoryDesc: The northern shires were brought under Norman control and redistributed to Norman tenants-in-chief; large areas remained recorded as waste or heavily devalued in the Domesday survey of 1086.

flows.label: Refugees → Scotland

summary: In the winter of 1069–70, after repeated northern risings and a Danish landing, William I's army moved through Yorkshire and the surrounding shires destroying villages, food stores, farm implements and livestock. Orderic Vitalis, writing two generations later and generally sympathetic to William, condemned the campaign and stated that more than 100,000 people died of the resulting famine. Simeon of Durham and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle describe the same devastation. Modern historians accept that a deliberate scorched-earth campaign took place and that famine followed, but reject Orderic's figure as far larger than the region's likely population; they also divide over the Domesday 'waste' entries, which David Palliser and others have argued reflect administrative and fiscal categories as much as physical destruction, while Paul Dalton and others read them as evidence of real and lasting depopulation. The episode is treated in the Cambridge World History of Genocide as a case study in deliberate destruction of a civilian resource base.
contested: Orderic Vitalis's figure of more than 100,000 famine deaths is rejected as demographically impossible, and the meaning of the Domesday 'waste' entries — physical devastation versus fiscal or record-keeping categories — is disputed among specialists.

sources.title: William the Conqueror's Harrying of the North, 1069–1070 (The Cambridge World History of Genocide, vol. 1)
World History Encyclopedia: William the Conqueror's Harrying of the North

deathsNote: The upper bound is Orderic Vitalis's figure for famine deaths, given around 1125 and rejected by modern historians as exceeding the plausible population of the affected shires. No lower bound is established; that a severe famine with heavy mortality followed the campaign is not disputed, but its scale has never been reconstructed.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The deliberate destruction of crops, food stores, livestock and settlements and the ensuing famine are documented by Orderic Vitalis, Simeon of Durham and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
baselineWhat: The population of Yorkshire and the northern shires before the Norman devastation
baselineNote: The estimate is reconstructed from Domesday Book, compiled in 1086, using household multipliers: England as a whole is put at 1.5-2.25 million, with Yorkshire and the northern shires at roughly 150,000. Domesday records around 60 per cent of Yorkshire vills as wholly or partly 'waste' seventeen years after the harrying, though historians dispute how much of that reflects killing, flight, or fiscal exemption. Orderic Vitalis's claim of 100,000 dead is generally treated as rhetorical.

title: Turkmen Settlement of Anatolia after Manzikert
actors: Seljuk and independent Turkmen groups occupied the Anatolian plateau after the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert, displacing or absorbing the Greek- and Armenian-speaking Christian population over the following century
peopleRange: No figures. Byzantine writers — Michael Attaleiates, Anna Komnene, later Niketas Choniates — describe the flight of populations from the plateau to the coasts and to Constantinople, and Syriac and Armenian chronicles record similar movements; none give numbers. The rival modern reconstructions rest on the same narrative material supplemented by episcopal lists, saints' lives, and later Ottoman tax registers read backwards.
territoryDesc: Most of the Anatolian plateau passed permanently out of Byzantine control, organised from the 1080s as the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum with its capital eventually at Konya; Byzantium retained the western river valleys and the coasts.

flows.label: Christian flight from the plateau → Constantinople and the coasts
Turkmen groups → the Anatolian plateau

summary: The Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071 did not itself lose Anatolia, but the civil wars that followed opened the plateau to Turkmen groups who settled it over the next generation, and by the 1080s a Seljuk sultanate was established in the interior. What happened to the existing Christian population is one of the sharper disputes in medieval history. Speros Vryonis's 'The Decline of Medieval Hellenism in Asia Minor' (1971) argued for large-scale disruption, flight and the destruction of the Christian ecclesiastical structure, producing eventual Islamisation. Claude Cahen and, more recently, A. C. S. Peacock and Alexander Beihammer have emphasised continuity, negotiated accommodation, intermarriage and gradual conversion, with Christian communities persisting for centuries. Both readings work from the same thin body of chronicles; no demographic reconstruction is possible. The entry records a securely documented transfer of sovereignty over a very large territory accompanied by undocumented but real displacement.
contested: Whether the Turkmen settlement of Anatolia involved mass displacement and destruction of the Christian population, as Vryonis argued, or gradual accommodation and conversion, as Cahen, Peacock and Beihammer hold, is unresolved and carries a modern Greek–Turkish political charge.

sources.title: Britannica: Battle of Manzikert
Britannica: Anatolia — Seljuq expansion
The Turks in Anatolia before the Ottomans (The New Cambridge History of Islam, vol. 2)

deathsNote: No usable figures. The chronicles describe raids, sieges and famine over a century of intermittent warfare without totals, and the scholarly dispute is about the character of the change rather than a measurable death toll.
baselineWhat: The population of Byzantine Anatolia on the eve of Manzikert
baselineNote: There is no census. McEvedy and Jones put Asia Minor at roughly 7 million around 1000 CE, and Russell's estimates for the Byzantine provinces are of the same order; some Byzantinists argue for 8-10 million at the eleventh-century peak. The incoming Turkmen population is generally reckoned much smaller, in the low hundreds of thousands, so the demographic change in the following centuries was mainly conversion and language shift rather than replacement.

title: The Rhineland Massacres of 1096
actors: Bands accompanying the People's Crusade, chiefly under Count Emicho of Flonheim, attacked the Jewish communities of the Rhineland and the Danube while local bishops and burghers variously sheltered or abandoned them
peopleRange: No figure for survivors displaced. Several of the affected communities — Worms, Mainz, Cologne — were effectively destroyed, and survivors fled or were forcibly baptised, with Emperor Henry IV subsequently permitting the forcibly converted to return to Judaism. The evidence is three Hebrew chronicles (the Mainz Anonymous, Solomon bar Simson and Eliezer bar Nathan), Latin annals, and the memorial books (Memorbücher) listing the dead by name, which give the episode an unusually firm documentary base for its date.

flows.label: Jewish refugees from Mainz → Cologne and its surrounding villages

summary: In the spring and early summer of 1096, as contingents assembled for the First Crusade, armed bands attacked Jewish communities along the Rhine and into the Danube valley — Speyer, Worms, Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Metz, Regensburg and Prague — demanding conversion and killing those who refused. The Hebrew chronicles composed within a generation, together with Latin annals and the German memorial books, record the killings community by community and describe many Jews killing themselves and their families rather than accept baptism. Robert Chazan's reconstruction from these sources puts the total dead in the low thousands rather than the higher figures sometimes quoted. Church and imperial authorities did not sanction the attacks — several bishops attempted to shelter Jews and Henry IV afterwards allowed forced converts to revert — but no perpetrators were punished. The events are treated in modern scholarship as a decisive turning point in the position of Jews in Latin Christendom.
contested: The precise death toll is uncertain: the Hebrew chronicles are near-contemporary and detailed but written as martyrological narratives, and modern estimates range from about two thousand to eight thousand.

sources.title: Genocidal Massacres of Jews in Medieval Western Europe, 1096–1392 (The Cambridge World History of Genocide, vol. 1)
The Rhineland Massacres of Jews in the First Crusade: Memories Medieval and Modern (Medieval Concepts of the Past, CUP)
Fordham Medieval Sourcebook: Emico and the Slaughter of the Rhineland Jews

deathsNote: The range spans the estimates derived from the Hebrew chronicles and the memorial books; Robert Chazan's reconstruction sits near the lower end, at roughly three thousand. The uncertainty comes from the martyrological form of the Hebrew sources and from incomplete coverage of the smaller communities.
violenceNote: The killings, the plundering and burning of Jewish quarters and the destruction of synagogues and Torah scrolls are documented in the Hebrew chronicles of 1096, in Latin annals and in the German memorial books.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of the Rhineland and Danube communities attacked in 1096
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The only near-contemporary evidence is the Hebrew crusade chronicles and the Christian annals, which give community sizes for Mainz, Worms, Speyer and Cologne that historians read as symbolic as often as literal. Estimates of Ashkenazi Jewry in the German lands at the end of the eleventh century range from a few thousand to more than twenty thousand, and the reported death tolls (roughly 2,000 to 12,000) span nearly the same range, so no ratio can be constructed.

title: The Crusader Capture of Jerusalem and the Massacre of 1099
actors: The armies of the First Crusade stormed Fatimid-held Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and killed or enslaved much of its Muslim and Jewish population before establishing a Latin kingdom
peopleRange: No count. Survivors were ransomed or expelled: a letter from the Cairo Geniza records Jewish captives ransomed by the Egyptian Jewish community, and Arabic sources record the garrison and some inhabitants leaving under terms. Jerusalem's population before the siege is usually estimated at twenty to thirty thousand, and the city was substantially emptied of Muslims and Jews, who were subsequently barred from residence in the Latin kingdom's capital. The evidence is Latin crusade narratives, Arabic chronicles written later, and the Geniza letters, which are contemporary documentary material.
territoryDesc: Jerusalem and its hinterland became the capital of the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, which held the city until 1187.

flows.label: Ransomed and expelled survivors → Egypt
Muslim refugees → Damascus

summary: The First Crusade took Jerusalem by storm on 15 July 1099 after a five-week siege, and the killing that followed was extensive enough to shock even sympathetic Latin writers: the Gesta Francorum and Raymond of Aguilers describe streets filled with the dead, and Ibn al-Athir, writing much later, gives seventy thousand killed in the al-Aqsa mosque alone. Jews who had taken refuge in a synagogue were burned there according to Ibn al-Qalanisi. Benjamin Kedar's study of the whole source tradition shows the highest Arabic figures exceed any plausible estimate of the city's population, and Geniza letters from Egypt document Jewish captives being ransomed and Christian sources record survivors expelled or ransomed rather than killed to a man. The massacre was nonetheless a large-scale killing of a civilian population and became a fixed point in both Latin triumphalism and later Muslim memory of the crusades.
contested: Casualty figures range from Ibn al-Athir's 70,000 to modern estimates an order of magnitude lower; Benjamin Kedar's source-critical study shows the highest figures exceed the city's likely population and that a substantial number of inhabitants were ransomed or expelled rather than killed.

sources.title: Crusaders and Mass Killing at Jerusalem in 1099 (The Cambridge World History of Genocide, vol. 1)
Britannica: Crusades — The siege of Jerusalem
World History Encyclopedia: The Capture of Jerusalem, 1099 CE

deathsNote: The low end reflects modern minimalist readings constrained by the city's likely population and by evidence of ransoming; the high end approaches the whole non-Frankish population of the city. Ibn al-Athir's 70,000 and the Latin accounts of blood to the knees are rhetorical and are treated as such by Kedar and subsequent scholarship.
violenceNote: The killing of the civilian population and the burning of a synagogue with those sheltering in it are documented in the Gesta Francorum, Raymond of Aguilers, Ibn al-Qalanisi and Ibn al-Athir, and assessed critically by Benjamin Kedar.
baselineWhat: The population of Jerusalem at the time of the Crusader siege
baselineNote: Estimates for Fatimid Jerusalem in 1099 run from about 20,000 to 30,000, swollen by refugees from the surrounding countryside who had taken shelter behind the walls. Crusader letters claim tens of thousands killed and later Arabic sources up to 70,000; Benjamin Kedar's review of the evidence, which draws on a Cairo Geniza letter about the ransom of captives, suggests a far lower toll of some thousands, with many survivors enslaved or ransomed and the rest expelled.

title: The Jingkang Incident and the Southward Flight of the Song
actors: Jurchen Jin armies conquered northern China, sacked the Song capital and deported the imperial house, driving a mass migration south
peopleRange: Song and Jin sources record the deportation of the captured court in convoys said to number some 14,000-15,000 people including the emperors Huizong and Qinzong, consorts, officials and craftsmen. The far larger movement is the flight of northern civilians across the Huai and Yangzi, which historians reconstruct from the Song household registers: registered households in the southern circuits rose sharply between the 1100s and the 1160s while the north was lost to the Jin. Estimates of the migration run from about one million to five million or more, and rest on register interpolation rather than any direct count; households were units of taxation, not people, so conversions are contested.
territoryDesc: The Jin dynasty took all of north China to the Huai River; the Song court re-established itself at Lin'an (Hangzhou) as the Southern Song

flows.label: Song imperial house and court deported to Manchuria
Northern refugees to the Yangzi delta and Lin'an

summary: In 1126-27 Jurchen armies of the Jin dynasty besieged and sacked Bianjing (Kaifeng), capital of the Northern Song, and carried the retired emperor Huizong, the reigning emperor Qinzong, the imperial clan, court women, officials and skilled artisans north into captivity in what Chinese historiography calls the Jingkang Incident. Song accounts describe the seizure of thousands of women of the palace and elite households and their distribution among Jin commanders; these accounts are partly recorded in captivity narratives whose detail is disputed. A surviving prince re-founded the dynasty at Lin'an as the Southern Song, and continued warfare until the treaty of 1142 fixed the frontier at the Huai River. Behind the court came one of the largest population movements in Chinese history, as northern gentry, officials and peasants crossed into the Yangzi valley and the south-east; historians reconstruct this from Song household registers rather than from any contemporary count, and estimates range from about one million to five million. The migration permanently shifted China's demographic and economic centre of gravity to the south.
contested: The scale of the southward migration depends on how Song household registers are converted into people, and estimates differ by a factor of several.

sources.title: Jingkang incident
Jin-Song wars
Southern Song dynasty

deathsNote: No defensible range exists. The sieges of Kaifeng, the campaigns of 1126-42 and the accompanying famine and flight killed large numbers, but Song and Jin sources give no usable totals and the census discontinuity between the two states makes demographic inference unreliable.
violenceNote: Song captivity narratives and official histories record the seizure and sexual enslavement of palace and elite women, the removal of artisans as forced labour, and starvation during the sieges of Kaifeng.
baselineWhat: The population of the Northern Song empire on the eve of the Jurchen conquest
baselineNote: The Song household registers of 1102-1110 recorded about 20 million households; because they counted taxable adult males unevenly, historical demographers convert this to a total population near 100 million, with estimates ranging from 90 to 120 million. Roughly half lived in the northern provinces the Jin took.
shareCaveat: The five million figure is an estimate of net southward migration reconstructed from later register shifts, not a count of individuals moved, and the flight ran over two decades.

title: Almohad Forced Conversion and the Flight of Andalusi Jews and Christians
actors: The Almohad caliphate abolished dhimmi status across the Maghrib and al-Andalus, requiring conversion to Islam, and Jewish and Christian communities converted, fled or were destroyed
peopleRange: No figures. The evidence is Jewish responsa and letters, Maimonides' Epistle on Forced Conversion and his family's own flight from Córdoba through Fez to Egypt, Hebrew chronicles such as Abraham ibn Daud's and the elegies of Abraham ibn Ezra listing destroyed communities, and Arabic and Latin sources on the collapse of the Mozarabic church. All are qualitative. Communities named as destroyed or dispersed include Córdoba, Lucena, Seville, Fez, Marrakesh, Tlemcen and Sijilmasa, but no source counts the people involved.

flows.label: Andalusi Jews → the Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia
Maghribi Jews → Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean

summary: The Almohad movement that took Marrakesh in 1147 and crossed into al-Andalus rejected the dhimma arrangement under which Jews and Christians had lived under Muslim rule, and required conversion to Islam. Jewish communities across the Maghrib and al-Andalus responded by outward conversion, by flight to the Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia, to Provence or to Egypt, or were destroyed; the Mozarabic Christian communities of al-Andalus, already reduced, effectively disappeared, with many deported to North Africa. Maimonides' family left Córdoba and eventually settled in Fustat, and his Epistle on Forced Conversion is addressed to Jews living outwardly as Muslims. The episode ended the long period in which al-Andalus sustained large protected non-Muslim communities. Numbers cannot be recovered; recent scholarship, including the Brill volume on forced conversion, has also debated how systematic and how sustained Almohad enforcement actually was, as against its representation in later Jewish memory.
contested: How systematically the Almohads enforced conversion, and over how long, is debated: recent scholarship questions whether the persecution was as uniform as later Jewish and Christian sources present it, while accepting that communities were destroyed and dispersed.

sources.title: Again on Forced Conversion in the Almohad Period (Forced Conversion in Christianity, Judaism and Islam, Brill)
The Jews of Muslim Spain (The Cambridge History of Judaism, vol. 5)
Britannica: Almohads

deathsNote: No usable figures. Hebrew sources record killings at particular places, notably in the initial Almohad advance across the Maghrib, but give no totals, and the dominant outcomes recorded are conversion and flight rather than mass killing.
violenceNote: The suppression of synagogues and churches and the abolition of protected status for Jews and Christians is documented in Jewish responsa and chronicles, in Maimonides' Epistle on Forced Conversion, and in the Brill scholarship cited.
baselineWhat: The Jewish and Christian populations of al-Andalus and the Maghrib under Almohad rule
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Twelfth-century al-Andalus and the Maghrib have no surviving population registers, and reconstructions of Andalusi Jewry rest on the Cairo Geniza correspondence, communal responsa and later expulsion-era data — sources that document communities without sizing them. Published estimates differ by an order of magnitude, and the Mozarab Christian population is even less well attested.

title: The Baltic Crusades: Conquest of Livonia and Prussia
actors: The Sword Brothers and then the Teutonic Order, with crusader contingents and German and Polish settlers, conquered the pagan Livs, Estonians, Latgalians and Old Prussians and built a monastic state over their lands
peopleRange: No reliable figures. The Old Prussian population before the conquest is estimated by modern historians at roughly one to two hundred thousand, extrapolated from later settlement patterns, Order rent rolls and colonisation charters, and those estimates are contested. Populations were displaced by two long revolts (1242–1249 and 1260–1274) and their suppression, by the Order's policy of resettling submitted groups away from their territories, and by the arrival of German and Polish colonists in the towns and countryside. No counts survive.
territoryDesc: Livonia and Prussia — approximately modern Latvia, Estonia, the Kaliningrad oblast and parts of northern Poland — were organised as the monastic state of the Teutonic Order, with German towns founded under Kulm and Lübeck law and the land distributed to Order officials, bishops and settlers.

flows.label: German settlers → Prussia
Submitted Prussian groups resettled by the Order

summary: From the mission and crusade in Livonia around 1200 to the final suppression of Prussian resistance in the 1270s and 1280s, the Baltic crusades conquered the last pagan peoples of the southern and eastern Baltic and replaced their societies with a monastic state. Henry of Livonia's chronicle and Peter of Dusburg's Chronicon terrae Prussiae, both written from inside the enterprise, record campaigns of devastation, the killing and enslavement of populations, forced baptism and the razing of strongholds; the Great Prussian Uprising of 1260–1274 and its suppression were especially destructive. Conquest was followed by systematic colonisation: German and Polish settlers were brought in under charter, towns were founded, and the surviving Prussian population was reduced to a subordinate rural stratum whose language died out by about 1700. No population figures survive from the conquest itself, and modern estimates of the pre-conquest Prussian population and of losses are extrapolations from later records.
contested: Pre-conquest population estimates and the scale of losses are extrapolations from later Order records and are disputed; nationalist historiography in Poland, Germany and the Baltic states has read the same evidence very differently.

sources.title: Britannica: Northern Crusades
World History Encyclopedia: Northern Crusades
Britannica: Teutonic Order

deathsNote: No usable figures. Peter of Dusburg and Henry of Livonia describe killings, enslavement and the devastation of whole districts across nearly a century of intermittent war, but neither they nor any later source supplies totals, and no modern reconstruction attempts one.
violenceNote: Killings, the burning of settlements and the enslavement of captives are documented by Henry of Livonia's chronicle and Peter of Dusburg's Chronicon terrae Prussiae, both written from within the crusading enterprise.
baselineWhat: The pagan Baltic and Finnic population of Livonia and Prussia at the start of the crusades
baselineNote: No records exist for the pre-conquest period; estimates come from archaeological settlement surveys and back-projection from the Order's own later land registers. Henryk Lowmianski's reconstruction gives Prussia roughly 170,000-200,000, and the Livonian lands - Estonians, Latgalians, Livs, Curonians, Semigallians - are put at 250,000-350,000. The full plausible range is about 350,000-600,000.
shareCaveat: The conquest ran for nearly a century against a denominator that is a single-date estimate with a very wide margin.

title: The Fourth Crusade and the Sack of Constantinople
actors: A Venetian-transported crusade army diverted to Constantinople, stormed and sacked the city in April 1204, and partitioned the Byzantine empire among Latin rulers
peopleRange: No count. Constantinople's population, plausibly several hundred thousand before 1204, fell steeply as inhabitants fled the sack and the subsequent Latin occupation; Byzantine elites and clergy regrouped at Nicaea, Trebizond and Epirus, where successor states formed. Niketas Choniates, himself a refugee, describes the flight of the population in detail but gives no numbers, and no register survives.
territoryDesc: The Byzantine empire was dismembered under the Partitio Romaniae: a Latin Empire at Constantinople, a Venetian maritime domain, and crusader lordships in Greece, with Byzantine successor states at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond.

flows.label: Byzantine refugees → Nicaea
Byzantine refugees → Trebizond
Byzantine refugees → Epirus

summary: The Fourth Crusade, unable to pay Venice for its transport, was diverted first to Zara and then to Constantinople, where after intervening in a Byzantine succession dispute it stormed the city on 12–13 April 1204 and sacked it for three days. Niketas Choniates, an eyewitness, records systematic plunder, killings, rape and the desecration of churches including Hagia Sophia; Villehardouin, on the crusader side, records the scale of the booty without demur. Britannica's summary gives approximate campaign losses of about 20,000 on the crusader side and 30,000 on the Byzantine, with civilian deaths unknown; no contemporary source provides a civilian toll. The empire was partitioned among the victors, its relics and treasures dispersed to Latin churches, and although Byzantine rule was restored at Constantinople in 1261 the state never recovered its former reach. Pope John Paul II expressed regret for the sack in 2001; that is a statement of contrition, not a formal legal finding.
contested: No reliable civilian death toll exists for the sack; the casualty figures in circulation derive from campaign summaries rather than from any contemporary count.

sources.title: Britannica: Sack of Constantinople (1204)
World History Encyclopedia: 1204 — The Sack of Constantinople
The Byzantine empire and the Balkans, 1204–1453 (The Cambridge History of War)

deathsNote: No defensible figures for civilian deaths. Contemporary accounts describe killing during three days of sack without totals; the figures of roughly 20,000 crusader and 30,000 Byzantine losses that appear in reference summaries refer to the campaign and are not derived from a count of the sack itself.
violenceNote: Niketas Choniates, an eyewitness, documents rape, the plundering and burning of houses and the desecration and stripping of churches including Hagia Sophia; Villehardouin corroborates the scale of the plunder.
baselineWhat: The population of Constantinople on the eve of the Fourth Crusade's assault
baselineNote: Reconstructed from the walled area, grain supply and pilgrim descriptions rather than any register. Magdalino and others put the twelfth-century city at roughly 400,000, the largest in Christendom; more conservative estimates run to 150,000-250,000, and the city never recovered its size after 1204.

title: The Albigensian Crusade and the Conquest of Languedoc
actors: A papally proclaimed crusade of northern French lords under Simon de Montfort, later the French crown, made war on the counts of Toulouse and their subjects to suppress Cathar heresy, ending with the annexation of Languedoc
peopleRange: No figures. Populations fled sacked towns, dispossessed southern nobles (the faidits) were driven into exile or into resistance, and surviving Cathar believers emigrated to Lombardy and Catalonia; the numbers are not recorded. The evidence is the crusade's own narrative sources — Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay for the crusaders, the Canso de la Crosada from the southern side — together with the later inquisition registers, which document communities of believers in detail but were compiled after the war.
territoryDesc: The county of Toulouse and much of Languedoc passed under the control of the French crown by the Treaty of Paris of 1229, ending the region's political autonomy.

flows.label: Cathar believers and exiles → Lombardy
Exiles → Catalonia

summary: Innocent III proclaimed a crusade against heresy in Languedoc in 1208, and the twenty-year war that followed transferred the region to northern control. Its notorious moment came at Béziers on 22 July 1209, when the town was stormed and its population killed; the papal legate Arnaud Amalric reported to Rome that nearly twenty thousand had been killed regardless of rank, age or sex, a figure that exceeds most estimates of the town's population and that Britannica notes alongside the caution that chroniclers' figures from this period are often exaggerated. Mass burnings of identified heretics followed at Minerve in 1210 and Lavaur in 1211. The war ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1229, which brought Languedoc under the French crown, and was followed by the papal inquisition established in the 1230s. Mark Gregory Pegg has argued the crusade should be read as genocidal in intent; other specialists, including R. I. Moore, dispute that reading and question whether an organised 'Cathar church' existed as the crusaders described it.
contested: Both the death tolls and the character of the war are disputed: Arnaud Amalric's 20,000 at Béziers is widely regarded as inflated, campaign-wide totals of hundreds of thousands to a million that circulate in popular accounts have no evidentiary basis, and scholars including Mark Gregory Pegg and R. I. Moore disagree over whether the crusade was genocidal and whether an organised Cathar church existed at all.

sources.title: Britannica: Massacre at Béziers (1209)
Britannica: Albigensian Crusade
The Albigensian Crusade and the Early Inquisitions into Heretical Depravity, 1208–1246 (The Cambridge World History of Genocide, vol. 1)
World History Encyclopedia: Albigensian Crusade

deathsNote: This range applies to the sack of Béziers alone, the one episode with a contemporary figure: Arnaud Amalric's letter to Innocent III claims nearly 20,000, while modern estimates of the town's population put the real toll substantially lower. No defensible total exists for the twenty-year war; figures of hundreds of thousands or a million that circulate in popular accounts rest on nothing.
violenceNote: The sack of Béziers, the mass burnings of identified heretics at Minerve and Lavaur and the destruction of towns are documented by Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, the Canso de la Crosada and Arnaud Amalric's own dispatch.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Thirteenth-century Languedoc was never enumerated, and estimates for its population are back-projections from later hearth-tax records; the Cathar community itself is known mainly from inquisition registers, which record a few thousand perfecti and an unknown penumbra of believers. Chronicle figures for the crusade's massacres, such as the 15,000-20,000 said to have died at Béziers, are literary rather than counted.

title: The Mongol Conquest of China and the Census Collapse
actors: Mongol armies under Chinggis Khan, Ögedei and Khubilai destroyed the Jin empire in northern China and then the Southern Song, killing, deporting artisans and reordering the population under the Yuan dynasty
peopleRange: No count. Documented movements include the deportation of craftsmen and skilled workers northward, the enrolment of captured populations as bondservants of Mongol nobles, and large-scale flight from north China to the Song south during the Jin wars. The evidence is the Jin and Yuan dynastic histories and the surviving census returns, which are tax registers of households the state could reach rather than counts of people.
territoryDesc: All of China was brought under a single non-Chinese dynasty for the first time: the Jin empire fell in 1234, the Southern Song in 1279, and the Yuan ruled from Dadu (Beijing).

flows.label: Flight from north China → the Southern Song
Deported artisans → Mongolia and the Mongol heartland

summary: The Mongol wars in China ran for nearly seventy years, from the first attacks on the Jin in 1211 to the destruction of the Southern Song in 1279. The demographic evidence is a registration record with an enormous gap: the Jin census of 1207 recorded roughly 7.6 million households and about 45 million people in north China, while the Mongol registration of north China in the 1230s recorded under two million households. That collapse has often been read directly as tens of millions of deaths. Specialists are more cautious. Yuan registration was far less thorough than Jin registration, much of the population escaped enrolment or was assigned to Mongol nobles as bondservants and so left the ordinary registers, and there was heavy flight to the south. The Cambridge Economic History of China and the demographic work of Ho Ping-ti treat much of the apparent loss as administrative. Real mortality in the north from warfare, famine and epidemic was nonetheless severe, and the conquest of the Song, achieved partly by negotiated surrenders, was less destructive than the northern wars.
contested: Whether the fall from roughly 45 million registered people in Jin north China to a fraction of that under early Mongol registration represents deaths or the breakdown and narrower scope of household registration is the central dispute; popular figures of 30 to 60 million deaths for the Mongol conquest of China rest on the raw arithmetic and are not accepted by specialists.

sources.title: Population Change (The Cambridge Economic History of China)
Britannica: China — The Yuan, or Mongol, dynasty
Genocide, Extermination and Mass Killing in Chinese History (The Cambridge World History of Genocide, vol. 1)

deathsNote: The upper figure is the commonly quoted death toll derived from subtracting Mongol-era registration totals from Jin-era ones. Specialists including Ho Ping-ti and the contributors to the Cambridge Economic History of China attribute a large part of that gap to changes in registration coverage, flight and the removal of populations into noble households. Real excess mortality in north China was heavy but has never been separately reconstructed, so no defensible lower bound exists.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The killing of urban populations at Zhongdu and elsewhere, the deportation and assignment of artisans and captives, and the devastation of the north China countryside are documented in the Jin and Yuan dynastic histories.
baselineWhat: The registered population of Jin northern China and Southern Song China on the eve of the Mongol conquest
baselineNote: Chinese household registers are the best pre-modern demographic series anywhere: the Jin census of 1207 recorded about 8.4 million households and 53.5 million people, and Southern Song registers imply a comparable or larger population, for a combined total usually given as 100-120 million around 1200. The Yuan census of 1290 counted about 58.8 million. Historians divide over how much of that fall represents deaths and how much represents the collapse of registration, tax flight and the loss of southern records.

title: The Mongol Conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire
actors: Chinggis Khan's armies destroyed the Khwarazmian empire, sacked Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv, Nishapur, Herat and Urgench, killed or deported their populations and drove captive levies ahead of their assaults
peopleRange: No count. The documented movements are of craftsmen and skilled workers deported eastward to Mongolia and to Mongol-controlled cities — a systematic practice recorded by Juvayni and by Chinese sources — and of refugees into India, Iran and Anatolia, among them Turkic groups whose migration underlies the later Anatolian principalities. The Persian chroniclers Juvayni, Rashid al-Din and Ibn al-Athir give enormous figures for the dead but none for the displaced.
territoryDesc: Transoxiana, Khwarazm and Khurasan were absorbed into the Mongol empire; the irrigation systems of the Merv oasis and Khwarazm were wrecked and several major cities never regained their former size.

flows.label: Deported craftsmen → Mongolia and the Mongol heartland
Refugees → Afghanistan and northern India

summary: Chinggis Khan's invasion of the Khwarazmian empire in 1219, provoked by the killing of a Mongol trade mission, destroyed the largest Islamic state of its day in two years. Bukhara and Samarkand fell in 1220, Urgench, Merv, Nishapur and Herat in 1221; where cities resisted, the Mongols expelled the population, separated out artisans for deportation, and killed the remainder. The Persian chroniclers give figures that dominate the event's reputation: Juvayni reports 1.3 million killed at Merv and Ibn al-Athir gives comparable totals elsewhere, with claims for Nishapur and Herat above a million. Modern specialists reject these. John Masson Smith's work on the logistics of Mongol siege warfare, and David Morgan's assessment of the Persian sources, argue that the cities concerned could not have contained such populations and that the numbers function as expressions of catastrophe rather than counts. That the campaign killed on a very large scale, wrecked the irrigation agriculture of Khurasan and Khwarazm, and permanently reduced several great cities is not disputed; the arithmetic is.
contested: The chroniclers' city-by-city death tolls — 1.3 million at Merv, comparable figures for Nishapur and Herat — are rejected by modern specialists including John Masson Smith and David Morgan as exceeding any plausible population; how far the campaign caused long-term demographic decline in Iran, as against destruction that was later made good, is also debated.

sources.title: Britannica: Iran — The Mongol invasion
Mongol Invasions of Khurasan (A History of Herat, chapter 1)
Mongol Genocides of the Thirteenth Century (The Cambridge World History of Genocide, vol. 1)

deathsNote: The range reflects modern reassessments rather than the chronicles. Juvayni, Rashid al-Din and Ibn al-Athir give city totals that sum to well over five million and, in some readings, above ten; John Masson Smith's analysis of siege logistics and city sizes and David Morgan's source criticism treat these as impossible, leaving a very large but unquantified toll of which the range here is a conservative modern bracket.
violenceNote: The killing of urban populations, the selection and deportation of artisans, the use of captive levies (hashar) in assaults and the destruction of cities and irrigation works are documented by Juvayni, Rashid al-Din and Ibn al-Athir and assessed in the modern scholarship cited.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Estimates of the Khwarazmian empire's population range from under 5 million to over 10 million depending on how much of Iran, Khurasan and Transoxiana is counted and at what date, and the empire itself had existed in its full extent for barely a decade. The medieval chroniclers' city figures - Juvayni's 1.3 million dead at Merv, comparable numbers for Nishapur and Urgench - are rejected as arithmetically impossible by modern scholars, and no fiscal register survives to replace them.
