title: Deportation of Sicily's Muslims to Lucera and the Colony's Destruction
actors: Emperor Frederick II deported the remaining Muslim population of western Sicily to a segregated colony at Lucera in Apulia; in 1300 the Angevin king Charles II destroyed the colony and enslaved or dispersed its inhabitants
peopleRange: Estimates of the Lucera colony's size cluster between about 15,000 and 20,000, with some scholars suggesting that up to 60,000 people were moved in total across the two decades of transfers. The figures come from Hohenstaufen and Angevin fiscal and administrative records — tax assessments, grain levies and the accounts of the 1300 dispersal — and from chronicles; they are administrative estimates rather than a census, and modern historians treat the higher totals with caution.
territoryDesc: Muslim landholding in western Sicily was extinguished and the lands redistributed; the site of Lucera in Apulia became a royal colony, and after 1300 was repopulated with Christians and renamed Civitas Sanctae Mariae.

flows.label: Muslims of western Sicily → Lucera, Apulia

summary: After suppressing a long Muslim revolt in the mountains of western Sicily, Frederick II from 1223 deported the island's remaining Muslim population to Lucera in Apulia on the mainland, where they were settled as a royal colony — taxed directly by the crown, permitted their mosques and law, and supplying the emperor with archers and craftsmen. The transfer removed Islam from Sicily after three and a half centuries and created an isolated Muslim community of perhaps fifteen to twenty thousand in the middle of Latin Christendom. The colony survived Frederick's death and the Angevin conquest until 1300, when Charles II, under pressure from the papacy and needing money, had it destroyed: the inhabitants were seized, enslaved and sold, some killed, the mosques demolished, and the town repopulated with Christians. Julie Taylor's study of the community is the standard modern account. The episode is unusually well documented for a medieval forced transfer because the crown taxed the colony directly and left records.
contested: The size of the colony is uncertain, with estimates ranging from about 15,000 to as many as 60,000 moved in total, and the number killed as opposed to enslaved in the 1300 destruction is not recoverable.

sources.title: Medievalists.net: The Muslim Colony of Luceria Sarracenorum (Lucera)
The kingdom of Sicily under the Hohenstaufen and Angevins (The New Cambridge Medieval History)
Centro Primo Levi: The Last Muslims in Italy

deathsNote: No reliable toll. The 1300 destruction of Lucera involved killings as well as mass enslavement and sale, but the Angevin records document the sale of captives rather than a count of the dead.
violenceNote: The enslavement and sale of the colony's inhabitants and the demolition of its mosques in 1300 are documented in Angevin administrative records and analysed in Julie Taylor's study of the community.
baselineWhat: The Muslim community of Sicily deported to Lucera, which is also the only population for this event that was ever counted
baselineNote: No independent count survives of the Muslims remaining in western Sicily when Frederick II began the deportations in 1223. Estimates of the Lucera colony itself range from about 15,000-20,000, the figure preferred by Abulafia, to as many as 60,000 in older literature; when Charles II destroyed the colony in 1300 its inhabitants were sold into slavery or dispersed. Sicily's Muslim population had been several hundred thousand under Islamic rule and had already collapsed through conversion, emigration and the rebellions of the 1190s-1220s.

baselineSources.title: History of Islam in southern Italy — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: Baseline and affected figure are the same estimate seen from two sides, so the ratio is near 100 per cent by construction; what it records is that the community was moved and then destroyed in its entirety.

title: The Mongol Invasions of Korea and the Deportation of Captives
actors: Mongol armies invaded Goryeo Korea repeatedly over three decades, taking captives on a large scale, while the Goryeo court sheltered on Ganghwa Island until it submitted in 1259
peopleRange: The Goryeosa, the official dynastic history compiled in the fifteenth century from Goryeo records, states that in the campaign of 1254 alone 206,800 people were taken captive and that the number of the slain could not be counted. That is a court-recorded administrative figure rather than a chronicler's rhetorical number, which makes it unusually specific for the period, but it covers one campaign of six and cannot be extended to the whole war; totals for the other campaigns are not given.
territoryDesc: Goryeo survived as a kingdom but became a subordinate son-in-law state of the Yuan, with northern territories detached into Mongol commanderies and the court obliged to intermarry with the imperial house.

flows.label: Goryeo court and population → refuge on Ganghwa Island
Korean captives → Liaodong and the Mongol territories

summary: Between 1231 and 1259 Mongol armies invaded Korea six times. The Goryeo military government moved the court to Ganghwa Island, out of reach of an army without a navy, and left the mainland population to absorb the invasions. The Goryeosa records that the 1254 campaign alone carried off 206,800 captives, and describes the burning of settlements and the killing of those who resisted; the nine-storey wooden pagoda of Hwangnyongsa, one of the great monuments of Korean Buddhism, was destroyed in the invasion of 1238. Goryeo submitted in 1259 and was drawn into the Yuan orbit as a subordinate kingdom whose rulers married Mongol princesses, and was subsequently made to build and man the fleets for the failed invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281. The captive figure is one of the few precise numbers in any thirteenth-century account of Mongol warfare, though it covers a single campaign.
contested: The 206,800 captive figure comes from the Goryeosa, compiled in the fifteenth century from earlier records; it is unusually specific but rests on a single source, and no comparable figures survive for the other five campaigns.

sources.title: Koryŏ in the Mongol Empire (The Cambridge History of the Mongol Empire)
World History Encyclopedia: Goryeo

deathsNote: No usable figures. The Goryeosa states for 1254 that those killed 'could not be counted', which is an admission of ignorance rather than an estimate, and gives no totals for the other campaigns.
violenceNote: The taking of captives, the burning of settlements and the destruction of the Hwangnyongsa pagoda in 1238 are recorded in the Goryeosa and in the Korean monastic record.
baselineWhat: The population of Goryeo Korea at the time of the first Mongol invasion
baselineNote: Goryeo kept household registers but the totals do not survive intact. Korean historical demographers reconstruct a thirteenth-century population of roughly 3 million, with estimates ranging from about 2.5 to 5 million depending on assumptions about household size and the large unregistered slave and temple population.
shareCaveat: The 206,800 figure comes from a single Goryeosa entry for captives taken in the campaign of 1254 and is treated by many historians as a chronicler's round number rather than a count; it is not a total for all three decades.

title: Reconquista Conquests and the Displacement of Andalusi Muslims
actors: The crowns of Castile and Aragon conquered Córdoba, Valencia, Seville and Murcia, expelled or subordinated their Muslim inhabitants, and redistributed the land to Christian settlers under repartimiento
peopleRange: No reliable totals. James I's own chronicle, the Llibre dels fets, states that fifty thousand Muslims left the city of Valencia under the surrender terms of 1238; Castilian accounts of the surrender of Seville in 1248 speak of the city being emptied of its Muslim population, with chroniclers' figures running from one hundred thousand to three hundred thousand. All are royal or court numbers produced to magnify the achievement. The firmest evidence is the repartimiento registers — the land-distribution books compiled for Valencia, Seville and Murcia — which record what was redistributed to whom rather than how many left.
territoryDesc: The Guadalquivir valley, the kingdom of Valencia and Murcia were annexed to Castile and Aragon between 1236 and 1266, leaving Granada as the sole Muslim polity in Iberia.

flows.label: Muslims of Valencia and Murcia → the emirate of Granada
Muslims of Seville → North Africa

summary: The Christian conquests of the mid-thirteenth century — Córdoba in 1236, Valencia in 1238, Seville in 1248, Murcia definitively in 1266 — transferred the greater part of al-Andalus to Castile and Aragon and were followed by systematic redistribution of urban property and farmland to Christian settlers recorded in the repartimiento books. Muslim populations were treated differently from place to place: some, particularly rural communities in Valencia and Aragon, remained as Mudéjars under charters guaranteeing religion and custom; others were expelled outright, as at Seville, or left under surrender terms, as James I records for the city of Valencia. The Mudéjar revolt of 1264–1266 in Andalusia and Murcia was followed by further expulsions and a second wave of Christian settlement. The result over two generations was a substantial movement of Muslims to Granada and North Africa and a repopulation of the conquered south by settlers from the north. The 1492 conquest of Granada and the expulsion of Spain's Jews in the same year fall outside this entry's window.
contested: The numbers of Muslims who left are known only from royal chronicles written to celebrate the conquests; the repartimiento registers show what was redistributed but not how many people departed, and modern estimates vary widely.

sources.title: Britannica: Reconquista
Troubled Times: The Aftermath of the Mudejar Revolt, Granadan Invasions and Mudejar Emigration, 1276 to 1327 (A Forgotten Community, Brill)
Britannica: Valencia, medieval kingdom of Spain

deathsNote: No significant aggregate death toll is documented. Most of the major cities surrendered on terms rather than being stormed, and the recorded outcome was expulsion, emigration and subordination rather than mass killing; the suppression of the 1264–1266 revolt involved fighting for which no totals survive.
baselineWhat: No defensible aggregate exists for the Muslim population of the territories conquered between 1236 and 1300
baselineNote: Component estimates exist but do not add to a reliable total: Guichard and Burns put the kingdom of Valencia at roughly 200,000 Muslims at its conquest, and the repartimiento land registers of Seville, Cordoba and Murcia record settler allotments rather than the displaced population. Estimates for the Guadalquivir valley vary several-fold, and the sequence of expulsions after the 1264 Mudejar revolt is documented qualitatively rather than numerically.

title: The Mongol Invasion of the Rus Principalities
actors: Batu's Mongol army destroyed the Rus principalities city by city, sacked Kyiv in December 1240, and imposed tributary rule through the Golden Horde
peopleRange: No figures. Populations fled the destroyed towns of the Vladimir-Suzdal and Kyivan lands, and the centre of gravity of Rus settlement shifted north-east and west; skilled craftsmen were deported to Horde centres, a practice reflected in the disappearance of certain enamel and filigree techniques from Rus archaeology for generations. The evidence is the Rus chronicles, the eyewitness report of the papal envoy John of Plano Carpini, who travelled through Kyiv in 1246, and excavation of destruction layers and mass graves at Ryazan, Kyiv and elsewhere.
territoryDesc: The Rus principalities became tributaries of the Golden Horde, their princes required to obtain patents of rule from the khan; the arrangement lasted formally until 1480.

flows.label: Flight from the sacked towns of the north-east
Refugees from Kyiv → Galicia-Volhynia

summary: Batu's campaign of 1237–1241 destroyed the political order of the Rus lands. Ryazan fell in December 1237, Vladimir in February 1238, and Kyiv in December 1240 after a short siege; the chronicles record the storming and burning of dozens of towns. John of Plano Carpini, passing through in 1246, described bones and skulls lying in the fields and reported that Kyiv had been reduced to some two hundred houses whose inhabitants lived in servitude. Archaeology corroborates destruction layers and mass graves at several sites, and a marked decline in urban crafts. The princes who survived became tributaries of the Golden Horde, travelling to Sarai for patents to rule and collecting tribute for the khan. No population or casualty figures exist: the chronicles record which towns were taken and burned, not how many died, and Carpini's observations are impressionistic. Modern Russian, Ukrainian and Mongolist historiographies differ sharply over how devastating and how lasting the effects were.
contested: The long-term demographic and economic impact of the invasion is disputed between historiographies that treat it as a catastrophe setting the region back for centuries and those that emphasise recovery, continuity and the Horde's role as a functioning imperial overlord.

sources.title: Britannica: Batu
World History Encyclopedia: The Mongol Invasion of Europe
The Mongols and Europe (The Cambridge History of the Mongol Empire)

deathsNote: No defensible figures. The Rus chronicles record the destruction of named towns without counting the dead; Carpini's account of bones in the fields is descriptive; excavated mass graves establish that killing was extensive at particular sites but support no aggregate.
violenceNote: The storming and burning of towns, the killing of their inhabitants and the deportation of craftsmen are documented in the Rus chronicles, in John of Plano Carpini's eyewitness report and in excavated destruction layers and mass graves.
baselineWhat: The population of the Rus principalities on the eve of the Mongol invasion
baselineNote: There is no census. Estimates rest on archaeological survey of towns and settlement density and on later fiscal records: George Vernadsky put the Rus lands at about 7.5 million before the invasion, Soviet demographers such as Urlanis nearer 5 million, so a range of 5-8 million is the usual scholarly span. Excavations at Kyiv, Ryazan and Vladimir show destruction layers and mass graves consistent with the chronicles' account of city-by-city sacking.

baselineSources.title: Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus' — Wikipedia

title: The Mongol Invasion of Hungary
actors: Batu's and Subutai's Mongol armies destroyed the Hungarian royal army at Mohi and devastated the kingdom for a year before withdrawing on the death of the Great Khan Ögedei
peopleRange: No count. The population fled to fortified places, to Transdanubia, to the Dalmatian coast — where Béla IV himself took refuge — and into the forests; Master Roger of Torre Maggiore, who was captured and escaped, describes the flight and the famine that followed in his Carmen miserabile. Béla's post-invasion policy of inviting Cuman and German settlers and licensing stone castles is indirect evidence of depopulation in the central plain. No register survives.
territoryDesc: The kingdom was not annexed: the Mongols withdrew in 1242 without establishing rule, and Hungary was reconstituted under Béla IV with a new programme of fortification and resettlement.

flows.label: Flight from the Great Plain → the Dalmatian coast
Flight to fortified Transdanubia

summary: In April 1241 the Mongol army destroyed Béla IV's forces at Mohi and spent the following year systematically ravaging Hungary, crossing the frozen Danube in the winter to reach Transdanubia before withdrawing in spring 1242 after Ögedei's death. Master Roger's Carmen miserabile, written by a survivor, describes massacre, the burning of settlements and a famine in which the surviving population starved. The scale of loss is disputed. Britannica's summary reports that Hungary lost about half its population, with roughly sixty per cent losses on the Great Plain — locally total — and about twenty per cent in Transdanubia, figures derived from settlement archaeology and the disappearance of villages from later charters. Other Hungarian historians argue for a considerably lower overall loss, in the range of fifteen to twenty per cent, holding that many settlements recorded as abandoned were re-established and that the charter evidence overstates permanent depopulation. Hungary's population before the invasion is usually put at around two million.
contested: Estimates of Hungary's population loss range from about fifteen to twenty per cent to about half, depending on whether abandoned-village evidence from later charters is read as permanent depopulation or as temporary flight followed by resettlement.

sources.title: Britannica: Hungary — The Mongol invasion; the last Árpád kings
Britannica: Battle of Mohi
The Mongols and Europe (The Cambridge History of the Mongol Empire)

deathsNote: The range applies the competing loss estimates to a pre-invasion population usually put at about two million: the lower end reflects historians who argue for fifteen to twenty per cent loss, the upper the reading reported by Britannica that Hungary lost about half its people. Deaths from the ensuing famine of 1242, described by Master Roger, are included and cannot be separated from those killed outright.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Massacre, the burning of settlements and the famine of 1242 are documented by Master Roger of Torre Maggiore's Carmen miserabile, written by an eyewitness who was himself captured.
baselineWhat: The population of the Kingdom of Hungary on the eve of the Mongol invasion
baselineNote: Hungarian historical demography reconstructs the kingdom's mid-thirteenth-century population from later charters, settlement archaeology and the tax registers of the following century. György Györffy and others put it at roughly 2 million, with published estimates ranging from about 1.5 to 2.5 million. Estimates of the invasion's mortality — from 15 to 50 per cent, varying sharply between the Great Plain and the forested and mountainous regions — are correspondingly uncertain.

title: The Mongol Sack of Baghdad and the End of the Abbasid Caliphate
actors: Hülegü's Mongol army besieged and stormed Baghdad, executed the last Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim, and killed or dispersed much of the city's population
peopleRange: No count. Survivors fled the city and the surrounding Sawad, and Baghdad's population was a fraction of its former size for generations; Christian and Jewish residents were exempted from the killing under Hülegü's orders, on the intercession of his Christian wife according to the Syriac and Armenian sources, and remained. Estimates of the city's pre-siege population range from about two hundred thousand to a million, all extrapolations from area and later evidence rather than records.
territoryDesc: The Abbasid caliphate as a political institution was extinguished and Iraq was incorporated into the Ilkhanate, ruled from Tabriz; Baghdad ceased to be an imperial capital.

flows.label: Refugees → Syria

summary: Hülegü, sent west by his brother the Great Khan Möngke, besieged Baghdad in January 1258; the city surrendered on 10 February and was given over to a week or more of killing and plunder. The caliph al-Musta'sim was executed, reportedly rolled in a carpet and trampled to avoid spilling royal blood, ending five centuries of Abbasid caliphate. Figures for the dead vary wildly across the sources: Hülegü's own report to Louis IX gives about two hundred thousand, later Persian writers such as Wassaf give two million, and the intermediate tradition often gives eight hundred thousand. Modern assessments, including John Masson Smith's work on Mongol logistics, put the plausible toll far lower, in the tens of thousands to low hundreds of thousands, constrained by estimates of the city's population and the practicalities of killing over a limited period. Recent work in Medical History has also reassessed whether epidemic disease, rather than the sack alone, accounts for part of the mortality reported in the sources. The destruction of Baghdad's libraries is widely reported but its extent is debated.
contested: Death figures range from Hülegü's own claim of about 200,000 to later claims of two million; modern estimates are far lower. The scale of the destruction of Baghdad's libraries and the claim that the Tigris ran black with ink are also questioned as later embellishment.

sources.title: Britannica: Hülegü
Britannica: Iraq — The later Abbasids
'Plague and the Mongol conquest of Baghdad (1258)? A reevaluation of the sources', Medical History (CUP)
World History Encyclopedia: Ilkhanate

deathsNote: The low end reflects modern minimalist estimates constrained by the city's plausible population and the logistics of the sack; the high end is the figure most commonly transmitted in the Arabic and Persian tradition. Hülegü's own dispatch claimed about 200,000 and Wassaf claimed two million; neither is a count. Recent work has argued that epidemic disease may account for part of the mortality attributed to the sack.
violenceNote: The killing of the population, the plunder and burning of the city and the destruction of libraries and mosques are documented by Rashid al-Din, Ibn al-Fuwati, Bar Hebraeus and the Armenian chronicler Grigor of Akner, though the extent of the library destruction is disputed.
baselineWhat: The population of Baghdad at the time of the Mongol siege
baselineNote: Medieval chroniclers give death tolls from 200,000 to 2 million, figures modern historians reject as impossible. Estimates of the city's actual population in 1258, based on its built area and its long decline from the ninth-century Abbasid peak, cluster between about 250,000 and 400,000.

title: The Expulsions of the Jews from England and France
actors: Edward I expelled the Jews of England in 1290; Philip IV expelled those of France in 1306 and seized their property; after readmission, Charles VI expelled them again and definitively in 1394
peopleRange: For England in 1290, modern estimates from Exchequer and tallage records put the community at roughly 2,000 to 3,000 people; medieval chroniclers gave 15,000 to 17,000, figures no longer accepted. For France in 1306 the commonly cited figure is around 100,000, an estimate derived from later chronicles and from modern extrapolation from the royal fiscal records generated by the confiscation of Jewish property and debts, with scholarly estimates running from about 50,000 to 125,000. The English figure rests on unusually good administrative evidence; the French one does not.

flows.label: England 1290 → Flanders and northern France
France 1306 → Provence, Savoy and the Empire
France 1394 → Italy and the Rhineland

summary: England and France were the first major European kingdoms to expel their Jewish populations outright. Edward I's edict of 18 July 1290 gave the Jews of England until 1 November to leave, following decades of punitive taxation that had exhausted the community's wealth, the Statute of the Jewry of 1275 banning lending at interest, and the executions of 1278–1279 over coin-clipping charges; the crown took the outstanding debts and the property. Philip IV of France ordered mass arrests on 22 July 1306, confiscated the property and expelled the community, recalling them in 1315 under fiscal pressure; further expulsions followed in 1322 and, definitively, in 1394 under Charles VI. In each case the expulsion was accompanied by confiscation, and in each case fiscal motive is visible in the record. England's Jews did not return in organised form until the seventeenth century.
contested: The size of the French community expelled in 1306 is uncertain, with estimates from about 50,000 to 125,000; the medieval English chroniclers' figure of 15,000 to 17,000 has been replaced by modern estimates around 2,000 to 3,000 based on Exchequer records.

sources.title: The National Archives (UK): Jews in England 1290
Britannica: Judaism — Marginalization and expulsion
Jewish Virtual Library: Expulsions of the Jews

deathsNote: These were expulsions rather than killings, and no significant death toll is documented for either edict. English chronicles record a group of expelled Jews drowned by a ship's master in the Thames estuary in 1290, an incident for which the master was prosecuted; it involved a small number of people and stands out precisely because it was exceptional.
violenceNote: The mass arrest of France's Jews on a single day in July 1306 preceding their expulsion and the confiscation of their property is documented in the French royal records.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of England and of France on the eve of the expulsions
baselineNote: Modern scholarship puts England's Jews at 2,000-3,000 in 1290, well below the 16,000 given by older chronicles, reconstructed from the Exchequer of the Jews and tallage rolls. France's Jewish population in 1306 is estimated at anywhere from 50,000 to 140,000, from royal confiscation records. The combined figure is therefore almost entirely French and carries a wide margin.

baselineSources.title: History of the Jews in France

shareCaveat: The expulsions were intended to be total, so the numerator and the denominator are estimates of the same community and the ratio approaches 100% by construction rather than by measurement.

title: Muhammad bin Tughluq's Transfer of Delhi to Daulatabad
actors: The Delhi sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq ordered the transfer of his capital and its population from Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan, some 1,100 kilometres south, and reversed the decision within a few years
peopleRange: No count. Ibn Battuta, who was in Delhi within a decade of the events and is hostile to the sultan, describes the city being emptied and a search made for anyone who stayed behind; Ziauddin Barani and Isami give similar accounts. Modern historians, including Peter Jackson in his study of the Delhi Sultanate, read these as describing the compulsory removal of the court, the administrative and religious elites and their households — a substantial but bounded population — rather than the whole city, and treat 'the city was left empty' as a rhetorical formula. Delhi's population at the time is itself unknown.
territoryDesc: Daulatabad, the former Yadava capital of Devagiri, was rebuilt as a second capital to govern the newly annexed Deccan; the project was abandoned and Delhi resumed its role.

flows.label: Delhi → Daulatabad (Devagiri)
Return to Delhi after the project was abandoned

summary: Around 1327 Muhammad bin Tughluq, having extended Delhi Sultanate authority deep into the Deccan, ordered his capital moved to Daulatabad and required the population of Delhi to move with it. The march of more than a thousand kilometres, described by Ibn Battuta and by the court historian Barani, killed an unrecorded number on the road; within a few years the sultan reversed the policy and ordered a return, and Delhi took years to recover. The episode became the standard example of the sultan's reputation for grand schemes badly executed, a reputation established by hostile contemporaries. Britannica's account of the Tughluq reign describes the aim as settling Muslim nobles in the south and holding them under the sultan's control. Modern scholarship qualifies the picture further: the compulsion is not in doubt and is documented by an eyewitness, but historians read the transfer as directed at the court, administration, ulama and their dependants rather than at every inhabitant, and note that Daulatabad functioned as a genuine second capital and remained an important city afterwards.
contested: Whether the whole population of Delhi was moved or only the court, administrative and religious elites and their households is disputed; the sources are hostile to the sultan and modern historians including Peter Jackson read 'the city was emptied' as rhetorical.

deathsNote: No figures. Ibn Battuta and Barani describe deaths on the march south and among those who returned, but give no numbers and are writing to condemn the policy rather than to count its cost.
baselineWhat: The population of Delhi at the time of the ordered transfer of the capital to Daulatabad
baselineNote: No count survives. Fourteenth-century Delhi was among the largest cities in the world, and modern urban-size reconstructions (Chandler's series and later revisions) put it in the range of 200,000-400,000 in this period. The chroniclers Barani and Ibn Battuta describe the city as emptied but give no numbers, and modern historians disagree over whether the whole population or only the court and administrative classes were ordered to move.

title: The Black Death Massacres and Expulsions of Jewish Communities
actors: Town councils, guilds, flagellant bands and local lords across the Holy Roman Empire, the Rhineland, Alsace, Switzerland, Aragon and Provence killed, burned or expelled Jewish communities accused of poisoning wells during the plague
peopleRange: No aggregate. Several hundred Jewish communities were destroyed or dispersed across German-speaking Europe alone; the Nuremberg Memorbuch and other memorial books list the localities and, in many cases, the dead by name, and surviving municipal records document confiscations and cancelled debts. Survivors moved east, and the persecutions of 1348–1351 are conventionally treated as a principal driver of the shift of Ashkenazi settlement into Poland and Lithuania. Neither the killed nor the displaced have been totalled.

flows.label: Survivors → Poland and Lithuania

summary: As plague spread through Europe in 1348 and 1349, Jewish communities were accused of causing it by poisoning wells. Confessions extracted under torture at Chillon on Lake Geneva in September 1348 were circulated to towns along the Rhine and became the template for the accusation. Pope Clement VI issued two bulls condemning the charge and pointing out that Jews were dying of the plague as well, without effect. At Basel in January 1349 the community was burned in a wooden house built for the purpose; at Strasbourg on 14 February 1349, before the plague had even reached the city, several hundred to two thousand Jews were burned and the survivors expelled, after a coup by the guilds against a council that had protected them. Similar destructions followed at Mainz, Cologne, Erfurt, Frankfurt, Brussels and hundreds of smaller places. Municipal debt to Jewish lenders was extinguished along with the lenders in many cases. Surviving communities were expelled and moved east, reshaping the geography of Ashkenazi Jewry.
contested: No aggregate death toll has been established; the memorial books and municipal records document the destroyed communities in detail but historians have not produced a defensible total, and figures for individual towns such as Strasbourg range widely.

sources.title: Genocidal Massacres of Jews in Medieval Western Europe, 1096–1392 (The Cambridge World History of Genocide, vol. 1)
The Shock of the Black Death (Persecution and Toleration, CUP)
Jewish Virtual Library: The Black Death

deathsNote: No defensible aggregate exists. Individual episodes are documented — Strasbourg's is variously given as several hundred to two thousand, Basel's as several hundred — and the memorial books name thousands of dead across hundreds of localities, but no scholar has produced a total for the wave as a whole.
violenceNote: The burnings of whole communities, the extraction of confessions under torture at Chillon and the seizure and destruction of Jewish property are documented in municipal records, the Chillon depositions, the memorial books and contemporary chronicles.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of the Holy Roman Empire and neighbouring lands attacked during the Black Death, around 1348
baselineNote: There is no census; Salo Baron's estimates and later work on the Memorbücher and town records put the Jewish population of the German lands at roughly 80,000-150,000 in the mid-fourteenth century, spread over some 1,000 settlements, of which more than 500 communities were destroyed or dispersed in 1348-51.

title: Ottoman Sürgün Resettlement and the Devşirme Child Levy
actors: The Ottoman state compulsorily resettled Anatolian Muslim and nomadic populations into the conquered Balkans, moved Balkan populations into Anatolia, and levied Christian boys from Balkan villages for conversion and service to the sultan
peopleRange: No totals for this period. Sürgün — compulsory transfer by imperial order — is documented in sultanic decrees and in the early tahrir survey registers, which record settlers moved into newly taken Balkan districts and, in the other direction, groups moved into Anatolia; the registers name communities rather than count movements. For the devşirme, the levy is usually estimated at one to three thousand boys a year at its height in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, with an aggregate over the whole life of the institution often put at around 200,000; those figures are extrapolations from scattered levy registers, of which the earliest detailed survivals postdate this entry's window.
territoryDesc: Ottoman rule was extended across Thrace, Bulgaria, Macedonia, Serbia and Greece between the crossing to Gallipoli in 1354 and the middle of the fifteenth century, with Edirne as capital from the 1360s.

flows.label: Anatolian Turkmen and yörük settlers → Thrace and the Balkans
Devşirme recruits → Anatolia and the sultan's household

summary: Ottoman expansion into the Balkans was accompanied by two systematic instruments of population policy. Sürgün was the compulsory transfer of populations by imperial decree: Turkmen and nomadic groups from Anatolia were moved into newly conquered Balkan districts to secure them, and Balkan populations were moved in the other direction; the practice was later used on a large scale to repopulate Istanbul after 1453. The devşirme was a periodic levy of Christian boys, chiefly from Balkan villages, who were taken from their families, converted to Islam, and trained for the Janissary corps or the palace service, from which the highest offices of the empire were filled. The characterisation of the devşirme is disputed: Ottoman-centred scholarship, notably Halil İnalcık's, presents it as a recruitment mechanism that gave peasant boys access to the empire's highest positions, while Balkan and much Western scholarship treats it as a tribute in children taken by force from subject communities; both descriptions rest on the same evidence of compulsion and of subsequent careers.
contested: Whether the devşirme is best described as a child tribute exacted by force or as a route of social mobility into the Ottoman elite is disputed between Ottomanist scholarship, notably that of Halil İnalcık, and Balkan national historiographies; the compulsion itself is not in dispute.

sources.title: Britannica: devşirme
Britannica: Janissary
The incorporation of the Balkans into the Ottoman Empire, 1353–1453 (The Cambridge History of Turkey, vol. 1)

deathsNote: Neither sürgün nor devşirme was lethal by design and no death toll is associated with them. They were instruments for moving and appropriating populations, and the sources record transfers and levies rather than killing.
violenceNote: The compulsory levy of Christian boys from their families for conversion and state service is documented in Ottoman kanunname legislation and levy registers and described in the Cambridge History of Turkey.
baselineWhat: The Anatolian and Balkan populations subject to Ottoman forced resettlement and the child levy
baselineNote: No denominator can be reconstructed for this window. The Ottoman tahrir registers that would allow one begin only in the later fifteenth century, after the period covered here; V. L. Ménage and later scholars estimate the devşirme took on the order of 1,000-3,000 boys a year from the Balkan Christian villages, but the sürgün resettlements moved whole households in numbers never centrally totalled, across territories whose populations were changing hands throughout.

title: Early Ming State-Organised Resettlement under the Hongwu Emperor
actors: The Hongwu emperor's government moved peasant households from densely settled Shanxi and the Yangtze delta into war-devastated north China, transferred wealthy families to the capital, and settled hereditary military households in frontier colonies
peopleRange: Estimates for state-organised resettlement under Hongwu and his son Yongle range from roughly one million to more than seven million people; Cao Shuji's multi-volume Zhongguo yimin shi is the standard reconstruction and sits within that range. The evidence is imperial edicts recorded in the Ming shilu — which document specific transfers such as the removal of 5,300 wealthy households to Nanjing in 1391 — together with county gazetteers, land-registration records and later lineage genealogies. There was no migration register, and the ubiquitous north Chinese family tradition of descent from migrants gathered at the great pagoda tree of Hongdong in Shanxi is a folk memory rather than a record.

flows.label: Shanxi households → the depopulated North China Plain
Wealthy Jiangnan households → Nanjing
Military colonists → the northern frontier garrisons

summary: The wars that ended Mongol rule left large parts of the North China Plain and the Huai region depopulated. The Hongwu emperor's response was compulsory resettlement on a scale that reshaped the demography of northern China: households were moved from crowded Shanxi and from the lower Yangtze into the emptied prefectures of Hebei, Henan and Shandong, given land, tools and tax remissions, and forbidden to return; wealthy and potentially troublesome families from the Yangtze delta were transferred to the new capital at Nanjing, 5,300 households in a single order in 1391; and hereditary military households were settled in self-supporting agricultural colonies along the northern and southwestern frontiers. The policy was administrative rather than punitive in intent, but it was compulsory and enforced. The totals are reconstructions: the edicts survive, the migration itself was never counted, and the folk tradition of the Hongdong pagoda tree, from which millions of north Chinese families trace descent, is a memory of the process rather than evidence of its scale.
contested: The scale of early Ming resettlement is reconstructed from edicts, gazetteers and genealogies rather than from any register, and estimates differ by several million; the Hongdong pagoda tree tradition, though nearly universal in north China, is folk memory and scholars debate how much historical migration it encodes.

sources.title: ChinaKnowledge: Ming Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor
'From Migration Legends to Regional Identity: the Formation of the Ming-Qing State', Journal of Chinese Humanities (Brill, 2024)
Britannica: Hongwu

deathsNote: No significant death toll is associated with the resettlement programme itself, which was intended to restore agricultural production and came with land grants and tax remissions. Deaths on the moves are not recorded.
baselineWhat: The population of Ming China at the census of 1393
baselineNote: The Hongwu registration of 1393 recorded 60,545,812 people in 10.65 million households. Modern historical demographers regard this as an undercount produced by a tax register: Martin Heijdra and Cao Shuji put the true figure at somewhere between 65 and 85 million.

title: Timur's Campaigns: Isfahan, Delhi and Baghdad
actors: Timur (Tamerlane), ruling from Samarkand, campaigned across Iran, Central Asia, the Caucasus, India and the Levant, storming cities, massacring populations and deporting craftsmen to his capital
peopleRange: No totals. The documented and repeated practice was the deportation of artisans, scholars and skilled workers to Samarkand and Kesh to build and staff Timur's capital, recorded by his court historians and by the Castilian envoy Ruy González de Clavijo, who saw the deported craftsmen and their colonies at Samarkand in 1404; the Delhi campaign of 1398 carried off large numbers of captives, including the stonemasons said to have built the Bibi Khanum mosque. None of these movements is quantified in a usable way.
territoryDesc: Timur built an empire from Anatolia and the Levant to the Indus and the Syr Darya, ruled from Samarkand; it fragmented within a generation of his death.

flows.label: Deported craftsmen from Delhi → Samarkand
Deported artisans from Iraq and Syria → Samarkand

summary: Timur's campaigns between 1370 and his death in 1405 produced a series of city massacres that are among the best-known of the period. At Isfahan in 1387, after the killing of his tax collectors, his troops are reported by the Persian sources to have killed some seventy thousand people and to have built towers of skulls. At Delhi in December 1398 he sacked the city for several days after, according to his own memoirs and the Zafarnama tradition, ordering the execution of about a hundred thousand prisoners taken before the battle. At Baghdad in 1401 the Persian sources report ninety thousand heads built into towers. Every one of these figures comes from a chronicle tradition — much of it commissioned by Timur himself, for whom the reputation for terror was an instrument of war — and the round numbers are conventional. The other consistent feature of the campaigns, the systematic deportation of craftsmen to Samarkand, is corroborated independently by Clavijo's embassy account.
contested: All the massacre figures derive from chronicles, several of them written under Timur's own patronage, for whom a reputation for terror served military purposes; the widely repeated claim that Timur's campaigns killed seventeen million people, or five per cent of the world's population, has no evidentiary basis and is not accepted by specialists.

sources.title: Britannica: Sack of Delhi (1398)
Encyclopaedia Iranica: ISFAHAN vi. Medieval Period
World History Encyclopedia: Timur
Genocidal Massacres in Medieval India (The Cambridge World History of Genocide, vol. 1)

deathsNote: The range is an aggregation of the individual figures the chronicle tradition gives for the major massacres — about 70,000 at Isfahan in 1387, about 100,000 prisoners at Delhi in 1398, about 90,000 at Baghdad in 1401, with others at Sabzavar, Tikrit and Aleppo — treated as an order of magnitude rather than a count. Those figures are conventional round numbers from sources partly written under Timur's patronage. The often-quoted total of 17 million has no basis.
violenceNote: The city massacres, the execution of prisoners before Delhi and the deportation of craftsmen to Samarkand are documented in the Zafarnama tradition, in Timur's own memoirs and, for the deported craftsmen, independently by Ruy González de Clavijo's embassy account of 1404.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: the campaigns ran from Anatolia to Delhi across 35 years and a dozen distinct polities
baselineNote: The often-repeated claim that Timur's wars killed 17 million people, about 5 per cent of a world population then around 350-375 million, traces to a nineteenth-century estimate and has no documentary basis. Individual sieges are better attested - the tower of skulls at Isfahan in 1387, put by chroniclers at 70,000, and the sack of Delhi in 1398 - but they come from court histories with their own reasons to exaggerate. There is no reconstructible population for the whole set of territories he campaigned in over 1370-1405.

title: Timur's Invasions of Georgia and the Depopulation of the Kartli Lowlands
actors: Timur's armies repeatedly invaded the Christian kingdom of Georgia, sacking towns and carrying off captives
peopleRange: No usable figure exists. Persian court chronicles - Nizam al-Din Shami's and Sharaf al-Din Yazdi's Zafarnama - describe the enslavement of whole districts and the sack of Tbilisi in 1386 in the conventional idiom of victory literature, and Georgian chronicles describe flight to the mountains and to Imereti; both are literary rather than statistical. Modern historians infer serious and lasting depopulation of the eastern Georgian lowlands from settlement abandonment and later tax and church records rather than from any count.
territoryDesc: Kartli and Kakheti reduced to tributary status; Georgian kingdom fragmented in the following decades

flows.label: Captives from Tbilisi and Kartli to Samarkand and Transoxiana

summary: Between 1386 and 1403 Timur invaded Georgia eight times, taking Tbilisi in 1386 and capturing King Bagrat V, and returning repeatedly to devastate Kartli and Kakheti when Georgian rulers renounced tribute. Persian chronicles written for Timur's court describe cities stormed, populations enslaved, vineyards and churches destroyed and captives marched to Transoxiana, while Georgian chronicles record flight into the mountains and into western Georgia. The scale is not recoverable: chronicle numbers are rhetorical, and archaeologists and historians instead infer heavy depopulation of the eastern lowlands from abandoned settlements and from the weakened, fragmented kingdom of the fifteenth century. Georgia survived as a Christian tributary state but never recovered its earlier position, and the invasions are conventionally treated as the end of the Georgian golden age.
contested: Whether the campaigns caused a demographic collapse or a severe but recoverable disruption is debated, and all contemporary numbers are propagandistic.

sources.title: Timurid invasions of Georgia
Kingdom of Georgia
Timur (Tamerlane)

deathsNote: No defensible range can be given. The chronicles report slaughter at Tbilisi and in later campaigns without figures that can be checked, and no independent demographic reconstruction of medieval Georgian mortality exists.
violenceNote: Timurid court chronicles themselves record the storming of towns, the destruction of churches and the removal of captives, and Georgian chronicles corroborate the church destruction.
baselineWhat: The population of the kingdom of Georgia before Timur's campaigns
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Georgia in the late fourteenth century has no surviving fiscal register or census, and modern estimates of its population are extrapolated from monastic and chronicle references. Georgian historiography holds that the eight invasions between 1386 and 1403, following the Black Death, reduced the country severely and that the Kartli lowlands never fully recovered, but no baseline figure can be defended.

title: The Ming Occupation of Đại Việt and the Deportation of Its Elites
actors: The Ming Yongle emperor annexed Đại Việt as the province of Jiaozhi, deported its ruling house, officials, scholars and craftsmen to China, and imposed Ming law, dress and ritual until a twenty-year insurgency expelled the occupation
peopleRange: No reliable total. The Ming shilu and the Vietnamese Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư record the deportation of the Hồ ruling family and their officials to Nanjing, and repeated levies of craftsmen, scholars, physicians and skilled workers sent north — among them the architect Nguyễn An, later credited with work on the imperial palaces in Beijing. The numbers given in the Vietnamese record are polemical and those in the Chinese record are partial; the deportations plainly involved thousands rather than a general population transfer.
territoryDesc: Đại Việt was annexed outright as the Ming province of Jiaozhi, administered by Ming prefectures and counties for twenty years, before independence was restored under Lê Lợi and recognised by the Ming in 1428.

flows.label: Deported Vietnamese elites, scholars and craftsmen → Nanjing

summary: The Ming invaded Đại Việt in 1406 on the pretext of restoring the deposed Trần dynasty, and in 1407 annexed it outright as the province of Jiaozhi. The Hồ rulers and their officials were deported to China, and further levies removed scholars, physicians and skilled craftsmen north over the following years. The occupation imposed Ming administrative structures, taxation, dress and ritual, and its officials collected and removed or destroyed Vietnamese books and records — an act that Vietnamese tradition regards as an attempt to erase the country's separate cultural existence and that modern scholarship treats as a deliberate, if partly rationalised, programme of assimilation. Resistance culminated in Lê Lợi's insurgency from 1418; the Ming withdrew in 1427 and recognised Vietnamese independence in 1428. Nguyễn Trãi's Bình Ngô đại cáo, the proclamation of victory, is the classic Vietnamese account of the occupation and is a work of political rhetoric as well as a record.
contested: Vietnamese and Chinese accounts of the occupation differ sharply on its character and on the extent of the removal and destruction of Vietnamese books; the numbers deported are not reliably recorded in either tradition.

sources.title: The Ming Invasion of Vietnam, 1407–1427 (East Asia in the World, CUP)
'Our mountains and rivers have changed: Nature and empire in the Ming colonisation of Đại Việt, 1407–28', Journal of Southeast Asian Studies (CUP)
Britannica: Le Loi

deathsNote: No usable figures. Twenty years of occupation and insurgency produced fighting, reprisals and famine described in both traditions, but neither the Ming shilu nor the Vietnamese chronicles supply totals, and the figures in Nguyễn Trãi's proclamation are rhetorical.
violenceNote: The deportation of craftsmen and scholars and the collection and removal or destruction of Vietnamese books and records are documented in the Ming shilu and in the Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư and analysed in the Cambridge scholarship cited.
baselineWhat: The population of Đại Việt registered by the Ming administration of Jiaozhi province after the conquest of 1407
baselineNote: Ming records of the registration of Jiaozhi report roughly 3.12 million registered persons together with some 2 million people classed as unregistered upland groups; modern estimates of Đại Việt's population around 1400 run from about 3 to 5 million. Registration figures under a hostile occupation are likely to understate the true population.

title: The Aztec Triple Alliance: Conquest, Tribute Resettlement and Mass Sacrifice
actors: The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan subjugated city-states across central Mesoamerica, planted colonists in frontier provinces, and took war captives for sacrifice at the imperial temples
peopleRange: No aggregate figure exists. The Codex Mendoza and the Matricula de Tributos record tribute obligations from 38 provinces and roughly 400 subject towns, and colonial-era sources describe the planting of Nahua colonists in garrison settlements such as Oztoma and Alahuiztlan on the Tarascan frontier and in Oaxaca, but numbers are given only sporadically. Populations of destroyed or resettled towns are described in the annals of Tlatelolco and Texcoco in qualitative terms.
territoryDesc: An imperial tribute domain covering much of central and southern Mexico from the Gulf coast to the Pacific, excluding the Tlaxcalan and Tarascan states.

flows.label: Nahua military colonists settled at the Tarascan frontier garrisons

summary: From the formation of the Triple Alliance in 1428 the Mexica of Tenochtitlan and their allies conquered a tribute empire across central Mesoamerica, imposing tribute recorded in pictorial registers, installing governors and garrisons, and settling Nahua colonists in frontier provinces after the removal or destruction of local populations. Warfare was structured partly around the taking of captives: prisoners from campaigns and from the ritualised xochiyaoyotl or flower wars with Tlaxcala and Huexotzinco were sacrificed at the Templo Mayor and provincial temples. Sources on the scale of sacrifice are unreliable in a specific way: the dedication of the rebuilt Templo Mayor in 1487 is reported in colonial-era annals as involving 20,000 to 80,400 victims, figures modern scholars treat as ideological rather than countable, while excavation of the Huei Tzompantli skull rack beneath Mexico City from 2015 has recovered hundreds of skulls and confirms institutionalised display of sacrificial dead. The empire's structure — tribute, garrison colonies and captive-taking — is what the Spanish conquest of 1519-1521, already in the atlas, dismantled and partly reused.
contested: The scale of human sacrifice: numbers in the colonial annals are regarded by most scholars as propagandistic, and estimates of annual victims range from the low hundreds to twenty thousand, with some historians arguing Spanish sources inflated the practice to justify conquest and others pointing to the tzompantli excavations as corroboration of large-scale ritual killing.

deathsNote: No defensible total can be given. Colonial-era annals report tens of thousands sacrificed at single dedications; these are rhetorical. Archaeology at the Huei Tzompantli establishes that sacrifice was institutionalised and repeated over decades but cannot yield an empire-wide rate. Deaths in the wars of conquest themselves were never recorded.

title: The Ayutthayan Capture of Angkor and the Removal of the Khmer Court
actors: The Ayutthaya kingdom captured the Khmer capital and, by Thai chronicle accounts, carried off its court, artisans and population
peopleRange: No reliable figure. Thai chronicles compiled long after the event describe the deportation of the Khmer royal family, Brahmans, court dancers, artisans and large numbers of ordinary people to Ayutthaya, in the standard Southeast Asian idiom in which manpower rather than land was the prize of war. Michael Vickery and other historians have shown that the chronicle accounts are late, mutually inconsistent and partly retrojected, and that the conventional date of 1431 is itself uncertain; archaeology shows continued occupation at Angkor after the fifteenth century rather than sudden abandonment.
territoryDesc: Angkor region passed under Ayutthayan control; the Khmer political centre moved south-east to the Phnom Penh-Longvek region

flows.label: Khmer court, Brahmans and artisans deported to Ayutthaya

summary: Thai chronicle traditions describe a siege of Angkor Thom of some seven months ending with the city's capture by Ayutthaya, conventionally dated to 1431, after which the Khmer king was killed or fled and an Ayutthayan prince was installed. The same chronicles say the victors removed the Khmer royal family, Brahman ritual specialists, court dancers, artisans and a mass of ordinary people to Ayutthaya, a practice consistent with the wider Southeast Asian pattern in which war was fought for manpower rather than territory, and Khmer court culture is generally held to have entered Siamese royal practice through this transfer. The Khmer political centre subsequently shifted to the Phnom Penh and later Longvek region, though the reasons - military pressure, trade, hydraulic decline - are debated. Modern scholarship, particularly Michael Vickery's, treats the chronicle accounts as late and unreliable, questions the 1431 date, and rejects the older narrative of a sudden and total abandonment of Angkor; archaeological work shows continued occupation of the Angkor region for generations afterwards. The episode is included here for the deportation of population it is recorded as involving, while noting that its scale cannot be established.
contested: The date, the scale of any deportation, and whether Angkor was abandoned at all are all disputed; the Thai chronicle accounts are late and are treated sceptically by modern historians.

sources.title: Fall of Angkor
Ayutthaya Kingdom
Angkor

deathsNote: No figures exist. The chronicles record a long siege and the killing of the Khmer king, but give no toll, and no independent evidence bears on mortality.
violenceNote: Thai chronicle traditions describe a siege of several months before the city fell; no other form is documented by an identifiable source.
baselineWhat: The population of Greater Angkor, the low-density urban complex and its hinterland, at its height
baselineNote: Klassen, Evans and colleagues' 2021 demographic model, built from airborne laser scanning of the Angkor region and mound-density analysis, puts Greater Angkor at roughly 700,000-900,000 people at its peak in the thirteenth century, with the walled civic-ceremonial core holding on the order of 20,000-25,000. Angkor's population in the 1430s was substantially lower after decades of hydraulic decline and political contraction, but the size of that decline is not quantified, so this baseline is a peak figure and not a 1431 figure.

title: The Inca Mitma: State Resettlement across Tawantinsuyu
actors: The Inca state uprooted conquered communities and moved them across the empire as mitmaqkuna colonists, replacing them with loyal populations
peopleRange: Highly uncertain. Colonial Spanish chroniclers who interviewed Inca administrators — Cieza de Leon, Garcilaso de la Vega, Cobo — describe the systematic transfer of whole communities, and modern anthropological and linguistic reconstruction, notably by John Murra and later scholars, suggests that something between a quarter and a third of the empire's population lived as mitmaqkuna. Because estimates of Tawantinsuyu's population itself range from about 6 million to 14 million, the resulting figure ranges from roughly 1.5 million to well over 4 million people over the course of a century; more conservative readings, treating the quarter-to-third claim as applying to specific provinces rather than the empire, give figures in the low hundreds of thousands. The central estimate here is deliberately rough. Archaeological confirmation exists for particular transfers, including the state maize estates of the Cochabamba valley settled with colonists drawn from dozens of highland groups, documented in a 1556 Spanish visita that lists their origins.
territoryDesc: Population transfers spanned Tawantinsuyu from present-day Ecuador and southern Colombia to central Chile and north-western Argentina.

flows.label: Aymara and other highland colonists resettled into the Cochabamba maize valleys
Chimu craftsmen from Chan Chan transferred to Cusco after the conquest of the north coast

summary: The Inca state used compulsory resettlement, mitma, as a routine instrument of rule: communities judged rebellious were moved far from their homelands and replaced by populations of proven loyalty, while colonists were planted to open new agricultural land, garrison frontiers or supply specialised crafts. Transferred groups, the mitmaqkuna, retained their dress and ethnic identity but owed labour and allegiance to the state and were registered in the census system recorded on khipu. The most fully documented case is the Cochabamba valley, converted into a state maize estate worked by colonists drawn from a long list of highland groups, itemised in a Spanish inspection of 1556. Craft specialists were also relocated wholesale, including metalworkers and weavers from the defeated Chimu kingdom brought to Cusco. The Spanish conquest inherited a landscape of displaced populations and layered its own reducciones on top of it — a system the atlas already covers. Mitma is probably the largest state-organised population transfer in the pre-Columbian Americas and its absence from the atlas was a substantial gap.
contested: The scale, which depends on unresolved estimates of Tawantinsuyu's total population and on whether the chroniclers' claim that a quarter to a third of subjects were mitmaqkuna described the empire as a whole or particular provinces.

deathsNote: No death toll can be established and the system was not primarily lethal: mitmaqkuna were resettled as productive subjects with land and obligations rather than killed or enslaved. Chroniclers describe deaths in transit and from moving people between radically different altitudes and disease environments, but nothing was counted, and the catastrophic mortality of the sixteenth century belongs to the Spanish conquest entries.
violenceNote: Spanish colonial inspections such as the 1556 Cochabamba visita, which recorded the origins and labour obligations of resettled colonists, document the labour service required of mitmaqkuna.
baselineWhat: The population of Tawantinsuyu, the Inca empire, on the eve of the Spanish invasion
baselineNote: There is no census. Modern reconstructions work back from early colonial tribute counts, Andean archaeology and epidemic modelling, and differ by a factor of two: Cook's range for the Andes is roughly 4 to 15 million, with about 9 million his preferred figure, while Rowe's older reconstruction gave about 6 million and some settlement-based estimates reach 12-14 million. A figure of roughly 10 million for the empire in the 1520s sits in the middle of that literature and should be read as an order of magnitude.
