shareCaveat: The mitmaqkuna total accumulates across roughly a century of successive conquests, while the denominator is a single snapshot for the empire at its greatest extent, so the ratio understates how heavily particular conquered provinces were moved.

title: The Indian Ocean and Red Sea Slave Trades, 1450–1750
actors: Swahili coast, Omani, Yemeni, Indian and later Portuguese, Dutch and French merchants shipped enslaved Africans, Malagasy, Indians and Southeast Asians across the Indian Ocean to Arabia, Persia, India and the European colonies of the Indies and the Mascarenes
peopleRange: Much weaker evidence than for the Atlantic. The East African and Red Sea traffic out of sub-Saharan Africa is included in the roughly five million figure given in the standard syntheses for all the non-Atlantic trades between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, most of it after 1750; Ralph Austen's tentative census is the basis of most estimates. Separately, Richard Allen's work on European slave trading in the Indian Ocean between 1500 and 1850 counts hundreds of thousands of people moved by the Portuguese, Dutch, French and English within the ocean basin — from Madagascar, Mozambique, Bengal, the Coromandel coast, Arakan and the Indonesian archipelago to Goa, Batavia, Ceylon, the Cape and the Mascarenes. There is no register comparable to the Atlantic voyage database and no reliable total for 1450-1750.

flows.label: Mozambique and the Swahili coast → Arabia
Madagascar → Batavia and the Dutch East Indies
Bengal and Arakan → Batavia
Mozambique → the Cape Colony

summary: The Indian Ocean carried an old and continuous traffic in enslaved people that the arrival of European companies redirected rather than created. East Africans and Malagasy were shipped north to Arabia, the Persian Gulf and India; Portuguese Goa, Dutch Batavia and Ceylon, and later French Mauritius and Bourbon drew enslaved labour from Madagascar, Mozambique, Bengal, Arakan, Sulawesi and Bali; the Dutch East India Company both bought slaves and took them as war captives, as at Banda. The Arakanese and Portuguese raiding of Bengal in the seventeenth century, which supplied thousands of captives a year to Chittagong and Batavia, is among the better-documented episodes. Volumes are poorly recorded because much of the traffic was carried in small vessels by merchants who kept no registers surviving today, and because European company records document only part of it. Modern estimates come from Austen for the African trades and from Richard Allen for European slave trading within the ocean, and both authors present their figures as provisional.
contested: The volume of the Indian Ocean and Red Sea trades before 1750 is unknown within wide margins, and historians disagree over how much European company activity added to a pre-existing traffic as against redirecting it.

sources.title: Klas Rönnbäck, 'The Slave Trades out of Africa' (African Economic History Network, PDF)
Richard B. Allen, 'European Slave Trading in the Indian Ocean, 1500-1850' (Ohio University Press)

deathsNote: No defensible total. Mortality in transit is documented episodically in Dutch and Portuguese company records — losses on Madagascar and Bengal voyages were sometimes very heavy — but the absence of comprehensive registers means no aggregate can be constructed.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Raiding for captives on the Bengal and Malagasy coasts, the holding of enslaved people in company and private hands at Batavia, Goa and the Cape, and the sale of women and children into domestic and sexual servitude are documented in Dutch East India Company and Portuguese records analysed by Richard Allen and others.
baselineNote: No single denominator exists. The trades drew captives from the East African interior, Madagascar, the Horn, South Asia and the Indonesian archipelago across three centuries, and none of these source regions was enumerated in the period. Estimates of the volume itself are contested and rest on scattered customs records and merchant accounts rather than the systematic shipping data available for the Atlantic.

title: The Trans-Saharan Slave Trade, 1450–1750
actors: Saharan and North African merchants, and the Moroccan and Ottoman states that taxed and used them, moved enslaved people north across the desert from the Sahel and the Sudan to Morocco, Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli and Egypt
peopleRange: No count exists and every figure is a reconstruction. Ralph Austen's census-style estimates, built from the records of desert entrepôts, North African markets and travellers' reports, remain the standard basis; textbook syntheses drawing on Lovejoy, Manning and Toledano put the combined trans-Saharan, Red Sea and Indian Ocean traffic out of sub-Saharan Africa at roughly five million people for the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries as a whole, of which the trans-Saharan route was the largest component before the nineteenth century. Because these estimates rest on scattered market and caravan observations rather than shipping registers, they are far weaker than the Atlantic figures and are given as orders of magnitude by their own authors.

flows.label: Central Sudan → Fezzan and Tripoli
Niger bend → Marrakesh and Morocco
Darfur and Kordofan → Egypt along the Forty Days Road

summary: The desert trade in enslaved people, already centuries old by 1450, continued and in places intensified through the early modern period. Captives were taken in raiding and warfare in the Sahel and the savanna belt, marched to desert-edge markets such as Timbuktu, Agades, Kano and Kobbei, and carried north by caravan to Morocco, the Ottoman Regencies of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli, and Egypt, where they were absorbed into domestic service, agriculture, the military and the harem. The Moroccan conquest of Songhay in 1591 and the later creation by Mawlay Isma'il of a standing army of enslaved black soldiers, the Abid al-Bukhari, are the clearest instances of state organisation of the traffic. Women and children formed a much larger share of this trade than of the Atlantic trade, and mortality on the desert crossing was high. The volume is genuinely unknown: the figures in circulation derive from Austen's reconstructions and later syntheses and should be read as orders of magnitude rather than counts.
contested: The volume of the trans-Saharan trade is disputed within wide margins because it rests on inference from caravan and market reports rather than records of individual shipments, and comparisons with the Atlantic trade are frequently made for political purposes on both sides.

sources.title: Klas Rönnbäck, 'The Slave Trades out of Africa' (African Economic History Network, PDF)
Encyclopedia.com: Slave Trade

deathsNote: No total exists. Contemporary travellers describe heavy mortality on the desert crossings and the routes are marked by burial sites, and historians generally assume losses at least as high as those of the Atlantic middle passage, but there is no series of records from which a figure could be derived.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: The predominance of women and children among those carried north, their use as domestic and sexual slaves, and the castration of some boys for the eunuch trade are described in Arabic chronicles, market records and European travellers' accounts and are summarised in the historiography reviewed by Austen and Rönnbäck.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: the trade drew captives from the whole Sahel and Sudanic belt over three centuries and dozens of polities
baselineNote: Ralph Austen's censuses of the Saharan trade, built from North African market records, caravan accounts and demand estimates, give roughly 4,000-7,000 captives a year in this period, or on the order of 1.5 million between 1450 and 1750, with wide error margins. The populations raided - Kanem-Bornu's tributaries, the Hausa lands, the Niger bend, Darfur and Kordofan - were never enumerated, changed constantly with the rise and fall of states, and cannot be aggregated into a single base.

title: The Fall of Constantinople and the Ottoman Repopulation of the City
actors: Mehmed II took Constantinople, allowed a three-day sack in which the surviving inhabitants were enslaved, then repopulated the city by compulsory transfer of families from across the empire
peopleRange: The figures come from narrative sources, not registers. Byzantine and Ottoman chroniclers of the siege (Doukas, Kritovoulos, Sphrantzes, Leonard of Chios) put the city's population before the siege at 40,000-50,000, far below its medieval peak, and describe some 4,000 killed and roughly 50,000 survivors enslaved or ransomed; these are round numbers written for effect. The repopulation is better evidenced: Mehmed ordered families deported (surgun) from Anatolia and Rumelia, Muslim, Christian and Jewish alike, and the survey of 1477-78 counts about 16,300 households in the city, implying perhaps 60,000-70,000 residents a quarter-century after the conquest. The number moved under compulsion cannot be separated cleanly from voluntary settlement.
territoryDesc: The last territory of the Roman/Byzantine state passed to the Ottomans, who made the city their capital; the remaining Byzantine successor states at Mistra (1460) and Trebizond (1461) followed within a decade, the latter's population also subject to deportation and resettlement.

flows.label: Enslaved inhabitants dispersed into Anatolia
Surgun transfers from Anatolia → Istanbul
Surgun transfers from Rumelia → Istanbul

summary: Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453 after a seven-week siege, and by the custom of the day a city taken by storm was given over to plunder; the chroniclers describe three days of sack in which churches were stripped, thousands were killed and the bulk of the surviving population was enslaved, with the wealthier ransomed. Mehmed II then set about restoring the city as an imperial capital, issuing orders that brought settlers from all over the empire, some by inducement and many by surgun, the compulsory transfer of designated households. Muslims from Anatolia, Orthodox Christians from Rumelia and the Aegean, Armenians and Jews were installed by quarter, a pattern repeated at Trebizond, Karaman and elsewhere as new territories were absorbed. The 1477-78 survey shows a city of roughly 16,300 households, restored in size but wholly recomposed. The killing and enslavement figures rest on partisan narrative accounts and are not verifiable; the transfer policy is documented in Ottoman administrative records and surveys.
contested: The number killed and enslaved in the 1453 sack rests entirely on chroniclers with strong confessional interests, and historians disagree on how much of the city's later population arrived by compulsion rather than by the tax exemptions and property grants Mehmed also offered.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Fall of Constantinople, 1453
Harvard University, Mapping Cultural Space Across Eurasia: Repopulation and deportation (surgun)

deathsNote: The figure of about 4,000 killed during the assault and sack comes from the eyewitness and near-contemporary chroniclers of the siege and is the only number in circulation; it is a chronicler's estimate, not a count, and no modern reconstruction has been able to test it. Deaths among those enslaved and dispersed afterwards are unrecorded.
violenceNote: The killing and mass enslavement during the three-day sack, the plunder of churches including Hagia Sophia, and the compulsory transfer of households under surgun are described by the Byzantine and Italian chroniclers of the siege and by Ottoman administrative sources respectively.
baselineWhat: The population of Constantinople on the eve of the Ottoman siege
baselineNote: Steven Runciman and subsequent scholarship estimate 40,000-50,000 inhabitants in 1453, a remnant of a city that had held several hundred thousand before the Fourth Crusade of 1204; large parts of the walled area were by then fields and ruins. The surrendered towns and the compulsory transfers of 1453-78 brought in populations from across the Balkans and Anatolia.
shareCaveat: The 60,000 figure spans both the enslavement of the city's inhabitants in 1453 and the compulsory resettlement of people brought in from elsewhere, who were never part of this denominator.

title: The Đại Việt Conquest of Champa and the Sack of Vijaya
actors: Lê Thánh Tông of Đại Việt invaded Champa, stormed its capital Vijaya, and reduced the kingdom to a small southern remnant, opening central Vietnam to Vietnamese settlement
peopleRange: The figures come from the Vietnamese court annals, the Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư, which record that when Vijaya fell in March 1471 some 60,000 Cham were killed and 30,000 taken captive, including the king Trà Toàn and members of the royal family. These are victory claims written by the conquering court and are treated by historians as conventional or rhetorical rather than as counts. The subsequent movement is better attested in kind than in number: Cham communities dispersed south to Panduranga, west to Cambodia and across the maritime world to the Malay peninsula and Aceh, while Vietnamese soldier-settlers were established on the conquered land in military colonies, the beginning of the sustained southward expansion known as the nam tiến.
territoryDesc: The Cham territories from the Hải Vân pass south to Cape Varella were annexed and organised as the province of Quảng Nam; Champa survived only as the small principality of Panduranga in the far south, itself finally absorbed in 1832.

flows.label: Cham survivors → Panduranga
Cham refugees → Cambodia
Vietnamese military colonists → the annexed Cham lands

summary: In 1470-71 Lê Thánh Tông led a large invasion of Champa in response to Cham raids on the Vietnamese south, and in March 1471 stormed the Cham capital of Vijaya. The Vietnamese annals claim 60,000 Cham killed and 30,000 captured, among them the king; the city was destroyed and the kingdom's northern and central territories annexed and settled with Vietnamese military colonists. Champa, which had existed as a Hindu and later partly Muslim polity on the central Vietnamese coast for more than a millennium, was reduced to the small southern principality of Panduranga and never recovered; Cham communities dispersed to Cambodia, the Malay world and Hainan, where their descendants remain. The conquest is the decisive episode in the nam tiến, the long southward movement of Vietnamese settlement that would eventually reach the Mekong delta. Its numbers rest entirely on the annals of the victors and are not independently corroborated by Cham inscriptions or external sources.
contested: The figures of 60,000 killed and 30,000 captured come solely from the Vietnamese court annals and are generally regarded as conventional victory numbers rather than counts.

sources.title: EBSCO Research Starters: Battle of Vijaya
EBSCO Research Starters: Vietnamese-Cham Wars

deathsNote: The upper figure of 60,000 killed at the fall of Vijaya is the claim of the Đại Việt court annals and is the only number available; historians treat such figures in Southeast Asian court chronicles as rhetorical, and there is no independent evidence — archaeological or documentary — by which to test it. No lower bound can be established.
violenceNote: The storming and destruction of Vijaya, the killing and enslavement of its inhabitants and the desecration of Cham religious sites are recorded in the Vietnamese court annals, the principal surviving account of the campaign.
baselineWhat: No defensible figure exists for the population of Champa in 1471
baselineNote: Cham records were largely destroyed and Vietnamese chronicles give only casualty and captive claims - 60,000 killed and 30,000 taken at Vijaya - which historians treat as conventional round numbers rather than demography. There is no settlement survey or register from which a kingdom-wide population could be reconstructed, and published guesses vary by an order of magnitude.

title: Crimean and Nogai Slave Raiding in Eastern Europe
actors: The Crimean Khanate and allied Nogai hordes, as Ottoman vassals, raided Muscovy, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Ukrainian lands for captives who were sold through Crimean ports into the Ottoman world
peopleRange: Estimates for the whole early modern period run from roughly one and a half to three million people carried off from the East European lands, and are reconstructions rather than counts. Mikhail Kizilov's study, which reads Christian, Muslim and Jewish sources together, sets out both the basis and the weakness of these figures: they derive from customs receipts at Kefe (Caffa), from the ransom levies raised by Muscovy and Poland-Lithuania, from Ottoman and Crimean records of the slave tax, and from travellers' descriptions of the markets, none of which covers the traffic as a whole. Individual raids are better recorded: the great raids of 1521, 1571 and 1666 are each credited with tens of thousands of captives in contemporary reports.

flows.label: Ukrainian lands → Kefe (Caffa) slave market
Muscovite frontier → Crimea
Crimea → Istanbul and the Ottoman markets

summary: For nearly three centuries the steppe frontier of Eastern Europe was subject to organised raiding for captives, conducted by the Crimean Khanate and the Nogai hordes and feeding a slave market centred on the Ottoman port of Kefe. Raiding parties, sometimes numbering tens of thousands of horsemen, struck deep into Muscovy, Ukraine, Podolia and Volhynia, burning settlements and driving off people and livestock; the great raid of 1571 reached and burned Moscow itself. The captives were marched to the Crimea, sold, and dispersed across the Ottoman world as domestic slaves, concubines, agricultural workers and galley rowers. Both Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth built defensive lines and raised dedicated ransom taxes, and the Cossack hosts emerged in part as a response. Estimates of the total taken run between about one and a half and three million; Kizilov's work shows how they are assembled from customs, ransom and market records and why they remain provisional. The traffic declined as Russian power advanced into the steppe and ended with the Russian annexation of the Crimea in 1783, outside this era.
contested: The total number of captives is estimated within a range of roughly one and a half to three million and rests on partial customs and ransom records; the subject is also politically freighted in modern Russian, Ukrainian and Crimean Tatar historical writing.

sources.title: Mikhail Kizilov, 'Slave Trade in the Early Modern Crimea From the Perspective of Christian, Muslim, and Jewish Sources', Journal of Early Modern History (Brill)
Encyclopedia.com: Crimean Khanate

deathsNote: No total exists. Contemporary accounts describe killing during raids, the abandonment of the old and the very young who could not walk, and deaths on the march across the steppe to the Crimea; none of this was recorded systematically, and the estimates in circulation concern captives taken rather than people killed.
violenceNote: The seizure of women and children as the most valuable captives, their sale into domestic and sexual servitude and to the galleys, and the burning of settlements during raids are documented in the Ottoman, Crimean, Polish, Muscovite and Jewish ransom sources examined by Kizilov.
baselineWhat: The population of the raided lands - Muscovy, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Ukrainian steppe frontier - around the midpoint of the raiding era
baselineNote: There is no census. Standard reconstructions put Muscovy at roughly 6-7 million and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth at 9-10 million around 1600, giving an order of magnitude of 16 million for the territories exposed to the raids. Estimates of captives taken between 1500 and 1700 range from about 1.5 million (Fisher) to 2-3 million (Kizilov and others), reconstructed from Ottoman customs registers at Kefe, ransom accounts and chronicle notices.

baselineSources.title: Crimean–Nogai raids into East Slavic lands — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The captive total accumulates over 275 years and roughly ten generations, while the denominator is a single-year snapshot of populations that were themselves growing; the annual rate implied is on the order of 5,000-10,000 people a year, not 12 per cent of a standing population.

title: Muscovy's Subjugation of Novgorod: The Deportations of 1478-1489 and the Sack of 1570
actors: Grand Prince Ivan III and later Tsar Ivan IV annexed the Novgorod Republic, deported its landholding and merchant families to central Muscovy and settled Muscovite servitors on their estates
peopleRange: Roughly 20,000-40,000 people. Muscovite chancery records and the Novgorod land cadastres (pistsovye knigi) record the removal of several thousand boyar, merchant and landholding households between 1484 and 1489 — figures of 7,000-8,000 families are commonly given — with their lands redistributed to Muscovite pomeshchiki. Household-to-person conversion is an estimate. Chronicle death tolls for the 1570 sack range from 1,500 named in Ivan IV's own synodikon of the disgraced to 27,000 or 60,000 in later chronicle and foreign accounts; most historians treat the higher figures as inflated.
territoryDesc: The Novgorod Republic's territories, extending from the Baltic hinterland to the White Sea and the northern Urals, were absorbed into the Grand Duchy of Moscow.

flows.label: Novgorod boyar and merchant families deported to Moscow and the central provinces

summary: Ivan III ended the independence of the Novgorod Republic in 1478, and over the following decade his government deported the city's landowning, merchant and clerical elites into central Muscovy, confiscating their estates and replacing them with Muscovite service gentry — one of the earliest systematic elite transfers in Russian state practice. The veche bell, the symbol of the city's self-government, was removed to Moscow. In January 1570 Ivan IV, alleging a treasonous conspiracy with Poland-Lithuania, brought his oprichnina troops to Novgorod and conducted a sack lasting several weeks. Estimates of those killed vary by more than an order of magnitude: the tsar's own synodikon lists about 1,500 names, while the Novgorod chronicles and foreign observers such as Heinrich von Staden give figures in the tens of thousands. The city never regained its former commercial position. The entry fills a gap in the atlas between the Mongol invasion of Rus and Russia's eastward expansion after 1552.
contested: The death toll of the 1570 sack, which ranges from about 1,500 in Ivan IV's own commemorative list to 27,000-60,000 in chronicle and foreign accounts.

sources.title: Republic of Novgorod — Wikipedia
Massacre of Novgorod — Wikipedia
Ivan III of Russia — Wikipedia
Oprichnina — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The low end is the count of names in Ivan IV's synodikon of the disgraced, compiled at his own order; the high end comes from the Novgorod Third Chronicle and from foreign accounts including that of the oprichnik Heinrich von Staden. The disagreement turns on whether chronicle round numbers describe a count or a rhetorical enormity, and on whether famine and plague deaths in the following year are folded in.
violenceNote: The Novgorod chronicles and the account of the oprichnik Heinrich von Staden describe the killings, drownings in the Volkhov and torture during the 1570 sack.
baselineWhat: No defensible figure exists for the population of Novgorod and its lands across the 1478-1570 span
baselineNote: The Muscovite cadastres (pistsovye knigi) compiled after annexation record taxable peasant households in the Novgorod pyatiny but not a total population, and estimates of the city itself range from about 20,000 to 35,000 in the late fifteenth century. The affected figure combines two events almost a century apart - the deportation of landholding and merchant families in 1478-89 and the sack of 1570, whose death toll is variously given as 2,000 to 15,000 - so no single-year denominator fits it.

title: The Conquest of Granada and the Forced Conversion of Its Muslims
actors: Castile and Aragon conquered the Nasrid emirate of Granada, then set aside the surrender terms and required its Muslim population to convert to Christianity or leave
peopleRange: No count exists. The emirate's population at the surrender is usually put at 250,000-300,000 on the basis of later Castilian tax and parish records and estimates of its cultivated area; the number who emigrated to North Africa under the emigration clauses of the 1491 Capitulations, and again after the forced conversions of 1500-02, is unknown and modern guesses run from a few tens of thousands to well over a hundred thousand. The great majority stayed and were baptised, becoming the population later called Moriscos.
territoryDesc: The Nasrid emirate of Granada, the last Muslim polity in the Iberian peninsula, roughly the modern provinces of Granada, Malaga and Almeria, was annexed to the Crown of Castile; its ruling family went into exile in Morocco and its lands were redistributed to Castilian settlers, nobles and the Church.

flows.label: Granada → Fez and the Maghreb
Malaga coast → North Africa

summary: The war of 1482-92 ended eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia when Granada surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella on 2 January 1492. The Capitulations of Santa Fe guaranteed the inhabitants their religion, law, property and the right to emigrate; the population of Malaga, taken by storm in 1487, had already been enslaved en masse, and thousands were sold or ransomed. From 1499 Archbishop Cisneros pressed mass baptisms in Granada, provoking the revolt of the Albaicin and the Alpujarras in 1499-1501; its defeat was followed by a Castilian pragmatic of February 1502 requiring all Muslims in Castile to convert or leave, extended to Navarre in 1515 and to the Crown of Aragon in 1525-26. Most converted rather than emigrate, creating the Morisco population expelled a century later. Numbers are poorly recorded: the emirate's population is reconstructed from later Castilian fiscal surveys rather than counted, and the volume of emigration is not documented.
contested: How many Granadan Muslims emigrated rather than converted, and whether the 1502 pragmatic is best read as a breach of the 1491 Capitulations or as a response to the Alpujarras revolt, are both disputed.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World): Granada (Spain)
Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World): Moriscos

deathsNote: No usable death toll exists. The ten-year war, the storming of Malaga and the suppression of the 1499-1501 revolt all involved killing and mass enslavement, but the chronicles give no consistent figures and no modern reconstruction has produced a defensible total.
violenceNote: The mass enslavement of Malaga's inhabitants in 1487 and the public burning of Arabic manuscripts and the closure of mosques under Cisneros from 1499 are recorded in Castilian royal and municipal documents and in the Arabic and Castilian chronicles of the war.
baselineWhat: The Muslim population of the Nasrid emirate of Granada at the start of the war of conquest
baselineNote: Miguel Ángel Ladero Quesada and other historians of the conquest estimate the emirate at roughly 300,000 people, with wider ranges of 250,000-500,000; the figures are reconstructed from Castilian settlement and tax records compiled after 1492 rather than from any Nasrid census. Perhaps 100,000 left for North Africa during and after the war, and those who remained were required to convert after 1499-1502.

title: The Demographic Collapse of the Indigenous Americas
actors: European colonisation of the Americas was followed by a population collapse whose causes — imported epidemics, war, enslavement, forced labour and the destruction of subsistence systems — are weighted differently by different scholars
peopleRange: This is one of the most contested numbers in history and every figure must be attributed. For the hemisphere in 1492: Alfred Kroeber estimated 8.4 million and Ángel Rosenblat 13.4 million; Henry Dobyns proposed 90 to 112.5 million; William Denevan's regional synthesis gives about 54 million, the figure most often used as a middle position; Koch and colleagues' 2019 reconstruction gives about 60 million falling to roughly six million by 1600, a decline of about 90 per cent. Linda Newson's survey stresses that these totals are built from regional estimates of very unequal quality and that the causes varied by region with settlement density, contact intensity and the labour regime imposed. There is no census; the numbers are reconstructions from tribute records, mission registers, carrying-capacity models and archaeology.
summary: Between 1492 and the mid-seventeenth century the indigenous population of the Americas fell catastrophically, and the size of that fall depends almost entirely on an unobservable starting figure. The published estimates for 1492 span more than an order of magnitude, from Kroeber's 8.4 million and Rosenblat's 13.4 million at one end to Dobyns's 90-112 million at the other, with Denevan's roughly 54 million and Koch and colleagues' roughly 60 million occupying the middle. Nearly all specialists agree that imported epidemic disease — smallpox, measles, typhus, influenza — was the largest single killer, because it struck populations with no prior exposure and repeatedly, but Newson and others argue that disease cannot be treated as an independent variable: mortality was highest where conquest, enslavement, forced labour in mines and fields, tribute exaction, forced resettlement and the destruction of food systems left populations unable to care for the sick, and falling fertility then prevented recovery. Some regions were emptied within a generation, others declined slowly, and a few populations stabilised and grew again. Because the figure has become politically charged, this atlas gives the range and the scholars attached to each end rather than adopting a single number.
contested: Everything about the magnitude is disputed: the 1492 baseline ranges from about 8 million to over 100 million depending on method, and the weighting of epidemic disease against violence, enslavement and coerced labour is argued about both as a matter of evidence and as a matter of moral framing.

sources.title: Linda A. Newson, 'The Demographic Collapse of Native Peoples of the Americas, 1492-1650' (British Academy, PDF)
Koch et al., 'Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492', Quaternary Science Reviews (2019) — open access copy, UCL Discovery
Robert McCaa, 'The Population of Mexico from Origins to Revolution' (University of Minnesota)

deathsNote: The bounds are not a measurement but the consequence of the disputed baseline. A minimalist starting population of the Rosenblat or Kroeber type implies a loss on the order of ten million; Denevan's roughly 54 million and Koch's roughly 60 million imply losses in the tens of millions; Dobyns's figures imply a loss approaching one hundred million. The overwhelming majority of these deaths are attributed by nearly all scholars to imported epidemic disease rather than to direct killing, but Newson and others insist the epidemics acted on populations already broken by conquest, enslavement, forced labour and famine, so the categories cannot be cleanly separated.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Newson's survey documents systematic killing, enslavement and ill treatment under the early encomienda and the mine labour drafts as contributory causes of the decline alongside epidemic disease, and these forms are recorded in the Spanish crown's own inquiries and in mission and tribute records.
baselineWhat: The Indigenous population of the Americas on the eve of European contact in 1492
baselineNote: There is no census. Modern reconstructions from carrying-capacity models, early colonial tribute and mission counts and archaeological survey range from about 40 million to over 100 million; Denevan's widely used consensus figure is roughly 54 million, and Koch and colleagues (2019) model about 60 million. Lower-end estimates (Ubelaker, Rosenblat) fall below 15 million for some regions, so the figure carries an uncertainty of tens of millions.

baselineSources.title: Population history of Indigenous peoples of the Americas
Koch et al. (2019), Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492, Quaternary Science Reviews

title: The Expulsion of the Jews from Spain
actors: Ferdinand and Isabella ordered all Jews who would not convert to Christianity to leave Castile and Aragon within four months
peopleRange: Contested by a factor of ten or more. Early modern chroniclers gave 160,000, 300,000 or even 800,000; these are rhetorical. Modern work using Castilian and Aragonese tax registers, community lists and the records of returning converts has cut the figure sharply: the Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World reports over ten thousand leaving by the Mediterranean coast in 1492-93 and 'possibly as many as forty to fifty thousand' overall, while noting even that may be high because many who left returned and converted by 1499. Henry Kamen's revision, which puts the Jewish population of Spain at well under 100,000 and departures at roughly 40,000-50,000, is now widely but not universally accepted; other scholars retain figures of 100,000 or more.

flows.label: Castile → Portugal
Aragon → Ottoman lands
Andalusia → North Africa

summary: The edict issued at Granada on 31 March 1492 gave the Jews of Castile and Aragon until the end of July to accept baptism or leave, forbidding them to take gold, silver or coined money. Many converted; the rest dispersed to Portugal, Navarre, North Africa, Italy and above all the Ottoman Empire, where Bayezid II received them and where the Jewish population of Istanbul and Salonica grew sharply. A substantial minority returned within a few years and were baptised, which is one reason the figures are so hard to pin down. The scale is genuinely disputed: traditional totals of several hundred thousand rest on chroniclers rather than records, and archival work since the 1980s has produced figures around a tenth of those. What is not disputed is that a Jewish communal presence that had existed in Iberia for over a millennium was ended by state order.
contested: The number expelled ranges from about 40,000 in Henry Kamen's revision to 200,000 or more in older accounts; the difference turns on estimates of Spain's Jewish population and on how many converted or returned rather than emigrating.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World): Jews, Expulsion of (Spain; Portugal)
Jewish Virtual Library: The Expulsion of the Jews from Spain

deathsNote: There was no organised killing. Deaths occurred on the roads and at sea, from shipwreck, disease, robbery and the conditions of a forced departure in high summer, and are described in Jewish and Christian narrative sources; no reliable total exists and no modern scholar has proposed one.
violenceNote: The edict of 31 March 1492 ended the legal residence of Jews as such in the Spanish kingdoms and barred them from removing precious metals or coin, a combination of expulsion and confiscation recorded in the text of the edict itself and in the Crown's implementing orders.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of Castile and Aragon at the time of the Alhambra Decree
baselineNote: Estimates rest on tax rolls of the aljamas and on the accounts of chroniclers, and differ by more than a factor of two. Ladero Quesada and Henry Kamen argue for roughly 80,000; Haim Beinart and older traditions give 200,000 or more. The number is politically freighted because it bears directly on how many left versus how many converted. About 100,000 sits at the lower-middle of the range.

baselineSources.title: History of the Jews in Spain — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: Both the number expelled and the size of the community are disputed by roughly the same factor, and many who left returned within a few years and converted, so the ratio is uncertain at both ends.

title: The Spanish Conquest of the Caribbean and the Collapse of the Taíno
actors: Spanish settlers on Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Jamaica and Cuba seized land and distributed the indigenous population in encomiendas, raided neighbouring islands for slaves, and within two generations the Taíno had all but disappeared as a distinct population
peopleRange: The starting population is one of the most contested figures in demographic history. Bartolomé de Las Casas wrote of three to four million on Hispaniola; Sherburne Cook and Woodrow Borah reconstructed about eight million; Ángel Rosenblat put it near 100,000; Massimo Livi Bacci's re-examination of the Spanish counts and the island's carrying capacity argues for a few hundred thousand at most. What is documented is the direction and speed of the fall: Spanish tribute counts recorded roughly 60,000 tributary Indians in 1508 and about 26,000 in the repartimiento of 1514, and by mid-century the Taíno were reported to have ceased to exist as a separate community. Tens of thousands more were carried in from the Bahamas and the Lucayan islands, which were emptied, and from the Venezuelan pearl coast.
territoryDesc: The Greater Antilles and the Bahamas passed under Spanish rule; land was distributed to settlers and the surviving indigenous population was resettled around mines, farms and mission villages, with the Bahamas depopulated entirely by slave raiding.

flows.label: Lucayans seized from the Bahamas → Hispaniola
Taíno redistributed to mines and encomienda estates
Captives from the pearl coast → Hispaniola

summary: Within a generation of 1492 the indigenous societies of the Greater Antilles were destroyed. Settlers were granted encomiendas entitling them to the labour and tribute of named indigenous communities; villages were broken up and relocated to serve gold placers and estates, and when local labour ran short, raiding parties emptied the Bahamas and the coasts of Venezuela and Central America. Old World epidemics, above all the smallpox outbreak of 1518-19, arrived on top of forced labour, famine and the dislocation of subsistence agriculture, and the compounding of these causes is why the collapse was so fast. The scale of the loss is disputed by more than an order of magnitude, with high estimates from Las Casas and from Cook and Borah, minimal estimates from Rosenblat, and Livi Bacci arguing that even a few hundred thousand starting population implies near-total destruction. The Spanish crown's own investigations, the Laws of Burgos of 1512-13 and the New Laws of 1542 were responses to reports of the collapse, and failed to stop it.
contested: Whether Hispaniola held a few hundred thousand or several million people in 1492, and how far the collapse should be attributed to epidemic disease rather than to enslavement, forced labour and the destruction of subsistence agriculture, remain unresolved.

sources.title: Massimo Livi Bacci, 'The Decline of the Taino, 1492-1542: A Re-Vision' (PDF, University of Connecticut)
Encyclopedia.com: Taino (Arawak) Indians
Encyclopaedia Britannica: encomienda

deathsNote: No defensible total exists because the starting population is unknown to within an order of magnitude. Whatever the baseline, the surviving records show that the great majority of the Taíno died within about fifty years; scholars differ on the mix of epidemic disease, forced labour in the placers, famine caused by the disruption of cultivation, and outright killing, with Livi Bacci emphasising the labour and subsistence collapse and others emphasising imported pathogens.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Forced labour under the encomienda and in the gold placers, punitive campaigns against resisting caciques, and the destruction and forced relocation of villages are documented in the Spanish crown's own inquiries, the Jeronymite interrogatory of 1517 and the reports of Bartolomé de Las Casas, whose numbers but not whose account of the practices are disputed.
baselineWhat: The indigenous (Taíno and neighbouring) population of the Greater Antilles in 1492
baselineNote: No defensible single figure exists. Estimates for Hispaniola alone span more than two orders of magnitude — from a few tens of thousands implied by recent genetic work, through Karen Anderson Córdova's maximum of about 500,000, to Las Casas's claim of over three million; Jamaica and Puerto Rico together are put at a maximum of about 600,000. Because the plausible range is so wide, any percentage built on it would be an artefact of the estimate chosen rather than a finding.

title: The Forced Conversion of the Jews of Portugal and the Lisbon Massacre
actors: King Manuel I of Portugal decreed expulsion, then blocked departure and had the Jewish population forcibly baptised; a Lisbon crowd later massacred the converts
peopleRange: No count. Portugal's Jewish population had been swollen by refugees admitted from Castile in 1492 on payment of an entry fee, and contemporary estimates of that influx run from 20,000 to over 100,000 without documentary support. The point of the 1497 measures was that almost nobody left: Manuel restricted embarkation to Lisbon and had those who assembled there baptised by force, so the displacement here is a conversion in place rather than an exodus. Emigration of New Christians followed over the next decades, much of it clandestine, and is not quantified.

flows.label: Jewish children → São Tomé (1493)
New Christian emigration → the Low Countries and beyond

summary: John II had already, in 1493, seized some two thousand children of Castilian Jewish refugees and shipped them to the newly settled island of São Tomé, where most died. His successor Manuel I decreed the expulsion of Jews and Muslims on 5 December 1496 as a condition of his marriage to a Spanish princess, but did not want to lose the community: he restricted departure to a single port, and in October 1497 had the Jews gathered at Lisbon baptised en masse. Conversion by force created a large New Christian population that was legally Catholic and socially marked, and in April 1506 a Lisbon crowd, incited by friars during plague and famine, killed converts in the streets over roughly three days; the toll is usually given as between one and four thousand and rests on contemporary accounts rather than a count. Emigration was formally barred until 1507 and restricted repeatedly thereafter. The Portuguese Inquisition, established in 1536, pursued the descendants of these forced converts for two centuries.
contested: The size of the Jewish population of Portugal in 1497 and the death toll of the 1506 Lisbon massacre are both known only from narrative sources and vary widely between them.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World): Jews, Expulsion of (Spain; Portugal)
Jewish Virtual Library: The Expulsion of the Jews from Spain

deathsNote: The range is for the Lisbon massacre of April 1506 and comes from contemporary and near-contemporary narratives, including the account attributed to Solomon ibn Verga and reports by foreign residents; there was no official count. Deaths among the children deported to São Tomé in 1493 were reported as very high by contemporaries but were never enumerated.
violenceNote: The seizure of Jewish children for deportation to São Tomé in 1493 and for forced baptism in 1497, and the killing of converts at Lisbon in 1506, are documented in Portuguese royal chronicles, in Jewish narrative sources and in the correspondence of foreign merchants resident in Lisbon.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of Portugal after the arrival of refugees from Castile and Aragon
baselineNote: Portugal's own Jewish community is generally put at 20,000-30,000 before 1492. Between 20,000 and 60,000 Castilian refugees were admitted in 1492 on payment of an entry tax, giving totals in the sources from about 40,000 to 100,000. The figures derive from Portuguese crown revenue records and contemporary chroniclers, and are contested.

title: Barbary Corsair Captive-Taking in the Mediterranean
actors: Corsairs operating from Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli and Salé, under Ottoman or Moroccan authority, seized European ships and raided coastal villages, holding captives for ransom or forced labour; European corsairs from Malta, Livorno and Spain did the same to Muslim shipping and coasts
peopleRange: The best-known figure is Robert Davis's estimate that as many as a million to 1.25 million Europeans were taken and held in North Africa between 1500 and 1800. Davis derived it not from a count of captives but from a model: he estimated the standing slave populations of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli from contemporary observers and then calculated how many new captives would have been required to maintain those populations given mortality, ransom and conversion. The method has been criticised as producing figures well above what ransom, consular and redemptionist-order records support, and other historians work with substantially lower numbers. The corresponding traffic in the other direction — Muslims taken by Maltese, Tuscan and Spanish corsairs and put to the galleys — is less studied and less quantified.

flows.label: Raids on the Italian coast → Algiers
Raids on the Spanish coast → Salé
The 1627 raid on Iceland → Algiers and Tunis
Muslim captives taken by Maltese corsairs held at Valletta

summary: For three centuries the western Mediterranean was a zone of reciprocal captive-taking. Corsairs sailing from the Ottoman regencies of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli and from Moroccan Salé took merchant ships and landed on the coasts of Italy, Spain, the Balearics, Corsica and occasionally as far as Ireland and Iceland, carrying off villagers to be ransomed, put to the oars or set to labour; Christian corsairs from Malta, Livorno and the Spanish presidios raided Muslim shipping and coasts in the same way. Redemptionist religious orders such as the Trinitarians and Mercedarians raised money to ransom Christian captives and kept records that survive; the 1627 raid that took some four hundred people from Iceland and the sacking of Italian coastal villages are among the best-documented episodes. Robert Davis's estimate of a million or more European captives between 1500 and 1800 brought the subject wide attention and is contested on method: it is a model-based reconstruction from estimated standing slave populations, not a count. The trade in both directions collapsed only with European naval dominance in the nineteenth century, and the topic is now frequently mobilised in polemics about the comparative history of slavery.
contested: Robert Davis's figure of about a million European captives is derived from a demographic model of standing slave populations rather than from records, and other historians regard it as too high; the reciprocal enslavement of Muslims by Christian corsairs is far less quantified and is often omitted from popular accounts.

sources.title: Ohio State University Department of History: Robert C. Davis, 'Christian Slaves, Muslim Masters'
History News Network: 'Historian Claims in New Book that More than a Million White Europeans Were Captured by North African Slave Traders'

deathsNote: No total exists. Captives died in raids, at the oars of galleys, in the bagnios of the North African ports and in Christian galleys and prisons; Davis's model assumes heavy mortality among slaves in order to generate its capture figures, which makes any death estimate derived from it circular.
violenceNote: Galley service and labour in the bagnios, indefinite detention pending ransom, the taking of women and children in coastal raids and their sale into domestic and sexual servitude are documented in ransom and consular records, the archives of the redemptionist orders and captivity narratives from both sides of the sea.
baselineNote: No single denominator exists: captives were taken from the coasts and shipping of Italy, Spain, France, Portugal, Greece, and as far as Ireland and Iceland, over two and a half centuries. Robert Davis's estimate of 1-1.25 million European captives between 1530 and 1780 is itself an extrapolation from replacement rates in the North African slave populations and has been criticised as high; other historians suggest figures a third to a half as large.

title: The Khivan and Bukharan Slave Trade and Turkmen Raiding of Persia and Russia
actors: Turkmen and Kazakh raiders captured Persians, Russians and others for sale in the slave markets of Khiva and Bukhara
peopleRange: Russian officers who occupied Khiva in 1873 recorded the emancipation of roughly 29,300-40,000 slaves, most of them Persian; the Russian envoy Baron von Meyendorff estimated around 40,000 Persian slaves in the Bukhara khanate in 1820, and British travellers gave comparable orders of magnitude. Cumulative estimates of Iranians enslaved in Central Asia between 1500 and 1900 run to around a million, notably in Thomas Ricks's work, extrapolated from market and raiding accounts rather than counted. Contemporary numbers come from Russian and British travellers, diplomats and military reports.

flows.label: Captives from Khorasan and northern Persia to the Khiva slave market
Russian and Volga captives to Bukhara

summary: For centuries the khanates of Khiva and Bukhara were the principal slave markets of Central Asia, supplied chiefly by Turkmen raiders of the Yomut and Tekke tribes who took captives from Shia Persian Khorasan - religious opinion in the Sunni khanates treating Shia Persians as lawfully enslavable - and also by raids on Russian settlements, shipping on the Caspian and caravans. Slaves worked as agricultural labourers on irrigated estates, as artisans and in households; the trade was central to the economies of the oasis khanates. Captured Russians became a recurring pretext for Russian intervention, from the disastrous Khivan expedition of 1839-40 to the conquest of 1873, when General Kaufman's forces occupied Khiva and the khan was compelled to abolish slavery; Russian officers recorded the emancipation of tens of thousands, most of them Persian. Bukhara's slavery was formally abolished in 1873 as well, and finally with the fall of the emirate in 1920. Cumulative totals across the early modern period are extrapolations from traveller and diplomatic accounts, not counts.
contested: Cumulative totals for the number enslaved over three centuries are extrapolations from traveller reports; only the 1873 emancipation figure has a contemporaneous administrative basis, and Russian sources had an interest in emphasising the trade as justification for conquest.

sources.title: Khivan slave trade
Bukharan slave trade
Khivan campaign of 1873 and the emancipation of slaves

deathsNote: No death toll can be established. Raiding, forced marches across the Karakum and conditions of captivity killed an unknown number; travellers described high mortality on the routes from Khorasan but produced no figures.
violenceNote: Russian and British diplomatic and traveller accounts, and the Russian emancipation records of 1873, document forced agricultural and domestic labour, the taking of children and the sale of women as concubines.
baselineWhat: No single population can serve as a denominator for nearly four centuries of raiding across Persia, the Russian steppe frontier and Central Asia
baselineNote: The captives were taken from Khorasan and the Persian plateau, Russian and Ukrainian frontier settlements, and neighbouring Central Asian peoples over some 370 years, with no continuous source population. The firmest numbers are terminal: Russian forces recorded roughly 40,000 slaves freed in Khiva at the 1873 conquest and comparable numbers in Bukhara, and nineteenth-century Persian estimates of one million captives taken overall are extrapolations rather than counts.

title: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade to 1750
actors: Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, English, French and Danish merchants, licensed by their states and supplied by African polities and traders, shipped captive Africans across the Atlantic to American plantations and mines
peopleRange: These are the best-documented forced migration figures of the pre-modern world. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, built from the records of some 36,000 individual voyages, estimates 12.52 million captives embarked and 10.7 million disembarked across the whole trade to 1866; roughly 4.5 to 5 million of those embarkations had occurred by 1750, the great majority after 1650 as the sugar colonies of the Caribbean and Brazil expanded. The database's own methodology notes that documented voyages cover about 85 per cent of embarkations, and that the totals are estimates built by extrapolation from shipping records, port registers and customs data rather than a complete count. The figures exclude those who died between capture and embarkation, who are not counted anywhere.

flows.label: West Central Africa → Brazil
Gold Coast → the Caribbean
Bight of Benin → Jamaica and Saint-Domingue
Bight of Biafra → mainland North America

summary: Between 1501 and 1750 something on the order of five million people were carried from Africa across the Atlantic as slaves, part of a traffic that reached 12.5 million embarkations before it ended. The trade grew slowly in the sixteenth century, when Portuguese and Spanish shipping predominated, then expanded sharply from the 1640s as Dutch, English and French planters developed sugar in the Caribbean and as Brazil's plantation economy grew; by the first half of the eighteenth century well over a million people were being shipped every twenty-five years. Captives were obtained through warfare, raiding, judicial enslavement and debt within Africa and sold at coastal factories to European carriers; the largest single source region was West Central Africa. Mortality on the Atlantic crossing averaged in the region of twelve to fifteen per cent over the period, falling over time, and further deaths occurred during capture, the march to the coast and confinement in barracoons, none of which appear in the shipping records. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, which underlies all modern figures, is explicit that its totals are estimates extrapolated from documented voyages rather than a census.
contested: The database's totals are widely accepted but its compilers note that a higher overall figure — they cite 15.4 million departures as an alternative — would imply that documented voyages cover only two-thirds of the trade; deaths before embarkation are undocumented and are estimated by inference rather than counted.

sources.title: SlaveVoyages: Estimates — Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
SlaveVoyages: Methodology of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade estimates
Klas Rönnbäck, 'The Slave Trades out of Africa' (African Economic History Network, PDF)

deathsNote: The lower bound is the implied number who died at sea before 1750: the database's own embarked and disembarked totals imply an average loss of roughly one captive in eight on the Atlantic crossing, which on four to five million embarkations gives something over half a million deaths in transit. The upper bound adds the deaths that occurred between capture and embarkation — in the wars and raids that produced captives, on the march to the coast and in coastal barracoons — which are not recorded in any source and are estimated by historians at a further fraction comparable to or greater than shipboard mortality. No count of the latter exists and every figure for it is an inference.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Chaining and confinement in barracoons and below decks, the shipping of children as a substantial minority of captives, sexual violence aboard ship and punishment regimes are documented in the shipping records, surgeons' logs, parliamentary inquiries and captives' own narratives that underlie the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database.
baselineWhat: No single population can serve as a denominator for two and a half centuries of embarkations from the whole Atlantic coast of Africa
baselineNote: The Slave Voyages database reconstructs embarkations and disembarkations voyage by voyage, but the source populations were dozens of polities from Senegambia to Angola whose sizes over 250 years cannot be reconstructed; Manning's modelling of Atlantic Africa suggests populations in the tens of millions, but the deaths, dislocations and captures within Africa are not captured by any denominator. A percentage here would be spurious.

title: The Portuguese Conquest of Goa and Malacca
actors: Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa and Malacca for the Portuguese crown, killing or expelling their Muslim populations and installing a garrisoned trading empire across the Indian Ocean
peopleRange: No counts survive. Portuguese chronicles record that Albuquerque, on retaking Goa in November 1510, ordered the killing of the city's Muslim inhabitants over several days, a figure of about six thousand being repeated in the Portuguese sources; at Malacca in 1511 the Muslim, Javanese and Gujarati population was killed, enslaved or driven out while Hindu, Chinese and Burmese merchants were spared and their property protected, on Albuquerque's own account. The sultan and his court withdrew to Bintan and then founded Johor, taking a substantial following with them. All these numbers come from the conquerors' own chronicles and Albuquerque's letters, written to justify and celebrate the campaigns, and cannot be checked.
territoryDesc: Goa became the capital of the Estado da Índia and Malacca its eastern anchor, giving Portugal control of the straits through which the spice trade between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea passed; the sultanate of Malacca was destroyed and its successor state established at Johor.

flows.label: Sultan's court and followers → Bintan and Johor
Muslim merchants relocate trade to Aceh, Banten and Java
Goa: Muslim population killed or expelled, city resettled

summary: Portugal's seaborne empire in Asia was founded on the seizure of two entrepôts. Goa was taken in 1510 and, after being lost and retaken, its Muslim inhabitants were massacred on Albuquerque's orders; the city became the capital of the Estado da Índia and the seat of a Portuguese settler and mixed-descent population. Malacca, the greatest emporium of Southeast Asia, fell in August 1511 after a short campaign; Albuquerque's letters describe the killing and expulsion of the Muslim population and the deliberate sparing of Hindu, Chinese and other merchants whose trade Portugal wished to keep. The sultanate re-formed at Bintan and then at Johor, and much of the Muslim commercial network shifted to Aceh, Banten and Brunei, so that Portuguese Malacca never recovered the traffic it had captured. The scale of killing and expulsion is known only from Portuguese narrative sources; there are no independent counts, and the figures they give are contested.
contested: The numbers killed at Goa in 1510 and at Malacca in 1511 come only from Portuguese chronicles and Albuquerque's own dispatches, and historians differ over whether these are boasts, conventional figures or approximations.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: Portuguese Malacca

deathsNote: No reliable figure. The repeated Portuguese claim of about six thousand Muslims killed at Goa in 1510 is the only number of any precision and derives from the conquerors' chronicles; deaths at Malacca are described but not counted.
violenceNote: The massacre of Goa's Muslim inhabitants, the killing and expulsion of Malacca's Muslim community and the conversion or destruction of mosques are recorded in Albuquerque's own letters and in the Portuguese chronicles of the conquest.
baselineWhat: The populations of Goa and Malacca at the time of the Portuguese conquests
baselineNote: No count exists for either city. Tomé Pires, writing in the 1510s, describes Malacca as a port of extraordinary size and later estimates derived from him run from about 40,000 to 190,000 inhabitants; for Goa there is no comparable figure at all. Because the two cities' estimates differ by a factor of four and cannot be added to anything reliable, no denominator is offered.

title: The Spanish Conquest of Mexico and the Depopulation of the Central Highlands
actors: Cortés and his indigenous allies destroyed the Mexica capital and the Spanish crown replaced the Aztec tributary state with a colonial regime of encomienda, tribute and congregación resettlement
peopleRange: Central Mexico's population in 1519 is estimated between about 4.5 million and 25 million and its seventeenth-century nadir at about one to 1.5 million. Sherburne Cook and Woodrow Borah reconstructed 25.2 million in 1519 falling to 1.2 million by 1620; Ángel Rosenblat put 1519 at 4.5 million and the fall at under a quarter; Rudolph Zambardino's statistical critique gave five to ten million falling to about one million; William Sanders's archaeological surveys suggested roughly half the Cook-Borah figure. Robert McCaa's survey concludes the 1519 population was 'certainly five million, probably ten, and perhaps fifteen, if not twenty or twenty-five million'. Separately, the congregación programmes of the 1550s and 1590s resettled surviving communities into planned towns; the numbers moved are recorded case by case in Spanish administrative records but have never been totalled.
territoryDesc: The Aztec tributary empire and its neighbours became the Viceroyalty of New Spain; land and labour rights were granted to Spanish encomenderos, and surviving indigenous communities were regrouped into nucleated towns under Spanish and ecclesiastical supervision.

flows.label: Survivors expelled from Tenochtitlán after the siege
Congregación: dispersed villages regrouped into planned towns

summary: The siege of Tenochtitlán ended in August 1521 with the city starved, largely destroyed and its surviving inhabitants driven out; the campaign was fought by a few hundred Spaniards alongside tens of thousands of Tlaxcaltec and other indigenous allies, and a smallpox epidemic swept the city during the siege. The conquest state that followed rested on the encomienda, on tribute assessments inherited from the Mexica, and from the 1550s on congregación, the compulsory regrouping of dispersed settlements into towns to make labour and tithes easier to extract. Central Mexico then suffered the steepest recorded demographic collapse in the hemisphere, driven principally by successive epidemics — smallpox in 1520, measles in 1531, and the cocoliztli outbreaks of 1545 and 1576 that killed millions — compounded by forced labour, tribute demands, the disruption of agriculture and forced resettlement. The size of that collapse is disputed by a factor of five: the range of published estimates for 1519 runs from Rosenblat's 4.5 million to Cook and Borah's 25.2 million, and the choice of baseline determines whether the loss is counted in millions or tens of millions. McCaa notes that war mortality was of decidedly secondary importance beside epidemic disease, while stressing that overwork, ecological damage and forced relocation shaped who survived.
contested: The pre-conquest population of central Mexico, and therefore the absolute magnitude of the collapse, is disputed between the high reconstructions of Cook and Borah and the minimal figures of Rosenblat, with Zambardino, Sanders and McCaa occupying the middle ground.

sources.title: Robert McCaa, 'The Population of Mexico from Origins to Revolution' (University of Minnesota)
World History Encyclopedia: The Fall of Tenochtitlan
Encyclopaedia Britannica: encomienda

deathsNote: The range simply reflects the disputed baseline: Rosenblat's reconstruction implies a loss of roughly one million from a population of 4.5 million, Zambardino's four to nine million, and Cook and Borah's about 24 million by 1620. Nearly all scholars attribute the great majority of these deaths to imported epidemic disease rather than to killing; forced labour, tribute exaction, famine and resettlement are treated as aggravating factors that raised mortality and suppressed recovery. Deaths in the fighting itself, including the siege of Tenochtitlán, are a small fraction of the total.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The starvation siege and destruction of Tenochtitlán, the massacre at the Templo Mayor festival in 1520 and at Cholula in 1519, compulsory labour drafts, and the destruction of temples and codices are described in the Spanish conquistador accounts, in the indigenous testimony collected in the Florentine Codex and in the crown's own inquiries.
baselineWhat: The Indigenous population of central Mexico on the eve of the Spanish invasion in 1519
baselineNote: There is no census; every figure is a modern reconstruction from tribute lists, early colonial counts and carrying-capacity modelling, and scholars differ by a factor of five. The Berkeley school (Cook and Borah) put central Mexico at about 25 million; Sanders and Whitmore reconstruct 11-16 million; Zambardino argued for 5-10 million. About 15 million sits in the middle of the credible range. All schools agree the population fell to roughly 1-2 million by 1600.
