title: The Spanish Conquest of Peru and the End of Tawantinsuyu
actors: Pizarro's expedition seized and executed the Inca Atahualpa, took Cusco and destroyed the Inca state, and Spanish rule was consolidated by the execution of the last Inca at Vilcabamba in 1572
peopleRange: Estimates of the population of the Inca realm in 1520 range from about three million to fourteen million, with Noble David Cook's regional reconstruction of Peru giving a mid-range figure near nine million and minimalist estimates near three. Colonial tribute inspections give the falling side of the curve rather than its starting point: the visitas of the 1570s counted around 1.3 million in the area later covered by the Toledo assessments, and by the 1620s the tributary population had fallen further. The conquest itself displaced people mainly through the collapse of the Inca state's own resettlement system, which had moved large numbers of mitmaqkuna colonists, many of whom returned or were stranded when the state that placed them ceased to exist.
territoryDesc: Tawantinsuyu, the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas, spanning modern Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador and parts of Chile, Argentina and Colombia, was absorbed into the Viceroyalty of Peru; its lands, herds and labour obligations were reassigned to Spanish encomenderos and the crown.

flows.label: Political centre shifts from Cusco to the new Spanish capital at Lima
Neo-Inca state at Vilcabamba dispersed after 1572

summary: Francisco Pizarro's small force arrived during a war of succession between Atahualpa and Huáscar and in November 1532 seized Atahualpa at Cajamarca, killing much of his entourage; he was ransomed and then executed in 1533. Cusco was taken the same year, and after the failed siege of 1536-37 and decades of civil war among the conquerors, the rump Inca state at Vilcabamba was destroyed and Túpac Amaru executed in 1572. Epidemics preceded the Spaniards: smallpox is generally held to have reached the Andes around 1524-27, killing the Inca Huayna Capac and precipitating the succession war. The demographic decline that followed was severe but is documented only through colonial tribute inspections, which count taxable adults rather than people, and the pre-conquest baseline is disputed between roughly three and fourteen million. What the conquest added to disease was the seizure of land and herds, the encomienda, and from 1569 the systematic resettlement and labour drafts described separately.
contested: The population of the Inca realm at contact, and how much of the subsequent decline is attributable to epidemics that arrived before the Spaniards themselves, are both disputed.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: European Contact Overwhelms the Inca Empire — Francisco Pizarro's Conquest of Peru
Linda A. Newson, 'The Demographic Collapse of Native Peoples of the Americas, 1492-1650' (British Academy, PDF)

deathsNote: No defensible total for the conquest period alone. Deaths at Cajamarca and in the sieges and civil wars ran to thousands and are described in Spanish and mestizo chronicles without reliable counts; the far larger mortality came from epidemics beginning before 1532 and continuing through the sixteenth century, and cannot be separated from the wider collapse treated in its own entry.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The killing of Atahualpa's unarmed entourage at Cajamarca, the sack of Cusco, punitive campaigns during the risings of 1536-37 and the extirpation of Andean shrines are recorded in the accounts of the conquistadors themselves and in the indigenous and mestizo chronicles of Guaman Poma and Garcilaso de la Vega.
baselineWhat: The population of Tawantinsuyu, the Inca empire, on the eve of the Spanish invasion
baselineNote: There is no census. Reconstructions rest on early colonial tribute lists and visitas: John Rowe's back-projection gives about 6 million, Noble David Cook's Demographic Collapse: Indian Peru 1520-1620 offers a range of roughly 4 to 14 million with a working figure near 9 million, and some ecological reconstructions go higher still. The 9 million used here is a mid-point of Cook's range and should be read as an order of magnitude.

baselineSources.title: Population history of indigenous peoples of the Americas

shareCaveat: Most Andean population loss over the sixteenth century came from introduced epidemic disease rather than from the conquest campaigns, so a ratio against this baseline attributes to the invasion deaths with several causes.

title: Toungoo Burma's Wars of Conquest and the Deportation of Ayutthaya, Lan Na and Lan Xang
actors: The Toungoo kings of Burma conquered the Tai states and Siam and carried their populations back to Pegu as labour and soldiers
peopleRange: All figures come from Burmese, Thai and Lan Na chronicles compiled after the events, which use conventional and often rhetorical numbers. Chronicles state that tens of thousands were taken from Ayutthaya in 1564 and again in 1569, that Chiang Mai and the Lan Na towns were emptied of skilled populations in 1558, and that Vientiane's people were carried off in the 1560s-70s. A total on the order of 100,000 over the half-century is the conventional reading of these accounts; it cannot be verified against any record.
territoryDesc: At its height under Bayinnaung the Toungoo empire held Lower and Upper Burma, the Shan states, Lan Na, Lan Xang and Siam, the largest state in mainland Southeast Asian history to that date

flows.label: Captives from Ayutthaya to Pegu
Captives from Chiang Mai to Pegu

summary: Between 1548 and 1569 the Toungoo kings Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung conquered the Shan states, Lan Na, Lan Xang and Siam, and made deportation a standard instrument of rule: skilled artisans, monks, soldiers and whole village populations were marched to the capital at Pegu, where they supplied labour and manpower for the next campaign, and defeated royal families were resettled at the Burmese court. Ayutthaya was taken in 1564 and again in August 1569, when the Siamese royal house and a large part of the city's population were carried north. The empire could not hold together after Bayinnaung's death in 1581: Siam broke away under Naresuan, and in 1599 Pegu itself was sacked by an Arakanese and Toungoo coalition and its own population dispersed, an inversion of what it had done to others. Everything known about the numbers comes from chronicle traditions written for later courts, Burmese and Thai, which differ from each other and use figures for effect. The atlas already covers the later phase of these wars, including the 1767 sack of Ayutthaya, in its entry on deportation warfare between Burma and Siam in 1759-1828.
contested: Burmese and Thai chronicle traditions give different accounts of the same campaigns and different figures; modern national histories on both sides continue to use them for contrasting purposes.

sources.title: Burmese-Siamese War (1568-1569)
Bayinnaung

deathsNote: No usable toll. Chronicles describe heavy mortality in the sieges of Ayutthaya and Vientiane and among deportees on the marches to Pegu, and famine in Siam after 1569, but the numbers given are literary conventions rather than counts.
violenceNote: Burmese, Thai and Lan Na chronicles describe the mass removal of captured populations to Pegu for labour and military service.
baselineWhat: The combined population of Ayutthaya, Lan Na and Lan Xang in the mid-sixteenth century
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Mainland Southeast Asia has no sixteenth-century census; population estimates for Siam, Lan Na and Lan Xang derive from later fiscal registers, European travellers' guesses and modern back-projection, and published figures for the region around 1600 differ by a factor of two or more between Lieberman, Reid and Thai national historiography. Deportation counts in the Burmese and Thai chronicles are themselves formulaic.

title: Russian Eastward Expansion: Kazan, Astrakhan, Siberia and the Yasak
actors: Muscovy and then the Russian Empire conquered the Volga khanates and Siberia, imposed a fur tribute enforced by hostage-taking, and settled Russian colonists on indigenous land
peopleRange: No overall count. Kazan was stormed in 1552 with the killing of its defenders and the expulsion of Tatars from the city, where they were barred from residing inside the walls, and Tatar and Chuvash villages were displaced by monastic and service-gentry estates through the later sixteenth century. In Siberia the state's own records are fiscal rather than demographic: yasak registers count taxable adult males, from which the entire indigenous population of Siberia in the seventeenth century is reconstructed at roughly 200,000-230,000. Populations were moved as much by flight from tribute collection, hostage-taking and epidemic as by expulsion, and the resulting movements are not quantified.
territoryDesc: The khanates of Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556) brought the whole Volga to the Caspian under Moscow; the Siberian khanate fell after 1582 and Russian ostrogs reached the Pacific at Okhotsk in 1639 and the Kamchatka peninsula by the 1700s, adding roughly thirteen million square kilometres and its indigenous peoples to the Russian state.

flows.label: Tatars expelled from Kazan to outlying settlements
Russian servitors and settlers → eastern Siberia

summary: Ivan IV's storm of Kazan in October 1552 and the annexation of Astrakhan in 1556 removed the successor khanates of the Golden Horde and opened the Volga and the Urals to Russian settlement; Tatars were expelled from Kazan itself and lands were granted to monasteries and servicemen, with episodes of forced baptism through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. East of the Urals, expansion was carried out by Cossack bands and merchant companies building fortified ostrogs along the river systems, and was financed by the yasak, a fur tribute levied on indigenous households and enforced by taking hostages, the amanaty, from each clan. Resistance, notably by the Koryak and Chukchi and in the Kamchatka risings of 1731 and 1741, was met with punitive expeditions; smallpox epidemics from the 1630s onwards killed a very large share of Yakut, Tungus, Yukaghir and Itelmen populations, in some districts most of them. Russian historiography traditionally described this as the peaceful 'joining' of Siberia; a competing literature, and some indigenous organisations, describe it as conquest with genocidal effects. The documentary base is overwhelmingly the tribute registers of the conquering state.
contested: Whether Russian expansion into Siberia should be characterised as colonial conquest with catastrophic demographic consequences, or as a largely commercial incorporation, is disputed; so is how much of the indigenous population decline is attributable to imported epidemics rather than to tribute exactions, hostage-taking and punitive campaigns.

sources.title: S. V. Bakhrushin, 'Yasak (fur tribute) in Siberia in the seventeenth century', trans. in Alaska Journal of Anthropology (PDF)
Encyclopedia.com: Siberia

deathsNote: No defensible total. Indigenous Siberian populations fell steeply between the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, with smallpox the largest identified cause and punitive expeditions, hostage-taking and the disruption of hunting economies also implicated; because the only systematic records are tribute rolls of taxable men, the decline can be traced but not converted into a death toll.
violenceNote: The taking of clan hostages including children to guarantee yasak payment, punitive expeditions against non-paying clans, forced baptism campaigns in the Volga region and the requisition of indigenous labour and transport are documented in Russian government yasak registers and voevoda reports analysed by S. V. Bakhrushin and later Russian and Western historians of Siberia.
baselineWhat: The indigenous population of Siberia at the time of the Russian conquest, as reconstructed from the yasak tribute registers
baselineNote: B. O. Dolgikh's classic reconstruction from seventeenth-century yasak books gives roughly 216,000-227,000 indigenous Siberians in the early 1600s; later scholars regard this as a minimum because tribute rolls counted adult men liable to pay. The figure excludes the settled populations of the Volga khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan, conquered in 1552 and 1556, which numbered several hundred thousand more.

title: The French Wars of Religion, the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre and the Flight of the Huguenots
actors: The French crown, Catholic and Protestant nobles and urban militias killed, besieged and drove out confessional opponents across France
peopleRange: No defensible aggregate exists for wartime flight. Contemporary registers show Geneva, the Rhineland, England and the Dutch provinces receiving thousands of French Protestant refugees, with the largest surges after the massacres of 1572, and internal flight between towns was continuous; the register-based counts that support the much better documented exodus after the 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes, treated separately in this atlas, do not exist for the 1560s-1590s. Any single figure for this period would be a guess.

flows.label: French Protestants to Geneva
Huguenot refugees to England
Huguenot refugees to the Dutch provinces

summary: Between 1562 and 1598 France went through eight civil wars fought along confessional lines, punctuated by urban massacres, sieges and the expulsion of minority communities from towns that changed hands. The best known episode began in Paris on 24 August 1572, when the killing of Protestant leaders gathered for a royal wedding spread to the city's Huguenot population and then to at least a dozen provincial cities over the following weeks; historians generally estimate about 2,000 killed in Paris and perhaps 10,000 in total, against older accounts that ranged from 5,000 to 30,000. The massacres produced conversions, abjurations and a wave of emigration to Geneva, the Rhineland, England and the Dutch provinces, and they hardened the Huguenot 'places of safety' in the south and west. The wars ended with the Edict of Nantes of April 1598, which granted the Huguenots limited worship rights and fortified towns; the settlement held until Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, producing the far larger exodus recorded separately in this atlas. Estimates of total mortality from all causes over the whole period range widely, from about two to four million, and include famine and epidemic deaths as well as killing.
contested: Both the death toll of the St Bartholomew's Day massacres and the total mortality of the wars are disputed, the latter because the higher figures fold in famine and epidemic deaths in a period of poor demographic evidence; the degree of royal responsibility for ordering the 1572 killings beyond a small group of Protestant leaders is also debated among historians.

sources.title: French Wars of Religion (Wikipedia)
St. Bartholomew's Day massacre (Wikipedia)

deathsNote: The range is for the St Bartholomew's Day massacre and its provincial sequels: roughly 2,000 killed in Paris on modern estimates, with perhaps 10,000 across France in the following weeks. Older accounts gave 5,000 to 30,000 nationally. Total mortality for the wars as a whole is separately estimated at two to four million from all causes, a figure dominated by famine and disease and not by direct killing.
violenceNote: Killings, iconoclasm and the sacking of churches and houses by both confessions are documented in contemporary chronicles, municipal records and martyrologies used by modern historians of the wars.
baselineWhat: The Protestant (Huguenot) population of France at the outbreak of the wars
baselineNote: Estimates rest on the number of Reformed congregations, about 1,200-2,150 churches by 1562, and on regional consistory records; historians generally put the Huguenots at up to one in ten of a French population of some 18-20 million at the start of the wars, or roughly two million, falling to about 800,000 by the Edict of Nantes in 1598. Total war deaths across the eight wars are estimated at two to four million including famine and disease, and the great Huguenot emigration came later, after the 1685 revocation.
shareCaveat: The wars killed and displaced Catholics as well as Protestants, so a Huguenot denominator understates the population the fighting acted upon, while a national denominator would understate how heavily the burden fell on the Reformed minority.

title: The Dutch Revolt and the Exodus from the Southern Netherlands
actors: Spanish Habsburg armies reconquered the southern Netherlands, expelling or driving out Protestant townspeople to the northern provinces and abroad
peopleRange: Demographic reconstructions from city registers, guild rolls and church membership lists, associated above all with the work of J. G. C. A. Briels, put migration from the southern Netherlands to the northern provinces at roughly 100,000-150,000 over the later sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries; further thousands went to England, the Rhineland and the Baltic. The single clearest datum is Antwerp, whose population fell from about 100,000 before the 1584-85 siege to about 40,000 after it, when Protestants were given four years to settle their affairs and leave.

flows.label: Antwerp merchants and artisans to Amsterdam
Ghent and Flemish textile workers to Leiden and Haarlem
Flemish and Walloon refugees to London and East Anglia

summary: The revolt against Philip II's rule in the Low Countries, opened by the Duke of Alba's repression from 1567, was fought city by city, and the Spanish reconquest of the south between 1579 and 1585 emptied its Protestant communities. Sacks by unpaid Spanish troops set the pattern: Mechelen and Zutphen in 1572, Naarden the same year, the 'Spanish Fury' at Antwerp in November 1576, in which contemporaries claimed as many as 17,000 dead and a thousand buildings burned, and Maastricht in 1579. When Antwerp capitulated on 17 August 1585, Alexander Farnese allowed its Protestants four years to wind up their affairs and depart rather than expelling them outright, and the city lost some 60,000 of its 100,000 people. The northern provinces, England and the Rhineland absorbed the emigrants, and the transfer of Antwerp's merchants, printers and textile workers to Amsterdam, Leiden and Haarlem is treated in the standard economic histories as a foundation of the Dutch Golden Age. Casualty figures reported by sixteenth-century chroniclers for the sacks, particularly Antwerp 1576 and Maastricht 1579, are generally regarded as inflated.
contested: The scale of the sacks is disputed: figures such as 17,000 dead at Antwerp in 1576 or only 400 survivors of 30,000 at Maastricht in 1579 come from contemporary polemical accounts circulated as anti-Spanish propaganda and are treated with caution by modern historians, while the emigration totals are reconstructions from partial registers rather than counts.

sources.title: Fall of Antwerp (Wikipedia)
Spanish Fury (Wikipedia)
Eighty Years' War (Wikipedia)
Dutch Golden Age (Wikipedia)

deathsNote: The range covers civilians killed in the major sacks of the revolt (Mechelen, Naarden and Zutphen in 1572, Antwerp in 1576, Maastricht in 1579). The upper end reflects contemporary chronicle and pamphlet claims, notably 17,000 at Antwerp, which circulated as propaganda; the lower end reflects modern scepticism about those numbers. Deaths from the sieges' hunger and disease are not included and were probably larger.
violenceNote: Massacre, arson and the plunder of churches during the sacks are described in contemporary chronicles and city records on both sides, which modern historians use while discounting their casualty arithmetic.
baselineWhat: The population of the southern provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands at the start of the revolt
baselineNote: Hearth counts and urban registers put the seventeen provinces at roughly 3 million in the 1560s, with about 2 million in the ten southern provinces. The exodus was overwhelmingly urban: Antwerp fell from about 100,000 inhabitants in 1560 to roughly 42,000 by 1589, and Ghent, Bruges and Brussels lost comparable shares.
shareCaveat: The emigrants were drawn almost entirely from the Protestant urban population of Flanders and Brabant, a small fraction of the southern provinces, so the share against the whole population understates the effect on the towns.

title: The Toledo Reducciones and the Potosí Mita
actors: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo forcibly regrouped the Andean rural population into planned towns and instituted a rotating forced-labour draft to supply the silver mines of Potosí
peopleRange: The general resettlement of the 1570s is usually said to have moved on the order of 1.4 million people from thousands of scattered hamlets into roughly eight hundred to a thousand new towns; Jeremy Mumford's study of the general resettlement is the standard modern account and the figures derive from the visita records compiled for Toledo's inspection, which counted tributaries rather than people. The mita quota established for Potosí required about 13,500 conscripts a year drawn from sixteen highland provinces, roughly one adult man in seven from each community serving in rotation, travelling with their families for distances of hundreds of kilometres. Both figures are administrative targets recorded in colonial legislation, not counts of people actually moved, and evasion and flight were widespread.
territoryDesc: The rural settlement pattern of the central Andes, based on dispersed hamlets exploiting several ecological tiers, was replaced by grid-plan towns; vacated lands were declared surplus and passed to Spanish estates, and the mita drew labour from an arc of provinces stretching from Cusco to southern Bolivia.

flows.label: Mita conscripts from the Collao → Potosí
Mita conscripts from Cusco province → Potosí
Dispersed hamlets regrouped into reducción towns

summary: Between 1569 and 1581 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo carried out the largest programme of compulsory resettlement in the colonial Americas, uprooting the dispersed Andean settlement pattern and concentrating the rural population into new grid-plan towns, the reducciones, where tribute could be assessed, doctrine taught and labour drafted. In parallel he adapted the Inca institution of the mita into a rotating conscription that sent roughly 13,500 men a year, with their households, from sixteen provinces to the silver mines of Potosí and the mercury mine at Huancavelica. Conditions in the mines and refineries were lethal, though no reliable mortality series exists; the surviving records show sustained flight from mita provinces, the growth of a class of permanent migrants who had abandoned their home communities to escape the draft, and the passage of vacated community land into Spanish hands. Colonial administrators themselves recorded that the reducciones did not hold: by the end of the sixteenth century officials complained that taxpaying Indians were fleeing in growing numbers. Modern economic research has traced measurable long-run disadvantage in districts that were subject to the mita compared with adjacent districts that were not.
contested: How many people were actually moved, and how far the demographic decline of the mita provinces should be attributed to the labour draft and the resettlement rather than to epidemics affecting the whole Andes, are both disputed.

sources.title: University of Pennsylvania, Digital Indigenous Americas: 'Colonial Legislations as Framework for Dispossessions in the Central Andes — the Reducciones'
University of Pennsylvania, Digital Indigenous Americas: 'Colonial Legislations as a Framework for Dispossessions in the Central Andes — the Colonial Mita'
Jeremy Ravi Mumford, 'Vertical Empire: The General Resettlement of Indians in the Colonial Andes' (Duke University Press)

deathsNote: No defensible death toll exists. Mortality at Potosí and Huancavelica was notoriously high — mercury poisoning at Huancavelica, cave-ins, silicosis and cold at Potosí — and colonial critics from the seventeenth century onward wrote of millions dead, but those numbers are polemical and no record permits a count of mita deaths as against deaths from the epidemics that struck the same populations.
violenceNote: The compulsory labour draft, the burning or abandonment of old settlements to prevent return, and the campaigns to extirpate Andean shrines that accompanied resettlement are documented in Toledo's own ordinances and inspection records and analysed in the University of Pennsylvania project and in Mumford's study.
baselineWhat: The indigenous population of the Viceroyalty of Peru enumerated in Viceroy Toledo's general inspection of 1570-1575
baselineNote: Toledo's visita general, the first systematic count of the Andes, enumerated roughly 1.3-1.5 million tributary Indians and their dependants across the viceroyalty; the sixteen highland provinces made liable for the Potosí mita held on the order of a million of them. The pre-conquest Andean population was far larger, with estimates from about 4 to 12 million, so this baseline is already a post-collapse figure.
shareCaveat: The affected figure is close to the whole enumerated population because the reducciones resettled essentially everyone counted, while the mita draft that followed extended over roughly seven further generations, so the ratio measures the reach of one resettlement rather than the total number of people the programme touched over 1569-1750.

title: The Spanish Reduccion and Resettlement of the Philippine Lowlands
actors: Spanish colonial authorities and missionary orders concentrated dispersed Philippine populations into mission towns and imposed tribute and forced labour
peopleRange: Spanish tribute lists and missionary reports record most of the lowland Christianised population - on the order of half a million to a million people in the seventeenth century - resettled from scattered barangay hamlets into nucleated pueblos 'under the bell'. Linda Newson's demographic reconstruction from tribute records estimates a Philippine population of roughly 1.5-2 million at contact and substantial decline in the resettled lowlands. The figures rest on tribute counts kept for taxation, which under-record those who fled to the uplands.
territoryDesc: Lowland Luzon and the Visayas reorganised into pueblos, encomiendas and later provinces under the Spanish crown

flows.label: Dispersed barangay settlements gathered into mission pueblos

summary: From the 1570s Spanish colonial administrators and the Augustinian, Franciscan, Jesuit and Dominican orders pursued a policy of reduccion in the Philippines, gathering populations that had lived in scattered kin-based settlements into nucleated towns built around a church, in order to convert, tax and levy labour from them. Residents were subject to tribute, to the polo y servicios corvee that supplied labour for shipyards, fortifications and the Manila galleon trade, and to compulsory sale of produce; missionary and administrative records treat the concentration as largely complete in the Christianised lowlands of Luzon and the Visayas by the seventeenth century. Substantial numbers escaped by moving to the uplands or to unpacified areas, becoming the remontados and the still-independent peoples of the Cordillera and the Muslim south, whom Spain never subdued. Revolts against tribute and labour drafts recurred through the period. Linda Newson's reconstruction from tribute records finds significant population decline in the resettled lowlands from disease, labour drafts and disruption, though on nothing like the scale of Spanish America.
contested: How much of the lowland population was actually resettled, and how far demographic decline was caused by resettlement and labour drafts as opposed to introduced disease, are debated.

sources.title: History of the Philippines (1565-1898)
Polo y servicio (Spanish colonial forced labour in the Philippines)
Linda A. Newson, Conquest and Pestilence in the Early Spanish Philippines (University of Hawai'i Press)

deathsNote: No defensible range. Newson's tribute-based reconstruction shows regional population decline in the century after conquest, but disentangling deaths caused by resettlement, labour drafts and epidemics from ordinary mortality is not possible with the surviving records.
violenceNote: Spanish colonial and missionary records themselves document the polo y servicios labour draft and the suppression of indigenous religious practice in the reduccion towns.
baselineWhat: The population of the Philippine archipelago at the time of Spanish conquest
baselineNote: Linda Newson's reconstruction from early tribute records in Conquest and Pestilence in the Early Spanish Philippines (2009) gives about 1.5-1.6 million around 1570. Earlier estimates ranged from 500,000 to over 2 million; the tribute lists that underpin all of them counted taxable households in the pacified lowlands only.
shareCaveat: Reduccion applied to the Christianised lowlands; the Cordillera highlands and the Muslim sultanates of Mindanao and Sulu were largely outside it and are inside this denominator.

title: Portuguese Angola and the West Central African Slaving Wars
actors: Portugal established colonies at Luanda and Benguela and waged and financed wars against Ndongo, Kongo and their neighbours, exporting captives on a scale that made West Central Africa the largest single source of the Atlantic trade
peopleRange: West Central Africa — the Congo and Angola coasts — supplied more captives to the Atlantic trade than any other African region, on the order of 5.7 million across the whole trade according to the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, of which a substantial share was shipped before 1750 through Luanda and, from the 1610s, Benguela. Port-level series compiled from Portuguese customs and shipping records show Luanda alone dispatching thousands of captives a year through the seventeenth century. Numbers for those killed, enslaved and displaced inside Angola by the wars themselves do not exist: the Portuguese sources count exports, not the populations that produced them.
territoryDesc: Portuguese authority extended from Luanda (founded 1575) and Benguela (1617) up the Kwanza valley through a chain of forts and allied chieftaincies; the kingdom of Ndongo was broken, the kingdom of Kongo defeated at Mbwila in 1665 and fragmented, and the interior was reorganised around slaving polities such as Kasanje and Matamba.

flows.label: Captives from the Kwanza interior → Luanda
Luanda → Bahia and Pernambuco
Benguela → Rio de Janeiro

summary: From the foundation of Luanda in 1575 the Portuguese presence in West Central Africa was organised around the acquisition of captives, through direct campaigning up the Kwanza, through alliance with the Imbangala warrior bands, and through the purchase of people taken in wars fought by African states. Ndongo was progressively destroyed, its ruler Njinga waging a long resistance from Matamba; Kongo, a Christian kingdom that had dealt with Portugal on treaty terms since 1491, was defeated at Mbwila in 1665 and dissolved into civil war that itself generated captives. The Dutch occupation of Luanda in 1641-48 interrupted but did not end the traffic. The consequence was that this stretch of coast became the single largest source region of the Atlantic slave trade, and Brazil its principal destination. The scale of the internal disruption — populations moved out of raiding zones, states reorganised around the supply of captives, the depopulation of some districts and the fortification of others — is described in Portuguese and missionary sources and in African oral tradition, but has never been quantified.
contested: Historians differ over how far the Atlantic demand for captives caused the wars of the region as against intensifying conflicts that had other origins, and over the resulting demographic effect on West Central African populations, which cannot be measured.

sources.title: Maximiliano M. Menz and Wolfgang Lenk, 'Luanda, Global Capital of the Slave Trade', in Portuguese Colonial Cities (TeseoPress)
EBSCO Research Starters: The Ndongo Wars
SlaveVoyages: Estimates — Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade

deathsNote: No defensible figure exists. Portuguese campaign accounts and missionary reports describe heavy mortality in the wars of the Kwanza valley, in the great famines and epidemics that followed them, and among captives held at Luanda awaiting shipment, but the colonial records were kept to track exports and duties, not deaths, and no reconstruction has produced a total.
violenceNote: Campaigns that destroyed settlements and carried off their inhabitants, the holding of captives in coastal pens before shipment, and the taking of children among the captives are documented in Portuguese governors' correspondence, Capuchin missionary reports and the customs records analysed by Menz and Lenk.
baselineWhat: The population of West Central Africa during the Portuguese slaving wars
baselineNote: No population figure for the Kongo, Ndongo, Matamba and Ovimbundu lands in this period is reliable enough to serve as a denominator; Joseph Miller and John Thornton work instead from export series and from the demographic effects of removals on age and sex structure. What is well documented is the outflow: the Slave Voyages database records some 2.8 million captives embarked from West Central Africa between 1575 and 1750, the largest single regional stream of the Atlantic trade.
