title: Bandeirante Slave Raiding and the Destruction of the Guairá Missions
actors: Slave-raiding expeditions from São Paulo, the bandeiras, seized indigenous people across the Brazilian interior, destroying the Jesuit Guaraní missions of Guairá and extending Portuguese claims deep into Spanish territory
peopleRange: No reliable totals. Jesuit reports of the raids on the Guairá missions between 1628 and 1632 speak of tens of thousands of Guaraní carried off to São Paulo — figures of sixty thousand and more appear in mission correspondence and in later accounts — while the missionaries evacuated survivors south, leading several thousand people down the Paraná in 1631 in one of the largest organised flights of the colonial Americas. Figures for the total number of indigenous people enslaved by Paulista expeditions over the whole period range into the hundreds of thousands in some accounts; all rest on partisan Jesuit reporting or on later Brazilian narrative and none can be verified.
territoryDesc: Bandeira expeditions carried Portuguese presence west and south beyond the line of Tordesillas, destroying the Spanish Jesuit mission province of Guairá in what is now Paraná and helping fix the eventual boundaries of Brazil; they later opened the interior to the gold rushes of Minas Gerais and Goiás.

flows.label: Guaraní captives from Guairá → São Paulo
Mission Guaraní evacuated south down the Paraná

summary: From the late sixteenth century, expeditions from the frontier town of São Paulo ranged over the Brazilian interior in search of indigenous captives to work the sugar and wheat farms of the south, and later in search of gold. Between 1628 and 1632 large bandeiras under Antônio Raposo Tavares and others attacked the Spanish Jesuit reductions of Guairá, west of the Paraná, destroying the mission towns and driving their Guaraní inhabitants back to São Paulo in coffles; the Jesuits evacuated what remained of the population downriver in 1631 and resettled it further south. Raiding continued against the missions of Itatín and Tape until the Guaraní, permitted firearms by the Spanish crown, defeated a bandeira at Mbororé in 1641. Portuguese law repeatedly restricted and then permitted indigenous enslavement — the crown prohibited it in principle in 1570, 1609 and 1680 while allowing capture in 'just war' and the ransom of captives from other Indians — and the traffic continued under those exceptions. Brazilian nationalist historiography long celebrated the bandeirantes as pioneers of the nation's territory; that commemoration is now contested in Brazil precisely because of the slaving.
contested: The numbers of Guaraní enslaved come from Jesuit reports written to press the Spanish crown for protection, and are disputed; so is the modern commemoration of the bandeirantes in Brazil, where monuments to them have become a focus of public argument.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: Bandeiras
EBSCO Research Starters: Jesuits in Colonial Brazil

deathsNote: No defensible total. Jesuit accounts describe heavy mortality during the raids and on the forced marches to São Paulo, and epidemics repeatedly swept both the mission towns and the captive populations; the sources are partisan and record neither captives nor deaths systematically.
violenceNote: The burning of mission towns, the killing of those who resisted, the marching of captives in chains to São Paulo and the seizure of children are described in Jesuit reports and Spanish colonial complaints, and summarised in the reference literature on the bandeiras.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: the bandeiras ranged over the whole Brazilian interior for 140 years, and only the mission populations were ever counted
baselineNote: The raids ran from Sao Paulo across Guaira, the Parana-Paraguay basin, Minas Gerais and the Amazon fringe between 1580 and 1720, acting on dozens of unenumerated indigenous societies. The only counted population is that of the Jesuit reductions: the Guaira missions held on the order of tens of thousands of Guarani when they were destroyed in 1628-32, and the Parana-Uruguay reductions to which the survivors fled numbered around 40,000 in the 1640s. Estimates of Brazil's indigenous population in 1500 range from about 2.4 million (IBGE, following Rosenblat) to 5 million or more, but none of these can be attached to the specific interior the bandeirantes raided.

title: The Japanese Invasions of Korea (Imjin War)
actors: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's armies invaded Chosŏn Korea twice, devastating the peninsula and carrying tens of thousands of Koreans to Japan as captives before withdrawing after his death
peopleRange: The best-attested figure concerns captives: the survey of the war's legacies in the Transactions of the Royal Historical Society reports Yang Liu's estimate that between 20,000 and 100,000 Koreans were forcibly taken to Japan, with many more seized during the fighting and abandoned when the Japanese withdrew. Among them were potters whose descendants founded the Satsuma and Arita ceramic traditions, and craftsmen and scholars deliberately selected. Internal displacement was on a far greater scale — the court fled to the Yalu, Seoul and Pyongyang were abandoned, and whole provinces were emptied — but was never counted. Korean records of cultivated land show a catastrophic fall between the pre-war and post-war surveys, which historians use as a proxy for demographic and economic ruin rather than as a population figure.
territoryDesc: Japanese forces occupied most of the peninsula in 1592 and the southern provinces again in 1597-98, building coastal fortresses; no territory was permanently transferred, and Japanese forces withdrew entirely in 1598.

flows.label: Korean captives, including potters, → Satsuma and Kyushu
Court and population flee north to Uiju on the Yalu
Flight from the southern provinces inland

summary: Hideyoshi launched some 158,000 troops against Korea in 1592, took Seoul within three weeks and Pyongyang soon after, and was checked by Korean naval victories under Yi Sun-sin, by local righteous armies and by Ming intervention; a second invasion in 1597 was confined to the southern provinces and ended with his death in 1598. The war was fought largely on Korean soil and its effects on the population were severe: cities and palaces burned, agriculture ruined and famine and epidemic following the armies. Japanese commanders sent home noses and ears taken from the dead as proof of service, interred at the Mimizuka mound in Kyoto, and carried off Korean captives in large numbers, some sold on to Portuguese traders, others settled in Japan as artisans; between 20,000 and 100,000 are estimated to have been taken. Korean sources describe massacres of civilians at Jinju in 1593 and in the southern provinces in 1597-98. No reliable death toll exists for either side; figures of a million or more Korean dead appear in popular accounts without a documentary basis.
contested: The number of Koreans taken to Japan is given as a wide range by different scholars, and the war's total mortality has never been reliably estimated; the interpretation of the war remains sensitive in Korean and Japanese public memory.

sources.title: 'Legacies of the Imjin War (1592-1598) in and beyond East Asia', Transactions of the Royal Historical Society (Cambridge University Press)
'Japan's Invasion of Chosŏn Korea and Abduction of Koreans' (Project MUSE)

deathsNote: No defensible total. Korean, Japanese and Ming sources describe heavy losses among soldiers and civilians, including the massacre of the population of Jinju in 1593, but none permits a count; the figures of a million or more Korean deaths that circulate in general accounts have no documentary basis, and specialist work has not replaced them with a reliable number.
violenceNote: The massacre of civilians at Jinju and in the southern provinces, the taking of noses and ears as trophies interred at the Mimizuka, and the abduction of craftsmen, scholars, women and children to Japan are documented in Korean court records, Japanese commanders' reports and Buddhist and missionary accounts discussed in the Royal Historical Society survey.
baselineWhat: The population of Chosŏn Korea on the eve of the Japanese invasion of 1592
baselineNote: Chosŏn household registers are known to be severe undercounts (they record roughly 4 million), and modern Korean historical demography (Kwon Tae-hwan, Tony Michell) reconstructs a population of roughly 9-14 million in the late sixteenth century. A round 10 million is the commonly used working figure; the war and the epidemics and famine that followed are thought to have cut it substantially.

title: Shah Abbas's Deportations and the Founding of New Julfa
actors: Shah Abbas I of Safavid Iran, retreating before Ottoman armies, applied a scorched-earth policy to the Armenian and Georgian borderlands and deported their populations into the Iranian interior
peopleRange: The Encyclopaedia Iranica, following the seventeenth-century Armenian historian Arakel of Tabriz who witnessed the events, states that more than 400,000 people were deported to Iran during the scorched-earth withdrawal of 1603-05, the main movement taking place between 21 October and 19 November 1604. They were driven across the Aras river in cold and rain, wintered at Khalkhal, Ahar and Meshkin, and in the spring distributed to Gilan, Mazandaran and the countryside between Isfahan, Shiraz and Hamadan, with selected merchants and artisans of Julfa settled at Isfahan in the new suburb of New Julfa. Arakel's figure is the only one available and is a contemporary estimate, not a count; the parallel deportations from Georgia during the campaigns of 1614-17 are described in Georgian and Persian chronicles with figures that Georgian historiography puts in the tens of thousands killed and over a hundred thousand deported, and that are not independently verifiable.
territoryDesc: The Armenian districts of Nakhichevan, Julfa and the Ararat plain, and later parts of Kakheti in eastern Georgia, were deliberately laid waste to deny supplies to advancing Ottoman armies, leaving a depopulated buffer along the frontier.

flows.label: Julfa on the Aras → New Julfa, Isfahan
Ararat plain → Gilan and Mazandaran
Kakheti, eastern Georgia → the Iranian interior

summary: In the winter of 1603-05, as Ottoman armies advanced into the Caucasus, Shah Abbas I ordered the destruction of crops and pastures across the frontier districts and the removal of their inhabitants into Iran. The Armenian population of Julfa on the Aras, a wealthy merchant town, was resettled at Isfahan in a purpose-built suburb, New Julfa, where the shah granted its merchants privileges and a monopoly of the Iranian silk export trade, making the community central to Eurasian commerce for a century. The mass of the deportees fared very differently: driven in autumn rains and cold across a river that many drowned in, wintered in the mountain districts of Azerbaijan and then scattered across the interior, they suffered heavy losses that contemporaries describe but do not count. Abbas repeated the policy in Georgia in 1614-17, deporting Kakhetian Georgians and settling Turkic tribes in their place; Georgian tradition treats these campaigns as a national catastrophe and the figures it gives are not independently attested. The events are documented above all by Arakel of Tabriz, an Armenian eyewitness, alongside Persian court chronicles.
contested: The figure of 400,000 deportees comes from a single contemporary Armenian historian and cannot be checked; the death toll of the Georgian campaigns of 1614-17 is given in far higher numbers by Georgian national historiography than by Persian sources.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: 'Julfa i. Safavid Period'

deathsNote: No count exists. Arakel of Tabriz and other contemporaries describe large numbers drowning in the Aras, dying of cold and hunger on the winter march and perishing in the malarial lowlands of Gilan and Mazandaran where many were settled; the proportion who died is variously described as very heavy but was never counted, and no modern reconstruction has produced a figure.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The deliberate burning of crops and pastures, the forced winter march and the resettlement of deportees on state and crown lands are described by the eyewitness Armenian historian Arakel of Tabriz and summarised in the Encyclopaedia Iranica.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: no register exists for the Armenian and Georgian borderlands the campaign emptied
baselineNote: The deportee totals come from contemporary chroniclers, above all Arakel of Tabriz, who gives figures in the hundreds of thousands for the 1604-05 removal from Julfa, Nakhichevan and the Ararat plain, and from Georgian and Ottoman accounts of the Kakheti campaigns of 1614-17, in which perhaps 60,000-100,000 were killed and 100,000-130,000 deported. There is no independent enumeration of the population of eastern Armenia or Kakheti before the campaigns, so any denominator would be circular, resting on the same chronicles as the numerator.

title: The Beaver Wars and the Dispersal of the Wendat, Neutral and Erie
actors: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) confederacy, armed by Dutch and English traders, destroyed or absorbed neighbouring nations and emptied large areas of the eastern Great Lakes; French and Algonquian allies fought back
peopleRange: Tens of thousands. The Wendat (Huron) confederacy, estimated at 20,000-30,000 people before 1634 on the basis of Jesuit Relations censuses of longhouses, was reduced by epidemics and then dispersed in 1649-1650, its survivors scattered to Quebec, to Michilimackinac and into Haudenosaunee towns as adoptees. The Petun, Neutral, Erie and Susquehannock were dispersed in turn between 1650 and 1680. Numbers rest on Jesuit missionary counts, which are reasonably careful for the Wendat and much weaker for the others; there is no independent check.
territoryDesc: Southern Ontario, the Niagara peninsula, the Ohio country and much of the lower Michigan peninsula were largely emptied of settled villages for decades and held as Haudenosaunee hunting territory.

flows.label: Wendat survivors fleeing to the French settlement at Quebec (Wendake)
Wendat and Neutral captives adopted into Haudenosaunee towns

summary: Competition over the fur trade and over captives to replace population lost to epidemics drove a long series of wars in which the Haudenosaunee confederacy attacked and dispersed its neighbours. The Wendat confederacy, already halved by smallpox in the 1630s, was broken in 1649-1650 when its principal towns were destroyed; the Petun, Neutral, Erie and later the Susquehannock followed. Survivors were killed, fled westward and northward, or were adopted into Haudenosaunee communities in numbers large enough that Jesuit observers reported adoptees outnumbering the original population of some towns. The wars emptied southern Ontario and the Ohio country of settled villages for a generation and reshaped the map of the eastern Great Lakes before the Great Peace of Montreal in 1701. The atlas covered New England's Pequot and King Philip's wars but nothing of the interior; this is the largest Indigenous-driven displacement in seventeenth-century North America.
contested: How far the dispersals were driven by the fur trade, by mourning-war captive-taking to replace epidemic losses, or by European arms supply — a long-running argument in the historiography — and whether contemporary Jesuit population figures are reliable.

sources.title: Beaver Wars — Wikipedia
Iroquois — Wikipedia
Wyandot people — Wikipedia
Great Peace of Montreal — Wikipedia

deathsNote: No count exists. The range is a scholarly order-of-magnitude estimate across nearly a century, and folds together killing in raids, deaths in flight and famine, and the smallpox and measles epidemics of the 1630s-1660s that preceded and enabled the dispersals; separating war deaths from epidemic deaths is not possible with the Jesuit sources available.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The Jesuit Relations, written by missionaries resident among the Wendat and later among the Haudenosaunee, record the destruction of the Wendat towns and the adoption of captives including children.
baselineWhat: The Iroquoian-speaking nations of the lower Great Lakes destroyed or dispersed in the wars - Wendat (Huron), Tionontate (Petun), Neutral, Erie and Susquehannock - around 1600
baselineNote: Reconstructed from Jesuit Relations village and longhouse counts and archaeological settlement survey rather than any census. Trigger put the Wendat at about 20,000-30,000 before the epidemics of 1634-40, with the Neutral of comparable size and the Erie and Petun smaller; totals for the five nations are usually placed between 60,000 and 110,000.
shareCaveat: The 1600 baseline precedes the smallpox and measles epidemics of 1634-40, which had already cut these nations by roughly half before the Haudenosaunee campaigns began, so the share understates how much of the surviving population was killed, adopted or dispersed.

title: The Dutch Conquest and Depopulation of the Banda Islands
actors: The Dutch East India Company under Jan Pieterszoon Coen destroyed the population of the Banda Islands to secure a monopoly of nutmeg and mace, and repopulated the islands with company planters and enslaved labourers
peopleRange: The islands are generally reckoned to have held on the order of 13,000 to 15,000 people before 1621; after the campaign contemporaries counted around a thousand survivors still on the islands. Several hundred were shipped to Batavia as slaves, of whom many died; others escaped to the Kei and Aru islands and to Seram, where Bandanese communities survive. All these figures derive from Dutch East India Company reports and correspondence, which counted the population as a labour and revenue problem; there was no census, and the pre-conquest total is an estimate.
territoryDesc: The Banda archipelago, then the world's only source of nutmeg and mace, was taken into direct company ownership; its land was divided into perken, plantation blocks granted to company servants who worked them with enslaved labour imported from elsewhere in the archipelago.

flows.label: Bandanese deported as slaves → Batavia
Refugees → Kei and Aru islands
Refugees → Seram and Ambon

summary: The Dutch East India Company had sought a monopoly of the Banda spice trade since 1609, when a Bandanese ambush killed a company admiral and much of his party. In 1621 Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen arrived with a large force, occupied Lonthor, and in the campaign that followed the islands' population was killed, starved on the slopes to which it had fled, deported or driven overseas; forty-four leading orang kaya were tortured and executed by Japanese mercenaries in company service after a summary process. Contemporary reports describe roughly a thousand people remaining on islands that had held on the order of fifteen thousand. The company then divided the nutmeg groves into perken worked by imported enslaved labour under Dutch planters, an arrangement that lasted until the nineteenth century. A body of scholarship, including work published as 'Genocide in the Spice Islands', argues the destruction meets the definition of genocide; the Dutch government has not made any formal determination on the events of 1621.
contested: Whether the destruction of the Bandanese constitutes genocide is argued by historians and by Indonesian commentators; there has been no formal legal or governmental finding, and the pre-conquest population figure rests on company estimates.

sources.title: 'Genocide in the Spice Islands: The Dutch East India Company and the Destruction of the Banda Archipelago Civilisation in 1621' (National Cheng Kung University research output)

deathsNote: No count exists. Company correspondence records the execution of forty-four orang kaya and describes people killed in the fighting, starved on the cliffs of Lonthor where they had taken refuge, drowned, and dying in transit to Batavia; historians infer that the great majority of a population of some fifteen thousand died, but the only figures are the estimated population before and the roughly one thousand counted afterwards.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The torture and beheading of the orang kaya, the driving of the population into the interior where many starved, the burning of villages and the enslavement of survivors on the confiscated nutmeg plantations are documented in the Dutch East India Company's own reports and Coen's correspondence.
baselineWhat: The population of the Banda Islands before the Dutch East India Company's campaign
baselineNote: Contemporary VOC and English accounts and modern reconstructions put the Bandanese at roughly 13,000-15,000 across Banda Neira, Lonthor and the smaller islands. After Coen's campaign of 1621 about 1,000 remained on the islands; roughly 1,700 were taken as slaves to Batavia and the rest were killed, starved or fled to Kei, Seram and elsewhere.

baselineSources.title: Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The baseline and the affected figure derive from the same small set of Dutch estimates, so the near-total share records the intent and outcome of the campaign rather than an independently measured proportion.

title: The Expulsion of the Moriscos from Spain
actors: Philip III and the Duke of Lerma ordered the deportation of Spain's Morisco population, the baptised descendants of its Muslims, to North Africa and beyond
peopleRange: Better documented than most early modern expulsions because the operation was administered and shipping was paid for. Henri Lapeyre's reconstruction from embarkation lists and treasury records gives about 272,000; Antonio Dominguez Ortiz and Bernard Vincent and the Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World give approximately 300,000, of whom around 120,000 came from Valencia alone, where Moriscos were perhaps a third of the population. Higher contemporary claims of 500,000 or more are not supported by the administrative record; a small number evaded expulsion or returned.

flows.label: Valencia → Algiers and the Maghreb
Murcia and Andalusia → Tunis
Aragon → France (mostly onward to North Africa)

summary: Between September 1609 and 1614 the Spanish monarchy deported the Moriscos, the descendants of Muslims forcibly converted a century earlier, on the grounds that their conversion was insincere and that they were a security risk in a Mediterranean contested with the Ottomans and the Barbary regencies. Expulsion proceeded kingdom by kingdom, beginning with Valencia, where it triggered armed resistance in the Muela de Cortes and the Vall de Laguar. Most were shipped to North Africa, where many were robbed or killed on arrival; others reached Constantinople, Tunis, France and Italy. Estimates of the number deported cluster around 272,000 to 300,000, drawn from embarkation and payment records rather than chronicles, making this one of the better-counted forced migrations before the nineteenth century. Valencia's rural economy was severely damaged and its seigneurial landlords opposed the measure. Some children were retained in Spain, and a minority of Moriscos evaded expulsion or returned.
contested: Whether mortality in transit and on arrival ran to a substantial fraction of those expelled is disputed; contemporary claims that a quarter or more died are not corroborated by the administrative record, and the retention of Morisco children in Spain is variously described as a charitable exemption and as a seizure.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World): Moriscos, Expulsion of (Spain)
'The expulsion of the Moriscos from Spain in 1609-1614: the destruction of an Islamic periphery', Journal of Global History (Cambridge)
Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World): Moriscos

deathsNote: No reliable total. Deaths came from fighting during the Valencian resistance, from shipwreck and overcrowding at sea, and from robbery and killing by Berber bands after landing in North Africa, all described in contemporary reports; the frequently repeated claim that a large proportion died has never been substantiated from records.
violenceNote: The stripping of subject status from a baptised Christian population and the retention in Spain of Morisco children below a set age against their parents' departure are set out in the expulsion decrees themselves and analysed by Dominguez Ortiz and Vincent.
baselineWhat: The Morisco population of Spain immediately before the expulsion decrees
baselineNote: Henri Lapeyre's reconstruction from the expulsion registers counted 272,140 people actually embarked or driven out, and allowing for evasion, deaths in transit and unrecorded departures most historians put the Morisco population of Spain in 1609 at about 300,000-330,000 — some 4 per cent of a Spanish population of roughly 8.5 million, but a quarter or more of the population of the kingdom of Valencia.
shareCaveat: Numerator and denominator come from the same expulsion registers, so the ratio measures how complete the expulsion was rather than what share of a wider population it touched; against Spain's total population the Moriscos were about 4 per cent.

title: The Plantation of Ulster
actors: The English Crown confiscated the lands of the Gaelic lords of Ulster after their flight and granted them to English and Scottish settlers, requiring the removal of the Irish tenantry from most of the granted land
peopleRange: Not counted. The plantation's population effect is measured through settler numbers rather than displacement: muster rolls and estate records indicate on the order of 20,000-40,000 adult British settlers in the six escheated counties by the 1630s, and a British population in Ulster as a whole, including the unofficial settlement of Antrim and Down, of perhaps 80,000 by 1640. The native Irish were legally to be removed from the lands of British undertakers to designated 'servitor' and native grantee estates; in practice large numbers stayed on as tenants because settlers could not be found, so the amount of actual physical removal is disputed and unquantified.
territoryDesc: Roughly half a million profitable acres across the six escheated counties of Armagh, Cavan, Coleraine (renamed Londonderry), Donegal, Fermanagh and Tyrone were confiscated from Gaelic lordships and regranted, mostly to English and Scottish undertakers and to the London livery companies, with further private plantation in Antrim and Down.

flows.label: Lowland Scotland → Ulster
England → Ulster

summary: After the Nine Years War and the departure of the earls of Tyrone and Tyrconnell in 1607, the Crown declared their lands forfeit and organised the systematic settlement of six Ulster counties. Grants to English and Scottish undertakers carried an obligation to plant British Protestant tenants and, on most estates, to remove the existing Irish occupiers to land set aside for them, a condition that was widely evaded because settlers were scarce and Irish tenants paid higher rents. Alongside the official scheme, private plantation in Antrim and Down brought in large numbers of Lowland Scots. The result was not a clearance but a layered settlement in which a substantial British Protestant population was established over a dispossessed Gaelic landowning class and a partly displaced tenantry, a configuration that shaped the 1641 rising and Ulster's subsequent history. Contemporary records document land transfers and settler musters far better than they document the movement of the displaced.
contested: How far the Irish tenantry was actually removed, as opposed to remaining illegally on undertakers' land, is disputed among historians of the plantation; so is whether the scheme is best described as colonisation, confiscation or a failed policy of segregation.

sources.title: Ulster Historical Foundation: The Plantation of Ulster
Encyclopedia.com: Ulster

deathsNote: The plantation itself was not accompanied by mass killing. Deaths belong to the preceding Nine Years War and to the rising of 1641, in which several thousand Protestant settlers were killed and many more died after being stripped and driven out in winter, with reprisal killings of Catholics following; those events are counted separately from the plantation.
baselineWhat: The Gaelic Irish population of Ulster at the start of the plantation
baselineNote: No census exists. Ireland's population around 1600 is generally reconstructed at roughly 1.4 million from later hearth-money returns worked backwards, with Ulster the least populous and most war-devastated province after the Nine Years' War; estimates for Ulster cluster around 150,000-250,000. By 1641 the planted British population of Ulster is estimated at about 40,000.

title: The Tokugawa Suppression of Christianity and the Shimabara Rebellion
actors: The Tokugawa shogunate banned Christianity, expelled missionaries and prominent converts, compelled apostasy through registration and testing, and destroyed the Shimabara rising of 1637-38
peopleRange: Japan's Christian population around 1600 is usually estimated at roughly 300,000 out of some twelve million, on the basis of Jesuit mission reports. The edict drafted by the monk Sūden and promulgated in 1614 expelled missionaries and leading Japanese Christians, and around a hundred, including the daimyo Takayama Ukon who died at Manila in 1615, were deported to Macao and the Philippines. The much larger movement was internal and involuntary in a different sense: the population of whole districts was compelled to register at Buddhist temples and to tread on Christian images, and the surviving Christian communities of the Nagasaki region went underground for two and a half centuries as the Kakure Kirishitan. There are no reliable totals for those executed, exiled or forced to apostatise.

flows.label: Missionaries and Japanese Christians deported → Manila
Missionaries and Japanese Christians deported → Macao

summary: Christianity, introduced by the Jesuits in 1549, was proscribed by Hideyoshi in 1587 and comprehensively banned by the Tokugawa shogunate in 1614, on the argument that it was a subversive foreign allegiance. Missionaries and prominent converts were expelled to Macao and Manila; those who remained or returned were hunted, and executions by crucifixion, burning and the pit followed through the 1620s and 1630s, with the numbers of martyrs recorded in mission accounts and in later Catholic canonisation processes. In 1637-38 an uprising in the Shimabara peninsula and the Amakusa islands, driven by taxation and famine as well as by religion, drew tens of thousands of peasants into the ruined castle of Hara; Britannica notes that an army of 100,000 was unable to dislodge them quickly, and when the castle fell in April 1638 the defenders were killed almost to a man, in numbers usually given as between 27,000 and 37,000. Afterwards the shogunate imposed temple registration on the whole population, required suspects to tread on Christian images, expelled the Portuguese and closed the country to most foreign contact. Christian communities survived in secret around Nagasaki and the offshore islands until the nineteenth century.
contested: The number killed at Hara castle is given variously between about 27,000 and 37,000 in Japanese sources, and historians disagree on how far the Shimabara rising was a religious revolt as against a tax rebellion in a Christianised district.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Shimabara Rebellion
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kirishitan
'Sūden's Anti-Christian Edict (1614)', Presses de l'Inalco (OpenEdition Books)
Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region: the beginning of the absence of missionaries and the hiding of Christians

deathsNote: The bulk of the range is the killing of the defenders of Hara castle in April 1638, put at between about 27,000 and 37,000 in Japanese accounts of the siege; to this the upper figure adds the several thousand Japanese Christians executed in the persecutions between 1614 and 1650, recorded in mission reports and later Catholic martyrologies but never comprehensively counted. Deaths from the famine that helped provoke the rising are not included.
violenceNote: Public executions of Christians, the use of torture including the pit to compel apostasy, the fumie image-treading tests, compulsory temple registration and the destruction of churches are documented in shogunal edicts, in Jesuit and Dominican mission reports and in the Nagasaki heritage record.
baselineWhat: The Japanese Christian (Kirishitan) population at the 1614 expulsion edict
baselineNote: Jesuit and mendicant mission reports, the only source, put converts at roughly 300,000 in a Japanese population of some 12-18 million; estimates in the literature run from about 200,000 to 750,000. The subsequent registration and apostasy-testing system (fumi-e, the temple registers) acted on this community and on the villages of Shimabara and Amakusa, where some 37,000 rebels were killed in 1637-38.

title: The Thirty Years War and the Depopulation of the German Lands
actors: Habsburg, Bavarian, Saxon, Danish, Swedish, French and mercenary armies fought across the Holy Roman Empire, living off the country and destroying, expelling and starving its civilian population
peopleRange: No count of refugees exists. Flight was continuous and often repeated: rural populations abandoned villages ahead of armies and returned or did not, towns absorbed and then expelled refugees, and confessional expulsions moved Protestants out of Bohemia, Austria and the Palatinate. The measurable quantity is population loss rather than displacement: parish registers, hearth and tax lists and later reconstructions show the population of the German lands falling from roughly 18-20 million to roughly 12-16 million, with losses above half in parts of Wurttemberg, Pomerania, Mecklenburg and Brandenburg and little or none in the north-west.
territoryDesc: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 redrew the Empire's internal religious and territorial settlement, confirmed Swedish and French gains on the Baltic and Rhine, and recognised the effective sovereignty of the imperial princes.

flows.label: Protestant exiles: Bohemia → Saxony
Palatinate → the Dutch Republic

summary: The war that began with the Bohemian revolt of 1618 and ended at Westphalia in 1648 was fought largely by armies that supported themselves by requisition, contribution and plunder in the territories they occupied. Its demographic effect was the worst in German history until the twentieth century: the standard modern reconstructions, including Peter H. Wilson's, put the population of the Empire's German lands as falling by roughly a fifth to a third, from about 18-20 million to about 12-16 million, with the great majority of deaths caused by typhus, plague, dysentery and hunger rather than by combat. Losses were extremely uneven, exceeding half the population in parts of the south-west, Mecklenburg and Pomerania while some north-western regions were barely touched. The sack of Magdeburg in May 1631 killed most of a city of around 20,000-25,000 and became the war's emblematic atrocity. Confessional expulsions, notably of Protestants from Bohemia and Austria after 1620 and the Habsburg re-Catholicisation programme, added a deliberate displacement to the general flight.
contested: Total deaths are estimated at between about 4.5 and 8 million; the disagreement turns on baseline population estimates, on how much of the recorded decline was permanent death rather than temporary flight, and on how far plague would have struck regardless of the war.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: Thirty Years' War
Encyclopedia.com: Thirty Years War
ICRC Humanitarian Law & Policy: 'The Thirty Years' War: the first modern war?'

deathsNote: The lower figure reflects cautious modern reconstructions from parish and fiscal records, which treat much of the apparent decline as flight and later recovery; the higher figure reflects readings that take the recorded shortfalls as mortality. Peter H. Wilson's Europe's Tragedy argues for a total in the region of five million and emphasises that most deaths were from epidemic disease and hunger produced by military requisition, not from battle.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The sack of Magdeburg, systematic requisition and burning of villages, rape and torture of peasants to extract hidden food and money, and confessional expulsion and church seizure are documented in army muster and contribution records, town chronicles, parish registers and the Simplicissimus literature, and are analysed by Peter H. Wilson and Geoffrey Parker.
baselineWhat: The population of the German lands of the Holy Roman Empire in 1618
baselineNote: Standard reconstructions from parish registers, hearth taxes and territorial surveys put the German lands at 18-21 million in 1618 and 13-16 million by 1650, a loss of roughly a fifth to a third. Losses were extremely uneven: near zero in parts of the northwest, over half in Mecklenburg, Pomerania and Wurttemberg.
shareCaveat: Much of the mortality was from typhus, plague and dysentery spread by moving armies and from famine rather than direct killing, and some of the recorded decline is flight that later reversed.

title: The Dutch Pacification of Formosa and the Lamey Island Massacre
actors: The Dutch East India Company subjugated the indigenous villages of southwestern Taiwan by punitive expedition, and cleared the inhabitants of Lamey Island from their home entirely
peopleRange: Only company records exist. The punitive campaign against Mattau in late 1635 and against neighbouring villages established what Tonio Andrade calls a pax hollandica over the plains around the Bay of Tayouan, with villages compelled to submit at annual assemblies. Lamey Island, a small island off the southwest coast now called Xiao Liuqiu, held several hundred to about a thousand people; in the campaign begun in 1636 the inhabitants were besieged in caves, several hundred died, and the survivors were removed to the mainland settlement at Tayouan, placed in Dutch and Sinkan households or shipped to Batavia. The island was emptied of its original population. Numbers come from the Zeelandia day-registers and company correspondence.
territoryDesc: The company extended control from its fort at Tayouan over the villages of the southwestern Taiwan plain and outlying islands, the first sustained external rule over any part of Taiwan; it ended with the Zheng conquest of 1662.

flows.label: Lamey islanders deported → Tayouan
Lamey captives shipped → Batavia

summary: After a decade of weakness on Taiwan the Dutch East India Company received reinforcements from Batavia in 1634 and used them to subdue the villages around its fort at Tayouan, burning Mattau in 1635 and compelling its neighbours to submit; Tonio Andrade describes the resulting settlement as a pax hollandica maintained by annual assemblies of village headmen holding company staves of office. The company also acted against the inhabitants of Lamey Island, who had killed the crews of two shipwrecked Dutch vessels; from 1636 successive expeditions drove the islanders into limestone caves, where large numbers died when the entrances were sealed and fires lit, and removed the survivors from the island altogether, distributing them among households at Tayouan and shipping others to Batavia. The island was subsequently leased out for cultivation. These campaigns are documented in unusual detail because the company kept daily registers at Fort Zeelandia, and they are among the best-recorded instances of a European trading company clearing an indigenous population in the seventeenth century.
contested: The population of Lamey before 1636 and the number who died in the caves are known only from Dutch company records, which give varying figures, and historians differ over whether the campaign is best described as a punitive expedition that went beyond its object or as a deliberate clearance.

sources.title: Tonio Andrade, 'How Taiwan Became Chinese' (Columbia University Press / Gutenberg-e)
Tonio Andrade, 'How Taiwan Became Chinese', Chapter 3: Pax Hollandica

deathsNote: No agreed figure. Company records describe several hundred islanders dying in the caves at Lamey in 1636 and further deaths in later sweeps and in transit; the figures given in different Dutch reports do not agree and no reconstruction has settled them. Deaths in the mainland campaigns against Mattau and its neighbours were far smaller and are recorded village by village.
violenceNote: The burning of Mattau, the smoking-out and killing of the Lamey islanders in their caves, and the distribution of surviving Lamey children and adults into Dutch and allied households are recorded in the Zeelandia day-registers and company correspondence used by Andrade.
baselineWhat: The indigenous population of the villages of south-western Taiwan under Dutch East India Company administration
baselineNote: The Company's own village registers, compiled for the annual landdag assemblies, counted about 68,600 people in some 315 villages at the 1650 enumeration — one of the earliest systematic population counts anywhere in maritime Asia. Lamey Island (Lambay, modern Xiaoliuqiu) held around 1,100 people, of whom several hundred died in the 1636 assault and the survivors were deported and dispersed.

title: The Pequot War, King Philip's War and the Enslavement of Native New Englanders
actors: New England colonial governments and their Native allies destroyed the Pequot and then the Wampanoag-led alliance, seizing their lands and selling captives into slavery in the Caribbean, Bermuda and beyond
peopleRange: Numbers are recorded in colonial court and treaty records rather than in censuses. In the Pequot War the surviving Pequots were divided among the victors and their allies as servants and captives, some shipped to the West Indies, and the 1638 Treaty of Hartford purported to abolish the Pequot name; in King Philip's War of 1675-76 colonial governments enslaved captured and surrendered Native people in large numbers, selling many overseas and binding others to colonial households. Margaret Ellen Newell's study of the colonial records finds that thousands of Native New Englanders were enslaved by the colonies, including people who surrendered under promises of clemency. The Native population of southern New England was reduced by war, flight and enslavement to a fraction of its pre-war size, with survivors concentrated in a small number of towns or dispersed north to Canada and west.
territoryDesc: Pequot country in southeastern Connecticut was divided among the colonies and their Mohegan and Narragansett allies after 1638; after 1676 most remaining Native land in southern New England passed to the colonies, and the surviving communities were confined to small reserved tracts.

flows.label: Native captives sold to Bermuda
Native captives sold to the West Indies
Refugees north to Canada and the Abenaki country

summary: Two wars broke Native political independence in southern New England. In May 1637 a Connecticut and Massachusetts force with Mohegan and Narragansett allies surrounded and burned the Pequot fort at Mystic, killing several hundred people, mostly non-combatants, in an attack that shocked even the colonists' Native allies; the survivors were hunted, enslaved and distributed, and the Treaty of Hartford of 1638 declared the Pequot nation dissolved. Forty years later Metacom, called King Philip by the English, led a broad alliance against colonial expansion; the war of 1675-76 destroyed or damaged dozens of towns on both sides and is among the deadliest per capita conflicts in the region's history. Colonial governments responded to victory by selling captives: Margaret Ellen Newell's research in the colonial court records shows that thousands of Native people were enslaved, including many who surrendered under promise of clemency, and that Indian slavery was an established institution in New England rather than an incident of war. Metacom was killed in August 1676 and his wife and son were among those sold overseas. The surviving Native population was left on small reserved tracts under colonial supervision.
contested: The number of Native people killed and enslaved is drawn from colonial records that had reason to understate enslavement, and estimates of the Native population of southern New England before 1675 vary widely, so the proportion killed or removed is uncertain.

sources.title: Brown University: 'Colonial enslavement of Native Americans included those who surrendered, too' (on Margaret Ellen Newell's research)
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Pequot War
Encyclopaedia Britannica: King Philip's War

deathsNote: The lower bound reflects conservative readings of the colonial records: several hundred Pequots killed at Mystic in 1637, and in King Philip's War roughly two to three thousand Native dead and perhaps eight hundred to a thousand colonists killed. The upper bound follows estimates that put Native wartime deaths in 1675-76 at five thousand or more, including deaths from exposure, starvation and disease among those driven from their villages during the winter, and colonist deaths at around two and a half thousand. There was no count of Native dead, and the colonial sources record their own losses far more carefully than those of their enemies.
violenceNote: The burning of the Mystic fort with its inhabitants inside, the destruction of villages and food stores on both sides, and the sale of captured Native adults and children into slavery in the Caribbean, Bermuda and the Atlantic islands are documented in the colonial court, treaty and shipping records examined by Newell.
baselineWhat: The Native population of southern New England on the eve of King Philip's War
baselineNote: Contemporary and modern reconstructions put the Native population of the war zone at roughly 10,000-15,000 by 1675 — about 4,000 Narragansett, 2,400 Nipmuc, 2,400 Massachusett and Pawtucket, and fewer than 1,000 Wampanoag and Pokanoket, plus Mohegan, Pequot and praying-town communities. This is already a post-epidemic figure: southern New England is thought to have held on the order of 100,000 people before the epidemics of 1616-19 and 1633.
shareCaveat: The baseline is a 1675 snapshot while the events run from 1636, and the epidemics that preceded them had already removed most of the region's people, so a share calculated here measures the wars only, not the wider collapse.

title: The Manchu Conquest of Ming China: Yangzhou, Jiading and the Queue Order
actors: Qing armies conquered Ming China, sacked cities that resisted, and imposed the shaving of the forehead and the wearing of the queue on all adult men on pain of death
peopleRange: No usable figures. Cities that resisted were sacked and their populations killed or dispersed — Yangzhou in 1645 is the best known — and southern provinces saw large-scale flight, but the Ming and early Qing population registers were fiscal instruments recording taxable adults, not censuses, and cannot support a displacement estimate. Manchu bannermen were settled in walled garrison quarters in Beijing and in provincial cities, from which Chinese residents were removed; this is documented in Qing administrative records without totals.
territoryDesc: The Ming empire, with the later addition of Taiwan in 1683, passed to the Qing; Beijing's inner city was cleared of its Chinese population for banner garrisons, and similar garrison quarters were established in provincial capitals.

flows.label: Manchu banner population → Beijing and provincial garrisons
Flight from the Jiangnan cities during the conquest

summary: Qing forces entered Beijing in 1644 after the fall of the Ming to rebel armies, and spent the following two decades subduing the south. Where cities resisted they were stormed and sacked: Yangzhou fell in May 1645 after a short siege and was given over to a massacre that a survivor, Wang Xiuchu, described in a memoir that became one of the most reproduced texts in Chinese history; Britannica reports the traditional figure of 800,000 dead while noting it is 'probably quite exaggerated'. Jiading and Jiangyin were similarly treated later that year, in both cases after resistance provoked by the order of July 1645 requiring every adult man to shave the front of his head and wear the Manchu queue, enforced with the slogan that one might keep one's hair or one's head. The conquest was accompanied by the collapse of the registered population, the devastation of Sichuan in the wars associated with the rebel Zhang Xianzhong and the Qing campaigns that followed, and famine and epidemic across large areas. Aggregate mortality for the Ming-Qing transition is often given in the tens of millions, but those figures are derived from fiscal registers that undercounted before the wars and were not restored for decades, and specialists treat them as unreliable.
contested: The Yangzhou death toll of 800,000 comes from a memoir and a tradition of anti-Manchu commemoration and is regarded as greatly exaggerated; aggregate population-loss figures for the Ming-Qing transition rest on tax registers rather than censuses and are disputed within very wide margins.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Yangzhou Massacre (1645)
Dahpon David Ho, 'Sealords Live in Vain: Fujian and the Making of a Maritime Frontier in Seventeenth-Century China' (UC San Diego, eScholarship PDF)

deathsNote: No defensible total. The traditional figure of 800,000 for Yangzhou alone is reported by Britannica as probably much exaggerated, and estimates of total mortality in the Ming-Qing transition, sometimes put at tens of millions, are extrapolations from registered-household figures that are tax records rather than population counts and that were disrupted by the wars themselves. Deaths came from storming and massacre, from the campaigns in Sichuan, and from the famine and epidemic that accompanied two decades of war.
violenceNote: The massacres at Yangzhou, Jiading and Jiangyin, including killing, rape and the burning of the cities, are described in survivor memoirs, above all Wang Xiuchu's account of Yangzhou, and the queue order imposing Manchu hairstyle and dress on pain of death is recorded in Qing edicts.
baselineWhat: The population of Ming China on the eve of the Qing conquest
baselineNote: Ming fiscal registers understate population badly because they counted tax units rather than people. Ho Ping-ti's reconstruction, still the standard, puts China's population around 1600 at roughly 150 million; other estimates for the late Ming range from about 100 to 160 million. The conquest and the accompanying famines and epidemics are thought to have cut it substantially before recovery under the Qing.

title: The Khmelnytsky Uprising and the Massacres of 1648-49
actors: Cossack forces under Bohdan Khmelnytsky, allied with Crimean Tatars and joined by Ukrainian peasants, destroyed Jewish and Polish Catholic communities across the eastern Commonwealth; Polish forces killed Ukrainians in reprisal
peopleRange: No count of refugees. Jewish survivors fled west into Poland proper, Silesia, Bohemia, Germany, the Dutch Republic and the Ottoman lands, and communal ransom records document large numbers of captives sold by the Tatar allies into the Crimean slave markets. The Jewish population of the affected palatinates before 1648 has been estimated by Shaul Stampfer at roughly 40,000, far below the 500,000 asserted in earlier accounts, which changes every derived figure.
territoryDesc: The uprising detached much of Ukraine from direct Polish-Lithuanian control and, after the Pereiaslav agreement of 1654, brought the Cossack Hetmanate under Muscovite protection, beginning the partition of Ukraine between Poland and Russia confirmed in 1667.

flows.label: Jewish refugees → Poland proper and central Europe
Captives sold to Crimean Tatar allies → Crimea

summary: The Cossack rebellion that began in 1648 destroyed the Polish-Lithuanian order in Ukraine and, with it, the network of Jewish communities that had grown up under noble patronage as estate managers, tax farmers and leaseholders. Jewish and Polish Catholic townspeople were killed at Nemyriv, Tulchyn, Polonne and elsewhere; the Tatar allies took large numbers as captives for the slave market rather than killing them. Nathan Hannover's chronicle Yeven Metsulah and other Hebrew accounts gave figures of 100,000 dead or more, and these passed into standard histories. Shaul Stampfer's demographic reassessment, working from the pre-1648 Jewish population of the region, concludes that around 18,000-20,000 Jews died, out of a population of roughly 40,000 in the affected area, a proportion that is catastrophic even though the absolute number is far below the traditional one. Ukrainian villagers were in turn killed in large numbers by Polish forces, and the wars that followed to 1657 and beyond devastated the region.
contested: Jewish deaths are estimated at about 18,000-20,000 by Shaul Stampfer against traditional figures of 100,000 or more derived from seventeenth-century Hebrew chronicles; the events are also read very differently in Jewish, Polish and Ukrainian national historiographies, with Khmelnytsky a national liberator in Ukraine and the author of a massacre in Jewish memory.

sources.title: Shaul Stampfer, 'What Actually Happened to the Jews of Ukraine in 1648?', Jewish History (PDF)
YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe: Khmelnytskyi, Bohdan

deathsNote: The low end is Shaul Stampfer's estimate of Jewish deaths, derived from reconstructing the pre-uprising Jewish population of the affected palatinates; the high end is the figure transmitted by seventeenth-century Hebrew chronicles such as Nathan Hannover's Yeven Metsulah and repeated in older historiography. The range covers Jewish victims only; Polish Catholic townspeople and clergy, and Ukrainian peasants killed in Polish reprisals, are additional and are not separately totalled.
violenceNote: The killing of Jewish and Polish Catholic townspeople, the destruction of synagogues and churches, and the sale of captives to the Crimean Tatars are described in the Hebrew chronicles collected as the 1648 gezeirot, in Polish and Ukrainian chronicles and in communal ransom records, and are analysed by Stampfer and in the YIVO Encyclopedia.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of the Ukrainian palatinates of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth on the eve of the uprising in 1648
baselineNote: Shaul Stampfer's reassessment of the tax and community records puts about 40,000 Jews in the affected Ukrainian lands out of roughly 170,000 in the Commonwealth, and estimates 18,000-20,000 deaths — far below the 100,000 or more of the older chronicle tradition. Polish Catholic nobles, clergy and townspeople were also killed and driven out in numbers that have never been counted.

title: The Cromwellian Conquest of Ireland and the Transplantation to Connacht
actors: The English Commonwealth reconquered Ireland, confiscated most Catholic-owned land, ordered Catholic landowners to move west of the Shannon, and transported thousands of Irish to the Caribbean colonies
peopleRange: Partly documented. The transplantation order of 1653-54 applied to Catholic proprietors and their households, not to the whole population: surviving transplanters' certificates record several thousand named landowners with families and servants, and historians' estimates of those who actually moved to Connacht and Clare run from a few thousand to around forty or fifty thousand people including dependants. Transportation to Barbados and the Leeward Islands, of prisoners of war, vagrants and children, is estimated at between about 10,000 and 50,000; the higher figures rest on contemporary claims rather than shipping records, and the whole subject has been distorted by later polemic. Overall population loss is a separate matter: William Petty's near-contemporary estimate of 616,000 deaths out of about 1.4 million is the origin of most later figures.
territoryDesc: Under the Act for the Settlement of Ireland (1652) and the Act of Satisfaction (1653), land in the other three provinces was confiscated to pay the army and the 'Adventurers' who had funded the war; Catholic landownership fell from roughly three-fifths of the profitable land of Ireland before 1641 to under a fifth by the 1660s and under a tenth by 1703.

flows.label: Catholic proprietors → Connacht and Clare
Transportation → Barbados and the Leeward Islands

summary: Cromwell landed in August 1649 and the reconquest was completed by 1653 after storms of Drogheda and Wexford in which garrisons and numbers of townspeople were killed, and a long attritional campaign against guerrilla resistance in which crops were burned and civilians moved or starved. The settlement that followed transferred most Catholic-owned land to soldiers and creditors and ordered Catholic proprietors to remove themselves and their households across the Shannon into Connacht and Clare by May 1654 on pain of death. Thousands of prisoners of war and others were shipped to the West Indies as indentured labour. Ireland's population fell steeply between 1641 and 1652; William Petty's contemporary estimate of 616,000 deaths, mostly from plague and famine, is the source of the often-repeated claim of a loss of a third or more, and modern historians such as Toby Barnard, John Cunningham and Micheal O Siochru accept a very large loss while treating Petty's arithmetic as unreliable. The scale, the intent and the appropriate label for these events remain among the most contested questions in Irish historiography.
contested: Whether the conquest and settlement amounted to attempted extermination or ethnic cleansing, as some historians and many nationalist accounts argue, or to a brutal but conventional early modern reconquest and land confiscation, is actively disputed; the death toll and the number transported to the Caribbean are both uncertain by a factor of several.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: Cromwellian Conquest
'Oliver Cromwell and the Cromwellian settlement of Ireland', The Historical Journal (Cambridge)
The Down Survey of Ireland project, Trinity College Dublin

deathsNote: The upper bound is William Petty's estimate of 616,000 excess deaths between 1641 and 1652, made in the 1670s from his own imperfect surveys and widely reproduced since; the lower bound reflects modern scepticism about Petty's baseline and arithmetic while still accepting a very heavy loss. Most of the deaths on any estimate were from famine and epidemic disease, including bubonic plague in 1649-52, aggravated by the deliberate destruction of crops and the movement of populations, rather than from direct killing.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The killing of the garrisons and some civilians at Drogheda and Wexford, the burning of crops and destruction of settlements in the guerrilla phase, the transportation of prisoners and vagrants to Caribbean plantations, and the confiscation and eviction under the Acts of Settlement are documented in Cromwell's own dispatches, in the Commonwealth's statutes and in the transplanters' certificates and Down Survey records.
baselineWhat: The population of Ireland on the eve of the 1641 rising and the Cromwellian reconquest
baselineNote: William Petty's contemporary calculation gave 1,466,000 for 1641 and 850,000 for 1652; modern estimates put the 1641 population at 1.5-2.1 million, of whom the great majority were Catholic. Petty reckoned 616,000 deaths from war, famine and plague, a figure most historians consider too high but which still frames estimates of a 15-25 per cent population loss. Catholic-owned land fell from about 60 per cent of Ireland in 1641 to under 10 per cent after the settlement.

baselineSources.title: Act for the Settlement of Ireland 1652 — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The transplantation order applied to Catholic landowners and their households, some thousands of families, not to the whole Catholic population, which mostly stayed as tenants under new landlords.

title: The Deluge: Swedish and Russian Invasion and the Depopulation of Poland-Lithuania
actors: Swedish and Muscovite armies invaded the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, sacking its cities and, in the Russian case, carrying off large numbers of Lithuanian and Belarusian captives and craftsmen
peopleRange: The Commonwealth's population is generally reckoned to have fallen from roughly 11 million before 1648 to about 6-7 million by 1660, a loss of a third or more, with some regions of Lithuania and Mazovia losing half. These are modern demographic reconstructions from hearth-tax rolls and parish registers rather than counts, and they cover the whole period from the Khmelnytsky uprising through plague, so the Deluge proper accounts for only part. Russian forces deported captives, especially skilled craftsmen, from Vilnius, Polatsk and other Lithuanian towns to Muscovy; the numbers are documented in Muscovite service records but not aggregated, and estimates run into the tens of thousands.
territoryDesc: Sweden occupied most of the Crown lands and Muscovy most of Lithuania; almost all was recovered at Oliwa in 1660, but the Truce of Andrusovo in 1667 confirmed Muscovite possession of Smolensk and left-bank Ukraine.

flows.label: Craftsmen and captives deported from Vilnius and Lithuanian towns to Muscovy

summary: Between 1655 and 1660 the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was invaded simultaneously by Sweden and Muscovy, in a catastrophe Polish historiography calls the Deluge. Warsaw, Krakow and Vilnius were captured and systematically plundered; Vilnius burned for days in 1655 and Warsaw was stripped of its libraries, archives and building materials. Muscovite forces deported captives from the Lithuanian towns, with skilled craftsmen resettled in Moscow. Jewish communities suffered heavily, both in the earlier Cossack uprising and at the hands of Polish irregulars who accused them of collaborating with the Swedes. Modern demographic reconstructions put the Commonwealth's overall population loss across 1648-1660 at around a third, comparable in proportion to the Thirty Years War in Germany, though war, famine and plague cannot be disentangled.
contested: How much of the Commonwealth's population loss belongs to the Deluge as against the 1648-1657 Cossack uprising and the plague waves of the 1650s.

sources.title: The Deluge — Wikipedia
Swedish invasion of Poland — Wikipedia
Russo-Polish War (1654-1667) — Wikipedia
Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The range is a modern demographic reconstruction of total population loss across 1648-1660 by Polish historians working from hearth taxes and parish records; it includes emigration and depressed births as well as deaths, and folds together the Cossack uprising, the Swedish and Russian invasions, famine and plague. No contemporary count exists.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Polish and Lithuanian chronicles and the surviving municipal records of Warsaw, Krakow and Vilnius document the sacking, burning and removal of church and library property.
baselineWhat: The population of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth on the eve of the Swedish and Muscovite invasions
baselineNote: Hearth-tax and poll registers, as reconstructed by Polish historical demographers, put the Commonwealth at roughly 10-12 million in 1650 and at about 6-7 million by 1660 after war, plague and famine - losses of a third or more, comparable to the Thirty Years War in Germany. The Muscovite deportations of Lithuanian and Belarusian townspeople and craftsmen are documented in campaign records but not separately counted.

title: The Qing Great Clearance: Evacuation of the Southern Seaboard
actors: The Qing state ordered the entire coastal population of the southeastern provinces moved inland and their villages destroyed, to starve the Zheng regime on Taiwan of supplies and recruits
peopleRange: No count survives, and Qing officials did not attempt one. The evacuation order of 1661, the qianjie ling, required the population of the coasts of Shandong, Jiangnan, Zhejiang, Fujian and Guangdong to move inland behind a demarcated boundary, commonly thirty to fifty li — roughly fifteen to twenty-five kilometres — with everything seaward of it burned and forbidden on pain of death. Dahpon David Ho's study of the Fujian coast describes a thousand-mile stretch of coast left in wreckage, with 'hundreds of thousands killed, and hundreds of thousands more uprooted and forced to flee to Southeast Asia, to inland provinces, or eastward to islands like Taiwan'. Local gazetteers record the abandonment of whole counties; the aggregate is unknown.
territoryDesc: A continuous strip of coastline from Shandong to Guangdong, in places tens of kilometres deep, was emptied and declared prohibited; boundary walls, ditches and guard posts were built to enforce it, and the zone was resettled only after the policy was lifted in stages from 1669 and finally in 1683.

flows.label: Fujian coast → interior prefectures
Guangdong coast → inland Guangdong
Refugees → Taiwan and Southeast Asia

summary: Unable to defeat the Zheng maritime regime at sea, the Qing court adopted in 1661 the most drastic internal displacement policy of the early modern world: the removal of the entire population of the southeastern seaboard behind an inland boundary, and the destruction of everything left behind. Villages, fishing fleets, salt pans and port towns were burned; people who crossed back over the line were liable to execution; and the evacuated population, dispossessed of the only livelihoods it knew, was largely left to fend for itself in already crowded interior districts. Contemporaries and later gazetteers describe famine, banditry and mass death among the evacuees, and substantial flight to Taiwan and to Southeast Asia. The policy was relaxed from 1669 in places and formally ended after the Qing conquest of Taiwan in 1683, after which the coast was resettled, in part by people from elsewhere. Dahpon David Ho, whose study of the Fujian coast is the fullest English-language treatment, describes it as one of the most devastating and sustained scorched-earth campaigns of its era, with hundreds of thousands killed and hundreds of thousands more uprooted.
contested: No figures for the numbers moved or killed exist; the characterisation of the policy's severity rests on local gazetteers and literati accounts written after the fact, and its demographic effect has never been reconstructed.

sources.title: Dahpon David Ho, 'Sealords Live in Vain: Fujian and the Making of a Maritime Frontier in Seventeenth-Century China' (UC San Diego, eScholarship PDF)

deathsNote: No count exists. Ho characterises the toll as hundreds of thousands killed, on the basis of gazetteer and official accounts of famine, exposure and executions along the boundary; because the evacuation destroyed the very registers and communities that might have recorded deaths, no number can be established, and the phrase should be read as a historian's characterisation rather than an estimate with a method behind it.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The burning of coastal settlements, the destruction of boats and salt works, and the execution of those found seaward of the boundary are recorded in Qing edicts and provincial memorials and in the local gazetteers used by Ho.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The evacuation zone was defined as a strip measured in li inland from the shore across five provinces rather than by any administrative unit, so no register corresponds to it; and the Qing fiscal registers of the 1660s count ding, taxable adult males, not people. Contemporary and modern estimates of the numbers moved range from several hundred thousand to well over a million, and the deaths from the resulting famine are not counted at all.

title: The Battle of Mbwila, the Kongo Civil Wars and the Emptying of the Kingdom
actors: Portuguese Angola and rival Kongo royal houses fought wars that broke up the kingdom and fed captives into the Atlantic trade
peopleRange: No census exists. The scale rests on the trans-Atlantic slave-trade voyage database, which records roughly 500,000-600,000 people embarked from the Loango-Congo coast between 1660 and 1740, and on John Thornton's reconstruction of the civil wars from Kongo, Portuguese and Capuchin correspondence; Thornton argues a large share of those embarked in this period were prisoners of the Kongo wars. The figure of about 200,000 is a conservative middle estimate of Kongo-origin captives, not a count.
territoryDesc: The kingdom's core between the Congo river and the Angolan highlands fragmented into competing polities based on Kibangu, Mbula and Soyo; the capital Mbanza Kongo (Sao Salvador) was abandoned from 1678 to 1709

flows.label: Kongo captives to Luanda and the Atlantic ships

summary: At Mbwila (Ulanga) in October 1665 a Portuguese-Angolan force with African allies defeated and killed King Antonio I of Kongo, an outcome that removed the kingdom's central authority. Rival branches of the royal family then fought for the throne for two generations; the capital Mbanza Kongo was abandoned in 1678 and only reoccupied under Pedro IV in 1709, after the Antonian movement of Beatriz Kimpa Vita was suppressed and its leader burned in 1706. Prisoners taken in these wars were sold to Portuguese and Dutch traders at Luanda, Cabinda and Soyo, and the region became one of the largest sources of captives in the Atlantic trade. Historians differ on whether the wars drove the slave trade or the trade drove the wars: John Thornton emphasises internal dynastic politics with slaving as a consequence, while other scholars stress European demand as the motor. Kongo survived as a title and a set of provinces but never recovered its former reach.
contested: Whether the civil wars generated the slave exports or were generated by them, and what share of Loango-Congo embarkations were Kongo war captives, remain matters of scholarly disagreement.

sources.title: Kingdom of Kongo
Battle of Mbwila
Kongo Civil War
Slave Voyages: Estimates of the trans-Atlantic slave trade

deathsNote: No usable death toll exists. Contemporary Portuguese accounts of Mbwila claim thousands of Kongo dead including the king and much of the nobility, and the later wars were fought largely as raids on villages; deaths in captivity and on the Atlantic crossing are counted in the slave-trade entries rather than here.
violenceNote: Capuchin missionary reports and Portuguese colonial correspondence describe villages burned and their inhabitants enslaved during the succession wars.
baselineWhat: The population of the Kingdom of Kongo on the eve of the Battle of Mbwila
baselineNote: John Thornton's reconstruction, built from Capuchin mission baptismal registers, provincial tribute lists and territorial extent, puts the kingdom at roughly half a million in the mid-seventeenth century. It is the most carefully evidenced population estimate for any pre-colonial Central African state, but it still rests on extrapolation from mission districts to the kingdom as a whole.
shareCaveat: The 200,000 accumulates across 75 years of intermittent civil war, so it spans roughly three generations while the denominator is a single-year estimate.

title: The Spanish-Chamorro Wars and the Reduccion of the Mariana Islands
actors: Spanish forces with Filipino auxiliaries fought the CHamoru of the Marianas and removed the surviving northern islanders to Guam
peopleRange: Pre-contact CHamoru population estimates vary widely, from about 40,000 to over 100,000 across the archipelago, and rest on early Spanish accounts, mission counts and archaeological survey rather than any census. By the first Spanish counts around 1700 fewer than 5,000 remained, and the survivors of Rota, Tinian, Saipan and the northern islands had been concentrated on Guam and in a handful of mission villages. The number physically moved cannot be separated from the number who died.
territoryDesc: The northern Mariana Islands were emptied of settled population for most of the following century and administered from Guam

flows.label: Northern Marianas islanders removed to Guam

summary: A Jesuit mission established on Guam in 1668 under Spanish protection provoked three decades of intermittent war with the CHamoru, whose canoes and villages were destroyed by Spanish soldiers and Filipino auxiliaries in repeated campaigns. Between 1698 and 1700 the surviving inhabitants of Rota, Tinian, Saipan and the northern islands were removed to Guam and settled in mission villages under the policy of reduccion, so that they could be catechised, taxed and controlled; the northern islands were left largely uninhabited for a century. The CHamoru population collapsed to a small fraction of its pre-contact level. Guampedia and CHamoru scholars set out the debate over causation: introduced smallpox, influenza and other epidemics account for most of the deaths in nearly all accounts, but the wars, the destruction of the seafaring economy and forced concentration compounded them, and some CHamoru writers apply the term genocide while others emphasise disease and reject it. Spanish records are the principal source and were produced by the colonising power.
contested: Whether the CHamoru collapse is best described as genocide or as an epidemic catastrophe compounded by war and reduccion is disputed among CHamoru and other scholars; pre-contact population figures are also unresolved.

sources.title: Guampedia: Spanish response to CHamoru depopulation
Guampedia: Envisioning the past - near extinction
Spanish-Chamorro Wars

deathsNote: No count exists. The CHamoru population fell by something on the order of 90 per cent between 1668 and 1700; the great majority of deaths in almost all scholarly accounts are attributed to introduced epidemic disease, with killings in the wars a smaller though significant component. The proportions cannot be recovered from the Spanish sources.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Spanish and Jesuit accounts record the burning of villages, destruction of canoes and forced concentration into mission settlements.
baselineWhat: The CHamoru population of the Mariana Islands when Spanish mission and military operations began in 1668
baselineNote: Estimates rest on early Spanish mission counts, village and canoe tallies and later archaeological survey; Rogers and others put the pre-contact CHamoru population at roughly 40,000, with published figures from about 30,000 to over 100,000. By the 1700 reduccion, when the northern islanders had been removed to Guam, Spanish counts recorded fewer than 5,000 survivors.

title: The Indian Slave Trade of the English Southeast
actors: Carolina traders armed Indigenous allies to raid for captives, who were enslaved on southern plantations or shipped to the Caribbean and the northern colonies
peopleRange: Alan Gallay's reconstruction from colonial shipping, customs and militia records in The Indian Slave Trade (2002) estimates that between 24,000 and 51,000 Indigenous people were enslaved by the English and their Native allies in the Southeast between 1670 and 1715 — the figure most often cited, and the basis for the estimate here. Gallay notes that before 1720 Carolina exported as many or more Native slaves as it imported Africans. The raids on Spanish Florida's mission provinces in 1702-1706 alone are estimated to have carried off 10,000-12,000 Apalachee and Timucua, from Spanish mission registers and English accounts.
territoryDesc: The Spanish mission chain across Apalachee and Timucua in northern Florida was destroyed and the region depopulated of settled Indigenous towns.

flows.label: Apalachee and Timucua captives taken from the Florida missions to Charles Town
Native captives shipped from Charles Town to the West Indies

summary: From the founding of Charles Town in 1670 the Carolina colony built a trade in Indigenous captives, supplying guns and goods to allied nations — the Westo, later the Yamasee, Creek and Chickasaw — in exchange for people taken in raids. The largest single campaign, led by Governor James Moore against the Spanish mission provinces of Florida in 1702-1706, destroyed the Apalachee missions and carried off many thousands. Captives were held on Carolina plantations or shipped to the West Indies, Virginia and New England, where escape was harder. Alan Gallay's reconstruction puts the total enslaved at 24,000-51,000, exceeding the colony's African imports of the same period. The system helped depopulate the interior Southeast, drove the coalescence of refugee peoples into new confederacies, and collapsed with the Yamasee War of 1715-1717, when the colony's principal suppliers turned on it. The atlas had no entry for Indigenous enslavement in colonial North America outside New England.
contested: The totals, which rest on Gallay's inference from partial shipping and militia records; other historians accept the order of magnitude while regarding the upper bound as insecure.

deathsNote: No count exists for deaths in raids, in transit or in slavery. Spanish accounts of the Apalachee raids describe killings and the torture of mission Indians; Gallay argues that mortality from the slaving wars and the epidemics they spread was a principal cause of Indigenous population decline in the Southeast, but does not put a number to it.

Wood's reconstruction of the colonial South from colonial censuses, trader estimates and mission records puts the region's Indigenous population at roughly 199,000 in 1685, falling to about 90,000 by 1730. The estimate is built from named nations rather than a single count and carries wide uncertainty.
