title: The Huguenot Exodus after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
actors: Louis XIV outlawed Protestantism in France, quartered dragoons on Protestant households to force conversion, and banned emigration; between one in five and one in three Huguenots fled anyway
peopleRange: Estimated rather than counted, because emigration was illegal and clandestine. France's Protestant population before the Revocation is usually put at 700,000-900,000. Departures are conventionally estimated at 140,000-200,000 over roughly two decades, reconstructed from the registers of the receiving churches and relief funds in the Dutch Republic, England, Brandenburg-Prussia, Switzerland and the Cape, which recorded refugees for charitable and settlement purposes. Contemporary French official figures were suppressed and contemporary Protestant claims of 400,000 or more are not supported by the receiving records.

flows.label: France → Geneva and the Swiss cantons
La Rochelle and the west → England and Ireland
France → the Dutch Republic
France → Brandenburg-Prussia
France → the Cape of Good Hope

summary: From the late 1670s the French Crown escalated pressure on the Protestant minority protected since 1598 by the Edict of Nantes: churches were demolished, professions closed, and from 1681 dragoons were billeted on Protestant households with licence to coerce conversions. The Edict of Fontainebleau of October 1685 revoked toleration entirely, ordered ministers into exile within a fortnight and forbade lay Protestants to leave the kingdom. Perhaps 140,000-200,000 left in defiance of that ban, most to the Dutch Republic, England, the Swiss cantons and Brandenburg-Prussia, whose Edict of Potsdam invited them; smaller groups reached Ireland, Scandinavia, North America and the Dutch Cape Colony. The refugees were disproportionately urban, skilled and literate, and the receiving states competed for them, which is why their arrival is comparatively well recorded. Those who stayed were legally Catholic; clandestine worship in the Cevennes and elsewhere led to the Camisard war of 1702-10.
contested: The total number of emigrants is estimated from receiving-country records rather than counted, and ranges from about 140,000 to over 200,000; the older claim that the exodus caused France's relative economic decline is disputed by economic historians.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World): Huguenots
The Huguenot Society of Great Britain and Ireland: Huguenot History

deathsNote: There was no mass killing. Deaths arose from the dragonnades, from imprisonment and galley sentences imposed on those caught attempting to leave, and from the hazards of clandestine flight; the numbers are small relative to the displacement and are not reliably totalled.
violenceNote: The dragonnades' use of billeting, beatings and sleep deprivation to compel abjuration, the sentencing of intercepted emigrants to the galleys and of women to prisons such as the Tour de Constance, the demolition of temples, and the removal of Protestant children to Catholic instruction are set out in the Revocation edict and its enforcement orders and in the refugee testimonies collected in the receiving countries.
baselineWhat: The Protestant population of France before the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
baselineNote: French Protestants are usually estimated at 800,000-900,000 in the early 1680s, out of a French population of about 20 million, concentrated in Languedoc, the Cévennes, Poitou, Béarn and Normandy. Estimates of the emigration to the Dutch Republic, England, Brandenburg-Prussia, Switzerland and the colonies range from about 140,000 to 200,000, that is roughly one in five of the Protestant population.

title: Aurangzeb's Deccan Wars and the Maratha Conflict
actors: Aurangzeb moved the Mughal court and army to the Deccan for a quarter-century, annexing Bijapur and Golconda and campaigning against the Marathas, at enormous cost to the region's population
peopleRange: No counts exist. The Mughal army in the Deccan, with its camp followers, was described by contemporaries as a moving city of several hundred thousand people that consumed the countryside it passed through; Maratha campaigning and Mughal counter-campaigning turned much of the western Deccan into a zone of raiding, forced requisition and flight. Mughal revenue records document the collapse of assessed revenue in war-affected districts, which historians read as evidence of depopulation and abandoned cultivation, but they do not count people.
territoryDesc: The sultanates of Bijapur (annexed 1686) and Golconda (1687) were extinguished and their territories added to the Mughal empire, which reached its greatest extent; Maratha territory was overrun repeatedly but never held, and the Mughal position in the Deccan collapsed after Aurangzeb's death in 1707.

flows.label: Populations displaced by campaigning across the Deccan plateau

summary: Aurangzeb spent the last twenty-five years of his reign in the Deccan, annexing the Muslim sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda and attempting to destroy the Maratha polity founded by Shivaji; he captured and executed Shivaji's son Sambhaji in 1689 but, as Britannica notes, even after nearly two decades of struggle he failed to subdue the Marathas. The war was fought as a series of sieges and scorched-earth raids across a wide plateau, with both sides living off the country; contemporary chroniclers describe deserted villages, abandoned cultivation and famine, and a severe famine and plague in the Deccan in the opening years of the eighteenth century that court chronicle attributes with a death toll around two million — a figure from a single chronicle tradition that cannot be verified. Aurangzeb also reversed his predecessors' policy towards non-Muslims, reimposing the jizya in 1679, prohibiting the building and repair of Hindu temples and ordering demolitions. His religious policy is the subject of sharp modern dispute: it is central to Hindu nationalist accounts of Mughal rule, while historians including Audrey Truschke argue that temple destruction was targeted and political rather than systematic, a reading that is itself contested. The demographic cost of the Deccan wars has never been reconstructed.
contested: Whether Aurangzeb's religious measures amounted to systematic persecution or to targeted political acts is disputed between Hindu nationalist historiography and a body of academic work associated with Audrey Truschke and others; the two-million death toll for the Deccan famine of 1702-04 rests on a single court chronicle.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: India — Aurangzeb
Encyclopedia.com: Aurangzeb

deathsNote: No defensible total. Contemporary chroniclers report famine and plague in the Deccan in the early 1700s killing on the order of two million, but the figure comes from court chronicle rather than any count and cannot be tested; deaths in the sieges, raids and reprisals of the quarter-century war were never recorded systematically by either side.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The execution of Sambhaji in 1689, the devastation of the countryside by both armies, and the orders to demolish Hindu temples and schools are recorded in Mughal court chronicles and imperial orders and summarised in the Britannica account.
baselineWhat: The population of the Deccan sultanates and the Maratha lands during Aurangzeb's campaigns
baselineNote: Shireen Moosvi's reconstruction from the Ain-i-Akbari puts Mughal India at roughly 145 million around 1600, and Maddison's series gives about 165 million for the subcontinent in 1700, but neither can be disaggregated to Bijapur, Golconda and the Maratha country with any confidence, and no revenue survey of the newly annexed Deccan comparable to the northern Mughal records survives for the war years. Contemporary accounts describe famine and heavy mortality in the Deccan in the 1690s and 1700s without giving numbers.

title: The Great Migrations of the Serbs from Ottoman Territory to Habsburg Lands
actors: Serb populations fled Ottoman reprisals after failed Habsburg offensives, moving north under their patriarchs into Habsburg Hungary
peopleRange: The 1690 migration is variously given as 30,000-40,000 people, as 37,000 families (which would imply well over 150,000 people), or as around 60,000-70,000; the discrepancy comes from the ambiguity of the word 'families' in the surviving Habsburg and church documents and from later national historiography. A second, smaller migration followed in 1737-39. Estimates rest on Habsburg settlement records, the invitation charters of Emperor Leopold I and Serbian Orthodox church sources, none of which is a census.

flows.label: Kosovo and Old Serbia to the Habsburg military frontier and Vojvodina

summary: In 1689-90 a Habsburg army advanced deep into Ottoman Rumelia with Serb and Albanian support; when it was thrown back, Ottoman and Tatar forces conducted reprisals and Patriarch Arsenije III Carnojevic led a large body of Serbs north across the Danube and Sava under privileges granted by Emperor Leopold I. A second movement followed the failed Habsburg campaign of 1737-39 under Patriarch Arsenije IV. The migrants were settled in southern Hungary, Srem, Banat and along the military frontier, where they formed the demographic basis of later Vojvodina and of the Serbian Orthodox metropolitanate of Karlovci. The size of the 1690 movement is disputed, with sources giving 30,000-40,000 people or 37,000 families; the demographic effect on Kosovo and Old Serbia, and whether it opened the way for Albanian settlement there, is one of the most politically contested questions in Balkan historiography, argued differently by Serbian and Albanian historians.
contested: The size of the 1690 migration and its demographic consequences for Kosovo are disputed between Serbian and Albanian historiography, with Serbian accounts treating it as a mass exodus that emptied Kosovo and Albanian accounts treating it as smaller and more localised.

sources.title: Great Migrations of the Serbs
Arsenije III Crnojevic, Serbian Patriarch
Vojvodina

deathsNote: No death toll can be established. Contemporary accounts describe Ottoman and Tatar reprisal killings in 1690 and heavy mortality from hunger and disease among the migrants during the winter crossing, but no figures were recorded.
baselineNote: No usable denominator exists and the question is politically contested. Ottoman tax registers for the sanjaks of Old Serbia and Kosovo record households rather than a comparable population total, and the size of the Orthodox Serb population there around 1690 is disputed between Serbian and Albanian historiography. Even the migration figure is unsettled: Patriarch Arsenije III's own account speaks of some 30,000 souls, later Habsburg and Serbian sources of 37,000 families or up to 80,000 people.

title: The Great Serb Migration of 1690
actors: Serbs who had supported the Habsburg advance fled Ottoman reprisals as the front collapsed, and were settled by Emperor Leopold I in southern Hungary under charters of religious and communal autonomy
peopleRange: Contested, from a few thousand to well over 100,000. Patriarch Arsenije III Čarnojević, the migration's leader, wrote of 'more than 30,000 souls' in 1690 and 'more than 40,000' in 1696; a later Serbian monastic chronicle gives 37,000 families, which would imply several hundred thousand people. Sima Ćirković regards even 40,000 as an exaggeration lacking corroboration beyond the patriarch's own claims, and Noel Malcolm argues the 37,000-family figure derives from a single unreliable source written decades afterwards. The evidence is thus overwhelmingly ecclesiastical correspondence and later chronicle, not registers.

flows.label: Serbs from Kosovo, the Morava valley and Belgrade to Habsburg southern Hungary

summary: During the Great Turkish War, Habsburg armies advanced deep into Ottoman Rumelia in 1689 and were joined by Serb auxiliaries; when the front collapsed the following year, Patriarch Arsenije III led a large body of Serbs northwards ahead of Ottoman reprisals. Emperor Leopold I issued privileges in 1690-1691 recognising the patriarch as head of the Serbian Orthodox Church in the Monarchy and granting the migrants ecclesiastical and communal autonomy, arrangements that survived until 1912 and underpinned Serb settlement in the Military Frontier and in what became Vojvodina. The size of the movement is genuinely uncertain and politically charged, because Serbian and Albanian national historiographies have used it to argue about who subsequently populated Kosovo. The migration is included here for its lasting demographic effect on the middle Danube rather than for any secure headcount; a second, smaller migration followed in 1737-1739.
contested: Both the number of migrants and whether the movement left Kosovo substantially depopulated of Serbs — a claim central to Serbian national historiography and disputed in Albanian historiography and by revisionist historians such as Noel Malcolm.

deathsNote: No usable figure. Contemporary accounts describe deaths in flight from hunger and disease and Ottoman reprisal killings against communities that had collaborated with the Habsburgs, but nothing was counted.
baselineWhat: The Serb Orthodox population of the Ottoman territories the migration came from
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The Ottoman tax registers (defters) for Kosovo, Raška and the Morava valley in the late seventeenth century have not been reconstructed into an agreed population figure, and the subject is bound up with a live political dispute over the ethnic history of Kosovo. Even the size of the migration is contested: the sources can be read as 30,000 souls or 30,000 families, a difference of roughly fivefold, and Serbian, Albanian and Ottoman historiographies read them differently.

title: The Ottoman Iskan: Forced Settlement of Nomadic Tribes
actors: The Ottoman state ordered Turkmen, Yoruk and Kurdish tribal confederations to settle in designated villages, chiefly in the Raqqa region and Cukurova
peopleRange: Ottoman settlement registers (iskan defterleri) list tribes and households rather than individuals. The 1690s Raqqa programme assigned tens of thousands of households from the Boz Ulus, Yeni Il, Danismendli and Afshar confederations; at conventional household multipliers this implies well over 100,000 people, and the programme was repeated for decades because tribes returned to their pastures. The figure given is an order-of-magnitude reading of those registers, as analysed by Ottoman historians including Cengiz Orhonlu and Yusuf Halacoglu.

flows.label: Turkmen confederations ordered from Anatolian pastures to Raqqa

summary: From 1691 the Ottoman government made the settlement of pastoral tribes a systematic policy, ordering named confederations to occupy fixed villages on depopulated land, above all along the Euphrates around Raqqa, and holding tribal leaders responsible for keeping their people there. The stated aims were to end raiding on caravan routes and settled villages, to bring nomads onto the tax registers, and to repopulate abandoned districts. Enforcement was uneven: many tribes fled back to their highland pastures and were ordered south again in successive decrees through the eighteenth century, and settlement in the malarial Euphrates lands carried heavy mortality. A parallel and better-documented campaign, the Firka-i Islahiye of 1865, used a reform army to settle tribes in Cukurova and the Amanus. The policy is one of the clearest early-modern instances of a state moving populations to make them legible and taxable rather than to punish them.
contested: Ottoman historians disagree over how much of the settlement policy was ever enforced in practice and how far the registers describe intentions rather than accomplished moves.

sources.title: Iwamoto, 'A study on the turning point of the Ottoman policy toward nomads' (AJAMES)
Yoruks

deathsNote: No death toll was recorded. Ottoman documents and later scholarship note high mortality among tribes settled in the malarial Euphrates plains, and punitive expeditions against tribes that fled, but neither was counted.
baselineWhat: No defensible figure exists for the nomadic population of the Ottoman provinces subject to the settlement decrees
baselineNote: Ottoman registers record the named Turkmen, Yoruk and Kurdish confederations as taxable households and tent-groups assigned to specific villages, not as a counted population, and the coverage of the iskan decrees shifted across six decades between Raqqa, Cukurova and western Anatolia. Sixteenth-century estimates that roughly a quarter of Anatolia's population was nomadic cannot safely be carried forward to 1700.

title: War Captives, Tribute and Sacrifice in Dahomey and Asante
actors: The kingdoms of Dahomey and Asante raided neighbours for captives, sold most into the Atlantic trade and held or killed the rest
peopleRange: No figure can be attributed to these two states alone. The trans-Atlantic voyage database estimates roughly 2 million people embarked from the Bight of Benin and about 1.2 million from the Gold Coast between 1700 and 1867; Dahomey and Asante supplied a large but unquantified share, alongside many other suppliers, and both states also retained captives internally as agricultural and household slaves. Figures for people killed at Dahomey's annual customs come from European visitors' accounts and vary by an order of magnitude.

flows.label: Dahomean captives to Ouidah
Asante captives to Cape Coast and Elmina

summary: From the early eighteenth century Dahomey, based at Abomey, and Asante, based at Kumasi, organised warfare in part around the capture of people: campaigns against neighbouring states produced prisoners who were sold at the coast, settled as unfree labour on royal plantations, or held for the annual ceremonies. Dahomey took the coastal ports of Allada and Ouidah in the 1720s and thereafter traded directly with European ships; Asante expanded over the Akan states and northern savanna polities and took tribute in people as well as gold. Both kingdoms continued taking captives after the Atlantic trade was suppressed, redirecting them into domestic slavery and, in Dahomey's case, into palm-oil production. European observers described human sacrifice at Dahomey's annual customs on a large scale, but Robin Law and other historians argue that visitors' numbers were inflated and that the ceremonies were smaller and more political than the accounts suggest. British conquest of Asante (1896-1901) and French conquest of Dahomey (1892-94) ended both systems, and both powers cited slaving and sacrifice as justification for their own conquests.
contested: The scale of human sacrifice at Dahomey's annual customs, and the degree to which European abolitionist and imperial writers exaggerated it to justify conquest, are actively disputed.

sources.title: Dahomey
Annual Customs of Dahomey
