Slave Voyages: Estimates

deathsNote: There is no defensible aggregate. Deaths in the wars themselves are unrecorded; deaths at Dahomey's annual customs were reported by European visitors in figures from dozens to several hundred a year, which Robin Law regards as unreliable; mortality among captives held or shipped is accounted for in the Atlantic trade entries.
violenceNote: European traders' and missionaries' accounts, and later British and French colonial reports, describe enslavement of captives and ritual executions at Abomey and Kumasi.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The raided zone shifted continually over two centuries across the Bight of Benin hinterland, the Volta basin and the northern savanna, and no population counts exist for any of it before the colonial enumerations of the 1900s. Even the raiding states' own populations are guesses: eighteenth-century Dahomey is put at 200,000-350,000 and Asante at anywhere from 1 to 3 million.

title: The Dzungar Invasions of the Kazakh Steppe and the 'Great Disaster'
actors: The Dzungar Khanate invaded the Kazakh jüzes, driving nomadic populations west and south in mass flight
peopleRange: No count exists. Kazakh oral tradition and nineteenth-century Kazakh and Russian historiography describe the flight of the Middle and Junior jüzes towards the Syr Darya, Khiva, Bukhara and the Volga, and the claim that a third or more of the Kazakh people perished is a figure from that tradition rather than from records. Russian frontier correspondence and Central Asian chronicles record the arrival of large numbers of destitute Kazakhs on the Syr Darya and near Russian frontier lines, without enumeration.
territoryDesc: Dzungar control extended over the Kazakh eastern pastures and Semirechye; the Junior jüz accepted Russian protection in 1731

flows.label: Kazakh flight from Semirechye towards the Syr Darya and Transoxiana
Junior jüz flight west towards the Ural and Volga

summary: In 1723 the Dzungar Khanate launched a large campaign against the Kazakh jüzes at a moment when they were weakened by winter losses and internal division, seizing pastures and towns in Semirechye and along the Syr Darya. Kazakh tradition calls the ensuing years the Aqtaban shubyryndy, the 'barefoot flight' or Great Disaster, remembering mass movement of whole clans westward and southward with heavy loss of livestock and people, conflict with the Khivan, Bukharan and Kalmyk populations into whose lands they moved, and famine. Kazakh forces under Abulkhair and others won the counter-battles remembered as Bulanty and Anyrakay in the late 1720s, but the disaster led the Junior jüz to accept Russian protection in 1731, beginning the process that ended in Russian annexation over the following century. The claim that a third of the Kazakh population died rests on oral tradition and later national historiography, not on records; the Dzungar Khanate itself was destroyed by the Qing in 1755-58, an event recorded separately.
contested: The scale of mortality and displacement rests on Kazakh oral tradition and later national historiography rather than records, and the conventional figure of a third of the population is not independently supportable.

sources.title: Kazakh-Dzungar Wars
Dzungar Khanate
Abul Khair Khan and the Russian protectorate of 1731

deathsNote: No defensible range. Kazakh tradition speaks of the loss of a third of the people, a figure that functions as a memorial rather than a measurement; there are no records against which it can be tested.
baselineWhat: The Kazakh population of the three jüzes before the Dzungar invasions
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. The Kazakh khanates kept no registers, and the earliest usable counts are Russian imperial administrative surveys from more than a century later, which cannot be projected back across the disruption of the Aqtaban shubyryndy itself. Published estimates of the early eighteenth-century Kazakh population range from about one to three million and rest on assumptions about herd sizes and pasture capacity rather than on evidence.

title: The Expulsion of the Salzburg Protestants
actors: Prince-Archbishop Leopold Anton von Firmian expelled the Protestant peasantry of the archbishopric of Salzburg; Prussia and other Protestant states organised their reception
peopleRange: Well documented for an eighteenth-century expulsion because both the expelling and receiving states kept lists. The emigration patent of 31 October 1731 was followed by the departure of roughly 20,000-21,000 people, the great majority of the archbishopric's crypto-Protestant population; Prussian settlement records account for some 17,000 resettled in East Prussia, with smaller parties reaching other German states, the Dutch Republic and the new colony of Georgia in North America.

flows.label: Salzburg → East Prussia (Gumbinnen district)
Salzburg → Ebenezer, Georgia

summary: Protestantism had survived clandestinely among the mountain peasantry of the prince-archbishopric of Salzburg long after the Counter-Reformation. After Protestant villagers organised and appealed to the Corpus Evangelicorum, Archbishop Firmian issued an emigration patent in October 1731 requiring unpropertied Protestants to leave within eight days and property-holders within one to three months, in midwinter and in breach, the Protestant powers argued, of the Peace of Westphalia. Around 20,000 left. Frederick William I of Prussia offered them land in the depopulated Gumbinnen district of East Prussia and organised their transport; most of the emigrants walked north across Germany in publicised columns that became a European media event, and a small party was settled at Ebenezer in Georgia. Children below a certain age were initially retained by the Salzburg authorities to be raised Catholic, and their release was a principal demand of the Protestant states negotiating on the emigrants' behalf.
contested: Whether the retention of Protestant children by the Salzburg authorities was systematic or exceptional was disputed at the time between the archbishopric and the Corpus Evangelicorum, and the winter timing of the expulsion of the unpropertied is still argued over as either deliberate harshness or administrative rigidity.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World): Salzburg Expulsion
German History in Documents and Images: 'The Salzburg Protestants are Driven out of Austria and Settle in Prussia in the Year 1732'

deathsNote: There was no mass killing. Deaths occurred among the very young and old on the winter march north and on the Atlantic passage to Georgia, and are recorded individually in the Prussian settlement registers and the Ebenezer records rather than as a total.
violenceNote: The stripping of residence rights from a subject population on grounds of confession, and the retention of emigrants' children by the Salzburg authorities for Catholic upbringing, are recorded in the emigration patent and in the diplomatic correspondence of the Corpus Evangelicorum, and are treated in Mack Walker's study of the expulsion.
baselineWhat: The population of the Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg
baselineNote: The archbishopric held roughly 190,000-200,000 people in the early eighteenth century. About 20,000 crypto-Protestants, drawn overwhelmingly from the Pongau, Pinzgau and Lungau valleys, were expelled under the emigration edict of 1731; most were resettled in East Prussia.
shareCaveat: The expelled were concentrated in a few Alpine valleys; against the population of those valleys the share was a large fraction rather than the tenth the territory-wide ratio suggests.

title: Nader Shah's Sack of Delhi
actors: Nader Shah of Iran defeated the Mughal army at Karnal, occupied Delhi, and ordered a general massacre of the city's inhabitants after a riot against his troops
peopleRange: No count exists of those displaced. Persian and Mughal accounts describe the flight of much of the surviving population from the city after the massacre of 22 March 1739, and the removal of craftsmen and of thousands of women and children with the returning Iranian army; the figures given for the latter, running to several thousand, come from the same chronicles that report the killing and are not independently verifiable. The Mughal treasury, the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor and Timur Ruby were carried off, and Nader remitted Indian taxation for three years on the strength of the plunder.
territoryDesc: Mughal territory west of the Indus, including Kabul, Ghazni, Peshawar, Sindh and the western Punjab, was ceded to Iran; the Mughal emperor was restored to a throne with its prestige and treasury destroyed.

flows.label: Craftsmen and captives carried off with Nader's army → Khorasan

summary: Nader Shah, having seized power in Iran and driven out the Afghans and Ottomans, invaded the Mughal empire in 1738-39, destroyed Muhammad Shah's far larger army at Karnal in February 1739, and entered Delhi in March. A rumour of Nader's death provoked a riot in which several hundred of his soldiers were killed; on 22 March he ordered a general massacre, which continued through the day until the Mughal emperor's plea induced him to stop. Contemporary Persian and Mughal accounts put the dead variously between twenty and thirty thousand, with some later sources giving far higher figures; the killing was accompanied by looting, burning of quarters of the city and mass rape, and by the systematic extraction of the imperial treasure. Nader restored Muhammad Shah to a throne stripped of its wealth and of the territories west of the Indus, and withdrew with a plunder train that included the Peacock Throne. The blow is generally regarded as decisive in the disintegration of Mughal authority, opening the way to Maratha, Afghan and eventually British power in northern India.
contested: The number killed on 22 March 1739 is given as twenty to thirty thousand in most contemporary accounts, with figures up to and beyond a hundred thousand in some later sources; there was no count and the chroniclers were writing for patrons on both sides.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nadir Shah
Encyclopedia.com: Nadir Shah

deathsNote: The range is the one given in the contemporary Persian and Indo-Persian accounts of the massacre of 22 March 1739 and adopted in most modern narratives; higher figures appear in later chronicles and in colonial-era retellings and are not supported by the earlier sources. The dead were overwhelmingly civilians killed in a single day of ordered killing within the city.
violenceNote: The ordered massacre of the civilian population, the burning of quarters of the city, rape and the carrying off of women, children and craftsmen with the returning army are described in the Persian and Indo-Persian chronicles of the campaign and in eyewitness accounts collected shortly afterwards.
baselineWhat: The population of Delhi (Shahjahanabad) at the time of the sack
baselineNote: No census exists. Estimates derived from the walled city's area, its ward structure and European travellers' accounts range from about 400,000 to 2 million, with recent work favouring the lower end. The massacre of 22 March 1739 is generally put at 20,000-30,000 killed in a single day.

title: Ahmad Shah Durrani's Invasions of Northern India and the Sikh Ghallugharas
actors: The Afghan Durrani empire repeatedly invaded the Punjab and the Ganges plain, sacking cities, enslaving captives and attacking Sikh communities
peopleRange: No records of displacement survive. Persian court chronicles of the Durrani campaigns, Maratha letters from the Panipat campaign and later Sikh accounts all give figures, but they are literary rather than statistical. Maratha correspondence after the third battle of Panipat in January 1761 describes tens of thousands of camp followers killed or taken; the number of women and children carried off as slaves is given in some accounts as about 22,000, a figure repeated in later histories without independent support.
territoryDesc: Durrani rule was asserted over the Punjab, Kashmir, Sindh and, briefly, Delhi; the Punjab passed to Sikh misls by the 1760s-70s

flows.label: Captives taken from Panipat and Delhi towards Afghanistan

summary: Between 1747 and 1767 Ahmad Shah Durrani invaded India eight times from Kandahar, sacking Delhi in 1757 and plundering Mathura and Vrindavan on the same campaign, and in January 1761 destroying the Maratha army at Panipat in one of the bloodiest battles of the century. Maratha accounts describe tens of thousands killed in the battle and its aftermath, and large numbers of camp followers, chiefly women and children, taken north as slaves. Durrani forces also attacked the Sikh communities of the Punjab in two episodes remembered as the Ghallugharas: the smaller in 1746 and the Vadda Ghallughara of February 1762, in which Sikh tradition records between 10,000 and 30,000 killed, many of them families travelling with the fighting bands, followed by the demolition of the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar. The evidence is uneven: Persian chronicles written for the Durrani court, Maratha letters written in defeat and Sikh accounts compiled later each have their own purposes, and modern historians treat all of the figures as approximate. By the 1770s the Sikh misls had taken the Punjab and Durrani power had receded.
contested: All the casualty and captive figures come from partisan chronicles; the toll of the Vadda Ghallughara in particular rests on Sikh traditional accounts written after the event and is not independently corroborated.

sources.title: Ahmad Shah Durrani
Third Battle of Panipat
Vadda Ghalughara

deathsNote: The range aggregates the Panipat battle and its aftermath, where Maratha and Afghan accounts together suggest tens of thousands of soldiers and camp followers killed, with the sack of Mathura and the Ghallugharas. The figures are chronicle estimates, frequently rhetorical, and modern historians regard the higher end as unverifiable.
violenceNote: Persian, Maratha and Sikh chronicles record massacres of non-combatants, enslavement of captives and the destruction of temples at Mathura and of the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Eighteenth-century Punjab was not enumerated — the first census of the province came in 1855 — and the size of the Sikh community in the 1760s is unknown, with estimates of the dead in the Vadda Ghallughara of 1762 ranging from 10,000 to 30,000 out of an unrecorded base. Figures for captives taken in the Durrani invasions come from court chronicles and are not reconcilable with any population total.

title: The East African and Indian Ocean Slave Trade and the Zanzibar Plantations
actors: Omani and Swahili merchants and the Sultanate of Zanzibar organised slave raiding and trading from the East African interior for plantations on the coast and for markets across the Indian Ocean
peopleRange: The evidence is far weaker than for the Atlantic. Ralph Austen's conservative census, summarised by AP Central, has the East African coast exporting over 300,000 enslaved people in the nineteenth century, of whom about two-thirds remained in Africa on Zanzibar, the Zanzibari coastal possessions or in Somalia, with a further roughly 500,000 in the Red Sea trade drawn mainly from the Gulf of Aden region. EBSCO records approximately 600,000 people sold in the Zanzibar markets between 1830 and 1873, and a British estimate of 1895 that three quarters of the island's 200,000 inhabitants were still enslaved. Far fewer records were kept than in the Atlantic and abolitionist sources carry an evident bias, so all figures are estimates.

flows.label: Lake Nyasa and the interior -> Kilwa and Bagamoyo
Mainland ports -> Zanzibar clove plantations
Zanzibar -> Oman, the Gulf and western India

summary: From the late eighteenth century the Omani sultanate, which moved its capital to Zanzibar in 1840, built a plantation economy on the islands of Zanzibar and Pemba growing cloves with enslaved labour, and financed caravans that reached the Great Lakes and the eastern Congo. Captives taken in the interior were marched to Kilwa and Bagamoyo, sold in the Zanzibar market and either retained on the islands and the Swahili coast or shipped to Oman, the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea and western India. EBSCO records approximately 600,000 people sold at Zanzibar between 1830 and 1873. British pressure produced Sultan Barghash's decree of 1873 prohibiting the seaborne slave trade, the further decree of 1890 under Sultan Ali bin Said and the abolition decree of 6 April 1897; Michelle Liebst's study in the Law and History Review argues that the sultans' own reformist motives have been understated and British agents too readily credited as abolitionists. Abolition was slow in effect: only about a tenth of those eligible completed the required paperwork in the first year, since freedom had to be applied for and housing and income proved.
contested: The volume of the East African and Red Sea trades is disputed, with abolitionist-era estimates now regarded as inflated in some accounts and as conservative in others; the extent to which the sultans of Zanzibar acted under British coercion rather than from their own policy is argued by Liebst against the standard narrative.

sources.title: AP Central (College Board): The African Diaspora in the Indian Ocean
EBSCO Research Starters: Zanzibar Outlaws Slavery
Michelle Liebst, 'The Sultans of Zanzibar and the Abolition of Slavery in East Africa', Law and History Review (Cambridge)

deathsNote: No toll can be established. Mortality on the caravan routes from the interior to the coast was described as very high by missionary and consular observers, notably David Livingstone, and mortality in the dhow crossings and in the barracoons was also high, but these accounts are impressionistic and were produced in the service of an abolitionist campaign. No registers exist from which deaths could be counted, and deaths in the raiding that supplied the caravans are wholly unquantified.
violenceNote: The AP Central summary of Austen's work, EBSCO and Liebst's article document raiding and abduction in the interior, plantation labour on Zanzibar and Pemba, and the market in women and children for domestic service and concubinage across the Indian Ocean.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Captives were taken across a vast and unenumerated interior stretching from the Great Lakes to the Congo basin and Lake Nyasa; the first population data for these regions are colonial estimates from the 1900s. Historians such as Ralph Austen and Patrick Manning reconstruct export volumes of roughly a million or more for 1750-1900, but only as flows, not as shares of a known base population.

title: The Highland Clearances
actors: Scottish landowners, backed by the courts and sheriff officers, evicted tenant communities from the Highlands and Islands to make way for sheep farming and later for deer forests
peopleRange: There is no single count and the evictions were spread over a century. Historic UK records that between 1811 and 1821 the Duchess of Sutherland and the Marquis of Stafford removed roughly 15,000 people from the Sutherland estates to make room for some 200,000 sheep, the largest and best-documented single clearance, and puts total Highland emigration in the period at about 70,000, forced and voluntary combined. Britannica dates the removals from the mid-to-late eighteenth century into the mid-nineteenth. The figures come from estate papers, sheriff court records, emigration agents' lists and the decennial censuses from 1801, not from any register of evictions.
territoryDesc: Interior straths and glens across Sutherland, Ross, Inverness-shire and the Hebrides were converted from mixed township agriculture to large sheep walks and, later, sporting estates; the evicted were resettled on coastal crofts too small to live on, or emigrated. The Crofters Holdings (Scotland) Act of 1886 finally gave security of tenure to those who remained.

flows.label: Strathnaver -> coastal crofting townships, Sutherland
Hebrides and west Highlands -> Nova Scotia and British North America
Highland emigration -> Australia

summary: Over roughly a century, landowners in the Scottish Highlands and Islands replaced tenant townships with commercial sheep farming. Britannica describes the process as the forced eviction of inhabitants primarily to introduce sheep, running from the mid-eighteenth century into the mid-nineteenth. The Sutherland clearances of 1811-21, in which Historic UK records about 15,000 people removed, became the notorious case: houses were unroofed and burned to prevent return, and in Strathnaver in 1814 two elderly people died in a burning cottage. Many of the displaced were resettled on coastal crofts and kelp shores that could not support them; others emigrated to British North America and Australia, sometimes under landlord-assisted schemes and, in cases such as Barra in 1851, under outright coercion. Emigrant ships carried typhus. The Crofters Act of 1886 ended the legal basis of the removals.
contested: Historians differ over how far the clearances should be described as forced expulsion and how far as an agrarian transformation driven by market forces and population growth, with T. M. Devine's work stressing the wider Scottish and Lowland context; the number evicted has never been established.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Highland Clearances
Historic UK: The Highland Clearances

deathsNote: There was no significant direct death toll: the clearances were evictions, not killings. Deaths that occurred were incidental - people who died during evictions, such as the two elderly people burned in a cottage at Strathnaver in 1814, and passengers who died of typhus and other disease on emigrant ships, including on a voyage to Halifax in 1826. Mortality among the resettled on inadequate coastal holdings during the Highland potato famine of 1846-56 was real but was not separately counted.
violenceNote: Historic UK records the burning and unroofing of houses to prevent tenants returning, and the forcible embarkation of tenants such as the Barra families of 1851; the practice is documented in estate papers, sheriff court proceedings and contemporary press accounts.
baselineWhat: The population of the Scottish Highlands and Islands at Webster's enumeration of 1755, near the start of the clearances
baselineNote: Alexander Webster's 1755 count, the first usable population survey of Scotland, gives about 1.27 million for the country as a whole, of which the Highland counties held roughly a quarter — on the order of 340,000. The region's population then grew to a peak of about 400,000 in the 1840s before sustained decline; Tom Devine's work on the clearances uses this series.
shareCaveat: The clearances ran for more than a century while the regional population first grew by a fifth and then fell, so measuring evictions against a single 1755 snapshot compresses several distinct phases into one ratio.

title: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade at its Peak and its Suppression
actors: Portuguese, British, French, Spanish, Dutch, Brazilian, Cuban and North American traders, in partnership with African states and merchants, shipped captives across the Atlantic until the trade was suppressed
peopleRange: These are the best-documented forced-migration figures of the pre-industrial world. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, built from the records of some 36,000 voyages and estimated by its compilers to cover 80-85 per cent of all slaving voyages, puts the whole trade at 12.52 million captives embarked and about 10.7 million disembarked; roughly 4.8 million had been embarked before 1750, leaving about 7.7 million for 1750-1866. More than half of all Africans carried across the Atlantic went in the eighteenth century, and almost 4 million in the nineteenth, most of them to Brazil and Cuba after Britain and the United States outlawed the trade in 1807-08. The estimates are reconstructions from voyage records, not a headcount.

flows.label: Bight of Benin -> Bahia and Brazil
West Central Africa -> Rio de Janeiro
Gold Coast -> the British Caribbean
Upper Guinea -> Cuba

summary: The Atlantic trade reached its greatest volume in the second half of the eighteenth century and continued illegally for decades after abolition. Britain and the United States outlawed the traffic in 1807-08 and the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron intercepted vessels thereafter, but Brazilian and Cuban demand kept the trade running until Brazil suppressed it in 1850-51 and the last documented crossing reached Cuba in 1866-67. Slavery itself outlasted the trade: emancipation came in the British colonies in 1833-38, the French in 1848, the United States in 1865, Cuba in 1886 and Brazil in 1888. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database gives 12.52 million embarked and 10.7 million disembarked over the whole trade, with roughly 7.7 million of those embarkations falling after 1750. The gap between the two totals is the mortality of the Middle Passage.
contested: Estimates of mortality and depopulation inside Africa, caused by the wars and raids that supplied the coast, are far weaker than the shipping figures and are disputed; so is the effectiveness of naval suppression, which some historians argue prolonged mortality by encouraging faster, more crowded vessels.

sources.title: SlaveVoyages: Estimates - Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
SlaveVoyages: Methodology of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade estimates
Klas Ronnback, 'The Slave Trades out of Africa' (African Economic History Network)
Encyclopedia Virginia: The Transatlantic Slave Trade

deathsNote: The range is the shortfall between embarkations and disembarkations after 1750, derived from the voyage database itself: about 1.8 million captives died in the Middle Passage across the whole trade, of which roughly 1.0-1.4 million fall in this period. It excludes deaths during capture, the march to the coast and detention in barracoons, for which no comparable records exist and which some scholars believe were of similar or greater magnitude.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: The forms are documented in the voyage records, court and captured-ship papers assembled by the SlaveVoyages project and in the abolition-era parliamentary inquiries on which the database and the African Economic History Network survey draw.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: the captives came from a coastal belt stretching from Senegambia to Angola and from societies far inland, none of them enumerated
baselineNote: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database records about 7.7 million people embarked between 1750 and 1867, roughly two thirds of the entire Atlantic traffic, of whom some 6.7 million disembarked. There is no single population from which they were drawn: estimates of the population of West and West-Central Africa in 1750 range from roughly 25 million to well over 50 million, they rest on backward projection from twentieth-century censuses rather than evidence, and the trade's demographic effect was concentrated on particular regions - the Bight of Biafra, the Loango coast, Angola - rather than spread evenly.

title: The Trans-Saharan Slave Trade, 1750-1900
actors: Saharan and Sahelian states, merchant networks and raiding polities carried enslaved people north across the desert to North African and Ottoman markets
peopleRange: No count exists and every figure is a reconstruction. The African Economic History Network's survey reports that around five million people were trafficked out of sub-Saharan Africa across the trans-Saharan, Red Sea and Indian Ocean routes between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, with roughly two-thirds of that total on the trans-Saharan route, and that the nineteenth century was the busiest period for the non-Atlantic trades. Ralph Austen's census-style estimates, built from the records of desert entrepots, North African market registers and travellers' accounts, remain the basis of most calculations, and the figure given here - on the order of one and a half million for 1750-1900 - is an apportionment of those estimates to this period rather than an independent count.

flows.label: Central Sudan (Bornu, Sokoto) -> Fezzan and Tripoli
Timbuktu and the Niger bend -> Morocco
Darfur and Wadai -> Egypt by the Forty Days Road

summary: While the Atlantic trade was being suppressed, the desert routes remained active and in some decades expanded. Slaving states of the central Sudan such as Sokoto and Bornu, and the Nilotic raiding frontier in Darfur and the Bahr al-Ghazal, supplied captives who were marched north to Fezzan, Ghadames, Ghat and Tripoli, to Morocco, and along the Forty Days Road to Egypt, for sale into domestic service, concubinage, military slavery and agricultural labour in North Africa and the Ottoman lands. Women and children predominated, in contrast to the Atlantic trade, and castration for the eunuch market was practised at a small number of centres with very high mortality. Ottoman prohibitions from the 1850s, French and British pressure on the Saharan termini, and eventually colonial occupation of the Sahel reduced the traffic, but caravans were still being intercepted at the end of the century and slavery persisted in law in parts of the region into the twentieth. Volume estimates rest on entrepot records and travellers' counts, not on registers of any kind.
contested: The volume of the trade is contested in both directions: Austen's census has been criticised as too low by scholars who think the desert routes were systematically under-recorded, and as too high by others who regard the travellers' counts on which it partly rests as unrepresentative.

sources.title: Klas Ronnback, 'The Slave Trades out of Africa' (African Economic History Network)
AP Central (College Board): The African Diaspora in the Indian Ocean - on Ralph Austen's estimates

deathsNote: No death toll can be established. Mortality on the desert crossings was high - contemporary European travellers described caravan routes marked by remains - and mortality among boys castrated for the eunuch trade was extreme, but there are no records from which a figure could be built. Deaths in the raiding wars that supplied the caravans are equally unquantified.
violenceNote: The African Economic History Network survey and the syntheses of Austen, Lovejoy and Toledano on which it draws document the taking of captives in raids, the predominance of women and children destined for domestic service and concubinage, and the practice of castration for the eunuch market.
baselineWhat: No single population can serve as a denominator for 150 years of captive-taking across the Sahel and Sahara
baselineNote: Ralph Austen's estimates, the standard series, are built from caravan and market records at the North African and Ottoman end rather than from any count of the raided populations, which spanned Bornu, Hausaland, Darfur, Wadai and the Nile Sudan. There is no census of these polities in this period and no defensible aggregate to divide by.

title: The Expulsion of the Acadians (le Grand Derangement)
actors: British colonial authorities in Nova Scotia deported the French-speaking Catholic Acadian population and dispersed it among the Thirteen Colonies, Britain and France
peopleRange: Roughly 10,000 people out of an Acadian population usually put at 14,000-18,000 were deported or driven into flight between 1755 and 1764. Parks Canada puts the first phase, from the Halifax Council's order of 28 July 1755 through 1762, at 6,000-7,000 removed, with about 2,000 more escaping to Canada and Ile Saint-Jean or taking refuge along the Miramichi; the British capture of Ile Royale and Ile Saint-Jean in 1758 produced a second wave. The figures rest on British transport manifests, colonial council minutes and parish registers rather than on any census, and totals differ between accounts.
territoryDesc: The diked farmland of the Bay of Fundy marshlands, built up by Acadian settlers over a century, was confiscated and from 1759 granted to New England Planters and other British settlers; Acadians who returned in the 1780s and 1790s found their lands occupied and resettled on poorer ground in western Nova Scotia, Cape Breton, Prince Edward Island, eastern New Brunswick and the Gaspe.

flows.label: Grand-Pre and Minas Basin -> Massachusetts and the Thirteen Colonies
Ile Saint-Jean -> France (Saint-Malo)
Colonial exile -> Louisiana (the Cajun settlement)

summary: After the fall of Fort Beausejour in June 1755 the Nova Scotia Council, judging the Acadians' refusal of an unqualified oath of allegiance a security risk in the approaching war with France, ordered their deportation on 28 July 1755. Troops burned settlements, seized livestock and loaded families onto transports for the British seaboard colonies, England and France; Parks Canada puts the removals of 1755-62 at 6,000-7,000 people, with about 2,000 escaping to Canada, Ile Saint-Jean or the Miramichi. A second phase followed the capture of Ile Royale and Ile Saint-Jean in 1758. Families were separated at embarkation, several transports were lost at sea, and colonies that received deportees frequently refused to settle them. Many later moved again to French Louisiana, where their descendants became the Cajuns; those who returned after 1763 found their diked farmland granted to New England Planters.
contested: The total deported and the number who died are both uncertain, and historians differ over whether the deportation is best explained as a wartime security measure or as a deliberate removal of a population whose land was wanted.

sources.title: Parks Canada, Fort Beausejour-Fort Cumberland: The Great Upheaval
University of Maine Canadian-American Center: Acadian Deportation, Migration, and Resettlement

deathsNote: There is no death register. The best-documented losses are at sea in 1758, when a large share of those shipped from Ile Saint-Jean drowned or died of disease, including the several hundred lost when the transports Duke William and Violet foundered. Wider estimates that between a third and a half of all deportees died of smallpox, typhus, shipwreck and exposure in the receiving colonies rest on colonial correspondence and burial registers rather than counts, and are not agreed.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Parks Canada and the University of Maine's Canadian-American Center describe the burning of settlements, the confiscation of land and livestock, and the detention of Acadian men in churches and forts pending embarkation.
baselineWhat: The Acadian population of Nova Scotia and the surrounding French settlements in 1755
baselineNote: French and British colonial censuses of the 1750s give an Acadian population of about 14,100 at the start of the deportations; roughly 11,500 were deported and a 1764 census found some 2,600 still in Nova Scotia having evaded capture.

title: The Qing Destruction of the Dzungars
actors: The Qianlong emperor's armies destroyed the Dzungar (Zunghar) Mongol confederation and repopulated its lands
peopleRange: The Dzungar population before the campaigns is generally put at about 600,000, an estimate drawn from Qing and Russian reports of household and tribute numbers rather than from a census. Survivors were absorbed into other Mongol and Kazakh groups, enslaved, or fled to Russian territory; Encyclopedia.com's account records that Qianlong then repopulated the Ili region with Manchu and Mongol settlers, to which the Qing later added Han and Hui colonists and Turkic Muslim cultivators moved from the southern oases. There is no count of the displaced.
territoryDesc: Dzungaria and the Tarim basin were annexed and administered as the 'New Frontier', Xinjiang, garrisoned from Ili and repopulated with settlers; Britannica records that the Qing consolidated control of the region and constituted it a formal province in 1884.

flows.label: Dzungar survivors -> flight to the Kazakh steppe and Russian territory
Turkic cultivators resettled from the southern oases -> the Ili valley

summary: Qianlong exploited a Dzungar civil war to conquer Dzungaria in 1755 in alliance with the pretender Amursana, withdrawing after a rapid campaign. When Amursana revolted at being denied full authority, the emperor returned with overwhelming force and, in the words of the Encyclopedia.com account, set about the universal destruction of the Oirat population, issuing edicts for the killing of adult males and the distribution of women and children. Smallpox swept the survivors. The Dzungars, a people of about 600,000, ceased to exist as a political and largely as an ethnic entity within three years; their genealogies and records were destroyed, their settlements eliminated, and the Ili valley resettled with populations brought in from elsewhere. Scholars disagree on the proportions: Encyclopedia.com summarises Owen Lattimore as putting 50 per cent exterminated, 20 per cent dead of smallpox and 30 per cent surviving, Peter Perdue as 30 per cent exterminated, 40 per cent dead of smallpox and 30 per cent surviving, and Ilya Zlatkin as holding that only 7 per cent survived. The conquest brought the whole of Xinjiang under Qing rule.
contested: Whether the destruction of the Dzungars should be classed as a genocide is argued among historians of Inner Asia, and the estimates of how many were killed as against how many died of smallpox or survived differ by a wide margin between Lattimore, Perdue and Zlatkin.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of Russian History): Zunghars
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Dzungar
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Xinjiang - History

deathsNote: The range applies the competing scholarly proportions to a pre-campaign population of about 600,000. Peter Perdue's figures - 30 per cent exterminated and 40 per cent dead of smallpox - give roughly 420,000 deaths; Owen Lattimore's - 50 per cent exterminated and 20 per cent of smallpox - give a similar total by a different route; Ilya Zlatkin's claim that only 7 per cent survived gives about 560,000. The lower bound reflects scepticism about the 600,000 baseline itself, which rests on Qing and Russian estimates rather than enumeration. The split between deaths by killing and deaths by epidemic is precisely what the scholars disagree about.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Encyclopedia.com's account, drawing on the Qing edicts and campaign records, documents orders for the killing of the Oirat population, the enslavement and distribution of women and children, and the deliberate destruction of Dzungar genealogies, documents and settlements.
baselineWhat: The population of the Dzungar Khanate immediately before the Qing campaigns of 1755-1758
baselineNote: Peter Perdue, following the Qing official Wei Yuan, puts the Dzungars at roughly 600,000 people in about 200,000 households before the campaigns; Wei Yuan's account states that some 40 per cent died of smallpox, 20 per cent fled to Russia and the Kazakhs, and 30 per cent were killed by Qing forces. Estimates of the pre-war population range from about 500,000 to 800,000.

title: Deportation Warfare between Burma, Siam and their Neighbours
actors: Konbaung Burmese and Siamese armies fought wars whose object was the capture and forced resettlement of populations, alongside Manipuri, Arakanese, Mon and Lao victims
peopleRange: Burmese and Siamese chronicles and British East India Company reports give partial figures: tens of thousands deported from Ayutthaya after its sack in 1767; roughly 20,000 taken from Arakan after the Burmese conquest of 1784-85, with British Bengal officials reporting some 200,000 Arakanese refugees in Chittagong district by the late 1790s; repeated deportations of Mon, Shan, Manipuri and Lao communities; and the Siamese removal of much of the population of Vientiane to the Khorat plateau after 1827-28, usually put in the tens of thousands to over 100,000. The chronicle numbers are conventional and the East India Company figures are administrative estimates, so a combined total near half a million is an order of magnitude rather than a count.

flows.label: Captives from Ayutthaya to Upper Burma
Arakanese refugees to British Chittagong
Vientiane Lao resettled on the Khorat plateau by Siam

summary: In mainland Southeast Asia in this period war was fought principally for people rather than land, and both the Konbaung dynasty of Burma and the Siamese kingdoms of Ayutthaya and Bangkok systematically deported the populations of defeated states to repopulate their own core regions. Burmese armies sacked Ayutthaya in 1767 and marched captives, including royalty, monks and artisans, to Upper Burma; the Manipur valley was repeatedly raided in the campaigns Manipuris remember as the Seven Years' Devastation; and the conquest of Arakan in 1784-85 was followed by deportations to Burma and by a large refugee flight into British-held Chittagong, which East India Company officials put at around 200,000 by the late 1790s and which became a source of Anglo-Burmese friction. Siam did the same in the other direction, resettling Mon, Lao, Khmer and Malay communities in its own provinces, most drastically after the destruction of Vientiane in 1827-28, when much of the Lao population of the middle Mekong was moved to the Khorat plateau. Numbers rest on royal chronicles, which use conventional figures, and on East India Company correspondence; they should be read as orders of magnitude. The transfers reshaped the ethnic map of Burma, Thailand and Laos in ways still visible.
contested: Chronicle figures for captives are conventional rather than counted, and Thai, Burmese and Lao national histories differ on responsibility and scale.

sources.title: Burmese-Siamese wars
Konbaung conquest of Arakan (1784-85)
Lao rebellion (1826-1828) and the destruction of Vientiane

deathsNote: No defensible range. Chronicles and later accounts describe heavy mortality in the sack of Ayutthaya, in the Manipur raids, in Arakan and on the forced marches themselves, but the only quantities available are conventional chronicle figures and colonial estimates of survivors.
violenceNote: Burmese, Siamese and Lao chronicles and contemporary British East India Company reports describe deportees held as royal service manpower, the burning of captured capitals and the removal or destruction of royal and religious objects.
baselineWhat: The combined population of the mainland Southeast Asian polities that fought and were raided in these wars: Burma, Siam, the Lao states, Arakan, Manipur and the Mon and Shan lands
baselineNote: There are no censuses before the nineteenth century. Lieberman's reconstructions in 'Strange Parallels' and McEvedy and Jones's estimates put Burma at roughly 4-5 million around 1800, Siam at 2-3 million, and the Lao principalities and Manipur together under a million, giving an order of magnitude of 8 million for the region the deportation wars covered. The first Burmese administrative counts under British rule and the Siamese corvee registers are the only direct evidence, and both post-date most of the wars.
shareCaveat: The captive total accumulates across seventy years and a dozen separate wars, while the denominator is a single snapshot; particular targets, such as the Lao of Vientiane after 1828 or the Mon of Pegu, lost a far larger share of their populations than the regional ratio suggests.

title: The Alta California Mission System
actors: Franciscan missionaries backed by Spanish and then Mexican soldiers congregated coastal Native Californians at twenty-one missions, where baptised people were not free to leave
peopleRange: Mission registers, which the Franciscans kept meticulously and which survive, record at least 87,787 baptisms of Native Californians between 1769 and the 1830s and 63,789 deaths by the end of 1832. The resident population peaked at just over 21,000 in the 1820s. These are among the best documentary series for any pre-modern event in the atlas, though they record baptisms rather than a headcount of people compelled, and say nothing about those who evaded the missions. Estimates of California's pre-contact Indigenous population range from about 133,000 to over 700,000; the coastal peoples drawn into the missions were a subset.
territoryDesc: Twenty-one mission establishments with attached ranch lands running from San Diego to Sonoma, controlling most of the productive coastal zone; the lands were secularised by Mexico from 1833-1834 and largely passed to private grantees rather than to Indigenous communities.

flows.label: Chumash and other coastal peoples congregated at the missions

summary: Beginning at San Diego in 1769, Franciscan missionaries established twenty-one missions along the Alta California coast, drawing surrounding Indigenous communities into settlements organised around compulsory labour, religious instruction and residential segregation of unmarried women and girls. Once baptised, a neophyte was not free to leave: departure was treated as flight, and soldiers were sent to retrieve runaways, a practice documented in mission and presidio correspondence. Mortality was extreme — the registers record 63,789 deaths against 87,787 baptisms — driven by introduced disease, crowded dormitories, poor nutrition and high infant and maternal death rates, so that the system depended on continuous new recruitment from further inland. Resistance included the Chumash revolt of 1824. Mexican secularisation from 1833 dispersed the mission populations without restoring their land, leaving survivors as labourers on the ranchos. Historians and Native Californian communities disagree sharply over whether the missions are best described as coercive confinement or as religious congregation, a dispute that surfaced publicly around the 2015 canonisation of Junipero Serra. The atlas began its California coverage only in 1846.
contested: Whether the mission system constituted forced confinement and a cause of demographic collapse, as most modern scholarship and many California Indian communities hold, or a religious and protective enterprise whose mortality was driven by disease beyond the missionaries' control, as the Catholic Church and some historians have argued.

sources.title: Spanish missions in California — Wikipedia
Junipero Serra — Wikipedia
Chumash people — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The figure is the number of deaths of Indigenous neophytes recorded in the mission burial registers to 31 December 1832 — an unusually firm count, though it excludes deaths of people who fled and those in communities affected by mission-borne epidemics without entering the system. The overwhelming majority were from introduced disease, malnutrition and childbirth rather than direct killing; historians disagree over how far the conditions of confinement caused that mortality.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Mission and presidio correspondence, including the 1799 complaint of Father Antonio de la Concepcion Horra and the reports of visiting officials, document compulsory labour, the pursuit of runaways, corporal punishment and sexual violence by soldiers.
baselineWhat: The Native Californian population of the coastal strip between San Diego and San Francisco Bay from which the missions drew converts, in 1769
baselineNote: Sherburne Cook's reconstruction from mission registers and ethnographic territory estimates puts the coastal mission zone at roughly 64,000-72,000 people in 1769, within a statewide native population he estimated at about 310,000. Later scholarship (Cook's revision, Milliken) supports a coastal figure in the same range.
shareCaveat: The affected figure counts baptisms accumulated over 65 years, including children born inside the missions and recruits drawn from progressively further inland, so it exceeds the 1769 coastal population and the resulting share passes 100 per cent.

title: The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 under East India Company Rule
actors: The English East India Company held the revenue rights of Bengal and continued collection through a catastrophic harvest failure
peopleRange: Contemporary Company estimates put deaths at around a third of Bengal's population, roughly ten million of some thirty million; these rest on Warren Hastings's 1772 report and on revenue officers' district impressions rather than any enumeration. Modern historians, including Rajat Datta and Tim Dyson, regard one third as too high and put mortality lower, in the range of one to two million upward, while agreeing the mortality was catastrophic in the worst districts of western and northern Bengal and Bihar. No censuses existed and the surviving evidence is revenue correspondence.
summary: After a failed monsoon in 1768 and a worse one in 1769, famine struck Bengal and Bihar in 1769-71 in the period of dual government, when the East India Company held the diwani or right to collect land revenue while nominal administration remained with the Nawab. The Company maintained and in some districts increased revenue collection through the famine, its servants engaged in private grain trading, and relief was minimal; contemporary critics in Britain, including Edmund Burke and the Company's own later reviewers, condemned the conduct of its servants, and Warren Hastings reported in 1772 that about a third of the population had died. Modern historians dispute that figure: Rajat Datta's work on Bengal's grain markets argues that the famine was primarily a subsistence crisis driven by harvest failure and market fragmentation and that the one-third figure is unsupportable, while others emphasise the Company's revenue extraction and the absence of the customary relief obligations of Indian rulers. Large districts were depopulated, cultivation reverted to jungle, and the disaster contributed directly to the Regulating Act of 1773 and to the permanent settlement debate. It remains one of the largest mortality events attributed in part to a colonial administration's policy.
contested: Whether mortality reached the traditional figure of ten million, and how far East India Company revenue policy and grain speculation caused rather than aggravated the famine, are both actively disputed.

sources.title: Great Bengal famine of 1770
Company rule in India
Warren Hastings

deathsNote: The high figure is the traditional one-third-of-population estimate originating in Warren Hastings's 1772 report to the Company's directors and repeated for two centuries. The low figure reflects modern revisionist demography, particularly Rajat Datta's argument that the population base and the mortality rate were both overstated. There was no enumeration of any kind, so both ends are reconstructions.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: East India Company correspondence and contemporary British parliamentary criticism, including Burke's, documented continued revenue collection and grain engrossing during mass starvation.
baselineWhat: The population of the Bengal Presidency territories under East India Company revenue administration
baselineNote: There was no census before 1872. Company officials and later writers, above all W. W. Hunter in 'The Annals of Rural Bengal', worked from a presumed population of about 30 million for Bengal and Bihar and concluded that roughly a third of it, some 10 million people, died in 1769-71. Modern historians treat both the base and the death toll as rough, with estimates of mortality ranging from about 1.2 million to 10 million.
shareCaveat: The famous 'one third of Bengal' figure is a ratio inferred from an estimated base, not a count; treating it as a measured share would give the arithmetic a precision the eighteenth-century evidence does not support.

title: The Partitions of Poland-Lithuania
actors: Russia, Prussia and Austria annexed the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in three stages and abolished the state
peopleRange: The partitions transferred roughly 12-14 million inhabitants — the figure derives from the Commonwealth's own hearth-tax census of 1789 and from the partitioning powers' subsequent land surveys — to three foreign monarchies without physically moving them. There was no mass expulsion at the time; the displacement came later, in the emigration of tens of thousands after the 1794, 1830 and 1863 risings and in the Siberian deportations covered separately.
territoryDesc: The entire territory of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, about 733,000 km2 at its 1772 extent, divided between the Russian Empire (roughly 62 per cent), the Kingdom of Prussia (about 20 per cent) and the Habsburg Monarchy (about 18 per cent). Poland did not reappear as a state until 1918.
summary: In three partitions in 1772, 1793 and 1795, Russia, Prussia and Austria annexed the whole of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the largest state in central Europe, and erased it from the map for 123 years. The final partition followed the defeat of the Kosciuszko Uprising in 1794; the three powers agreed in 1797 to suppress the name of the kingdom entirely. Roughly 12-14 million people passed under new sovereigns. Partition was not accompanied by mass expulsion, but it created the political conditions for later coercive population measures in the atlas — the confinement of Jews to the Pale of Settlement in the annexed Russian provinces, the Siberian exile of insurgents after 1831 and 1863, and Prussian settlement policy in Poznania. It is the largest single act of territorial extinction in modern European history and its absence from the atlas would be conspicuous.

sources.title: Partitions of Poland — Wikipedia
Kosciuszko Uprising — Wikipedia
Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The partitions themselves were diplomatic and administrative acts and produced no mass death toll. The associated fighting — the Confederation of Bar, the 1794 uprising and the Praga massacre in which Russian troops killed several thousand civilians in a Warsaw suburb — caused deaths in the thousands to low tens of thousands.
baselineWhat: The population of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth before the first partition
baselineNote: The Commonwealth held no modern census; estimates from hearth-tax and church records put its population at roughly 12-14 million in 1772, falling to about 8.8 million in the reduced state counted by the 1789-91 fiscal census. The three partitions transferred all of it: Russia took roughly 62 per cent of the territory and 45 per cent of the people, Austria about 18 per cent of the land and 32 per cent of the people, and Prussia about 20 per cent of the land and 23 per cent of the people.

title: Russia's Annexation of the Crimean Khanate, the 1778 Deportation of Crimea's Christians and the Destruction of the Zaporozhian Sich
actors: Catherine II's government destroyed the Zaporozhian Sich, deported Crimea's Greek and Armenian population to the Azov coast, and annexed the Crimean Khanate
peopleRange: About 31,000 Greeks, Armenians, Georgians and Vlachs were removed from Crimea to the northern Azov littoral in 1778-1779; the figure comes from the resettlement registers kept by Suvorov's command and by Metropolitan Ignaty, and is unusually well documented for the period. Perhaps 100,000 or more Crimean Tatars emigrated to Ottoman lands in the two decades after annexation, a figure reconstructed from Russian provincial returns and Ottoman settlement records and regarded as approximate. The Zaporozhian Cossack host of some 10,000-20,000 was dispersed, part of it fleeing to Ottoman territory to found the Danubian Sich.
territoryDesc: The Crimean Khanate — the Crimean peninsula (about 26,100 km2) together with the Kuban and the steppe north of the Black Sea — was annexed by the Russian Empire in April 1783; the Zaporozhian lands were absorbed into New Russia and granted to Russian and foreign colonists.

flows.label: Crimean Greeks and Armenians deported to Mariupol and the Azov coast
Zaporozhian Cossacks fleeing to the Ottoman Danube delta

summary: In June 1775 Russian troops surrounded and razed the Zaporozhian Sich, the fortified centre of the Cossack host on the lower Dnieper, dissolving its autonomy and opening the steppe to state-directed colonisation; part of the host fled to Ottoman territory. In 1778-1779 the government removed the Khanate's Christian population — some 31,000 Greeks and Armenians — to the Azov coast, where they founded Mariupol and Nakhichevan-on-Don, a measure intended both to protect co-religionists and to strip the khan of his tax base. The Khanate, nominally independent since 1774, was annexed outright in April 1783. Emigration of Crimean Tatars to the Ottoman Empire followed in waves; the much larger exodus of 1856-1866 is treated separately in the atlas. The episode fills the gap between the atlas's Russian eastward expansion entry, which ends around 1750, and the nineteenth-century Caucasus and Crimean entries.
contested: Whether the 1778 removal of the Christians is best read as protection, as economic warfare against the Khanate, or as forced deportation; Russian, Greek, Armenian and Crimean Tatar historiographies weight these differently.

sources.title: Annexation of Crimea by the Russian Empire — Wikipedia
Crimean Khanate — Wikipedia
Zaporozhian Sich — Wikipedia
Mariupol Greeks — Wikipedia

deathsNote: There was no massacre. Deaths arose from the winter march of the deported Christians and from the first years on the unprepared Azov steppe, where contemporary Greek accounts report heavy mortality; no count was made. The destruction of the Sich was accomplished with little bloodshed.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Russian military correspondence and the resettlement registers record the razing of the Sich and the abandonment of Greek and Armenian property in Crimea.
baselineWhat: The population of the Crimean Khanate on the eve of Russian annexation, together with the Zaporozhian Host
baselineNote: Ottoman and early Russian administrative counts are fragmentary; Alan Fisher's reconstruction puts the Khanate at roughly 300,000-500,000 people, of whom about 31,000 Greeks and Armenians were deported to the Azov coast in 1778, with the Zaporozhian Sich adding some 50,000 Cossacks and dependants before its destruction in 1775. Crimean Tatar emigration to Ottoman lands after 1783 removed a further large share, variously estimated at 80,000-100,000 in the first decade.
shareCaveat: The affected figure sums three distinct groups - deported Christians, emigrating Crimean Tatars and dispersed Cossacks - drawn from partly overlapping territories, so the ratio is approximate.

title: The Loyalist Exodus from the United States
actors: Revolutionary state governments confiscated Loyalist property and banished Loyalists by statute; some 60,000 white Loyalists, 15,000 enslaved and free Black people and thousands of Haudenosaunee allies left for British territory
peopleRange: About 60,000 white Loyalists together with roughly 15,000 Black people — most of them enslaved and taken by their owners, some 3,000 free Black Loyalists evacuated under British protection — left the thirteen states between 1775 and 1785. The figures are reconstructed from British evacuation lists, including the Book of Negroes compiled at New York in 1783, from Loyalist Claims Commission files, and from settlement returns in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec; Maya Jasanoff's Liberty's Exiles gives a total in this range. Roughly 2,000 Haudenosaunee, mainly Mohawk under Joseph Brant, resettled on the Grand River in Upper Canada.
territoryDesc: Loyalist settlement led to the creation of New Brunswick in 1784 and of Upper Canada in 1791, and to the Haldimand Grant on the Grand River for the Six Nations.

flows.label: Loyalist evacuation from New York to the Bay of Fundy and Nova Scotia
Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia to Sierra Leone, 1792
Mohawk and other Six Nations allies to the Grand River

summary: During and after the American Revolutionary War, the revolutionary states passed confiscation and banishment acts against those who remained loyal to the Crown, seizing estates and in several states making return a capital offence. Around 60,000 white Loyalists left, together with some 15,000 Black people: enslaved people carried out by their owners, and about 3,000 who had been promised freedom for reaching British lines and were evacuated from New York in 1783 on the strength of the Book of Negroes, over American objections. Most went to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec, some to Britain, the Bahamas and Jamaica; about 1,200 Black Loyalists, disappointed by conditions in Nova Scotia, sailed on to Sierra Leone in 1792. Britain's Haudenosaunee allies, whose villages had been destroyed by the Sullivan expedition of 1779, resettled on the Grand River. The 1783 Treaty of Paris recommended restitution of confiscated property; the states largely ignored it. The atlas had almost nothing for North America between the Acadian expulsion and Indian Removal.
contested: Whether the departures are best characterised as expulsion, given the confiscation and banishment statutes, or as flight from a civil war in which loyalties were mixed and coercion uneven across states.

United Empire Loyalist — Wikipedia

deathsNote: There was no mass killing associated with the exodus itself, though Loyalists suffered tarring, whipping and lynching at the hands of committees and mobs, and mortality was high among Black Loyalists in the first Nova Scotian winters. No counts were kept.
violenceNote: State confiscation and banishment statutes and the files of the British Loyalist Claims Commission document the seizure of property and the stripping of citizenship.
baselineWhat: The population of the Thirteen Colonies at the outbreak of the Revolution
baselineNote: Colonial population series compiled from tax lists and militia returns, and reproduced by the US Census Bureau's historical statistics, put the Thirteen Colonies at roughly 2.4-2.5 million in 1775, including about half a million enslaved people. Estimates of Loyalist sympathisers run to a fifth or a third of the free population, of whom about 60,000 whites and 15,000 Black Loyalists actually left.

title: The Mysore Deportations of the Mangalorean Catholics and the Kodavas
actors: Tipu Sultan's Mysore state deported the Catholic population of the Kanara coast and the Kodavas of Coorg to Seringapatam
peopleRange: The figures come almost entirely from Catholic church records, Portuguese and Italian missionary correspondence and later British accounts: they give about 60,000-80,000 Mangalorean Catholics seized in 1784, roughly 20,000 dying on the march or in captivity, and 15,000-20,000 surviving to return after Tipu's death in 1799. Comparable figures for the Kodavas, in the range of tens of thousands, come from Coorg court and British sources. Indian historians including Irfan Habib and Mohibbul Hasan regard the numbers as inflated by hostile sources; no Mysore state records survive to test them.

flows.label: Mangalorean Catholics marched to Seringapatam
Kodavas deported from Coorg

summary: Following the Treaty of Mangalore in 1784, Tipu Sultan ordered the seizure of the Catholic population of South Kanara, whom he regarded as having sided with the British and the Portuguese, and their march inland to Seringapatam, where they were held, put to labour and in many cases forcibly converted; church records describe the episode as the Captivity, lasting until Tipu's death at Seringapatam in 1799. A parallel deportation removed Kodavas from Coorg in 1785 after a revolt, again with forced conversion. The scale is disputed: the surviving figures come from missionary and British sources with strong reasons to indict Tipu, and Indian historians have argued that the deportations were punitive and political rather than religious, and smaller than the church accounts claim. Tipu is a politically charged figure in present-day India, celebrated as an anti-colonial ruler in some accounts and denounced as a persecutor in others, and this episode is central to that argument. The atlas records it as a documented mass deportation whose numbers rest on contested sources.
contested: The scale and the motive are both disputed: church and British sources describe a religious persecution of 60,000-80,000 people, while several Indian historians treat the figures as inflated and the motive as punishment for collaboration.

sources.title: Captivity of Mangalorean Catholics at Seringapatam
Tipu Sultan

deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Church registers, missionary correspondence and later British accounts describe forced conversion, destruction of churches and forced labour at Seringapatam; Mysore's own records do not survive.
baselineWhat: The Catholic population of the Kanara coast on the eve of Tipu Sultan's 1784 deportation
baselineNote: Estimates rest on Mysore court chronicles, contemporary Portuguese and British East India Company reports, and later Catholic parish reconstructions; they put the Kanara Catholic community at roughly 60,000-80,000, of whom about 60,000 were marched to Seringapatam and perhaps 15,000-20,000 returned after 1799. The parallel deportation of Kodavas from Coorg is reported in Mysore sources at figures - up to 85,000 - that most historians regard as inflated.
