title: The Australian Frontier Wars and Aboriginal Dispossession
actors: British colonists, native police and colonial governments dispossessed Aboriginal peoples across the Australian continent, killing them in massacres and confining survivors on reserves and missions
peopleRange: No count exists of Aboriginal people displaced, and none was attempted at the time. Dispossession advanced with the pastoral frontier: land was occupied under leases and grants that made no provision for existing inhabitants, waterholes and food resources were taken, and survivors were drawn onto stations as unpaid or rationed workers, or gathered onto government reserves and mission stations under colonial protection legislation from the 1860s onwards. Aboriginal populations were not enumerated in colonial censuses, and estimates of the pre-1788 population of the continent range from about 300,000 to over a million.
territoryDesc: The whole of the Australian continent, some 7.6 million square km, was taken into British and then colonial possession without treaty and without recognition of prior ownership; the doctrine that the land had belonged to no one was overturned by the High Court of Australia only in 1992.

flows.label: Retreat before the pastoral frontier in Queensland and central Australia
Survivors gathered onto reserves and mission stations

summary: From the first British settlement in 1788 to the end of the nineteenth century, the occupation of Australia proceeded through a series of local frontier conflicts as pastoralists took land and water and Aboriginal groups resisted. The University of Newcastle's Colonial Frontier Massacres project, which defines a massacre as the deliberate killing of six or more relatively undefended people in a single operation, has documented 438 massacre sites across the continent between 1788 and 1930, with approximately 10,657 people killed, a figure the project describes as indicative rather than definitive and deliberately conservative. The Yoorrook Justice Commission's presentation of the Victorian data records 50 massacres there between 1834 and 1860, with 978 Aboriginal people and 10 colonists killed, and 47 of the 50 carried out by colonists. Alongside the killing, introduced disease, the destruction of food resources and the confinement of survivors on reserves and missions under protection legislation transformed Aboriginal society. Systematic removal of Aboriginal children, which became large-scale in the twentieth century and was investigated in the 1997 Bringing Them Home inquiry, has its legislative origins in the protection acts of this period.
contested: The scale of frontier killing has been the subject of Australia's 'history wars': Keith Windschuttle argued that massacre accounts were exaggerated or fabricated, while Lyndall Ryan's team and Henry Reynolds hold that the documented record is a floor rather than a ceiling, since killings were usually carried out in secret. The Newcastle project itself notes its figures are conservative and that the full story may never be known.

sources.title: University of Newcastle: Colonial Frontier Massacres in Australia, 1788-1930
Yoorrook Justice Commission (Victoria): Victorian Massacres

deathsNote: The lower figure is the count of people killed at documented massacre sites compiled by the University of Newcastle's Colonial Frontier Massacres project for 1788-1930, built from newspapers, government records, archives and oral histories under a strict corroboration standard; it counts only killings of six or more people in a single operation and the project describes it as indicative and conservative. The upper figure reflects the broader estimates of total Aboriginal deaths in frontier violence advanced by historians such as Henry Reynolds, which include smaller-scale killings, shootings by native police in the course of dispersal, and deaths that left no documentary trace. Neither includes the far larger mortality from introduced disease and the destruction of subsistence.
violenceNote: The University of Newcastle's Colonial Frontier Massacres project and the Yoorrook Justice Commission document massacres of Aboriginal people by colonists, settler parties and native police, and the destruction of camps and denial of access to water and food resources, drawing on newspapers, official records, archives and Aboriginal oral history.
baselineWhat: The Aboriginal population of the Australian continent at the beginning of British colonisation
baselineNote: Estimates for 1788 are contested and have risen over time: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown's early figure of about 300,000 was long standard, Noel Butlin argued for 1-1.5 million on epidemiological grounds, and the Australian Bureau of Statistics has cited a range from at least 315,000 to 750,000 or more, with some scholars going higher. By the 1901 census the Aboriginal population had fallen to roughly 90,000-95,000. Frontier death tolls are similarly disputed, from Lyndall Ryan's massacre-project count of 11,000-14,000 to national estimates of 30,000 (Reynolds) and 100,000 or more (Ørsted-Jensen and Evans).

baselineSources.title: Colonial Frontier Massacres in Australia, 1788–1930 (University of Newcastle)

shareCaveat: Both the 1788 population and the death toll are disputed by factors of three or more, so any share derived from them carries a very wide margin.

title: Convict Transportation to Australia and the Norfolk Island Penal Settlements
actors: The British state transported convicted prisoners from Britain and Ireland to penal colonies in Australia and secondary punishment stations
peopleRange: Convict transportation was recorded in detail: British and colonial registers record more than 162,000 convicts carried on some 800 voyages between 1788 and 1868, about 25,000 of them women, landing in New South Wales, Van Diemen's Land, Moreton Bay and Western Australia. The National Museum of Australia gives the same total; the registers are among the most complete records of any forced migration in this atlas.

flows.label: Convicts transported from Britain and Ireland to New South Wales
Reoffenders sent to Norfolk Island

summary: From the arrival of the First Fleet in January 1788 until the last transport reached Western Australia in 1868, Britain sent more than 162,000 convicted men, women and children to Australia, a sentence of exile that in most cases was permanent because few could afford the return passage. Convicts were assigned as unpaid labour to settlers and to public works, and their labour underwrote the colonial economy. Reoffenders and those convicted in the colonies were sent to secondary punishment stations, chief among them Norfolk Island, occupied as a penal settlement from 1788 to 1814 and again from 1825 to 1855, along with Macquarie Harbour and Port Arthur, where conditions were deliberately severe and prompted parliamentary inquiry in Britain. Irish political prisoners from the rebellion of 1798 and the Young Ireland movement, and Canadian and Chartist prisoners, were transported alongside those convicted of theft. Eleven of the sites are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list as evidence of the global convict system. The dispossession of Aboriginal peoples that the settlement caused is covered elsewhere in the atlas.
contested: Historians differ over how far convict labour should be described as slavery, forced labour or penal servitude, and over the severity of the system relative to British prisons of the period.

sources.title: National Museum of Australia: convict transportation peaks
Convicts in Australia

deathsNote: Voyage mortality, very high on the Second Fleet of 1790 when about a quarter of those embarked died, fell to around one per cent after surgeons were made responsible for convict health. There was no mass death toll; deaths came from shipboard disease, punishment and labour accidents, and the total has not been aggregated.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: British and colonial penal records, parliamentary inquiries into the secondary punishment stations, and the UNESCO World Heritage documentation record penal labour and the punishment regime.
baselineWhat: The population of Great Britain and Ireland at the start of transportation to New South Wales
baselineNote: Britain's first census in 1801 counted about 10.5 million in Great Britain, and Ireland's population in the 1790s is estimated at roughly 4.5-5 million, giving about 14.5 million around 1788. Both figures grew rapidly over the transportation era: by 1868, when transportation ended, the combined population was over 30 million despite the Irish Famine.
shareCaveat: The 162,000 accumulates over eighty years, during which the population of Britain and Ireland roughly doubled; the informative comparison is against the number of people convicted at assizes and quarter sessions, not the general population.

title: The Domestic Slave Trade of the United States
actors: Slaveholders and professional traders in the Upper South sold and marched roughly a million enslaved people to the cotton and sugar districts of the Deep South and Southwest
peopleRange: About one million enslaved people were moved from the Upper South to the Lower South between roughly 1790 and 1860, of whom the majority were sold through the trade and the remainder carried with migrating owners. The figure is a demographic reconstruction rather than a count: it is derived from the decennial federal censuses by comparing the enslaved populations that each state should have had from natural increase with the populations recorded, and is set out in these terms by the Equal Justice Initiative and Encyclopedia Virginia. Family effects are estimated separately: on these reconstructions more than half of enslaved people in the Upper South were separated from a parent or a child, and about a third of their marriages were broken by forced migration.

flows.label: Richmond and the Chesapeake -> Mississippi
Alexandria and Baltimore -> New Orleans
North Carolina -> the Alabama Black Belt

summary: When Congress closed the Atlantic trade to the United States in 1808, the enslaved population of the Chesapeake and the Carolinas was already growing by natural increase while the cotton frontier of the Gulf states was opening. The result was an internal traffic that moved roughly a million people south and west over seven decades, by coastwise vessel, by steamboat down the Ohio and Mississippi after 1811, on foot in chained coffles, and from the 1830s by rail. Slave-trading firms maintained pens and auction houses in Richmond, Alexandria, Baltimore, Charleston and above all New Orleans. The trade is documented in bills of sale, trader ledgers, newspaper advertisements, court records and the federal censuses, and its scale is inferred from interstate population differentials. Its most-cited social consequence is the routine breaking of families: on standard reconstructions more than half of enslaved people in the exporting states lost a parent or child to sale.
contested: The share of the million who were sold by traders rather than carried by migrating owners is estimated differently by different historians, and the profitability and demographic logic of the trade remain subjects of economic-history debate.

sources.title: Equal Justice Initiative: Domestic Slave Trade
Encyclopedia Virginia: The Transatlantic Slave Trade (with the post-1808 domestic trade)

deathsNote: There is no separate death toll for the internal trade, and it was not a killing operation: deaths occurred on coffle marches, in slave pens and in the shift to the harsher labour regimes of the sugar and cotton districts, but they are not separable in the records from the general mortality of enslavement. The trade's documented harm is measured in sales and family separations rather than in deaths.
violenceNote: The Equal Justice Initiative and Encyclopedia Virginia document the sale of children away from parents, the sale of women into sexual exploitation, and the use of whipping and confinement in trading pens, drawing on sale records, advertisements, court cases and the narratives of formerly enslaved people.
baselineWhat: The enslaved population of the United States at the 1860 census, at the end of the interstate trade
baselineNote: The 1860 federal census counted 3,953,760 enslaved people. The same population was 697,681 at the 1790 census and grew roughly fivefold by natural increase over the trade's span, so the census at the close of the period is the only denominator that yields a share resembling the historiographical finding that about one enslaved person in four in the Upper South was sold or moved south.
shareCaveat: The denominator is an end-of-period snapshot: measured against the 697,681 enslaved people counted in 1790, when the trade began, the million people sold south would exceed 100 per cent.

title: The Haitian Revolution, the War of Extermination and the Expulsion of the French
actors: Enslaved insurgents overthrew the plantation regime of Saint-Domingue; French forces under Leclerc and Rochambeau waged a campaign of extermination; after independence Dessalines ordered the killing or expulsion of the remaining French
peopleRange: Roughly 25,000-30,000 white colonists and a comparable number of free people of colour left Saint-Domingue between 1791 and 1804, going to Cuba, Jamaica, the United States and France; port and refugee registers in Santiago de Cuba, Charleston, Philadelphia and New Orleans provide partial counts, and around 9,000-10,000 of those first sheltering in Cuba were re-expelled to Louisiana in 1809, a movement documented in Spanish and American customs records. The colony's enslaved population, about 500,000 in 1789 by French colonial censuses, was not displaced abroad but was transformed by the revolution.
territoryDesc: Saint-Domingue, the wealthiest colony in the Caribbean, became the independent state of Haiti on 1 January 1804; its 27,750 km2 passed out of French control and plantation property was confiscated.

flows.label: Colonists and free people of colour fleeing to Santiago de Cuba
Refugees expelled from Cuba to New Orleans, 1809

summary: The rising of enslaved people in the northern plain of Saint-Domingue in August 1791 began a thirteen-year war that ended slavery in the colony and produced the second independent state in the Americas. Napoleon's expedition of 1802 under Leclerc, and after his death under Rochambeau, attempted to restore slavery and conducted what French officers themselves described as a war of extermination, including mass drownings and the use of dogs against prisoners; the insurgents responded in kind. After independence was declared on 1 January 1804, Jean-Jacques Dessalines ordered the killing of the remaining French population, and between February and April 1804 an estimated 3,000-5,000 people were killed, with priests, foreign nationals and skilled workers largely exempted. Tens of thousands of colonists and free people of colour had already fled to Cuba, Jamaica, the United States and France, reshaping the population of New Orleans and other port cities. The atlas covered the Caribbean's Indigenous collapse and the slave trade but not the revolution that ended slavery there.
contested: The characterisation of the 1804 killings, described by some historians as a genocide of the colony's white population and by others as the terminal act of a war in which the French had themselves pursued extermination; and the size of the toll, which contemporary accounts by survivors and by the Haitian state differ over.

sources.title: Haitian Revolution — Wikipedia
1804 Haiti massacre — Wikipedia
Jean-Jacques Dessalines — Wikipedia
Saint-Domingue — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The range covers those killed in the 1804 massacre of the remaining French population, estimated from survivor accounts and contemporary correspondence; no register was kept. The revolution as a whole is generally estimated to have caused well over 150,000 deaths among the formerly enslaved population and some 50,000 among French troops and colonists, most from disease, but these totals are reconstructions from military returns and colonial censuses rather than counts.
violenceNote: French officers' own dispatches under Rochambeau and the proclamations and correspondence of Dessalines document the mass drownings, executions and the 1804 killings.
baselineWhat: The total population of the French colony of Saint-Domingue on the eve of the revolution
baselineNote: Colonial returns for 1789 give roughly 500,000 enslaved people, about 30,000 whites and about 28,000 free people of colour, a total usually stated as around 520,000-560,000; the enslaved count is generally regarded as an undercount because planters under-declared for tax.
shareCaveat: The affected figure counts mainly the colony's white and French population, killed or expelled, together with French expeditionary troops who were never part of the colonial population; measured against the whole colony it looks small, while it represents most of a resident group of only some 30,000.

title: The Pale of Settlement: Residence Restriction of Russia's Jews
actors: The Russian imperial state confined its Jewish subjects to a designated western zone of residence and periodically expelled them from cities and villages within and beyond it
peopleRange: The imperial census of 1897 counted 4,899,300 Jews in the Pale, about 94 per cent of the empire's Jewish population and roughly 11 per cent of the Pale's total inhabitants — a direct enumeration and one of the more reliable figures in the atlas. Expulsions within the system moved smaller but substantial groups: the 1891-1892 expulsion from Moscow removed some 20,000-30,000 people, and the May Laws of 1882 barred new Jewish settlement in rural villages inside the Pale itself.
territoryDesc: A zone of about 25 western provinces of the Russian Empire, covering much of present-day Belarus, Lithuania, Moldova, Ukraine and eastern Poland, within which Jews were required to reside.

flows.label: Expulsion of Jews from Moscow into the Pale, 1891-1892

summary: From decrees of 1791 and 1794 onward, the Russian Empire required its Jewish subjects — acquired chiefly through the partitions of Poland — to live within a defined western zone, the Pale of Settlement, with exemptions for narrow categories such as merchants of the first guild, university graduates and certain artisans. The system was a legal confinement rather than a camp: it restricted where people could live, trade, own land and attend school, and was tightened by the May Laws of 1882, which barred Jews from villages within the Pale, and by quotas on secondary and higher education. Expulsions were periodically enforced, most visibly from Moscow in 1891-1892. The Pale held nearly five million people at the 1897 census and was abolished only in 1917. The atlas already covers the pogroms and emigration of the 1880s and 1890s; the residence regime that framed them is a distinct and larger confinement system.

sources.title: Pale of Settlement — Wikipedia
Pale of Settlement — YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe
May Laws — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The residence regime itself was not lethal; it operated through law, policing and expulsion orders. Deaths associated with Russian Jewry in this period arose from the pogroms of 1881-1884, 1903-1906 and the civil war, which the atlas covers in separate entries.
violenceNote: Imperial legislation itself, catalogued in the YIVO Encyclopedia, established the residence, education and occupational disabilities and the expulsion powers used against Jews resident outside the Pale.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of the Russian Empire at the 1897 imperial census
baselineNote: The 1897 census, the empire's only full one, recorded 5,189,401 Jews by religion, of whom roughly 4.9 million lived within the Pale of Settlement; they made up about 12 per cent of the Pale's population and a much higher share of its towns. At the Pale's creation in 1791 the Jewish population of the empire was on the order of one million, so the restricted population grew fivefold over the system's life.
shareCaveat: The affected figure is essentially the census count of Jews inside the Pale, so the ratio approaches 100 per cent by construction: it describes the completeness of the residence restriction, not a share of people singled out within the group.

title: The War in the Vendee and the Republican Repression
actors: French Republican armies suppressed a royalist and Catholic peasant insurrection in western France, burning villages and conducting mass executions and punitive sweeps
peopleRange: No reliable displacement figure exists. Whole communes were burned by the colonnes infernales in the winter of 1793-1794 and their inhabitants scattered; the department's population is estimated by the demographer Jacques Hussenet's team to have fallen by roughly 15-20 per cent, from a combination of death and flight. The basis is parish registers and post-revolutionary compensation claims, reconstructed in the 2007 collective study 'Detruisez la Vendee!'.
summary: A peasant and royalist rising against conscription and the civil constitution of the clergy broke out in the Vendee and neighbouring departments in March 1793 and was suppressed by Republican forces over the following three years. After the insurgent defeat at Savenay in December 1793 the Convention ordered the region devastated; General Turreau's colonnes infernales burned farms, crops and villages, and mass executions were carried out at Nantes under Jean-Baptiste Carrier, including the drownings in the Loire. Estimates of the dead range from about 117,000 to 200,000 out of a pre-war population of around 800,000, with the Hussenet team's figure of roughly 170,000 the most widely cited. Since Reynald Secher's 1986 book the question of whether the repression constituted a genocide has been fiercely argued in France; most academic historians of the Revolution, including Jean-Clement Martin, reject the term while accepting that the Convention ordered exterminatory measures. The event is the largest instance of state mass killing in western Europe between the Wars of Religion and the twentieth century.
contested: Whether the repression amounted to genocide, as Reynald Secher and some Vendean commemorative organisations argue, or to an exceptionally brutal counter-insurgency without genocidal intent, as Jean-Clement Martin and most academic specialists hold; the French state has never adopted either characterisation.

sources.title: War in the Vendee — Wikipedia
Colonnes infernales — Wikipedia
Reynald Secher — Wikipedia
Vendee — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The lower figure is the reconstruction by Jacques Hussenet and colleagues from parish registers and claims records, covering insurgents, civilians and Republican soldiers; the upper end reflects older estimates and those of authors such as Secher who count a wider area and longer period. The disagreement turns on which departments and years are included and on whether Republican military deaths are counted alongside civilian ones.
violenceNote: The Convention's own orders to Turreau, the trial records of Jean-Baptiste Carrier in 1794 and the reports of Republican officers themselves document the burnings, the Nantes drownings and rapes by the columns.
baselineWhat: The population of the insurgent region — the 'Vendée militaire' spanning parts of four western departments
baselineNote: The insurgent territory covered the Vendée and adjoining parts of Loire-Inférieure, Maine-et-Loire and Deux-Sèvres, with a population usually put at about 800,000 on the basis of the revolutionary-era departmental returns. Estimates of the dead on both sides range from 117,000 to 450,000, and the historians' dispute over whether the repression constituted genocide turns partly on which end of that range is accepted.

title: The Sokoto Caliphate: Jihad, Slave Raiding and the Plantation Economy
actors: The Sokoto Caliphate conquered the Hausa states and raided the non-Muslim Middle Belt for captives held as agricultural slaves
peopleRange: Paul Lovejoy and other historians of West African slavery estimate that by the end of the nineteenth century the Sokoto Caliphate held between one and two and a half million enslaved people, one of the largest slave populations anywhere in the modern world, concentrated on plantations around Kano, Sokoto and Zaria. The estimates derive from British colonial assessments made at conquest in 1900-1903, from caravan and market records, and from Arabic chronicles and correspondence of the caliphate itself; they are reconstructions, not censuses.
territoryDesc: A caliphate covering much of present-day northern Nigeria and parts of Niger, Cameroon and Burkina Faso, organised in some thirty emirates

flows.label: Captives from the Middle Belt to the plantations of Kano and Zaria

summary: The jihad proclaimed by Usman dan Fodio in 1804 overthrew the Hausa city-states and created the Sokoto Caliphate, which by the 1830s governed a population estimated in the millions across some thirty emirates. Warfare with non-Muslim polities on its southern and eastern frontiers - in the Middle Belt, Adamawa and around Lake Chad - was a continuing source of captives, since Islamic law as applied in the caliphate permitted enslavement of non-Muslims taken in jihad; captives were settled on plantations producing grain, cotton and indigo for the caliphate's cities, and were also sold into the trans-Saharan trade. Historians including Paul Lovejoy and Jan Hogendorn estimate the enslaved population at one to two and a half million by 1900, a share of total population comparable to the American South before abolition. Frontier populations fled to hill refuges and defensible sites, a settlement pattern colonial officials later recorded across the Jos plateau and the Middle Belt. Britain conquered the caliphate in 1900-1903 and abolished the legal status of slavery gradually, in a way designed to avoid disrupting the emirate economy, with slavery persisting in practice well into the twentieth century.
contested: The size of the enslaved population rests on reconstructions from British colonial assessments and market records rather than counts, and estimates differ by more than a factor of two; the balance between religious reform and slave-raiding economics in the caliphate's expansion is debated.

sources.title: Sokoto Caliphate
Fula jihads
Slavery in Nigeria

deathsNote: No defensible range. Slave raiding, the wars of the jihad and the caravan routes north all caused substantial mortality, described in Arabic chronicles and by nineteenth-century European travellers such as Heinrich Barth, but no figures exist.
violenceNote: Arabic chronicles of the caliphate, nineteenth-century European travellers including Heinrich Barth, and British colonial slavery assessments documented captive-taking including of children, plantation labour and concubinage.
baselineWhat: The population of the Sokoto Caliphate at its height
baselineNote: The caliphate is usually estimated at 10-20 million people by 1837, the most populous state in West Africa; the figures derive from nineteenth-century European travellers' accounts, later colonial enumeration and modern reconstruction rather than any census. Hogendorn and Lovejoy estimate that enslaved people made up between a quarter and a half of that population, with at least one million and perhaps 2.5 million held in slavery by 1900 — proportionally comparable to the American South.

title: The Musket Wars and the Invasion of the Chatham Islands
actors: Maori iwi armed with muskets acquired through European trade conquered and displaced rival iwi across New Zealand; Ngati Mutunga and Ngati Tama invaded the Chatham Islands and subjugated the Moriori
peopleRange: Around 30,000 people are estimated to have been enslaved or forced to migrate during the wars, out of a Maori population of perhaps 100,000-150,000; the figure comes from historians' reconstruction, chiefly R. D. Crosby's synthesis of iwi oral tradition, missionary accounts and Native Land Court testimony, and is an estimate rather than a count. Whole iwi abandoned their territories: Ngati Toa migrated from Kawhia to Kapiti, Te Ati Awa and Ngati Mutunga from Taranaki to the Wellington region and then to the Chathams. In 1835 about 900 Ngati Mutunga and Ngati Tama seized the brig Lord Rodney and landed on Rekohu, where the Moriori population of roughly 1,600 fell to 101 by 1862, recorded in colonial censuses.
territoryDesc: Large-scale redrawing of iwi territory across the North Island, the northern South Island and the Chatham Islands, with consequences for later Native Land Court and Treaty of Waitangi determinations of customary ownership.

flows.label: Ngati Toa migration from Kawhia to Kapiti and the Cook Strait
Ngati Mutunga and Ngati Tama invasion of the Chatham Islands, 1835

summary: From about 1806 the spread of muskets through the Bay of Islands trade set off four decades of intertribal warfare across New Zealand, in which as many as 3,000 battles and raids were fought, an estimated 20,000-40,000 people died and around 30,000 were enslaved or driven from their lands. Whole iwi relocated hundreds of kilometres, permanently altering the map of customary territory before British annexation in 1840. In November 1835 about 900 Ngati Mutunga and Ngati Tama, themselves displaced from Taranaki, seized a European vessel to reach Rekohu, the Chatham Islands, where they killed a proportion of the Moriori — whose tradition of non-violence, Nunuku's law, led them to submit rather than fight — and enslaved the remainder, prohibiting marriage and taking their land. The Moriori population fell from roughly 1,600 to 101 by 1862. In 2001 the Waitangi Tribunal's Rekohu report found on both Moriori and Ngati Mutunga claims and recorded the killings and enslavement; the New Zealand Crown apologised to Moriori in a 2020 settlement. The atlas covered the New Zealand Wars and the raupatu but not the preceding intertribal upheaval.
contested: Whether the Chatham Islands invasion is properly termed a genocide, a description used by some Moriori representatives and historians and resisted by others as anachronistic; and the reliability of casualty estimates for the Musket Wars, which rest largely on oral tradition recorded decades later.

sources.title: Musket Wars — Wikipedia
Moriori — Wikipedia
Moriori genocide — Wikipedia
Wharekauri / Rekohu / Chathams inquiry and the Rekohu report — Waitangi Tribunal

deathsNote: The range given by historians of the Musket Wars, principally R. D. Crosby, built from iwi tradition, missionary observation and later Native Land Court evidence; it covers killings in battle and raids and does not separate deaths from the epidemics and food shortages that accompanied mass migration. On the Chathams, roughly 10 per cent of about 1,600 Moriori were killed in the initial invasion, with most of the subsequent decline caused by enslavement, disease and prohibition of marriage.

atrocityFindings.body: Waitangi Tribunal (New Zealand)
atrocityFindings.finding: Rekohu: A Report on Moriori and Ngati Mutunga Claims in the Chatham Islands (2001), which recorded the 1835 invasion, killings and enslavement of Moriori and addressed both peoples' claims against the Crown

violenceNote: The Waitangi Tribunal's Rekohu report and the 1862 Moriori petition to the Crown document the killings and the enslavement of the Moriori survivors.
baselineWhat: The Maori population of New Zealand at the start of the musket wars, together with the Moriori of the Chatham Islands
baselineNote: Estimates of the Maori population around 1800 range from 85,000 to 110,000, back-projected from the first colonial counts of the 1850s; by 1857-58 the count was about 56,000. The Moriori numbered roughly 1,600-2,000 when Ngati Mutunga and Ngati Tama landed on Rekohu in 1835, and fewer than 200 by 1862.
shareCaveat: Deaths and displacement in this period are inseparable from the epidemic mortality that accompanied European contact over the same decades, so the ratio attributes to warfare losses with mixed causes.

title: Merina Expansion, Forced Labour and the Wars of Unification in Madagascar
actors: The Merina monarchy of Antananarivo conquered most of Madagascar and imposed unpaid state labour (fanompoana) and military levies on its subjects
peopleRange: Madagascar had no census in this period. Gwyn Campbell's demographic reconstruction from mission registers, army returns and slave-trade records concludes that the wars and the labour system caused heavy population loss in the conquered provinces and among conscripts, with army mortality on campaign frequently above a third; he estimates the enslaved population within Imerina rose to a substantial fraction of its inhabitants by mid-century. No count of people displaced survives.
territoryDesc: Merina authority extended from the central highlands over roughly two-thirds of Madagascar by the 1830s, including the Betsileo, Sakalava and Betsimisaraka lands

flows.label: Captives from the coastal provinces to Imerina

summary: From about 1810 Radama I, armed and trained under an agreement with the British governor of Mauritius, conquered the Betsileo, Sakalava and eastern coastal kingdoms and brought most of Madagascar under Merina rule. Conquest was financed and staffed by fanompoana, an unpaid labour obligation owed to the sovereign that was extended into military service, porterage, mining and construction, and by the enslavement of captured populations, who were moved to the highlands. Under Ranavalona I (1828-61) campaigns against the Sakalava and Bara continued and fanompoana was extended further; Gwyn Campbell's work on the period argues that campaign mortality, disease and the labour regime together produced a demographic decline in both the conquered provinces and Imerina itself. The queen's persecution of Christian converts and the 1835 ban on Christianity are better known in European accounts than the labour system, which historians now regard as the more consequential. Merina rule was itself ended by the French conquest of 1895.
contested: The scale of population loss is reconstructed rather than recorded, and Ranavalona I's reign is portrayed very differently in nineteenth-century missionary accounts and in later Malagasy nationalist historiography.

sources.title: Kingdom of Imerina
Ranavalona I
Gwyn Campbell, 'Slavery and Fanompoana: the Structure of Forced Labour in Imerina (Madagascar), 1790-1861', Journal of African History

deathsNote: No reliable toll. Campbell's estimates of army losses on individual campaigns run into the tens of thousands, largely from disease and hunger rather than combat, but these are reconstructions from incomplete returns rather than records of deaths.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Missionary correspondence and Merina court records, analysed by Campbell, document the fanompoana labour obligation and the enslavement of war captives.
baselineWhat: The population of Madagascar at the beginning of Merina expansion under Radama I
baselineNote: Gwyn Campbell's demographic work on nineteenth-century Madagascar, drawing on Merina court records, missionary observations and later French colonial counts, puts the island's population in the early nineteenth century at roughly 2 million, with estimates ranging from about 1.5 to 2.5 million. Campbell argues the population then stagnated or fell under the pressure of fanompoana labour service, military levies and the resulting famines and epidemics.

title: The Mfecane / Difaqane in Southern Africa
actors: Warfare and state formation among Nguni and Sotho-Tswana chiefdoms, in a period of drought and expanding slave and ivory trading, displaced populations across the southern African interior
peopleRange: No count of any kind exists for a pre-literate region in a period before colonial administration. The evidence is oral tradition recorded decades later, missionary and trader observation from the edges of the affected area, archaeology of abandoned settlement sites, and palaeoclimatic reconstruction. South African History Online records that much of the movement was flight to defensible mountain and river positions rather than long-distance migration, but that Ngoni groups reached present-day Tanzania and Malawi and Kololo groups reached Zambia. Any displacement figure would be an invention.
territoryDesc: The upheavals produced the Zulu kingdom under Shaka and the Sotho, Swazi, Ndebele and Gaza states, redistributed control of the highveld and the Natal coastlands, and left tracts of country temporarily emptied - a fact later used by settler and apartheid-era historiography to support an 'empty land' claim to the interior.

flows.label: Ndebele under Mzilikazi -> the highveld and Matabeleland
Ngoni migrations -> Malawi and Tanzania
Kololo -> the upper Zambezi

summary: Between roughly 1815 and 1840 a period of intense warfare, state formation and migration reshaped the interior of southern Africa. South African History Online sets out the causes now generally accepted: severe drought from about 1800 to 1820, intensified by the Tambora eruption of 1815 and remembered in oral tradition as the time of eating up everything; competition among chiefdoms for the ivory and slave trade through Delagoa Bay; the military and political consolidation associated with Shaka's Zulu kingdom; and the destabilising pressure of the Cape Colony frontier, the arms trade and slave raiding from the south and east. The consequences were the formation of the Zulu, Sotho, Swazi, Ndebele and Gaza states, the movement of Ngoni and Kololo groups as far as Tanzania, Malawi and Zambia, and depopulation of parts of the highveld into which Boer trekkers moved from 1836. Julian Cobbing's intervention in 1988 argued that the whole concept had been constructed by colonial and apartheid historiography to present black-on-black destruction and to justify white land claims.
contested: The Mfecane is one of the most contested topics in African historiography. Julian Cobbing argued in 1988 that it was a settler myth obscuring European slave raiding; Christopher Saunders, in Carolyn Hamilton's Mfecane Aftermath, replies that Cobbing oversimplified a diverse earlier literature that did not uniformly ignore colonial violence. Traditional death estimates of one to two million are now generally regarded as exaggerated.

sources.title: South African History Online: The Mfecane - Understanding a Period of Transformation in Southern Africa
Christopher Saunders, 'Pre-Cobbing Mfecane Historiography', in Carolyn Hamilton (ed.), Mfecane Aftermath (Cambridge Core)

deathsNote: The figure of one to two million deaths repeated in older accounts has no demographic basis: there was no census, no tax register and no administration in the affected region, and South African History Online records that contemporary historians consider these estimates exaggerated and much of the disruption to have been flight rather than mortality. No replacement figure has been established, and giving one would be false precision. Deaths certainly occurred from warfare, famine and the collapse of food production, and are attested in oral tradition and in the accounts of missionaries and traders.
violenceNote: South African History Online records documented warfare, famine and the destruction of communities across the affected region, drawing on oral traditions collected in the nineteenth century, missionary and trader accounts, and the archaeology of abandoned settlements; the scale and the attribution of that violence are the substance of the Cobbing debate.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists, and the event's historiography is itself contested. Julian Cobbing's 1988 critique reframed the Mfecane as driven substantially by Portuguese slave raiding from Delagoa Bay and Cape labour demand rather than by Zulu state formation alone, and in the ensuing debate both the death tolls - traditionally given as one to two million - and the underlying population of the interior were shown to rest on colonial-era assertion. Estimates of the Bantu-speaking population between the Limpopo and the Cape frontier around 1815 range from about 1.5 to 4 million.

title: The Burmese Invasions of Assam and Manipur and the Depopulation of the Brahmaputra Valley
actors: Konbaung Burmese armies occupied the Ahom kingdom of Assam and the Manipur valley, causing mass killing, enslavement and flight
peopleRange: Assamese chronicles (buranjis) and early British administrative reports describe the valley as half-emptied by 1826, with tens of thousands killed or carried off to Burma and large numbers fleeing to British Bengal, Goalpara, Cachar and the hills; Manipuri tradition remembers the parallel period as chahi taret khuntakpa, the Seven Years' Devastation, with much of the valley population dead or in flight to Cachar. British officials arriving in 1826 recorded abandoned villages and reverted cultivation. The figures are impressionistic - chronicles and colonial estimates, no enumeration - and a total of a few hundred thousand displaced is an order of magnitude.
territoryDesc: Assam and Manipur passed from Burmese occupation to British control under the Treaty of Yandabo, 1826

flows.label: Assamese flight west to Goalpara and British Bengal
Manipuris fleeing to Cachar

summary: Invited in by rival Assamese factions, Burmese armies invaded Assam three times between 1817 and 1821 and then occupied the Ahom kingdom until 1825, while separately devastating the Manipur valley from 1819. Assamese chronicles and early British reports describe systematic killing, mutilation, enslavement and the removal of captives to Burma, with the population fleeing into the hills, into Cachar and westwards into British territory; the period is remembered in Assam as the manor din, the time of the Burmese. Manipur's parallel experience, the Seven Years' Devastation, emptied much of the valley and drove a large refugee population into Cachar under Gambhir Singh. The refugee pressure and Burmese activity on the Bengal frontier were a proximate cause of the First Anglo-Burmese War of 1824-26, after which the Treaty of Yandabo transferred Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim to British control, ending the Ahom kingdom. No enumeration of the losses exists; the evidence is chronicle testimony and the observations of British officers who found abandoned settlements and jungle-covered fields.
contested: All figures are impressionistic; Assamese and Manipuri chronicle traditions and British colonial accounts, which had an interest in justifying annexation, are the only sources.

sources.title: Burmese invasions of Assam
Seven Years' Devastation (chahi taret khuntakpa), Manipur
Treaty of Yandabo, 1826

deathsNote: No defensible range. Assamese and Manipuri accounts describe very heavy mortality from killing, famine and disease, and British officials described a depopulated valley, but no counts exist and colonial estimates were made after the fact by an interested party.
violenceNote: Assamese buranji chronicles and early British administrative reports record killings, mutilation, the burning of villages and the marching of captives into servitude in Burma.
baselineWhat: The population of the Brahmaputra valley and the Manipur valley before the Burmese invasions
baselineNote: No count exists for the Ahom kingdom or Manipur before 1817. The first census of the region, taken in 1872 after fifty years of British rule and considerable in-migration, counted about 2.1 million in Assam and about 126,000 in Manipur, which cannot be projected back through a period of mass killing, enslavement and flight. Historians of the period record only that it is impossible to estimate how many were killed, deported to Burma or fled to Bengal, and describe a sharp fall in population.
shareCaveat: The affected figure is a modern estimate of killings, enslavement and flight with no contemporary count behind it.

title: The Russian Conquest of the Caucasus and the Circassian Expulsion
actors: The Russian Empire conquered the North Caucasus and expelled the Circassian (Adyghe), Ubykh and Abaza populations of the north-western Caucasus to the Ottoman Empire
peopleRange: Estimates vary by a factor of three and the difference is politically live. Britannica records that resettlement pressure began in 1860, that the expulsion was largely accomplished by 1864, and puts about 400,000 Circassians displaced, nearly all of whom chose the Ottoman Empire over relocation within Russia. Ottoman reception records and later reconstructions give higher totals, and Walter Richmond's study for Rutgers University Press argues that hundreds of thousands were deported on top of very heavy mortality, with about 200,000 Circassians remaining when the final Russian assault began in November 1861 and roughly three quarters of the population destroyed by 1864. The figures rest on Russian military correspondence, Ottoman provincial settlement registers and demographic back-projection, not on a census of the deported.
territoryDesc: The mountain and coastal districts of the north-western Caucasus - the Kuban valley, the Black Sea littoral around Sochi and the Ubykh lands - were emptied of their inhabitants and settled with Cossacks and Russian and other colonists; the Caucasus as a whole was incorporated into the empire.

flows.label: Black Sea coast (Sochi, Tuapse) -> Samsun and Ottoman Anatolia
Kuban and Circassia -> Ottoman Rumelia and the Marmara provinces
North Caucasus -> Ottoman Syria (Aleppo and the Golan)

summary: The Russian campaign to subdue the North Caucasus ran from the early nineteenth century to the surrender of Imam Shamil in 1859 in the east and the defeat of the western Circassians in 1864. In the north-west, where resistance had been sustained by a mountain population Russia could not garrison, the army adopted a policy of clearance: villages and crops were destroyed and the inhabitants offered relocation to the plains under Russian administration or emigration to the Ottoman Empire. Britannica records that from 1860 the population was pressed eastward toward the Kuban and that nearly all chose emigration instead, about 400,000 people, with many thousands dying of starvation and disease on the way. Embarkation on the Black Sea coast in overcrowded vessels, and reception in Ottoman ports without adequate provision, produced very high mortality. Circassians today form large diasporas in Turkey, Jordan, Syria and Israel. On 20 May 2011 the Parliament of Georgia became the first legislature to recognise the events as genocide; the Russian Federation rejects that characterisation, treating the emigration as a wartime consequence rather than a policy of destruction.
contested: Whether the expulsion constitutes genocide is disputed between Circassian organisations and the Georgian parliament, which recognised it in 2011, and the Russian government, which rejects the term; the number expelled and the number who died are also disputed, with Britannica's 400,000 displaced at the low end and Richmond's figures at the high end.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Circassian
Walter Richmond, The Circassian Genocide (Rutgers University Press, 2013) on JSTOR
RFE/RL: Georgia Recognizes Russian 'Genocide' Of Ethnic Circassians

deathsNote: The high end is Walter Richmond's figure of at least 600,000 Circassians dead from massacre, starvation and exposure, derived from Russian archival material and demographic reconstruction and used by Circassian organisations seeking recognition of a genocide. The low end reflects more conservative readings that treat the mortality as concentrated in the embarkation camps, the sea crossing and the first Ottoman winter, and that regard the pre-war population estimates on which the higher figures rest as too high. Britannica states only that many thousands died of starvation and disease en route. Russian official historiography disputes the higher figures and the intent they are used to establish.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: Parliament of Georgia
atrocityFindings.finding: Resolution recognising the nineteenth-century expulsion of the Circassians by the Russian Empire as genocide and ethnic cleansing - the first such recognition by a national legislature

violenceNote: Richmond's archival study documents the burning of villages, the destruction of crops and stores to compel departure, and killings during the final campaign; Britannica records the deaths from starvation and disease during the deportation itself.
baselineWhat: The Circassian, Ubykh and Abaza population of the north-western Caucasus before the expulsion
baselineNote: The baseline is contested and politically charged. Russian imperial administrative estimates of the 1860s imply somewhat under a million; Western scholarship, including Richmond and Shenfield, works with a pre-war population of roughly 1-2 million; Circassian national historiography, citing an 1830 figure, claims more than 4 million. The 1897 Russian census found only about 150,000 Circassians remaining in the Caucasus. Estimates of those expelled run from 500,000 to 1.5 million and of the dead from 400,000 (McCarthy) to over a million (Shenfield).
shareCaveat: Both numerator and denominator are disputed by a factor of three or more, and Russian, Turkish and Circassian sources differ systematically; the resulting percentage should be treated as an order of magnitude rather than a measurement.

title: The Seminole Wars and the Removal of the Seminole from Florida
actors: The United States fought three wars in Florida to take Seminole land and deport the Seminole and Black Seminoles to Indian Territory
peopleRange: United States Army records show 3,612 Seminoles relocated to Indian Territory by 1842, with several hundred more removed after the Third Seminole War; between about 350 and 500 remained in Florida. Black Seminoles removed alongside them, some of whom were subsequently claimed as slaves, are counted inconsistently in the records. The Seminole population before the wars is not reliably known, so removal rates are estimates.
territoryDesc: The Seminole were confined to a central Florida reservation by the 1823 Treaty of Moultrie Creek and then required by the 1832 Treaty of Payne's Landing to leave Florida entirely; the survivors' refuge in the Everglades became the basis of the modern Florida reservations.

flows.label: Seminole and Black Seminole deportation to Indian Territory
Removal from the Florida panhandle to the central peninsula reservation, 1823

summary: The atlas records Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears; the Florida wars were its longest and costliest theatre and are usually treated separately. The first conflict began in 1817-18 when Andrew Jackson led forces into Spanish Florida in pursuit of Seminoles and of people who had escaped slavery in Georgia, destroying Seminole, Mikasuki and Black Seminole towns. After the United States acquired Florida in 1821, the Treaty of Moultrie Creek confined the Seminole to a central reservation, and the 1832 Treaty of Payne's Landing, whose validity the Seminole disputed, required them to move to Indian Territory. Resistance produced the Second Seminole War of 1835-1842, in which fewer than 2,000 Seminole fighters held off a force that grew beyond 30,000; when pursuit failed, American commanders turned to destroying villages and crops to force surrender by starvation. By 1842, 3,612 Seminoles had been deported west; a Third war from 1855 to 1858 pushed most of the remainder out, leaving a few hundred in the Everglades. The Seminole Tribe of Florida regards the three conflicts as a single war and its members as never having surrendered.
contested: The legitimacy of the Treaty of Payne's Landing was disputed at the time and remains so; the number of Seminole and especially of Black Seminoles removed, and the fate of those claimed as slaves after removal, are poorly documented, and estimates of Seminole deaths in the wars are little more than informed guesses.

sources.title: Seminole Wars (Wikipedia)

deathsNote: About 1,500 United States soldiers died in the Second Seminole War, the great majority from disease rather than combat, and these are the only well-recorded deaths. Seminole military and civilian deaths, including those from hunger and exposure after the destruction of villages and crops and during removal, were never counted; the upper bound is an estimate combining army losses with the fragmentary evidence for Seminole mortality.
violenceNote: The deliberate destruction of villages and food crops as a means of forcing surrender is documented in United States Army correspondence and orders of the Second Seminole War and in the standard military histories drawn on by the cited account.
baselineWhat: The Seminole and Black Seminole population of Florida at the start of the First Seminole War
baselineNote: Estimates rest on US Army returns, agency counts and treaty rolls rather than a census; the Seminole population of Florida around 1820 is usually put at 4,000-6,000, including several hundred to a thousand Black Seminoles. The Seminole were themselves a recently formed population of Creek and other refugees plus people escaping slavery.
shareCaveat: The affected figure accumulates deaths, deportations and flight across four decades of three separate wars, during which the population was continually replenished by new arrivals and reduced by removal, so it can approach or exceed a single-year baseline.

title: The Massina and Umarian Jihads in the Western Sudan
actors: Fulani jihad states under Seku Amadu and later Umar Tal conquered the middle Niger, settled nomads and enslaved captured non-Muslim populations
peopleRange: No numerical records exist. Evidence comes from Arabic chronicles produced by the jihad states themselves, from oral traditions collected in the twentieth century, and from French colonial reports written decades later. The states are known to have resettled pastoral Fulbe into planned villages around Hamdullahi and to have taken large numbers of Bambara and other captives, but no chronicle gives usable totals.
territoryDesc: The Massina Empire controlled the inland Niger delta from Hamdullahi; the Umarian state at its height ran from the upper Senegal across Kaarta and Segu to Massina

flows.label: Captives from Segu and Kaarta to the jihad states

summary: In 1818 Seku Amadu, drawing on the example of Usman dan Fodio's Sokoto jihad, defeated the Bambara of Segu and founded the Massina Empire, building a new capital at Hamdullahi and requiring nomadic Fulbe to settle in supervised villages under a strict religious code. In 1852 Umar Tal, a Tijani cleric returning from Mecca and Sokoto, launched a second jihad from the upper Senegal, taking Kaarta in 1855 and Segu in 1861 and then turning on the fellow-Muslim state of Massina, sacking Hamdullahi in 1862; he died in 1864 during the revolt that followed. Both movements combined religious reform with conquest: non-Muslim populations, chiefly Bambara, were enslaved in large numbers, and pastoral groups were compelled to settle. The Umarian state's wars depopulated parts of the middle Niger shortly before the French advance of the 1880s and 1890s, which used the disorder as a justification for conquest. Coverage of the Sokoto jihad already exists in this atlas; these two jihads to its west were separate states with separate systems.
contested: The chronicles are partisan documents written by the jihad states or their opponents, and modern accounts differ over how far the wars were religious reform, Fulbe political expansion, or slave-raiding enterprises.

sources.title: Massina Empire
Toucouleur Empire
Umar Tal (Britannica)

deathsNote: No credible toll survives. The sack of Hamdullahi in 1862 and the siege that followed are described in chronicles as producing very heavy loss of life, but the accounts give no numbers that can be checked.
violenceNote: Arabic chronicles of both states and later French colonial reports record enslavement of captives and the destruction of non-Muslim shrines and practices.
baselineNote: No enumeration exists for the middle Niger in the nineteenth century. The Massina and Umarian states left tax and settlement records that historians use qualitatively, but the population of the conquered Bambara, Fulbe and Songhay territories is unknown, and the first counts come from French colonial administration after 1890, by which time the wars had already reshaped settlement.

title: Muhammad Ali's Egypt: The Conquest of Sudan, Slave Levies, Conscription and Corvee
actors: Muhammad Ali's Egyptian state invaded Sudan for slaves and gold, conscripted Egyptian peasants by force and requisitioned mass corvee labour
peopleRange: Egyptian and European consular records give partial figures: the 1820-22 Sudan campaign was intended to raise tens of thousands of slave soldiers, and contemporaries record about 20,000 captives sent north to the training camps at Aswan and Manfalut, where the great majority died; conscription took several hundred thousand Egyptian peasants into the army and navy over the reign; and the corvee assembled work gangs of 100,000 or more at a time on canals. The figure given is a rough aggregate of people forcibly moved, not a record.
territoryDesc: Egyptian rule was extended over Sennar, Kordofan and much of the Nile Sudan, later reaching Khartoum, founded as the provincial capital in 1821

flows.label: Sudanese captives marched to the Aswan and Manfalut camps
Egyptian peasants requisitioned for the Mahmudiyya canal

summary: In 1820 Muhammad Ali sent an army under his son Ismail into Sudan, explicitly to secure gold and slaves for a new conscript army; Sennar and Kordofan were taken, Khartoum founded, and captives were marched north, most of whom died of dysentery and other diseases in the camps before they could be trained. When the resistance leader Nimr of Shendi killed Ismail in 1822, the Daftardar's reprisal campaign devastated the Ja'aliyyin districts. Unable to fill the ranks with Sudanese, the state turned to conscripting Egyptian peasants, who fled villages, mutilated themselves and hid to avoid the levy, and to the corvee, which assembled vast unpaid work gangs for the Mahmudiyya canal, the barrages and the cotton estates; European consuls and Egyptian chroniclers report very high mortality on the canal works. Historiography is divided between accounts that treat the reign as the foundation of a modern state and those that emphasise the coercion on which it rested. Al-Jabarti and later Egyptian historians recorded both.
contested: Death tolls for the Mahmudiyya canal corvee range from a few thousand in official accounts to 100,000 in some European contemporary reports, and no reliable basis exists for choosing between them.

sources.title: Muhammad Ali of Egypt
Egyptian conquest of Sudan (1820-1824)

deathsNote: The range aggregates campaign deaths in Sudan, mortality among enslaved recruits at Aswan (contemporaries describe the great majority of about 20,000 dying), and corvee deaths on the canals, for which contemporary European estimates run as high as 100,000 and Egyptian official accounts far lower. None rests on systematic records.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Egyptian chronicles including al-Jabarti, European consular correspondence and later Sudanese accounts describe the slave levies, the Shendi reprisals and mortality in the corvee.
baselineWhat: The population of Egypt during Muhammad Ali's rule
baselineNote: Egypt's first modern census, taken in 1846-48, counted about 4.5 million people, and the French expedition's earlier estimates and Daniel Panzac's demographic work suggest a similar order for the 1820s. Conscription took perhaps 250,000-300,000 peasants into the army over the period, corvée levies for the Mahmudiyya canal and other works ran to hundreds of thousands with heavy mortality, and the Sudan campaigns seized tens of thousands of captives from beyond Egypt's own population.
shareCaveat: The affected figure combines Egyptian conscripts and corvée labourers with Sudanese captives who were never part of the Egyptian denominator.

title: The Greek War of Independence and its Reciprocal Massacres
actors: Greek insurgents and Ottoman and Egyptian forces destroyed and expelled each other's civilian communities during the war that created the Greek state
peopleRange: No census framework exists for either side. The Muslim and Jewish population of the Peloponnese, tens of thousands strong before 1821, was effectively eliminated by killing and flight in the first year of the revolt; the Greek population of Chios, put at around 100,000 before the Ottoman reprisal of 1822, was reduced to a small remnant by killing, enslavement and flight, with large numbers sold in Ottoman slave markets. Ibrahim Pasha's Egyptian campaign in the Morea in 1825-28 depopulated districts and deported an unknown number to Egypt. The figures come from consular reports, insurgent and Ottoman correspondence and later compilations, and are estimates rather than counts.
territoryDesc: The London Protocol of 1830 and the settlement of 1832 detached the Peloponnese, Attica, Boeotia and the Cyclades from the Ottoman Empire as an independent Greek kingdom of roughly 47,000 square km, the first successful secession from Ottoman rule in the Balkans and the model for those that followed.

flows.label: Chios captives -> Ottoman slave markets, 1822
Muslim survivors of the Morea -> Ottoman Rumelia
Deportations from the Morea under Ibrahim Pasha -> Egypt

summary: The revolt that began in the Peloponnese in March 1821 was accompanied from the outset by the destruction of civilian communities on both sides. Insurgent forces killed much of the Muslim and Jewish population of the Morea, most notoriously at the capture of Tripolitsa in September 1821; Ottoman authorities executed the Ecumenical Patriarch and killed and imprisoned Greeks in Constantinople and elsewhere in reprisal, and in 1822 the punishment of Chios killed and enslaved the great bulk of an island population of about 100,000, an event that became a European cause through Delacroix's painting. Ibrahim Pasha's Egyptian expedition of 1825-28 devastated the Morea and deported captives to Egypt. Intervention by Britain, France and Russia, and the destruction of the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino in 1827, secured Greek independence, recognised in 1830 and settled in 1832. The war established the pattern of reciprocal expulsion that recurred through the Balkan secessions of the following century.
contested: Casualty and enslavement figures for Tripolitsa and Chios differ sharply between Greek, Turkish and Western accounts, and modern Turkish historiography, including work published by the Turkish Historical Society, disputes the standard Greek accounts of the massacres of 1821 as much as Greek historiography disputes Ottoman accounts.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Greece - the Greek War of Independence
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Greek Independence Day

deathsNote: No side counted. The lower bound aggregates the more conservative modern readings of the principal episodes - the killings at Tripolitsa in 1821, the reprisals in Constantinople, Smyrna and Cyprus, the destruction of Chios in 1822 and the campaigns in the Morea - while the upper bound follows nineteenth-century consular and journalistic estimates, which were often produced by partisans of one side. Deaths from famine and epidemic during the eight years of war are additional and were never estimated at all.
violenceNote: Contemporary consular despatches, insurgent and Ottoman correspondence and the accounts summarised by Britannica document massacres of civilians by both sides, the enslavement of women and children from Chios, the burning of towns and villages and the destruction of mosques and churches.
baselineWhat: The population of the regions that rose in 1821 and became the Greek state - the Peloponnese, eastern Rumeli and the Aegean islands
baselineNote: Ottoman registers for these provinces are incomplete; the standard anchor is the Capodistrias census of 1828, which counted about 753,000 people in liberated Greece after seven years of killing, famine and flight. Working backwards, historians put the pre-war population at roughly 900,000, including some 40,000 Muslims in the Peloponnese, almost all of whom were killed or expelled by 1822.

title: The Black War and the Removal of the Tasmanian Aboriginal People
actors: British colonists and the colonial government of Van Diemen's Land fought and then removed the Aboriginal population of Tasmania to an island settlement
peopleRange: The National Museum of Australia records that approximately 200 surviving Aboriginal Tasmanians were gradually relocated to the Wybalenna settlement on Flinders Island after 1830, following George Augustus Robinson's 'friendly mission'. The population from which they came had already fallen from an estimated 15,000 before colonisation to fewer than 2,000 by 1818, principally through disease, violence and dispossession. The pre-colonial estimate is an anthropological reconstruction; the Wybalenna figures come from the settlement's own returns, which are among the few reliable counts in the episode.
territoryDesc: The island of Tasmania, some 68,400 square km, passed entirely into colonial possession; the survivors were held on Flinders Island in the Bass Strait, and the remnant was moved again to Oyster Cove on the Tasmanian mainland in 1847.

flows.label: Tasmanian Aboriginal survivors -> Wybalenna, Flinders Island
Wybalenna remnant -> Oyster Cove, 1847

summary: Conflict between colonists and Aboriginal Tasmanians escalated from about 1824 as pastoral settlement spread across the island's midlands. Lieutenant-Governor George Arthur declared martial law in 1828, which, as the National Museum of Australia records, designated Aboriginal Tasmanians open enemies of the state without legal protection. In October 1830 more than 2,200 settlers, soldiers, police and convicts - roughly a tenth of the colony's European population - formed the 'Black Line', a cordon dragged across the settled districts intended to drive the remaining Aboriginal people onto the Tasman Peninsula; it captured two people and killed two. Removal was then achieved by negotiation through George Augustus Robinson, and about 200 survivors were taken to Wybalenna on Flinders Island, where the National Museum records that most died within a few years: forty remained by 1847, when the settlement was closed and the remnant moved to Oyster Cove, and by 1876 all but one had died. Aboriginal Tasmanian descent communities survive today through the Bass Strait islands.
contested: Whether the destruction of the Tasmanian Aboriginal population constitutes genocide is disputed, as is the number killed in the Black War: Keith Windschuttle's challenge to the documentary basis of massacre accounts and Lyndall Ryan's response are the central exchange, and both the killing figures and the balance between violence and disease are argued.

sources.title: National Museum of Australia: The Black Line
University of Newcastle: Colonial Frontier Massacres in Australia, 1788-1930

deathsNote: Estimates of Aboriginal Tasmanians killed in the Black War itself generally fall between six hundred and a thousand, against roughly two hundred colonists killed, and rest on colonial newspapers, government correspondence and depositions rather than on records of the dead. The Black Line operation of 1830, despite mobilising a tenth of the colony's settler population, killed only two people. The far larger element in the population collapse - from perhaps 15,000 before colonisation to fewer than 2,000 by 1818, as the National Museum of Australia records - was introduced disease, the loss of land and food resources, the abduction of women by sealers and the resulting failure of reproduction, and this is not captured in any killing figure. Mortality at Wybalenna itself, where most of the 200 removed died within a few years, was from respiratory disease and despair in confinement.
violenceNote: The National Museum of Australia documents the declaration of martial law removing legal protection from Aboriginal Tasmanians, the Black Line operation, and the confinement of survivors at Wybalenna where most died; the abduction of Aboriginal women and children by sealers and settlers is recorded in colonial depositions and in the Colonial Frontier Massacres project's sources.
baselineWhat: The Aboriginal population of Tasmania at the time of British settlement in 1803
baselineNote: Estimates of the pre-invasion Aboriginal Tasmanian population range from about 3,000 to 7,000, with Lyndall Ryan's figure of roughly 5,000-7,000 the most widely used; by the time the Black War began in 1824 perhaps 1,000 remained, and 220 or fewer were removed to Wybalenna on Flinders Island in the 1830s.
shareCaveat: The affected figure counts only those still alive to be removed to Flinders Island after two decades of frontier killing and introduced disease; measured against the 1803 population it therefore shows how few survived rather than how many were harmed.

title: The Java War and the Dutch Cultivation System
actors: The Dutch colonial state defeated Prince Diponegoro's revolt and then imposed compulsory export-crop cultivation on the Javanese peasantry
peopleRange: The Java War of 1825-30 depopulated large districts of central Java: the population of the Yogyakarta, Mataram and Gunung Kidul areas is recorded as falling from just over 400,000 to under 200,000 between 1825 and 1831, and about a third of Java's roughly six million people were directly affected. Under the Cultivation System no population was moved wholesale, but villagers were compelled to give land and labour to export crops; the famines of the 1840s in Cirebon and of 1849-50 in Demak and Grobogan produced heavy mortality and flight, with Demak's registered population reported to have fallen from about 336,000 to 120,000 and Grobogan's from about 89,500 to 9,000. These are Dutch colonial administrative figures and include flight as well as death.
territoryDesc: Dutch direct rule extended over the Javanese principalities; the courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta lost most remaining territory
summary: The Java War of 1825-30, fought between Prince Diponegoro and the Dutch colonial government with its Javanese allies, ended Javanese armed resistance to Dutch rule and left at least 200,000 Javanese dead, most from disease and starvation rather than combat, alongside some 15,000 dead on the Dutch side. To pay for the war and for the Netherlands' fiscal crisis, Governor-General Johannes van den Bosch introduced the Cultuurstelsel or Cultivation System in 1830, requiring villages to devote a share of land and labour to sugar, coffee and indigo delivered to the colonial state at fixed prices, enforced through Javanese headmen and the colonial bureaucracy. The system generated over 800 million guilders for the Dutch treasury before its dismantling in the 1860s and 1870s, and Indonesian historiography calls it tanam paksa, forced cultivation. Its critics, including the Dutch official Eduard Douwes Dekker writing as Multatuli in Max Havelaar and the parliamentarian Baron van Hoevell, blamed it for the famines of the 1840s in Cirebon and of 1849-50 in Demak and Grobogan, in which colonial records show district populations collapsing through death and flight. Economic historians continue to disagree about how far the famines were caused by the system itself as against harvest failure, rice-market disruption and local abuses.
contested: How far the Cultivation System caused the famines of the 1840s, and how much Javanese welfare fell under it, remain debated among economic historians; the collapse of district population figures reflects flight as well as death.

sources.title: Cultivation System (Cultuurstelsel)
Prince Diponegoro

deathsNote: The lower figure is the standard estimate of Javanese deaths in the Java War itself, most from disease and starvation, as given in Dutch military and colonial accounts and accepted in Peter Carey's history of Diponegoro. The upper figure adds the deaths in the Cirebon and Demak-Grobogan famines of the 1840s under the Cultivation System, which colonial district returns imply were very large but which cannot be separated cleanly from flight and from ordinary mortality.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Dutch colonial critics of the system, notably Baron van Hoevell and the parliamentary inquiries of the 1850s and 1860s, documented compulsory labour and the famines that followed.
baselineWhat: The population of Java at the end of the Java War, when the Cultivation System was imposed
baselineNote: Raffles' count of 1815 gave 4.6 million and is regarded as a substantial undercount; Boomgaard's revisions and the Dutch colonial censuses put Java at roughly 6 million around 1830, rising to about 16 million by 1870. The Cultivation System applied to the peasantry of the residencies under direct Dutch administration, the great majority of that population.

title: The French Conquest of Algeria and the Dispossession of its Land
actors: France conquered Algeria, expropriated tribal and religious land for settler colonisation and confined the rural population to reduced holdings
peopleRange: No count of the displaced exists. Dispossession worked through law and warfare together: military sequestration of the lands of tribes that resisted, the confiscation of habous religious endowments, cantonnement - the confinement of tribes to a fraction of their land with the remainder declared vacant - the senatus-consulte of 1863, which broke collective tribal tenure into individual title, and the Warnier law of 1873, which opened that title to sale. Settler landholding grew from almost nothing in 1830 to hundreds of thousands of hectares by 1870, and the European population of Algeria to roughly a quarter of a million. The Algerian rural population that lost land was recorded in French cadastral and military registers, not counted as displaced.
territoryDesc: Algeria was annexed to France, with the northern departments administered as part of the metropole from 1848 and the Saharan territories brought under military administration later in the century; the whole comprised roughly 2.38 million square km, of which the productive Tell was the object of settler colonisation.

flows.label: Tribes of the Tell -> interior and highland reserves under cantonnement
Exile of Algerian resistance leaders and communities -> Tunisia and the Levant

summary: France invaded in June 1830 and took Algiers by 5 July; EBSCO's account records that the victorious troops pillaged the city and desecrated mosques and cemeteries, and that Marshal Clauzel then began the wholesale seizure of Algerian land and property, establishing settler colonisation. Resistance under Abd al-Qadir controlled two-thirds of the country by 1840 and was broken only by Marshal Bugeaud's campaigns of razzias - punitive raids that destroyed villages, crops, orchards and herds - culminating in his surrender in 1847; the Kabyle insurrection of 1871 was the last general rising. Legal instruments completed what the army began: cantonnement, the senatus-consulte of 1863 and the Warnier law of 1873 converted collective tribal land into alienable individual title, transferring the best land to European settlers. The Algerian population fell substantially between 1830 and the early 1870s, with the famine and typhus of 1867-68 the sharpest single episode.
contested: The scale of Algerian population loss and its attribution are disputed: demographic reconstructions of French colonial census and military data have been read as showing very large excess mortality caused by warfare, dispossession and the resulting vulnerability to famine, while other historians attribute the bulk of the decline to the drought, locusts and epidemic of 1867-68. Whether the conquest should be characterised as genocidal is argued in Algerian and French public debate and is not a settled scholarly position.

sources.title: EBSCO Research Starters: France Conquers Algeria
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Algeria - French rule

deathsNote: The range covers excess mortality among the Algerian population between 1830 and about 1875, and every figure in it is a demographic reconstruction from French colonial census series whose early estimates of the pre-conquest population are themselves contested. Deaths came from the campaigns and razzias, including notorious episodes such as the suffocation of the Ouled Riah in the caves of the Dahra in 1845, from the destruction of crops and herds, and above all from the famine and typhus epidemic of 1867-68, whose severity is itself linked by some historians to dispossession and by others to drought and locusts. No contemporary authority counted the dead.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: EBSCO and Britannica document the pillage and desecration of mosques and cemeteries in Algiers in 1830, Bugeaud's razzia doctrine of destroying villages, crops and herds, and the confiscation of religious endowment land; these are recorded in French military correspondence and colonial legislation.
baselineWhat: The Muslim population of Algeria at the time of the French invasion in 1830
baselineNote: No Ottoman-era count survives. French military and administrative estimates from the 1830s and 1840s, and the demographic reconstructions of Kamel Kateb and Djilali Sari working back from the first reliable colonial censuses of the 1870s and 1880s, give figures between about 2 and 5 million; 3 million is the most commonly cited middle value. The scale of the population loss during the conquest — from war, famine and the typhus epidemics of 1867-68 — is contested for the same reason.

title: US Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears
actors: The United States federal government, acting under the Indian Removal Act, forced the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole nations and others from the eastern states to Indian Territory west of the Mississippi
peopleRange: Britannica puts the number removed during the 1830s at approximately 100,000 tribal members, counted from the muster rolls, ration returns and removal-agent accounts kept by the War Department, which are the basis for all figures. The best-documented single case is the Cherokee removal of 1838-39: the National Park Service records more than 16,000 Cherokee evicted, moved in fourteen detachments, with several thousand more Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek and Seminole moved in separate operations across two decades. The rolls are incomplete, and people who fled into the mountains or the Florida swamps were not enumerated.
territoryDesc: Removal transferred roughly 25 million acres of homeland in Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, Florida and the Carolinas to the states and to white settlers, in exchange for land in Indian Territory (present Oklahoma) that was itself progressively reduced by later cessions and by the allotment policy after 1887.

flows.label: New Echota (Cherokee) -> Tahlequah, Indian Territory
Choctaw homelands, Mississippi -> Indian Territory
Seminole Florida -> Indian Territory
