summary: The Indian Removal Act of 28 May 1830 authorised the president to exchange western land for tribal territory within state boundaries, and the Supreme Court's ruling in Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) that Indian nations were domestic dependent nations without standing in federal court removed a legal obstacle to state pressure. Removal followed by treaty, coercion and force: the Choctaw from 1831, the Creek and Chickasaw through the 1830s, the Cherokee under the disputed Treaty of New Echota after May 1838, when troops under General Winfield Scott held families in stockades before marching them west, and the Seminole only after the seven-year Second Seminole War of 1835-42. The National Park Service records more than 16,000 Cherokee removed and more than a thousand deaths on the journey itself, with several thousand more attributed to its consequences; Britannica states that up to a quarter of those displaced died. The removals opened roughly 25 million acres to settlement and cotton.
contested: Death tolls are estimates rather than counts and vary widely by nation and by author; the legitimacy of the Treaty of New Echota, signed by a minority faction, was disputed at the time and remains so.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indian Removal Act
National Park Service: Trail of Tears National Historic Trail - History and Culture
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Trail of Tears
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Cherokee Nation v. Georgia

deathsNote: The low end aggregates the reasonably well-documented losses on individual removals, of which the Cherokee figure of more than a thousand dead on the road, recorded by the National Park Service, is the firmest. The high end follows Britannica's statement that up to 25 per cent of those displaced died, applied to the roughly 100,000 removed, and counts deaths in the holding stockades, on the routes and in the first years in Indian Territory from exposure, dysentery, cholera and starvation. No contemporary authority counted the dead.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The National Park Service and Britannica document the confinement of Cherokee families in stockades pending removal, the seizure and looting of houses, livestock and crops, and the use of shackles on some detachments.
baselineWhat: The Native American population living east of the Mississippi when the Indian Removal Act was passed
baselineNote: Contemporary War Department and Indian Office estimates put the eastern Native population at roughly 120,000-125,000 in 1830. The five southeastern nations named in the removal treaties accounted for about 74,000 of that (Cherokee c.22,000, Muscogee c.22,700, Choctaw c.19,500, Chickasaw c.5,000, Seminole c.5,000); the rest were northern and Great Lakes nations also removed under the Act.

title: Siberian Exile after the Polish Uprisings of 1830 and 1863
actors: The Russian imperial authorities deported Polish, Lithuanian and Belarusian insurgents, their families and declassed gentry to Siberia and the interior provinces as convicts and administrative exiles
peopleRange: Roughly 20,000-40,000 people after the January Uprising of 1863 alone. Russian administrative records give about 18,600-22,000 sentenced to Siberia after 1863; Polish historiography, counting families who followed and those exiled to European Russia and the Caucasus, gives figures up to 40,000. Several thousand were exiled after the November Uprising of 1830-31, and the parallel 'declassing' of the petty szlachta in the western provinces in the 1830s-1860s stripped several hundred thousand of noble status and moved tens of thousands. The basis is imperial chancery and Siberian governorate registers, which Polish and Russian historians read differently.

flows.label: Polish insurgents deported from the Congress Kingdom and the western provinces to Irkutsk and eastern Siberia

summary: After the failed uprisings of 1830-31 and 1863-64 the Russian government deported large numbers of Polish, Lithuanian and Belarusian insurgents and their sympathisers to Siberia, some to hard labour (katorga) in the Nerchinsk mines and at Lake Baikal, most to administrative exile as settlers in Siberian and Volga provinces. Estates were confiscated, families were permitted or compelled to follow, and returns were restricted for decades; a rising by Polish exiles near Lake Baikal in 1866 was suppressed and its leaders executed. The exiles left a lasting Polish presence in Siberian towns and contributed to the scientific exploration of the region. The Polish word sybirak entered the language for those deported, and was reused for the Soviet deportations of 1940-41 already in the atlas. The deportations sit within the wider imperial exile and katorga system, through which several hundred thousand people passed in the nineteenth century.
contested: The totals, which range from about 20,000 in Russian administrative counts to 40,000 or more in Polish national historiography depending on whether accompanying families and exile within European Russia are included.

sources.title: January Uprising — Wikipedia
November Uprising — Wikipedia
Sybirak — Wikipedia
Katorga — Wikipedia

deathsNote: No aggregate death toll exists. Mortality on the marching route east and in the katorga mines was high and is documented in exile memoirs and later in George Kennan's 1891 investigation of the exile system, but Russian records did not track deaths of exiles systematically. Several hundred insurgents were executed in the Congress Kingdom and Lithuania during the suppression itself.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Imperial sentencing records and exile memoirs document the katorga labour sentences and the confiscation of insurgents' estates.
baselineWhat: The population of the Congress Kingdom of Poland at the time of the January Uprising
baselineNote: Russian administrative counts give the Kingdom of Poland about 4.8-5.2 million inhabitants in the early 1860s. Deportees also came from the Lithuanian, Belarusian and Ukrainian provinces of the Western Krai, whose populations are not included in this denominator.
shareCaveat: Deportees were drawn overwhelmingly from the szlachta, the clergy and the educated urban population rather than evenly from the whole; and the denominator excludes the Western Krai provinces that supplied many of them.

title: Indian Indentured Labour: the Girmitiya System
actors: British colonial authorities and plantation interests recruited indentured labourers in India for sugar and other plantation colonies after the abolition of slavery in the British Empire
peopleRange: Figures depend on what is counted. The Striking Women project records that Britain transported approximately two million Indian indentured workers to nineteen colonies between 1834 and the end of the First World War, including Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad, British Guiana, Natal, Ceylon, Malaya, Kenya and Uganda. Narrower counts confined to emigration under formal indenture contracts from Indian ports give totals nearer 1.3 to 1.5 million for the whole period 1834-1917, of which the great majority had departed by 1900. All figures derive from emigration depot registers, ships' articles and colonial immigration department returns, which are reasonably good records by nineteenth-century standards but which count contracts rather than people and omit re-indenture and unregistered movement.

flows.label: Calcutta -> Mauritius
Calcutta -> British Guiana and Trinidad
Calcutta -> Fiji
Madras -> Natal

summary: Emancipation in the British Empire in 1833-38 created a demand for plantation labour that was met by indenture: five-year contracts, called girmit by the labourers from the English word agreement, under which Indian workers were shipped to Mauritius from 1834 and then to the Caribbean, Natal, Fiji, East Africa and Malaya. The Striking Women project records recruitment concentrated in rural north India and the south, frequently by deception about destination and wages among people who could not read the contracts; voyages of ten to twenty weeks with mortality among Caribbean-bound migrants of around 17 per cent in the early decades; and annual mortality on the plantations of around 12 per cent. Labourers were subject to criminal sanctions for breach of contract, restricted movement under pass systems, and sex ratios heavily skewed towards men. Resistance took the form of petitions, desertion, sabotage and strikes, and the system - after a campaign in which Gandhi's South African career began - was formally abolished in 1917. The descendants of the girmitiyas form the Indian populations of Fiji, Mauritius, Guyana, Trinidad, Suriname and South Africa.
contested: Whether indenture is best understood as 'a new system of slavery', in Hugh Tinker's phrase, or as a coerced but genuinely contractual labour migration in which a substantial minority returned to India and some prospered, is a long-running historiographical dispute; totals differ by nearly a factor of two depending on which colonies and which forms of recruitment are counted.

sources.title: Striking Women (University of Leeds): Indentured labour from South Asia, 1834-1917
Harvard Law Review: 'The Agreement and the Girmitiya'

deathsNote: No aggregate death toll has been compiled, but the rates are documented: the Striking Women project records mortality of about 17 per cent on early Caribbean-bound voyages, from cholera, dysentery and other shipboard disease, and annual mortality of around 12 per cent on the plantations themselves. Applied across a migration of well over a million people those rates imply very large numbers of deaths, but the rates varied enormously by colony, decade and estate, and colonial immigration returns are not consistent enough to support a total.
violenceNote: The Striking Women project documents recruitment by deception, criminal penalties and corporal punishment for breach of contract, long hours and low wages, and restrictions on movement, drawing on emigration records, colonial inquiries and the testimony of former indentured workers.
baselineWhat: The population of India at the 1881 census, near the midpoint of the indenture era
baselineNote: The 1881 census of India, the first reasonably complete decennial enumeration, recorded about 253.9 million people across British India and the princely states. Emigration registers kept at Calcutta, Madras and later Bombay are the source for the roughly 1.3 million indentured emigrants shipped to Mauritius, the Caribbean, Natal, Fiji and elsewhere between 1834 and the early twentieth century.
shareCaveat: Recruitment was drawn overwhelmingly from a handful of districts in eastern United Provinces and Bihar and from the Tamil and Telugu districts of the Madras Presidency, so the all-India ratio of about half a per cent conceals emigration rates in the sending districts an order of magnitude higher.

title: The Irish Famine: Clearances and Mass Emigration
actors: Irish landlords, using powers created and enlarged by British poor-law legislation, cleared tenants from their estates during the potato failure, while some two million people emigrated
peopleRange: Estimates of eviction vary with the definition and the source. RTE's survey of the historiography reports that surviving police and court records for 1846-52, which begin systematically only in 1849, show at least 100,000 families - about half a million people - losing their homes, with a more realistic figure of between two-thirds and three-quarters of a million; Encyclopedia.com gives roughly half a million permanently expelled, counting only legally sanctioned evictions and excluding informal ejectments and 'voluntary' surrenders. Separately, about two million people emigrated from Ireland in the decade after 1845, and the population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to 6.6 million in 1851.
territoryDesc: Clearance consolidated smallholdings into larger farms and pasture, particularly in Clare, Tipperary, Cork and Mayo; Encyclopedia.com records that in Clare one person in ten was permanently expelled from house and holding between 1849 and 1854, and that eviction rates in Tipperary were twenty times those of Fermanagh.

flows.label: Connacht and Munster -> Boston and the United States
Limerick and Clare -> Quebec and Montreal
Dublin -> Liverpool and Britain

summary: Successive failures of the potato crop from 1845 destroyed the subsistence of Ireland's cottier and smallholding population. Britannica records approximately one million deaths from starvation and famine-related disease, the worst famine in nineteenth-century Europe. What makes the episode a clearance as well as a famine is the policy framework: the Gregory or quarter-acre clause of the Poor Law Amendment Act of June 1847 required tenants to surrender holdings over a quarter of an acre before qualifying for relief, and the new rating system made pauper tenants a direct cost to landlords. Evictions rose sharply from late 1847, peaked in 1850 and largely ended by 1854, carried out by 'crowbar brigades' that demolished houses to prevent return. Around two million people emigrated in the decade, some assisted by landlords clearing estates. Ireland's population had not recovered its pre-famine level a century and a half later.
contested: Whether British relief policy amounts to culpable negligence, to ideological adherence to laissez-faire, or - as some nationalist historians and legislators have argued - to genocide, is a long-running dispute; the number evicted is also unresolved because constabulary records begin only in 1849 and readmitted 'caretakers' were counted inconsistently.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Great Famine (Irish history)
RTE: 'That diabolical system' - evictions in famine Ireland
Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of Irish History and Culture): Famine Clearances

deathsNote: Britannica gives approximately one million deaths from starvation, typhus and other famine-related disease in 1845-49, the standard figure derived by comparing the censuses of 1841 and 1851 with projected population growth. Higher estimates up to about 1.5 million extend the period to 1852 and include excess deaths among emigrants in transit and on arrival, notably in the Quebec quarantine stations. Both ends are demographic reconstructions; civil registration of deaths did not begin in Ireland until 1864.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: RTE and Encyclopedia.com document the demolition and 'tumbling' of houses by crowbar brigades at eviction, recorded in constabulary returns, court proceedings and contemporary illustrated press.
baselineWhat: The population of Ireland at the census of 1841, before the famine
baselineNote: The 1841 census counted 8,175,124 people; because that census is thought to have undercounted, the population on the eve of the blight in 1845 is usually put at about 8.5 million. By the census of 1851 it had fallen to 6.55 million.
shareCaveat: The affected figure counts people formally evicted from their holdings; it is not the total displaced by the famine, which also included roughly a million deaths and 1-1.5 million emigrants in the same decade.

title: The New Zealand Wars and the Raupatu Land Confiscations
actors: The British Crown and colonial government invaded the Waikato and Taranaki and confiscated Maori land under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863
peopleRange: No count of the displaced was made. Whole hapu were driven from confiscated districts: Waikato iwi withdrew south of the Puniu river into what became the King Country, Taranaki and Bay of Plenty communities lost their cultivations and settlements, and the confiscated land was surveyed and allotted to military settlers. NZHistory records that the confiscations took most of the lower Waikato district, including areas occupied by tribes that had remained neutral and a third of the land of Ngati Haua. The scale of the displacement is documented in Waitangi Tribunal district inquiries rather than in any contemporary count.
territoryDesc: Te Ara and NZHistory record confiscations under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863 across the Waikato, Taranaki, Bay of Plenty and Hawke's Bay, commonly given as around 3.2 million acres, roughly 13,000 square km; some land was later returned or paid for, and the compensation court process was slow, partial and itself a source of grievance.

flows.label: Waikato iwi -> the King Country after the 1863-64 invasion
Taranaki hapu displaced from confiscated land

summary: Conflict over land sales began in the north in 1845 and resumed in Taranaki in 1860. In July 1863 Governor George Grey's forces crossed the Mangatawhiri into the Waikato, and after the defeat of the Kingitanga forces the government confiscated land under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, justified as punishment of rebellion; Premier Alfred Domett had proposed the policy in a memorandum of 5 May 1863, and Te Ara records that what began as a limited proposal broadened considerably, taking land from tribes that had fought against the Crown and from tribes that had not. The Maori King Tawhiao responded by prohibiting surveying, land sales, Native Land Court sittings, road-building and gold prospecting in his territory and refusing to negotiate until the land was returned. In the Waikato Raupatu Claims Settlement Act 1995 the Crown formally acknowledged that it had acted unjustly and in breach of the Treaty of Waitangi in invading the Waikato and wrongly characterising Waikato as rebels, that the confiscations were wrongful, and that they had caused lasting damage - the first of the modern Treaty settlements.
contested: The area confiscated, the proportion returned and the adequacy of the settlements are matters of continuing negotiation between iwi and the Crown; the characterisation of the wars themselves, long taught in New Zealand as 'Maori wars' and now generally as the New Zealand Wars, has been revised in official usage.

sources.title: NZHistory (Ministry for Culture and Heritage): Raupatu - the confiscations
Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Raupatu - confiscations
Waikato Raupatu Claims Settlement Act 1995 (New Zealand Legislation): the Crown apology

deathsNote: Total deaths in the New Zealand Wars between 1845 and 1872 are usually put at between two and three thousand, of whom the substantial majority were Maori; the figures come from military returns on the colonial side, which are reasonably reliable, and from estimates on the Maori side, which are not. Deaths from disease and displacement following confiscation, particularly among communities pushed off their cultivations, were not counted and are additional.

atrocityFindings.body: The Crown of New Zealand, in the Waikato Raupatu Claims Settlement Act 1995
atrocityFindings.finding: Formal acknowledgement and apology: that the Crown acted unjustly and in breach of the Treaty of Waitangi in sending its forces across the Mangatawhiri in July 1863 and in characterising Waikato as rebels, and that the ensuing confiscations under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863 were wrongful and caused lasting harm

violenceNote: NZHistory and Te Ara document the destruction and appropriation of Maori settlements and cultivations in the invaded districts and the confiscation of land from communities including those that had not taken up arms, findings confirmed by the Crown in its 1995 statutory apology.
baselineWhat: The Maori population of New Zealand at the census closest to the wars
baselineNote: The 1857-58 Maori census counted 56,049, a population already falling steeply from disease and estimated at 70,000-90,000 in 1840; by 1896 it had reached its nadir of about 42,000. The New Zealand Settlements Act 1863 was used to confiscate roughly 1.2-1.6 million hectares in Waikato, Taranaki, Bay of Plenty and Hawke's Bay, land belonging to particular iwi rather than to the Maori population as a whole.
shareCaveat: The confiscations fell on the iwi of the war zones, not on all Maori, so a national denominator understates how completely particular groups such as Waikato-Tainui and Taranaki iwi were dispossessed.

title: The Killing and Dispossession of the California Indians
actors: State-funded California militias, federal troops and settler vigilantes killed, enslaved and dispossessed the Native peoples of California during and after the Gold Rush
peopleRange: No displacement count exists. The measurable quantity is the population collapse: Benjamin Madley's reconstruction, summarised by the University of Toronto Scarborough, records California's Indian population falling from perhaps 150,000 in 1846 to about 30,000 by 1873, a figure also used by the State of California in its 2019 apology. Survivors were confined on federal reservations, indentured under California's 1850 Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, or dispersed as labourers. The pre-conquest baseline is itself an estimate derived from mission registers, early state censuses and anthropological reconstruction.
territoryDesc: Effectively the whole of the newly created state of California passed into settler and federal hands: eighteen treaties negotiated with California tribes in 1851-52, which would have reserved about 7.5 million acres, were never ratified by the US Senate and were kept secret for half a century, leaving most Native Californians without recognised land title.
summary: Following the American conquest and the discovery of gold in 1848, Native Californians were subjected to a sustained campaign of killing, abduction and dispossession. Benjamin Madley's An American Genocide documents state and federal officials organising and paying for militia expeditions, and shows the Indian population falling from roughly 150,000 to about 30,000 between 1846 and 1873. California's 1850 Act for the Government and Protection of Indians permitted the indenture of Native children and of adults convicted of vagrancy, producing a traffic in unfree labour. Eighteen treaties negotiated in 1851-52 were rejected by the Senate, leaving most survivors landless. On 18 June 2019 Governor Gavin Newsom issued a formal apology on behalf of the State of California, used the word genocide, cited roughly 16,000 Native people killed in organised massacres, and established a Truth and Healing Council.
contested: Whether the events meet the legal definition of genocide is argued by scholars and was affirmed by the State of California in 2019; the share of the population collapse attributable to killing rather than to disease, starvation and collapsed birth rates is also disputed.

sources.title: University of Toronto Scarborough: Benjamin Madley, An American Genocide (Yale University Press)
HISTORY: California Slaughtered 16,000 Native Americans. The State Finally Apologized

deathsNote: The lower figure is the number of killings Madley was able to document individually from militia claims, newspaper reports, army correspondence and settler accounts, and is a floor rather than an estimate. The higher figure, about 16,000, is the number of Native people killed in organised massacres cited by the State of California in its 2019 apology. Both are far smaller than the total population decline of roughly 120,000, most of which is attributed to disease, starvation, forced labour and the destruction of food sources.

atrocityFindings.body: State of California, Office of the Governor
atrocityFindings.finding: Formal apology to California Native Americans describing the violence of 1846-1873 as genocide, citing roughly 16,000 people killed in massacres and establishing a Truth and Healing Council

violenceNote: Madley's reconstruction, drawing on militia payment claims, army records, newspapers and settler testimony, documents massacres of villages, the killing of prisoners, the abduction of women and children, indenture under the 1850 Act and the burning of settlements and food stores.
baselineWhat: The Native population of California at the start of the American period in 1846
baselineNote: Sherburne Cook estimated about 150,000 Native people in California in 1845, down from roughly 310,000 before Spanish colonisation, falling to about 30,000 by 1870; Benjamin Madley's more recent reconstruction uses the same order of magnitude, roughly 150,000 in 1846 and 30,000 in 1873.

title: The Mexican Cession and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
actors: The United States invaded Mexico and annexed roughly half of its national territory by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
peopleRange: The transfer moved a border rather than a population. Around 100,000 Mexican citizens were living in the ceded territory, principally in New Mexico and California, and the treaty offered them United States citizenship or the option to remove to Mexico within a year; only a small minority moved south. Far larger numbers of Native people, whose lands the treaty transferred without their participation, were affected in the decades that followed. Neither group was counted at the time; the figures come from Mexican provincial returns and the 1850 US census.
territoryDesc: Britannica records the cession of more than 525,000 square miles (about 1,360,000 square km), comprising present-day California, Nevada, Utah, most of Arizona and New Mexico, western Colorado and parts of Wyoming, together with US confirmation of the Texas annexation and the Rio Grande boundary. The Gadsden Purchase added a further strip in 1853.
summary: War began in 1846 over the annexation of Texas and the disputed boundary between the Nueces and the Rio Grande, and ended with the occupation of Mexico City and the signing of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo on 2 February 1848. Mexico ceded more than 525,000 square miles for fifteen million dollars and the assumption of over three million dollars in claims by American citizens. Mexicans remaining in the ceded territory were promised citizenship and protection of property; in practice land titles in California and New Mexico were widely lost through subsequent litigation and settlement. The acquisition transferred sovereignty over Native nations across the Southwest to the United States and precipitated the political crisis over the extension of slavery into the new territories that ran towards the Civil War.
contested: Mexican and United States historiography differ sharply over the war's origins and legitimacy; the extent to which the treaty's property guarantees were honoured for Mexican landholders is disputed and has been litigated for more than a century.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mexican-American War

deathsNote: United States military deaths are recorded with reasonable accuracy at about 13,000, the great majority from disease rather than combat. Mexican military and civilian deaths were never systematically counted and are estimated from army returns, hospital records and city accounts; the usual range for the Mexican side is in the tens of thousands. The total given here is therefore an estimate combining a firm figure with a soft one.
baselineWhat: The Mexican citizens living in the territory ceded to the United States in 1848
baselineNote: Contemporary estimates put roughly 80,000-100,000 Mexican citizens in the ceded lands, the great majority of them in New Mexico, with perhaps 7,500-14,000 Californios and small settlements in Arizona and Colorado. The indigenous population of the same territory was considerably larger and was not counted as Mexican citizens; California alone held an estimated 150,000 Native people in 1848. The territory itself, some 1.36 million square kilometres, was about half of Mexico's national area.
shareCaveat: The denominator counts only Mexican citizens; the Native peoples of the cession, who were far more numerous and lost far more, are excluded from it because Mexico never enumerated them.

title: The Caste War of Yucatan and the Sale of Maya Captives to Cuba
actors: Maya insurgents rose against the Yucatecan state and held an independent territory at Chan Santa Cruz; Yucatecan and later Mexican forces suppressed them and sold captured Maya into labour in Cuba
peopleRange: Yucatan's population is generally reckoned to have fallen by roughly half in the first years of the war, from around 500,000 to about 300,000, through death, flight and displacement; the estimate comes from Mexican state censuses of 1846 and the 1850s, which are of uneven quality. Tens of thousands of Maya fled south into what became British Honduras and into the Peten, where they founded new settlements; the region's demographic history rests on British colonial and Guatemalan records. Between roughly 1848 and 1861 the Yucatecan authorities sold captured Maya as contract labourers to Cuban plantations; estimates run to about 1,000-2,000 people, and in 2020 marine archaeologists identified the wreck of the vessel La Union, used on that route.
territoryDesc: The Maya rebels held the eastern forests of the peninsula around Chan Santa Cruz as a de facto independent state from the 1850s until the Mexican army took the capital in 1901; the area became the federal territory of Quintana Roo in 1902.

flows.label: Maya refugees south into British Honduras
Captured Maya shipped as contract labourers to Cuba

summary: In 1847 Maya communities in eastern Yucatan rose against the creole landowning order in a war over land, taxes and church fees that nearly drove the Yucatecan state into the sea. The rebellion stabilised around the oracular shrine of the Talking Cross at Chan Santa Cruz, which sustained an autonomous Maya polity trading with British Honduras for half a century until the Mexican army captured it in 1901. Estimates of the dead range from 40,000 to 50,000, and the peninsula's population fell by roughly half through killing, disease and flight, with substantial Maya migration into British Honduras and the Peten. From 1848 the Yucatecan authorities raised revenue by selling Maya prisoners into indentured labour in Cuba, a traffic denounced in the Mexican congress and suspended and revived several times before ending in the early 1860s. The atlas covered nineteenth-century Indigenous dispossession in the United States, Argentina and Chile but not Mexico's longest Indigenous war.
contested: Population loss figures for Yucatan, which rest on censuses of uneven quality taken during and after the fighting, and the number of Maya shipped to Cuba, which the Yucatecan authorities had reason to understate.

sources.title: Caste War of Yucatan — Wikipedia
Yucatan — Wikipedia
Maya peoples — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The commonly cited range for deaths in the hostilities, drawn from Mexican state records and from the standard account by Nelson Reed; it covers combatants and civilians on both sides and does not separate deaths from the cholera and smallpox epidemics that swept the peninsula during the fighting. Wider estimates of total population loss, around 200,000, include flight and depressed births as well as death.
violenceNote: Yucatecan state decrees and Mexican congressional debates document the sale of Maya prisoners to Cuba, and contemporary reporting on both sides records village massacres.
baselineWhat: The population of the Yucatan peninsula on the eve of the rising in 1846, the large majority of it Maya
baselineNote: Yucatecan state counts and Nelson Reed's reconstruction put the peninsula at roughly half a million people in 1846, falling to around 300,000 by the mid-1850s through killing, flight to Belize and Guatemala, and famine. The Maya share is usually put at three-quarters or more.
shareCaveat: The affected figure mixes people killed, sold as captive labour to Cuba, and driven into the forest or across the border over a 54-year span, and it is drawn from state estimates rather than a count.

title: The Great Mahele, the Overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom and United States Annexation
actors: Land division under settler pressure transferred most Hawaiian land out of commoner hands; American residents backed by United States Marines deposed Queen Liliuokalani and the United States annexed the islands
peopleRange: There was no mass expulsion; the displacement was from land rather than from the islands. Under the Great Mahele of 1848 and the Kuleana Act of 1850, maka'ainana commoners received fee-simple title to only about 28,600 acres out of roughly 4 million acres divided — a figure taken directly from the Land Commission awards — while Crown, government and chiefly lands passed increasingly to settlers and sugar companies. The Native Hawaiian population, estimated at several hundred thousand at contact in 1778, had fallen to about 40,000 by the 1890s, overwhelmingly from introduced disease.
territoryDesc: The Hawaiian archipelago, about 16,635 km2, was annexed by the United States by joint resolution in July 1898 after the deposition of the monarchy in 1893; approximately 1.8 million acres of Crown and government land passed to the United States without compensation to the Hawaiian Kingdom or its people.
summary: The Great Mahele of 1848 converted Hawaiian communal land tenure into private title, dividing land between the king, the chiefs and the government; the Kuleana Act of 1850 allowed commoners to claim the plots they cultivated, but only about 28,600 acres were awarded to them, and subsequent legislation permitted foreigners to buy land outright. Within a generation the sugar industry controlled most productive land. In January 1893 a committee of American and European residents, supported by the landing of United States Marines from the USS Boston, deposed Queen Liliuokalani; President Cleveland's investigator James Blount concluded the overthrow had been unlawful and that US forces had been decisive, but no restoration followed. The Republic of Hawaii was annexed by the United States in July 1898 by joint resolution rather than treaty. In 1993 Congress adopted Public Law 103-150, in which the United States apologised to Native Hawaiians for the overthrow and acknowledged that they had never directly relinquished their claims to their national lands. Hawaii was absent from the atlas.
contested: The legality of the 1898 annexation, effected by joint resolution rather than by treaty, and whether the Hawaiian Kingdom's sovereignty was ever lawfully extinguished — positions held by Hawaiian sovereignty organisations and contested by the United States, which accepts wrongdoing in the 1893 overthrow but not the invalidity of annexation.

sources.title: Overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom — Wikipedia
Great Mahele — Wikipedia
Apology Resolution (Public Law 103-150) — Wikipedia
Public Law 103-150, 107 Stat. 1510 (1993) — US Government Publishing Office

deathsNote: The overthrow itself was accomplished without significant bloodshed; one policeman was wounded. The catastrophic decline of the Native Hawaiian population across the nineteenth century was caused by introduced epidemic disease rather than by state killing.

atrocityFindings.body: United States Congress
atrocityFindings.finding: Public Law 103-150 (1993) apologising to Native Hawaiians for the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii on 17 January 1893 with the participation of US agents and armed forces, and acknowledging that Native Hawaiians never directly relinquished claims to their inherent sovereignty or their national lands

violenceNote: The 1993 Apology Resolution records the suppression of the Hawaiian language in schools from 1896 and the transfer of Hawaiian national lands without consent or compensation.
baselineWhat: The Native Hawaiian population of the Kingdom of Hawaii at the time of the Great Mahele
baselineNote: Kingdom censuses counted 84,165 people in 1850 and 71,019 in 1853, almost all Native Hawaiian, giving roughly 88,000 at the 1848 land division; the pre-contact population is estimated at anywhere from 300,000 to 800,000. By annexation in 1898 Native Hawaiians were a minority in their own islands, and commoners had received less than one per cent of the land under the Mahele.

title: Norwegianization, Sami Land Dispossession and the Nordic Assimilation Regimes
actors: The Norwegian, Swedish and Finnish states pursued assimilation of the Sami and Kven through language bans, boarding schools, land laws and, in Sweden, the forced relocation of reindeer-herding families
peopleRange: No aggregate figure exists and the commission that examined the policy did not produce one. The affected population is the Sami of the three Nordic states, today estimated at 50,000-100,000 and smaller in the nineteenth century, together with the Kven and Forest Finns of northern Norway. Specific components are countable: Norway's 1902 land act barred land purchase by those who could not speak Norwegian, and under the Swedish-Norwegian reindeer grazing conventions of 1919 and 1930 several hundred North Sami families were compelled to move south within Sweden, in what Swedish scholarship calls the tvangsforflyttningar. Norway's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2023 on the basis of school records, church registers and testimony.
territoryDesc: Sami customary lands across northern Norway, Sweden and Finland were progressively brought under state ownership and settler and industrial use, culminating for Norway in the Alta dam dispute of 1979-1982.

flows.label: Forced relocation of North Sami reindeer-herding families southwards within Sweden after 1919

summary: From the mid-nineteenth century until well into the twentieth, Norway pursued a policy known as fornorsking — Norwegianization — that made Norwegian the sole language of school and church in Sami and Kven districts, tied land purchase to Norwegian language and names, and placed Sami children in state boarding schools. Sweden ran a parallel but differently structured system of segregated nomad schools for reindeer-herding Sami under the doctrine 'Lapp shall remain Lapp', and after the 1919 reindeer grazing convention with Norway compelled North Sami families to relocate south, breaking herding communities. Finland applied comparable schooling and land policies. In June 2023 a Truth and Reconciliation Commission appointed by the Norwegian parliament delivered a report finding that the assimilation policy had caused lasting harm to the Sami, Kven and Forest Finns, and the Storting has since debated redress; Sweden's Sami church and state processes have followed. The Nordic world was entirely absent from the atlas before this entry.
contested: Whether the assimilation policies are properly described as cultural genocide, a term used by some Sami organisations and rejected by the Norwegian commission, which used the language of harmful assimilation policy without applying a legal genocide finding.

sources.title: Norwegianization — Wikipedia
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission — Storting (Norwegian Parliament)
Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Norway) — Wikipedia
Nomad school — Wikipedia
Alta controversy — Wikipedia

deathsNote: There was no significant death toll. The policies operated through schooling, language law, land law and administrative relocation rather than killing; the harm documented by the Norwegian commission is cultural, linguistic and psychological.

atrocityFindings.body: Truth and Reconciliation Commission appointed by the Storting (Norway)
atrocityFindings.finding: Reported in June 2023 that the Norwegianization policy pursued against the Sami, Kven/Norwegian Finns and Forest Finns caused serious and lasting damage, and recommended redress and institutional reform

violenceNote: Norway's Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented the boarding-school removal of Sami and Kven children, the suppression of their languages and the legal disabilities attached to non-Norwegian names and speech.
baselineWhat: The Sami population of Norway, Sweden and Finland around 1900, when the assimilation regimes were at their most systematic
baselineNote: Sami population figures are contested because the states counted by language and livelihood rather than descent, and because assimilation policy itself suppressed registration. Norwegian censuses of the late nineteenth century recorded roughly 20,000 Sami, Swedish counts about 7,000 reindeer-herding Sami with more outside herding, and Finland on the order of 1,500-2,000, giving a contemporary total of roughly 30,000-40,000. Modern estimates of the Sami population, based on self-identification and electoral rolls, run from 50,000 to 100,000 across the four countries.
shareCaveat: The programmes ran for 130 years across three states and several generations, so a single-year population is not the number of people they acted on; the contemporary counts are also an artefact of assimilation policy and understate the population of Sami descent.

title: The Taiping Rebellion
actors: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom under Hong Xiuquan fought the Qing state and its provincial armies across the Yangzi valley and south China
peopleRange: No count exists. Population movement was enormous - flight from besieged cities, from armies living off the country and from the collapse of agriculture across Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Jiangxi and Hubei - and is visible in the collapse of registered population in county gazetteers and in the subsequent state-sponsored resettlement of emptied districts by migrants from other provinces. Registered-population figures conflate death, flight and the breakdown of registration itself, and cannot be separated.
territoryDesc: The Taiping held Nanjing as their capital from 1853 to 1864 and at their height controlled much of the lower and middle Yangzi valley; the suppression left the Qing dependent on provincially raised armies under figures such as Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, a decisive shift of military and fiscal power from the centre to the provinces.

flows.label: Refugees from the Yangzi delta -> Shanghai and the treaty ports
Flight south from the war zone -> Guangdong and overseas emigration

summary: Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate who believed himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ, founded a movement in Guangxi that in 1850 became a rebellion, captured Nanjing in 1853 and held it as the capital of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom until 1864. Britannica describes it as probably the most important event in nineteenth-century China and puts the death toll at an estimated 20 million. The war combined ideological revolution - land redistribution, the prohibition of opium, foot-binding and the traditional cults - with conventional campaigning of extraordinary destructiveness: repeated sieges of great cities, the systematic devastation of the richest agricultural region in the empire, and massacres by both sides on the fall of towns. Suppression fell to provincial armies raised by Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, assisted late in the war by foreign-officered contingents including the force commanded by Charles George Gordon. Nanjing fell in July 1864.
contested: The death toll is among the most uncertain of any modern conflict. Britannica's 20 million is the conventional figure; Chinese demographic studies based on the fall in registered population between the censuses of 1851 and the 1870s produce far larger losses, but registered-population decline mixes deaths with flight, with the concealment of households and with the collapse of the registration system in war zones, and cannot be read directly as mortality.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Taiping Rebellion

deathsNote: Britannica's estimate of 20 million lives is the standard figure and forms the lower bound. The upper bound reflects the higher end of published estimates, which extend the count to the famine and epidemic mortality that followed the destruction of agriculture in the lower Yangzi and to the concurrent Nian and Muslim rebellions' effects in the same years. All figures derive from comparing pre-war and post-war population registers rather than from any count of the dead, and the registers are unreliable precisely where the war was worst.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Britannica's account and the standard histories of the war document massacres on the capture of cities by both Taiping and Qing forces, prolonged sieges that starved urban populations, and the devastation of the countryside by armies living off the land.
baselineWhat: The registered population of Qing China on the eve of the rebellion
baselineNote: Qing Board of Revenue registers gave about 430 million people in 1851, the peak of the dynasty's recorded population. The war was fought mainly in Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Jiangxi, Hubei, Hunan and Guangxi, which together held roughly a third of that total, and the provinces of the lower Yangzi recorded the sharpest falls in the post-war registers. Death-toll estimates range from about 20 million to 70 million, and rest on comparing pre- and post-war registration rather than on direct counts.
shareCaveat: The war was regional, so a national denominator understates its weight: in the worst-hit Yangzi provinces the recorded population fell by a third or more.

title: The Plains Wars and the United States Reservation and Allotment System
actors: The United States confined the Native nations of the Great Plains to reservations by treaty and war, destroyed the bison herds, and then broke up the reservations under the Dawes Act
peopleRange: No aggregate count of people moved exists. The relevant magnitudes are territorial and institutional: the Fort Laramie treaty of 1851 assigned bounded territories to the Arapaho, Blackfoot, Cheyenne, Lakota and others; the 1868 treaty created the 60-million-acre Great Sioux Reservation; the Medicine Lodge treaties of 1867 moved the southern Plains nations to Indian Territory. Populations were then held on these tracts by ration dependence after the bison collapse, and the tracts were themselves progressively cut down.
territoryDesc: Britannica records that of the 138 million acres held by tribes in 1887 when the Dawes General Allotment Act was passed, roughly two-thirds - about 90 million acres, or some 364,000 square km - had passed into white hands by 1932 through allotment, the sale of 'surplus' land and fraud. This is additional to the far larger areas ceded under the treaties of 1851-68 and to the seizure of the Black Hills after gold was found there in 1874.

flows.label: Southern Plains nations -> Indian Territory under the Medicine Lodge treaties
Northern Plains -> the Great Sioux Reservation and its successor agencies

summary: Between the first Fort Laramie treaty of 1851 and the massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890, the United States converted the Great Plains from Native territory into reservations and then into settler property. Treaties assigned bounded territories and then reduced them; the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty guaranteed the Black Hills to the Oceti Sakowin, and the guarantee was broken after the gold rush of 1874. Military campaigns, the near-extermination of the bison herds on which Plains subsistence depended, and the withholding of rations enforced confinement. The Dawes General Allotment Act of 8 February 1887 then divided reservations into individual holdings of 80 to 160 acres and opened the remainder to sale: Britannica records that about two-thirds of the 138 million acres held in 1887 had been lost by 1932. Britannica dates the Plains Wars from the early 1850s to the late 1870s and the reservation and allotment regime carried the process into the twentieth century.
contested: Whether the treaties were negotiated with parties competent to cede the land, and the legal consequences of their breach, remain live: the Supreme Court held in 1980 that the taking of the Black Hills required just compensation, which the Oceti Sakowin have refused, seeking the land instead.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Plains Wars
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Treaties of Fort Laramie
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Dawes General Allotment Act

deathsNote: No defensible aggregate death toll exists for four decades of intermittent campaigning across the Plains. Army returns record United States military casualties reasonably well and Native casualties badly; deaths from starvation and disease on the reservations after the bison collapse were not counted at all. The best-documented episodes - the Sand Creek and Wounded Knee massacres - are given separately, and adding them to unrecorded campaign and reservation mortality would produce a false precision.
violenceNote: Britannica's accounts of the Plains Wars and the Fort Laramie treaties describe winter attacks on villages with the destruction of lodges, food stores and horse herds, and the use of ration control and the collapse of the bison herds to compel and maintain confinement on reservations.
baselineWhat: The Native population of the Great Plains at the opening of the treaty and reservation era
baselineNote: There was no census of the Plains nations; the figure rests on Indian Office agency estimates and later reconstructions, which put the Plains tribes at roughly 100,000-250,000 in the mid-nineteenth century, with the Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Kiowa, Crow, Blackfeet and the village peoples of the Missouri making up most of it. Smallpox and cholera epidemics of 1837 and 1849 had already cut the village nations severely.

title: Kanak Dispossession, the Reserves and the Evenements in New Caledonia
actors: France annexed New Caledonia, used it as a penal colony, confined the Kanak to reserves under the cantonnement policy and the indigenat code, and suppressed revolts; conflict between Kanak independence forces and loyalists in the 1980s ended with the Matignon Agreements
peopleRange: Under the cantonnement policy applied from the 1860s and systematised by the decrees of 1876 and 1897, Kanak clans were removed from the fertile west coast and valleys and confined to tribal reserves; by the early twentieth century the reserves amounted to roughly a tenth of the territory's land and held virtually the whole Kanak population, which colonial censuses put at around 27,000-30,000 by 1921, down from an estimated 50,000-70,000 at annexation. The land figures come from French colonial land registers and the population figures from colonial censuses, both of uncertain precision for the earliest period. Around 22,000 convicts and some 4,000 political deportees, including Communards and Algerian Kabyle insurgents, were transported to the colony between 1864 and 1897.
territoryDesc: New Caledonia, about 18,575 km2, annexed by France in 1853; most agricultural and pastoral land passed to settlers, the penal administration and mining companies, with Kanak reserves restricted to a small fraction until land reform from the 1970s began returning territory to clans.

flows.label: Kanak clans removed from the west coast plains to interior and east coast reserves
Convicts and Communard deportees transported from France

summary: France annexed New Caledonia in 1853 and used it from 1864 as a penal colony, transporting some 22,000 convicts and about 4,000 political deportees, among them Paris Communards and Algerian insurgents. Kanak clans were progressively removed from the best land under the cantonnement policy and confined to reserves governed by the indigenat, a code of administrative penalties and movement restrictions that lasted until 1946; the Kanak population fell by roughly half between annexation and the 1920s, chiefly from introduced disease and dislocation. A major revolt led by the chief Atai in 1878 was suppressed with an estimated 1,000-1,200 Kanak killed, and a further rising in 1917 was put down in the north. Political conflict over independence intensified in the 1980s in the period known as les Evenements, marked by the ambush of Kanak activists at Hienghene in 1984, in which ten men were killed, and the hostage-taking and assault on the Ouvea cave in May 1988, in which nineteen Kanak and two gendarmes died. The Matignon Agreements of June 1988 and the Noumea Accord of 1998 established a decolonisation process and a series of referendums, the last of which, in 2021, was boycotted by the pro-independence movement. New Caledonia was absent from the atlas.
contested: The Ouvea operation of May 1988, where inquiries and testimony have raised allegations of summary executions of captured Kanak that French military authorities denied and which no court has established; and the legitimacy of the 2021 referendum, held over the objection of pro-independence organisations.

sources.title: New Caledonia — Wikipedia
Kanak people — Wikipedia
Ouvea cave hostage taking — Wikipedia
Matignon Agreements — Wikipedia
Kanak and Socialist National Liberation Front — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The bulk of the toll is the suppression of the 1878 Atai revolt, estimated in French colonial and later scholarly accounts at about 1,000-1,200 Kanak dead along with some 200 settlers and militia; the upper end adds the 1917 rising and scattered punitive operations. The 1980s Evenements caused roughly 80 deaths in total, including the ten Kanak killed at Hienghene in 1984 and the nineteen Kanak and two gendarmes killed at Ouvea in 1988.
violenceNote: French colonial land registers and the indigenat regulations document the removals, forced labour requisitions and administrative detention of Kanak; the 1878 suppression is recorded in French military reports.
baselineWhat: The Kanak population of New Caledonia at the time of French annexation
baselineNote: Estimates of the Kanak population in 1853 range from about 40,000 to 70,000; disease, land seizure under the cantonnement policy and the repression of the 1878 and 1917 revolts reduced it to about 27,000 by 1921, its lowest recorded point, after which it recovered. By the 1980s Kanak numbered around 60,000-70,000, roughly 43 per cent of the territory's population.
shareCaveat: The event spans 135 years — the reserves, the indigénat, the 1878 and 1917 revolts and the 1980s Événements — while the denominator is an 1853 snapshot of a population that first collapsed by half and then recovered.

title: The Muslim Rebellions in Qing China and their Suppression
actors: Hui and other Muslim communities rose in Yunnan and in the north-west, and Qing armies under commanders including Zuo Zongtang suppressed the risings and resettled the surviving populations
peopleRange: No count exists. After the suppression of the north-western rising, surviving Hui communities were removed from the Wei valley and other districts of Shaanxi and resettled under supervision in Gansu and what became Ningsia and Qinghai, and thousands fled westward across the Russian frontier into Semirechye, where their descendants are the Dungans of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. In Yunnan, the destruction of the Dali sultanate was followed by the dispersal and partial destruction of Muslim communities. The evidence is Qing campaign memorials, resettlement orders and county gazetteers, not enumeration.
territoryDesc: Yunnan was restored to Qing control in 1873 after the fall of the Dali sultanate; in the north-west, Zuo Zongtang's campaigns recovered Shaanxi and Gansu and then Xinjiang from Yaqub Beg, whose state had ruled Kashgaria from 1865, and in 1884 Xinjiang was constituted a regular province of the empire.

flows.label: Hui of the Wei valley, Shaanxi -> forced resettlement in Gansu
Flight across the Russian frontier -> Semirechye (the Dungans of Central Asia)

summary: Two great Muslim risings shook the Qing empire in the same decades as the Taiping. Britannica records that a clash between Chinese and Muslim miners in Yunnan in 1855 escalated into massacres around Kunming in 1856 and then into a general rising that lasted seventeen years, under Du Wenxiu at Dali, and that a second rising beginning in 1862 spread across Shaanxi, Gansu and Xinjiang and lasted fifteen years, gaining momentum from Taiping and Nian pressure but never achieving unified leadership. Both were suppressed by dividing the rebel factions and by overwhelming military force, in the north-west under Zuo Zongtang, whose campaigns went on to destroy the state Yaqub Beg had established in Kashgaria and to restore Qing control of Xinjiang by 1877. Suppression was followed by the forced resettlement of surviving Hui populations away from their home districts and by the flight of communities across the Russian frontier. Britannica describes the damage and devastation caused by the rebellions as immeasurable and records that recovery was still incomplete in the early twentieth century.
contested: Casualty figures are extremely uncertain. Britannica gives estimates of 20 to 30 million casualties for the Muslim rebellions and notes that actual numbers were likely higher, but the underlying data are declines in registered population that conflate death, flight, resettlement and the collapse of registration in war zones.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: China - Muslim rebellions
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Panthay Rebellion
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Xinjiang - History

deathsNote: Britannica states that estimates of casualties in the Muslim rebellions run to 20-30 million and that the real figure was likely higher, but no reliable count exists. The commonly repeated multi-million figures - such as the near-disappearance of the Hui population of Shaanxi - derive from the collapse in registered population recorded in county gazetteers, which cannot distinguish people killed from people who fled, were resettled elsewhere or simply ceased to be registered. Because the underlying source cannot separate death from displacement, no range is given here.
violenceNote: Britannica records massacres of Muslim residents around Kunming in 1856 that touched off the Yunnan rising, and the devastation of Shaanxi, Gansu and Xinjiang in the fighting and its suppression, with communities destroyed or forcibly resettled.
baselineWhat: The Muslim (Hui and Turkic) population of Yunnan, Shaanxi, Gansu and the north-west before the risings
baselineNote: No Qing census recorded religion, so every figure is a reconstruction from later provincial gazetteers, Republican-era surveys and the resettlement records compiled after the suppression. Estimates put the Hui of Shaanxi at several hundred thousand, those of Gansu at over a million and the Hui of Yunnan at roughly a million, giving an order of magnitude of about three million, with a credible range of two to five million.

title: The Crimean Tatar and Nogai Exodus to the Ottoman Empire
actors: Crimean Tatars and Nogais left the Russian Empire for Ottoman territory after the Crimean War under official suspicion, land pressure and administrative encouragement
peopleRange: Figures are drawn from Russian provincial administration records of passports issued and from Ottoman settlement registers, and they do not agree. The usual range for Crimean Tatars and Nogais departing between the end of the Crimean War in 1856 and the mid-1860s is between roughly 150,000 and 200,000, with some accounts putting the combined total including the Nogai steppe communities considerably higher. Vladimir Hamed-Troyansky's study of Muslim refugee property notes that Crimean Tatar refugees were a substantial component of the wider Muslim migration into Ottoman territory in these decades. Both empires had reasons to over- or under-count and neither conducted a census of the movement.
territoryDesc: Large districts of the Crimean interior and the Nogai steppe north of the peninsula were substantially depopulated, and their land redistributed to Russian, Ukrainian, German and Bulgarian settlers; the Muslim share of Crimea's population fell sharply and continued falling until the deportation of 1944.

flows.label: Crimea -> Samsun and the Ottoman Black Sea coast
Nogai steppe -> Ottoman Rumelia (Edirne and the Dobruja)

summary: During the Crimean War many Crimean Tatars were suspected by the Russian authorities of sympathy with the Ottoman and allied forces, and after the peace of 1856 a large emigration began. It was driven by a combination of official suspicion, the requisitioning and reallocation of land, rumours of forced conversion and conscription, and the willingness of the Ottoman state to receive and settle Muslim migrants; Russian administrators issued passports readily and in places encouraged departure. Somewhere between 150,000 and 200,000 Crimean Tatars and Nogais crossed the Black Sea to Anatolia and Ottoman Rumelia in the decade after the war, mortality in transit and on arrival was high, and abandoned villages in the peninsula were resettled with Slavic and other colonists. The movement is the first of the great nineteenth-century Muslim migrations into Ottoman territory, and it merges with the Circassian expulsion of 1864 and the Balkan migrations of 1877-78 in Ottoman refugee administration.
contested: How far the exodus was coerced is disputed: Russian records present it as voluntary emigration under lawfully issued passports, while Crimean Tatar and much Turkish historiography treats it as expulsion by pressure, land seizure and official harassment. The totals differ correspondingly.

sources.title: Vladimir Hamed-Troyansky, 'Abandoned Land: Muslim Refugees' Property in the Post-Ottoman Balkans', Past & Present
Milena Methodieva, 'Becoming a Muhacir: Writings and Narratives of Displacement in the Late Ottoman Empire', International Journal of Middle East Studies (Cambridge)

deathsNote: No death toll was compiled. Contemporary Ottoman and consular reports describe heavy mortality from disease, exposure and hunger in the Black Sea crossing and in the reception camps and resettlement districts, but neither empire counted the dead among the migrants, and modern estimates would be guesses.
baselineWhat: The Crimean Tatar and Nogai population of Crimea and the adjoining Black Sea steppe before the post-Crimean War emigration
baselineNote: Russian imperial administrative counts put the Muslim population of the Crimean peninsula at roughly 250,000-300,000 in the 1850s, with Nogai communities on the mainland steppe in addition. Estimates of the emigration itself range from about 150,000 to over 300,000; by the 1897 census Crimean Tatars were a minority of about a third in their own peninsula.
shareCaveat: The affected figure mixes Crimean Tatars from the peninsula with Nogais from the mainland steppe, whose numbers are counted less reliably, so the ratio is sensitive to whether the steppe population is inside the denominator.

title: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 and the British Reprisals
actors: Sepoys of the Bengal Army, princely states and rural populations rose against East India Company rule; British forces suppressed the revolt with mass executions and the punitive clearance of Delhi
peopleRange: No count of the displaced exists. The largest documented movement was the expulsion of the population of Delhi after its recapture in September 1857: the city was emptied, its inhabitants driven out for months, quarters around the Red Fort demolished and property confiscated on a mass scale, with only partial and staged readmission afterwards. Villages across the North-Western Provinces and Awadh were burned in punitive columns. The evidence is British military and civil correspondence, prize-agent records and later Urdu memoir literature, not enumeration.
territoryDesc: The rebellion ended the East India Company: by the Government of India Act of 1858 the Crown assumed direct rule, a Secretary of State for India was appointed, the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and exiled to Rangoon, and the policy of annexing princely states by lapse was abandoned in favour of guaranteeing loyal rulers.

flows.label: Expulsion of the population of Delhi after September 1857
Bahadur Shah Zafar and family -> exile in Rangoon

summary: The revolt began at Meerut in May 1857, spread to Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow and much of the North-Western Provinces and Awadh, and combined a mutiny of the Bengal Army with rural and princely rebellion. Both sides killed civilians: the National Army Museum records the killing of about 120 British women and children at Kanpur after a surrender, an act that shaped the character of the British response. The reprisals that Indians called the Devil's Wind included summary hangings along the line of march, the execution of prisoners by being blown from guns, the burning of villages, and the expulsion and partial demolition of Delhi after its recapture in September 1857. The revolt was suppressed by mid-1858, Rani Lakshmi Bai was killed in June 1858, and the East India Company was abolished in favour of Crown rule. Even the name of the events is contested: mutiny in older British usage, first war of independence in Indian nationalist usage.
contested: The death toll is disputed by an order of magnitude. The Indian historian Amaresh Misra has argued for roughly ten million deaths in the decade after 1857, based on records of religious fighters killed, British labour-force records showing regional workforce reductions of a fifth to a third, and colonial correspondence; as Dawn reported, the British historian Saul David called this an overestimate and suggested hundreds of thousands, and Shabi Ahmad of the Indian Council of Historical Research suggested migration rather than killing explains much of the recorded depopulation.

sources.title: National Army Museum: Decisive events of the Indian Rebellion
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Indian Mutiny (Indian Rebellion of 1857)
Dawn: 'Millions died after 1857 war of independence: historian' (on Amaresh Misra's claim and the reaction to it)

deathsNote: The lower figure is the conventional estimate, referred to in the Dawn report, of about 100,000 Indian soldiers killed in the fighting and the reprisals. The upper figure covers wider estimates that include civilians killed in punitive columns and executions, and the famine and epidemic mortality that followed the destruction of agriculture in the affected districts. Amaresh Misra's much larger claim of around ten million deaths over the following decade is an outlier that Saul David and others have rejected as an overestimate, and it is not used here. British military and civilian deaths, which are recorded with reasonable accuracy, numbered in the low thousands.
violenceNote: The National Army Museum and Britannica document the killing of British civilians at Kanpur, the summary hanging and execution of prisoners by being blown from guns during the British reprisals, the burning of villages and the demolition of quarters of Delhi including buildings around the Red Fort and the conversion of mosques to other uses after 1857.
baselineWhat: The population of the North-Western Provinces, Oudh and the other territories in revolt
baselineNote: The first all-India census, in 1872, counted about 30.8 million in the North-Western Provinces and 11.2 million in Oudh. Back-projected to 1857 the rebellion's core territory held on the order of 40 million, out of a British Indian population approaching 200 million. All pre-1872 Indian population figures are reconstructions from revenue settlements.
shareCaveat: Reprisals, and the famine and dislocation that accompanied them, fell very unevenly - concentrated in the Doab, in Oudh and around Delhi, whose population was expelled wholesale in September 1857.

title: The Andaman Islands Penal Colony and the Great Andamanese
actors: The British Indian government transported convicts to a penal colony at Port Blair, whose establishment also destroyed the indigenous Great Andamanese
peopleRange: Colonial penal records are relatively good: about 200 rebels of 1857 arrived in March 1858, and the settlement received convicts continuously until 1938, with cumulative transportations usually put at around 80,000 from India and Burma. Indigenous population figures come from colonial censuses and later anthropological counts: the Great Andamanese numbered about 4,800 in 1858, 625 in 1901, 90 in 1930 and 28 in 1988, with 39 recorded in the 2011 census of India.

flows.label: Convicts transported from India to Port Blair

summary: After the rebellion of 1857 the British Indian government re-established a penal settlement in the Andaman Islands, landing its first 200 convicts at Port Blair in March 1858; escapes in the first months ended in recapture and mass hangings. Over eighty years the colony received roughly 80,000 transported convicts from India and Burma, who cleared forest, built the settlement and were subject to a labour and ticket-of-leave regime; the Cellular Jail, completed in 1906, held political prisoners in solitary confinement, among them Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and later Bengali and Punjabi revolutionaries, and became a centre of hunger strikes in the 1930s. The colony also destroyed the indigenous Great Andamanese, whose numbers fell from about 4,800 in 1858 to a few dozen, mainly through introduced pneumonia, measles and syphilis and through the 'Andaman Homes' in which children were gathered and died. Japanese forces occupied the islands from 1942 to 1945. Independent India closed the penal settlement and made the Cellular Jail a national memorial; how the colony and its political prisoners should be commemorated, and which prisoners, remains a live argument in Indian public life.
contested: Indian memory politics over the Cellular Jail, particularly the commemoration of Savarkar and his clemency petitions, is actively disputed; the historical record of the colony itself is comparatively well documented.

sources.title: Clare Anderson, 'The Andaman Islands Penal Colony: Race, Class, Criminality, and the British Empire', International Review of Social History
Cellular Jail
Minority Rights Group: Andaman Islanders

deathsNote: No cumulative toll exists. Mortality among convicts in the first decades was very high from malaria, dysentery and overwork, and 87 recaptured escapers were hanged in 1858; the destruction of the Great Andamanese, a fall of more than 99 per cent of the population, was caused chiefly by introduced disease rather than direct killing.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Colonial penal records and Clare Anderson's archival work document penal labour and indefinite detention; colonial reports describe the Andaman Homes into which indigenous children were taken.
baselineNote: The two populations involved have no common denominator. The roughly 80,000 convicts transported to Port Blair between 1858 and 1945 were drawn from the whole of British India, a population of hundreds of millions, so no meaningful share can be computed. The indigenous Great Andamanese, destroyed by the colony's diseases and punitive expeditions, are estimated at about 5,000 in 1858 and had fallen to 19 individuals by 1961.

title: The Conquest of the Desert and the Occupation of Araucania
actors: The Argentine and Chilean armies conquered the independent indigenous territories of the pampas, Patagonia and Araucania, killing, deporting and confining the Mapuche, Tehuelche, Ranquel and allied peoples
peopleRange: Neither state counted the displaced. In Argentina the campaigns culminating in General Julio Roca's advance of 1879 produced several thousand killed and captured; Encyclopedia.com records that survivors were placed in indigenous settlements or dispersed through rural villages, while women and children were assigned to wealthy families in Buenos Aires, and prisoners were held on Martin Garcia island and sent to Tucuman sugar estates. In Chile the Mapuche were confined to reducciones under titulos de merced. The order of magnitude - some tens of thousands of people killed, captured, deported or confined - rests on army reports, ecclesiastical records and later reconstruction, not on any register.
territoryDesc: Encyclopedia.com records that the Argentine campaigns took over 225,000 square miles - roughly 583,000 square km - of the pampas and northern Patagonia for stock-raising and agriculture, much of it granted to officers and to those who had financed the campaign. In Chile, according to Harvard's ReVista, Mapuche landholding fell from about five million hectares to some 500,000 hectares, roughly 50,000 square km lost, with the remainder held as reducciones.

flows.label: Patagonian and pampas captives -> Martin Garcia island and Buenos Aires
Mapuche of Araucania -> reducciones under titulos de merced

summary: Between 1861 and 1885 the Argentine and Chilean states extinguished the independent indigenous polities that had held the southern cone frontier since the sixteenth century. Chile's occupation of Araucania, begun in 1861 and completed after the Mapuche rising of 1881, confined the Mapuche to reducciones granted by title deed; Harvard's ReVista records their landholding falling from roughly five million hectares to about 500,000. In Argentina, campaigns from the 1870s culminated in Roca's advance of 1878-79, which Encyclopedia.com records as taking over 225,000 square miles and destroying organised indigenous resistance; the minister's stated aim was to expel, subjugate or wipe out the Indians. Captured families were separated, prisoners were shipped to Martin Garcia island and to sugar estates in the north, and women and children were distributed as servants to households in Buenos Aires. The land was distributed to soldiers and to the financiers of the campaign and opened to European settlement.
contested: Whether the Argentine campaigns constitute genocide is actively argued in Argentina, in scholarship and in public commemoration, with Roca's monuments and the national currency a recurrent flashpoint; the number killed and deported has never been established.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com (Encyclopedia of Latin American History): Conquest of the Desert
Harvard ReVista: Indigenous Displacement in Southern Chile
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Conquest of the Desert

deathsNote: No reliable toll exists. Argentine army despatches reported figures for indigenous people killed and captured in each expedition, but they were not compiled into a verified total, and deaths in captivity - on Martin Garcia, in transit and on the Tucuman estates - were not recorded at all. Scholars arguing that the campaigns were genocidal emphasise precisely these uncounted deaths; those who dispute the characterisation point to the absence of evidence for large-scale killing in the field. Presenting a number would give a false impression of precision.
violenceNote: Encyclopedia.com and Harvard's ReVista document the separation of families, the assignment of indigenous women and children to households in Buenos Aires, the internment of prisoners on Martin Garcia and their transfer to plantation labour, and the destruction and appropriation of indigenous settlements and herds.
baselineWhat: The independent Indigenous population of the pampas, Patagonia and Araucanía before the Argentine and Chilean military campaigns
baselineNote: No census covered the independent territories. The Mapuche of Araucanía south of the Bío-Bío are usually estimated at 100,000-150,000 in the 1860s, drawing on Chilean parish and military reports; the Ranquel, Tehuelche, Pehuenche and allied groups of the pampas and Patagonia are estimated at a further 20,000-30,000. About 150,000 is the low-to-middle end of the combined range.
shareCaveat: The figure combines two separate national campaigns against different peoples, and counts killed, deported and confined together, so the percentage measures the combined reach of both states rather than the fate of any single nation.

title: The Peruvian Slave Raids on Rapa Nui and the Confinement of the Islanders at Hanga Roa
actors: Peruvian slave ships carried off roughly half the population of Rapa Nui; Chile annexed the island in 1888 and leased it to a sheep-ranching company that confined the islanders to the village of Hanga Roa
peopleRange: More than 1,400 Rapa Nui — about half the island's population — were seized by Peruvian raiders in December 1862 and taken to work in Peru, principally in the guano islands and coastal plantations; the figure comes from Peruvian shipping records and the diplomatic correspondence that followed international protest. Almost all died of disease; of the small group repatriated in 1863, about fifteen survived to reach the island, bringing smallpox with them. The population fell to 111 by 1877 and reached a recorded low of 101 in 1892, from missionary and Chilean census counts. From the 1890s to 1966 the surviving population, numbering a few hundred rising to about a thousand, was confined by the ranch lease to the village of Hanga Roa.
territoryDesc: Rapa Nui, 164 km2, annexed by Chile in September 1888; most of the island was leased to the Williamson-Balfour Company as a sheep station until 1953, with the islanders restricted to Hanga Roa and its immediate surroundings.

flows.label: Rapa Nui taken by Peruvian slave ships to Callao and the guano islands

summary: In December 1862 a fleet of Peruvian vessels raided Rapa Nui and carried off more than 1,400 people, roughly half the population, to labour in Peru; among them were the island's ariki and the men who could read the rongorongo script. International protest led to an order for repatriation, but by then most had died of tuberculosis, smallpox and dysentery, and the handful who returned brought smallpox to the island. The population fell to 111 by 1877. Chile annexed Rapa Nui in 1888 under an agreement signed by the chief Atamu Tekena, whose terms — whether sovereignty alone or land was ceded — remain disputed between the Rapa Nui and the Chilean state. From the 1890s the island was leased to the Williamson-Balfour Company as a sheep ranch, and the islanders were prohibited from living or working outside Hanga Roa; the restriction lasted until 1966, when the island was reopened and Rapa Nui were granted Chilean citizenship. The episode is one of the most severe population collapses in Pacific history and the confinement is a long-running and well-documented one.
contested: The meaning of the 1888 Acuerdo de Voluntades, which Rapa Nui representatives read as ceding sovereignty while retaining land ownership and which Chile has treated as transferring the island; land claims arising from it remain before Chilean courts and international bodies.

sources.title: History of Easter Island — Wikipedia
Easter Island — Wikipedia
Rapa Nui people — Wikipedia
Blackbirding — Wikipedia

deathsNote: Of the more than 1,400 people taken in 1862-63, the overwhelming majority died in Peru of tuberculosis, smallpox and dysentery before repatriation could be effected; only about fifteen reached the island alive. The range reflects uncertainty over how many were taken and how many died before the repatriation order. The subsequent collapse of the island population to about 100 was driven by the smallpox epidemic the survivors carried back and by continued emigration and disease.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Peruvian shipping and diplomatic records and the reports of the French consul and Catholic missionaries document the seizure of islanders including children and the loss of the rongorongo tradition with the deaths of the literate elite.
baselineWhat: The population of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) immediately before the Peruvian slave raids of 1862-63
baselineNote: Estimates for 1862 cluster around 3,000-4,000, reconstructed from missionary accounts, the raiders' own records and back-projection from the census of 1877, which counted just 111 islanders.
