That collapse was caused by the raids, by smallpox and tuberculosis brought back by the few returnees, and by emigration to Tahiti and Peru; peak precontact population estimates are far higher and heavily disputed.
shareCaveat: The event spans a century, from the 1862 raids to the end of the Williamson-Balfour ranching regime that confined islanders to Hanga Roa until 1966, while the baseline is a single pre-raid snapshot of a population that fell to 111 and then recovered.

title: The Long Walk of the Navajo and the Bosque Redondo Reservation
actors: The United States Army, under Brigadier General James Carleton and Colonel Kit Carson, destroyed Navajo (Dine) subsistence, marched the survivors to eastern New Mexico and interned them with the Mescalero Apache at Bosque Redondo
peopleRange: New Mexico Historic Sites records more than 8,500 Dine and nearly 500 Nde (Mescalero Apache) held at Bosque Redondo at the peak in the winter of 1864. The EBSCO research summary notes about 6,000 Navajos gathered at Forts Canby and Wingate by March 1864 at the start of a series of marches, with more than 8,000 people eventually at Fort Sumner. The figures come from army ration returns and post records, which count rations issued rather than people, and Navajo oral history holds that more people were on the marches than the army recorded.
territoryDesc: The Treaty of 1868, signed on 1 June, allowed the Dine to return to a reservation of about 3.5 million acres straddling the Arizona-New Mexico line, a fraction of their former range; the reservation was later enlarged to roughly 15 million acres. Bosque Redondo itself was abandoned.

flows.label: Canyon de Chelly and Fort Canby -> Bosque Redondo (Fort Sumner)
Mescalero Apache country -> Bosque Redondo

summary: In 1863 General Carleton ordered a campaign against the Navajo; Kit Carson's troops burned cornfields, orchards and hogans and killed livestock, most notoriously in Canyon de Chelly, forcing surrender by starvation. From 1863 to 1866 more than fifty groups were marched up to 300-350 miles east to the Bosque Redondo reservation at Fort Sumner, journeys of eighteen to forty days on eight days' rations; people who could not keep up were shot, and hundreds died on the road. At Fort Sumner more than 8,500 Dine and nearly 500 Mescalero Apache were held together on alkaline land with failed crops, insufficient rations and epidemic disease; the Mescalero left without permission in November 1865. The experiment was abandoned and the Treaty of 1868 permitted the Dine to return to a reservation within their homeland, the only such return in the history of United States removal policy.
contested: The number who died on the marches and at Fort Sumner is not established; army records omit deaths that Navajo oral tradition records, and estimates differ substantially.

sources.title: New Mexico Historic Sites: Bosque Redondo Memorial - History
EBSCO Research Starters: Long Walk of the Navajos

deathsNote: There is no death register for either the marches or the reservation. New Mexico Historic Sites states that hundreds of Dine died as a result of the march conditions; deaths at Fort Sumner from dysentery, exposure, malnutrition and epidemic disease over four years are usually reckoned in the low thousands from ration returns and post correspondence. Navajo oral history records killings on the march, including of those unable to walk, that the army did not document, and the range given here is a reconstruction rather than a count.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: New Mexico Historic Sites and the EBSCO summary document the destruction of Navajo crops, orchards and livestock to compel surrender, the killing of stragglers on the marches, the confinement of the population at Fort Sumner and the labour imposed on internees to build irrigation works.
baselineWhat: The estimated Dine (Navajo) population at the start of Carleton's campaign
baselineNote: There was no count of the Navajo before the campaign; estimates from Army correspondence and later reservation rolls put the people at roughly 12,000-15,000. About 10,000 were marched to Bosque Redondo, where the peak camp population was 9,022 in spring 1865; several thousand evaded capture in the canyon country and to the west.

baselineSources.title: Bosque Redondo, New Mexico Historic Sites

title: The Pacific Labour Trade and Blackbirding
actors: Labour recruiters and planters took Pacific Islanders, by kidnapping, deception and contract, to work the sugar and cotton plantations of Queensland, Fiji and Samoa
peopleRange: The National Museum of Australia records that more than 62,000 Pacific Island men, women and children were brought to Queensland between 1863 and 1904 from about eighty islands, principally in what are now Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea and Fiji, some individuals more than once. Comparable but smaller traffics supplied Fiji, Samoa, New Caledonia and, notoriously, the Peruvian guano islands. The Queensland figures come from government immigration registers and shipping returns, which are relatively good records for arrivals and poor ones for the circumstances of recruitment.

flows.label: Vanuatu (New Hebrides) -> the Queensland canefields
Solomon Islands -> Queensland
Deportation from Australia under the 1901 Act, 1906-08

summary: The first 67 South Sea Islanders were landed at Brisbane in 1863 to work cotton and then sugar. Over the next four decades more than 62,000 people were brought to Queensland; the National Museum of Australia records that many were kidnapped - 'blackbirded' - or deceived about the length and conditions of their service. Queensland legislated repeatedly, in the Polynesian Labourers Act 1868 and the Pacific Labourers Act 1880, setting shipping standards and prohibiting forced recruitment, but enforcement was inconsistent and inspectors were sometimes bribed. Mortality among labourers in Queensland was several times that of the settler population. The trade ended not from concern for the labourers but from the White Australia policy: the Pacific Island Labourers Act 1901 provided for deportation, and between 1906 and 1908 over 7,500 people were removed, with about 2,500 permitted to remain. Queensland recognised Australian South Sea Islanders as a distinct ethnic group in 2000. The activist Faith Bandler, whose father had been taken from Ambrym, maintained that it was a form of slavery, while noting that in later years some signed three-year contracts.
contested: Whether the labour trade should be characterised as slavery or as a coercive but partly voluntary indenture is disputed: Australian South Sea Islander communities and Faith Bandler have argued the former, while some historians emphasise the substantial proportion of later recruits who re-engaged voluntarily and the regulation of the trade after 1880.

sources.title: National Museum of Australia: Islander labourers

deathsNote: No total was compiled. Deaths occurred during raids and recruiting incidents in the islands, on the voyages, and above all on the plantations, where mortality among Pacific Islander labourers ran at several times the rate for the European population of Queensland, chiefly from respiratory and gastrointestinal disease among people newly exposed to introduced pathogens. Queensland immigration records register deaths inconsistently and the island end of the trade was not recorded at all.
violenceNote: The National Museum of Australia documents kidnapping and deception in recruitment, including of women and children, and the plantation labour regime, drawing on Queensland government immigration records, parliamentary inquiries and the testimony of Australian South Sea Islander descendants.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Recruiting drew on the New Hebrides (Vanuatu), the Solomon Islands, New Caledonia and the Loyalties, the Gilberts and parts of island New Guinea, and pre-contact population estimates for these archipelagos differ by an order of magnitude - the New Hebrides alone has been put anywhere from 100,000 to 650,000 before the depopulation of the nineteenth century. The first reliable counts postdate the trade by decades, after epidemic collapse had already occurred.
shareCaveat: The 62,000 counts indentures rather than individuals; a substantial number of islanders were recruited more than once, so the figure overstates the number of people taken.

title: The Sand Creek and Wounded Knee Massacres
actors: United States volunteer and regular troops attacked and killed Cheyenne and Arapaho people at Sand Creek in 1864 and Lakota people at Wounded Knee in 1890
peopleRange: These were killings rather than removals. At Sand Creek the National Park Service records a camp of about 750 Cheyenne and Arapaho, mostly women, children and the elderly, who had gathered near Fort Lyon on the territorial governor's instructions to friendly Indians. At Wounded Knee the Lakota band under Spotted Elk (Big Foot) numbered several hundred and was already in army custody. Survivors of both dispersed to other camps and agencies; there is no separate displacement figure.
summary: On 29 November 1864 about 675 Colorado volunteer troops under Colonel John Chivington attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho camp on Big Sandy Creek that was flying a white flag and a United States flag; the National Park Service records roughly 230 people killed over eight hours, most of them women, children and the elderly, with mutilation of the dead afterwards. Manuscript letters by Captain Silas Soule and Lieutenant Joseph Cramer, rediscovered in 2000, record that about a hundred soldiers refused the order. Chivington was initially acclaimed and then discredited when the character of the attack became known, and the massacre precipitated the Cheyenne and Arapaho war that followed. On 29 December 1890, near Wounded Knee Creek in South Dakota, US Army troops disarming a Lakota band during the suppression of the Ghost Dance killed, by Britannica's estimate, between 150 and 300 Lakota; Britannica describes it as the climax of the army's efforts to repress the Plains Indians. Congress passed a resolution of deep regret for Wounded Knee on its centenary in 1990.
contested: The number killed at Wounded Knee is given in a wide range because burials and army counts disagree, and whether the Wounded Knee killings began as a firefight or as a massacre has been argued since 1891, including in the debate over the twenty Medals of Honor awarded to soldiers present.

sources.title: National Park Service: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site - History and Culture
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Sand Creek Massacre
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Wounded Knee Massacre

deathsNote: The range combines the two events. For Sand Creek the National Park Service and Britannica agree on approximately 230 Cheyenne and Arapaho killed, including some 150 women, children and elderly people, and thirteen Cheyenne chiefs and one Arapaho chief; the figure derives from survivor testimony and the later federal inquiries. For Wounded Knee Britannica gives 150 to 300 Lakota killed, the spread reflecting the difference between bodies buried in the mass grave and the wounded who died later or were never recovered.

atrocityFindings.body: United States Congress and the US Army (federal inquiries into Sand Creek, 1865)
atrocityFindings.finding: Federal investigations concluded that the attack on the Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek was a massacre of people who believed themselves under United States protection, and discredited Colonel Chivington

violenceNote: The National Park Service and Britannica document the killing of non-combatants, the mutilation of the dead at Sand Creek and the destruction of the camps, drawing on survivor testimony, the Soule and Cramer letters and the 1865 federal inquiries.
baselineNote: No single denominator is defensible: the two massacres struck different peoples twenty-six years apart. The Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho bands attacked at Sand Creek in 1864 numbered a few thousand in all, and the Lakota of the Sioux agencies counted roughly 25,000 people at the time of Wounded Knee in 1890. Combining them would imply a population that never existed as a single group.

title: The War of the Triple Alliance and the Destruction of Paraguay
actors: Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay fought Paraguay to the destruction of its army and government, occupied the country and annexed disputed territory
peopleRange: No displacement count exists, though the Paraguayan government evacuated the civilian population inland ahead of the allied advance and large numbers followed the army in the retreat to Cerro Cora. The demographic argument concerns deaths rather than displacement, and is one of the sharpest in Latin American history: Vera Blinn Reber argued in 1988 for a pre-war population of about 285,000 and a loss of some 8-18 per cent; Thomas Whigham and Barbara Potthast, using a newly recovered 1870 census in their 1999 'Paraguayan Rosetta Stone' article, put the pre-war population at 420,000-450,000 against 116,351 counted in 1870, implying a loss of 60-69 per cent, later revised slightly downward. The dispute is over the reliability of the 1846 and 1870 census fragments.
territoryDesc: Paraguay ceded roughly 140,000 km2 to Brazil and Argentina under the postwar treaties, losing about a quarter of the territory it had claimed; it was occupied by allied troops until 1876.

flows.label: Civilian population retreating inland with the Paraguayan army

summary: The war that began in late 1864 between Paraguay and the alliance of Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay ended in March 1870 with the death of Marshal Francisco Solano Lopez at Cerro Cora and the occupation of the country. It is generally regarded as the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history, and the scale of Paraguay's population loss is fiercely disputed: a 1999 study by Thomas Whigham and Barbara Potthast using a recovered 1870 census concluded the country lost around 60 per cent of its people, while Vera Blinn Reber had earlier argued for a far smaller loss, and both positions remain in print. Civilians were mobilised and evacuated inland, and mortality from disease, starvation and exposure during the long retreat exceeded battlefield deaths. Paraguay ceded about 140,000 km2 to its neighbours and was occupied until 1876. The atlas's Americas coverage jumped from the 1840s to the 1900s in South America outside the Southern Cone frontier wars; this fills the largest gap.
contested: Paraguay's population loss, with credible published estimates ranging from under 20 per cent to nearly 70 per cent depending on which census fragments are accepted; the debate between Reber and Whigham and Potthast is unresolved and continues with new archival work.

sources.title: Paraguayan War — Wikipedia
Paraguayan War casualties — Wikipedia
The Paraguayan Rosetta Stone: New Insights into the Demographics of the Paraguayan War, 1864-1870 — Latin American Research Review

deathsNote: The low end follows Vera Blinn Reber's 1988 reconstruction, which posits a smaller pre-war population and a loss of 8-18 per cent; the high end follows Whigham and Potthast's reading of the 1870 census, implying that 60 per cent or more of Paraguayans died. The disagreement is entirely about the pre-war population baseline and the completeness of the 1870 enumeration. Most deaths were from disease, starvation and exposure rather than combat.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Allied and Paraguayan military correspondence and the accounts of foreign observers with both armies record the destruction of towns, the executions ordered by Lopez during the retreat, and mass civilian starvation.
baselineWhat: The population of Paraguay on the eve of the war
baselineNote: Paraguay held no reliable census. Reconstructions from the 1846 population register by Whigham and Potthast put the pre-war population at roughly 420,000-450,000, against older claims of 800,000 to 1.3 million; the 1870-71 post-war count found about 116,000-231,000 survivors. Their 'Paraguayan Rosetta Stone' argues for a loss of around 60 per cent of the population and 90 per cent of adult men, while lower estimates put mortality nearer 20 per cent.

title: The Russian Conquest of Central Asia
actors: The Russian Empire conquered the Kazakh steppe, the khanates of Kokand, Bukhara and Khiva and the Turkmen lands, and settled Slavic colonists on nomadic pasture
peopleRange: No count of the displaced was made. The principal displacement was indirect and cumulative: Slavic peasant settlement on the Kazakh and Kirghiz steppe, encouraged from the 1890s and accelerating after the Trans-Siberian Railway was completed in 1895, took the winter pastures of nomadic communities and pushed them towards settled or semi-settled farming on poorer land, a process the Hamilton College survey of Russian Turkestan describes as the main social effect of the conquest. Settler numbers were recorded in resettlement administration files; the pastoralists displaced were not.
territoryDesc: Russian rule was extended over the Kazakh steppe, the Governorate-General of Turkestan created in 1867 with its capital at Tashkent, the Emirate of Bukhara and the Khanate of Khiva reduced to protectorates in 1868 and 1873, the Khanate of Kokand abolished and annexed in 1876, and the Transcaspian province established by 1882 - together some three million square km of steppe, oasis and desert.

flows.label: Kazakh pastoralists pushed off winter pasture by Slavic settlement
Russian and Ukrainian peasant settlers -> the steppe provinces

summary: Russian forces took Tashkent in 1865 and it became the seat of a Governorate-General in 1867 under Konstantin von Kaufman. Bukhara was defeated in 1868 and Khiva in 1873, both surviving as protectorates; Kokand was abolished and absorbed in 1876. The conquest of the Turkmen lands was the bloodiest phase: the Hamilton College survey records the storming of the Teke fortress of Geok Tepe in January 1881, in which approximately 14,000 Teke Turkmen were killed including those cut down in the pursuit, after which the Transcaspian province was organised with its centre at Ashkhabad. Kaufman's administration adopted a policy of non-interference in Muslim religious and customary life, on the assumption that exposure to Russian culture would produce assimilation on its own. The lasting demographic effect came later, through peasant settlement of the steppe after the Trans-Siberian Railway, which took pasture from nomadic communities and set the conditions for the revolt of 1916 and the famine of the early Soviet period.
contested: Russian, Soviet and post-Soviet Central Asian historiographies differ sharply over whether the conquest is best described as colonial subjugation or as incorporation, and casualty figures for the campaigns, including Geok Tepe, come almost entirely from the Russian side.

sources.title: Hamilton College, Central Asian History: Keller on Russian Turkestan

deathsNote: No aggregate exists for thirty years of intermittent campaigning. The one large documented figure is the storming of Geok Tepe in January 1881, where the Hamilton College survey records approximately 14,000 Teke Turkmen killed, most of them in the pursuit after the fortress fell; the count comes from Russian military reporting, which had reason both to exaggerate the victory and to understate the killing of non-combatants. Deaths in the sieges of Tashkent, Samarkand, Khiva and Kokand, and among pastoral communities dispossessed of pasture, were not recorded.
violenceNote: The Hamilton College survey of Russian Turkestan records the killing of roughly 14,000 Teke Turkmen at Geok Tepe in 1881, including in the pursuit of those who fled, and the destruction of the fortress and its settlement.
baselineWhat: The population of the Central Asian territories conquered or made protectorates by Russia - the Kazakh steppe, Turkestan, Bukhara and Khiva
baselineNote: The first all-Russian census of 1897 counted about 5.3 million in the Turkestan Governorate-General and roughly 2.5 million in the Steppe krai, with the protectorates of Bukhara and Khiva holding perhaps 2-2.5 million more, giving an order of magnitude of 9-10 million for the conquered lands. Slavic settlement followed: by 1911 over 1.5 million settlers had taken up land on the Kazakh steppe, and the resulting pressure on nomadic pasture led to the 1916 revolt and the flight of several hundred thousand Kazakhs and Kyrgyz to China.

title: The Kalaupapa Leprosy Settlement
actors: The Hawaiian Kingdom and its successor governments forcibly exiled people diagnosed with Hansen's disease to an isolated peninsula on Molokai under a compulsory segregation law
peopleRange: About 8,000 people were sent to the Kalaupapa and Kalawao settlements between 1866 and 1969, of whom roughly 90 per cent were Native Hawaiians; the figure comes from the settlement's admission registers, maintained continuously and now held by the state of Hawaii and the National Park Service, and is one of the firmer counts in the atlas. Children born to residents were routinely removed and placed for adoption. The scale is small, but the settlement is among the longest-running compulsory medical confinements anywhere and its documentation is exceptional.
territoryDesc: The Kalaupapa peninsula on the north shore of Molokai, cut off from the rest of the island by sea cliffs, designated a leprosy settlement in 1865-66 and since 1980 a National Historical Park.

flows.label: Patients shipped from Honolulu to the Kalaupapa peninsula

summary: Under the Hawaiian Kingdom's Act to Prevent the Spread of Leprosy of 1865, people diagnosed with Hansen's disease were arrested, examined and transported to the isolated Kalaupapa peninsula on Molokai, where they were landed — in the early years sometimes put over the side to swim ashore — and were not permitted to leave. The policy continued under the Republic, the Territory and the State of Hawaii, and was abolished only in 1969, more than two decades after sulfone drugs had made the disease treatable. Roughly 8,000 people were exiled over a century, about nine in ten of them Native Hawaiians, and families were broken up: children born at the settlement were taken from their parents. The settlement is best known outside Hawaii through Father Damien and Mother Marianne Cope, who worked there. A small number of former patients chose to remain after 1969 and the peninsula became a National Historical Park in 1980. It is one of the clearest and best-documented instances of compulsory confinement on medical grounds in the atlas.
contested: Whether the segregation policy was a defensible public health measure by the standards of its time or a form of racialised confinement, given that Native Hawaiians made up the overwhelming majority of those exiled and that isolation continued for decades after effective treatment existed.

sources.title: Kalaupapa Leprosy Settlement — Wikipedia
History and Culture — Kalaupapa National Historical Park, US National Park Service
Kalaupapa, Hawaii — Wikipedia

deathsNote: Most of the roughly 8,000 people sent to Kalaupapa died there, over a century, of Hansen's disease and of the conditions of the settlement, which in its first decades lacked adequate shelter, food and medical care. This is mortality within a long-term institution rather than a discrete death toll, and the burial records are incomplete.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Hawaiian Board of Health records and National Park Service historical documentation record the compulsory arrest and transport of patients and the removal of children born at the settlement.
baselineWhat: The Native Hawaiian population at the Kingdom of Hawaii census of 1866, the year the first patients were exiled to Kalaupapa
baselineNote: The 1866 Kingdom census counted 62,959 residents, of whom 58,765 were Native Hawaiian, a population already reduced by roughly 80 per cent since contact. Of the roughly 8,000 people exiled to Kalaupapa between 1866 and 1969, about 90 per cent were Native Hawaiian.

baselineSources.title: Kalaupapa Leprosy Settlement and National Historical Park — Wikipedia
Kalaupapa National Historical Park — National Park Service

shareCaveat: The 8,000 exiles accumulate over 103 years, while the baseline is the population of a single year in which the Native Hawaiian population was still falling steeply; the share of any one cohort sent to Kalaupapa was much smaller.

title: Australia's Aboriginal Protection Acts, Missions and Reserves
actors: Australian colonial and state governments confined Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to missions and reserves under protection legislation, controlling their movement, employment, marriage and wages
peopleRange: No national aggregate exists, because each colony and then state kept its own records under separate statutes. Queensland's Aboriginals Protection and Restriction of the Sale of Opium Act 1897 was the most far-reaching: state records document several thousand formal removal orders between 1897 and the 1970s, moving people to settlements such as Barambah/Cherbourg, Palm Island and Yarrabah, often hundreds of kilometres from their country and frequently mixing unrelated language groups. New South Wales, Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria operated parallel systems from 1869, 1905, 1911 and 1869 respectively. The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population recorded at the 1971 census, the first to count Indigenous people fully, was about 116,000.
territoryDesc: A national network of government settlements, church missions and gazetted reserves; the reserves were progressively revoked or converted to Aboriginal freehold and land trusts from the 1970s.

flows.label: Removal of Aboriginal people to the Barambah/Cherbourg settlement, Queensland
Removal of people deemed troublesome to the Palm Island settlement

summary: Between 1869 and the 1960s every Australian colony and state enacted protection legislation placing Aboriginal people under the authority of a Protector or Board with power to order where they lived, whom they married, what work they did and how their wages were held. People were moved onto missions and government settlements — Coranderrk, Cherbourg, Palm Island, Moore River, Yarrabah among many — where passes were needed to leave, families were separated, languages were suppressed and earnings were controlled by the state, the basis of the later 'stolen wages' claims settled in Queensland and New South Wales in the 2000s and 2010s. Palm Island in Queensland served explicitly as a place of banishment for those deemed disruptive. The legislation also supplied the legal machinery for child removal, which the atlas covers separately as the Stolen Generations for 1945-1970; the confinement regime itself ran for a century and reached a far larger population. Protection statutes were repealed between the 1960s and 1970s, following the 1967 referendum.
contested: How far the reserves and missions provided refuge from frontier violence, as their administrators claimed and as some Aboriginal accounts allow, and how far they functioned as coercive institutions; and the scale of the wages withheld, which state-run reparation schemes have compensated only partially, a point of continuing dispute.

sources.title: Aboriginals Protection and Restriction of the Sale of Opium Act 1897 — Wikipedia
Aboriginal Protection Act 1869 — Wikipedia
Aborigines Protection Board — Wikipedia

deathsNote: There was no mass killing under the protection regime, which followed the frontier violence the atlas covers separately. Mortality on settlements was high from tuberculosis, influenza and poor conditions, and is documented in settlement records and later inquiries, but was never aggregated nationally.
violenceNote: State archives of the protection boards, and the Bringing Them Home inquiry of 1997, document removal orders, controlled wages, restrictions on movement and the separation of children under the protection statutes.
baselineWhat: The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population of Australia around 1900, when the protection regime was being extended across the colonies
baselineNote: Official counts of the Aboriginal population around federation are unreliable because Aboriginal people were excluded from the census and remote populations were estimated rather than enumerated; the figures generally used are of the order of 90,000-100,000 for 1901, against modern estimates of 750,000 or more before 1788 and a counted population of 115,953 at the 1971 census, the first after the 1967 referendum. The protection acts, from Victoria's in 1869 to Queensland's 1897 Act and its successors, at their height controlled residence, employment, wages, marriage and the custody of children for most of that population.
shareCaveat: The regime ran for a century across separate colonial and state jurisdictions with different reach, so no single-year population corresponds to the number of people it confined or controlled.

title: The Colonisation of Hokkaido, Ainu Assimilation Policy and the Annexation of Ryukyu
actors: The Meiji state annexed Ezo as Hokkaido and settled it, imposed assimilation on the Ainu, and abolished the Ryukyu Kingdom, making it Okinawa prefecture
peopleRange: Neither the Ainu nor the Ryukyuans were displaced in a single mass movement, and neither was counted as displaced. The Ainu, numbering in the tens of thousands, lost access to their hunting and fishing grounds as Hokkaido was surveyed and allotted to settlers, and particular communities were relocated wholesale in connection with the territorial exchanges with Russia in the 1870s and 1880s. Ryukyuans were not moved; their kingdom was abolished and its king removed to Tokyo. The evidence is Meiji administrative records and later ethnographic and legal history.
territoryDesc: Ezo province was renamed Hokkaido in 1869 and placed under a Colonisation Office, and roughly 83,400 square km were surveyed, allotted and settled with mainland Japanese migrants and soldier-farmers. The Ryukyu Kingdom, a tributary of both China and Satsuma, was reorganised as a Japanese domain in 1872 and abolished in 1879, its roughly 2,280 square km becoming Okinawa prefecture.

flows.label: Japanese settlers and soldier-farmers -> Hokkaido
The Ryukyuan royal house -> removal to Tokyo, 1879

summary: In 1869 the new Meiji government renamed Ezo as Hokkaido and established a Colonisation Office to survey, allot and settle it, an undertaking that brought hundreds of thousands of mainland Japanese migrants north over the following decades. Britannica records that the Ainu, the indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuriles, were largely assimilated under the growing Japanese presence. Ainu land rights were not recognised in the allotment system, salmon fishing and deer hunting were restricted, and the Hokkaido Former Aborigines Protection Act of 1899 completed a policy of assimilation, granting small agricultural plots on conditions and promoting Japanese language and schooling in place of Ainu practice. In the south, the Ryukyu Kingdom, which had paid tribute to both China and Japan, was declared a Japanese domain in 1872 and abolished in 1879, its king removed to Tokyo and its territory made Okinawa prefecture over Chinese objection. Japan recognised the Ainu as an indigenous people by Diet resolution in 2008 and by statute in 2019.
contested: Whether Meiji policy towards the Ainu is best characterised as assimilation, colonisation or cultural destruction is argued in Japanese and international scholarship; the legality of the Ryukyu annexation was disputed by Qing China at the time and the question of Okinawan self-determination remains politically live.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ainu
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Hokkaido
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ryukyu Islands

deathsNote: There was no significant direct death toll: neither the colonisation of Hokkaido nor the annexation of Ryukyu involved mass killing. Ainu population decline in the nineteenth century came from introduced disease, the disruption of subsistence and intermarriage and assimilation, and was not separately recorded; the losses are visible only in the shrinking number of people registered as Ainu.
violenceNote: Britannica records the assimilation of the Ainu under Japanese settlement and the framework of the 1899 Hokkaido Former Aborigines Protection Act, which promoted Japanese language and agriculture in place of Ainu language, subsistence and custom.
baselineWhat: The Ainu population of Hokkaido together with the population of the Ryukyu Kingdom at annexation
baselineNote: The Kaitakushi count of 1873 recorded 16,272 Ainu in Hokkaido, already much reduced. The Ryukyu Kingdom's population at its abolition in 1879 is estimated at roughly 310,000. Both figures come from early Meiji administrative counts of uncertain completeness, and Ainu numbers are further blurred by assimilation policy, which removed the category itself from later records.
shareCaveat: Two very different populations are combined here; the Ainu, on whom assimilation and dispossession bore hardest, are under 6% of the total, so an aggregate share badly dilutes what happened to them.

title: Canada's Numbered Treaties, the Reserve and Pass System, and the North-West Resistance
actors: The Dominion of Canada took title to the western interior by the Numbered Treaties, confined First Nations to reserves, restricted their movement by an extra-legal pass system and suppressed Metis and Cree resistance in 1885
peopleRange: No single displacement figure covers the process. Between 1871 and 1877 Treaties 1 to 7 covered the territory from the Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains, with Treaties 8 to 11 extending to the Beaufort Sea by 1921; reserve allocations ranged from 160 to 640 acres per family of five, alongside annuities of three to five dollars and promises of schools, tools and hunting rights on unoccupied Crown land. The populations settled on those reserves were counted in treaty pay-lists rather than censuses. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission separately recorded that more than 150,000 First Nations, Metis and Inuit children passed through the residential school system, most of them after 1900.
territoryDesc: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada records that the Numbered Treaties covered the territory between the Lake of the Woods, the Rocky Mountains and the Beaufort Sea - the present Prairie provinces, northern Ontario and the Northwest Territories - opening it to railway construction and settlement while reserving small allotments to the signatory nations.

flows.label: Plains Cree bands -> reserves after the 1885 resistance
Red River Metis -> dispersal westward after 1870

summary: Canada acquired Rupert's Land in 1870 and secured title to the western interior through eleven Numbered Treaties beginning in 1871, negotiated as the bison herds collapsed and famine spread across the plains. First Nations were settled on reserves whose acreage was fixed per family, and the oral undertakings made at the negotiations, recorded in Indigenous accounts, differ in important respects from the written texts. The Red River Resistance of 1869-70 and the North-West Resistance of 1885 arose from Metis land insecurity and First Nations starvation; after the defeat at Batoche in May 1885 Louis Riel was hanged at Regina on 16 November 1885 and other leaders were imprisoned or executed, dispersing Metis leadership. In the same year the Department of Indian Affairs introduced the pass system, requiring an Indian agent's written permission to leave a reserve; the Canadian Encyclopedia records that its architect Hayter Reed acknowledged it had no basis in law, and it persisted in varying degrees of enforcement into the 1930s and in places the early 1940s. The residential school system, which the Truth and Reconciliation Commission described in 2015 as an instrument of cultural genocide, expanded in the same decades.
contested: The Numbered Treaties are read by the Crown as land surrenders and by many signatory nations as agreements to share the land, a divergence rooted in the difference between the written texts and the oral undertakings; the legality of the pass system was doubted by its own architect.

sources.title: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada: Treaties and agreements
The Canadian Encyclopedia: Pass System in Canada
The Canadian Encyclopedia: North-West Rebellion (Resistance)
Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada: Honouring the Truth, Reconciling for the Future (summary of the final report)

deathsNote: The 1885 fighting was small in scale - the Canadian Encyclopedia records twelve government personnel and six Metis fighters killed at Duck Lake, with heavier losses at Fish Creek and Batoche - and does not account for the period's main mortality, which came from the starvation and epidemic disease that followed the collapse of the bison herds on the plains in the late 1870s and 1880s. That mortality was never counted, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's work on deaths in residential schools concerns mainly the twentieth century.

atrocityFindings.body: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada
atrocityFindings.finding: Concluded that the establishment and operation of the residential schools was a central element of a policy 'that can best be described as cultural genocide', and recorded that more than 150,000 First Nations, Metis and Inuit children attended

violenceNote: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented the removal of children into residential schools and the suppression of Indigenous languages and ceremonies, and the Canadian Encyclopedia documents the pass system's confinement of people to reserves without legal authority.
baselineWhat: The First Nations and Metis population of the western interior - present-day Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the North-West Territories - at the start of the treaty process
baselineNote: There was no reliable census of the region before Confederation. Canadian historical demography puts the total First Nations population of Canada at about 125,000 in 1867, including roughly 10,000 Metis in the West; the western interior share is usually reconstructed at 30,000-40,000 First Nations plus 10,000-12,000 Metis from treaty annuity rolls, fur-trade post records and Hudson's Bay Company censuses. The range across authorities is wide, roughly 35,000 to 60,000.

title: The Criminal Tribes Acts and the Settlement of India's 'Criminal Tribes'
actors: The British Indian government designated whole communities as hereditary criminals and subjected them to registration, restricted movement and closed settlements
peopleRange: By the 1940s roughly 150 communities had been notified under the Acts, covering an estimated 3.5 million to 13 million people depending on which provincial lists and which definitions are counted; the higher figure is the one commonly cited by Indian denotified-tribe organisations and derives from provincial registers and census categories. Tens of thousands at a time were held in industrial and agricultural settlements run by provincial governments and by the Salvation Army. The counts come from colonial provincial registers, which were themselves the instrument of the policy.
summary: The Criminal Tribes Act of 1871, extended and consolidated in 1911 and 1924, empowered provincial governments in British India to declare entire communities - typically nomadic, pastoral or itinerant groups such as the Sansi, Kanjar, Pardhi, Lodha, Yerukula and Chhara - as criminal by heredity. Members were required to register, to report at roll calls sometimes several times a night, to carry passes, and to remain within specified areas; those judged incorrigible could be confined in settlements, some of them fenced, where labour was compulsory and children could be separated from parents into reformatory schools. Provincial governments contracted the running of several settlements to the Salvation Army and to industrial employers, who obtained a captive workforce. The system rested on a theory of hereditary criminality drawn from contemporary European criminology and from colonial anxieties about mobile populations, and it criminalised occupation and movement rather than acts. India repealed the Acts in 1952 and the affected groups became the 'denotified tribes', but many were immediately brought under Habitual Offenders Acts, and their descendants continue to report police harassment and social stigma; the Indian government's own commissions, including the Renke Commission of 2008, have documented their continuing marginalisation.
contested: The number of people covered by the Acts varies widely between colonial provincial registers and later Indian estimates, and there is scholarly disagreement about how far the settlements were used as against surveillance in place.

sources.title: Criminal Tribes Act
Denotified tribes of India
Nomadic and denotified communities and the Renke Commission (Wikipedia overview)

deathsNote: No significant death toll is attributable to the system as such. It operated by registration, restriction and confinement rather than killing, though mortality in some settlements from disease and poor conditions was reported by inspectors; no figures were compiled.
violenceNote: Colonial settlement records and later Indian government commissions document compulsory residence and labour in the settlements and the removal of children of registered families into reformatory schools.
baselineWhat: The population of the communities notified as 'criminal tribes' in British India at independence
baselineNote: At independence in 1947 some 13 million people in 127 notified communities were subject to the legislation, though only a fraction were entered on the local police registers at any time and fewer still were held in the closed industrial and agricultural settlements; the 1949-52 repeal is usually described as decriminalising about 2.3 million registered individuals. The descendant category of denotified and nomadic tribes numbers around 60 million people in India today.

title: The Aceh War and the Dutch Conquest of Northern Sumatra
actors: The Netherlands invaded and subjugated the Sultanate of Aceh over four decades of counter-guerrilla warfare
peopleRange: No systematic count of displacement was kept. Dutch military records describe the repeated burning of villages, the destruction of the sultanate's capital and the concentration of population inside a fortified perimeter around Kutaraja from 1884, with flight into the interior; Acehnese casualties and refugee movement were recorded only in aggregate operational reports. Standard estimates of Acehnese deaths across the war range from about 60,000 to 100,000, against roughly 37,000 dead on the Dutch side including auxiliaries, most from disease.
territoryDesc: The Sultanate of Aceh, roughly the area of the modern Indonesian province, annexed to the Netherlands East Indies
summary: The Netherlands invaded Aceh in 1873 after failing to obtain its submission by treaty, killing the sultan and taking the capital, but faced four decades of guerrilla resistance led by the ulama and territorial chiefs. From 1884 the Dutch withdrew to a fortified line around Kutaraja, then from 1898 the campaigns of J. B. van Heutsz and his adviser Christiaan Snouck Hurgronje returned to mobile columns that pursued resistance leaders, burned villages and attacked fortified settlements, including assaults on Kuta Reh and other highland villages in which whole communities including women and children were killed. Dutch military records themselves describe these operations, and Dutch historians have since debated whether the highland assaults, notably at Kuta Reh in 1904 where several hundred villagers including women and children were killed, amounted to massacres. Acehnese deaths across the war are usually put at 60,000-100,000 and Dutch and auxiliary deaths at around 37,000. The sultanate was abolished, Aceh incorporated into the Netherlands East Indies, and grievances from the war fed into later Acehnese resistance to both Dutch and Indonesian rule.
contested: Acehnese and Dutch casualty estimates vary widely and there is no agreed count; the characterisation of specific operations such as Kuta Reh as massacres has long been debated in the Netherlands.

sources.title: Aceh War
Kuta Reh massacre, 1904
J. B. van Heutsz
Aceh

deathsNote: Both ends are estimates of Acehnese dead across four decades, derived from Dutch military reporting and later reconstructions; they include combatants and civilians and cannot be disaggregated. Dutch and colonial-army losses of roughly 37,000, mostly to disease, are separately recorded in Dutch military statistics.
violenceNote: Dutch military records and reporting on the Kuta Reh assault of 1904, together with later Dutch historical research, document village burning and the killing of non-combatants.
baselineWhat: The population of the Sultanate of Aceh at the Dutch invasion of 1873
baselineNote: No census was taken before the conquest; Dutch colonial estimates of the 1870s put Aceh at roughly 500,000-800,000, and the first reliable count, the Netherlands Indies census of 1930, recorded about 1 million for the residency. The mid-point of the colonial range is used here and should be treated as approximate.

title: The April Uprising, the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78 and the Muhacir Migrations
actors: Ottoman irregulars suppressed the Bulgarian April Uprising of 1876, and the Russian invasion and the creation of Bulgaria, Serbia, Montenegro and Romania then drove the Muslim population of the Balkans into the Ottoman Empire
peopleRange: The figures for the Muslim exodus come from Ottoman refugee commission registers and modern reconstructions and vary widely. Nedim Ipek's count, cited by Vladimir Hamed-Troyansky in Past & Present, is that by 1879 the Ottoman Empire hosted 1,230,000 Muslim refugees from the Balkans; Kemal Karpat puts total war refugees at about 1.5 million; Justin McCarthy calculates 515,000 Muslims leaving Bulgaria specifically, and Milos Jagodic about 71,000, mainly Albanians, leaving Serbian territory. A medical commission in Istanbul recorded over half a million refugees passing through the capital alone. Bulgarians were also displaced in 1876-78, principally within the region, and were not separately enumerated.
territoryDesc: The Treaty of Berlin of July 1878 replaced the larger Bulgaria of San Stefano with an autonomous Principality of Bulgaria and the province of Eastern Rumelia, confirmed the independence of Serbia, Montenegro and Romania with enlarged borders, gave Bosnia-Herzegovina to Austro-Hungarian administration and Kars, Ardahan and Batum to Russia, removing most of the Ottoman Empire's remaining European territory.

flows.label: Bulgarian provinces -> Istanbul and Anatolia (muhacirs)
Nis and southern Serbia -> Kosovo and Macedonia (Albanian muhacirs)
Black Sea coast -> Izmir and western Anatolia

summary: In April 1876 a Bulgarian rising was crushed by Ottoman regular and irregular forces. The Bulgarian News Agency's account records that estimates of Bulgarian deaths range from the 12,000 reported by the British diplomat Walter Baring and the 15,000 reported by the American consul Eugene Schuyler to later nineteenth-century figures of 25,000-40,000, with modern scholarship generally accepting 15,000-30,000; eighty settlements were burned, two hundred more sacked, and around 10,000 Bulgarians imprisoned. Gladstone's pamphlet on the 'Bulgarian horrors' and the European press campaign that followed made intervention politically possible, and Russia declared war in April 1877. The Russian advance and the establishment of Bulgaria, and the enlargement of Serbia and Montenegro, then produced the largest single displacement in Ottoman history: on Nedim Ipek's count the empire was hosting 1,230,000 Balkan Muslim refugees by 1879. Refugee property left behind was appropriated under land laws that the new Balkan states inherited from the Ottoman code of 1858.
contested: The Bulgarian death toll of 1876 was disputed at the time between the Ottoman inquiry and the British and American consular investigations and is still given in a wide range; Justin McCarthy's much larger estimates of Muslim civilian deaths in 1877-78 are contested by other historians on grounds of method and of his use of Ottoman population figures.

sources.title: Bulgarian News Agency (BTA): April 1876 Uprising - Backgrounder
Vladimir Hamed-Troyansky, 'Abandoned Land: Muslim Refugees' Property in the Post-Ottoman Balkans', Past & Present
Milena Methodieva, 'Becoming a Muhacir', International Journal of Middle East Studies (Cambridge)

deathsNote: The range covers two different bodies of dead. The lower figure is the modern consensus range of 15,000-30,000 Bulgarian civilians killed in the suppression of the April Uprising in 1876, reported by BTA and derived from the Baring and Schuyler consular investigations against the much lower Ottoman inquiry figures. The upper figure reflects estimates of Muslim civilian deaths during and after the war of 1877-78, of which the best known is Justin McCarthy's calculation of roughly 260,000 dead among the Muslim population of Bulgaria, arrived at by comparing Ottoman population registers with post-war Bulgarian censuses; McCarthy's method and his conclusions are disputed by other historians of the period. Deaths in flight from disease, cold and hunger dominate the upper figure.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: British Foreign Office (Walter Baring's consular report to Parliament) and the United States consulate (Eugene Schuyler)
atrocityFindings.finding: Official investigations into the suppression of the April Uprising reported roughly 12,000 and 15,000 Bulgarians killed respectively, against much lower figures from the Ottoman government's own inquiry

violenceNote: BTA's account, drawing on the Baring and Schuyler investigations and on later scholarship, documents the burning of eighty settlements and sacking of two hundred more, killings of civilians, rape, looting and the imprisonment of some 10,000 Bulgarians in 1876; comparable acts against Muslim villagers during the Russian advance are documented in the Ottoman refugee commission records used by Hamed-Troyansky.
baselineWhat: The Muslim population of the Ottoman Balkan territories that became Bulgaria, Eastern Rumelia and the enlarged Serbian, Montenegrin and Romanian states
baselineNote: Justin McCarthy's reconstruction from Ottoman population registers (nüfus defterleri) puts the Muslim population of the Danube and Edirne provinces at roughly 1.5 million before the war; Bulgarian and Russian sources give lower Muslim shares and higher Christian ones, and the ethnic arithmetic of these registers is contested on all sides. The figure should be read as an order of magnitude within a disputed range.
shareCaveat: The affected figure combines Muslims who fled or were expelled with those who died, and also includes Bulgarian Christians killed in the suppression of the April Uprising, so numerator and denominator do not describe the same population.

title: The Famines of British India, 1876-1902
actors: Successive monsoon failures in British India produced famines whose mortality is attributed by different historians to colonial revenue, trade and relief policy or to drought and limited state capacity
peopleRange: Famine displacement was recorded through the relief system rather than by enumeration of migrants. Millions entered government relief works and camps at the height of the crises of 1876-78 and 1896-1902, subject to distance and task tests designed to deter all but the destitute; large numbers migrated from the Deccan and the Central Provinces towards towns and canal districts, and famine years produced surges in emigration under indenture. The relief-works returns count attendances rather than people, and no displacement total exists.

flows.label: Deccan famine districts -> Madras relief works and city
Central Provinces -> the Punjab canal colonies

summary: Between 1876 and 1902 British India suffered a sequence of severe famines: the Great Famine of 1876-78 in the Madras Presidency, Bombay Deccan, Mysore and Hyderabad; the famine of 1896-97; and that of 1899-1900. Each followed monsoon failure associated with El Nino events, and each occurred in a colony with railways capable of moving grain, an export trade that continued through the crises, a land revenue demand that continued to be collected, and a relief doctrine shaped by the fear of encouraging dependence, which imposed wage and task tests on relief works. Famine Commissions reported in 1880, 1898 and 1901 and produced the Famine Codes. Mike Davis's Late Victorian Holocausts argues that the deaths were the product of imperial economic and political decisions rather than of drought alone; Tirthankar Roy replies that famines resulted from geography and low state capacity, that pre-colonial famine data are too poor to support claims that famines became more frequent under British rule, and that railways, irrigation and administrative capacity ended famine mortality after about 1900. Both positions are held by serious scholars and neither is adjudicated here.
contested: This is one of the most politically live disputes in imperial history. Mike Davis, and more recently Jason Hickel and co-authors, attribute tens of millions of deaths in this period to colonial policy; Tirthankar Roy of the London School of Economics rejects what he calls the colonial-mentality theory in favour of a state-capacity explanation, and disputes both the causal claim and the comparative frequency claim. Mortality estimates themselves vary by a factor of three or more.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Late Victorian Holocausts (Mike Davis)
Tirthankar Roy, 'Colonialism did not cause the Indian famines' (History Reclaimed)
Tirthankar Roy, 'Colonialism and Indian Famines: A Response' (Developing Economics)

deathsNote: The lower end aggregates the official Famine Commission estimates and the more conservative demographic reconstructions from census intervals for the three major famines: roughly five and a half million for 1876-78 and about a million for 1899-1900 on official figures. The upper end follows Mike Davis's Late Victorian Holocausts, which puts deaths in the El Nino famines of 1876-1902 across India, China and Brazil in the tens of millions and gives figures for India at the top of the published range; these rest on higher assumptions about normal mortality and on nineteenth-century estimates such as William Digby's. Indian vital registration was incomplete throughout, so every figure derives from comparing decennial censuses with projected population, and Roy argues that the population declines observed in 1872-81 and 1891-1901 cannot bear the causal weight placed on them.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
baselineWhat: The population of British India, including the princely states, at the 1881 census
baselineNote: The 1881 census counted about 253.9 million people, rising to 287.3 million in 1891 and 294.4 million in 1901 — the flat decade of the 1890s itself reflecting famine mortality. Excess-death estimates for the Great Famine of 1876-78 run from about 5.5 million to 10 million and for the famines of 1896-97 and 1899-1902 from about 6 million to 19 million, with the higher figures associated with Mike Davis and the lower ones with historians who emphasise drought and disease over policy.

baselineSources.title: Timeline of major famines in India during British rule — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The famines struck particular provinces — Madras, Bombay, the Deccan, the Central Provinces and later much of northern India — so a subcontinental denominator understates local mortality, which reached a fifth or more of the population in the worst-hit districts.

title: The Ploughing Campaign and the Invasion of Parihaka
actors: The New Zealand government imprisoned Maori protesters without trial and invaded the pacifist settlement of Parihaka in Taranaki
peopleRange: New Zealand government records and the Waitangi Tribunal's Taranaki inquiry document several hundred ploughmen and fence-builders arrested from 1879 and held without trial in South Island gaols under special legislation; about 1,600 Armed Constabulary and volunteers entered Parihaka on 5 November 1881, and most of the settlement's residents, numbering roughly 1,500-2,000, were dispersed to other districts under a pass system, with houses and cultivations destroyed.
territoryDesc: The invasion secured for settlement the Taranaki land confiscated after the wars of the 1860s, which Parihaka's residents had been ploughing and fencing in protest

flows.label: Maori prisoners held without trial in Dunedin and other South Island gaols

summary: At Parihaka in Taranaki, Te Whiti o Rongomai and Tohu Kakahi built a community that resisted the survey and sale of confiscated land by non-violent means: from 1879 their followers ploughed settlers' paddocks and rebuilt fences across surveyed lines. The government responded by arresting several hundred men and holding them without trial in South Island prisons under successive Maori Prisoners Acts, where some died. On 5 November 1881 about 1,600 Armed Constabulary and volunteers marched on the settlement, met by children singing and by people sitting silently on the marae; the leaders were arrested and tried, houses were demolished, crops and livestock destroyed and most residents were dispersed, with those permitted to return required to carry passes. Evidence presented to the Waitangi Tribunal's Taranaki inquiry, whose report was published in 1996, included accounts of rapes committed during the occupation. In 2017 the Crown signed Te Kawenata o Rongo with the people of Parihaka, apologising formally for the invasion and its consequences and providing a reconciliation package, later given legislative form.
contested: Nineteenth-century official accounts presented the invasion as the peaceful enforcement of law; the Waitangi Tribunal and the 2017 Crown apology accept that it involved unlawful imprisonment, destruction of property and serious abuses.

sources.title: NZHistory: Te ra o te pahua - invasion of the pacifist settlement at Parihaka
Parihaka
New Zealand Government: Crown apology to Parihaka
RNZ: Tears as Crown apologises for Parihaka atrocities

deathsNote: There was no mass killing: the settlement did not resist. Some of the ploughmen imprisoned without trial in South Island gaols died in custody, a number not precisely recorded, and deaths followed from the destitution caused by the destruction of homes and crops.

atrocityFindings.body: Crown of New Zealand (Te Kawenata o Rongo)
atrocityFindings.finding: The Crown apologised for the 1881 invasion of Parihaka, the imprisonment without trial of its people, the destruction of the settlement and the lasting harm caused, and agreed a reconciliation package with Parihaka

violenceNote: The Waitangi Tribunal's Taranaki inquiry and the 2017 Crown apology record imprisonment without trial, the destruction of houses and cultivations, and evidence of rapes during the occupation.
baselineWhat: The residents of Parihaka at the time of the November 1881 invasion
baselineNote: Parihaka was the largest Maori settlement in the country, with a resident population usually put at 1,500-2,000 and several thousand present on the day of the invasion. About 1,600 armed constabulary and volunteers entered on 5 November 1881; most residents were dispersed to their home districts, houses were destroyed and cultivations laid waste, and hundreds of ploughmen and fencers had already been arrested and held without trial in South Island jails.

baselineSources.title: NZHistory - Te ra o te pahua: invasion of the pacifist settlement at Parihaka

shareCaveat: The figure of about 1,600 is used in the sources both for the constabulary force that entered Parihaka and for the residents dispersed, so numerator and denominator here are close by coincidence as much as by measurement.

title: The Putumayo Rubber Atrocities
actors: The Peruvian Amazon Company under Julio Cesar Arana held Huitoto, Bora, Andoke, Ocaina and neighbouring peoples in debt bondage on rubber stations, enforced by armed overseers
peopleRange: No count of those held exists; company payroll and rubber-delivery records were partial and self-serving. Roger Casement, sent by the British Foreign Office in 1910, estimated the Indigenous population of the Putumayo had fallen from around 50,000 to some 8,000-10,000 over three decades, and the figure of about 30,000-40,000 deaths derives from his and subsequent reconstructions. Later Colombian and Peruvian anthropological work, and the 1924-1930 relocation of 6,719 Indigenous people documented in Peruvian government records, extended the toll. All figures are estimates from missionary, consular and company sources, not enumerations.
territoryDesc: The Putumayo basin, disputed between Peru and Colombia, was administered de facto by the company through a chain of rubber stations until the boundary settlement of 1922.
summary: Between the 1880s and 1913 the rubber enterprise built by Julio Cesar Arana in the Putumayo basin, incorporated in London in 1907 as the Peruvian Amazon Company, extracted rubber through the compulsory labour of Huitoto, Bora, Andoke, Ocaina and related peoples, held by debt, hostage-taking of women and children, and armed overseers, many of them Barbadian labourers recruited by the company. The system was exposed by the American engineer Walter Hardenburg and the Iquitos newspaper La Sancion, and investigated in 1910-1911 by the British consul Roger Casement, who described it in his report to the Foreign Office — published as a parliamentary Blue Book in 1912 — as a system not merely of slavery but of extermination, documenting floggings, mutilation, starvation, rape and mass shootings. A House of Commons Select Committee on Putumayo reported in 1913. Estimates of Indigenous deaths across the period run to 30,000-40,000, with the Huitoto population reduced by around nine-tenths; the company was wound up but no perpetrator in Peru was convicted. The atlas had nothing on the Amazon rubber boom.
contested: The death toll, for which no enumeration exists and estimates range from tens of thousands to figures above 200,000 in some Colombian accounts; and, in Peru, the historical assessment of Arana, who was later elected a senator.

sources.title: Putumayo genocide — Wikipedia
Peruvian Amazon Company — Wikipedia
Casement Report — Wikipedia
Julio Cesar Arana — Wikipedia
Rubber boom — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The commonly cited range, derived from Casement's population estimates and from later anthropological reconstruction of Huitoto and Bora numbers; higher figures circulate in Colombian accounts but rest on the same thin base. Deaths came from shooting, flogging, starvation and disease under the labour regime, in proportions that were never recorded.

atrocityFindings.body: Select Committee on Putumayo, House of Commons, United Kingdom
atrocityFindings.finding: 1913 report following Roger Casement's investigation, finding that the Peruvian Amazon Company's operations rested on the enslavement and systematic ill-treatment of the Indigenous population of the Putumayo

violenceNote: Roger Casement's 1911 report to the British Foreign Office and the depositions of thirty Barbadian company employees taken by him document the floggings, mutilations, shootings, starvation, rapes and hostage-taking of women and children.
baselineWhat: The indigenous population of the Putumayo–Caraparaná–Igaraparaná rubber district at the start of the boom
baselineNote: No census was taken; the figure of roughly 50,000 Huitoto, Bora, Andoke, Ocaina, Resígaro and Muinane derives from Roger Casement's 1911 investigation and Peruvian Amazon Company station registers, and later scholarship estimates that around nine in ten of the targeted populations were destroyed. Individual data points support the scale of collapse: the Resígaro numbered fewer than thirty by 1911, and the Último Retiro station's workforce fell from about 2,000 to about 200 by 1912.

title: The United States Indian Boarding School System
actors: The United States federal government and church partners removed Native American, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian children from their families into distant boarding schools to eliminate their languages and cultures
peopleRange: No enrolment total exists for the nineteenth century alone. The Department of the Interior's 2022 investigation identified 408 federally operated boarding schools in 37 states and territories across the whole period 1819-1969. The single best-documented institution, the Carlisle Indian Industrial School opened in October 1879, took more than 7,800 American Indian and Alaska Native children between 1879 and 1918, according to the National Park Service. Enrolment in the system expanded rapidly through the 1880s and 1890s as the Indian Office made schooling a condition of rations and treaty payments.

flows.label: Lakota agencies, Dakota Territory -> Carlisle, Pennsylvania
Southwest reservations -> eastern boarding schools

summary: From 1879 the United States built a national system of off-reservation boarding schools on the model of Carlisle, founded by Richard Henry Pratt, whose stated aim was to 'kill the Indian, save the man'. Children were taken from their families, often under pressure or coercion, renamed, had their hair cut, were forbidden to speak their languages or practise their religions, and were set to manual labour that supported the institutions themselves. The Department of the Interior's Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative Investigative Report, released in May 2022, identified 408 federal schools operating between 1819 and 1969 and marked or unmarked burial sites at approximately 53 of them, with the number expected to rise; it was the first comprehensive federal inventory of the policy. The National Park Service records more than 7,800 children at Carlisle to 1918 and about 200 buried in its cemetery, whose remains the Army has since been returning to their communities.
contested: How many children died in the schools is unresolved: the federal investigation is still identifying burial sites, and school records of deaths, discharges and 'outing' placements are incomplete and inconsistent.

sources.title: US Department of the Interior: Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative Investigative Report (press release, 2022)
National Park Service: Carlisle Federal Indian Boarding School National Monument site bulletin

deathsNote: No total exists for the nineteenth century. The firmest single figure is the National Park Service's estimate of about 200 children who died at Carlisle and were buried there between 1879 and 1918. The Interior Department's 2022 report identified burial sites at roughly 53 federal schools and stated that the number would grow as the investigation continued; because records were kept inconsistently and many children died after being sent home ill, any aggregate would be a guess.

atrocityFindings.body: United States Department of the Interior
atrocityFindings.finding: Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative Investigative Report: identified 408 federal Indian boarding schools operating 1819-1969 in 37 states, documented policies of renaming children, cutting hair and prohibiting Indigenous languages and religions, and located marked or unmarked burial sites at approximately 53 schools

violenceNote: The Department of the Interior's 2022 investigative report documents the removal of children from their families, the suppression of Indigenous names, languages and religious practice, the use of manual labour in place of academic instruction, and confinement in institutions from which children were not free to leave.
baselineWhat: The American Indian and Alaska Native population of the United States as enumerated in the 1880 census
baselineNote: The 1880 federal census counted 306,543 American Indians, and the 1890 census 248,253 — the recorded nadir of the Indigenous population of the United States. Both counts are undercounts, since census enumeration of people on reservations and in Indian Territory was incomplete, and Native Hawaiians were counted separately (about 40,000 in the 1890s).
