title: Menelik II's Conquest of the Southern Lands and the Gabbar System
actors: The Shewan and then Ethiopian imperial armies of Menelik II conquered the Oromo, Sidama, Kafficho, Wolayta and other southern polities and imposed tribute, land alienation and servile labour
peopleRange: No count exists. Imperial and provincial records show the settlement of naftanya (rifle-bearing) soldier-settlers on conquered land and the reduction of much of the local population to gabbar status, owing labour and tribute to them; the great famine and rinderpest epizootic of 1888-92, which coincided with the campaigns, killed an estimated third of the population of the northern and central highlands on the standard estimate of Richard Pankhurst, itself derived from contemporary missionary and traveller accounts rather than enumeration.
territoryDesc: The Ethiopian empire roughly doubled in area, incorporating the Oromo lands, Kaffa, Wolayta, Sidama, the Ogaden and the southern peripheries into the borders of the modern state

flows.label: Northern soldier-settlers (naftanya) settled on conquered southern land

summary: Between the 1870s and 1900 Menelik II, first as king of Shewa and from 1889 as emperor, conquered the Oromo, Gurage, Wolayta, Sidama, Kafficho, Konso and Somali lands to the south, west and east, roughly doubling the territory of the Ethiopian state and fixing the borders of modern Ethiopia in negotiations with the European colonial powers. Conquered populations were placed under the gabbar system, in which they owed labour, produce and tribute to naftanya soldier-settlers granted rights over their land, and slave-taking and slave trading, though formally restricted by Menelik's edicts, continued on a large scale. Contemporary European observers, including the Russian officer Alexander Bulatovich, described very heavy population loss in the conquered south, and Oromo nationalist historians have argued that the campaigns killed or displaced a large share of the southern peoples; Ethiopian historians such as Bahru Zewde treat the period primarily as state formation comparable to other nineteenth-century expansions and regard the highest claims as unsupportable. The campaigns coincided with the Great Ethiopian Famine of 1888-92, caused by a rinderpest panzootic that destroyed the cattle herds, which independently killed an estimated third of the population of the north. The historical assessment of Menelik's conquests remains one of the most contested questions in Ethiopian politics.
contested: Whether the southern conquests constituted colonial subjugation with mass mortality, as Oromo nationalist historiography argues, or state formation with harsh but conventional tributary consequences, as much Ethiopian historiography holds, is actively disputed; no figures for deaths or displacement are supportable from records.

sources.title: Menelik II
Ethiopian Empire
Famines in Ethiopia, including the Great Famine of 1888-1892

deathsNote: No defensible range. Claims that the conquests killed millions come from Oromo nationalist historiography extrapolating from Bulatovich's contemporary impression that the population of the conquered lands had halved; Ethiopian and international historians regard this as unsupportable, and the concurrent rinderpest famine of 1888-92 makes attribution to the campaigns impossible.
violenceNote: Ethiopian imperial administrative practice and contemporary European accounts document the gabbar system of compulsory labour and tribute owed by conquered populations to soldier-settlers.
baselineWhat: No defensible denominator: the conquered southern polities were never enumerated and the scale of their population is disputed as part of a live political argument
baselineNote: There was no census in Ethiopia before 1984. McEvedy and Jones put the whole Ethiopian region at roughly 11 million around 1900. Claims that the conquests of 1880-1900 killed or destroyed half the population of the south rest chiefly on the Russian officer Alexander Bulatovich's contemporary impression, repeated in Oromo nationalist historiography; other historians regard the figure as unsupportable. The gabbar system that followed tied conquered cultivators to naftanya settlers across Wollega, Arsi, Sidama, Kaffa and Wolayta, but its extent is documented in land grants rather than in population counts.

title: Anti-Jewish Pogroms, the May Laws and Emigration from the Russian Empire
actors: Mobs attacked Jewish communities across the south-western Russian Empire while the imperial government restricted Jewish residence, trade and settlement, driving mass emigration
peopleRange: Emigration is measured from receiving-country arrival records rather than Russian departure records, which did not exist for most emigrants. Somewhere in the region of three quarters of a million Jews left the Russian Empire between 1881 and 1900, chiefly for the United States, with about two million leaving in the whole period to 1914. Separate and better documented is the expulsion of Jews from Moscow beginning in 1891, which removed on the order of twenty to thirty thousand people to the Pale of Settlement. Both figures are reconstructions from immigration statistics, communal aid-society records and police orders.
territoryDesc: The May Laws of 1882 barred Jews from settling anew outside towns and shtetls within the Pale of Settlement, restricted their acquisition of rural property and their trading on Sundays and Christian holidays, tightening a residence regime that already confined most of the empire's five million Jews to the western provinces.

flows.label: Pale of Settlement -> New York and the United States
Expulsion from Moscow (1891) -> the Pale of Settlement
Odessa -> London's East End

summary: After the assassination of Alexander II in March 1881, waves of anti-Jewish riots swept the south-western provinces of the Russian Empire, destroying homes, shops and synagogues. The government's response was restrictive rather than protective: the Temporary Regulations of May 1882, known as the May Laws, prohibited new Jewish settlement outside towns within the Pale of Settlement and curtailed Jewish landholding and trade, and were followed by quotas on secondary and higher education and, from 1891, the expulsion of most Jews from Moscow. The combination of periodic violence and legal disability produced the largest Jewish migration in history: hundreds of thousands left in the 1880s and 1890s, with the total passing two million by 1914. The killing associated with pogroms was limited in this period; the great lethal pogroms came after 1903 at Kishinev and during the revolutionary violence of 1905-06 and the civil war.
contested: The degree of official instigation of the 1881-84 riots is disputed: older accounts held that the government organised them, while more recent scholarship in the YIVO Encyclopedia and elsewhere emphasises official passivity, local economic conflict and the state's use of the violence to justify restriction rather than its authorship of it.

sources.title: YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe: Russian Empire
Center for Israel Education: May Laws are instituted in Russia

deathsNote: The pogrom wave of 1881-84 killed comparatively few people - deaths were counted in the tens rather than the thousands - and its damage was overwhelmingly to property, livelihoods and personal security. Mass killing in pogroms belongs to the period after 1903. Presenting a death range for 1881-1900 would misrepresent an episode whose principal effect was expulsion and emigration rather than slaughter.
violenceNote: The YIVO Encyclopedia and the Center for Israel Education document the destruction and looting of Jewish homes, shops and synagogues, rapes committed during the riots, and the legal disabilities of the May Laws and the residence regime that placed Jews outside the ordinary rights of imperial subjects.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of the Russian Empire at the 1897 imperial census
baselineNote: The 1897 census, the empire's only general census, recorded 5,215,805 Jews by religion, about 94 per cent of them in the Pale of Settlement and Congress Poland; the same population was roughly 4 million when the pogroms began in 1881. The emigration figure counts departures to the United States, Britain, Argentina and Palestine over two decades.
shareCaveat: The denominator is a mid-period census while the numerator accumulates emigration over twenty years; measured against the roughly 4 million Jews of 1881 the share would be noticeably higher.

title: The Scramble for Africa and the Berlin Conference
actors: European powers partitioned almost the entire African continent among themselves, formalising the rules of claim at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85
peopleRange: Partition displaced sovereignty rather than, in the first instance, people; the population movements it produced - labour migration, flight from conquest columns, resettlement onto reserves and concessions - occurred within the individual colonies and are recorded, where they are recorded at all, in colonial administrative papers. No aggregate figure for people displaced by the partition itself is meaningful.
territoryDesc: By 1900 the great majority of Africa's roughly 30 million square km was under European claim or control - British, French, Portuguese, Belgian, German, Italian and Spanish - with only Ethiopia and Liberia substantially outside it. Borders were drawn on maps in Europe with little reference to existing polities, and the doctrine of effective occupation adopted at Berlin obliged claimants to establish administration on the ground, driving the conquest campaigns of the following two decades.
summary: The Berlin West Africa Conference, convened by Bismarck and sitting from November 1884 to February 1885, brought fourteen states together to settle rival claims in the Congo basin. Its General Act declared the Congo basin neutral, guaranteed free trade and navigation on the Congo and the Niger, prohibited the slave trade in the region, and set out the conditions on which European claims to African coasts would be recognised. Britannica records that although colonisation had already begun, its pace greatly accelerated after the conference. The partition that followed was carried out by treaty with African rulers, by concession company, and by military conquest - against the Asante, the Sokoto Caliphate, the Mahdist state in Sudan, the Ndebele, Dahomey, Samori Ture's empire and many others - and left almost the whole continent under European claim by 1900. The conference is often described as having divided Africa; more precisely, it set the rules by which the powers agreed to recognise each other's divisions.
contested: Historians differ over how much causal weight the Berlin Conference itself carries, some treating it as the trigger of the partition and others as a codification of a process already under way; the degree to which treaties signed by African rulers were understood by them as cessions of sovereignty is disputed in almost every case.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Berlin West Africa Conference
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Congo Free State

deathsNote: There is no aggregate toll for the partition. Deaths occurred in the conquest campaigns and in the labour and taxation regimes that followed, and the largest of these - the Congo Free State rubber regime, the French Algerian and Saharan campaigns, the Sudan campaigns, and after 1900 the German suppression of the Herero and Nama - are counted separately where the evidence allows. Aggregating them here would double-count and would imply a precision the sources do not support.
baselineWhat: The population of the African continent at the close of the partition
baselineNote: There was no census of most of Africa in this period. McEvedy and Jones' regional series and the demographic reconstructions used by Frankema and Jerven put the continent at roughly 120-140 million around 1900. The partition acted on essentially the whole continent: by 1900 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained outside European rule.

title: The Congo Free State and the Rubber Regime
actors: Leopold II of Belgium held the Congo basin as a personal possession and extracted rubber and ivory through forced labour enforced by the Force Publique and concession company militias
peopleRange: No displacement count exists for a territory that was never censused under Leopold's rule. Villages fled into the forest to escape rubber quotas, whole districts were depopulated by flight as well as by death, and hostage-taking - the seizure of women and children to compel men to bring in rubber - was systematic. The scale of the population change is inferred from the first colonial censuses after 1908, from missionary station records and from the anthropological reconstruction of particular societies such as Jan Vansina's work on the Kuba, not from contemporary counts.
territoryDesc: The Congo Free State covered almost the entire Congo river basin, coextensive with the modern Democratic Republic of the Congo, recognised at the Berlin Conference as Leopold's personal holding rather than a Belgian colony; from 1891-92 the state and its concession companies claimed ownership of all 'vacant' land and its produce, which in practice meant the wild rubber on which the population depended for nothing and the state for everything.

flows.label: Flight from rubber districts into the forest and across the river

summary: Leopold II obtained international recognition of the Congo Free State in 1885 and from the early 1890s converted it into an extraction economy based on wild rubber. Quotas were imposed on villages and enforced by the Force Publique and by armed sentries employed by concession companies: hostages were taken, villages burned, and - as the CEPR summary of the economic-history literature records - sentries were required to produce a human hand for every cartridge fired, to prevent ammunition being used for hunting. Edmund Morel publicised the system from the shipping records, and Roger Casement's consular report of 1904 confirmed the accusations; the Congo Reform Association that the two founded is often described as the first mass human rights organisation. A commission of inquiry appointed by Leopold reported in 1905, and under pressure from Belgium, Britain, the United States, France and Germany the Belgian state annexed the territory in 1908, paying Leopold substantial compensation. The regime lasted about fourteen years in its most intense form and its effects on wealth, health and institutions in the former concession areas are measurable more than a century later.
contested: The figure of ten million dead, associated with Adam Hochschild and Jan Vansina and cited in the economic-history literature, is disputed because there was no pre-conquest census against which to measure it; critics note that the baseline population is a reconstruction and that much of the mortality came from sleeping sickness and smallpox epidemics whose spread was accelerated, but not initiated, by the labour regime. Defenders reply that the epidemics were themselves a product of forced movement, hunger and the destruction of village life.

sources.title: CEPR / VoxEU: King Leopold's ghost - the legacy of labour coercion in the DRC
EBSCO Research Starters: Belgium Confiscates Congo Free State from King Leopold II
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Congo Free State

deathsNote: The upper figure is the estimate attributed to Hochschild and Vansina and reported in the CEPR summary and by EBSCO: roughly ten million people, about half the population of the Congo, dead between 1880 and 1920 from violence, disease, starvation and collapsed birth rates. It is a reconstruction from post-1908 censuses projected backwards, not a count, and it covers a longer period than Leopold's rule alone. The lower figure reflects more conservative readings that confine the estimate to the concession districts and to the years of the rubber regime and that attribute a larger share of the epidemic mortality to causes independent of the labour system. No contemporary authority counted the dead.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: British Foreign Office (the Casement Report) and the Commission of Inquiry appointed by Leopold II
atrocityFindings.finding: Casement's 1904 consular report confirmed the accusations of mutilation, hostage-taking, killing and forced labour in the rubber districts, and the commission appointed in response reported in 1905, leading to Belgian annexation in 1908

violenceNote: The Casement report of 1904, the 1905 commission of inquiry and the missionary photographic record documented hostage-taking of women and children, the severing of hands, floggings with the chicotte, the burning of villages and killings by Force Publique soldiers and company sentries enforcing rubber quotas.
baselineWhat: The population of the Congo basin at the founding of the Congo Free State
baselineNote: No usable starting figure exists, and the dispute over it is central to the historiography. E. D. Morel's contemporary estimate of 20 million, from which the familiar claim that half the population died derives, rests on no enumeration; the first colonial census, in 1924, counted about 10 million. Louis and Stengers call the starting figures 'wild guesses', Vansina and Hochschild accept a decline on the order of ten million, and recent demographic work suggests a documented decline of about 1.2-1.5 million. With the base itself contested by a factor of two, a percentage would be meaningless.

title: The Mahdist State in Sudan: Forced Migration to Omdurman and the Famine of 1889
actors: The Khalifa Abdallahi's Mahdist state moved western Sudanese tribes to the capital, deported opponents and requisitioned grain during a catastrophic famine
peopleRange: Estimates rest on Egyptian and British intelligence reports, on the memoirs of European captives such as Rudolf Slatin and Josef Ohrwalder, and on the reconstructions of P. M. Holt and M. W. Daly. Omdurman grew from nothing to a city of perhaps 150,000 within a few years, substantially through ordered migration of the Ta'aisha and other Baqqara from Darfur and Kordofan; the figure of roughly 200,000 covers that movement plus tribes displaced by campaigns and famine, and is an order-of-magnitude estimate.
territoryDesc: The Mahdist state held most of the former Turco-Egyptian Sudan from Dongola to the Ethiopian marches

flows.label: Baqqara of Kordofan and Darfur ordered to Omdurman

summary: After the fall of Khartoum in 1885 and the Mahdi's death, the Khalifa Abdallahi consolidated power by ordering the migration (hijra) of his own Ta'aisha kinsmen and other western tribes to the new capital at Omdurman, moving whole communities several hundred miles and settling them as a garrison population. Tribes that resisted were attacked and deported, and grain was requisitioned for the capital and the armies. Between 1888 and 1892 Sudan suffered a famine remembered as sanat sitta, the year six, caused by drought, locusts, cattle disease and the disruption and requisitioning of agriculture; contemporaries described mass death and depopulated districts. Anglo-Egyptian writers after the reconquest claimed Sudan's population fell from around 8 million to 2 or 3 million under Mahdist rule, a claim later historians including Holt and Daly regard as propaganda built on invented baselines, though they accept the losses were severe. The state was destroyed by the Anglo-Egyptian campaign of 1896-98, in which some 11,000 Mahdist fighters were killed at Omdurman in a single morning.
contested: The Anglo-Egyptian claim that Sudan lost half or more of its population under the Mahdiyya was used to justify the reconquest and is rejected by modern historians as unsupported, though the famine's severity is not in doubt.

sources.title: Mahdist State

Mahdist State (Encyclopedia.com)

deathsNote: The low end reflects historians' cautious reading of famine mortality in the affected provinces; the high end reflects the larger figures in colonial-era accounts, which modern scholarship treats as inflated. Deaths combine famine, epidemic disease and campaign killings, and none of the figures rest on records.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: European captives' memoirs and Egyptian intelligence reports, used by Holt and Daly, describe grain requisitioning, forced migration and punitive campaigns against dissenting tribes.
baselineWhat: The population of the Sudan at the start of the Mahdist state
baselineNote: Contemporary Egyptian administrative estimates and the reconstruction by H. A. MacMichael put the Sudan at roughly 7-8.5 million before the Mahdiyya, falling to 2-3 million by the Anglo-Egyptian reconquest in 1898. Those figures were compiled by the incoming colonial administration and had an obvious interest in blackening the Mahdist record; modern historians accept a large decline from war, the famine of 1889 and epidemic disease but regard the specific numbers as unreliable.

title: Abdur Rahman Khan's Subjugation of the Hazarajat and the Pashtun Settlement of Northern Afghanistan
actors: The Afghan emir Abdur Rahman Khan conquered the Hazarajat and Kafiristan, enslaved and displaced their populations and moved Pashtun communities north
peopleRange: Afghanistan kept no population records. The widely repeated statement that more than half the Hazara population was killed, enslaved or driven out in 1891-93 originates in British political reporting and Hazara accounts and is reproduced by Minority Rights Group among others; it is an impression rather than a measurement. Hazara refugee communities established in Quetta in British India and in Mashhad in Iran date from these years, as do the Pashtun nomad and settler communities placed on Hazara and Uzbek land.
territoryDesc: The Hazarajat and Kafiristan were brought under direct Kabul control; land in the Hazarajat and in the northern provinces was granted to Pashtun settlers and nomads

flows.label: Hazara refugees to Quetta in British India
Ghilzai Pashtuns transferred to the northern provinces

summary: Abdur Rahman Khan, installed as emir in 1880, spent two decades imposing central authority on regions that had governed themselves. Between 1891 and 1893 his forces, reinforced by tribal militias promised land and captives and operating under a declaration of jihad against the Shia Hazaras, fought a war in the Hazarajat in which villages were destroyed, men killed, women and children sold in slave markets, and land redistributed to Pashtun tribes; survivors fled to Quetta in British India and to Mashhad in Iran, where their descendants remain. In 1895-96 the emir conquered Kafiristan, converted its population by force and renamed it Nuristan. He also carried out the naqlin, the transfer of Ghilzai Pashtun families to the Uzbek and Turkmen lands north of the Hindu Kush, to hold the frontier and dilute non-Pashtun majorities, a policy whose effects still shape northern Afghanistan's demography. Hazara organisations describe the campaigns as genocide; the term is contested among historians, some of whom emphasise the campaigns' political and fiscal aims and the absence of measurable population data.
contested: Whether the Hazarajat campaigns constitute genocide, and the claim that more than half the Hazara population perished or fled, are disputed; both rest on estimates rather than records.

sources.title: Minority Rights Group: Hazaras in Afghanistan
Hazaras
Pashtun colonization of northern Afghanistan

deathsNote: No count exists and none of the figures in circulation rests on records. Contemporary British political officers described very heavy Hazara losses in 1891-93, and accounts agree that killing, enslavement and flight together removed a large share of the population from the Hazarajat, but the proportion is an estimate.
violenceNote: British Indian political reporting and Hazara and Nuristani accounts describe massacres, enslavement, the burning of villages and forced conversion in Kafiristan.
baselineWhat: The Hazara population of central Afghanistan before Abdur Rahman Khan's campaigns
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Afghanistan held no census until 1979, and estimates of the nineteenth-century Hazara population derive from British Indian political officers' reports and from the emir's own court chronicle, the Siraj al-Tawarikh, neither of which is a count. The widely repeated claim that more than half the Hazara were killed, enslaved or driven out rests on these same sources and cannot be given a denominator without circularity.

title: The Hamidian Massacres of the Armenians
actors: Ottoman troops, Hamidiye irregulars and urban mobs killed Armenians across the eastern Anatolian provinces and in Constantinople during the reign of Sultan Abdulhamid II
peopleRange: No count of the displaced was made. The Armenian National Institute's account records that tens of thousands fled the country, thousands were forcibly converted to Islam, and the destitute - people whose homes, workshops and stock had been plundered - numbered in the hundreds of thousands. Emigration from the eastern provinces to Russia, the Balkans, Egypt and the United States accelerated sharply after 1896. The figures come from missionary and consular reporting and Armenian communal records rather than from Ottoman administrative sources.

flows.label: Eastern Anatolia -> Russian Armenia and the Caucasus
Constantinople -> emigration to the United States

summary: The killings began in the Sasun district in the summer of 1894, when troops and Kurdish irregulars suppressed resistance to double taxation, and spread after Armenian political demonstrations in Constantinople in September 1895 were broken up with violence. Through the autumn of 1895 massacres moved south and east from Trebizond across the Armenian provinces; the worst single episode was at Urfa, where the Armenian National Institute records approximately 3,000 people burned in the cathedral. A further round followed the seizure of the Ottoman Bank by Armenian revolutionaries in August 1896, in which five to six thousand people were killed in Constantinople over three days. Estimates of the total dead range from about 80,000 to 300,000; the Armenian National Institute gives 100,000 to 300,000 and the EBSCO summary reports that Abdulhamid II is said to have killed more than 100,000. Plunder was systematic, forced conversions were widespread, and the events are widely treated in Armenian and Western scholarship as a precursor to the deportations and killings of 1915.
contested: Death tolls vary by a factor of three or more between sources. Turkish official historiography treats the events as intercommunal violence and the suppression of an armed separatist movement rather than as state-directed massacres, a position that Armenian institutions and most Western scholarship reject; the relationship between 1894-96 and 1915 is argued in the same terms.

sources.title: Armenian National Institute: Hamidian (Armenian) Massacres, 1894-1896
EBSCO Research Starters: the Hamidian massacres of Armenians

deathsNote: The upper end, 300,000, is the maximum in the range given by the Armenian National Institute and derives from missionary, consular and Armenian Patriarchate compilations made at the time. The lower end reflects the more conservative contemporary European estimates and later scholarly revisions. EBSCO notes that only rough estimates exist even for individual towns - 920 killed at Trebizond on 2 October 1895, nearly 6,000 in Constantinople after the Ottoman Bank raid - and that the Ottoman state produced no reliable count. There is no independent census against which to check any of the figures.
violenceNote: The Armenian National Institute and EBSCO document the massacre of civilians, the burning of the cathedral at Urfa with its congregation inside, forced conversions to Islam and the systematic plunder and destruction of Armenian homes and businesses, drawing on missionary, consular and Patriarchate reporting.
baselineWhat: The Armenian population of the Ottoman Empire before the massacres
baselineNote: The figure is politically contested. Ottoman official statistics of the 1890s recorded about 1.0-1.1 million Armenians, the Armenian Patriarchate claimed roughly 2.6 million, and European consular and later scholarly estimates generally fall between 1.5 and 2 million. The mid-range figure is used here with that spread flagged.

title: Weyler's Reconcentracion in Cuba
actors: The Spanish captain-general Valeriano Weyler ordered the rural population of Cuba into fortified towns to deny support to the independence insurgency
peopleRange: Estimates of those concentrated range from about 300,000 to more than 500,000, out of a Cuban population of roughly 1.6 million; the figures come from Spanish military orders and provincial returns, from American consular reporting and from the 1899 US census of Cuba, which recorded a population sharply lower than the 1887 Spanish census and was used to infer the loss. Deaths among the reconcentrados are most often put at 150,000-170,000, with some scholars arguing for figures above 200,000.
territoryDesc: The order applied first to Pinar del Rio and later to most of the island; rural districts were declared free-fire zones and crops and livestock outside the fortified lines destroyed.

flows.label: Rural population of Pinar del Rio concentrated into garrisoned towns

summary: Appointed captain-general in February 1896 to suppress the Cuban war of independence, Valeriano Weyler issued a series of reconcentracion orders requiring the rural population to move into fortified towns within a fixed period, on pain of being treated as insurgents; crops and livestock outside the lines were destroyed to deny the rebels supply. The towns had no capacity to feed or house the influx, and the concentrated population died in very large numbers of hunger, dysentery, yellow fever and smallpox. Most estimates put deaths at 150,000-170,000, or roughly a tenth of the island's population, over about two years. American newspapers made the camps a central justification for intervention in 1898, and the policy became the template later applied by the British in South Africa and the United States in the Philippines — both already in the atlas, which had no entry for the Cuban original. Weyler was recalled in October 1897 and the orders rescinded; he was never prosecuted and remained a senior figure in Spain.
contested: The death toll, with estimates from about 100,000 to more than 400,000; and whether the policy is properly described as genocidal, as some scholars such as John Lawrence Tone's critics have argued, or as a counter-insurgency measure whose lethality flowed from administrative failure rather than intent.

sources.title: Reconcentration policy — Wikipedia
Valeriano Weyler — Wikipedia
Valeriano Weyler — The World of 1898, Library of Congress

deathsNote: The range most commonly given in the scholarship, inferred from the gap between the Spanish census of 1887 and the American census of 1899 and from contemporary consular and relief reporting. Lower estimates around 100,000 come from those who attribute more of the population gap to emigration and depressed births; higher figures above 300,000 appear in Cuban nationalist accounts. Deaths were overwhelmingly from starvation and epidemic disease inside the concentration towns rather than from killing.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Weyler's own published orders, American consular dispatches and contemporary relief reporting document the forced concentration, the destruction of rural crops and property, and the starvation inside the towns.
baselineWhat: The population of Cuba at the outbreak of the 1895 war of independence
baselineNote: The Spanish census of 1887 counted 1,631,687 inhabitants and the island is generally estimated at about 1.8 million by 1895; the first US census of 1899 found 1,572,797, a shortfall usually read as the demographic mark of the war and of reconcentracion itself.
shareCaveat: The order applied only to the rural population; measured against the roughly two-thirds of Cubans who lived outside the fortified towns, the share concentrated was considerably higher.

title: Reconcentration in the Philippine-American War
actors: United States Army commanders, notably Brigadier General J. Franklin Bell in Batangas and Laguna, ordered rural populations into guarded 'protected zones' and destroyed crops, livestock and dwellings outside them
peopleRange: Glenn May's study of Batangas, published in Philippine Studies, puts about 300,000 people inside the reconcentration zones of Batangas and Laguna between December 1901 and April 1902; in Batangas town more than 30,000 people were crowded into an area laid out for 3,000. Comparable but smaller zones were used in Marinduque, Samar and elsewhere. The figures come from US Army returns and Bell's own telegraphic circulars, and from parish burial registers.
territoryDesc: Everything outside the zones in Batangas and Laguna was treated as hostile country: standing crops, rice stores, draft animals and houses were burned or confiscated to deny support to Filipino forces.

flows.label: Rural barrios of Batangas -> guarded zones in the town centres

summary: After conventional Filipino resistance collapsed, US commanders adopted the reconcentration method that Spain had used in Cuba, ordering rural inhabitants into guarded zones around garrison towns and treating the emptied countryside as a free-fire and free-forage area. The most systematic application was Bell's campaign in Batangas and Laguna from December 1901, which May estimates confined about 300,000 people. Crowding, poor sanitation and the destruction of food stocks produced epidemics of malaria, dysentery, typhoid and cholera; parish burial registers in Lipa and Batangas town show mortality several times the pre-concentration norm. The US Office of the Historian states that as many as 200,000 Filipino civilians died in the war as a whole from fighting, epidemics and food shortages. The policy, together with the killings that followed the Balangiga attack on Samar, was the subject of a US Senate inquiry and of courts-martial in 1902.
contested: How many died as a direct result of reconcentration is strongly disputed: contemporaries and later writers offered figures from a few thousand to Leon Wolff's 54,000 for Batangas, while May's parish-register analysis supports a far smaller count of excess deaths during the concentration months and attributes most mortality to epidemic disease amplified by crowding.

sources.title: US Department of State, Office of the Historian: The Philippine-American War, 1899-1902
Glenn A. May, 'Was the Philippine-American War a Total War?' / reconcentration in Batangas, Philippine Studies (Ateneo de Manila)
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Philippine-American War

deathsNote: The US Office of the Historian gives over 20,000 Filipino combatant deaths and 'as many as 200,000' civilian deaths for the whole war from fighting, cholera and malaria epidemics and food shortages; some demographic reconstructions run higher and others lower. The share attributable specifically to reconcentration cannot be isolated with confidence: May's burial-register work finds about 1,700 excess deaths in two Batangas parishes during the four concentration months, with far heavier mortality in the cholera months that followed.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Crop and house destruction, the zones themselves, the 'water cure' and summary killings were documented in US Army records, the 1902 Senate Committee on the Philippines hearings and the courts-martial of Generals Smith and Waller.
baselineWhat: The population of Batangas and Laguna provinces, where General J. Franklin Bell's reconcentration order applied most systematically, at the 1903 census
baselineNote: The 1903 Philippine census, the first after the war, counted 257,715 in Batangas and 148,606 in Laguna. Because it was taken after the war's mortality, the pre-war population of the two provinces was higher, and estimates of excess deaths in Batangas alone run to about 100,000. Reconcentration was also imposed in Marinduque, Albay, Samar and parts of Panay, whose populations are not in this baseline.
shareCaveat: The 300,000 figure covers reconcentration across several provinces while the denominator covers only Batangas and Laguna, and the denominator is a post-war census, so the ratio is inflated at both ends.

title: The Boxer War, the Amur Massacres and the Russian Occupation of Manchuria
actors: Russian troops and Cossacks expelled and drowned the Chinese population of Blagoveshchensk and the Amur left bank and occupied Manchuria; the Eight-Nation Alliance occupied Beijing and imposed the Boxer Protocol on the Qing
peopleRange: Some 4,000 Chinese lived in Blagoveshchensk before July 1900 and most of that population was driven into the Amur; the inhabitants of the Qing enclave of the Sixty-Four Villages east of the river, numbering in the tens of thousands, were expelled and their settlements burned. Larger displacement followed the Russian occupation of Manchuria and the Russo-Japanese War fought across it in 1904-05. The figures come from Russian provincial and military records and Qing reporting, and are contested.
territoryDesc: Russia occupied the whole of Manchuria from 1900 and did not withdraw as promised, a refusal that precipitated the Russo-Japanese War; the Qing enclave of the Sixty-Four Villages on the left bank of the Amur, guaranteed by the 1858 Treaty of Aigun, was destroyed and its inhabitants expelled, ending Chinese habitation there.

flows.label: Blagoveshchensk and the Sixty-Four Villages -> forced crossing of the Amur into China

summary: The Boxer rising and the Qing court's declaration of war on the powers in 1900 brought an Eight-Nation expedition to Beijing and a Russian invasion of Manchuria. In early July 1900 the military governor of the Amur province, General Gribskii, ordered the removal of the Chinese population of Blagoveshchensk; the Chinese were marched to the river and driven into it by Cossacks who fired on those who hesitated, and, as the Smith College study records, most drowned in three successive operations. Russian Cossacks and settlers then attacked and burned the villages of the Qing enclave on the left bank, ending Chinese settlement there. The Boxer Protocol of September 1901 imposed a vast indemnity on China, permitted foreign garrisons and required the execution or punishment of officials, and the occupying armies looted Beijing and its palaces. Russia retained Manchuria after the protocol, and the territory then became the battlefield of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05, after which the southern part passed into Japanese control.
contested: The number killed at Blagoveshchensk is uncertain, with figures from about 3,000 to 5,000 and higher in Chinese accounts; Gribskii's motive, whether suspicion of the Chinese or an alleged wish to protect them from the townspeople, was disputed even in the Russian inquiry that followed.

sources.title: Smith College Scholarworks: The Blagoveshchensk Massacre and Beyond (Smith College history publication)
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Boxer Rebellion

deathsNote: Estimates of Chinese deaths in the Blagoveshchensk drownings and the destruction of the Sixty-Four Villages run from about 3,000 to 5,000 in Russian-based accounts and higher in Chinese ones; the Smith College study records that most of the assembled Chinese perished and that thousands of Chinese residents of the city died. Deaths in the Boxer war as a whole, including Chinese Christians killed by Boxers, foreign missionaries, and Chinese killed in the punitive expeditions, run into the tens of thousands and are counted separately.
violenceNote: The forced river crossings, the shooting of those who refused and the burning of the Sixty-Four Villages are documented in Russian provincial and military records and in the Qing protests examined in the Smith College study.
baselineWhat: The Chinese population of Blagoveshchensk and the Sixty-Four Villages East of the Amur, the communities cleared in July 1900
baselineNote: Russian administrative estimates put roughly 30,000-35,000 Chinese and Manchu inhabitants in the Sixty-Four Villages enclave on the Amur left bank, with several thousand more Chinese residents and labourers in Blagoveshchensk itself. The Russian occupation of Manchuria that followed covered a far larger population, put at 8-14 million.

shareCaveat: The denominator covers only the Amur left-bank clearances; the wider Boxer War and the occupation of Manchuria acted on millions more.

title: The Indigenat, Forced Labour and Conscription in French West and Equatorial Africa
actors: The French colonial administration conscripted African men for military service and public works and punished evasion under the indigenat code
peopleRange: French records are partial but give orders of magnitude: about 200,000 West and Equatorial Africans were conscripted as tirailleurs in the First World War and a comparable number in the Second; at least 127,000 men were requisitioned for the Congo-Ocean railway between 1921 and 1934, brought from as far as Chad and Oubangui-Chari; and tens of thousands fled French territory for the Gold Coast, Gambia and Liberia to escape recruitment. No single total for people moved exists.

flows.label: Labour requisitioned from Oubangui-Chari and Chad to the Congo-Ocean railway
Tirailleurs conscripted for service in France

summary: Across French West Africa and French Equatorial Africa the indigenat, a summary disciplinary code applied to colonial subjects, underpinned a system of unpaid prestation labour, forced crop cultivation and requisition for public works. The largest single project, the Congo-Ocean railway from Brazzaville to Pointe-Noire (1921-34), drew workers by force from across Equatorial Africa; Britannica records 15,000-20,000 African deaths and Stanford historian J. P. Daughton puts the toll at at least 20,000, from disease, exhaustion and violence. Military conscription for the two world wars removed roughly 200,000 men in each conflict, and recruitment drives helped provoke the Volta-Bani war of 1915-16, one of the largest anti-colonial revolts in French Africa, suppressed with heavy loss of life. Whole communities fled across borders to British territory to avoid recruiters, a movement colonial officials recorded with alarm. Forced labour was abolished in April 1946 by the law carried by Felix Houphouet-Boigny, and the indigenat was ended the same year.
contested: Death tolls for the Congo-Ocean railway and for the suppression of the Volta-Bani war are estimates from incomplete administrative records and vary substantially between authors.

sources.title: Congo-Ocean Railway (Britannica)
Stanford: deadly railroad project in Congo reveals colonial-era abuses
Indigenat
Volta-Bani War

deathsNote: The range combines 15,000-20,000 railway deaths (Britannica) or at least 20,000 (Daughton) with deaths in the Volta-Bani repression, usually put at tens of thousands including famine deaths, and with unquantified mortality in other labour requisitions. Combat deaths of conscripted tirailleurs in Europe are not included here.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: French administrative records, the 1927 Gide and Londres exposes and Daughton's archival work document requisition of labour, punitive expeditions and village burning during recruitment.

baselineNote: Colonial enumerations, themselves rough head-tax counts, put French West Africa at about 14-15 million and French Equatorial Africa at about 3 million in the 1930s. These counts were made by the same administration that levied the labour and were widely understood to undercount, since registration meant liability.

title: The Second Boer War: Farm Burning and the Concentration Camps
actors: British forces under Lords Roberts and Kitchener burned Boer farms and interned Boer civilians and African labourers in fenced camps in the Transvaal, Orange River Colony, Cape Colony and Natal
peopleRange: Roughly 110,000-120,000 Boer women, children and elderly men and about 115,000-140,000 black Africans passed through the camps; totals differ because the camp registers were kept separately for the two systems and the African camps were poorly recorded. The British National Archives education resource counts forty-five camps for Boer internees and sixty-four for black Africans. The figures rest on British camp returns, the reports of Emily Hobhouse and of the Fawcett Ladies Commission, and later reconstruction of the African camp registers.
territoryDesc: Kitchener's scorched-earth policy destroyed some 30,000 farmsteads and several small towns across the two Boer republics, together with crops and livestock, and the country was divided by blockhouse lines; the republics were annexed as the Transvaal and Orange River Colonies.

flows.label: Burned farms of the Transvaal and Orange Free State -> camps at Bloemfontein and elsewhere

summary: From 1900 the British army answered Boer guerrilla warfare by burning farms and removing the civilian population that supported the commandos into fenced camps served by the railway lines. The National Archives records forty-five camps for Boer internees and sixty-four separate camps for black Africans, many of whom had worked on Boer farms and were held under worse conditions and set to labour. Overcrowding, poor rations, contaminated water and epidemics of measles, typhoid and dysentery killed tens of thousands, most of them children. Emily Hobhouse's 1901 report and the subsequent Fawcett Commission forced improvements and made the camps a scandal in Britain. The camps are widely treated as an early instance of the mass internment of a civilian population by a modern state, though they were not established with the purpose of killing.
contested: The death tolls, particularly for the African camps whose records were far less complete, and the question of whether the high mortality reflected deliberate policy or administrative incompetence, remain disputed.

sources.title: The National Archives (UK), The South African War: How did the British conduct war in 1899-1902?
The National Archives (UK), The South African War: Source 8a (concentration camps)
South African History Online: Deaths in the Black concentration camps of the Second Anglo-Boer War

deathsNote: The UK National Archives states that about 26,000 Boer women and children died and over 14,000 black inmates, mainly of disease and malnutrition; the commonly cited camp registers give 27,927 Boer deaths. Estimates for the African camps range from roughly 14,000 to over 20,000 because those registers are incomplete. Deaths were overwhelmingly from epidemic disease and undernourishment in the camps rather than from killing.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Farm burning, internment and the use of African inmates as labour are documented in British military records and in the reports of Emily Hobhouse and the Fawcett Commission, summarised by the UK National Archives.
baselineWhat: The white republican population of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State at the outbreak of war in 1899
baselineNote: The Transvaal census of 1896 counted about 245,000 whites and the Orange Free State roughly 78,000, giving some 320,000 Boer civilians; the two republics also held around 900,000 black African inhabitants. About 116,000 Boers and a comparable number of Africans were interned, and roughly 28,000 Boers, four-fifths of them children, died in the camps along with an estimated 20,000 Africans.

shareCaveat: Roughly half of the affected figure consists of black Africans interned in separate camps, who are not part of the white republican baseline; against the Boer population alone the internment rate was about a third.

title: The Deportation of the Yaqui to Yucatan
actors: The government of Porfirio Diaz and the Sonoran state authorities deported Yaqui families from the Yaqui river valley to henequen plantations in Yucatan and to Oaxaca, and opened their land to settlers and irrigation companies
peopleRange: Encyclopedia.com records that between 1902 and 1908 approximately 8,000 to 15,000 of some 30,000 Yaqui were deported. Others fled north across the border into Arizona, where Yaqui communities were founded that survive today, or into the Bacatete mountains. The figures rest on Mexican federal and Sonoran state deportation records, plantation registers in Yucatan, and the reporting of the American journalist John Kenneth Turner, whose 1910 book Barbarous Mexico publicised the traffic.
territoryDesc: The fertile bottomlands of the Yaqui river in southern Sonora, which the Yaqui had defended against Spanish and Mexican claims since the seventeenth century, were surveyed, sold to companies and settlers and brought under irrigation as the population was removed; some land was returned when President Lazaro Cardenas created a Yaqui zone in 1937.

flows.label: Yaqui valley, Sonora -> henequen plantations of Yucatan
Flight north across the border to Arizona

summary: After decades of war over the Yaqui river lands, the Diaz government adopted a policy of removing the Yaqui population altogether. Families were rounded up in Sonora, marched or shipped to San Marcos and Veracruz and sent on to Yucatan, where they were sold to henequen planters at a fixed price per head and worked under conditions that contemporaries described as slavery; smaller numbers went to sugar estates in Oaxaca and Morelos. Encyclopedia.com records approximately 8,000 to 15,000 of some 30,000 Yaqui deported between 1902 and 1908. Mortality on the journey and on the plantations was very high, and few returned. Others fled to Arizona, where refugee Yaqui communities were established, or continued armed resistance from the Bacatete mountains, which persisted into the 1920s. The traffic was exposed internationally by John Kenneth Turner in 1910 and was one of the abuses that discredited the Diaz regime; deportations ended with the revolution, and the survivors' descendants were among those who returned to Sonora in the following decades.
contested: The number deported and the number who died are both uncertain, resting on incomplete state records and on campaigning journalism; some accounts describe the policy as genocidal in intent, while others treat it as a labour-supply and land-clearance measure, and no formal determination has been made.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: Yaqui (history, deportation to Yucatan and population figures)
Evelyn Hu-DeHart, 'Development and Rural Rebellion: Pacification of the Yaquis in the Late Porfiriato', Hispanic American Historical Review (Duke University Press)

deathsNote: No count was kept. Contemporary and later accounts describe mortality of a half to two thirds among deportees within a few years, from the journey itself, from tropical disease to which highland and desert people had no resistance, and from the working regime on the henequen estates; applying those rates to the deportation estimates yields several thousand deaths. Turner's contemporary reporting alleged higher mortality still. All figures are inferences rather than records.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: The sale of deportees to planters, the separation of families and the seizure of Yaqui land are documented in Mexican federal and Sonoran records, in Yucatecan plantation accounts and in Turner's contemporary investigation, and are summarised in Hu-DeHart's scholarship.
baselineWhat: The Yaqui population of the Yaqui river valley and the surrounding Sonoran towns around 1900
baselineNote: No reliable enumeration exists because Yaquis avoided Mexican census-takers and many worked outside the valley; historians of the deportations (Hu-DeHart, Padilla Ramos) work with a figure of roughly 20,000-30,000 Yaquis in Sonora at the turn of the century. The upper end is used here and the range should be read as wide.

title: The Deportation of Pacific Islanders from Queensland under the White Australia Policy
actors: The new Commonwealth of Australia ended Pacific Islander labour recruitment and deported most of the Islanders living in Queensland
peopleRange: Commonwealth and Queensland administrative records give reasonably firm figures: about 62,000 Islanders had been brought to Queensland between 1863 and 1904 under the labour trade; the Pacific Island Labourers Act 1901 provided for deportation, and roughly 7,000-7,500 people were removed between 1906 and 1908, with about 1,600-2,500 exempted on grounds of long residence, marriage or land ownership.

flows.label: Deportations to the New Hebrides (Vanuatu)
Deportations to the Solomon Islands

summary: One of the first acts of the Australian federal parliament in 1901 was the Pacific Island Labourers Act, which prohibited further recruitment of Islanders after 1904 and required those in Australia to be deported after 1906, part of the legislative package known as the White Australia policy. Most of those affected were ni-Vanuatu and Solomon Islanders who had been recruited, sometimes by deception or force, for the Queensland sugar industry; some had lived in Australia for thirty years, had married and had children born in the colony. About 7,000 to 7,500 were removed on chartered ships between 1906 and 1908, in some cases landed on islands other than their own, where returnees without kin or language faced real danger; a campaign by churches and Islander petitioners secured exemptions for around 1,600-2,500. Those who stayed became the Australian South Sea Islander community, which the Commonwealth formally recognised as a distinct cultural group in 1994 and Queensland in 2000. The recruitment side of this history is covered by the atlas's entry on the Pacific labour trade; this entry concerns the state expulsion that ended it.
contested: How many of the deportees were returned to their own islands, and how many died as a result, was not systematically recorded at the time.

sources.title: Pacific Island Labourers Act 1901
Australian South Sea Islanders

deathsNote: There was no mass death toll in the deportation itself. Contemporary missionary reports record deaths among returnees landed on unfamiliar islands, but these were not counted.
violenceNote: Commonwealth legislation and deportation records document the compulsory removal of long-resident Islanders and their exclusion from Australia.
baselineWhat: The Pacific Islanders resident in Queensland at Federation
baselineNote: The 1901 Commonwealth census counted about 9,300 Pacific Islanders in Queensland out of roughly 10,000 in Australia, the surviving residue of some 62,000 recruitments to the sugar plantations between 1863 and 1904. Under the Pacific Island Labourers Act 1901 about 7,500 were deported between 1906 and 1908; roughly 1,600-2,500 were exempted and allowed to remain, forming the Australian South Sea Islander community.

title: The Herero and Nama Genocide in German South West Africa
actors: The German colonial army under Lieutenant General Lothar von Trotha drove Herero communities into the Omaheke desert, issued an extermination proclamation, and held Herero and Nama survivors in labour and death camps while expropriating their land and cattle
peopleRange: Most of the Herero population, generally put at 60,000-80,000 before the war, was driven from its grazing lands; survivors were dispersed into camps, into German farms and mines as forced labourers, or across the border into British Bechuanaland, where several thousand remained. Nama communities were deported to camps including Shark Island at Luederitz. The figures rest on German colonial and missionary records and on the 1918 British 'Blue Book' report, and on later demographic reconstruction.
territoryDesc: Herero and Nama land and cattle were confiscated by decree in 1905-07 and redistributed to German settlers and companies; the surviving population was barred from owning cattle or land and placed under pass laws, a dispossession whose effects on land ownership in Namibia persist.

flows.label: Waterberg -> flight east into the Omaheke sandveld and Bechuanaland
Nama prisoners -> Shark Island camp, Luederitz

summary: After Herero communities rose against land seizure and settler abuses in January 1904, German forces defeated them at the Waterberg in August and pursued survivors into the waterless Omaheke, sealing the water holes. On 2 October 1904 von Trotha issued a proclamation ordering that Herero found in German territory be fired upon; a similar campaign followed against the Nama from 1905. Survivors were held in camps, the worst of them on Shark Island at Luederitz, where mortality was extreme, and were set to forced labour on railways, farms and in mines. On 28 May 2021 the German government, in a joint declaration with Namibia, stated that it would officially call the events 'what they were from today's perspective: a genocide', and pledged 1.1 billion euros over thirty years for reconstruction and development, while stating that legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from the declaration. Ovaherero and Nama traditional authorities have rejected the declaration's terms and its exclusion of their representatives from the negotiations.
contested: Germany accepts the description 'genocide' only 'from today's perspective' and denies that it creates a legal obligation to pay reparations, arguing the 1948 Genocide Convention is not retroactive; Ovaherero and Nama representatives dispute both that position and the legitimacy of a settlement negotiated between two governments without them, and the pre-war population figures on which the death estimates rest are themselves debated.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: German-Herero conflict of 1904-07
PBS NewsHour: Germany recognizes colonial killings in Namibia as genocide (28 May 2021)
German Practice in International Law (University of Bonn): Reconciliation Without Reparation - the German-Namibian Joint Declaration
Amnesty International: Namibia - Germany must deliver reparatory justice for its brutal colonial past (2025)

deathsNote: The most commonly cited figures, repeated in the German government's 2021 statements and in press accounts of them, are about 65,000 Herero and at least 10,000 Nama dead; Britannica states that roughly 75 percent of the Herero population died. Lower estimates follow authors who argue the pre-war Herero population was smaller than the German colonial estimate of 80,000; higher ones include deaths in the camps and in flight through the Omaheke. Deaths came from shooting, from thirst and starvation in the desert, and from disease, exhaustion and abuse in the camps.

atrocityFindings.body: Government of the Federal Republic of Germany (Joint Declaration with the Republic of Namibia)
atrocityFindings.finding: Germany acknowledged the 1904-08 events in German South West Africa as, in Foreign Minister Heiko Maas's words, 'what they were from today's perspective: a genocide', and pledged 1.1 billion euros over thirty years, while stating that legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from the declaration.

atrocityFindings.body: German Bundestag
atrocityFindings.finding: In 2004 the German Minister for Economic Cooperation and Development apologised at Waterberg for the killings; the Bundestag debated and rejected reparations claims, and Germany's position that no legal liability arises has been maintained since, a stance analysed and criticised in the Bonn University international-law commentary.

violenceNote: Von Trotha's proclamation, the sealing of the desert water holes, the camps at Shark Island and Windhoek, forced labour and sexual violence against detained women are documented in German colonial and missionary archives and in the 1918 British Blue Book, and are summarised by Britannica and in the scholarship underlying Germany's 2021 declaration.
baselineWhat: The Herero and Nama populations of German South West Africa before the 1904 war
baselineNote: German colonial estimates and the 1985 UN Whitaker Report give roughly 80,000 Herero and 20,000 Nama before the war, though estimates for the Herero range from 60,000 to 100,000. The 1911 colonial census counted about 15,000 Herero and 9,800 Nama, implying that 50-80 per cent of the Herero and about half the Nama died, in the Omaheke desert, in the concentration camps at Shark Island and elsewhere, or in flight to Bechuanaland.
shareCaveat: The affected figure is close to the whole pre-war population because the campaign, the camps and the expropriation of Herero and Nama land and cattle applied to both peoples in their entirety.

title: The Maji Maji Rebellion and its Suppression in German East Africa
actors: German colonial forces and their auxiliaries suppressed a mass rising in southern German East Africa by destroying villages, crops and food stores across the southern highlands and the Rufiji and Kilombero valleys
peopleRange: No count of the displaced exists. German punitive columns burned villages and food stores across a belt of southern Tanganyika from the Rufiji delta to the Songea highlands, emptying whole districts; survivors dispersed into the bush or into neighbouring chiefdoms, and some areas remained depopulated for a generation. Contemporary German military reports and later oral-history collection describe the scale but give no reliable numbers.
territoryDesc: The rising was provoked by forced cotton cultivation, head tax and labour demands; its defeat consolidated German control of the southern districts and was followed by administrative reforms under Governor Rechenberg, while much of the affected country lost its population and its cultivation for years.
summary: From July 1905 a broad rising spread across southern German East Africa, drawing together many peoples around the maji water medicine that fighters believed would turn bullets to water. German forces, heavily outgunned in weapons if not in numbers, met the rising with machine guns and then with a deliberate scorched-earth campaign that destroyed villages, standing crops and grain stores across the affected districts. The resulting famine, rather than combat, caused most of the deaths and continued after the fighting ended in August 1907. Encyclopedia.com summarises the death toll at roughly 250,000, and the campaign is generally treated as one of the deadliest colonial counter-insurgencies in Africa. Germany and Tanzania have since 2017 discussed the return of remains and objects taken during the period, but there has been no formal determination equivalent to the 2021 Namibian declaration.
contested: The death toll rests on colonial estimates and later demographic inference rather than any count, and figures between roughly 75,000 and 300,000 appear in the literature; historians also differ over how far the famine was an intended instrument of policy rather than a consequence of the fighting.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: Maji Maji Revolt, Africa
Tanzania Network (Tanzania-Netzwerk e.V.): Maji Maji war - our demands to Germany

deathsNote: Encyclopedia.com gives about 250,000 deaths, most caused by the famine that followed the German scorched-earth campaign rather than by fighting. The lower bound reflects historians who regard the widely repeated figures as extrapolations from colonial district reports; the higher end includes deaths from famine and disease over several years after 1907. There was no census, and all figures are reconstructions.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The burning of villages and food stores, the resulting famine and the forced cultivation regime that provoked the rising are documented in German colonial military and administrative records and in the oral testimony collected by the Maji Maji Research Project in the 1960s.
baselineWhat: The population of German East Africa at the time of the rising, of which the southern districts affected held a substantial minority
baselineNote: German colonial administrative estimates, the only figures available and themselves rough, put the colony at roughly 7-7.7 million before the First World War. The rising and the famine created by the deliberate destruction of crops and food stores were concentrated in the Matumbi, Ngindo, Pogoro, Bena and Ngoni districts of the south; Iliffe and others estimate 75,000 to 300,000 deaths there, chiefly from starvation.

title: Compulsory Cultivation, Portage and Labour Recruitment in the Belgian Congo
actors: The Belgian colonial state and concession companies compelled Congolese to grow set crops, work in mines and move their villages to roads and cordons
peopleRange: Colonial statistics counted crops and workers rather than displaced people. By the late 1930s roughly 800,000 Congolese households were subject to compulsory cotton cultivation, and the Union Miniere and other companies recruited hundreds of thousands of workers, often from distant districts, under multi-year contracts. Village regrouping along roads and river routes, and the sleeping-sickness cordons of the 1920s-30s, moved an unknown but large number of communities; no total exists.

flows.label: Labour recruitment from Kasai to the Katanga mines

summary: Belgium annexed the Congo Free State in 1908 after the rubber atrocities, but retained compulsion in altered form: the cultures obligatoires required peasants to plant fixed acreages of cotton, rice or palm; the head tax forced entry into the cash economy; and recruitment agencies supplied labour to the Katanga copper mines and Kasai diamond fields under penal contracts. Administrators regrouped villages along roads for tax collection and medical control, and the sleeping-sickness campaigns of the 1920s and 1930s created cordons, screening camps and lazarets that moved and confined populations. Resistance was punished by force, most severely in the Pende revolt of 1931 in Kwilu, suppressed with several hundred deaths. During the Second World War the effort de guerre intensified quotas for copper, rubber and palm oil and lengthened compulsory labour days. Belgium abolished most compulsory cultivation only in the 1950s; the system is far less studied than the Free State period that preceded it.
contested: Belgian colonial historiography long treated the post-1908 period as reformist by contrast with the Free State; recent scholarship stresses the continuity of compulsion, and the balance between the two readings remains disputed.

sources.title: Belgian Congo
Pende revolt

deathsNote: No aggregate exists. Mortality in mine and plantation labour camps was high in the 1910s and 1920s and fell after companies invested in stabilised workforces; deaths in the 1931 Pende repression are usually put in the hundreds. Excess mortality from the compulsory cultivation regime has not been quantified.
violenceNote: Belgian colonial ordinances, company records and the parliamentary and missionary criticism of the interwar years document compulsory cultivation, penal labour contracts and detention for tax and labour default.
baselineWhat: The population of the Belgian Congo at the first colony-wide count
baselineNote: The colonial administration's first full enumeration, in 1924, put the Congo at about 10 million people; by 1958 the count had reached roughly 13.5 million. Under the cultures obligatoires regime peasants were required to plant set acreages of cotton, rice or palm, villages were moved to roadsides and cordons sanitaires for administrative convenience and sleeping-sickness control, and the Union Minière and other companies recruited hundreds of thousands of workers for the Katanga mines under quota systems administered through chiefs.
