title: Japan's Annexation of Korea and the Colonial Land Survey
actors: Japan annexed Korea by treaty in August 1910 and its Government-General carried out a cadastral land survey that transferred large areas to the state, to the Oriental Development Company and to Japanese settlers, displacing Korean cultivators
peopleRange: Displacement was gradual and is measured by emigration rather than by any register: Korean migration to Manchuria and to Japan rose sharply after the land survey of 1912-18, and by the mid-1920s several hundred thousand Koreans were living in Manchuria and well over 100,000 in Japan, with the numbers continuing to grow through the 1930s. Britannica records that dispossessed cultivators either took to slash-and-burn farming in the hills or emigrated to Manchuria and Japan in search of work, and that the Korean communities in those places descend from them. The evidence is the colonial Government-General's own statistics and Japanese and Chinese immigration records.
territoryDesc: The whole of Korea, about 220,000 square kilometres, was annexed and administered by a Government-General under military rule until 1919. The land-survey ordinance required registration of holdings and voided the rights of those who failed to register or whose title was customary or communal; village and clan lands were expropriated as no individual could claim them, and much of the confiscated land was sold cheaply to Japanese buyers and to the Oriental Development Company.

flows.label: Dispossessed Korean cultivators -> labour migration to Osaka and industrial Japan
Northern Korea -> settlement in Manchuria (Jiandao)

summary: Japan established a protectorate over Korea in 1905 and annexed it by the treaty of 22 August 1910, abolishing the Korean state and governing through a Government-General under a military governor. Between 1912 and 1918 a cadastral survey required all landholders to register title; customary, communal and clan holdings, and those of cultivators who did not or could not register, were voided, and Britannica records that many farmers were thereby deprived of their land, much of which was sold cheaply to Japanese purchasers. The dispossessed moved to marginal hill cultivation or emigrated to Manchuria and to industrial Japan, forming the communities from which the present Korean populations of those places descend. The March First Movement of 1919 was suppressed with several thousand deaths and mass arrests, after which Japan replaced military rule with a nominally civil 'cultural policy'. Rice was exported to Japan in growing quantities through the 1920s while Korean per capita consumption fell.
contested: The legal validity of the 1910 treaty is disputed between South Korea, which regards it as void because it was imposed under duress, and Japan, which has maintained that it was validly concluded and was rendered null by the 1965 normalisation treaty; the extent of land actually confiscated by the survey is debated among economic historians.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Korea under Japanese rule
Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Korea as a Colony of Japan, 1910-1945

deathsNote: Annexation and the land survey were not directly lethal. The principal identified death toll of the period is the suppression of the March First Movement of 1919: Japanese official figures gave about 550 deaths, while Korean nationalist sources give roughly 7,500 killed, 16,000 wounded and 46,000 arrested. The gap between the two is a longstanding dispute over the counting of casualties in a nationwide series of demonstrations.
violenceNote: The abolition of Korean statehood and nationality, the voiding of customary land title and the suppression of the Korean language and press in the colonial period are documented in the Government-General's own ordinances and statistics, summarised by Britannica and Columbia's Asia for Educators.
baselineWhat: The population of Korea at the time of the Japanese annexation
baselineNote: The Government-General's household registration counted about 13.1 million in 1910, but registration was incomplete and the figure rose to 17.3 million by 1920 largely through better enumeration; demographers therefore put Korea's actual population in 1910 at roughly 16-17 million. The colonial cadastral survey of 1910-18 registered land titles in ways that transferred large holdings to the state and to the Oriental Development Company.

title: The Mexican Revolution: Displacement and Flight to the United States
actors: The contending armies and factions of the Mexican Revolution, and the federal forces before them, drove civilians from the countryside and across the northern border; the United States admitted large numbers as refugees and briefly interned others
peopleRange: Robert McCaa's demographic reconstruction, using two-sex inverse projection against the 1930 census, puts emigration losses at fewer than 400,000 out of a total demographic cost of about 2.1 million, of which he attributes roughly 175,000-200,000 to war-related refugee movement specifically. Internal displacement was far larger and was never counted; whole districts of Morelos, Chihuahua and Durango were emptied at points in the fighting. The evidence is Mexican and United States census data, US immigration records and McCaa's projections.

flows.label: Chihuahua -> El Paso and the United States border
Morelos villages depopulated in the Zapatista war -> Mexico City and elsewhere

summary: The decade of revolution that followed the fall of Porfirio Diaz in 1911 was fought largely in the countryside and destroyed the security of rural populations across northern and central Mexico. Federal and revolutionary armies alike conscripted men, requisitioned crops and livestock, burned villages and, in Morelos, concentrated the rural population under General Victoriano Huerta's commanders in an effort to deny support to the Zapatistas. Civilians left for the cities, for the mining towns and in very large numbers across the northern border, where United States immigration policy was permissive until the 1920s and where the Mexican-descended population of the south-west grew rapidly. McCaa's reconstruction puts the total demographic cost of the revolution at about 2.1 million, comprising roughly 1.4 million excess deaths, 550,000 lost births and under 400,000 net emigration; earlier writers had attributed a far larger share of the population shortfall to migration. The revolution also produced the 1917 constitution, whose Article 27 provided the legal basis for the agrarian redistribution of the following decades.
contested: The share of Mexico's population shortfall between 1910 and 1930 attributable to deaths as against emigration and lost births was long disputed; McCaa's projections shifted the consensus toward a far higher death figure and a lower migration figure than mid-century accounts had assumed, and the 1921 census is regarded as unreliable.

sources.title: Robert McCaa, 'Missing Millions: The Human Cost of the Mexican Revolution', University of Minnesota Population Center
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mexican Revolution

deathsNote: McCaa's inverse projection gives about 1.4 million excess deaths for 1910-1920, within a total demographic cost of 2.1 million including 550,000 lost births. Older estimates of 1 to 2 million 'deaths' often conflated deaths, lost births and emigration. A large share of the excess mortality was caused by the 1918-19 influenza pandemic, whose effects McCaa's method does not fully separate from those of the fighting, which is the principal reason for the range.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Forced conscription, summary executions, requisitioning and the burning of villages by federal and revolutionary forces alike are documented in Mexican military records, contemporary reporting and the scholarship on the Morelos campaign.
baselineWhat: The population of Mexico at the 1910 census, the last before the Revolution
baselineNote: The Porfirian census of 27 October 1910 counted 15,160,369 people. The 1921 census counted 14,334,780, a fall of about 800,000 despite a decade of natural increase; historical demographers attribute the shortfall to war deaths, the 1918 influenza pandemic, lost births and emigration to the United States.
shareCaveat: The 400,000 figure is the estimated net migration to the United States and does not include the far larger internal displacement within Mexico, which was never counted.

title: The Italian Conquest of Libya and the Deportation of Libyans to Italy
actors: Italy invaded the Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica in 1911, carried out mass reprisals at Tripoli, deported Libyan notables and captives to penal islands in Italy, and from 1923 fought a reconquest of the interior
peopleRange: Approximately 5,000-6,000 Libyans were deported to Italy over the colonial period, of whom roughly 4,000 were transported between 1911 and 1918, according to the study by Francesca Di Pasquale in the International Review of Social History; they were held on Ustica, the Tremiti islands, Favignana, Ponza and in the military prison at Gaeta. Far larger numbers were displaced within Libya by the fighting and by the flight of populations into Egypt, Tunisia and the interior, which was never counted.
territoryDesc: Italy annexed Tripolitania and Cyrenaica by decree in November 1911, a claim the Ottoman Empire conceded at Ouchy in 1912; effective Italian control was limited to the coast until the reconquest campaigns launched in 1923, which by 1926 had taken the Jebel and Fezzan and set the stage for the concentration camps of Cyrenaica after 1929.

flows.label: Tripoli -> deportation to the penal island of Ustica
Cyrenaica -> deportation to the Tremiti islands

summary: Italy declared war on the Ottoman Empire in September 1911 and landed at Tripoli, Benghazi and other coastal points. Rachel Simon, writing in 1914-1918-Online, records that after attacks on Italian forces on 23-26 October 1911 Italy punished the local population severely, killing over 4,000. Alongside the reprisals, Italy deported Libyan notables, suspected resisters and their families to penal islands off the Italian coast: Di Pasquale's study records 900 Libyans on Ustica of whom 127 died, about 17 percent, and 1,366 on the Tremiti islands of whom 437 died, about a third, from cholera, cold and overcrowding. Italian control was largely confined to the coastal towns until the Fascist government launched the reconquest of the interior from 1923, a campaign of columns, aerial bombing and the destruction of encampments that continued past 1926 and led to the mass internment of the Cyrenaican population in camps from 1929, outside the period covered here.
contested: Total Libyan deaths in the whole colonial war from 1911 to 1932 are contested, with Libyan official figures of several hundred thousand and Italian scholarly estimates lower; the figures for the 1911-26 phase alone are not separately established.

sources.title: Francesca Di Pasquale, 'The "Other" at Home: Deportation and Transportation of Libyans to Italy During the Colonial Era (1911-1943)', International Review of Social History (Cambridge University Press)
Rachel Simon, 'Italo-Turkish War 1911-1912', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War

deathsNote: Simon records over 4,000 killed in the Tripoli reprisals of October 1911 alone. Di Pasquale documents mortality of 17 percent on Ustica and about a third on the Tremiti islands among deportees. Totals for Libyan deaths in the fighting, in reprisals and from war-driven famine and displacement between 1911 and 1926 are not established; Libyan accounts of the whole colonial war to 1932 run far higher, and Italian scholarship lower.
violenceNote: The October 1911 reprisals, the deportation of civilians to Italian penal islands and the mortality there are documented in Italian military and prison-administration archives analysed by Di Pasquale and summarised by Simon.
baselineWhat: The population of the Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica at the Italian invasion
baselineNote: Late Ottoman and early Italian estimates put the two provinces together at roughly 800,000 to 1 million in 1911; there was no census. The Italian census of 1936 counted 848,600 Libyans, after a quarter-century of war, famine, flight to Egypt and the Cyrenaica concentration camps.
shareCaveat: The 5,000 refers to Libyans deported to Italian penal islands; the far larger Cyrenaica concentration camps of 1929-1934, which confined perhaps 100,000 people and killed tens of thousands, fall outside this event's dates.

title: The Balkan Wars and their Reciprocal Expulsions
actors: The armies of Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro, and Ottoman forces, drove out and killed civilians of the opposing religion or nationality across Macedonia, Thrace, Kosovo and Epirus as the frontiers moved
peopleRange: Berna Pekesen, writing for the Leibniz Institute of European History, records roughly 400,000 Muslim refugees reaching Ottoman territory after the First Balkan War of 1912 and about 135,000 more after the Second in 1913; Christian populations were also displaced in the opposite direction, notably Bulgarians from Aegean Macedonia and Greeks from areas taken by Bulgaria. The Turkish Coalition of America's annotated map, prepared by Justin McCarthy, puts Muslim deaths and forced exile in the conquered areas of Ottoman Europe together at around 1.5 million and Muslim mortality there at 27 percent, figures that other demographers regard as high. The evidence is Ottoman and Balkan state records, the Carnegie Endowment's 1914 international commission report, and later demographic reconstruction.
territoryDesc: The Ottoman Empire lost almost all its remaining European territory apart from eastern Thrace and Edirne; Macedonia was partitioned between Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria, Albania became independent, and the new borders cut across settlement patterns that had been mixed for centuries.

flows.label: Muslim refugees from Macedonia and Thrace -> Ottoman Istanbul and Anatolia
Bulgarians from Aegean Macedonia and Thrace -> Bulgaria

summary: The Balkan League's victory over the Ottoman Empire in 1912 and the allies' war among themselves in 1913 redrew the map of south-eastern Europe and were accompanied by systematic violence against civilians identified with the losing side. The Carnegie Endowment sent an international commission which reported in 1914 on massacres, village burning and forced conversion by all the belligerents. Pekesen records about 400,000 Muslim refugees moving into Ottoman territory after the first war and roughly 135,000 more after the second, while Christian populations moved in the opposite direction. A Bulgarian-Ottoman convention annexed to the 1913 Treaty of Constantinople provided for a limited exchange of populations along the new border, the first such instrument in the region. The wars established the practice of moving populations to match frontiers that would be applied on a far larger scale in 1923.
contested: The scale of Muslim mortality is the sharpest dispute: Justin McCarthy's demographic reconstruction, widely cited in Turkey, is much higher than the figures used by Greek, Serbian and Bulgarian historiography, and each national tradition emphasises the atrocities committed against its own population.

sources.title: Berna Pekesen, 'Expulsion and Emigration of the Muslims from the Balkans', European History Online (Leibniz Institute of European History, Mainz)
Report of the International Commission to Inquire into the Causes and Conduct of the Balkan Wars (Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 1914)
Turkish Coalition of America: 1912-1913 Balkan Wars - Death and Forced Exile of Ottoman Muslims, annotated map by Justin McCarthy
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Balkan Wars

deathsNote: There is no agreed civilian death toll. McCarthy's reconstruction, cited by the Turkish Coalition of America, implies well over half a million Muslim deaths in the conquered areas, a figure other demographers consider too high because it treats unexplained population shortfalls as deaths rather than as unrecorded migration. Lower estimates count documented massacres and epidemic deaths among refugees. Combatant deaths on all sides added roughly 150,000 more.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: International Commission to Inquire into the Causes and Conduct of the Balkan Wars (Carnegie Endowment for International Peace)
atrocityFindings.finding: The commission's 1914 report found that all the belligerent armies and irregular bands had burned villages, massacred civilians and driven out populations of the opposing religion, and described the wars as having been fought with the object of changing the composition of the population.

violenceNote: Massacres, village burning, forced conversions and the destruction of mosques and churches by all the belligerents were documented on the ground by the Carnegie Endowment's international commission in 1913 and published in its 1914 report.
baselineWhat: The population of the Ottoman European provinces (Rumelia) lost in 1912-1913, across the vilayets of Salonica, Monastir, Kosovo, Scutari, Janina and Adrianople
baselineNote: Ottoman population statistics of 1911-1912 and the reconstructions built on them (Karpat; Justin McCarthy) give roughly 5-6 million inhabitants in the European provinces transferred to Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece, Montenegro and the new Albanian state, of whom something over 2 million were Muslims. Ottoman counts of non-Muslims are widely held to be understated, and Greek, Bulgarian and Serbian counts of the same districts differ sharply.

baselineSources.title: Report of the International Commission to Inquire into the Causes and Conduct of the Balkan Wars (Carnegie Endowment, 1914)

shareCaveat: The affected figure aggregates refugees and expellees of every community — Muslim, Bulgarian, Greek and Serb — moving in opposite directions across the same territory, so it counts movements rather than a single displaced group.

title: The Ikhwan Hijar: Saudi Settlement of the Bedouin
actors: Abdulaziz Ibn Saud's state settled bedouin tribes in religious agricultural colonies and used them to conquer central and western Arabia
peopleRange: There was no census. Standard accounts describe between 120 and 200 hijar settlements founded from 1912, the largest of which, al-Artawiyah and al-Ghatghat, held several thousand people each; totals of 50,000-100,000 settled bedouin are commonly given in the literature on Ibn Saud's state-building, based on British political-agent reporting and later Saudi accounts rather than on registers.
territoryDesc: Ikhwan forces were central to the Saudi conquest of Hail (1921), the Hijaz including Mecca, Medina and Jeddah (1924-25) and the Asir

flows.label: Ikhwan forces from the Najd hijar into the Hijaz

summary: From 1912 Abdulaziz Ibn Saud encouraged and then organised the settlement of nomadic tribes in hijar, agricultural colonies built around wells and a mosque, where Wahhabi missionaries taught a strict doctrine and where the settlers, the Ikhwan, could be mobilised as a standing force. The first and largest was al-Artawiyah; over the following fifteen years between 120 and 200 such settlements were founded. Sedentarisation broke the tribes' seasonal migration and their autonomy, and the Ikhwan became the shock troops of Saudi expansion, taking Hail in 1921 and the Hijaz in 1924-25, where the sack of Taif in September 1924 killed several hundred civilians and prompted flight from Mecca. When Ibn Saud restrained raiding across the new borders with Iraq and Transjordan, the Ikhwan revolted and were defeated at Sabilla in March 1929, after which their leaders were imprisoned and their settlements disarmed. The hijar system nonetheless established the pattern of settled bedouin communities that persisted in the Saudi state.
contested: Numbers of settlements and settlers derive from British political reporting and later Saudi narratives, and the extent to which settlement was voluntary or compelled is described differently in each.

sources.title: Ikhwan
Al Artawiyah
Battle of Sabilla

deathsNote: The settlement programme itself was not lethal. Deaths came in the campaigns it enabled: several hundred civilians at Taif in 1924 by most accounts, and around a thousand at Sabilla in 1929, both figures from British reporting and later histories rather than records.
violenceNote: British political agents' reports and later histories of the Saudi conquest document the killings at Taif in 1924.
baselineNote: No defensible denominator exists. Central Arabia was never enumerated before the Saudi census of 1974, and estimates of the nomadic population of Najd in the 1910s and 1920s are guesses drawn from British political reports; the number of hijar settlements (roughly 200 by the late 1920s) and their estimated 50,000-60,000 residents is better attested than the bedouin population from which they were drawn.

title: The Persecution and Deportation of the Ottoman Greeks (the Greek Genocide)
actors: Ottoman and later Turkish nationalist authorities expelled Greek populations from eastern Thrace and the Aegean coast, deported Pontic and Anatolian Greeks into the interior and into labour battalions, and destroyed Greek communities in Pontus
peopleRange: Roughly 150,000-200,000 Greeks were driven from eastern Thrace and the Aegean littoral in 1913-14, many crossing to Greece and the islands; deportations of Pontic and Anatolian Greeks into the Anatolian interior followed from 1916 and again in 1921-22; and the flight of 1922 removed most of the remainder. Combined with the exchange of 1923 this removed a population that Ottoman and Patriarchate counts placed at between 1.5 and 2.5 million. The figures rest on Ottoman statistics, Ecumenical Patriarchate registers, Greek state refugee records and League of Nations reporting, which differ substantially from one another.
territoryDesc: Greek communities that had lived on the Aegean coast, in Cappadocia, in Bithynia and along the Black Sea for millennia were removed; their churches, schools and property were confiscated or destroyed, and the process was completed by the compulsory exchange of 1923.

flows.label: Pontic Greeks -> deportation marches into the Anatolian interior
Aegean littoral -> expulsion to Lesbos, Chios and mainland Greece, 1914

summary: From 1913 the Ottoman government pursued a policy of removing Greek populations from strategically sensitive coasts and border districts, beginning with a boycott and then expulsions from eastern Thrace and the Aegean littoral in 1914 in which about 150,000 people crossed to Greece. Greek men of military age were conscripted into unarmed labour battalions where, as Tigran Martirosyan records in 1914-1918-Online, conditions were frequently lethal. From 1916 Pontic Greeks were deported inland in columns comparable to the Armenian deportations, and the fighting of 1919-22 in Pontus and western Anatolia destroyed most of the remaining communities. Greek and diaspora institutions and the International Association of Genocide Scholars characterise the whole sequence as genocide; the Hellenic Parliament established 19 May as a day of remembrance for the genocide of the Greeks of Pontus by Law 2193/1994 and extended commemoration to all Greeks of Asia Minor by Law 2645/1998. Turkey rejects the characterisation and treats the events as part of a reciprocal war between states and communities.
contested: Turkey denies that a genocide occurred and points to Muslim deaths and displacement caused by the Greek army's occupation of western Anatolia in 1919-22; the death toll is disputed, with figures from about 300,000 to 900,000 for the Greek population of the Ottoman Empire in this period, and the greek-genocide.net project places the total victim toll of the whole period at 1 to 1.5 million.

sources.title: Greek Genocide Resource Center: A General Overview of the Greek Genocide
Greek Genocide Resource Center: Hellenic Parliament Genocide Recognition, Law 2193/1994
Tigran Martirosyan, 'Labour Battalions (Ottoman Empire/Middle East)', 1914-1918-Online
Assyrian International News Agency: IAGS resolution of December 2007 on the Assyrian and Greek genocides

deathsNote: Estimates of Greek deaths in the Ottoman Empire between 1914 and 1923 range from about 300,000 to 900,000; the greek-genocide.net project puts the toll of the whole period at 1 to 1.5 million. The disagreement turns on the pre-war Greek population, on whether deaths in the 1919-22 war and in the labour battalions are counted, and on whether deaths from hunger and epidemic during deportation are attributed to policy. Turkish accounts give far lower figures and set them against Muslim civilian deaths in the Greek-occupied zone.

atrocityFindings.body: Hellenic Parliament
atrocityFindings.finding: Law 2193/1994 designated 19 May as a day of remembrance for the genocide of the Greeks of Pontus; Law 2645/1998 designated 14 September as a day of remembrance for the genocide of the Greeks of Asia Minor as a whole.

atrocityFindings.body: International Association of Genocide Scholars
atrocityFindings.finding: Resolution of December 2007 holding that the Ottoman campaign against Christian minorities between 1914 and 1923 constituted a genocide against Armenians, Assyrians and Pontian and Anatolian Greeks.

atrocityFindings.finding: Turkey rejects the genocide characterisation of the treatment of Ottoman Greeks and frames the events of 1919-23 as a war of national liberation in which Muslim civilians also suffered mass killing and displacement.

violenceNote: Expulsions, deportation marches, the labour battalions and the destruction of Greek villages and churches are documented in Ottoman records, in Greek and Patriarchate archives, in Allied consular and relief reporting, and in the 1914-1918-Online account of the labour battalions.
baselineWhat: The Greek Orthodox population of the Ottoman Empire on the eve of the First World War
baselineNote: The Ottoman census of 1914 recorded 1,792,206 Greek Orthodox subjects; the Ecumenical Patriarchate's own count was higher, at about 2.5 million, and Western estimates cluster around 1.8-2 million. Scholarly estimates of Greek deaths between 1913 and 1923 range from about 300,000 to 900,000, with the survivors leaving in the 1922 flight and the 1923 exchange.

title: The Natives Land Act of 1913 in South Africa
actors: The Parliament of the Union of South Africa barred Africans from buying or leasing land outside designated reserves and outlawed sharecropping, and white farmers evicted African tenant families across the Orange Free State and the Transvaal
peopleRange: No count was made of those evicted. Sol Plaatje's Native Life in South Africa, written as the Act took effect, describes families with their stock on the roads of the Orange Free State moving between provinces in search of land, and contemporaries and later historians agree that tens of thousands of sharecropping and rent-tenant households were displaced in the first years, with the process continuing for decades. The evidence is legislative, contemporary reportage and later oral history rather than any enumeration.
territoryDesc: The Act scheduled about 7 percent of the land area of the Union as areas in which Africans, then roughly two thirds of the population, could acquire land; the remainder was closed to African purchase or lease. The Native Trust and Land Act of 1936 raised the scheduled share to about 13.5 percent. The 1913 line became the baseline for later restitution claims in post-apartheid South Africa.

flows.label: Evicted sharecropping families of the Orange Free State -> reserves, towns and other provinces

summary: The Natives Land Act, assented to in June 1913, prohibited Africans from buying or leasing land outside scheduled areas amounting to roughly 7 percent of the Union, and specifically outlawed the sharecropping and rent-tenancy arrangements by which many African families farmed on white-owned land. Its anti-squatting provisions were intended to convert independent African cultivators into wage labourers or servants on white farms. Evictions began immediately, most sharply in the Orange Free State, and Sol Plaatje's contemporary account records families and their livestock moving along the roads between provinces in midwinter. The Act did not immediately apply in the Cape, where it conflicted with the qualified franchise, and its full application was worked out over the following decades. It is generally treated as the legal foundation of the reserve system that apartheid later elaborated into the bantustans.
contested: The number of families evicted and the speed with which the Act took effect in different provinces are debated, and some historians argue that it accelerated a process of tenant eviction already under way rather than initiating it.

sources.title: South African History Online: The Natives Land Act of 1913
O'Malley Archive (Nelson Mandela Foundation): 1913 Natives Land Act No 27

deathsNote: There was no significant direct death toll. The Act operated through law, eviction and impoverishment rather than killing, though Plaatje recorded deaths of children and livestock among families forced onto the roads in winter.
violenceNote: The statutory exclusion of Africans from land ownership outside the reserves and the eviction of tenant families are documented in the Act itself, in Sol Plaatje's contemporary account and in the South African History Online summary.
baselineWhat: The African population of the Union of South Africa at the 1911 census
baselineNote: The 1911 census, the first of the Union, recorded 4,019,006 Africans out of a total population of 5,973,394. The Act reserved about 7 per cent of the country's land for African occupation, raised to roughly 13 per cent by the 1936 Native Trust and Land Act, and outlawed sharecropping and labour tenancy on white-owned farms.

title: The East African Campaign: Conscripted Carriers and Civilian Famine
actors: British, German, Belgian and Portuguese forces conscripted African porters for the East African campaign and requisitioned food and livestock across British East Africa, German East Africa, Nyasaland and Mozambique
peopleRange: The British Carrier Corps and its counterparts recruited or conscripted very large numbers of African men across East and Central Africa; Mahon Murphy, writing in 1914-1918-Online, records that no fewer than 95,000 carriers died, around 10 percent of the total manpower used, which implies an order of a million men moved away from their homes for military transport. Numbers rest on British military labour returns, which were themselves incomplete, and on colonial district reports.
territoryDesc: German East Africa was occupied by British, Belgian and Portuguese forces during the campaign and divided after the war under League of Nations mandates: Tanganyika to Britain, Ruanda-Urundi to Belgium, and the Kionga triangle to Portugal.

flows.label: Recruitment districts of British East Africa and Nyasaland -> campaign lines in German East Africa

summary: The four-year campaign in East Africa was fought across country without roads or railways, so both sides moved supplies on the heads of conscripted African porters. Recruitment was formally voluntary in places and openly compulsory in others, and men were taken from their farms for long periods, often far from home. Murphy records that no fewer than 95,000 carriers died, about 10 percent of the manpower used, overwhelmingly from dysentery, malaria and exhaustion rather than combat, with the influenza pandemic that reached the region in October 1918 adding heavily to the toll. The removal of adult labour and the requisitioning of food and livestock produced serious famine in parts of German East Africa, Kenya and Nyasaland in 1917-18. Civilian mortality is not reliably known and is usually estimated at several hundred thousand across the region.
contested: Civilian deaths from the famine and epidemics that accompanied the campaign are not counted anywhere and estimates vary by an order of magnitude; the extent to which carrier recruitment was voluntary is also disputed between colonial records and later oral history.

sources.title: Mahon Murphy, 'Carrier Corps', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Peter Gatrell, 'Refugees', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War

deathsNote: The lower figure is Murphy's count of carrier deaths in 1914-1918-Online, which he describes as a minimum drawn from British military records; the upper end includes civilian deaths from the war-driven famine and the 1918-19 influenza in the campaign zone, which no administration counted and which historians reconstruct only in outline. Deaths were caused by disease, exhaustion and hunger rather than by killing.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Compulsory carrier recruitment and the requisition of food and livestock are documented in British, German and Belgian military and colonial records, summarised by Murphy in 1914-1918-Online.
baselineWhat: The African population of the territories from which carriers were conscripted and food requisitioned
baselineNote: Contemporary colonial estimates give roughly 7.5 million for German East Africa, 2.5-4 million each for British East Africa and Uganda, about 1.2 million for Nyasaland, and several million more in Northern Rhodesia and Portuguese East Africa. All are administrative estimates rather than censuses and carry wide margins.
shareCaveat: The 1 million is usually the number of carriers conscripted across the campaign; civilian famine and epidemic deaths caused by requisitioning and the removal of male labour, often put at several hundred thousand, are additional.

title: The Internment of Enemy Aliens in the First World War
actors: Britain, Germany, France, Russia, Austria-Hungary, Canada, Australia, the United States and others interned resident civilians of enemy nationality and other groups judged suspect
peopleRange: Matthew Stibbe, writing in 1914-1918-Online, records that between 1914 and 1920 the European belligerents interned more than 400,000 enemy aliens, and that counting enemy aliens together with other suspect groups as many as 800,000 civilians in Europe experienced some form of internment during the war and its aftermath, with a further 50,000-100,000 non-combatants interned in the rest of the world. National figures include over 32,000 civilians interned in Britain in 1914-19, German civilian detainees rising from 48,513 in June 1915 to 111,879 in October 1918, about 6,890 interned in Australia, and about 2,300 held as dangerous enemy aliens in the United States. The figures come from national internment administrations and Red Cross inspection records.

flows.label: London and British cities -> Knockaloe camp, Isle of Man
Ukrainian and other Austro-Hungarian subjects in Canada -> internment camps including Castle Mountain and Spirit Lake

summary: The First World War produced the first systematic mass internment of civilians by modern states on grounds of nationality. Britain interned over 32,000 German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman civilians, the largest camp being Knockaloe on the Isle of Man, which held over 20,000 men; Germany's civilian detainee population rose to nearly 112,000 by October 1918, including deported Belgian and French civilians. Canada interned 8,579 people under the War Measures Act, the great majority of them Ukrainians and other subjects of Austria-Hungary, and required a further 80,000 to register and report; internees were set to labour in national parks and on railways. Australia interned about 6,890 and deported up to 6,150 in 1919. Naturalised citizens, women and children were caught up in the systems, and many internees lost businesses and homes, with property confiscated or sold under enemy-property legislation. Camps were generally not lethal, but prolonged confinement produced the condition contemporaries called barbed-wire disease. Canada formally acknowledged the injustice of its internment operations and in 2005 established a recognition fund.
contested: Whether internment was a genuine security measure or a response to press-driven public hostility is debated, and the extent to which internees' confiscated property was ever restored is contested in several countries.

sources.title: Matthew Stibbe, 'Enemy Aliens and Internment', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Colin Holmes, 'Knockaloe, 1914-1918: Civilian Internment in Wartime', Historical Human Rights Atlas (Leibniz Institute of European History, Mainz)
Canadian War Museum: 'Enemy Aliens' - The Internment of Ukrainian Canadians
Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21: Enemy Aliens - Internment in Canada 1914-1920

deathsNote: There was no large death toll in most Allied and Central Power civilian camps; deaths were from illness, accident at forced labour and, in a small number of cases, shooting by guards. Mortality was far higher in Ottoman and Russian internment and among civilians deported into labour by Germany, which are treated in the entries on those events.

atrocityFindings.body: Government of Canada / Parliament of Canada
atrocityFindings.finding: Canada acknowledged the injustice of the First World War internment operations, and the Internment of Persons of Ukrainian Origin Recognition Act of 2005 established a fund to commemorate and educate about the internment of 8,579 people under the War Measures Act.

violenceNote: Detention without charge on grounds of nationality, compulsory labour in Canadian camps and the confiscation of enemy property are documented in national internment records and summarised by Stibbe and by the Canadian War Museum.
baselineWhat: The resident enemy-alien civilian populations of the belligerent states in 1914
baselineNote: No aggregate denominator was ever compiled. Internment figures themselves are reasonably well established — Matthew Stibbe and the Internment research literature put the worldwide total of civilians interned at around 800,000 — but the population at risk was made up of enemy-national residents, naturalised subjects and minorities suspected by association, counted differently or not at all in a dozen states with incompatible nationality laws.

baselineSources.title: Civilian internment in the First World War — Wikipedia

title: The German Invasion and Occupation of Belgium and Northern France
actors: The German army invaded neutral Belgium and northern France in August 1914, executed civilians during the advance, and from 1916 deported Belgian and French civilians to Germany and to labour battalions behind the front
peopleRange: Michael Amara, writing in 1914-1918-Online, records that the German invasion between August and October 1914 caused more than 1.5 million Belgian civilians to flee, of whom about 1 million reached the Netherlands by October 1914 and around 200,000 reached Great Britain; the number in France rose to 325,000 by November 1918, and roughly 600,000 Belgians, about 8 percent of the population, spent the war abroad. Figures come from Belgian, Dutch, British and French relief and registration records.
territoryDesc: Almost all of Belgium and ten departments of northern France were placed under German military government for four years; the invasion route saw the deliberate destruction of Louvain's university library, Dinant, Aarschot and other towns, and the occupied zone was systematically stripped of machinery, livestock and raw materials.

flows.label: Antwerp and the Belgian interior -> the Netherlands, October 1914
Belgian coast -> Britain
Deportation of Belgian workers to Germany, 1916-17

summary: The German invasion of neutral Belgium in August 1914 was accompanied by mass executions of civilians in reprisal for alleged franc-tireur resistance, and by the burning of Louvain, Dinant and other towns; roughly 6,000 Belgian and French civilians were killed in these episodes. More than 1.5 million Belgians fled, most crossing into the Netherlands during the siege of Antwerp in October 1914, and some 600,000 remained abroad for the duration. From October 1916 to February 1917, after voluntary recruitment failed, around 60,000 Belgians were deported to Germany to work in the war economy, a measure abandoned in early 1917 after international protest and practical failure; compulsory labour battalions continued in the occupied zones of France and Belgium. The occupation regime requisitioned food and industrial plant, and Belgium depended for its subsistence on the Commission for Relief in Belgium. The deportations and the 1914 killings were among the principal charges in Allied war-crimes lists at the end of the war.
contested: The 1914 killings were contested at the time between German claims of civilian resistance and Allied accounts of unprovoked reprisal; later historical work has largely rejected the franc-tireur justification, though the death totals for individual towns are still refined.

sources.title: Michael Amara, 'Refugees (Belgium)', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Larissa Wegner, 'Occupation during the War (Belgium and France)', 1914-1918-Online

deathsNote: About 6,000 Belgian and French civilians were killed in the reprisal executions of August-September 1914, a figure established by John Horne and Alan Kramer from German and Belgian records. The upper bound adds deaths among deported workers, deaths from undernourishment during the occupation and civilian deaths under bombardment, which are not separately counted.
violenceNote: The 1914 reprisal executions, the burning of Louvain and its library, and the 1916-17 labour deportations are documented in German and Belgian military and administrative records and summarised in the 1914-1918-Online articles by Amara and Wegner.
baselineWhat: The population of Belgium in 1914
baselineNote: Belgium's population was about 7.6 million in 1914, per the pre-war national statistics. The occupied departments of northern France added roughly 2 million more people under the same regime, so the total population subject to the occupation was closer to 9.6 million.

baselineSources.title: German occupation of Belgium during World War I — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: Most of the 1.5 million who fled in the autumn of 1914 returned within months once the front stabilised; the roughly 120,000 Belgians and French deported for forced labour from 1916 were a much smaller and differently constituted group.

title: Japan's South Seas Mandate and Wartime Displacement in Micronesia
actors: Japan seized Germany's Micronesian colonies, settled them heavily under a League of Nations mandate, and in wartime conscripted, relocated and interned islanders across the western Pacific
peopleRange: Composite, and each element is separately documented. The 1939 census of the Nan'yo mandate recorded 77,257 Japanese, Korean and Okinawan settlers against 51,723 indigenous islanders out of 129,104 inhabitants; on Saipan almost 90 per cent of the population was Japanese by 1937. Wartime removals include the deportation of about 1,200 Nauruans to Chuuk in 1943, of whom 463 died before the survivors returned in 1946, and the forced march and internment of roughly 18,000 Chamorros on Guam into camps at Manenggon and elsewhere in July 1944 — both figures from postwar Australian, Nauruan and United States military records. Islanders across the Carolines and Marshalls were moved off land taken for airfields and fortifications; those numbers were not systematically recorded.
territoryDesc: The Caroline, Marshall and Northern Mariana Islands, held by Japan from 1914 under a Class C League of Nations mandate from 1920 and administered as the Nan'yo-cho; after 1945 they passed to the United States as the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. On Guam, the United States after 1944 condemned a large share of the island's land — by some accounts around two thirds at its peak — for military use.

flows.label: Nauruans deported by Japan to Chuuk, 1943
Chamorros forced-marched into the Manenggon internment camp, Guam, July 1944

summary: Japan occupied Germany's Micronesian possessions in 1914 and administered them from 1920 as a League of Nations mandate, developing sugar, phosphate and fisheries and settling so many Japanese, Okinawan and Korean migrants that by 1939 settlers outnumbered indigenous islanders across the mandate and made up nine tenths of the population of Saipan. Islander land was alienated to settlers and to the colonial administration. During the Pacific War the administration conscripted islanders for labour on airfields and fortifications, moved communities away from military installations, and in 1943 deported about 1,200 Nauruans to Chuuk, where 463 died of starvation and bombing before the survivors were repatriated in 1946. On Guam, occupied by Japan from December 1941, the Chamorro population was subjected to forced labour and, as United States forces approached in July 1944, marched inland and interned in camps at Manenggon and elsewhere; between about 1,000 and 2,000 Chamorros are estimated to have died under the occupation. After the war the United States took much of Guam's land for bases, a grievance that produced land-return legislation from the 1970s. Micronesia was absent from the atlas apart from the Marshall Islands nuclear relocations.
contested: Responsibility and redress for wartime treatment of islanders: Guam's Chamorros pursued United States compensation for decades, obtained in the 2016 Guam World War II Loyalty Recognition Act, while claims against Japan have generally been treated by Tokyo as settled by the postwar peace instruments — a position disputed by claimant groups.

sources.title: South Seas Mandate — Wikipedia
Battle of Guam (1944) — Wikipedia
Manenggon — Wikipedia
Chamorro people — Wikipedia
Nauruans — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The range aggregates the 463 Nauruan deaths on Chuuk, recorded in Australian and Nauruan administration records, with estimates of 1,000-2,000 Chamorro deaths under the Japanese occupation of Guam, drawn from postwar United States Navy investigations and the Guam War Claims Review Commission. Islander deaths from forced labour, starvation and bombing elsewhere in the mandate were not systematically counted and are excluded.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Postwar United States Navy war crimes investigations on Guam and Australian administration records on Nauru document the forced labour, internment, beheadings and massacres of Chamorros and the deaths of deported Nauruans.
baselineWhat: The indigenous Micronesian population of the islands Japan took over as the South Seas Mandate
baselineNote: The first Japanese census of the mandate, in 1920, counted 48,505 islanders. Japanese settlement then transformed the territory: by the early 1940s roughly 96,000 Japanese, Okinawan and Korean settlers lived in the mandate, outnumbering the indigenous population by nearly two to one.

baselineSources.title: History of the Federated States of Micronesia — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The affected figure includes both islanders relocated, conscripted or interned and Japanese settlers displaced by the fighting and later repatriated, so the numerator draws on a wider population than the indigenous denominator.

title: The Russian Empire's Wartime Deportation of Jews, Germans and Others
actors: The Russian army command deported Jews, ethnic Germans, Poles, Roma and others from the western borderlands and from occupied Galicia into the interior of the empire as suspect populations
peopleRange: Peter Gatrell, writing in 1914-1918-Online, gives roughly 420,000 German colonists expelled from the Polish provinces in December 1914, about 600,000 Russian Jews displaced, mainly in spring 1915, some 300,000 civilian foreign citizens deported, about 120,000 civilians deported by the Russian occupation regime in Galicia and Bukovina, and about 30,000 East Galician Jews deported to the interior. The total refugee population of the empire reached 4.9 million by January 1917 on official data, and over 6 million on Siobhan Peeling's revised estimate; deportees are a subset of that. Figures come from army orders, Tatiana Committee and zemstvo relief registration, and later scholarship.
territoryDesc: The deportations emptied strips of the western borderlands of populations judged unreliable, and were accompanied by scorched-earth destruction during the retreat of 1915; the Pale of Settlement was effectively broken as Jews expelled from the front zone were permitted to settle in the interior.

flows.label: Western borderlands -> deportation into the Russian interior
Occupied Galicia -> deportation to the Volga provinces

summary: From the first months of the war the Russian high command treated whole categories of the population of the western borderlands as security risks and ordered their removal. Ethnic Germans were expelled from the Polish provinces in December 1914, Jews were driven from the front zone in large numbers in the spring and summer of 1915 amid hostage-taking and army pogroms, and the Russian occupation administration in Galicia and Bukovina deported civilians including Ukrainian Greek Catholic clergy and Jews into the interior. Gatrell puts German colonists expelled at about 420,000 and Jews displaced at about 600,000. The deportations were carried out at short notice, often with the destruction of property, and combined with voluntary flight to create a refugee population of nearly 5 million by January 1917, which strained the empire's administration and contributed to the political crisis of 1917. One consequence was the effective collapse of the Pale of Settlement, as expelled Jews were permitted to live in interior provinces previously closed to them.
contested: The line between deportation and flight is often impossible to draw in the Russian records, so estimates of how many were forcibly removed rather than displaced by the fighting vary widely.

sources.title: Peter Gatrell, 'Resettlement', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Siobhan Peeling, 'Refugees (Russian Empire)', 1914-1918-Online

deathsNote: No reliable death toll exists for the deportations as such. Mortality among deportees and refugees from typhus, cholera and exposure during transport and in reception points was substantial and is documented in relief agency reporting, but was never counted separately from wartime civilian mortality generally.
violenceNote: Deportation orders, hostage-taking from Jewish communities and property destruction during the 1915 retreat are documented in Russian army orders and relief-agency records analysed by Gatrell and Peeling.
baselineWhat: The Jewish and ethnic German populations of the Russian Empire, concentrated in the western borderlands from which the army deported
baselineNote: The 1897 imperial census counted 5.2 million Jews, almost all confined to the Pale of Settlement, and about 1.8 million ethnic Germans. By 1914 these had grown to roughly 5.5 and 2.4 million. Poles, Roma, Muslims and others were also deported and are not in this denominator.
shareCaveat: The deportations fell on specific frontline provinces rather than on these communities empire-wide; in Kurland, Kovno and occupied Galicia the share removed was far higher than the ratio shows.

title: The Sayfo: The Assyrian, Syriac and Chaldean Genocide
actors: Ottoman forces, gendarmes and allied Kurdish tribal irregulars destroyed Assyrian, Syriac and Chaldean communities in Hakkari, Tur Abdin, Diyarbekir, Urmia and the Bohtan valleys
peopleRange: Whole communities of the Hakkari mountains fled into Persia and then, with the Russian collapse in 1917-18, retreated some 500 kilometres south to British lines, where about 50,000 survivors were placed in the Baquba refugee camp near Baghdad in 1918; others fled from Tur Abdin into Syria. There was never a census of the Ottoman Syriac population, so both the pre-war base and the number displaced rest on church registers, missionary counts and British and Russian military reporting.
territoryDesc: The Assyrian tribal districts of Hakkari were emptied and never resettled by their inhabitants; survivors were resettled in British-administered Iraq and in Syria, and the historic monasteries and villages of Tur Abdin lost most of their population.

flows.label: Hakkari -> flight to Urmia in Persia, 1915
Urmia -> retreat to British lines and the Baquba camp, 1918

summary: Alongside the deportation of the Armenians, Ottoman forces and allied tribal irregulars attacked the Syriac-speaking Christian communities of south-eastern Anatolia and north-western Persia from 1914, in events remembered in Syriac as the Sayfo, the sword. The mountain tribes of Hakkari were driven out in 1915 and took refuge around Urmia; the villages of Tur Abdin and the Diyarbekir province were attacked and their inhabitants killed or dispersed. When Russian forces withdrew in 1917-18 the surviving population made a long retreat southward under attack, and about 50,000 were placed by the British in the Baquba camp in Mesopotamia. Britannica states that upwards of 250,000 Assyrians were killed during the First World War. The International Association of Genocide Scholars resolved in December 2007, by 83 percent of voting members, that the Ottoman campaign against Christian minorities between 1914 and 1923 constituted a genocide against Armenians, Assyrians and Pontian and Anatolian Greeks; Turkey rejects that characterisation.
contested: Turkey denies that a genocide took place; the death toll rests on estimates of a pre-war population that was never counted, with figures from about 150,000 to 300,000 in circulation, and some historians treat the killings as part of the Armenian genocide rather than as a distinct event.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Assyrian Genocide
International Association of Genocide Scholars: Resolutions (including the 2007 resolution on the Assyrian and Greek genocides)
Assyrian International News Agency: International Genocide Scholars Association Officially Recognizes Assyrian, Greek Genocides (December 2007)
Assyrian International News Agency: Text of the Assyrian, Armenian and Pontic Greek genocide resolution as adopted by Sweden (2010)

deathsNote: Britannica gives upwards of 250,000 Assyrians killed during the First World War and notes the figure may not include all victims. The range reflects disagreement over the pre-war Syriac population of the Ottoman Empire and Persia and over whether deaths from starvation and epidemic during the 1918 retreat are counted. Deaths came from massacre, from exposure and hunger during flight, and from epidemics in the refugee concentrations at Urmia and Baquba.

atrocityFindings.body: International Association of Genocide Scholars
atrocityFindings.finding: Resolution adopted in December 2007 with 83 percent support, holding that the Ottoman campaign against Christian minorities of the Empire between 1914 and 1923 constituted a genocide against Armenians, Assyrians and Pontian and Anatolian Greeks, and calling on Turkey to acknowledge it and apologise.

atrocityFindings.body: Riksdag of Sweden
atrocityFindings.finding: On 11 March 2010 the Swedish parliament adopted a resolution recognising the 1915 killings of Armenians, Assyrians/Syriacs/Chaldeans and Pontic Greeks as genocide and calling on Turkey to come to terms with its history.

atrocityFindings.body: Republic of Turkey, Ministry of Foreign Affairs
atrocityFindings.finding: Turkey rejects the genocide characterisation of the 1915 events, including as applied to Christian communities other than the Armenians, and treats parliamentary recognitions as political rather than historical or legal determinations.

violenceNote: Massacres, abductions of women and children, and the destruction of villages, churches and monasteries are documented in Syriac chronicles and survivor testimony, in Russian, British and American consular and military reporting, and in the material assembled for the 2007 IAGS resolution.
baselineWhat: The Assyrian, Syriac and Chaldean population of the Ottoman Empire and the adjoining Persian border districts in 1914
baselineNote: Ottoman censuses recorded these communities by millet rather than ethnicity and undercounted them; church registers and the estimates used by Gaunt and other historians of the Sayfo put the total at roughly 500,000-620,000 across Hakkari, Tur Abdin, Diyarbekir, Urmia and Mosul province. Assyrian organisations give higher pre-war figures, Turkish official accounts lower ones.
shareCaveat: Both numerator and denominator are contested: death estimates for the Sayfo range from about 150,000 to 300,000 and the pre-war population is itself disputed, so the resulting share carries an uncertainty of tens of percentage points.

title: The Armenian Genocide
actors: The Ottoman government under the Committee of Union and Progress arrested the Armenian leadership, deported the Armenian population of Anatolia into the Syrian desert, and confiscated its property; killings were carried out by gendarmes, the Special Organisation and irregulars
peopleRange: Peter Gatrell, writing in 1914-1918-Online, puts the number of Armenians deported at about 1.2 million and records that of roughly 850,000 deportees only some 300,000 were alive in early 1916. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum describes deportations from the six eastern provinces spreading to virtually the whole empire. The figures rest on Ottoman administrative and interior ministry records, German and American diplomatic reporting, missionary and Near East Relief records, and the postwar Ottoman courts-martial files, and are reconstructed rather than counted.
territoryDesc: Armenian property, land, businesses and churches were confiscated under the 'abandoned properties' laws of 1915 and after and redistributed to Muslim settlers, refugees and the state; the historic Armenian population of Anatolia was effectively removed, and Armenian communal and religious buildings were destroyed or converted over the following decades.

flows.label: Erzurum and the eastern provinces -> death marches to Deir ez-Zor on the Euphrates
Cilicia and Maras -> Aleppo transit and the Syrian desert camps
Van and Bitlis survivors -> Russian Armenia and Yerevan

summary: On 24 April 1915 the Ottoman authorities arrested several hundred Armenian intellectuals and community leaders in Constantinople, and from May the government ordered the deportation of the Armenian population of the eastern provinces, a policy given legal form by the Temporary Law of Deportation of 27 May 1915 and extended over the following months to almost the whole empire. Columns of deportees were marched south through Anatolia to holding camps along the Euphrates around Deir ez-Zor; convoys were robbed, women and children were abducted, and large numbers were killed outright or died of hunger, thirst and disease. Ronald Grigor Suny, writing in 1914-1918-Online, gives a conservative estimate of 600,000 to 1 million killed or dead on the marches; the USHMM states that at least 664,000 and possibly as many as 1.2 million died; the Armenian National Institute and many states use the figure of 1.5 million for the period 1915-1923. Postwar Ottoman courts-martial in 1919-20 convicted leading Unionists in absentia. The Republic of Turkey rejects the characterisation of the events as genocide, describing them as wartime relocation with heavy mortality on all sides, while more than thirty states, the European Parliament, the International Association of Genocide Scholars and, since 2019 and 2021, the United States Congress and President have recognised them as genocide.
contested: Turkey disputes both the characterisation as genocide and the higher death tolls, arguing that the deportations were a security measure in wartime and that Muslim civilians died in comparable numbers; Armenian institutions and most genocide scholars hold that the deportations were intended to destroy the Armenian population, and the death toll itself ranges in serious scholarship from about 600,000 to 1.5 million.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: The Armenian Genocide (1915-16) in Depth
Ronald Grigor Suny, 'Armenian Genocide', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Peter Gatrell, 'Resettlement', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Armenian Genocide
Armenian National Institute: Frequently Asked Questions about the Armenian Genocide
Armenian National Institute: United States House of Representatives Resolution 296 (2019)

deathsNote: Suny's article for 1914-1918-Online gives a conservative range of 600,000 to 1 million and favours 600,000-800,000 killed; the USHMM gives at least 664,000 and possibly 1.2 million; the Armenian National Institute and the recognising resolutions of many parliaments use 1.5 million for 1915-1923. The disagreement turns on the pre-war Armenian population, which Ottoman censuses and the Armenian Patriarchate counted differently, on whether deaths after 1918 and forced converts are included, and on how deaths from starvation and disease during deportation are classified. Turkish official accounts give far lower figures and attribute the deaths chiefly to wartime conditions.

atrocityFindings.body: Ottoman courts-martial, Constantinople
atrocityFindings.finding: Special military tribunals convened in 1919-20 tried members of the Committee of Union and Progress for the deportation and massacre of Armenians; Talat, Enver and Cemal and others were convicted in absentia and sentenced to death.

atrocityFindings.body: International Association of Genocide Scholars
atrocityFindings.finding: Resolved in 1997 that the Ottoman campaign against the Armenians constituted genocide, and in December 2007 that the Ottoman campaign against Christian minorities between 1914 and 1923 constituted a genocide against Armenians, Assyrians and Pontian and Anatolian Greeks.

atrocityFindings.body: United States House of Representatives
atrocityFindings.finding: H.Res.296, adopted 29 October 2019 by 405 votes to 11, affirmed that it is US policy to commemorate the Armenian Genocide and to reject efforts to associate the US government with its denial.

atrocityFindings.body: Republic of Turkey, Ministry of Foreign Affairs
atrocityFindings.finding: Turkey rejects the genocide characterisation, describing the 1915 events as a wartime relocation carried out under military necessity in which Muslims and Armenians alike suffered heavy losses, and has proposed a joint historical commission rather than accepting parliamentary determinations.

violenceNote: These forms are documented in Ottoman interior ministry and courts-martial records, in German and American consular reporting collected by Ambassador Morgenthau and by Johannes Lepsius, and in Near East Relief and missionary archives, and are set out in the USHMM and 1914-1918-Online accounts.
baselineWhat: The Armenian population of the Ottoman Empire on the eve of the genocide
baselineNote: The figure is contested and politically charged. The Armenian Patriarchate's 1913-14 count gave about 2.1 million in some 2,925 towns and villages; Ottoman government statistics gave about 1.2-1.3 million; Arnold Toynbee and most later historians settle between 1.6 and 2.1 million. Recent scholarship generally states that around two million Armenians lived in Ottoman territory within a total Anatolian population of 15-17.5 million.
shareCaveat: The denominator is itself disputed — Ottoman figures are roughly 40 per cent lower than Armenian ones — so the share killed swings between about two-thirds and nearly the whole population depending on which count is used.

title: The Great Famine of Mount Lebanon and Ottoman Syria
actors: The Allied naval blockade of the eastern Mediterranean, Ottoman requisitioning and a land blockade imposed by the Fourth Army commander Cemal Pasha, and a locust invasion in 1915, together destroyed the food supply of Mount Lebanon and Syria
peopleRange: Roughly a third of the population of Mount Lebanon emigrated during and immediately after the famine, principally to Egypt, the Americas and West Africa, and many more moved from the mountain to Beirut and the coastal towns in search of food. The figures rest on Ottoman and French Mandate administrative estimates, missionary and consular reporting and church records; there was no census.

flows.label: Mount Lebanon villages -> Beirut and emigration overseas

summary: From 1915 the population of Mount Lebanon and the Syrian interior faced the combined effect of the Allied blockade of the eastern Mediterranean, the Ottoman army's requisitioning of grain, pack animals and transport for the Sinai and Palestine fronts, a land blockade of the largely Maronite mountain imposed by Cemal Pasha, and a locust plague that destroyed the 1915 crops across Syria and Palestine. Prices rose beyond reach, relief was obstructed, and mortality was extreme: contemporary and later estimates put deaths in Mount Lebanon at 150,000-200,000, roughly a third of its population, giving the district what is often described as the highest per capita wartime mortality of any bounded territory in the First World War, with a further large toll in the Syrian interior. Another third of the population emigrated. The famine is a central event in modern Lebanese memory and contributed to the case for a separate Lebanese entity under the French Mandate.
contested: Responsibility is disputed between accounts emphasising the Allied blockade, accounts emphasising Ottoman requisitioning and Cemal Pasha's deliberate isolation of the mountain, and accounts emphasising the locusts and the collapse of the silk economy; the death toll rests on estimates rather than registration.

sources.title: Middle East Monitor: Remembering the Great Famine of Mount Lebanon (1914-1918)
Libnanews: Lebanon History - The Great Famine of Mount Lebanon during the First World War
The National: Lebanon's dark days of hunger - the Great Famine of 1915-18

deathsNote: Estimates for Mount Lebanon itself are 150,000-200,000 dead, about a third of the population, a figure repeated in Lebanese and international accounts and drawn from contemporary missionary, consular and church reporting rather than from registration. Wider estimates for Ottoman Syria as a whole, including Damascus, Aleppo and the interior, run to 300,000-500,000. Deaths were from starvation and the diseases that accompany it.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The blockade, the requisitioning of food and transport and the isolation of Mount Lebanon are documented in Ottoman, French, British and American consular and missionary reporting summarised in the cited accounts.
baselineWhat: The population of the Mutasarrifate of Mount Lebanon on the eve of the First World War
baselineNote: Ottoman administrative counts for the autonomous Mutasarrifate give roughly 400,000-415,000 inhabitants around 1913-14. Estimates of famine deaths in Mount Lebanon run from 100,000 to 200,000, that is a quarter to a half of the population, the highest proportional loss of any territory in the war; for Ottoman Syria as a whole, deaths are put at roughly 500,000.

baselineSources.title: Great Famine of Mount Lebanon — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The 200,000 is a death toll rather than a displacement count, and it is the upper end of a range running from 100,000; against the wider Syrian population the share is much lower.

title: The Serbian Retreat through Albania and the Occupation of Serbia
actors: Austro-Hungarian, German and Bulgarian forces overran Serbia in autumn 1915; the Serbian army, government and large numbers of civilians retreated across the Albanian mountains to the Adriatic, and the occupiers interned civilians and requisitioned food
peopleRange: Mile Bjelajac, writing in 1914-1918-Online, records that about 169,828 soldiers and civilians were evacuated from the Adriatic coast, with roughly 153,000 reaching Allied territory by late 1915; a far larger number set out and did not complete the retreat. Civilians displaced within Serbia by the invasion and by the occupation regimes are not counted. Figures come from Serbian army and Allied evacuation records.
territoryDesc: Serbia was partitioned between Austro-Hungarian and Bulgarian military administrations from late 1915 until 1918; the Bulgarian zone in Macedonia and the Morava valley pursued forcible assimilation, closing Serbian schools and churches and suppressing the 1917 Toplica rising with heavy civilian killing.

flows.label: Kosovo -> retreat through the Albanian mountains to Durres and Vlore
Adriatic ports -> evacuation to Corfu

summary: The combined Austro-Hungarian, German and Bulgarian offensive of October 1915 broke the Serbian front, and rather than surrender the army, the government and a large body of civilians withdrew across the mountains of Albania and Montenegro in winter. Bjelajac describes an ordeal in snow without food, clothing or medical supplies which killed large numbers of soldiers and civilians before the survivors reached the Adriatic; about 169,828 people were evacuated by Allied shipping, most to Corfu, where many more died. Serbia itself was placed under Austro-Hungarian and Bulgarian occupation, with internment of civilians in camps, requisitioning, and, in the Bulgarian zone, a campaign of forcible assimilation and the violent suppression of the Toplica rising in 1917. Bjelajac gives Serbian military losses including 79,000-81,000 dead in captivity, and states that civilian casualties of war and occupation have never been fully established, running to hundreds of thousands from epidemics, famine, camps and reprisals. The Serbian male population fell by between 17 and 30 percent across counties by the 1921 census.
contested: Civilian mortality in Serbia in 1914-18 has never been established and figures used in Serbian, Austrian and Bulgarian historiography differ substantially; the typhus epidemic of 1915 and the deaths of the retreat are variously attributed to war conditions or to the conduct of particular armies.

sources.title: Mile Bjelajac, 'Serbia', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Peter Gatrell, 'Refugees', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War

deathsNote: Serbia's total war losses, military and civilian, are usually put at between 300,000 and over 1 million out of a pre-war population of about 4.5 million, the widest proportional loss of any belligerent. Bjelajac gives 29,249 killed in action, 43,027 dead of wounds and disease in hospital and 79,000-81,214 dead in captivity, and states civilian losses from epidemic, famine, camps and reprisals have never been fully established. The lower bound counts documented military and epidemic deaths; the higher includes contested estimates of civilian mortality.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Reprisal killings of civilians in 1914, internment of Serbian civilians by the occupying powers, requisitioning and the Bulgarian assimilation campaign are documented in Austro-Hungarian and Serbian records and in the neutral expert reports summarised by Bjelajac.
baselineWhat: The population of the Kingdom of Serbia in 1914, including the territories annexed in the Balkan Wars
baselineNote: Serbia's census of 1910 recorded about 2.9 million in the pre-1912 kingdom; the addition of Vardar Macedonia and other Balkan War gains brought the total to roughly 4.5 million by 1914. Serbia's wartime losses, military and civilian, are usually put at 1-1.25 million, among the highest proportional losses of the war.

title: The Central Asian Revolt of 1916 and the Urkun
actors: The Russian imperial government conscripted Central Asians for rear labour service, and after the resulting revolt punitive detachments and Russian settlers killed Kyrgyz and Kazakh communities and drove survivors over the Tien Shan passes into Chinese Turkestan
peopleRange: Estimates of those who fled into Chinese Xinjiang in the winter of 1916-17, an exodus remembered in Kyrgyz as the Urkun, run from about 100,000 to over 300,000, with large numbers dying on the passes and many later returning to a homeland whose pastures had been taken by settlers. The Institute for Security and Development Policy records that tens of thousands died attempting to escape over the mountain passes. The figures rest on Russian provincial and military reporting, Soviet-era estimates and later Kyrgyz and Kazakh demographic reconstruction.
territoryDesc: Land in the Semirechye had already been transferred to Slavic settlers before the revolt, and after its suppression further pasture was confiscated and Kyrgyz communities were pushed off the best land in the Issyk-Kul basin and the Chu valley.

flows.label: Issyk-Kul and Semirechye -> flight over the Tien Shan passes into Chinese Turkestan

summary: On 25 June 1916 the Russian government, exempting Central Asians from military service but needing labour, decreed the conscription of men aged 19 to 43 from Turkestan and the Steppe for rear work on the front. The decree fell on populations already resentful at land seizures for Slavic settlement and at wartime requisitions, and revolt spread through Samarkand, Ferghana, the Semirechye and the Kazakh steppe, with attacks on officials and settlers. Punitive detachments and armed settlers responded with massacres, the burning of encampments and the confiscation of livestock. The Kyrgyz of the Issyk-Kul basin fled over the Tien Shan into Chinese territory in the autumn and winter, and large numbers died of cold, hunger and attack on the passes. The Institute for Security and Development Policy states that about 270,000 Central Asians were killed and that the Kyrgyz lost roughly 40 percent of their population. The revolt and the flight remain politically sensitive: Kyrgyzstan marked the centenary in 2016, and Russian commentators criticised the commemoration.
contested: Death tolls range widely and the Kyrgyz share of the losses is debated; whether the killings amounted to genocide is argued by some Kyrgyz historians and rejected by Russian officials and by others who emphasise the mutual violence between nomads and settlers, and the centenary commemorations in 2016 became a diplomatic irritant.

sources.title: Institute for Security and Development Policy: The Revolt of 1916 in Russian Central Asia
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty: Remembering The Great Urkun 100 Years Later

deathsNote: The Institute for Security and Development Policy gives about 270,000 Central Asians killed by Russian forces, with the Kyrgyz losing roughly 40 percent of their population. Lower estimates of around 100,000-150,000 are used by other historians, who separate deaths in punitive operations from deaths on the flight into China and from later famine, and who note that some of the population loss represents emigrants who did not return rather than deaths. Deaths occurred by killing, by exposure and starvation on the mountain passes, and in the disorder that followed.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The labour conscription decree, the punitive operations, the burning of encampments and the seizure of livestock and pasture are documented in Russian provincial and military records and summarised in the Institute for Security and Development Policy study.
baselineWhat: The indigenous Muslim population of Russian Turkestan and the Steppe oblasts subject to the labour conscription decree
baselineNote: The 1897 imperial census counted about 5.3 million in the Turkestan governorate-general; with continued growth and the Steppe oblasts included, the population liable to the June 1916 labour decree was roughly 7 million. The Kyrgyz of Semirechye, who bore the worst of the reprisals and the flight to China, numbered under a million within that total.
shareCaveat: Losses were extremely concentrated: as much as 40% of the ethnic Kyrgyz population is estimated to have died or fled to China, a far higher share than a ratio against the whole of Turkestan conveys.

title: The Ottoman Deportation of Kurds from Eastern Anatolia
actors: The Ottoman government and army deported Kurdish tribal populations from the eastern provinces westward and southward and dispersed them among Turkish-speaking populations in central and western Anatolia
peopleRange: Estimates are unreliable. Studies of the eastern provinces, principally Ugur Umit Ungor's work for Oxford University Press, describe the deportation of Kurdish tribes from Bitlis, Erzurum, Mus and Palu towards Konya and the south in the winter of 1916, with figures of around 300,000 for that wave and up to 700,000 for the war as a whole appearing in the literature; Ungor stresses that there are no reliable statistics. The evidence is Ottoman interior ministry correspondence and army records rather than any enumeration.
territoryDesc: The policy was part of a wider programme of demographic engineering in eastern Anatolia in which deported Kurds were to be settled in dispersed groups not exceeding a set proportion of the local Turkish population, while Muslim refugees from the Balkans and the Caucasus were settled in the emptied districts.

flows.label: Bitlis, Mus and Erzurum -> deportation to Konya and central Anatolia

summary: As the Russian army advanced into eastern Anatolia in 1916, the Ottoman government ordered the removal of Kurdish tribal populations from the frontier provinces and their resettlement in the Turkish-speaking interior, where they were to be dispersed in small groups so as to assimilate. The deportations were carried out in winter with little provision, and mortality from cold, hunger and epidemic was heavy; an early estimate by Safrastian held that half of those deported died. The policy formed part of a broader programme of population engineering in the region that also encompassed the Armenian deportations and the settlement of Muslim refugees, and it was resumed in a different form by the Turkish Republic in the 1920s and 1930s. The episode is poorly documented compared with the Armenian deportations and remains little known outside specialist scholarship.
contested: Both the number deported and the mortality are uncertain, and no formal count was made; whether the deportations are best understood as a wartime security measure or as part of a deliberate demographic engineering programme is debated, with Ungor arguing the latter.

sources.title: Ugur Umit Ungor, 'Deportations of Kurds, 1916-34', in The Making of Modern Turkey: Nation and State in Eastern Anatolia, 1913-1950 (Oxford University Press)
Oxford University Press: The Making of Modern Turkey - Nation and State in Eastern Anatolia, 1913-1950

deathsNote: No count exists. Contemporary and early estimates, including Safrastian's 1948 figure that half the deportees died, imply losses in the low hundreds of thousands, but these rest on impressionistic reporting rather than records; Ungor notes that establishing the mortality would require a separate study. Deaths were caused by exposure, hunger and epidemic during winter deportation rather than by systematic killing.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
