violenceNote: The forced removal, the dispersal quotas and the assimilationist purpose are documented in Ottoman interior ministry correspondence analysed in Ungor's study.
baselineWhat: The Kurdish population of the eastern Ottoman provinces of Van, Bitlis, Erzurum, Diyarbekir and Mamuretülaziz on the eve of the First World War
baselineNote: The 1914 Ottoman census recorded religion rather than ethnicity, so Kurdish numbers are reconstructed from provincial administrative reports and later Turkish republican counts; estimates for the eastern provinces run from about 1 million to 1.5 million. Any figure is an approximation of a population that was itself mobile and partly nomadic.

title: Displacement and the Emigre Exodus of the Russian Civil War
actors: The Bolshevik government, the White armies and the intervening powers fought across the former Russian Empire; defeated forces and civilians evacuated from the Crimea, the Baltic and the Far East and were resettled abroad under League of Nations arrangements
peopleRange: Siobhan Peeling, writing in 1914-1918-Online, records that estimates of the number of citizens of the former Russian Empire settled around the world by 1921 range from 1 to 3 million; Alexandre Sumpf notes about 200,000 in Berlin alone and 80,000 in France. Internal displacement was far larger and was never counted, since the war moved across the whole empire and coincided with the return of millions of wartime refugees, prisoners and demobilised soldiers. The evidence is League of Nations High Commission records, receiving-state registration and emigre organisations, all incomplete.
territoryDesc: The war ended with the Bolshevik reconquest of most of the former empire, the loss of Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Bessarabia, and the establishment of Soviet republics in Ukraine, Belarus, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

flows.label: Evacuation of Wrangel's forces and civilians from the Crimea to Constantinople, November 1920
Petrograd and the north-west -> Berlin
Vladivostok and the Far East -> Harbin

summary: The civil war that followed the Bolshevik seizure of power drove the largest political emigration in Europe of the period. The evacuation of General Wrangel's army and accompanying civilians from the Crimea in November 1920 put some 150,000 people ashore at Constantinople; others left through the Baltic ports, through Poland and through Vladivostok and Harbin. Estimates of the number of former Russian subjects settled abroad by 1921 range from 1 to 3 million, concentrated in Berlin, Paris, Prague, Belgrade, Harbin and Constantinople. Soviet decrees of 1921-22 stripped most of them of citizenship, leaving them stateless, and the League of Nations responded by appointing Fridtjof Nansen High Commissioner for Refugees and creating the Nansen passport, an identity certificate that allowed stateless refugees to cross borders. The arrangement was the foundation of the modern international refugee regime, and Nansen received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922 for this and for his work on prisoner repatriation and Russian famine relief.
contested: The size of the emigration is genuinely uncertain, with defensible estimates spanning 1 to 3 million; the circumstances of departure, poor record keeping and the movement of emigres between countries make any single figure unreliable.

sources.title: Siobhan Peeling, 'Emigration (Russian Empire)', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Alexandre Sumpf, 'Russian Civil War', 1914-1918-Online
The Nobel Prize: Fridtjof Nansen, Peace Prize 1922 - facts

deathsNote: Deaths in the civil war as a whole, including the terrors, the epidemics and the 1921-22 famine, are usually put at 7 to 12 million, but they are treated in the separate entries on the terrors and the famine. The emigration itself was not directly lethal, though many died of typhus and destitution in the transit camps around Constantinople and Gallipoli in 1920-21.

atrocityFindings.body: League of Nations
atrocityFindings.finding: Appointed Fridtjof Nansen High Commissioner for Russian Refugees in 1921 and adopted in July 1922 the arrangement creating the Nansen certificate of identity for stateless Russian refugees, the first international travel document for refugees.

violenceNote: Soviet decrees of 1921-22 deprived emigres of citizenship, rendering them stateless, which is the fact that produced the League of Nations Nansen passport arrangement.
baselineWhat: The population of the former Russian Empire at the outbreak of revolution
baselineNote: The empire's population was about 166 million in 1914 on official estimates, and the territory of the future USSR held roughly 140-147 million in 1917-20. Estimates of the white emigration range from about 900,000 to 2 million, with the League of Nations Nansen office registering around 1.5 million Russian refugees in the early 1920s; total excess deaths from the civil war, famine and epidemics are put at 7-12 million.
shareCaveat: The affected figure counts emigres only; internal displacement, famine flight in 1921-22 and the flight of Cossack and Jewish communities during the pogroms involved many millions more and are not in the numerator.

title: Racial Massacres and Expulsions in the United States: East St Louis, Elaine, Tulsa and Rosewood
actors: White mobs, often with the participation or acquiescence of local police and, in Tulsa and Elaine, of National Guard and federal troops, killed African Americans and burned their neighbourhoods and towns across the United States
peopleRange: The largest single displacement was at Tulsa, where the Oklahoma Historical Society records that more than a thousand homes and businesses in the Greenwood district were destroyed, the vast majority of the city's African American residents were made homeless and thousands spent the winter of 1921-22 in tents. Roughly 6,000 African Americans left East St Louis after the July 1917 massacre, and the entire African American population of Rosewood, Florida, was driven out permanently in January 1923. Figures come from the 2001 Oklahoma commission report, contemporary Red Cross relief records and the 1993 Florida legislative study.
territoryDesc: The Greenwood district of Tulsa, an unusually prosperous Black commercial and residential quarter, was burned to the ground; the town of Rosewood, Florida, was destroyed and never rebuilt, and its land passed to others.

flows.label: East St Louis -> flight across the Mississippi to St Louis, July 1917
Rosewood, Florida -> permanent flight of the surviving residents, January 1923

summary: Between 1917 and 1923 a series of massacres destroyed African American communities in the United States, driven by competition over jobs and housing during the Great Migration, by the return of Black servicemen after the First World War, and by white resistance to Black economic independence and organisation. In East St Louis in July 1917 a mob killed dozens of people and burned Black neighbourhoods. In the Red Summer of 1919 violence struck Chicago, Washington and other cities; in Elaine, Arkansas, in October 1919, a Black sharecroppers' union meeting was attacked and posses and federal troops killed a number of people usually estimated between 100 and 240. At Tulsa on 31 May and 1 June 1921 a white mob, deputised by the authorities and joined by aircraft dropping incendiaries according to survivor testimony, destroyed the Greenwood district; the Oklahoma Historical Society records credible death estimates between fifty and three hundred, more than a thousand homes and businesses burned and thousands of Black Tulsans held under armed guard, and no white person was ever imprisoned for the killings or the arson. At Rosewood, Florida, in January 1923 the Black population of the town was killed or driven out and the settlement destroyed. Florida's legislature compensated Rosewood survivors in 1994, and Oklahoma's 1997-2001 commission recommended reparations for Tulsa survivors, which the legislature declined to pay.
contested: Death tolls at Tulsa and Elaine remain uncertain because bodies were removed and no reliable inquest was held; the Oklahoma commission concluded that victims were buried in unmarked graves, and searches for them have continued. Whether the events should be described as riots or as massacres was itself contested for decades, and reparations claims have been rejected by courts on limitation grounds.

sources.title: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture: Tulsa Race Massacre
National Endowment for the Humanities: The 1921 Tulsa Massacre
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tulsa race massacre of 1921

deathsNote: No aggregate count exists. The Oklahoma Historical Society gives credible estimates of fifty to three hundred dead at Tulsa; the 2001 Oklahoma commission documented unmarked graves whose excavation has continued since 2020. Elaine is usually put at 100-240 Black dead and five white; East St Louis at 39-150; Rosewood at 6-30 or more. The ranges reflect the removal and concealment of bodies, the absence of inquests and the reluctance of contemporary authorities to count Black victims.

atrocityFindings.body: Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot of 1921 (established by the Oklahoma Legislature in 1997, reported 2001)
atrocityFindings.finding: The commission established the scale of the destruction of Greenwood, found evidence of victims buried in unmarked graves and of the deputisation of white civilians by city authorities, and recommended that reparations be paid to surviving victims; the legislature did not enact reparations.

atrocityFindings.body: Florida Legislature
atrocityFindings.finding: In 1994, following an academic study commissioned by the legislature, Florida enacted a compensation act for the survivors and descendants of the 1923 destruction of Rosewood, the first such payment by a US state for a racial massacre.

violenceNote: The killings, the mass detention of Black residents under armed guard and the burning of Greenwood and Rosewood are documented in the 2001 Oklahoma commission report, in contemporary Red Cross relief records and in the 1993 Florida legislative study.
baselineWhat: The combined Black population of the four communities attacked - East St Louis, Illinois; Tulsa's Greenwood district; Phillips County, Arkansas; and Rosewood, Florida - around 1920
baselineNote: A constructed sum, not a single published figure: roughly 10,000-11,000 Black residents in East St Louis in 1917, close to 10,000 in Tulsa's Greenwood district in 1921, some 20,000-25,000 Black residents of Phillips County (where Black residents outnumbered white by about ten to one in the Elaine area), and 200-300 at Rosewood. Component figures come from the 1920 federal census and the state commissions of inquiry.

baselineSources.title: Encyclopedia of Arkansas - Elaine Massacre of 1919
Oklahoma Historical Society - Tulsa Race Massacre

shareCaveat: The denominator is a sum of four local Black populations assembled by hand, and the Phillips County component covers a whole county while the violence fell on part of it, so the percentage should be read as an order of magnitude only.

title: The Armenian-Azerbaijani War and the Massacres of Baku, Shusha and Zangezur
actors: Armenian, Azerbaijani and Ottoman forces and local militias killed and expelled each other's civilian populations across the contested South Caucasus
peopleRange: Contemporary relief agencies and the short-lived Caucasus republics reported several hundred thousand refugees moving between Armenian- and Azerbaijani-populated districts, with figures of 300,000-500,000 commonly cited; the counts come from Near East Relief, British occupation authorities and the rival governments' own claims, all with an interest in the totals, and no census-quality data exists for these years.
territoryDesc: Contested control of Karabakh, Zangezur, Nakhchivan and the Baku province, settled only by the Soviet delimitations of 1920-23

flows.label: Armenians from Karabakh and Nakhchivan to Yerevan
Azerbaijanis from Zangezur eastward

summary: As the Russian imperial front dissolved, the newly declared republics of Armenia and Azerbaijan fought over Karabakh, Zangezur and Nakhchivan while communal massacres consumed mixed districts. In Baku, fighting between Bolshevik-Dashnak forces and Azerbaijani Musavatists in the 'March Days' of 1918 left thousands of Muslim civilians dead, and in September 1918 Ottoman-backed forces of the Army of Islam entered the city and killed large numbers of Armenians; estimates for each episode run from several thousand to tens of thousands and are strongly contested along national lines. In March 1920 the Armenian quarter of Shusha was destroyed and its population killed or driven out, with death estimates ranging from about 500 to 20,000. Hundreds of thousands of civilians fled in both directions, and the surviving refugee flows helped fix the ethnically separated map that Soviet delimitation formalised in 1921-23. Armenian and Azerbaijani historiographies differ sharply on sequence, responsibility and numbers for almost every episode in this period.
contested: Every major figure and the question of who initiated each massacre are disputed between Armenian and Azerbaijani historiography, with Turkish and Russian archival readings adding further divergence.

sources.title: Armenian-Azerbaijani war (1918-1920)
March Days, Baku, 1918
Shusha massacre, 1920

deathsNote: The lower bound reflects conservative scholarly tallies of the identifiable massacres (Baku March and September 1918, Shusha 1920, and village-level killings in Karabakh, Zangezur and Nakhchivan); the upper bound reflects the maximal claims of the Armenian and Azerbaijani national historiographies, each of which counts the other side's victims low and its own high. There was no neutral authority in the region to record deaths.
violenceNote: British occupation reports, Near East Relief workers and the rival republics' own commissions of inquiry recorded mass killings and the burning of Armenian and Azerbaijani quarters and villages.
baselineWhat: The combined population of the Armenian and Azerbaijani republics in the contested South Caucasus
baselineNote: No reliable census covered the period. Russian imperial estimates of 1916 and the figures used by the two short-lived republics give Armenia roughly 1.3 million - swollen by refugees from Ottoman Anatolia and then thinned by famine - and Azerbaijan about 2 million. Both are contested and unstable given the refugee movements of these years.
shareCaveat: The 400,000 counts killings and expulsions on both sides across three years and includes refugees who had arrived from Ottoman territory and are not in this denominator.

title: The Soviet Reconquest of Central Asia, the Basmachi War and Flight to Afghanistan
actors: Soviet forces suppressed the Kokand autonomy and the Basmachi insurgency, requisitioned grain and drove tens of thousands across the Afghan and Chinese frontiers
peopleRange: Soviet and Afghan records are fragmentary. The destruction of Kokand in February 1918 and the punitive operations that followed emptied towns in the Fergana valley; the famine of 1917-1919 in Turkestan, driven by cotton monoculture, the collapse of grain imports and requisitioning, killed a very large number and dispersed more. Emigration to Afghanistan during the insurgency and again during collectivisation in 1929-32 is usually estimated at 200,000 or more, including much of the Turkmen and Uzbek population of the border districts, together with movement into Xinjiang and Iran.
territoryDesc: The Kokand autonomy, the Emirate of Bukhara and the Khanate of Khiva were abolished and their territory incorporated into Soviet republics

flows.label: Flight across the Amu Darya into Afghanistan

summary: Between 1918 and the mid-1930s Soviet power was imposed on Central Asia by force. Red Army units sacked Kokand in February 1918, killing thousands and ending the short-lived Turkestan autonomy; Bukhara was bombarded and its emir driven into Afghanistan in 1920, and Khiva's khanate was abolished. The resulting insurgency, called basmachi (bandits) by the Soviet authorities, was fought across the Fergana valley and the eastern Bukharan mountains for more than a decade, with village burning and food requisitioning on both sides. Requisitioning and the collapse of the cotton-for-grain economy produced a severe famine in Turkestan in 1917-19 and again in the Kazakh steppe in 1919-22. Collectivisation and the campaign against nomadic pastoralism from 1929 renewed the fighting and pushed a further wave of Uzbeks, Tajiks and above all Turkmen across the Amu Darya into Afghanistan, where they formed lasting communities, before the frontier was sealed. The atlas already covers the Kazakh famine of 1930-33 and the 1916 revolt; this entry covers the intervening reconquest.
contested: Soviet historiography treated the insurgency as banditry and the emigration as flight of class enemies; post-Soviet Central Asian accounts treat both as national resistance and expulsion, and casualty figures were never independently established.

sources.title: Basmachi movement
Kazakh famine of 1919-1922

deathsNote: The wide range reflects what is being counted. Combat and reprisal deaths in the insurgency are usually put in the low hundreds of thousands; adding the famine deaths in Turkestan and the Kazakh steppe in 1917-22, which several historians estimate at a million or more, produces the upper figure. Soviet authorities published no reliable totals.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Soviet military records, Comintern and Party correspondence and later Central Asian historiography document requisitioning, punitive expeditions and the destruction of villages in the Fergana valley.
baselineWhat: The population of Soviet Central Asia outside Kazakhstan — the Uzbek, Turkmen, Tajik and Kirghiz territories — at the census of 1926
baselineNote: The Soviet census of 1926 recorded roughly 7.5 million people across the Uzbek SSR, the Turkmen SSR, the Tajik ASSR and the Kirghiz ASSR, the region of the Basmachi war and the flight to Afghanistan and Xinjiang. The count follows the famine of 1917-21 in Turkestan, which itself killed hundreds of thousands.

title: The Finnish Civil War Prison Camps
actors: The victorious Finnish White government interned captured Red Guards, their families and suspected supporters in prison camps and tried them before special treason courts
peopleRange: About 80,000 Reds were captured at the end of the war in May 1918 and held initially across some sixty-four camps, consolidated to thirteen by the summer; the largest were at Tammisaari, Suomenlinna, Hameenlinna, Riihimaki, Lahti and Tampere. The figures come from Finnish state prison-camp administration records and the special court files, compiled in the national accounting of the war's victims.

flows.label: Captured Red Guards from Tampere and southern Finland -> Tammisaari and other camps

summary: The Finnish Civil War of January to May 1918 ended with the defeat of the Red Guards, and roughly 80,000 prisoners were taken into camps while special treason courts processed their cases. Food was scarce in Finland that spring, rations in the camps were inadequate, and malnutrition combined with a summer epidemic to produce very high mortality: about 11,600 prisoners died in the camps, most of them between May and September 1918. The special courts issued 555 death sentences of which 113 were carried out, on top of several thousand summary executions during and immediately after the fighting, including roughly 290 in Tampere and 247 in Vyborg. Total deaths from the war and its aftermath came to about 36,000 in a country of some three million. Most prisoners were released under amnesties during 1918-19, but the camps and the terror left a division in Finnish society that lasted for decades; a state-funded national project later compiled a database of all those who died in the conflicts of 1914-22.
contested: Whether the camp deaths should be attributed to a deliberate policy of punishment or to Finland's acute food crisis and administrative collapse in 1918 is debated by Finnish historians; the totals themselves are among the best documented of any event in this period.

sources.title: Finland 100: The price of the Finnish civil war - sentences, executions, prison camps, deaths
Matthew Stibbe, 'Enemy Aliens and Internment', 1914-1918-Online (context on the European internment systems of 1914-20)

deathsNote: About 11,600 prisoners died in the camps, chiefly of malnutrition and of the disease that swept them in the summer of 1918; adding the 113 executions ordered by the treason courts and deaths shortly after release brings the camp-related toll to roughly 12,500-13,500. These figures come from Finnish state records compiled in the national war-victims project, and are relatively well established. Around 36,000 people died in the war and its aftermath in total.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Mass internment, camp starvation and the summary executions of 1918 are documented in Finnish state prison-camp and treason-court records and in the national compilation of war victims.
baselineWhat: The population of Finland at the time of the civil war
baselineNote: Finnish official statistics put the population at about 3.13 million in 1918. The camps held some 80,000 people, close to the entire Red Guard establishment of roughly 75,000-100,000 combatants and supporters; about 12,500 died in the camps of hunger and disease within a year, the highest camp mortality in interwar Europe relative to population.

title: The Anti-Jewish Pogroms of the Russian Civil War
actors: White Volunteer Army units, Ukrainian People's Republic detachments, independent warlord bands and, in a smaller number of cases, Red Army units attacked Jewish towns and villages in Ukraine and Belarus
peopleRange: Several hundred thousand Jews were driven from their homes in the shtetls of Ukraine and Belarus by the pogroms and by the destruction of their livelihoods; contemporary Jewish relief organisations registered hundreds of thousands of destitute and homeless survivors, and the violence contributed to renewed emigration to Poland, western Europe, the United States and Palestine. Figures rest on the records of Jewish relief committees, the Kyiv-based investigating commissions and the material collected by Nokhem Shtif and Elias Tcherikower.

flows.label: Jewish communities of Podolia and Volhynia -> flight westward into Poland and beyond

summary: Between 1918 and 1921 more than a thousand pogroms were recorded across Ukraine and Belarus as authority collapsed and armies moved back and forth. Nicolas Werth, in the Sciences Po Mass Violence encyclopedia, records approximately 150,000 Jewish victims, 125,000 in Ukraine and 25,000 in Belarus, with 1919 the deadliest year; other counts of those killed outright are lower, in the range of 50,000-100,000, with the remainder dying of wounds, hunger and epidemic. The perpetrators included the White Volunteer Army, whose Ukrainian campaign of 1919 was accompanied by systematic pogroms, detachments nominally under the Ukrainian People's Republic, independent bands under warlords such as Hryhoriv, and, less often, Red Army units, some of whose members were shot for it. Communities were robbed, houses burned, women raped and entire shtetl populations killed. The violence was documented at the time by Jewish investigating commissions whose archives were later published, and it is widely regarded as the largest killing of Jews in Europe between the Chmielnicki massacres and the Holocaust.
contested: Responsibility is politically contested, above all the degree of responsibility of Symon Petliura and the Ukrainian People's Republic, an argument that ran through the 1926 assassination of Petliura and the acquittal of his assassin in Paris in 1927; the death toll ranges in serious work from about 50,000 to 200,000 depending on whether deaths from wounds, hunger and epidemic are included.

sources.title: Nicolas Werth, 'Crimes and Mass Violence of the Russian Civil Wars (1918-1921)', Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance encyclopedia
Nokhem Shtif, The Pogroms in Ukraine, 1918-19: Prelude to the Holocaust (Open Book Publishers, open access)
Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Pogrom

deathsNote: Werth gives approximately 150,000 Jewish victims for 1918-22. Counts restricted to those killed outright in identified pogroms are lower, commonly 50,000-60,000; totals that include deaths from wounds, exposure, hunger and the typhus that followed the destruction of communities reach 150,000-200,000. The disagreement is between narrow and broad definitions of victim and between the different investigating commissions' records.
violenceNote: Killings, mass rape and the burning and looting of Jewish quarters were documented contemporaneously by Jewish investigating commissions in Kyiv whose archives underlie Shtif's account and Werth's summary.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of the Ukrainian lands during the Russian Civil War
baselineNote: The 1897 census counted about 1.9 million Jews in the nine Ukrainian provinces and the 1926 Soviet census 1.57 million in the Ukrainian SSR, bracketing a wartime population of roughly 1.6 million. Estimates of those killed in the pogroms range from about 50,000 to 200,000, with several hundred thousand more left homeless, orphaned or destitute across more than a thousand recorded pogroms.

baselineSources.title: Pogroms during the Russian Civil War — Wikipedia
History of the Jews in Ukraine — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The affected figure counts people made homeless or refugees rather than killed, and the two are often conflated in the literature.

title: The New Borders of Central Europe: Refugees after Trianon, Versailles and Neuilly
actors: The peace treaties of 1919-20 redrew the borders of Austria-Hungary and Germany, and the successor states and France expelled or pressured out officials, settlers and minorities while Bulgaria and Greece agreed a 'voluntary' exchange under the Treaty of Neuilly
peopleRange: Miklos Zeidler, writing in 1914-1918-Online, records that over 400,000 Hungarian refugees fled the neighbouring states into the new frontiers of Hungary between 1918 and 1924, out of about 3 million Hungarians left outside them. Comparable movements included roughly 100,000-150,000 Germans leaving Alsace-Lorraine for Germany after 1918, several hundred thousand Germans leaving the territories ceded to Poland, and, under the Greek-Bulgarian convention annexed to the 1919 Treaty of Neuilly, about 92,000 Bulgarians moving from Greece to Bulgaria and about 45,000-50,000 Greeks from Bulgaria to Greece. Figures come from national refugee administrations, the mixed commissions and the League of Nations.
territoryDesc: Zeidler records that historic Hungary lost about 189,907 square kilometres and 10.6 million people at Trianon, retaining 92,963 square kilometres and 7.6 million people; Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France, Posen and West Prussia to Poland, and further territory by plebiscite, and Bulgaria lost western Thrace and its Aegean coastline under the Treaty of Neuilly.

flows.label: Hungarian officials and families from Transylvania and Slovakia -> rump Hungary
Germans leaving Alsace-Lorraine -> Germany
Bulgarians of western Thrace and Macedonia -> Bulgaria under the Neuilly convention

summary: The peace settlements of 1919-20 moved borders across populations that had not moved, and produced a decade of departures, expulsions and negotiated transfers. Hungary, reduced by Trianon to less than a third of its former territory, received over 400,000 refugees from the successor states between 1918 and 1924, many of them officials, teachers and railwaymen dismissed or pressured out, some living for years in railway wagons at Budapest stations. France removed a large part of the German population that had settled in Alsace-Lorraine since 1871, sorting inhabitants by identity card into four categories. Germans left the territories ceded to Poland in large numbers under emigration and option provisions. In the Balkans the Convention respecting Reciprocal Emigration annexed to the Treaty of Neuilly of 27 November 1919 created a nominally voluntary but state-organised exchange between Greece and Bulgaria, supervised by a mixed commission under League of Nations auspices, which moved roughly 140,000 people in total and served as the immediate model for the compulsory exchange agreed at Lausanne in 1923.
contested: Whether these movements are best described as expulsion, pressured emigration or voluntary migration differs by case and is contested in each national historiography; the Hungarian figure of over 400,000 in particular is used politically in arguments about Trianon.

sources.title: Miklos Zeidler, 'Trianon, Treaty of', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Peter Gatrell, 'Refugees', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Berna Pekesen, 'Expulsion and Emigration of the Muslims from the Balkans', European History Online (Leibniz Institute of European History)

deathsNote: These transfers were not accompanied by mass killing and no significant death toll is attributed to them; hardship, destitution and deaths from illness among refugees living in temporary accommodation are recorded but not quantified.
violenceNote: Loss of citizenship and public employment, option clauses and the state-supervised emigration conventions are set out in the treaties themselves and in the mixed commission records summarised by Zeidler and Gatrell.
baselineWhat: The population living in the territories transferred from Hungary, Germany, Austria and Bulgaria by the postwar peace treaties
baselineNote: Trianon transferred about 10.6 million of the Kingdom of Hungary's 20.9 million inhabitants to Romania, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia; Versailles transferred roughly 6.5-7 million from Germany, chiefly to Poland; Neuilly and Saint-Germain moved smaller numbers from Bulgaria and Austria. Adding these gives roughly 18 million people whose sovereign changed, based on the prewar censuses used in the treaty negotiations.
shareCaveat: The refugees were a specific slice of the transferred population — officials, railwaymen, teachers, landowners and urban minorities who lost position or feared the new states — not a random sample, so the low percentage understates how completely the treaties displaced the groups that did move.

title: The Red Terror, the White Terror and the First Soviet Camps
actors: The Cheka and the Soviet government took hostages, carried out mass executions and created a network of concentration and forced-labour camps; White governments and armies conducted their own executions and reprisals
peopleRange: Werth records about 50,000 prisoners held in seven concentration camps in Tambov province alone by late July 1921 during the suppression of the peasant rising there, and about 500,000 people arrested by the Cheka in the course of the peasant wars. A camp network was established by decree in September 1918 and by 1921 held roughly 40,000-60,000 inmates nationally; the Solovki special camp opened in 1923. Figures come from Cheka and OGPU administrative records opened after 1991.

flows.label: Tambov and other rebel provinces -> northern camps and, from 1923, Solovki

summary: Following the attempt on Lenin's life and the killing of the Petrograd Cheka chief, the Soviet government proclaimed the Red Terror in September 1918, authorising the execution of hostages drawn from former officers, clergy, landowners and the bourgeoisie and the confinement of class enemies in concentration camps. Werth estimates 10,000 to 15,000 people shot in the mass executions of September-October 1918 alone and observes that the Cheka executed more people in a few weeks than the tsarist regime had sentenced to death in ninety-two years. Camps established by decree in 1918 grew into a network that by 1921 held tens of thousands, and the suppression of the Tambov peasant rising in 1921 saw seven camps holding around 50,000 people, including hostage families, with monthly mortality of 15 to 20 percent in the autumn. White governments and armies carried out their own executions and reprisals, on a smaller scale but including mass shootings at Omsk, Ufa and elsewhere. The Solovki special-purpose camp, opened in 1923 in a confiscated monastery, became the model for the later Gulag.
contested: Totals for the Red Terror range from Cheka-reported figures of around 12,700 executions to estimates by later historians of 100,000 to 250,000 or more, depending on whether military-front executions, hostage shootings and deaths in camps are included; White Terror totals are less well documented and were smaller in scale but are similarly contested.

sources.title: Nicolas Werth, 'Crimes and Mass Violence of the Russian Civil Wars (1918-1921)', Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance encyclopedia
Alexandre Sumpf, 'Russian Civil War', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War

deathsNote: Werth documents 10,000-15,000 executions in the first weeks of the Red Terror in autumn 1918 and camp mortality of 15-20 percent a month in Tambov in autumn 1921. Estimates of total Red Terror victims range from official Cheka figures of about 12,700 through 50,000 to 100,000 in cautious reconstructions and up to 250,000 or more in wider counts that include front-line and military-tribunal executions and deaths in detention. White Terror deaths are generally put in the tens of thousands, with the anti-Jewish pogroms treated separately.
violenceNote: Hostage-taking, mass execution and the concentration camps of 1918-21 are documented in Soviet decrees and in Cheka and camp administration records opened after 1991 and summarised by Werth.
baselineWhat: The population of the territory under Soviet control during the civil war
baselineNote: The Soviet census of 1920 counted 136.8 million in the areas it could reach, with substantial territory - the western borderlands, parts of Central Asia, the Far East - unenumerated because of the fighting. Population figures for these years are unusually poor, and the war, famine and epidemics of 1918-1923 were themselves moving the total sharply.
shareCaveat: Camp figures for this period are point-in-time inmate counts, not cumulative totals of everyone detained, executed or taken hostage, and the executions of the Red and White terrors are estimated separately and very uncertainly.

title: De-Cossackization on the Don
actors: The Bolshevik Party's Orgburo and Red Army and Cheka units on the Don carried out executions, hostage-taking and deportations against the Don and Kuban Cossacks and confiscated their land
peopleRange: There is no full count. Nicolas Werth records about 17,000 people deported from five stanitsy to forced labour in the mines in October-November 1920, and the wider campaign involved the expulsion of Cossack families from their stanitsy, the resettlement of land-poor peasants and returning Red Army men in their place, and flight with the retreating White armies; several tens of thousands more left with Denikin and Wrangel in 1920. The evidence is Soviet party and Cheka documentation opened in the 1990s.
territoryDesc: Cossack land tenure, the legal basis of the Don and Kuban hosts, was abolished; stanitsa land was redistributed to incoming peasant settlers, and the Don and Kuban host territories were dissolved as administrative units.

flows.label: Don stanitsy -> deportation to forced labour in the Donbas mines

summary: On 24 January 1919 the Orgburo of the Bolshevik Central Committee issued a secret circular directing merciless mass terror against wealthy Cossacks and against all Cossacks who had taken any part in the struggle against Soviet power, together with the confiscation of grain and the resettlement of outsiders on Cossack land. Executions of hostages and of former officers followed in the Don stanitsy, provoking a major Cossack rising in March 1919. Werth records about 8,000 Cossacks executed in February and March 1919 and some 17,000 people deported from five stanitsy to forced labour in the mines in the autumn of 1920, and describes the campaign as an early instance of the Soviet state acting against a whole social category. The policy was suspended, resumed and formally moderated at different points, and the deportations of families continued into 1921. The Russian Federation's 1991 law on the rehabilitation of repressed peoples and a 1992 decree addressed the repression of the Cossacks.
contested: Whether de-Cossackization amounted to genocide against a distinct people, or was a class-directed repression of a privileged military estate, is disputed among historians and was politically charged in the post-Soviet rehabilitation debates; the total number killed is not established.

sources.title: Nicolas Werth, 'Crimes and Mass Violence of the Russian Civil Wars (1918-1921)', Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance encyclopedia
Encyclopedia.com: Circular Letter from the Orgburo of the Central Committee concerning relations with the Cossacks, 24 January 1919 (document text)

deathsNote: Werth documents about 8,000 executions in February-March 1919 from Soviet records; totals for the whole campaign including deaths in deportation, in the mines and during the suppression of the 1919 rising are estimated by different historians between roughly 10,000 and 45,000, and some Cossack organisations claim far higher figures. The archival base is partial and no comprehensive count has been made.
violenceNote: The Orgburo circular of 24 January 1919, execution lists and deportation orders were published from Soviet party and Cheka archives after 1991 and are summarised by Werth.
baselineWhat: The Cossack population of the Don Host territory in 1917
baselineNote: The Don Host oblast held roughly 3.5 million people in 1917, of whom about 1.5 million were registered Cossacks, the estate targeted by the Orgburo directive of January 1919; the Kuban Host added a further 1.3 million or so Cossacks. Estimates of those killed or deported in the campaign vary from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand, and the archival basis remains contested.

title: The Polish-Soviet War and the Peace of Riga
actors: Poland and Soviet Russia fought for the borderlands of the former Russian Empire and divided Belarus and Ukraine between them at Riga in March 1921, leaving large minorities on each side and prompting option, repatriation and settlement programmes
peopleRange: Around 1.1 million people were repatriated in each direction under the Riga agreements between 1921 and 1924, including prisoners of war, wartime refugees returning to Poland from the Russian interior and people exercising the treaty's option clauses; the numbers come from the Polish-Soviet mixed repatriation commissions. Roughly 4-5 million Ukrainians and Belarusians remained on the Polish side of the new border and a comparable population of Poles on the Soviet side.
territoryDesc: The Riga border ran far east of the Curzon Line, leaving Minsk on the Soviet side but placing western Belarus and western Volhynia and eastern Galicia within Poland. Poland subsequently settled military colonists on land in the eastern voivodeships, a policy that fed the conflicts of the following decades.

flows.label: Repatriation of Poles and returning wartime refugees from Soviet territory
Repatriation of Soviet prisoners and optants eastward

summary: Fighting between Poland and Soviet Russia began in 1919 in the vacuum left by the collapse of the German and Russian empires, reached Kyiv in May 1920 and Warsaw in August, and ended in an armistice in October 1920 and the Treaty of Riga of 18 March 1921. Jerzy Borzecki records that the treaty fixed a border well east of the Curzon Line, leaving Poland a national state with large Ukrainian and Belarusian minorities, allowing former subjects of the Russian Empire on Polish territory to opt for Polish citizenship, and providing for the return of cultural property and a payment of 30 million gold rubles. Large repatriation and option movements followed on both sides, restoring wartime refugees to their homes and moving optants across the new line. The treaty also settled the fate of the short-lived Ukrainian People's Republic, whose forces had been Poland's allies and whose interned soldiers remained in Polish camps. Mortality among prisoners of war on both sides was heavy, and the numbers are a longstanding dispute between Polish and Russian historians.
contested: The number of Soviet prisoners of war who died in Polish camps in 1920-21 is disputed: joint Polish-Russian archival work published in 2004 concluded that roughly 16,000-20,000 died of epidemic and privation, while Russian official statements have alleged far higher figures and deliberate killing, which Polish historians reject.

sources.title: Jaroslaw Centek, 'Polish-Soviet War 1920-1921', 1914-1918-Online International Encyclopedia of the First World War
Jerzy Borzecki, 'Riga, Treaty of', 1914-1918-Online

deathsNote: Combatant deaths on both sides are usually put in the tens of thousands. The largest identified civilian and prisoner mortality is among prisoners of war: roughly 16,000-20,000 Soviet prisoners died in Polish camps according to the joint Polish-Russian documentary publication of 2004, and a comparable number of Polish prisoners died in Soviet hands. Typhus among troops, prisoners and civilians in the war zone accounts for most of the deaths.
violenceNote: Prisoner-of-war internment and its mortality on both sides are documented in the joint Polish-Russian archival publication of 2004 and in the Riga treaty records summarised by Borzecki.
baselineWhat: The population of the eastern borderlands assigned to Poland at Riga - the Wilno, Nowogrodek, Polesie, Wolyn, Lwow, Stanislawow and Tarnopol voivodeships
baselineNote: The Polish census of 1921, taken shortly after the treaty, counted about 27.2 million in Poland as a whole, of which the seven eastern voivodeships held roughly 9-10 million, a majority of them Ukrainians, Belarusians and Jews rather than Poles; by the 1931 census the same area held about 13 million. The Riga treaty's repatriation provisions moved roughly 1.1 million people between Poland and Soviet Russia in 1921-24, including prisoners of war, refugees returning from wartime evacuation and opting populations.
shareCaveat: The 1.1 million counts treaty repatriations in both directions, most of them people returning home from wartime evacuation rather than newly expelled, so the ratio should not be read as a measure of expulsion.

title: The Volga Famine
actors: Drought struck a countryside already stripped by Soviet grain requisitioning, civil war and the collapse of transport; the Soviet government eventually admitted foreign relief agencies, principally the American Relief Administration and Nansen's International Committee
peopleRange: Millions of people abandoned the famine provinces of the Volga, the southern Urals and southern Ukraine for the towns, the railway lines and the grain-growing regions, and Soviet and relief agency reporting describes hundreds of thousands crowding railway stations; there was never a registration of the displaced. About 25-30 million people lived in the officially declared famine areas at the height of the crisis, and the Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine records around 3.5 million people in Ukraine's recognised famine zones without food by March 1922.

flows.label: Volga famine provinces -> flight to the cities and railway lines

summary: A severe drought in 1921 fell on a peasantry whose seed grain and reserves had been taken by the forced requisitioning of war communism and whose transport and administration had broken down in the civil war. The famine that followed centred on the middle and lower Volga, the southern Urals, the Crimea and southern Ukraine. The Soviet government appealed for international help in July 1921 and admitted the American Relief Administration under Herbert Hoover, Nansen's International Russian Relief Committee, the Save the Children Fund and others, whose kitchens at their peak fed some 10 million people. The Warwick University Modern Records Centre records the League of Nations describing it as the worst famine in Europe in modern times as regards both numbers affected and mortality, and gives estimates of victims from 1 million to 10 million with 5 million the most frequently quoted. Relief in Ukraine was delayed because Moscow initially declined to recognise the Ukrainian famine areas while grain was still being moved out of and exported from Ukraine.
contested: Whether the famine should be counted as a policy-driven catastrophe or a natural disaster aggravated by war is debated: the drought was real, but requisitioning, the seizure of seed grain, continued grain exports and the delayed recognition of the Ukrainian famine zones are documented policy contributions. Death estimates span an order of magnitude.

sources.title: University of Warwick Modern Records Centre: Famine in Russia, 1921-1922 (digital collection)
Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Famine of 1921-3

deathsNote: The Warwick Modern Records Centre states that estimates of famine victims from starvation or associated disease vary from 1 million to 10 million, with 5 million the figure most often quoted. The Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine documents 235,000 recorded deaths in five southern Ukrainian gubernias in the winter of 1921-22 alone and suggests the Ukrainian total may have exceeded a million. The range reflects the absence of vital registration, the concurrent typhus and cholera epidemics, and disagreement over the baseline population.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Forced grain requisitioning including seed grain, and continued grain movement and export during the famine, are documented in Soviet decrees and in the relief agencies' reporting collected by the Warwick Modern Records Centre and the Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine.
baselineWhat: The population of the famine-stricken provinces of the Volga, the Urals, southern Ukraine and Crimea
baselineNote: Soviet and American Relief Administration surveys placed roughly 30 million people in the declared famine zone, of whom the ARA was feeding about 10 million at the peak in mid-1922. Excess deaths are usually estimated at about 5 million; the displacement figure counts those who left the famine provinces as refugees, recorded incompletely by railway and provincial authorities.
shareCaveat: The affected figure counts famine refugees, not deaths; mortality in the same zone was several times higher.

title: The Burning of Smyrna and the Exodus of the Anatolian Greeks
actors: Turkish nationalist forces entered Smyrna in September 1922 after the collapse of the Greek army in Anatolia; the Greek and Armenian quarters burned and the surviving Christian population was evacuated or deported
peopleRange: American relief sources cited by the Greek Genocide Resource Center record about 213,480 refugees of various nationalities evacuated from Smyrna to Greece on Allied and chartered shipping in September and October 1922. Across Anatolia and eastern Thrace as a whole roughly 1.2 million Greek Orthodox refugees reached Greece in 1922-24, counted by the Greek census of 1928 and by the Refugee Settlement Commission established under League of Nations auspices.
territoryDesc: The Greek and Armenian quarters of Smyrna, one of the largest commercial cities of the eastern Mediterranean, were destroyed by fire; Greek and Armenian property throughout western Anatolia and eastern Thrace passed to the Turkish state and to Muslim refugees.

flows.label: Smyrna quayside -> evacuation to Piraeus and the Aegean islands
Eastern Thrace -> flight into Greek Macedonia and Thrace

summary: The Greek army's front in Anatolia broke in August 1922 and Turkish forces entered Smyrna on 9 September. Massacres in the Armenian quarter were reported by foreign consuls and missionaries, and on 13 September a fire destroyed the Armenian and Greek quarters while the Turkish quarter was largely spared. Hundreds of thousands of civilians were driven onto the quayside and were eventually taken off by Allied and chartered shipping, about 213,000 according to American relief figures, while men of military age were separated and marched into the interior in labour columns from which few returned. The fire's origin is disputed: Greek, Armenian and several foreign eyewitnesses attributed it to Turkish troops, while Turkish accounts attribute it to retreating Greek and Armenian arsonists. The exodus from Smyrna was the largest single episode in a movement that brought about 1.2 million Orthodox refugees into Greece and was formalised by the compulsory exchange agreed at Lausanne in January 1923.
contested: Responsibility for the fire is disputed between Greek, Armenian and foreign eyewitness accounts blaming Turkish forces and Turkish accounts blaming retreating Greek and Armenian irregulars; the number who died in the fire and the massacres ranges in the sources from about 10,000 to well over 100,000.

sources.title: Greek Genocide Resource Center: The Smyrna catastrophe, September 1922 (documentation and eyewitness accounts)
MERIP (Middle East Research and Information Project): The Greek-Turkish Population Exchange
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Greco-Turkish wars

deathsNote: Contemporary estimates vary enormously. An early dispatch put deaths at about 1,000 with unknown further losses in the burning districts; the American consul George Horton estimated at least 100,000 dead, and an American relief official was quoted at 120,000. Population comparisons before and after leave roughly 190,000 people unaccounted for, but an unknown share of those were deported inland or evacuated elsewhere rather than killed. Deaths came from massacre, from the fire, from drowning at the quayside and from the deportation of men into the interior.
violenceNote: Massacres, the separation and deportation of men of military age, and the destruction of the Christian quarters were reported at the time by foreign consuls, naval officers and missionaries whose accounts are collected by the Greek Genocide Resource Center.
baselineWhat: The Greek Orthodox population of Anatolia and Ottoman Thrace before the First World War
baselineNote: The Ottoman census of 1914 recorded 1,729,738 Greeks in the empire; the Ecumenical Patriarchate claimed closer to 2.5 million, and modern estimates cluster between 1.6 and 2 million. The figure used is the Ottoman count, which is the most systematic enumeration available and is generally treated as a floor.

baselineSources.title: Population exchange between Greece and Turkey — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: Large numbers of Anatolian Greeks had already been deported, conscripted into labour battalions or killed between 1914 and 1922, so the 1922-23 exodus is measured against a population that had already been reduced.

title: The Kanto Massacre of Koreans
actors: Vigilante groups, police and army units killed Koreans, Chinese and Japanese leftists in Tokyo, Yokohama and the surrounding prefectures in the days after the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923
peopleRange: Thousands of Koreans were taken into police custody or into army-run protective detention during and after the killings, and an unknown number left Japan afterwards; the earthquake itself displaced well over a million people in Tokyo and Yokohama, but that displacement was a natural disaster rather than a policy act and is not counted here.
summary: In the confusion after the earthquake of 1 September 1923, rumours that Koreans were poisoning wells, setting fires and preparing an uprising were spread and repeated by police and official channels, and martial law was declared. Vigilante groups formed and, together with police and soldiers, killed Koreans and some Chinese and Japanese who were mistaken for them, checking identity by pronunciation at street barricades; the anarchist Osugi Sakae and his partner and nephew were killed by a military police officer, and labour organisers were killed at Kameido. Estimates of Korean deaths range from the Japanese Home Ministry's contemporary figure of about 230 through independent Japanese investigations in the range of 2,600 to the roughly 6,000 recorded by Korean student investigators at the time and repeated in the Harvard-Yenching Institute's account of recent scholarship, which argues the state both induced the killings by spreading rumours and mobilising police and soldiers under martial law and then concealed its role through cursory prosecutions. A small number of vigilantes were tried and received light sentences. Successive Japanese governments have not issued a formal acknowledgement of state responsibility, and in recent years the national government has said it has found no records allowing it to establish the facts, while the governor of Tokyo has declined since 2017 to send the customary memorial message to the annual commemoration.
contested: The number of Koreans killed is disputed from roughly 230 in the contemporary Japanese official count to about 6,000 in Korean investigations, and the Japanese government has not accepted state responsibility, stating that it has not found records that would allow the facts to be ascertained; the Republic of Korea and Korean and Japanese civil-society organisations dispute that position.

sources.title: Harvard-Yenching Institute: research on the Great Kanto Earthquake and the massacre of Koreans - state and popular responsibility
Kenji Hasegawa, 'The Massacre of Koreans in Yokohama in the Aftermath of the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923', Monumenta Nipponica (Sophia University)
Brown University Library, Center for Digital Scholarship: Behind the Accounts of the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923

deathsNote: The Japanese Home Ministry's contemporary count was about 230 Koreans killed; the Japanese scholar Yamada Shoji and others working from local records reach figures in the low thousands; Korean investigators at the time compiled about 6,000, the figure cited in the Harvard-Yenching account. Several hundred Chinese labourers and a number of Japanese, including Osugi Sakae and the Kameido labour organisers, were also killed. The disparity reflects the absence of any official investigation, the destruction and non-release of records, and disputes over which killings to include.

atrocityFindings.body: Government of Japan
atrocityFindings.finding: The Japanese government has stated that it has not found records within the government that would allow the facts of the massacre to be ascertained, and has declined to conduct an official investigation or issue a formal acknowledgement of state responsibility; Japanese and Korean scholars and civil-society organisations dispute this position.

violenceNote: The killings, the role of official rumour and of police and soldiers under martial law, and the subsequent prosecutions are documented in Japanese police and judicial records, in contemporary Korean investigations and in the scholarship summarised by Hasegawa and the Harvard-Yenching Institute.
baselineWhat: The Korean population resident in Japan in 1923
baselineNote: Japanese Home Ministry registration figures put the Korean population of Japan at roughly 80,000 in 1923, of whom perhaps 20,000-25,000 lived in Tokyo and Kanagawa prefectures, the area of the massacre. Registration was incomplete and some estimates for the national Korean population run higher.

title: The Greek-Turkish Population Exchange under the Treaty of Lausanne
actors: Greece and Turkey, under a convention signed at Lausanne on 30 January 1923 and supervised by a Mixed Commission under League of Nations auspices, compulsorily exchanged their Orthodox Christian and Muslim populations
peopleRange: Roughly 1.2-1.5 million Orthodox Christians moved from Anatolia and eastern Thrace to Greece, most of them before the convention was signed, and about 350,000-500,000 Muslims moved from Greece to Turkey; the usual combined figure is about 1.6 million. MERIP gives approximately 1.5 million Orthodox Christians and roughly 500,000 Muslims. The counts come from the Mixed Commission's records, the Greek census of 1928 and the reports of the Refugee Settlement Commission, and differ because many Orthodox refugees had already fled in 1922 and were retrospectively brought under the convention.
territoryDesc: Property left behind on both sides was liquidated by the Mixed Commission and set against the property of the incoming population; villages and urban quarters changed occupants entirely, and the settlement of refugees in Greek Macedonia and Thrace changed the demography of northern Greece decisively.

flows.label: Orthodox Christians of Anatolia -> Greek Macedonia and Thrace
Muslims of Greece -> Anatolia

summary: The Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations, signed at Lausanne on 30 January 1923, provided in Article 1 for a compulsory exchange from 1 May 1923 of Turkish nationals of the Greek Orthodox religion established in Turkey and Greek nationals of the Muslim religion established in Greece, exempting under Article 2 only the Greeks of Constantinople and the Muslims of western Thrace. Religion, not language or self-identification, was the criterion, so Turkish-speaking Orthodox Christians of Cappadocia went to Greece and Greek-speaking Muslims of Crete and Epirus went to Turkey. Fridtjof Nansen, League of Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, had promoted the exchange as a means of resolving the refugee crisis created by the 1922 collapse, and a Mixed Commission supervised transfers and property liquidation. Much of the movement had already occurred as flight in 1922; the convention retroactively made it permanent and stripped those transferred of the right to return. The Permanent Court of International Justice was asked in 1925 to interpret 'established' in Article 2 and held that it meant residence of a lasting nature under the convention's own terms rather than under national law. It was the first compulsory exchange of populations codified in an international treaty and was cited as a precedent for later transfers.
contested: Whether the exchange should be regarded as a humanitarian settlement of an existing refugee emergency or as the international legalisation of ethnic cleansing is disputed among historians and lawyers; the numbers on each side and the treatment of the exempted communities in Istanbul and western Thrace remain contentious between Greece and Turkey.

sources.title: Republic of Turkiye, Ministry of Foreign Affairs: Lausanne Peace Treaty VI - Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations, 30 January 1923 (full text)
Permanent Court of International Justice, Advisory Opinion of 21 February 1925: Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations (Lausanne Convention VI, Article 2)
MERIP: The Greek-Turkish Population Exchange
The Nobel Prize: Fridtjof Nansen, Peace Prize 1922 - facts

deathsNote: The exchange itself was not a killing operation, and no reliable death toll exists for the transfers. Mortality among refugees in the Greek reception camps in 1922-24 from typhus, malaria and destitution was heavy and is usually estimated in the tens of thousands, but it is not separable from the deaths of the 1922 flight that preceded the convention.

atrocityFindings.body: Permanent Court of International Justice
atrocityFindings.finding: Advisory Opinion of 21 February 1925 interpreting Article 2 of the Lausanne Convention, holding that 'established' denotes residence of a lasting nature determined by the convention itself and by the Mixed Commission, not by Turkish or Greek municipal law.

violenceNote: The convention itself stripped those transferred of nationality and of the right to return without the permission of the receiving government, as recorded in its published text.
baselineWhat: The two communities made subject to the compulsory exchange: the Orthodox Christians of Turkey and the Muslims of Greece
baselineNote: The Mixed Commission's own accounting covered roughly 1.2-1.3 million Orthodox Christians moved from Anatolia and eastern Thrace to Greece, most of whom had already fled in 1922, and about 355,000-500,000 Muslims moved from Greece to Turkey. The exempted communities, the Greeks of Istanbul, Imbros and Tenedos and the Muslims of Western Thrace, together numbered a few hundred thousand and are excluded from the baseline.

baselineSources.title: Population exchange between Greece and Turkey — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The exchange was designed to be exhaustive, so the share approaches 100 per cent by construction and measures the completeness of the convention rather than its intensity; against the combined population of Greece and Turkey, some 18 million in 1923, the exchange moved about a tenth of all inhabitants.

title: Reza Shah's Forced Sedentarization of Iran's Nomadic Tribes
actors: The Pahlavi state disarmed Iran's nomadic confederations and compelled them to settle in fixed villages under army supervision
peopleRange: Nomads are usually estimated to have made up a quarter or more of Iran's population of roughly 12-15 million in the 1920s, so the confederations targeted - Qashqai, Bakhtiari, Lur, Kurd, Baluch, Shahsavan, Turkmen and others - comprised on the order of two to three million people, of whom a large share were subjected to forced settlement (takht-e qapu) at some point in the 1930s. There was no enumeration; the estimate rests on Iranian government and army records, on British and Russian consular reporting, and on later anthropological reconstructions, notably by Lois Beck for the Qashqai.

flows.label: Qashqai pastoralists prevented from migrating and settled in the Fars lowlands

summary: Reza Shah's programme of state centralisation in the 1920s and 1930s treated Iran's large nomadic confederations, which had their own armed forces and often their own external relations, as the principal obstacle to a unitary state. The army campaigned against the Lurs, Kurds, Baluch, Qashqai, Bakhtiari and Turkmen, executed or imprisoned tribal leaders including the Bakhtiari khans and the Qashqai ilkhani's family, disarmed the tribes, and from the early 1930s applied a policy known as takht-e qapu, forcing pastoral groups to abandon seasonal migration and settle in fixed villages, sometimes at the point of army guns and often in lowland areas unsuited to their herds. Anthropological and historical accounts, including Lois Beck's work on the Qashqai, describe mass loss of livestock, disease among people and animals kept in unsuitable climates, impoverishment and substantial mortality; forced dress reform and conscription accompanied the settlement. The policy collapsed almost immediately after the Anglo-Soviet occupation of Iran and Reza Shah's abdication in 1941, when large numbers of tribespeople resumed migration. No figures were compiled at the time, and the scale of mortality remains a matter of reconstruction from tribal memory and later fieldwork.
contested: No enumeration was made, so both the number settled and the mortality attributed to settlement rest on later reconstruction; Iranian nationalist accounts present the policy as necessary state-building and modernisation, while affected communities and much anthropological work describe it as coercive and destructive.

sources.title: Reza Shah
Qashqai people
Bakhtiari people

deathsNote: No defensible range. Contemporary and later accounts describe heavy mortality among forcibly settled pastoralists from disease, malnutrition and loss of herds, and executions of tribal leaders and fighters during the disarmament campaigns, but the Pahlavi state kept no relevant records and no reconstruction has produced a credible total.
violenceNote: Historical and anthropological studies of the Qashqai and Bakhtiari, including Lois Beck's fieldwork, document the imprisonment and execution of tribal leaders, army enforcement of settlement, and the confiscation of herds and destruction of tent camps.
baselineWhat: The nomadic and semi-nomadic tribal population of Iran at the start of the Pahlavi sedentarisation campaign
baselineNote: Iran held no census before 1956. Estimates by Lambton, Amanolahi and others put the nomadic confederations - Qashqai, Bakhtiari, Lur, Kurdish, Baluch, Shahsevan and Turkmen - at roughly a quarter of a national population of some 10-12 million in the 1920s, that is about 2.5-3 million. The 1956 census, after two decades of forced settlement and post-Reza Shah re-nomadisation, counted far fewer.
shareCaveat: Both figures are estimates made without a census; the affected total is a reconstruction of how many were subject to settlement orders, not a register of people moved.

title: New Zealand Rule in Western Samoa: The Mau, Black Saturday and the Exiles
actors: The New Zealand administration of the mandated territory of Western Samoa banned the Mau movement, deported its leaders and shot into a crowd in Apia
peopleRange: New Zealand administration records and later official histories give the figures: nine or eleven killed on 28 December 1929 depending on the count used, the deportation of the movement's leading figures including Olaf Nelson in 1928 and again in 1933, and about 1,500 Mau supporters taking to the bush in 1930 while pursued by some 150 marines, sailors and military police supported by seaplanes.

flows.label: Mau leaders deported to New Zealand

summary: New Zealand governed Western Samoa under a League of Nations mandate from 1920, after a period in which its failure to quarantine a ship had allowed an influenza epidemic to kill about a fifth of the population. Samoan opposition coalesced in the Mau, a movement for self-government that organised boycotts, refused taxes and maintained its own police; the administration responded by banning it, deporting its leaders and, on 28 December 1929, firing on a Mau parade in Apia, killing the paramount chief Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III and eight others along with one New Zealand policeman. In January 1930 the administrator declared the Mau seditious, and about 1,500 supporters withdrew into the bush pursued by marines and military police; arrests of men were followed by demonstrations organised by Samoan women. The movement was recognised and the bans lifted after the New Zealand Labour government took office in 1935-36, and Samoa became independent in 1962. In 2002 the New Zealand Prime Minister formally apologised in Apia for the actions of the colonial administration, including Black Saturday and the deportation of Samoan leaders.
contested: Whether the shooting on Black Saturday began with the crowd or the police was disputed at the time; the New Zealand apology of 2002 accepts the administration's responsibility.

sources.title: NZHistory: Black Saturday
Archives New Zealand: the rise of the Mau and the fall of colonial rule in Samoa
New Zealand Government: Prime Minister apologises to Samoa
Mau movement

deathsNote: Contemporary and later New Zealand accounts record eight or ten Samoans and one New Zealand policeman killed on 28 December 1929, with Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III dying of his wounds the next day; the small variation reflects whether those who died later of injuries are included.

atrocityFindings.body: Government of New Zealand
atrocityFindings.finding: In 2002 the Prime Minister of New Zealand formally apologised to Samoa for the actions of the New Zealand administration, including the deaths on Black Saturday in 1929 and the banishment of Samoan leaders

violenceNote: New Zealand administration records, later official histories and the 2002 apology document the shooting of Mau demonstrators and the arrest and deportation of the movement's leaders.
baselineWhat: The Samoan population of the mandated territory of Western Samoa
baselineNote: The 1921 census counted 36,422 people in Western Samoa, a figure still depressed by the 1918 influenza epidemic, which the New Zealand administration had allowed ashore and which killed roughly a fifth of the population; by the late 1920s the territory held about 40,000-45,000.
shareCaveat: The 1,500 covers those exiled, imprisoned or shot; the Mau commanded the allegiance of a large majority of Samoans, which a ratio of punished individuals to population does not capture.

title: Italy's Deportation of the Cyrenaican Population into Camps
actors: Italian forces under Pietro Badoglio and Rodolfo Graziani cleared the population of the Jebel Akhdar and interned them in camps on the Sirtica coast
peopleRange: Scholarly estimates give roughly 100,000 to 120,000 Libyans interned in about twenty concentration camps in the Sirtica between 1929 and 1934, the bulk of the semi-nomadic population of the Jebel Akhdar, together with their herds. The camps were closed in 1934. The figures come from Italian colonial military and administrative records and the reconstructions of Libyan and Italian historians, summarised in the International Review of Social History.

flows.label: Jebel Akhdar -> camps at El Agheila, Soluch, Sidi Ahmed el-Magrun and Agedabia

summary: To end the Senussi resistance led by Omar al-Mukhtar, Italian commanders removed the population that sustained it. Between 1929 and 1931 the semi-nomadic communities of the Jebel Akhdar were driven south to the coastal plain of the Sirtica and held behind wire in about twenty camps, their livestock confiscated or destroyed, while a barbed-wire barrier some 270 kilometres long was built along the Egyptian frontier to cut off supply. Historians estimate that 100,000 to 120,000 people were interned and that 40,000 to 48,000 died of hunger, disease and executions in the camps. Omar al-Mukhtar was captured and hanged before an assembly of internees at Soluch in September 1931, and the campaign was declared over in January 1932. The camps were dissolved in 1934, and survivors returned to a devastated region. Libyan and Italian scholars, notably Ali Abdullatif Ahmida, characterise the episode as genocide; the Italian state has not accepted that characterisation, though the treaty of friendship signed at Benghazi in 2008 included an Italian expression of regret for the colonial period and a substantial compensation package.
contested: Whether the clearance and internment of Cyrenaica constituted genocide is disputed between Libyan and some international scholars and the Italian state, which has apologised for colonialism in general terms without accepting that characterisation.

sources.title: The Other at Home: Deportation and Transportation of Libyans to Italy during the Colonial Era (1911-1943), International Review of Social History (Cambridge University Press)

deathsNote: The range of 40,000 to 48,000 deaths among internees, from starvation, disease, exposure and execution, is the figure given in the scholarly literature summarised in the International Review of Social History. Italian colonial records did not systematically register deaths in the camps, so the figures derive from population comparisons before and after the clearance as well as from camp reports.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: The forced removal of the Jebel population, the confiscation and slaughter of herds, the conditions in the Sirtica camps and the public execution of captured resistance leaders are documented in Italian colonial military records and the historical literature reviewed in the International Review of Social History.
baselineWhat: The population of Cyrenaica at the start of the Italian clearances
baselineNote: E. E. Evans-Pritchard, working from Italian administrative figures, put Cyrenaica's population at about 225,000 before the campaign, most of it the semi-nomadic Bedouin of the Jebel Akhdar. Italian forces deported roughly 100,000-110,000 of them to camps on the Sirtica coast between 1929 and 1934; Italian and Libyan estimates of deaths in the camps and the clearances range from about 40,000 to 70,000, and Cyrenaica's livestock herds, the population's livelihood, were reduced by well over half.

title: The Mexican Repatriation in the United States
actors: United States federal, state and county authorities pressed or deported Mexicans and Mexican Americans, many of them US citizens, to Mexico during the Depression
peopleRange: Estimates of those who left the United States for Mexico between 1929 and 1936 range from about 400,000 to two million, with figures around one million commonly cited; researchers estimate that roughly 60 per cent were United States citizens by birth, most of them children. The wide range reflects the mixture of formal deportation, county-organised transport, and departures under pressure that were never recorded as removals; the evidence comes from Mexican and United States immigration statistics, county relief records and later scholarship cited in the California legislature's 2005 apology.

flows.label: Los Angeles and the southwestern United States -> central Mexico
Midwestern industrial cities -> northern Mexico

summary: As unemployment rose after 1929, federal immigration raids, county welfare policies and public campaigns pressed people of Mexican descent to leave the United States. Los Angeles County organised trains to the border and other counties followed; relief was withheld from Mexican families, and highly publicised raids such as that in La Placita in Los Angeles in February 1931 spread fear well beyond those actually detained. A majority of those who went were United States citizens, chiefly the American-born children of Mexican immigrants, and many had no legal process at all. Estimates of the total run from 400,000 to two million. Labour demand in the Second World War reversed the flow, and the Bracero programme began recruiting Mexican workers in 1942. In 2005 the California legislature passed the Apology Act for the 1930s Mexican Repatriation Program, formally apologising for the state's role in the unconstitutional removal of United States citizens and legal residents; no comparable federal apology has been issued.
contested: The total is uncertain by a factor of five because most departures were coerced rather than formally ordered and were not recorded as removals, and because Mexican and United States entry and exit statistics do not match.

sources.title: Immigration History (Immigration and Ethnic History Society): Mexican Repatriation (1929-1936)
California Senate Bill 670 (2005), Apology Act for the 1930s Mexican Repatriation Program

deathsNote: There was no significant death toll. The harm consisted in the loss of citizenship rights, homes, property and family separation, and in the destitution of families arriving in a Mexico unprepared to absorb them; deaths in transit were not systematically recorded and were not a defining feature of the episode.

atrocityFindings.body: Legislature of the State of California
atrocityFindings.finding: Passed the Apology Act for the 1930s Mexican Repatriation Program in 2005, apologising for the unconstitutional removal and coerced emigration of an estimated two million people, roughly 1.2 million of them United States citizens

violenceNote: The removal of United States citizens without due process and the use of immigration raids and detention to induce departure are documented in county and federal records and are recited in the findings of the California Apology Act of 2005.
baselineWhat: The Mexican-origin population of the United States at the 1930 census
baselineNote: The 1930 US census, the only one to record 'Mexican' as a race, counted about 1,692,000 people of Mexican origin, falling to about 1,592,000 in 1940 despite natural increase. The number repatriated is disputed: Gratton and Merchant estimate about 355,000 movements to Mexico in the 1930s, Hoffman over 400,000 for 1929-37 and Rosales 600,000 for 1929-36, while a California legislative inquiry claimed up to 1.8 million; formal deportations numbered about 82,000.
shareCaveat: The headline figure of one million sits at the high end of a 300,000-2,000,000 range whose central scholarly estimates are closer to 350,000-600,000, so the resulting share could be overstated by a factor of two or three.

title: Soviet Dekulakization and the Special Settlements
actors: The Soviet Politburo and the OGPU expropriated and deported peasant families labelled kulaks from the grain-growing regions to closed 'special settlements' in the Urals, Siberia, Kazakhstan and the far north
peopleRange: Roughly 1.8 million people were deported in 1930-31 alone: about 560,000 in the first wave of February-May 1930 (some 115,000 families) and 1,244,000 in the wave of May-September 1931 (about 265,000 families), with further waves through 1933 bringing the total to roughly 2.1 million. Only 1,317,000 were still registered as 'specially displaced' on 1 January 1932, the shortfall of about half a million reflecting deaths and escapes. A further 284,000 people were arrested as 'first category' kulaks between February and September 1930. The figures come from OGPU and NKVD registration and transport records opened after 1989 and compiled by V. N. Zemskov, V. P. Danilov and the Memorial society; they are administrative counts rather than estimates, though they undercount those who fled before deportation.

flows.label: Ukrainian grain districts -> Narym special settlements, western Siberia
North Caucasus -> Urals special settlements
Volga region -> Northern Krai and Komi settlements

summary: Following the Politburo decision of 30 January 1930 'on measures for the liquidation of kulak households', the OGPU expropriated, arrested or deported peasant families classified as kulaks in order to break resistance to collectivization. Households in the 'first category' were shot or sent to camps, those in the 'second' were deported with their families to remote 'special settlements' under commandant supervision, and those in the 'third' were resettled on poor land within their own districts. Roughly two million people were moved between 1930 and 1933, most of them to the Urals, western Siberia, the Northern Krai and Kazakhstan, where they were set to logging, mining and land clearance with little shelter or food. Mortality in the settlements was severe, reaching about 14 per cent of the registered population in 1933 alone. The special settlement regime, with its commandant offices and travel bans, became the administrative model later applied to whole deported nationalities.
contested: Historians differ over the total deported and over how many died, because OGPU registers count only those who reached the settlements and were still registered there, and because deaths from flight, transit and the 1932-33 famine overlap.

sources.title: Memorial, Russia's Necropolis of Terror and the Gulag: The Liquidation of the Kulaks, 1930-1932
Nicolas Werth, Mass Crimes under Stalin (1930-1953), Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance
Lynne Viola, The Role of the OGPU in Dekulakization, Mass Deportation, and Resettlement in 1930, Carl Beck Papers
