deathsNote: Zemskov's registers record about 151,000 deaths among special settlers in 1933 alone, a rate of some 14 per cent, and roughly 390,000 deaths in the settlements between 1932 and 1940; Werth notes that about 500,000 of those deported in 1930-31 were lost to death or flight by January 1932. The lower bound counts registered deaths in the settlements, the higher bound adds deaths in transit, in the first unregistered months and among those who fled.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Confiscation of houses, livestock and tools, the shooting of 'first category' kulaks, and the compulsory labour regime in the settlements are documented in OGPU and NKVD operational orders and settlement reports published after 1989 by Memorial and in the Danilov-Viola document series.
baselineWhat: The rural population of the Soviet Union at the start of collectivisation
baselineNote: The 1926 Soviet census counted 147 million people, about 82 per cent of them rural, giving roughly 120 million peasants by 1930. OGPU records, published after 1991, show about 1.8-2.1 million people deported to special settlements in 1930-31 and some 2.4 million by 1933, of whom several hundred thousand died in transit or in the settlements.
shareCaveat: Those deported were drawn from a designated category of a few per cent of peasant households, so a share of the whole rural population understates how far the campaign reached inside the group it targeted.

title: The Gulag: The Soviet Forced-Labour Camp System
actors: The OGPU and later the NKVD and MVD held prisoners under sentence in a nationwide network of forced-labour camps and colonies and in exile settlements
peopleRange: About 18 million people passed through the camps and labour colonies of the Gulag between 1929 and 1953, according to the NKVD and MVD registration statistics assembled by V. N. Zemskov and summarised by Anne Applebaum, with a further six to seven million held in exile or special settlement. The camp and colony population peaked at roughly 2.5 million in early 1953. These are administrative counts from the camp administration's own annual returns; they exclude prisoners of the ordinary prison system, those shot before sentence and deportees never registered.

flows.label: Sentenced prisoners from European Russia -> Kolyma camps, Far East
Sentenced prisoners -> Vorkuta and the Arctic coal camps

summary: The Chief Administration of Camps, created in 1930, turned political and criminal imprisonment into an instrument of economic development, concentrating prisoners in remote regions to cut timber, mine gold, coal and nickel, and build canals, railways and cities. The system expanded with each wave of repression, absorbing dekulakized peasants, victims of the Great Terror, deported nationalities, Poles and Balts, returning Soviet prisoners of war and postwar nationalist insurgents. Camp records opened after 1991 show a population that peaked at about 2.5 million in 1953 and roughly 18 million passing through over two decades, alongside a parallel exile system. Recorded deaths in the camps and colonies exceed 1.6 million, concentrated in the famine year of 1933 and the war years of 1942-43. The system was wound down after Stalin's death in 1953, and the Russian Law on the Rehabilitation of Victims of Political Repression of 1991 provided for the rehabilitation of those convicted on political grounds.
contested: Estimates of total deaths differ because the camp administration's registers exclude prisoners released while dying, deaths in transit and executions carried out outside the camps.

sources.title: Britannica: Gulag
Gulag: Soviet Forced Labor Camps and the Struggle for Freedom (Gulag History project, George Mason University and the National Park Service)
Memorial, Russia's Necropolis of Terror and the Gulag

deathsNote: The lower figure is the total of deaths recorded in the camp and colony registers between 1930 and 1956, compiled by Zemskov from NKVD-MVD returns. The higher figure reflects scholars including Applebaum who add deaths in transit, deaths of prisoners released in extremis so that they would not be counted, and mortality among exiles and special settlers held under the same administration.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Compulsory labour under production quotas tied to rations, beatings and punishment isolators, executions of prisoners during the terror of 1937-38 and starvation in the war years are documented in the camp administration's own records and in the survivor testimony collected by Memorial and the Gulag History project.
baselineWhat: The population of the Soviet Union at the 1939 census
baselineNote: The 1939 census recorded 170,557,093 people, and is the only usable Soviet count near the midpoint of the Gulag's existence (the 1937 census was suppressed and its organisers shot; the 1926 census gave 147 million). Archival work since 1991, chiefly by Zemskov, Getty and Khlevniuk, established that some 18 million passed through the camps and colonies between 1930 and 1953, with several million more in exile settlements.
shareCaveat: The 18 million is a cumulative throughput across 23 years and several demographic generations, not a population held at any one time — the peak simultaneous camp and colony population was about 2.5 million — so dividing it by a single-year census exaggerates the share of any living cohort that was imprisoned.

title: The Kazakh Famine and Forced Sedentarization (Asharshylyk)
actors: Soviet authorities under Filipp Goloshchyokin confiscated livestock and forced nomadic Kazakh pastoralists into sedentary collective farms
peopleRange: Estimates of those who fled range from about 600,000, the figure Werth gives for those who left for other regions, to roughly 1.5 million in Sarah Cameron's reconstruction, of whom some 200,000 crossed into China, Mongolia, Iran and Afghanistan and many never returned. Kazakhstan's population fell by 1.7 to 2 million between 1931 and 1933. The figures rest on Soviet census comparisons of 1926 and 1937-39, republican party reports and later demographic reconstruction rather than on any count of refugees.

flows.label: Kazakh steppe -> Xinjiang, China
Kazakh steppe -> western Siberia and the Russian republic

summary: Collectivization in Kazakhstan combined grain and meat procurement with a campaign to settle the nomadic and semi-nomadic population on collective farms. Livestock, the basis of the pastoral economy, collapsed from roughly 40 million head to about 4.5 million between 1928 and 1933 through requisition, forced slaughter and disease. The resulting famine killed between 1.1 and 1.5 million people, most of them ethnic Kazakhs, a loss of roughly a third to two-fifths of the Kazakh population, and drove hundreds of thousands across the borders into China, Mongolia and beyond. Kazakhstan is the only Soviet republic whose titular nationality became a minority in its own territory as a result. The famine is officially commemorated in Kazakhstan, but the state has not sought a genocide determination, and scholars differ over whether the catastrophe was an intended outcome of sedentarization policy or a consequence of it.
contested: Whether the famine amounted to genocide against Kazakhs is disputed; Kazakhstan commemorates it as a national tragedy without a formal genocide declaration, and historians differ over intent.

sources.title: Sarah Cameron, The Hungry Steppe: Famine, Violence, and the Making of Soviet Kazakhstan (Cornell University Press)
Nicolas Werth, Mass Crimes under Stalin (1930-1953), Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance

deathsNote: Werth gives 1.1 to 1.4 million dead of hunger or epidemic disease out of a population decline of 1.7 to 2 million; Cameron's reconstruction gives about 1.5 million, of whom roughly 1.3 million were Kazakhs. The disagreement turns on how flight and unrecorded return migration are separated from mortality in the census gap.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Livestock requisition, the destruction of pastoral households and the punishment of those who resisted sedentarization are documented in republican party and OGPU records used by Cameron and Werth.
baselineWhat: The Kazakh population of Kazakhstan at the 1926 Soviet census, the last before collectivisation
baselineNote: The 1926 census counted 3,637,612 Kazakhs; projections for 1930 put the figure nearer 3.9-4.1 million. The 1937 census counted 2,181,520. Scholarly estimates put deaths at 1.3-2.3 million, that is 38-42 per cent of all Kazakhs, and flight abroad and to other Soviet republics at 665,000 to 1.1 million, of whom perhaps 200,000-400,000 never returned.
shareCaveat: The 1.1 million figure is the upper estimate of those who fled and is separate from the 1.3-2.3 million who died, so displacement and mortality should not be added together.

title: Land Apportionment, the Native Land Husbandry Act and African Removals in Southern Rhodesia
actors: The settler government of Southern Rhodesia divided land by race and moved African families off land reserved for Europeans
peopleRange: Colonial reports and later studies indicate that between the 1930s and the early 1960s something on the order of 100,000 African families were moved from European areas into Native Reserves and Native Purchase Areas; at average family sizes of the period this implies roughly half a million people. The figure is a reconstruction from Native Affairs Department annual reports and later scholarship rather than a single official count.
territoryDesc: The 1930 Act allotted about 49 million acres to roughly 50,000 Europeans and about 29 million acres of reserves to more than a million Africans, with the rest unassigned

flows.label: African families moved from European farming areas into reserves

summary: The Land Apportionment Act of 1930 gave statutory form to racial land division in Southern Rhodesia, reserving the best-watered high-veld for European ownership and confining African freehold to designated Native Purchase Areas. Africans living as tenants or squatters in newly designated European areas were served with eviction notices and moved to reserves, a process that accelerated after the Second World War as settler immigration rose. The Native Land Husbandry Act of 1951 went further, allocating individual arable and grazing rights in the reserves, compelling destocking of cattle and cutting off land rights for those working in towns; it produced widespread rural resistance and was effectively abandoned in the early 1960s. The reserves became overcrowded and eroded, and the removals are a direct antecedent of the land question that dominated Zimbabwean politics after 1980. The 1969 Land Tenure Act extended the division further and falls outside this entry's period.
contested: Estimates of how many families were moved vary because colonial records counted eviction orders rather than people, and because some movement was gradual and administratively recorded as voluntary.

sources.title: Land Apportionment Act of 1930
Origins (Ohio State): Colonial land injustices in post-independence Zimbabwe

deathsNote: There was no significant direct death toll. The harm was dispossession, impoverishment and overcrowding in the reserves rather than killing; deaths from the resulting land pressure and malnutrition were never measured.
violenceNote: Native Affairs Department records and later historical studies document evictions, hut destruction and compulsory destocking.
baselineWhat: The African population of Southern Rhodesia at the time of the Land Apportionment Act of 1930
baselineNote: Colonial estimates put the African population of Southern Rhodesia at roughly 1.1 million in 1931 alongside about 50,000 Europeans; African numbers were estimated rather than fully enumerated until the sample censuses of the 1960s. By 1962 the African population had grown to roughly 3.6 million while the land division remained essentially unchanged.
shareCaveat: The removals ran for three decades over which the African population more than tripled, so the share against a 1931 baseline overstates the proportion of the population moved at any one time.

title: Japan's Seizure of Manchuria and Agricultural Settlement
actors: The Japanese Kwantung Army seized Manchuria, installed the puppet state of Manchukuo and settled Japanese farmers on land taken from Chinese cultivators
peopleRange: Japan planned to send one million households, roughly five million people, to Manchuria over twenty years from 1936; in the event about 270,000 to 320,000 Japanese agricultural settlers went, including 86,530 members of the Patriotic Youth Brigade between 1938 and 1945. The land they received was largely bought under compulsion or expropriated from Chinese and Korean cultivators through the Manchuria Colonization Company, displacing an uncounted but far larger number of Chinese farmers; the Kwantung Army also forced villagers in guerrilla districts into fortified 'collective hamlets'. Settler figures come from Japanese colonization ministry records; the displacement of Chinese cultivators was never systematically counted.
territoryDesc: The three northeastern provinces of China, about 1.3 million square kilometres, were detached from Chinese authority after the Mukden incident of 18 September 1931 and constituted as Manchukuo in March 1932 under the last Qing emperor Puyi, with Jehol added in 1933. Japan controlled the state through the Kwantung Army and Japanese officials until the Soviet invasion of August 1945.

flows.label: Nagano and other Japanese prefectures -> settlement villages in northern Manchuria

summary: Officers of the Kwantung Army staged an explosion on the South Manchurian Railway near Mukden on 18 September 1931 and used it as the pretext for occupying Manchuria, which was constituted the following year as the nominally independent state of Manchukuo. The League of Nations commission under Lord Lytton found in 1932 that the Japanese action could not be justified as self-defence and that Manchukuo did not rest on a genuine independence movement; when the League adopted the report in February 1933 Japan withdrew from the organisation. From 1936 Japan pursued a mass colonisation programme intended to place a million farming households in Manchuria, backed by a company that acquired land cheaply or by compulsion from Chinese cultivators, and by youth brigades of teenage boys. Around 270,000 settlers had gone by 1945. When the Soviet Union invaded in August 1945 the Kwantung Army withdrew southward and left the settler communities behind: of the more than 200,000 still in Manchuria, some 78,500 died in attacks, suicides, disease, starvation and exposure, and thousands of children were left with Chinese families. The repatriation of the survivors is treated separately.
contested: Japan maintained until 1945 that Manchukuo was an independent state responding to local self-determination, a claim the Lytton Commission and the Tokyo tribunal rejected; the scale of Chinese dispossession by the colonisation programme has never been quantified.

sources.title: Britannica: Manchukuo
Kevin McDowell, Japan in Manchuria: Agricultural Emigration in the Japanese Empire, 1932-1945, Eras (Monash University)
Nippon.com: Nagano museum relates hardships of Japanese agricultural emigrants to Manchuria

deathsNote: About 78,500 Japanese settlers died in 1945-46 during the Soviet invasion and the flight south, a figure from Japanese repatriation and prefectural records. Chinese deaths under the occupation of Manchuria - in the suppression of resistance, in forced labour on Japanese projects, and in the biological warfare experiments of Unit 731 near Harbin - are far less well counted; estimates for Chinese civilian deaths in the northeast across the whole occupation run into the hundreds of thousands.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: League of Nations Commission of Enquiry (Lytton Commission)
atrocityFindings.finding: Reported in 1932 that Japanese military action in Manchuria could not be regarded as self-defence and that Manchukuo was not the product of a genuine independence movement; the League adopted the report in February 1933

atrocityFindings.body: International Military Tribunal for the Far East
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that the seizure of Manchuria in 1931 was an act of aggressive war and part of a conspiracy to dominate East Asia

violenceNote: Compulsory land acquisition for settlers, forced concentration of villagers into guarded hamlets, conscripted labour on military construction and the killing of suspected resisters are documented in Japanese colonial administrative records and in the findings of the Tokyo tribunal.
baselineWhat: The population of Manchuria, the three northeastern provinces, when Japan seized it
baselineNote: Estimates for 1930-31 run at roughly 30-34 million, the great majority Han Chinese who had migrated from Shandong and Hebei over the preceding half century. The Manchukuo census of 1940 counted about 43 million, a rise driven by continued Chinese in-migration as well as Japanese and Korean settlement.
shareCaveat: Manchuria's population grew by roughly a third during the occupation through continued Chinese migration, so a 1931 denominator is unstable across the event's span.

title: The Japanese Military 'Comfort Women' System
actors: The Japanese armed forces established and regulated brothels in which women, most of them Korean and Chinese, were held for sexual servitude
peopleRange: Estimates of the number of women held in the comfort stations range from about 20,000, the figure argued by the Japanese historian Hata Ikuhiko, to 200,000 or more, the figure used by Korean and Chinese researchers and by campaigners; figures around 50,000 to 100,000 are common in the intermediate scholarship. Most were Korean, with large numbers of Chinese and smaller numbers of Taiwanese, Filipino, Indonesian, Burmese and Dutch women; the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation records 200 to 300 European women forced into prostitution in the Dutch East Indies and Indonesian victims of sexual violence numbering between 22,234 and 60,000 in different estimates. The wide range reflects the destruction of Japanese military records in 1945 and disagreement over what counts as coercion.

flows.label: Korea -> comfort stations in occupied China
Korea -> comfort stations in Southeast Asia

summary: From the early 1930s, and on a large scale after 1937, the Japanese armed forces set up 'comfort stations' at bases across China, Southeast Asia and the Pacific, staffed by women recruited through deception, debt, official pressure or outright abduction and held under military regulation. On 4 August 1993 Chief Cabinet Secretary Yohei Kono issued a statement acknowledging that the military had been directly or indirectly involved in the establishment and management of the stations, that recruitment was largely by private agents but often against the women's will, and that they had lived in misery under a coercive atmosphere; the statement extended apologies and remorse. In 1996 the United Nations Special Rapporteur on violence against women, Radhika Coomaraswamy, reported on the system as military sexual slavery and recommended state compensation. Japan created the Asian Women's Fund in 1995 to make payments from private donations with government support, an arrangement many survivors rejected as a way of avoiding state legal responsibility. A Japan-Republic of Korea agreement of December 2015 declared the issue resolved finally and irreversibly and provided a one-billion-yen Japanese contribution to a Korean foundation; the foundation was dissolved by Korea in 2018 and the dispute continues, with Seoul courts reaching opposing conclusions on Japan's sovereign immunity in 2021.
contested: Japan's government acknowledges military involvement and has apologised through the Kono Statement while disputing the term 'sexual slavery', the estimate of 200,000 victims and claims of systematic forcible abduction by officials; Korean, Chinese and many international bodies characterise the system as military sexual slavery and hold that Japan's legal responsibility is unsettled.

sources.title: Statement by the Chief Cabinet Secretary Yohei Kono on the result of the study on the issue of comfort women, 4 August 1993 (Asian Women's Fund digital museum)
Asian Women's Fund digital museum: the comfort women issue and the Asian Women's Fund
Report of the UN Special Rapporteur on violence against women, Radhika Coomaraswamy, on military sexual slavery in wartime, E/CN.4/1996/53/Add.1
NIOD Institute for War, Holocaust and Genocide Studies: the Japanese occupation and the Pacific War in numbers

deathsNote: No count of deaths exists. Women died of disease, violence, suicide and abandonment in war zones, and many did not return home, but the destruction of records and the shame that kept survivors silent for decades make any figure speculative. The harm of the system was primarily prolonged sexual violence and confinement rather than a countable death toll.

atrocityFindings.body: Government of Japan (Chief Cabinet Secretary Yohei Kono)
atrocityFindings.finding: Acknowledged in the statement of 4 August 1993 that the Japanese military was directly or indirectly involved in establishing and managing comfort stations, that women were in many cases recruited against their will and lived in coercive conditions, and extended apologies and remorse

atrocityFindings.body: United Nations Commission on Human Rights, Special Rapporteur on violence against women
atrocityFindings.finding: Reported in 1996 that the comfort stations constituted military sexual slavery in violation of international law and recommended that Japan accept legal responsibility and pay compensation to survivors

atrocityFindings.body: International Military Tribunal for the Far East and Allied national tribunals
atrocityFindings.finding: The Batavia court-martial of 1948 convicted Japanese officers of forcing Dutch women in Java into prostitution; the Tokyo tribunal recorded mass rape by Japanese forces as a war crime

violenceNote: The military's role in establishing and regulating the stations, the methods of recruitment and the confinement of the women are documented in surviving Japanese military and police records cited in the Kono Statement, in the Batavia trial records and in the survivor testimony collected by the UN Special Rapporteur.
baselineNote: No single denominator exists. The women were taken from colonial Korea and Taiwan, occupied China, the Philippines, the Netherlands Indies, Burma and elsewhere, so there is no one population from which the system drew. The numerator itself is contested: Japanese scholars' estimates range from about 20,000 (Hata) to 50,000-200,000 (Yoshimi), and no register of the system survives.

title: The Holodomor: Famine in Soviet Ukraine
actors: Soviet party and state organs seized grain, blacklisted villages and closed the borders of Ukraine and the Kuban to starving peasants
peopleRange: The defining act was holding a starving population in place rather than moving it. Under the directive of 22 January 1933 signed by Stalin and Molotov, which banned peasants from leaving Ukraine and the North Caucasus, about 220,000 people were intercepted by the OGPU by mid-March 1933 and roughly 190,000 were sent back to their villages; the internal passport system introduced on 27 December 1932 denied passports to collective farmers and so bound them to the countryside, and blacklisted villages were cut off from all goods. The interception figures come from OGPU reports published from the Soviet archives.
summary: Grain procurement quotas set far above what the 1932 harvest could yield were enforced in Soviet Ukraine and the Kuban by requisition brigades that confiscated seed grain and other foodstuffs, while villages that failed to meet quotas were 'blacklisted' and cut off from supply. The decree of 22 January 1933 sealed the republic's borders against peasants seeking food, and the internal passport system introduced weeks earlier tied collective farmers to their villages. Demographic reconstructions put excess deaths in Ukraine at roughly 3.5 to 5 million in 1932-33, within a Soviet-wide famine toll of at least 5 to 7 million that also devastated Kazakhstan, the Volga and the Kuban. The famine was denied by the Soviet state, excluded from the 1937 census results and not publicly acknowledged until 1986-87. Whether it constituted genocide against Ukrainians is a live political and scholarly dispute: Ukraine, the European Parliament, the German Bundestag and more than thirty other states and parliaments have declared it genocide, while the Russian government rejects that characterization and describes the famine as a shared tragedy of the peoples of the USSR.
contested: Whether the famine in Ukraine was a genocide directed at Ukrainians as a national group, or a Soviet-wide catastrophe of collectivization that struck Ukraine hardest, is disputed between Ukraine and many Western parliaments on one side and the Russian government and some historians on the other.

sources.title: Britannica: Holodomor
European Parliament resolution of 15 December 2022, '90 years after the Holodomor'
German Bundestag debate and resolution on the Holodomor, November 2022
National Museum of the Holodomor-Genocide, Kyiv: Why does Russia still deny the Holodomor?
Nicolas Werth, Mass Crimes under Stalin (1930-1953), Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance

deathsNote: The range is for Ukraine. Britannica cites a demographic study finding at least 3.9 million Ukrainian deaths; Werth gives 4 to 4.5 million for Ukraine and the Kuban together; the lower bound of about 3.5 million reflects the reconstructions of R. W. Davies and Stephen Wheatcroft, the higher figures those of Ukrainian demographers and of scholars who add unborn children. Soviet-wide famine deaths in 1931-34 are put at 5 to 7 million, including 1.1 to 1.5 million in Kazakhstan and 300,000 to 400,000 in the Volga region. All figures are reconstructions from census and registration data, since deaths were deliberately under-recorded.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: European Parliament
atrocityFindings.finding: Recognised the Holodomor as a genocide against the Ukrainian people, by 507 votes to 12, and called on other states to do the same

atrocityFindings.body: German Bundestag
atrocityFindings.finding: Adopted a cross-party motion in November 2022 classifying the Holodomor as genocide

violenceNote: Grain and food confiscation, the blacklisting of villages, and the police cordon that returned fleeing peasants are documented in Soviet party and OGPU directives published from the archives and cited by Werth and by the European Parliament resolution.
baselineWhat: The population of the Ukrainian SSR at the start of the famine
baselineNote: The 1926 Soviet census counted 29.0 million in the Ukrainian SSR and Soviet statistical estimates for the beginning of 1933 give about 31.9 million. The 1937 census, which recorded the resulting deficit, was suppressed and its organisers shot; its recovered returns underpin modern estimates of excess mortality.
shareCaveat: The Kuban, blockaded under the same decrees and heavily Ukrainian-speaking, lay outside the Ukrainian SSR and so outside this denominator; and excess deaths in Ukraine are estimated by demographers at 3.5-5 million, far above the figure carried in this entry.

title: La Matanza: the 1932 Massacre in Western El Salvador
actors: The Salvadoran military government suppressed a peasant and communist uprising by killing Pipil villagers across the western coffee districts
peopleRange: No count of people displaced exists. Survivors fled the western departments and many abandoned Pipil dress and language; some crossed into Guatemala and Honduras, but the flight was never registered. The killing itself is estimated at between 10,000 and 40,000 dead, with the most commonly used range 10,000-30,000, resting on contemporary diplomatic reporting, church records and later oral history rather than on any official count.

flows.label: Survivors fleeing the western departments toward Guatemala

summary: On 22 January 1932, amid the collapse of coffee prices and after the annulment of municipal and legislative election results, members of the Communist Party of El Salvador and Pipil peasants led by Farabundo Marti and Feliciano Ama rose in the western departments, seizing several towns and killing an estimated 2,000 people in the process. The government of General Maximiliano Hernandez Martinez declared martial law and put down the revolt within days, then carried out weeks of reprisal killings in which soldiers and civilian patrols executed men in and around the villages of Izalco, Nahuizalco, Juayua and Sonzacate, frequently identifying victims by indigenous dress, features or surnames. Estimates of the dead range from 10,000 to 40,000; because the victims were overwhelmingly Pipil non-combatants and because Pipil language and dress were largely abandoned afterwards, many scholars describe the killing as an ethnocide, though others emphasise its class and political character. Marti and Ama were executed. The episode became foundational to Salvadoran politics on both left and right; the guerrilla front of the 1980s took Marti's name, and the state offered no official reckoning for decades.
contested: The death toll is disputed across a wide range, with recent scholarship by historians including Erik Ching and Hector Lindo-Fuentes arguing for figures nearer the lower end than the 30,000 long cited; the characterisation of the killing as ethnocide or genocide as against political repression is also debated.

sources.title: La Matanza / 1932 Salvadoran peasant massacre (Wikipedia)

deathsNote: No official count was made. Contemporary estimates by foreign diplomats and clergy, later government-linked accounts and oral testimony collected from the 1970s produce a range of 10,000 to 40,000; the higher figures originate largely in later political usage, while recent archival work has tended to argue for the lower end. Around 2,000 people were killed by the rebels during the uprising itself.
violenceNote: Mass shootings and summary executions of villagers, and the targeting of people identifiable as indigenous by dress and language, are documented in contemporary diplomatic and church reporting and in the oral histories gathered by later Salvadoran and foreign historians.
baselineWhat: The population of El Salvador at the 1930 census
baselineNote: The 1930 Salvadoran census recorded about 1.44 million inhabitants. The killing was concentrated in the western coffee departments of Sonsonate, Ahuachapán, Santa Ana and La Libertad and fell overwhelmingly on Pipil (Nahua) communities, but the Indigenous share of the population is itself contested — census categories were based on dress and language and the state had an interest in minimising them — so no defensible Pipil denominator exists.

title: The Nazi Concentration Camp System before the War
actors: The SS and German police held political opponents, and then people classified as social, racial and religious undesirables, in camps outside judicial control
peopleRange: At least 100 early camps and detention sites were opened across Germany in 1933, holding roughly 45,000 to 50,000 people in that year alone under 'protective detention'. After consolidation under the SS the system comprised six main camps by 1939 - Dachau, Sachsenhausen, Buchenwald, Flossenbuerg, Mauthausen and Ravensbrueck - with a prisoner population of about 21,000 in the summer of 1939. Cumulatively, on the order of 200,000 people passed through the prewar camps, including some 30,000 Jewish men arrested after Kristallnacht in November 1938. The figures come from the camp administrations' own records and from the Museum's encyclopedia of camps and ghettos.
summary: Detention camps appeared in Germany within weeks of Hitler's appointment as chancellor in January 1933, initially run by the SA, the police and local authorities to hold communists, social democrats and trade unionists under 'protective detention' outside any court process. Dachau, opened in March 1933, became the model for a system that Heinrich Himmler consolidated under the SS Inspectorate of Concentration Camps. From 1936 the categories of prisoner widened to include Roma, Jehovah's Witnesses, homosexual men, repeat offenders and people labelled 'asocial', held for indefinite terms and marked with coloured triangles. Camps were sited to exploit prisoner labour in SS-owned quarries and brickworks. After the annexation of Austria and Kristallnacht in 1938 tens of thousands of Jewish men were seized and held for weeks or months, most being released on condition that they emigrate. The prewar system established the legal void, the labour regime and the personnel on which the wartime camps and killing centres were built.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Concentration Camps, 1933-1939
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Nazi Camps
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Dachau

deathsNote: Deaths in the prewar camps ran to several thousand, from beatings, shootings 'while attempting escape', suicide and disease; there was no systematic killing programme before the war. Camp death registers are incomplete and the range reflects differing treatment of deaths shortly after release.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Detention without judicial process, systematic beatings and punishment regimes, forced labour in SS enterprises and killings in custody are documented in camp records, Gestapo files and survivor testimony summarised by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.
baselineWhat: The population of Germany within its 1937 borders on the eve of the war
baselineNote: The May 1939 census counted about 69.3 million people in the Altreich and 79.4 million in the Greater German Reich including Austria and the Sudetenland. The pre-war camps drew from specific targeted groups within that population — Communists and Social Democrats, Jehovah's Witnesses, Jews, Roma, homosexual men and people classed as 'asocial' — rather than from the population at large.

title: Nazi Persecution of German Jews and the Refugee Exodus
actors: The German state stripped Jews of citizenship, employment and property, driving emigration that other states then restricted by quota
peopleRange: Of roughly 522,000 Jews living in Germany in January 1933, about 304,000 had emigrated by the outbreak of war in September 1939; from Austria, annexed in March 1938, roughly 117,000 of about 185,000 Jews had left by the same date. Around 10,000 children reached Britain on Kindertransport trains between December 1938 and September 1939. The figures come from German population statistics, Jewish community registers and refugee organisation records compiled by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.

flows.label: Germany and Austria -> Britain
Germany and Austria -> United States
Vienna -> Mandatory Palestine

summary: From April 1933 German law progressively excluded Jews from the civil service, the professions, education and the economy; the Nuremberg Laws of September 1935 removed their citizenship and criminalised marriage and sexual relations with 'Germans or kindred blood'. Expropriation accelerated after 1937, and in October 1938 about 17,000 Jews of Polish citizenship were expelled from Germany in the Polenaktion, many being stranded in the no man's land at Zbaszyn. The pogrom of 9-10 November 1938 destroyed hundreds of synagogues and thousands of businesses, killed at least 91 people and sent some 30,000 Jewish men to concentration camps, after which emigration became flight. Receiving states largely kept their doors narrow: the Evian conference of July 1938 produced no significant new quotas, the United States left its German quota partly unfilled, and in June 1939 the liner St. Louis was turned away from Cuba and the United States. Britain admitted about 10,000 unaccompanied children while restricting Jewish immigration to Palestine under the 1939 White Paper. Roughly two in five of the Jews who fled Germany and Austria found refuge in countries that Germany later occupied.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: The Nuremberg Race Laws
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: German Jewish Refugees, 1933-1939
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Kristallnacht
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: The Evian Conference
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Voyage of the St. Louis

deathsNote: At least 91 Jews were killed outright in the November 1938 pogrom, and several hundred more of the roughly 30,000 men then arrested died in the concentration camps in the following weeks; suicides in Germany and Austria in 1938-39 added several hundred more. Mass killing began only after the war started, so the toll of the prewar persecution itself was in the hundreds rather than the thousands.
violenceNote: The stripping of citizenship under the 1935 laws, the expropriation and destruction of Jewish property and synagogues in November 1938, and the mass arrests that followed are documented in German legal texts, police and insurance records, and the diplomatic reporting summarised by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of Germany when Hitler took power
baselineNote: The census of June 1933 counted 499,682 people of the Jewish faith in Germany, and the usual working figure including those defined as Jews by the Nuremberg Laws but not religiously affiliated is about 525,000. Austria added roughly 185,000 in March 1938 and the Czech lands about 118,000 in 1939. Roughly 300,000-330,000 Jews left Germany before the war and about 117,000 left Austria, so the combined outflow of about 400,000 is drawn from a wider base than the 1933 German figure.

baselineSources.title: History of the Jews in Germany — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The affected figure includes refugees from Austria and the Czech lands who are not in the 1933 German baseline, so the ratio overstates the share of German Jews who escaped; measured against the combined German and Austrian population of about 710,000 it is closer to 56 per cent.

title: The Simele Massacre and the Dispersal of Iraq's Assyrians
actors: The Iraqi army and allied irregulars killed Assyrian villagers in and around Simele, driving survivors into Syria
peopleRange: League of Nations and British records give roughly 600 to 3,000 Assyrians killed in Simele and some 60-100 surrounding villages in August 1933, with looting and destruction across the Dohuk and Zakho districts; several thousand fled immediately into French-mandate Syria, and the League of Nations subsequently organised the settlement of about 9,000-20,000 Assyrians along the Khabur river in Syria between 1935 and 1937. Figures come from League of Nations commission reports, British Royal Air Force and consular reporting, and Assyrian church records; the totals are small compared with most events in this atlas and are stated as recorded.

flows.label: Assyrian survivors resettled on the Khabur in Syria under League of Nations arrangements

summary: Assyrians displaced from Hakkari during the First World War had been settled in northern Iraq under British mandate and many served in the Iraq Levies; after Iraqi independence in 1932 their demands for autonomy and their association with British power made them politically exposed. In August 1933, after an armed clash near the Syrian border, Iraqi army units under Bakr Sidqi and allied Kurdish and Arab irregulars killed Assyrian villagers in Simele and dozens of surrounding villages, with League of Nations and British reports giving figures from 600 to 3,000 dead and describing summary executions of unarmed men. Survivors fled to Syria, and the League of Nations, which had guaranteed minority protection in Iraq, arranged their settlement on the Khabur river; the massacre and the League's failure to protect a minority it had underwritten contributed directly to Raphael Lemkin's formulation of the concept that became genocide, which he first presented to a legal conference in Madrid in 1933. Bakr Sidqi was feted in Baghdad and went on to lead a coup in 1936. Iraq has never conducted an official inquiry; the Iraqi Kurdistan parliament recognised the massacre in 2013 and Assyrian organisations mark 7 August as a memorial day. The scale of the killing is far smaller than most events in this atlas, and it is included for its role as a template of state violence against a minority and for the dispersal it began.
contested: The death toll ranges from about 600 in conservative League of Nations reporting to 3,000 or more in Assyrian accounts, and Iraqi accounts of the time presented the operation as the suppression of an armed rebellion.

sources.title: Simele massacre
Assyrians in Iraq
Raphael Lemkin and the origins of the concept of genocide, United States Holocaust Memorial Museum

deathsNote: The low figure is the count in British and League of Nations reporting immediately after the events; the high figure comes from Assyrian community sources and later accounts that include killings in outlying villages over the following weeks. No forensic investigation was carried out.

atrocityFindings.body: Kurdistan Regional Government parliament (Iraq)
atrocityFindings.finding: Formally recognised the 1933 killings of Assyrians at Simele as a massacre and designated 7 August as a day of commemoration in the Kurdistan Region.

violenceNote: League of Nations commission reports and British consular and Royal Air Force reporting documented the summary execution of unarmed Assyrian men and the looting and destruction of villages.
baselineWhat: The Assyrian population of Iraq at the time of the Simele massacre
baselineNote: League of Nations mandate records put the Assyrian refugee community resettled in northern Iraq from Hakkari and Urmia after the First World War at roughly 20,000-25,000; adding the longer-established Assyrian and Chaldean communities of the Mosul region gives a total of about 40,000, though definitions of who counted as Assyrian rather than Chaldean varied between the British administration, the Iraqi state and the churches. Iraq's 1932 population estimate did not enumerate the community separately.
shareCaveat: The 25,000 aggregates those killed with the far larger number displaced across 1933-37, including the roughly 9,000 who were settled along the Khabur in Syria, so it measures the dispersal of the community rather than the death toll, which is usually put in the hundreds to low thousands.

title: Turkey's Settlement Law and the Dersim Operations
actors: The Turkish state used the 1934 Settlement Law and emergency rule to disperse Kurdish and Alevi populations and suppressed Dersim by military operation
peopleRange: An unpublished Inspectorate report cited by Sciences Po's Mass Violence and Resistance project records 11,818 people deported from Dersim, and the Council of Ministers ordered on 6 August 1938 the removal of a further 5,000 to 7,000 people from prohibited zones to the west. Under the Settlement Law of 21 June 1934, which allowed the state to depopulate areas for cultural, political or military reasons and to resettle populations by degree of assimilation, tens of thousands of Kurds were moved westward in the 1930s. The figures rest on Turkish administrative and military records, most of which remained closed for decades, and on census comparisons.

flows.label: Dersim (Tunceli) -> forced resettlement in western Anatolia

summary: The Settlement Law of June 1934 authorised the Turkish government to move populations for cultural, political or military reasons and classified regions by the degree of assimilation required of their inhabitants, providing the legal basis for dispersing Kurdish communities westward. In December 1935 the Tunceli Law placed the province of Dersim, largely Kurdish-speaking and Alevi, under military emergency administration and renamed it. Military operations in the spring of 1937, following an armed clash, and a far larger campaign in August and September 1938 subdued the region: villages were bombed and burned, and inhabitants were killed or deported. An unpublished official Inspectorate report cited by scholars gives 13,160 civilians killed and 11,818 deported; Alevi and Kurdish accounts give higher figures, some in the tens of thousands. The subject was taboo in Turkey for decades. In November 2009 Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan publicly described the events as a massacre, and in November 2011 he apologised in parliament, citing archival records of 13,806 people killed, while opposition parties disputed his use of the episode against them. The Turkish state has held no judicial inquiry.
contested: The number killed is disputed between the official Inspectorate figure of about 13,160 cited by Erdogan in 2011 and Kurdish and Alevi accounts giving figures several times higher; whether the operations constituted genocide is argued by Kurdish organisations and rejected by the Turkish state.

sources.title: Martin van Bruinessen and others, Dersim Massacre, 1937-1938, Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance
Al Jazeera: Erdogan apologises to Kurds for mass killing, 24 November 2011
Hurriyet Daily News: First official apology for killings in Dersim

deathsNote: The lower figure comes from an unpublished Turkish Inspectorate report and is close to the 13,806 cited by Prime Minister Erdogan from state archives in 2011. Kurdish and Alevi organisations and some researchers give figures of 40,000 or more, counting deaths during the deportations and in the depopulated highlands. Turkish military archives on the operations have only partially been opened.

atrocityFindings.body: Prime Minister of Turkey (Recep Tayyip Erdogan)
atrocityFindings.finding: Stated in parliament on 23 November 2011, citing state archives, that 13,806 people had been killed in the Dersim operations, described the events as a massacre and apologised on behalf of the state

violenceNote: Aerial and artillery bombardment of villages, the burning of settlements, the deportation of survivors under the Settlement Law and the placement of Dersimi children with Turkish families are documented in Turkish military and administrative records examined by the researchers of the Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance project.
baselineWhat: The population of Dersim, renamed Tunceli province, at the 1935 Turkish census
baselineNote: The 1935 general census, taken the year the province was placed under the special Tunceli Law, recorded roughly 108,000 inhabitants, overwhelmingly Kurmanji- and Zazaki-speaking Alevis. The wider 1934 Settlement Law applied to Kurdish populations across the east - the same census recorded about 1.48 million Kurdish mother-tongue speakers nationally - but the deportations counted here were concentrated on Dersim.
shareCaveat: The denominator covers Dersim alone, while the Settlement Law dispersed Kurdish populations well beyond the province, so the share measures the Dersim operations rather than the whole programme.

title: Italy's Invasion of Ethiopia and the Addis Ababa Massacre
actors: Fascist Italy invaded and annexed Ethiopia, used chemical weapons against its forces and population, and massacred civilians in Addis Ababa in reprisal
peopleRange: No reliable count exists of Ethiopians displaced. The imperial family and government went into exile in 1936, tens of thousands fled the bombing and gas attacks of 1935-36 and the reprisals of 1937, and Italian plans envisaged settling large numbers of Italian colonists, of whom perhaps 100,000 had arrived in Italian East Africa by 1939. Displacement figures rest on Italian colonial administration records and later estimates rather than on any registration.
territoryDesc: Ethiopia, about 1.1 million square kilometres, was annexed on 9 May 1936 and merged with Eritrea and Italian Somaliland into Italian East Africa, with Victor Emmanuel III proclaimed emperor. Italian rule collapsed in 1941 when British and Ethiopian forces retook the country and Haile Selassie returned.

flows.label: Ethiopian imperial government -> exile in Britain, 1936

summary: Italy invaded Ethiopia from Eritrea and Somaliland on 3 October 1935 without declaration of war. Italian forces used mustard gas sprayed from aircraft against Ethiopian troops, civilians, livestock and water sources, in violation of the 1925 Geneva Protocol to which Italy was a party, and bombed field hospitals marked with the Red Cross. Addis Ababa fell in May 1936 and the country was annexed to Italian East Africa. The League of Nations condemned the invasion and imposed limited economic sanctions that excluded oil and were abandoned in 1936, an episode widely seen as demonstrating the League's ineffectiveness. Resistance continued, and after an attempt on the life of the viceroy Rodolfo Graziani on 19 February 1937, Italian soldiers, Blackshirts and civilians killed Ethiopians in Addis Ababa over three days in the massacre known as Yekatit 12; Ian Campbell's reconstruction from Italian, Ethiopian and diplomatic sources puts the dead at roughly 19,000 to 20,000, against Ethiopian claims of 30,000 and much lower Italian figures. Reprisals extended to the massacre of the monastic community of Debre Libanos in May 1937. No Italian was ever tried: Ethiopia's request for extradition of Italian officers after the war was not granted by the Allies.
contested: The death toll of the Addis Ababa massacre ranges from Italian estimates in the low thousands through Ian Campbell's roughly 19,000 to the Ethiopian figure of 30,000; Italy has never prosecuted those responsible for the gas attacks or the massacres, and the Italian state long minimised the use of chemical weapons, which was officially admitted only in 1996.

sources.title: Britannica: Italo-Ethiopian War, 1935-36
Ian Campbell, The Addis Ababa Massacre: Italy's National Shame (Hurst Publishers)
Museo delle Civilta, Rome: Yekatit 12

deathsNote: Ethiopian deaths across the invasion and occupation of 1935-41 are estimated between about 150,000 and 760,000; the Ethiopian government's postwar claim to the reparations commission was 760,000, while more conservative estimates count roughly 275,000 combatant and civilian deaths in the war of 1935-36 plus tens of thousands in the reprisals of 1937 and the guerrilla war. The Addis Ababa massacre of February 1937 accounts for an estimated 19,000 to 30,000 of the total, depending on the source. Italian deaths were far lower. All figures rest on estimates rather than registration.

atrocityFindings.body: League of Nations
atrocityFindings.finding: Condemned the Italian invasion of Ethiopia as a breach of the Covenant in 1935 and imposed economic sanctions on Italy

violenceNote: The use of mustard gas against troops and civilians, the killing of civilians in Addis Ababa in February 1937, the massacre of the clergy of Debre Libanos and the destruction of churches and villages are documented in Italian military orders and colonial records, in contemporary diplomatic and Red Cross reporting, and in Ian Campbell's archival reconstruction.
baselineWhat: The population of Ethiopia at the time of the Italian invasion
baselineNote: Ethiopia had no census before 1984; McEvedy and Jones and Italian colonial estimates put the population at roughly 10-12 million in the 1930s. Estimates of Ethiopian deaths from the war and occupation range from about 350,000 to the Ethiopian government's post-war claim of 760,000; the Yekatit 12 reprisal in Addis Ababa in February 1937 killed between 3,000 and 30,000 people over three days depending on the source, and was followed by the massacre at Debre Libanos.

title: The 1936-1939 Arab Revolt in Palestine and its Suppression
actors: British Mandate forces suppressed a Palestinian Arab revolt with collective punishment, house demolitions and mass detention, amid communal violence between Arabs and Jews
peopleRange: No refugee count was made. British Mandate records document the demolition of some 2,000 houses over the revolt, including the dynamiting of much of the old city of Jaffa in June 1936, which rendered several thousand people homeless - British estimates gave about 6,000 residents affected while the Palestine Arab authorities said far more - and the internment of roughly 9,000 people by 1939. Matthew Hughes's study of British records estimates that a substantial share of the adult male Palestinian Arab population was killed, wounded, imprisoned or exiled. The figures come from Mandate government reports, the Peel Commission and later archival research.
summary: A general strike and then armed revolt against British rule, Jewish immigration and land sales began in Palestine in April 1936, lapsed after the strike ended in October, and resumed as a full rural insurgency from 1937 to 1939. Britain deployed some 20,000-25,000 troops, imposed collective fines, curfews and administrative detention, demolished houses on a large scale - most conspicuously the dynamiting of a swathe of the old city of Jaffa in June 1936, presented as urban improvement and challenged unsuccessfully in the Mandate courts - and used punitive village searches and 'human shield' practices documented by Matthew Hughes from British military records. The Palestinian leadership was arrested or driven into exile, the Arab Higher Committee outlawed, and the revolt also produced substantial internal Palestinian violence against suspected collaborators. Estimates of the dead vary: around 5,000 Palestinian Arabs, several hundred Jews and around 260 British on standard reckonings, with Walid Khalidi and Hughes arguing for higher Arab figures. The Peel Commission of 1937 recommended partition with a compulsory transfer of population, the first official proposal of its kind, and the 1939 White Paper restricted Jewish immigration and land purchase. The suppression left Palestinian Arab political and military capacity severely weakened on the eve of the 1947-49 war.
contested: Death tolls are contested, with estimates for Palestinian Arab dead ranging from about 3,000 to over 5,000 and disagreement over how many were killed by British forces as opposed to in internal Palestinian factional violence; the characterisation of British methods is debated among historians.

sources.title: 1936-1939 Arab revolt in Palestine
Matthew Hughes, Britain's Pacification of Palestine (Cambridge University Press)
Peel Commission report, 1937

deathsNote: The lower figure follows British Mandate returns of Arab dead, which recorded around 3,000-5,000 killed by security forces and in intercommunal and intra-Palestinian violence, plus roughly 500 Jewish and 260 British dead. The higher figure comes from Walid Khalidi's and Matthew Hughes's assessments, which count deaths under-recorded by the Mandate administration, particularly in rural punitive operations.
violenceNote: Matthew Hughes's research in British military and colonial archives, and contemporary Mandate court proceedings over the Jaffa demolitions, documented punitive house destruction, mass administrative detention, beatings in custody and summary killings during village searches.
baselineWhat: The Palestinian Arab population of Mandate Palestine at the outbreak of the revolt
baselineNote: The 1931 mandate census counted 858,708 Arabs, Muslim and Christian, and government estimates for 1936 give about 950,000-980,000. The Jewish population at the same date was roughly 380,000, having risen sharply with the immigration of 1933-36 that helped trigger the revolt.

title: The Porajmos: Nazi Genocide of Roma and Sinti
actors: Nazi Germany and its allies registered, interned, deported and killed Roma and Sinti across occupied Europe
peopleRange: Roma and Sinti were first confined in municipal Zigeunerlager in Germany and Austria from 1936, then deported: about 2,500 from western Germany to the Lublin district in May 1940, 5,007 from Austria to the Lodz ghetto in autumn 1941, and around 23,000 to the so-called Gypsy family camp at Auschwitz-Birkenau from February 1943. Tens of thousands more were interned by Romania in Transnistria, by the Independent State of Croatia at Jasenovac and by Vichy France. Cumulative confinement figures on the order of 100,000 rest on camp registers, deportation lists and the reconstructions summarised by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.

flows.label: Austria -> Lodz ghetto, autumn 1941
Germany and occupied Europe -> Auschwitz-Birkenau family camp
Romania -> deportation to Transnistria

summary: Roma and Sinti were persecuted in Germany from 1933 under vagrancy and 'asocial' laws, then racially defined by the Reich Central Office for the Combating of the Gypsy Nuisance and the research unit of Robert Ritter, and confined from 1936 in municipal camps such as Marzahn in Berlin. Deportations began in 1940. In the occupied Soviet territories the Einsatzgruppen shot at least 30,000 Roma alongside Jews. Himmler's decree of 16 December 1942 sent about 23,000 Roma to a separate family camp at Auschwitz-Birkenau, where roughly 21,000 died of disease, starvation and gassing, including between 4,200 and 4,300 killed in a single night on 2 August 1944. Romania deported some 25,000 Roma to Transnistria, where about half died, and the Independent State of Croatia killed most of its Roma population at Jasenovac. Estimates of the total killed run from at least 250,000 to around 500,000. Survivors were long excluded from West German compensation on the ground that they had been detained for policing rather than racial reasons; Chancellor Helmut Schmidt formally acknowledged the genocide in March 1982.
contested: The total is uncertain because prewar Roma populations were never accurately counted and many killings, particularly in the occupied Soviet Union and the Balkans, were recorded without distinguishing Roma victims.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Genocide of European Roma (Gypsies), 1939-1945
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Auschwitz

deathsNote: The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives at least 250,000 European Roma killed, with a possible total of around 500,000. The range reflects missing prewar population data, the frequent recording of Roma victims simply as partisans or asocials, and disagreement over whether deaths in Romanian, Croatian and Hungarian custody are counted in full.

atrocityFindings.body: Federal Republic of Germany (Chancellor Helmut Schmidt)
atrocityFindings.finding: Formally acknowledged in March 1982 that the crimes committed against German Roma and Sinti constituted genocide

violenceNote: Racial registration and sterilisation, internment in municipal and concentration camps, mass shootings by the Einsatzgruppen and gassing at Auschwitz-Birkenau and Chelmno are documented in German police and camp records summarised by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.
baselineWhat: The Roma and Sinti population of Europe in the areas that came under Nazi German and Axis control
baselineNote: No pre-war state counted Roma reliably; the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum and the standard literature work from an estimated European Roma and Sinti population of roughly 1-1.5 million before the war, of which the territories under Axis control held perhaps 700,000-1 million. Death estimates range from about 130,000 to 500,000, with 250,000-500,000 the figure most often cited.
shareCaveat: Both numbers are estimates with wide bands - the death toll spans a fourfold range and no reliable pre-war census of Roma exists - so the percentage should be treated as indicative only.

title: Internal Displacement inside Spain during the Civil War
actors: Republican and Nationalist advances, aerial and naval bombardment and organised evacuations moved civilians within Spain and sent children abroad
peopleRange: No census of wartime internal refugees exists. Republican refugee-relief bodies registered several hundred thousand people at a time in Catalonia and the Levante alone, and figures of one to three million internally displaced across the Republican zone by 1938 are commonly cited in the literature; they rest on relief-agency registrations that double-count repeated moves and omit those who sheltered with relatives. The individually documented episodes are firmer: 15,000-50,000 people fled Malaga along the coast road in February 1937, and about 34,000 children were evacuated abroad from the northern zone in 1937, of whom 3,886 reached Britain on a single ship.

flows.label: Malaga to Almeria along the coast road, February 1937
Basque children evacuated from Bilbao to Britain, 1937
Refugees moving into Catalonia ahead of the Nationalist advance

summary: The atlas already records the Retirada, the flight of Republicans into France in 1939; the larger movement, however, happened inside Spain. Each Nationalist advance pushed civilians ahead of it into the shrinking Republican zone, and the Republic created refugee committees and a national evacuation apparatus that resettled people in Catalonia, the Levante and Madrid. The best-known single episode is the flight from Malaga on 8 February 1937, when between 15,000 and 50,000 people, mostly women, children and the elderly, walked the coast road toward Almeria while Nationalist warships and Italian and German aircraft attacked the column; deaths on the road are usually put around 3,000, though the Spanish state has said the true number is unknown and several modern historians argue for lower figures. From 1937 the Basque and Republican authorities also evacuated about 34,000 children abroad, to Britain, France, Belgium, the Soviet Union and Mexico; those sent to the USSR were largely unable to return until after 1956. Most internal refugees returned or were returned home after 1939, often into the classification and punishment system of the new regime.
contested: The aggregate number of internal refugees is not established, and the death toll on the Malaga-Almeria road is disputed between the figure of around 3,000 long used by memory associations and lower estimates by some historians; the Spanish government has stated that the number of dead and missing remains unknown.

sources.title: Malaga-Almeria road massacre (Wikipedia)
Evacuation of children in the Spanish Civil War (Wikipedia)
White Terror (Spain) (Wikipedia)

deathsNote: The range refers to civilians killed while fleeing Malaga in February 1937, the largest single documented killing of refugees in transit during the war; the higher end comes from contemporary accounts and Spanish memory associations, the lower from recent local studies working from burial and civil-register evidence. It does not attempt to count deaths from bombing, hunger and disease among displaced people across the whole war, for which no defensible figure exists.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: The strafing and shelling of the Malaga refugee column is documented by contemporary eyewitnesses including the Canadian surgeon Norman Bethune and by later Spanish local-history research.
baselineWhat: The population of Spain at the outbreak of the Civil War
baselineNote: The Spanish censuses of 1930 and 1940 counted 23.6 million and 26.0 million respectively, implying about 24.5 million in 1936. Displacement estimates rest on Republican refugee-service records and provincial relief registers; some 440,000 crossed into France in the Retirada of early 1939 and about 30,000 children were evacuated abroad.

title: The Spanish Civil War: the Retirada and the French Internment Camps
actors: Franco's forces drove the Republican population into exile and France interned the refugees in beach camps in Roussillon
peopleRange: About 465,000 people crossed the French border in the Retirada of January-February 1939, roughly 220,000 of them soldiers and 170,000 women, children and elderly civilians, arriving within a few weeks after the fall of Barcelona; earlier waves from the northern front in 1937 brought the wartime total of Spanish refugees in France to over half a million. Perhaps half returned to Spain during 1939, while tens of thousands remained, and about 20,000 Spanish republicans were later deported by the Germans to concentration camps, principally Mauthausen. Figures come from French prefectural and interior ministry registration and the collections of the French national museum of immigration history.

flows.label: Catalonia -> Argeles-sur-Mer and the Roussillon beach camps
Spanish republicans in French custody -> Mauthausen concentration camp

summary: The collapse of the Republican front in Catalonia in early 1939 pushed close to half a million people over the Pyrenees in a few weeks. France interned them on the beaches of Argeles-sur-Mer, Saint-Cyprien and Le Barcares behind wire, at first without shelter or sanitation, and later in camps such as Gurs, Bram and Rivesaltes; thousands died of dysentery, pneumonia and exposure in the first months. Many were pressed into labour companies, and after 1940 Vichy handed several thousand to the Germans; about 20,000 Spanish republicans were deported to Nazi concentration camps, of whom roughly half died, most at Mauthausen. Others returned to Spain, where the Francoist state prosecuted the defeated through military tribunals, held some 270,000 political prisoners at the peak in 1940 and used prisoner labour on public works. Tens of thousands were executed after the war ended, and Spanish and international researchers have documented mass graves still being exhumed under the memory laws of 2007 and 2022.
contested: The number of people executed by the Francoist authorities during and after the war is disputed, with estimates for postwar executions ranging from about 20,000 to 50,000 and wartime repression figures still being revised as graves are exhumed.

sources.title: Musee national de l'histoire de l'immigration (Paris): The Retirada, or post-war Spanish republican exile
Britannica: Spanish Civil War

deathsNote: This range covers deaths connected with the exile and its aftermath rather than the war itself: several thousand refugees died in the French camps in 1939, about 10,000 Spanish republicans died in Nazi concentration camps after deportation, and Francoist postwar executions are estimated at 20,000 to 50,000. Total deaths in the civil war of 1936-39, including combat and the repression carried out by both sides, are usually put at 500,000 or more and are counted separately.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Internment without charge in the French camps, labour companies, the deportation of Spanish republicans to Nazi camps, the postwar military tribunals and the removal of children from Republican families are documented in French prefectural archives, Mauthausen camp records and Spanish judicial and prison records examined under the historical memory laws.
baselineWhat: The population of Spain at the outbreak of the Civil War
baselineNote: Spain's 1930 census counted 23,563,867 and the 1940 census 26,014,278; interpolation puts the 1936 population at roughly 24.5 million. The Retirada of January-February 1939 carried about 465,000 people across the French border in a few weeks, of whom roughly half returned to Spain within the year.

title: China's Wartime Refugee Flight and the Yellow River Dyke Breach
actors: The Japanese invasion drove tens of millions of Chinese civilians from their homes, and Chinese Nationalist forces breached the Yellow River dykes to slow the advance
peopleRange: Estimates of Chinese civilians displaced during the war with Japan run from about 30 million to 95 million; figures of 80 to 100 million refugees are commonly cited in the scholarship on the basis of Nationalist government relief registration, provincial reports and postwar reconstruction, and all are approximations for a country whose population and administration were both in disarray. The Yellow River breach alone displaced nearly four million people across Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu, about a fifth of the population of the flooded districts, according to the reconstruction by Chris Courtney and colleagues from Chinese relief and postwar survey records.

flows.label: Lower Yangtze cities -> the wartime capital Chongqing and the southwest
Flooded districts of Henan -> Anhui and Jiangsu

summary: The Japanese advance from 1937 emptied cities and whole provinces: universities, factories and government offices moved west to Sichuan and Yunnan, and civilians fled ahead of the front in numbers that contemporary and later estimates place in the tens of millions, among the largest displacements of the century. On 9 June 1938 Chiang Kai-shek ordered the Yellow River dykes cut at Huayuankou in Henan to halt the Japanese advance on Wuhan. The flood inundated some 1.3 million hectares across 44 counties, displaced close to four million people and, over the nine years before the river was returned to its course in 1947, is estimated to have killed more than 800,000. The flooded zone contributed to the Henan famine of 1942-43, in which one to three million people died. Chinese war deaths overall are variously estimated at 14 to 20 million. The dyke breach was carried out by the Chinese government against its own population and was concealed at the time as a Japanese bombing.
contested: Refugee totals are estimates rather than counts and vary by a factor of three; responsibility for the consequences of the Yellow River breach, ordered by the Chinese Nationalist government but prompted by the Japanese invasion, is argued over in both Chinese and Japanese historiography.

sources.title: Disaster History: Yellow River flood, 1938-47 (project of Chris Courtney and colleagues)
Diana Lary, Drowned Earth: The Strategic Breaching of the Yellow River Dyke, 1938, War in History
Britannica: Sino-Japanese War, 1937-45

deathsNote: The range is for the Yellow River flood alone. Diana Lary gives half a million as the lowest estimate of deaths; the Disaster History project gives more than 800,000 deaths across Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu between 1938 and 1947, with postwar Chinese calculations reaching 893,303. Total Chinese deaths in the war with Japan, from combat, massacre, famine and disease, are usually put at 14 to 20 million and are not counted here.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The deliberate destruction of the dykes and the resulting inundation and famine are documented in Chinese military orders, relief agency records and the postwar surveys analysed by Diana Lary and by the Disaster History project.
baselineWhat: The population of China at the outbreak of the war with Japan
baselineNote: China had no reliable national census before 1953. Nationalist government estimates for the late 1930s ranged from 450 to 500 million, and modern reconstructions by Ho Ping-ti and the Maddison project put the population around 500 million in 1937. The 1953 census, the first modern enumeration, counted 582.6 million.
shareCaveat: The 80-95 million refugee estimate accumulates over eight years and counts people who fled repeatedly as the front moved; it is a Nationalist wartime relief figure rather than a registration count.

title: Deportation of Koreans from the Soviet Far East
actors: The Soviet Council of People's Commissars and the NKVD deported the entire Korean population of the Far Eastern Krai to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan
peopleRange: NKVD transport records report 171,781 people, in 36,442 families, moved in 124 trains between September and late October 1937; Soviet decrees and reports are the source, and the count is administrative rather than estimated. This was the first Soviet deportation of an entire nationality defined by ethnicity alone.

flows.label: Vladivostok and the Far Eastern Krai -> Kzyl-Orda and southern Kazakhstan
Far Eastern Krai -> Uzbekistan (Tashkent region)

summary: Decree 1428-326ss of 21 August 1937, signed by Stalin and Molotov, ordered the removal of the Korean population from the border districts of the Far Eastern Krai on the stated ground of preventing Japanese espionage; within weeks the order was extended to the whole krai. About 172,000 people were loaded into freight trains and carried some 6,000 kilometres to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, where they were settled on the steppe and in the Aral and Syr Darya districts, often without prepared housing before winter. Korean schools, newspapers and the Korean-language pedagogical institute were closed, and the deportees were placed under residence restrictions that were not lifted until the 1950s. The operation coincided with the arrest and execution of much of the Korean Soviet intelligentsia. It became the template for the wartime deportations of other nationalities.
contested: Death tolls are disputed: no register of mortality in transit and in the first winters was kept, and figures in circulation range from a few thousand to 40,000 or more.

sources.title: Jon K. Chang, False Narratives and the Reality of History: The Deportation of Soviet Koreans in 1937 (Researching Internal Displacement working paper)
Pavel Polian, Against Their Will: The History and Geography of Forced Migrations in the USSR (Central European University Press)

deathsNote: There is no reliable count. NKVD transport reports record only a few hundred deaths en route, which specialists regard as an undercount; Korean community and later Soviet-era estimates of deaths in transit and during the first winters in Central Asia run from about 16,500 to 40,000. The disagreement turns on whether deaths from exposure, hunger and disease in 1937-38 in the reception areas are counted.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: The confiscation of property, the closure of Korean-language institutions and the parallel arrest and execution of Korean party and cultural figures are documented in the Soviet decrees and NKVD reports cited by Polian and Chang.
baselineWhat: The Korean population of the Soviet Far Eastern Krai
baselineNote: NKVD operational records report 171,781 people deported in 124 trainloads between September and October 1937, and the 1937 Soviet census recorded a Korean population of similar size. The operation was designed to remove the entire community, so the recorded deportation total is effectively the population count.

baselineSources.title: Deportation of Koreans in the Soviet Union

shareCaveat: The deportation was total by design, so the ratio is close to 100% by construction; the denominator is derived from the same NKVD records as the numerator.

title: The Great Terror: Mass and National Operations of the NKVD
actors: The NKVD under Nikolai Yezhov arrested, shot or sent to camps quotas of 'anti-Soviet elements' and members of diaspora nationalities on Politburo authority
peopleRange: About 1.5 million people were arrested in the sixteen months from August 1937, of whom roughly 800,000 were sentenced to death and most of the remainder to camp terms. Operational order 00447 against 'former kulaks, criminals and other anti-Soviet elements' accounted for 767,000 sentences and 387,000 executions. The national operations produced their own totals: the Polish operation under order 00485 saw about 140,000 arrested and 111,000 shot, the German operation about 55,000 arrested and 42,000 shot, the Chinese Eastern Railway operation 33,108 condemned and 21,200 shot, and the Latvian operation 22,360 condemned and 16,573 shot. Under order 00486 some 40,000 wives of 'traitors to the motherland' were arrested and about 20,000 of their children placed in orphanages. All figures come from NKVD statistical returns opened after 1991 and compiled by Memorial and by Nicolas Werth.

flows.label: Sentenced survivors of the mass operations -> northern camps

summary: Between July 1937 and November 1938 the NKVD carried out centrally planned mass arrests under numbered operational orders that set regional quotas for execution and for camp sentences. Order 00447 targeted former kulaks, returning deportees, clergy and people with criminal records; a parallel series of 'national operations' targeted Soviet citizens of Polish, German, Latvian, Finnish, Greek, Korean, Chinese and other diaspora origins on the presumption that they were foreign agents. Sentences were passed in absentia by two- and three-man boards on the basis of lists. The Polish operation was proportionally the deadliest, with about four in five of those arrested shot. Wives of executed men were arrested under a separate order and their children placed in institutions. The operations were halted in November 1938 and Yezhov himself was shot in 1940; the Soviet state did not publish the statistics, which emerged from the archives after 1991 and are now maintained in the databases of the Memorial society.
contested: Totals rest on NKVD statistical returns whose completeness is debated, and burial sites for many of the executed have still not been identified.

sources.title: Nicolas Werth, Mass Crimes under Stalin (1930-1953), Sciences Po Mass Violence and Resistance
Memorial, Russia's Necropolis of Terror and the Gulag

deathsNote: NKVD returns record 681,692 executions for counter-revolutionary and state crimes in 1937-38; Werth gives about 800,000 death sentences over the sixteen months of the operations. The difference reflects sentences carried out in early 1939, deaths under interrogation and executions recorded under other headings.
violenceNote: Quota-based execution, sentencing by extrajudicial boards, the authorised use of physical pressure in interrogation, the arrest of wives and the placement of their children in orphanages are recorded in the NKVD operational orders themselves, published from the archives and catalogued by Memorial.
baselineWhat: The population of the Soviet Union at the suppressed census of January 1937
baselineNote: The 1937 census counted about 162 million people; Stalin rejected the result, had the organisers arrested, and ordered a new census in 1939 which returned 170.6 million. Modern demographers regard the 1937 figure as the more accurate of the two.
shareCaveat: The 'national operations' fell overwhelmingly on small diaspora nationalities — Poles, Germans, Koreans, Latvians and others — for whom the arrest rate ran to several per cent of the group, so a share of the whole Soviet population conceals how concentrated the targeting was.

title: The Nanjing Massacre
actors: The Japanese Central China Area Army killed prisoners and civilians and committed mass rape after capturing the Chinese capital
peopleRange: About 200,000 to 250,000 civilians who had not fled Nanjing sheltered in the Nanking Safety Zone established by a committee of foreign residents in an area of some four square kilometres; most of the city's prewar population of around one million had already left before the Japanese army arrived on 13 December 1937. The Safety Zone figures come from the committee's own records and the reports of its members, including John Rabe and Minnie Vautrin.
summary: Japanese forces entered Nanjing on 13 December 1937 after a pursuit up the Yangtze from Shanghai and, over roughly six weeks, executed surrendered Chinese soldiers and men of military age, killed civilians, burned large parts of the city and committed mass rape.
