Foreign residents who remained set up a Safety Zone that sheltered some 200,000 to 250,000 people and recorded what they saw in diaries, letters and films. The figures are sharply disputed. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East found in 1948 that over 200,000 Chinese civilians and prisoners of war were killed in and around the city in the first six weeks and recorded some 20,000 cases of rape in the first month; the Nanjing War Crimes Tribunal of 1947 put the toll at more than 300,000, the figure inscribed at the memorial hall in Nanjing and used by the Chinese government. Japanese scholars differ widely: Hata Ikuhiko's estimate is around 40,000, other Japanese historians give figures between 100,000 and 200,000, and a revisionist current in Japan claims the massacre was greatly exaggerated or fabricated. Successive Japanese governments have acknowledged that killings of non-combatants occurred while declining to endorse a figure, and the Japanese foreign ministry states that it is difficult to determine the number of victims.
contested: The death toll differs by an order of magnitude between the Chinese official figure of more than 300,000, the Tokyo tribunal's finding of over 200,000, mainstream Japanese scholarly estimates of 40,000 to 200,000, and Japanese revisionist claims of a few thousand or of fabrication.

sources.title: Britannica: Nanjing Massacre
Judgment of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, 1948
Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders
Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan: Japan's postwar record and history issues

deathsNote: The low end is the estimate of the Japanese historian Hata Ikuhiko, which counts killings within the city walls over a shorter period; the high end is the finding of the 1947 Nanjing War Crimes Tribunal and the figure maintained by China. The Tokyo tribunal's figure of over 200,000 sits between them. The disagreement turns on the geographic and temporal boundaries used, on whether executed prisoners of war are counted as massacre victims, on burial-society records whose reliability is contested, and on the politics of memory in both countries.

atrocityFindings.body: International Military Tribunal for the Far East
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that Japanese forces killed over 200,000 Chinese civilians and prisoners of war at Nanjing in the first six weeks of occupation and committed about 20,000 rapes in the first month; convicted General Matsui Iwane of failing to prevent the atrocities

violenceNote: The killings, mass rape and burning of the city are documented in the diaries and reports of the foreign Safety Zone committee, in Japanese soldiers' diaries, in burial society records and in the evidence heard by the Tokyo and Nanjing tribunals.
baselineWhat: The population remaining in Nanjing and its immediately surrounding counties when the city fell in December 1937
baselineNote: Nanjing held over a million people before the Japanese advance and much of the population fled; the International Committee for the Nanking Safety Zone estimated 200,000-250,000 civilians sheltering in the zone, to which are added residents outside it, some 70,000-90,000 disarmed Chinese soldiers, and the rural populations of the surrounding counties where killing also occurred - roughly half a million people in total.
shareCaveat: The death toll is contested - the Nanjing tribunal and Chinese accounts give 300,000, the Tokyo tribunal about 200,000, and Japanese scholars figures from 40,000 to 200,000 - and both toll and denominator depend on whether the surrounding counties and disarmed soldiers are included, so the percentage is unusually sensitive to definition.

title: The Parsley Massacre of Haitians in the Dominican Republic
actors: Dominican army and police units under Rafael Trujillo killed Haitians and Haitian-descended residents of the border region and drove survivors into Haiti
peopleRange: Tens of thousands of Haitians and people of Haitian descent fled or were expelled from the Dominican border provinces during and after October 1937; Haitian government registration of refugees and later scholarship suggest on the order of 25,000 to 40,000 crossed into Haiti, in addition to those killed. The figures rest on Haitian consular and refugee records, United States diplomatic reporting and later historical research, since the Dominican state suppressed documentation of the killings.

flows.label: Dominican border provinces -> Haiti across the Massacre and Dajabon rivers

summary: In late September and October 1937 Rafael Trujillo ordered the killing of Haitians in the Dominican border region. Soldiers and police, sometimes with civilian participation, used machetes and rifles over roughly a week, reportedly testing suspected Haitians by asking them to pronounce the Spanish word for parsley, perejil, a shibboleth that gave the episode its name; the bodies of many victims were thrown into the river that marks the frontier. Estimates of the dead range from about 4,000 to 20,000 or more, with figures of 12,000 to 15,000 common in the literature. The killings formed part of a wider policy of 'Dominicanisation' of the frontier that also expelled survivors and restricted Haitian labour and settlement. Under diplomatic pressure mediated by the United States, Cuba and Mexico, the Dominican Republic agreed in January 1938 to pay Haiti an indemnity of 750,000 US dollars, of which about 525,000 was actually paid, without any admission of responsibility or prosecution of those involved. In 2013 a Dominican constitutional court ruling retroactively stripped citizenship from many Dominicans of Haitian descent, an act critics linked to the same policy tradition.
contested: The death toll ranges from about 4,000 to more than 20,000; the Dominican state has never acknowledged responsibility or prosecuted anyone, and the 1938 indemnity was framed as a settlement of claims rather than as an admission.

sources.title: Britannica: Parsley Massacre

deathsNote: Estimates range from about 4,000, based on contemporary consular counts of identified victims, to 20,000 or more in Haitian and later accounts; figures of 12,000 to 15,000 are widely used. The Dominican government suppressed records and disposed of bodies in the rivers, so no count was ever possible, and the number remains an estimate built from refugee testimony and diplomatic reporting.
violenceNote: The killings, the expulsion of survivors and the subsequent exclusion of Haitians from the frontier zone are documented in Haitian and United States diplomatic reporting of 1937-38 and in the historical research summarised by Britannica.
baselineWhat: The Haitian and Haitian-descended population recorded as resident in the Dominican Republic
baselineNote: The Dominican census of 1935 counted 60,517 'foreign' members of the black population, overwhelmingly Haitians and their descendants, most of them in the border provinces and the sugar bateyes. Death-toll estimates range from about 14,000 to 40,000, with most scholars near 20,000, so the share killed is put at anywhere from a fifth to three-fifths of that community.
shareCaveat: The killings were concentrated in the northern border region rather than in the sugar zones, so the share of the border population affected was far higher than the national ratio implies.

title: The Annexation of Austria and the Sudetenland
actors: Nazi Germany annexed Austria by invasion and plebiscite and the Czechoslovak borderlands by the Munich agreement of the four powers
peopleRange: About 6.7 million Austrians and roughly 3.6 million inhabitants of the Sudeten districts passed under German rule. Some 150,000 to 200,000 Czechs, German-speaking anti-Nazis and Jews left or were driven from the ceded borderlands into rump Czechoslovakia between October 1938 and March 1939, and about 117,000 Jews left Austria by September 1939. Population figures come from the Czechoslovak and Austrian censuses; the movement figures from Czechoslovak refugee registration and refugee-organisation records.
territoryDesc: Austria, about 84,000 square kilometres, was incorporated into the Reich on 13 March 1938 and dissolved into Reichsgaue. The Sudeten borderlands, about 28,000 square kilometres, were ceded by Czechoslovakia under the Munich agreement of 30 September 1938; the remaining Czech lands were occupied on 15 March 1939 as the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, while Slovakia became a nominally independent state and Hungary and Poland took further Czechoslovak districts.

flows.label: Sudeten borderlands -> rump Czechoslovakia (Prague and the interior)
Vienna -> emigration abroad after the Anschluss

summary: German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938 and the country was annexed the next day, ratified by a plebiscite held under Nazi control. Persecution of Austrian Jews was immediate and more violent than anything yet seen in Germany, with public humiliations in Vienna, mass arrests and the creation of Adolf Eichmann's Central Office for Jewish Emigration, which forced emigration in exchange for expropriation. Six months later, at Munich on 30 September 1938, Britain, France, Germany and Italy agreed the cession of the Czechoslovak borderlands to Germany without Czechoslovak participation; German forces occupied them in the first ten days of October. Between 150,000 and 200,000 Czechs, Jews and German-speaking opponents of Nazism moved into what remained of Czechoslovakia, which Germany then dismembered in March 1939. The two annexations added roughly ten million people and 112,000 square kilometres to the Reich without war, and extended the concentration camp system with the opening of Mauthausen in August 1938.
contested: Whether the Anschluss represented annexation of an unwilling country or, as postwar Austrian state doctrine long held, the occupation of a first victim, remains politically contested in Austria; the plebiscite results were produced under conditions that precluded a free vote.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Nazi Territorial Aggression - The Anschluss
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Austria
Jewish Virtual Library: The Munich Agreement (1938)

deathsNote: Neither annexation was resisted militarily and there was no significant battle toll. Deaths arose from persecution rather than from the transfers of territory: several hundred Austrian Jews took their own lives in the weeks after the Anschluss, and thousands of Austrian political opponents were sent to Dachau and the newly opened Mauthausen camp.

atrocityFindings.body: International Military Tribunal, Nuremberg
atrocityFindings.finding: Found in its judgment that the seizure of Austria and of Czechoslovakia formed part of the Nazi plan of aggressive war, and convicted defendants on the count of crimes against peace

violenceNote: Mass arrests of political opponents and Jews after the Anschluss, the expropriation of Jewish property through Eichmann's emigration office, and the loss of Czechoslovak citizenship in the ceded districts are documented in German and Austrian administrative records summarised by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.
baselineWhat: The combined population of the territories Germany annexed in 1938: Austria and the Czechoslovak borderlands
baselineNote: The Austrian census of 1934 counted 6,760,233 people, and the Sudeten territory ceded at Munich held about 3.6 million, of whom roughly 2.8-2.9 million were German-speaking and some 700,000-800,000 Czech. Roughly 150,000-250,000 Czechs, Jews and political opponents left the ceded borderlands for rump Czechoslovakia in late 1938, and Austrian Jewish emigration ran to about 117,000 by 1941.

title: The Phoenix Islands Settlement Scheme and Gilbertese Resettlement to the Solomon Islands
actors: The British colonial administration of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands moved Gilbertese settlers to the Phoenix atolls and later to the Solomon Islands
peopleRange: Colonial records give roughly 1,000 Gilbertese settled on Nikumaroro, Manra and Orona from 1938, all evacuated by 1963 when the atolls proved unable to support them; a parallel and continuing movement to the Solomon Islands began with a pilot group of ten in 1954 and thirty men in 1955, and the Solomon Islands census of 1976 recorded 2,753 Gilbertese in the protectorate. The total moved across both schemes is on the order of 3,000 people.

flows.label: Gilbertese settlers to the Phoenix Islands
Evacuation to Gizo and Wagina in the Solomon Islands

summary: Faced with land shortage in the southern Gilbert Islands, the British colonial administration launched a settlement scheme in 1938 that moved about a thousand Gilbertese to the uninhabited Phoenix atolls of Nikumaroro, Manra and Orona, where they were to establish coconut plantations. Drought and thin soils made the settlements unviable, and in 1963 the administration evacuated the remaining settlers to Wagina and Gizo in the British Solomon Islands Protectorate. A parallel resettlement of Gilbertese directly to the Solomons continued from 1954 until the Governing Council effectively stopped it in 1971 over concerns about ethnic tension of the kind seen in Fiji; the 1976 Solomons census counted 2,753 Gilbertese. Participation was organised and encouraged by the administration rather than compelled at law, but the choices available to settlers were shaped by colonial land policy and by the phosphate economy that had already taken Banaba, whose people the atlas records separately. The Gilbertese communities in the Solomons were displaced again during the tensions of 1998-2003 and questions of land and citizenship have persisted.
contested: Whether the scheme should be classed as forced relocation or as assisted colonial settlement is genuinely ambiguous: it was administratively organised and driven by colonial land and phosphate policy, but settlers were recruited rather than removed at gunpoint.

sources.title: Phoenix Islands Settlement Scheme
Solomon Islands Encyclopaedia: Gilbertese re-settlement scheme

deathsNote: There was no significant death toll. Settlers suffered drought, water shortage and hardship on the Phoenix atolls, which was why the scheme was abandoned, but no mass mortality was recorded.
baselineWhat: The population of the Gilbert Islands at the time the resettlement scheme began, from whose overcrowded southern atolls the settlers were drawn
baselineNote: British colonial censuses of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands recorded roughly 28,000-30,000 people in the Gilberts in the 1930s. The scheme moved about 700 settlers to the Phoenix Islands from 1938 and later relocated roughly 2,000-3,000 in total, most of them onward to the Solomon Islands in 1963-64 after drought made the Phoenix atolls unviable.

title: Aktion T4 and the Murder of Disabled People
actors: German physicians and the Chancellery of the Fuehrer killed institutionalised disabled children and adults under a centrally organised programme
peopleRange: The programme's own internal accounting, the Hartheim statistics captured after the war, records 70,273 institutionalised people killed in the six gassing centres between January 1940 and August 1941. Victims were moved from asylums to the killing centres by bus and rail under the cover of transfers to specialist institutions. In all phases, including the killing of children by starvation and drugs and the decentralised 'wild euthanasia' of 1942-45, historians estimate about 250,000 deaths, and the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives 250,000 to 300,000 including at least 10,000 children.

flows.label: Austrian asylums -> Hartheim killing centre
Institutions in western Germany -> Hadamar killing centre

summary: Beginning in 1939 with the killing of disabled infants and young children in special paediatric wards, the Nazi state extended medical killing to institutionalised adults under an operation run from Tiergartenstrasse 4 in Berlin and authorised by a backdated note from Hitler. Physicians selected patients from questionnaires returned by asylums; those chosen were transported to six centres - Brandenburg, Grafeneck, Bernburg, Sonnenstein, Hartheim and Hadamar - and killed with carbon monoxide in gas chambers disguised as showers, their families receiving falsified causes of death. Public protest, notably the sermon of Bishop Clemens August von Galen in August 1941, led Hitler to halt the centralised gassing after 70,273 deaths, but killing continued in institutions by starvation and lethal medication until 1945. The programme supplied the personnel and the technique for the extermination camps of Operation Reinhard, where T4 staff including Christian Wirth and Franz Stangl were deployed. Postwar West German trials convicted a number of the doctors and administrators involved.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Euthanasia Program
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Gassing Operations

deathsNote: The figure of 70,273 for January 1940 to August 1941 comes from the programme's own statistics. Totals of 250,000 to 300,000 for all phases, given by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, add the child killings, the deaths from deliberate starvation diets and overdoses after 1941, and the killing of patients in occupied Poland and the Soviet Union. Records for the later decentralised phase are incomplete, which is what drives the range.

atrocityFindings.body: United States Military Tribunal, Nuremberg (Doctors' Trial)
atrocityFindings.finding: Convicted defendants of crimes against humanity for the euthanasia killings and for medical experimentation, and set out the Nuremberg Code

violenceNote: Selection by questionnaire, transport to gassing centres, falsified death certificates and the later use of starvation diets and lethal medication are documented in the T4 administrative files, the Hartheim statistics and the records of the postwar euthanasia trials.
baselineWhat: The population of German psychiatric hospitals, asylums and care institutions on the eve of the killing programme
baselineNote: Reich health statistics and the reconstructions by Friedlander and the USHMM put roughly 300,000 patients in German institutions in 1939. The 70,273 figure is the T4 organisation's own internal tally of people gassed at the six killing centres to August 1941; killing by starvation and lethal medication continued to 1945, bringing the total usually given for the whole euthanasia programme to 250,000-300,000 across Germany and the occupied territories.
shareCaveat: The 70,273 figure covers only the centrally organised gassings to August 1941; the full programme killed several times that number, so this share understates it.

title: Expulsions from Annexed Poland and the 'Heim ins Reich' Resettlement
actors: Himmler's Reich Commission for the Strengthening of Germandom expelled Poles and Jews from the annexed Polish provinces and settled ethnic Germans brought in from eastern Europe in their place
peopleRange: Roughly 900,000 to 1,000,000 Poles and Jews were expelled from the annexed provinces into the General Government or moved within them between 1939 and 1944, according to German resettlement office records; in the Zamosc region of the General Government a further 100,000 Polish villagers, including about 30,000 children, were cleared from their homes in 1942-43. About 500,000 ethnic Germans were settled in the annexed territories, drawn from roughly one million resettled under the 'Heim ins Reich' agreements from the Baltic states, Volhynia, Galicia, Bessarabia, northern Bukovina and Romania. At least 20,000 Polish children judged racially suitable were taken from their families for Germanization. Figures come from SS resettlement statistics and the postwar Polish and German reconstructions summarised by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.

flows.label: Wartheland -> General Government (expelled Poles and Jews)
Baltic Germans from Latvia and Estonia -> Wartheland
Germans of Bessarabia and Bukovina -> annexed Polish provinces

summary: Hitler appointed Himmler Reich Commissioner for the Strengthening of Germandom on 7 October 1939 with the task of making the annexed Polish provinces German. Poles and Jews were removed from their farms, shops and houses at short notice, usually with a suitcase each, and moved by train to the General Government; their property was handed to ethnic German settlers brought in under agreements with the Soviet Union, Italy, Romania and the Baltic states that repatriated about a million Volksdeutsche from eastern and southeastern Europe. Racial screening offices sorted both the expelled and the incoming, and at least 20,000 Polish children assessed as Germanizable were taken from their parents and placed with German families. The most systematic clearance in the General Government took place around Zamosc in 1942-43 as a first instalment of Generalplan Ost, the SS scheme for the settlement of eastern Europe by Germans and the removal, over decades, of tens of millions of Slavs. Generalplan Ost was never implemented as drafted, but the expulsions, the Germanization of children and the plunder of property were carried out and were charged at Nuremberg.
contested: Totals vary between roughly 900,000 and 1.7 million expelled depending on whether internal displacement inside the annexed provinces, the flight of 1939 and the later evacuation of ethnic Germans are counted.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Polish Victims
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Lebensraum
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: German Administration of Poland

deathsNote: Deaths arose from the conditions of the transports in winter, from the killing of those who resisted and from the shooting of villagers during the Zamosc clearances and the reprisals that followed; several thousand of the deported children died. No systematic count exists, and the range reflects Polish postwar estimates that include deaths in transit camps such as Lodz and Potulice alongside those killed during the operations.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.body: International Military Tribunal, Nuremberg
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that the deportation of populations from occupied territories and the Germanization programme, including the removal of children, constituted war crimes and crimes against humanity

violenceNote: The seizure of Polish farms and houses, the racial screening and removal of children, the use of expelled Poles as forced labour and the transit camps are documented in SS resettlement records introduced in evidence at Nuremberg and summarised by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.
baselineWhat: The population of the Polish territories annexed to the German Reich in 1939
baselineNote: The annexed provinces — the Reichsgau Wartheland, Danzig-West Prussia, Upper Silesia and Zichenau — held roughly ten million people, of whom about 8.9 million were Poles, around 600,000-700,000 Jews and some 600,000 ethnic Germans. Himmler's Reich Commission expelled several hundred thousand Poles and Jews eastward into the General Government and settled some 500,000-900,000 ethnic Germans brought 'home to the Reich' from the Baltic, Volhynia, Bessarabia and elsewhere.

baselineSources.title: Expulsion of Poles by Germany — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The affected figure combines Poles and Jews expelled from the annexed provinces with ethnic Germans resettled into them from outside, two movements in opposite directions, so it should not be read as a share of the annexed territories' population that was driven out.

title: Franco's Postwar Concentration Camps, Prisons and Forced-Labour System in Spain
actors: The Franco dictatorship interned, imprisoned and conscripted into labour battalions Spaniards classified as disloyal after the Republic's defeat
peopleRange: The Francoist camp inspectorate's own returns record 177,905 captured enemy soldiers held in about 100 camps at the war's end in April 1939 and 431,251 people as having passed through the camps by then; historians' totals for the whole 1936-1947 system range from roughly 500,000 (Javier Rodrigo) to 700,000-1,000,000 (Carlos Hernandez de Miguel), with Paul Preston counting close to 200 camps and Hernandez de Miguel about 300. The prison population, counted separately, stood between roughly 270,000 and 500,000 in 1939-1940 depending on which official series is used, falling to about 30,000 political prisoners by 1946. All figures rest on regime paperwork that was partly destroyed, so they are floors rather than settled counts.
summary: After the Republic's surrender in April 1939 the Franco regime kept in place the network of concentration camps built during the civil war and combined it with a greatly expanded prison system and with labour battalions. Classification commissions sorted prisoners into those released, those sent to workers' battalions and those handed to military courts under the Law of Political Responsibilities; the parallel scheme of 'redemption of sentences through work' let prisoners cut their terms by labouring for the state and for private construction, public-works and mining firms, and prisoner labour was used, among many projects, on the Valle de los Caidos monument begun in 1940. Alongside this, children of imprisoned, executed or exiled Republicans were placed in state and church institutions: by 1943 official records show 12,043 such children in state custody, and figures compiled by Judge Baltasar Garzon in 2008 from historical sources put more than 30,000 children under regime 'tutelage' between 1944 and 1954, a practice that victims' associations say later merged into decades of irregular adoptions known in Spain as the ninos robados. The last camp, Miranda de Ebro, closed in 1947. The subject was left largely untouched during the transition under what is commonly called the pacto del olvido; the 2007 Historical Memory Law and the 2022 Democratic Memory Law reopened it, while the 1977 Amnesty Law has continued to block criminal prosecutions.
contested: The number of postwar executions and prison deaths, the extent to which prisoner labour was coerced rather than incentivised, and above all the scale of the removal of children are disputed in Spain, where no court has established the facts and estimates for abducted or irregularly adopted children run from tens of thousands to figures around 300,000 advanced by victims' lawyers that historians regard as unverifiable.

sources.title: Francoist concentration camps (Wikipedia)
Campos de concentracion franquistas (Wikipedia, Spanish)
Valley of the Fallen (Wikipedia)
Lost children of Francoism (Wikipedia)
White Terror (Spain) (Wikipedia)

deathsNote: The range covers executions carried out after the war ended in April 1939: Paul Preston and others put post-war executions at roughly 20,000, while Spanish memory associations and some regional studies reach substantially higher totals; disagreement turns on incomplete civil registers, unrecorded burials and where to draw the line between wartime and postwar killing. Deaths from hunger, typhus and untreated illness inside the prisons and camps are counted separately and are usually estimated in the tens of thousands.
violenceNote: These forms are documented by historians of the Francoist repression including Javier Rodrigo, Carlos Hernandez de Miguel and Paul Preston, and, for the removal of children, in the 2008 judicial investigation opened by Judge Baltasar Garzon and in the case files compiled by victims' associations.
baselineWhat: The population of Spain at the 1940 census
baselineNote: The 1940 Spanish census (INE) recorded 26,014,278 inhabitants. Estimates of the numbers held in Francoist concentration camps, prisons and labour battalions after the Republic's defeat vary with what is counted; Javier Rodrigo's work on the camp system and prison-administration returns support an order of several hundred thousand passing through between 1939 and the mid-1940s.
shareCaveat: The 400,000 is a cumulative throughput over roughly eight years and overlaps with the Retirada population, since many who were interned in France and returned were imprisoned again in Spain.

title: The German-Soviet Partition of Poland
actors: Germany and the Soviet Union invaded and divided the Polish state between them under the secret protocol of the pact of 23 August 1939
peopleRange: About 35 million people lived in the Polish Republic in 1939; roughly 22 million came under German control and about 13 million under Soviet control. Within the German zone hundreds of thousands were expelled from the annexed western provinces into the General Government, and around 300,000 people fled eastward across the demarcation line in the autumn of 1939, many of them Jews. The Soviet zone produced its own deportations of about 320,000 people to the interior of the USSR in 1940-41. Population figures come from the Polish census of 1931 projected forward; the movement figures from German resettlement records, Soviet NKVD registers and refugee registration.
territoryDesc: Germany annexed about 92,000 square kilometres of western and northern Poland outright as Danzig-West Prussia, the Wartheland, Upper Silesia and the Ciechanow district, and administered a further 95,000 square kilometres as the General Government from 26 October 1939. The Soviet Union took about 200,000 square kilometres east of the Bug and San, incorporating them into the Ukrainian and Belorussian republics after staged elections in October 1939; Vilnius was handed to Lithuania. The Polish state ceased to exist as a territorial entity until 1945.

flows.label: Annexed Wartheland and Pomerania -> General Government
German-occupied Poland -> Soviet zone (refugees, autumn 1939)

summary: The German invasion of 1 September 1939 and the Soviet invasion of 17 September divided Poland along a line fixed by the secret protocol to the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and revised by the boundary and friendship treaty of 28 September. Germany annexed the western provinces directly to the Reich and placed the rest under a colonial administration, the General Government, seated in Krakow. The Soviet Union annexed the eastern half to the Ukrainian and Belorussian republics after elections conducted under military occupation, imposed Soviet citizenship, and deported categories of the population it judged hostile. Both occupiers moved at once against Polish elites: German forces shot thousands of teachers, priests, officials and landowners in the Intelligenzaktion of late 1939, while the NKVD shot about 21,857 Polish officers and officials in the spring of 1940. The partition lasted until the German attack on the Soviet Union in June 1941, after which the whole territory came under German rule.
contested: Russia's official presentation of the Soviet entry of 17 September 1939 as a protective measure for Ukrainians and Belorussians, rather than as an act of aggression carried out in agreement with Germany, is rejected by Poland, the Baltic states and most Western historians.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Invasion of Poland, Fall 1939
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: German Administration of Poland
Avalon Project, Yale Law School: Judgment of the International Military Tribunal - The Nazi Regime in Germany

deathsNote: The September campaign itself killed roughly 66,000 Polish soldiers and some 16,000 German soldiers, with civilian deaths from bombing and reprisals in the tens of thousands. Between October 1939 and mid-1940 German units shot at least 50,000 members of the Polish intelligentsia and other civilians in the annexed territories, and the NKVD shot 21,857 Polish prisoners in 1940. The figures are drawn from campaign records, German security-police reports and Soviet files; they exclude the far larger toll of the occupation that followed.

atrocityFindings.body: International Military Tribunal, Nuremberg
atrocityFindings.finding: Found the invasion of Poland to be a war of aggression and the German occupation policy in Poland to constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity

violenceNote: The shooting of Polish elites by German Einsatzgruppen and Selbstschutz units, the destruction of towns during and after the campaign, and the imposition of German and Soviet citizenship regimes on Polish citizens are documented in German security-police reports and Soviet decrees cited at Nuremberg and by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.
baselineWhat: The population of the Second Polish Republic
baselineNote: The 1931 census counted 32.1 million; the Polish government's estimate for mid-1939 was about 35.1 million, of whom roughly 69% Poles, 14% Ukrainians, 9% Jews and 3% Belarusians. The 1939 census returns were largely destroyed in the invasion.
shareCaveat: The 1.5 million figure is usually the count of those deported into the Soviet interior in 1940-41; German expulsions from the annexed western provinces and the wider wartime mortality are additional and counted elsewhere.

title: Japanese Wartime Mobilisation of Korean and Chinese Forced Labour
actors: The Japanese state and Japanese companies conscripted Korean, Chinese and Taiwanese workers for mines, shipyards and factories in Japan and its empire
peopleRange: Japanese government figures record roughly 670,000 Koreans brought to the Japanese home islands under labour mobilisation programmes between 1939 and 1945, rising to about 800,000 including those mobilised within Korea and in Sakhalin and the South Seas; South Korean official commissions have put the total number of Koreans mobilised for labour across the empire far higher, in the millions, counting short-term and local conscription. A Japanese foreign ministry survey completed in 1946 recorded 38,935 Chinese labourers forcibly transported to Japan, of whom 6,830 died there. The figures come from Japanese wartime labour administration records and the 1946 foreign ministry report, and from the Korean Truth Commission on Forced Mobilisation established in 2004.

flows.label: Korea -> coal mines and shipyards of Kyushu and western Japan
North China -> mines and construction sites in Japan

summary: From 1939 Japan met wartime labour shortages by recruiting, and from 1944 formally conscripting, workers from colonial Korea and Taiwan and by transporting Chinese prisoners and civilians to Japan. Labourers worked in coal and metal mines, shipyards, steel plants and construction under conditions of confinement, low or withheld pay and high accident and death rates; among the best documented cases are the Hanaoka mine, where Chinese labourers revolted in June 1945 and were killed in the suppression, and the Hashima and Takashima coal mines. Compensation claims have been litigated for decades. Japan holds that all claims arising from the colonial period were settled by the 1965 Treaty on Basic Relations and its claims agreement with the Republic of Korea, under which Japan provided grants and loans. On 30 October 2018 the Supreme Court of Korea held that the 1965 agreement did not extinguish individual claims for damages arising from illegal colonial rule and ordered Nippon Steel, and in a subsequent ruling Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, to compensate former labourers; Japan called the rulings a violation of international law, and the dispute led to trade restrictions in 2019. In March 2023 the South Korean government announced that a domestic foundation would pay the judgments, a solution rejected by some plaintiffs.
contested: Japan and South Korea disagree fundamentally over whether individual claims survived the 1965 treaty, and over the terminology, with Japan preferring 'former civilian workers from the Korean Peninsula' to 'forced labour'; the totals mobilised also differ greatly between Japanese wartime records and Korean commission findings.

sources.title: Nippon.com: What's at stake in the Japan-Korea wartime/forced labor dispute
Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan: Japan's postwar record and history issues
Judgment of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, 1948

deathsNote: There is no agreed figure. The 1946 Japanese foreign ministry survey recorded 6,830 deaths among 38,935 Chinese labourers taken to Japan, a rate of about 17 per cent. Deaths among Korean mobilised workers in mines, at construction sites, in the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and in shipwrecks such as the Ukishima Maru are estimated in the tens of thousands, with Korean and Japanese estimates differing by a wide margin because the underlying mobilisation totals are themselves disputed.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.body: Supreme Court of the Republic of Korea
atrocityFindings.finding: Held on 30 October 2018 that individual claims for damages for forced labour under Japanese colonial rule were not extinguished by the 1965 claims agreement, and ordered Nippon Steel to compensate four former labourers; Japan's government rejected the ruling as contrary to international law

atrocityFindings.body: International Military Tribunal for the Far East
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that forced labour of prisoners of war and civilians, including on the Burma-Siam railway, was carried out as a matter of policy and constituted war crimes

violenceNote: Conscription orders, confinement in company barracks, withheld wages and punishment of those who fled are documented in Japanese wartime labour records, in the 1946 foreign ministry survey of Chinese labourers and in the evidence accepted by the Korean courts.
baselineWhat: The population of colonial Korea at the 1940 census, the main source of wartime conscripted labour
baselineNote: The colonial census of 1940 counted about 23.5 million people in Korea. Estimates of mobilisation vary with definition: roughly 670,000-800,000 Koreans were taken to Japan proper for labour between 1939 and 1945, while counts that include mobilisation within Korea and across the empire run to several million; around 40,000 Chinese were also shipped to Japan.

baselineSources.title: Chinese and Korean forced labour in wartime Japan — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The numerator includes Chinese and Taiwanese labourers who are not part of the Korean denominator, and estimates of Koreans mobilised range from about 670,000 to over five million depending on whether mobilisation inside Korea is counted.

title: Forced Labour in the German War Economy
actors: German authorities under Fritz Sauckel's plenipotentiary office conscripted and deported civilians from occupied Europe to work in the Reich
peopleRange: By August 1944 about 7.6 million foreign civilian workers and prisoners of war were registered as working in the Reich, roughly a fifth of the German workforce; some 13 million people in total performed forced labour for Germany during the war, of whom about 8.4 million were foreign civilians deported into the Reich. Nearly three million Soviet citizens were deported as Ostarbeiter between 1942 and 1944 and at least 1.5 million Polish citizens from 1939. The figures come from German labour administration returns and from the documentation assembled for the German Forced Labour Compensation Programme, which made payments to about 1.66 million former labourers between 2001 and 2007.

flows.label: Occupied Soviet Union -> industrial western Germany (Ostarbeiter)
Occupied Poland -> agriculture and industry in southern Germany
France (Service du travail obligatoire) -> the Reich

summary: Labour shortages caused by conscription led Germany to draw workers from every occupied country, first by recruitment and then by force. Fritz Sauckel, appointed plenipotentiary for labour deployment in March 1942, organised round-ups in Poland, the occupied Soviet territories, France, the Netherlands and the Balkans; whole villages were emptied and people seized in street and cinema raids. A racial hierarchy governed treatment: workers from western Europe were relatively better placed, Poles and Soviet Ostarbeiter wore identifying badges, lived in guarded barracks, faced separate penal law and were fed at levels that produced widespread illness. Concentration camp prisoners were hired out to firms under a policy of extermination through labour, and camp satellites were built beside factories. Sauckel was convicted at Nuremberg and executed. After decades of litigation, the German state and German industry created the Foundation 'Remembrance, Responsibility and Future' in 2000, which paid compensation to about 1.66 million surviving forced labourers.
contested: Totals differ according to whether prisoners of war, concentration camp prisoners hired out to firms, and labourers conscripted within their own occupied countries are counted alongside civilians deported into the Reich.

deathsNote: There is no agreed total. Deaths among foreign civilian labourers in the Reich from malnutrition, disease, industrial accidents, punishment and Allied bombing are usually put in the hundreds of thousands; adding concentration camp prisoners worked to death in the camp economy and Soviet prisoners of war used as labour produces figures above two million. The lower bound counts civilian deportees, the upper bound the whole labour system.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.finding: Convicted Fritz Sauckel of war crimes and crimes against humanity for the deportation of civilians from occupied territories for slave labour

baselineNote: No single denominator is defensible: the deported workers came from more than a dozen occupied and allied countries, chiefly the occupied Soviet territories, Poland and France, whose combined population ran to roughly 200 million but which were never a single administrative or demographic unit. Ulrich Herbert's standard account records about 7.6 million foreign civilian workers and prisoners of war in the Reich in August 1944, with roughly 13.5 million passing through the system in all.

title: The Ghettos as a System of Confinement
actors: German occupation authorities, with Romanian and other allied administrations, confined Jewish populations in closed districts before deporting them
peopleRange: Researchers at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum have documented more than 1,300 ghettos, about 1,100 of them established by German authorities and some 150 more in the Romanian-administered Transnistria Governorate, almost all in occupied Poland, the occupied Baltic states and the occupied Soviet Union. Millions of Jews passed through them; the Warsaw ghetto held more than 400,000 people at its peak in 1941 and the Lodz ghetto about 164,000 at its sealing in 1940. The counts come from the Museum's multi-volume Encyclopedia of Camps and Ghettos, built from German administrative records, Jewish council records and survivor testimony.

flows.label: Warsaw ghetto -> Treblinka killing centre
Lodz ghetto -> Chelmno killing centre

summary: From late 1939 German authorities concentrated Jews in designated districts of towns and cities, first in occupied Poland and from 1941 in the occupied Soviet territories, sealing many of them with walls or fences and appointing Jewish councils to administer them. Ghettos served as holding pens and labour pools: inhabitants were set to work for German firms and the army while receiving rations far below subsistence. Overcrowding, hunger and epidemic typhus killed hundreds of thousands, with the Warsaw ghetto alone recording more than 80,000 deaths from starvation and disease before the deportations began. From 1942 the ghettos of the General Government were emptied to the killing centres of Operation Reinhard, and the last large ghettos in Poland and Lithuania were destroyed in 1943 and 1944. Armed resistance broke out in Warsaw in April 1943 and in Bialystok, Vilna and other ghettos. Theresienstadt, established in November 1941, was used both as a transit ghetto and as a propaganda showpiece.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Ghettos
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Warsaw
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Lodz
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Deportations to and from the Warsaw Ghetto

deathsNote: These figures count deaths inside the ghettos from starvation, cold, disease and shooting, not the far larger number of ghetto inhabitants murdered after deportation to the killing centres, who are counted in the Holocaust entry. Estimates rest on Jewish council burial records, German administrative returns and postwar reconstruction; the ghettos of the occupied Soviet Union, many of which existed only weeks before their inhabitants were shot, are the hardest to count.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Sealed confinement, starvation rations, compulsory labour and the shooting of those who left without permission are documented in German ordinances, Jewish council records and the diaries and archives kept in the ghettos themselves, notably the Oneg Shabbat archive of Warsaw.
baselineWhat: The Jewish population of German-occupied Poland, where most ghettos were established
baselineNote: The Polish census of 1931 and later community registers give about 3.3 million Jews in pre-war Poland, roughly 10 per cent of the population; Warsaw's ghetto alone held over 400,000 at its peak and Lodz about 164,000. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum has documented at least 1,143 ghettos in German-occupied eastern Europe, extending into the occupied Soviet territories, Romanian-administered Transnistria and, in 1944, Hungary, so the population confined was drawn from a wider pool than Poland alone.
shareCaveat: The numerator includes ghettoised Jews in the occupied Soviet Union, Transnistria and Hungary who are not in the Polish denominator, so the ratio is inflated; it also counts a cumulative flow through the ghettos rather than a standing population.

title: The South Tyrol Option Agreement
actors: Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy agreed that the German-speaking population of South Tyrol must choose between emigration to the Reich and assimilation in Italy
peopleRange: About 213,000 people were entitled to opt; roughly 185,000, some 86 per cent of those eligible, registered for German citizenship and emigration by the deadline of 31 December 1939, but only about 75,000 actually left before the transfers were suspended in 1943. Figures come from the joint German-Italian option commission's registers and from later Italian and Austrian historical accounts.

flows.label: South Tyrol -> Austria and the Reich (Tyrol, Vorarlberg and further afield)

summary: South Tyrol had been annexed by Italy in 1919 and subjected to a policy of Italianization that banned German-language schooling and public use of German. On 23 June 1939 German and Italian officials agreed that the province's German- and Ladin-speaking inhabitants would be given a choice: opt for German citizenship and resettlement in the Reich, or remain as Italian citizens and accept assimilation. The campaign that followed split families and villages between 'optants' and 'stayers'. About 185,000 registered to leave, though only some 75,000 had gone by 1943, when the German occupation of northern Italy made further transfers pointless. Most emigrants were settled in Austria rather than in the eastern territories originally envisaged. After the war Italy and Austria agreed in 1946 that optants could return and recover citizenship, and most of those who had left came back; the episode left a lasting division in South Tyrolean society.
contested: Whether the option constituted a free choice or coercion is disputed: both governments described it as voluntary, while South Tyrolean and Austrian accounts emphasise the propaganda, intimidation and the absence of any third possibility.

sources.title: House of Austrian History (Haus der Geschichte Oesterreich): 1939 Hitler-Mussolini Pact
The 1939 Option Agreement and the 'Consistent Ambivalence' of Fascist Policies towards Minorities in the Italian New Provinces, The Historical Journal (Cambridge University Press)

deathsNote: The option produced no significant death toll. It was an administered population transfer carried out under political pressure rather than by force of arms, and its harms were the division of communities, loss of property and the uprooting of those who left.
violenceNote: The requirement that those who stayed abandon their language and identity, and that those who left surrender Italian citizenship, is documented in the text of the 1939 agreement and in the administrative record examined in The Historical Journal.
baselineWhat: The German- and Ladin-speaking population of South Tyrol eligible to exercise the option in 1939
baselineNote: The joint German-Italian option registers recorded 246,036 eligible people, of whom 185,085 - about 75 per cent - opted for German citizenship and emigration; roughly 75,000 had actually left for the Reich by 1943, when the German occupation of northern Italy ended the transfer. The figures come from the option commission's own records.

title: The Holocaust
actors: Nazi Germany, its agencies and its allies and collaborators across occupied Europe systematically murdered Europe's Jews
peopleRange: Roughly three million Jews were deported by rail from ghettos, transit camps and cities across Europe to the killing centres and concentration camps, in addition to the roughly 1.5 to 2 million shot near their homes in the occupied Soviet territories and Poland. More than 1,300 ghettos and over 44,000 camps and incarceration sites of all kinds have been documented by researchers at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. The deportation figures rest on German railway and police transport lists, camp arrival records and the reconstruction of individual transports; the Museum and Yad Vashem have recovered the names of about 4.9 million victims.

flows.label: Hungary -> Auschwitz-Birkenau, May-July 1944
Warsaw ghetto -> Treblinka, summer 1942
Netherlands (Westerbork) -> Auschwitz and Sobibor
Thessaloniki -> Auschwitz-Birkenau, 1943

summary: The Holocaust was the state-organised murder of about six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1939 and 1945, carried out in three overlapping ways. From June 1941 the Einsatzgruppen and Order Police battalions, assisted by Wehrmacht units and local auxiliaries, shot Jewish communities at the edge of their own towns in the occupied Soviet territories, killing about 33,771 people at Babi Yar outside Kyiv alone on 29-30 September 1941 and at least 1.5 million in all. From 1939 Jews were concentrated in more than 1,300 ghettos, where hunger and disease killed hundreds of thousands. From December 1941 six killing centres using gas - Chelmno, then Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka under Operation Reinhard, and Auschwitz-Birkenau and Majdanek - received deportation trains from across the continent: approximately one million people were murdered at Auschwitz, about 925,000 at Treblinka, 435,000 at Belzec, at least 167,000 at Sobibor and at least 152,000 at Chelmno. The Wannsee conference of 20 January 1942 coordinated the deportation of Jews from the whole of Europe among the agencies of the German state. The concentration camp system, more than 44,000 camps and incarceration sites in all, worked prisoners to death in armaments production, and the last months of the war added the death marches westward from the evacuated camps. Alongside Jews, the Nazi state killed at least 250,000 Roma, some 3.3 million Soviet prisoners of war, about 1.8 million non-Jewish Polish civilians and 250,000 to 300,000 disabled people. The figure of six million rests on prewar and postwar census comparison, German transport and camp documentation and community-by-community reconstruction; Raul Hilberg's lower reconstruction of about 5.1 million and Yad Vashem's and the Museum's figure of close to six million mark the working range, and about 4.9 million victims have been identified by name.
contested: Scholarly estimates of the total range from roughly 5.1 million to over six million depending on method and on the treatment of the occupied Soviet territories; denial and minimisation of the Holocaust, which the evidentiary record and courts in several countries have rejected, is not part of that scholarly range.

The lower bound of about 5.1 million is Raul Hilberg's reconstruction from German documentation; higher figures around 6.2 million come from demographic reconstructions such as Wolfgang Benz's country-by-country study. The disagreement turns chiefly on the number shot in the occupied Soviet Union, where documentation is thinnest, and on how Jews who died of hunger and disease in ghettos and in flight are classified. Deaths of other groups killed by the Nazi state - Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, Polish civilians, disabled people - are counted in separate entries.

baselineNote: Standard demographic reconstructions, used by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum and Yad Vashem, put Europe's Jewish population at about 9.5 million in 1933-39, roughly 60 per cent of world Jewry, with the largest communities in Poland (about 3.3 million) and the Soviet Union (about 3 million). About six million were murdered, roughly two-thirds of the European Jewish population.

shareCaveat: The widely accepted death toll is about six million, roughly two-thirds of European Jewry; a smaller numerator counts only a subset, such as those held in ghettos and camps, and the resulting share will understate the whole.

title: The Katyn Massacre of Polish Prisoners
actors: The Soviet NKVD shot Polish officers, police and officials held prisoner after the Soviet occupation of eastern Poland
peopleRange: The Politburo decision of 5 March 1940 authorised the shooting of 14,700 prisoners of war held in the Kozelsk, Starobelsk and Ostashkov camps and 11,000 prisoners held in the western Ukrainian and Belorussian provinces. A 1959 memorandum from KGB chief Alexander Shelepin to Khrushchev states that 21,857 people were shot in total. These are Soviet internal documents, released by Russia in 1990-92 and reproduced in the record of the European Court of Human Rights.

flows.label: Kozelsk camp -> Katyn forest execution site

summary: After the Soviet occupation of eastern Poland in September 1939 the NKVD held tens of thousands of captured Polish officers, police, border guards, officials and landowners. On 5 March 1940 the Politburo approved a proposal by Lavrentiy Beria to shoot them without trial as 'hardened and uncompromising enemies of Soviet power'. About 21,857 people were killed in April and May 1940 at Katyn near Smolensk, in the NKVD prisons of Kalinin and Kharkov and at other sites. When German forces uncovered the Katyn graves in 1943 the Soviet Union blamed Germany, a claim it maintained until 13 April 1990, when the Soviet government acknowledged NKVD responsibility. In 2010 the Russian State Duma adopted a declaration attributing the massacre to Stalin and other Soviet leaders. The Russian criminal investigation was discontinued in 2004 and much of its file remains classified; the European Court of Human Rights found in 2013 that it could not examine the adequacy of that investigation but held that Russia had breached its duty to cooperate with the Court.
contested: Russia acknowledges Soviet responsibility but has not classified the killings as genocide or war crimes in domestic law, has kept much of the investigation file classified, and has resisted the legal rehabilitation of individual victims sought by Polish relatives.

sources.title: European Court of Human Rights, Janowiec and Others v. Russia (Grand Chamber, 2013)
Institute of National Remembrance (Poland): The Katyn Massacre - basic facts

deathsNote: The figure of 21,857 comes from the 1959 Shelepin memorandum and is the count used by the Polish Institute of National Remembrance and by the European Court of Human Rights; small variations reflect whether prisoners shot at related sites and those whose remains have not been located are included.

baselineNote: Soviet records indicate roughly 230,000-250,000 Polish servicemen and police were captured in September-October 1939; most rank-and-file conscripts were released or handed to Germany, while officers, police and officials were held in the Kozelsk, Starobelsk and Ostashkov camps and in NKVD prisons in the western oblasts. The Politburo decision of 5 March 1940 designated about 25,700 of these for execution, of whom 21,857 were shot — a figure confirmed by the Shelepin note released from the Soviet archives in 1992.

title: The Sanko Sakusen: Japanese Scorched-Earth Campaigns in North China
actors: The Japanese North China Area Army destroyed villages, food stores and populations in the Communist base areas of north China
peopleRange: No reliable count of those displaced exists. Chinese Communist wartime sources state that the population of the base areas of north China fell from about 44 million to 25 million between 1940 and 1942 through killing, flight and depopulation of cleared zones; Japanese and Western historians treat these figures as politically produced and unverifiable, but agree that the campaigns emptied large districts, created fortified strategic villages and blockade lines, and drove villagers into the mountains.
summary: After the Communist Hundred Regiments Offensive of August-December 1940 exposed the weakness of Japanese control in north China, the North China Area Army under Tada Hayao and from 1941 Okamura Yasuji adopted a counter-insurgency strategy of destroying the rural base of the guerrillas: burning villages, seizing or destroying grain, killing or removing inhabitants, and constructing blockade ditches, walls and strongpoints to seal off districts. Chinese sources named the strategy sanguang, 'burn all, kill all, loot all', which entered Japanese usage as sanko sakusen. Whole districts were declared depopulation zones. Estimates of the death toll are highly uncertain: the Japanese historian Himeta Mitsuyoshi has put deaths caused by the policy at about 2.7 million Chinese civilians, a figure repeated in Chinese accounts and questioned by other Japanese scholars as an extrapolation. There is no dispute among historians that the campaigns involved the systematic destruction of villages and the killing of non-combatants, which the Tokyo tribunal treated as part of the pattern of Japanese conduct in China.
contested: The death toll attributed to the campaigns rests on contested extrapolations, ranging from the 2.7 million figure of the Japanese historian Himeta Mitsuyoshi to far lower estimates by other Japanese scholars; Chinese base-area population figures were produced in wartime propaganda conditions.

sources.title: Hans van de Ven, Campaigns in China, 1937-1945, in The Cambridge History of the Second World War
Judgment of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, 1948

deathsNote: The upper figure is Himeta Mitsuyoshi's estimate of deaths caused by the Three Alls campaigns, widely cited in China; the lower figure reflects historians who count only documented massacres and village destructions in the north China plain. No systematic wartime registration existed in the affected districts, so all figures are extrapolations.

atrocityFindings.body: International Military Tribunal for the Far East
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that Japanese forces in China systematically killed civilians, destroyed towns and villages without military necessity and plundered on a large scale, and convicted senior commanders and ministers accordingly

violenceNote: Village burning, the destruction of grain stores and wells, the killing of inhabitants of guerrilla districts and the construction of blockade lines are documented in Japanese army operational orders, in Chinese base-area reports and in the evidence on Japanese conduct in China heard by the Tokyo tribunal.
baselineWhat: The population of the Chinese Communist base areas of north China before the Japanese scorched-earth campaigns
baselineNote: Chinese Communist wartime reporting, cited in Japanese and Western scholarship on the campaigns, records the population of the north China base areas falling from about 44 million to about 25 million between 1940 and 1945. The figure is a party administrative claim rather than a census, and the 19 million difference mixes deaths with flight to areas outside Communist control and with territory lost to Japanese occupation.

title: Soviet Annexation of the Baltic States and Mass Deportations
actors: The Soviet Union annexed Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in 1940 under the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, reoccupied them in 1944 after German withdrawal, and deported tens of thousands accused of nationalism, wealth, or wartime collaboration to Siberia and Central Asia in 1941 and again in 1949.
peopleRange: roughly 130,000–200,000-plus deported across the 1941 ('June deportation') and 1945–1953 waves combined, including about 90,000–95,000 in the single March 1949 Operation Priboi, plus tens of thousands of wartime refugees who fled west in 1944
territoryDesc: Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania

flows.label: Riga → Siberia
Vilnius → Kazakhstan

summary: The Soviet Union occupied and annexed the three Baltic republics in 1940, an act most Western governments never formally recognized. German occupation followed in 1941–44, after which the Red Army reoccupied the territories and Soviet rule was reimposed. Soviet security services deported tens of thousands of people—often entire families of suspected nationalists, wealthier farmers ('kulaks'), or wartime partisans and their supporters—to Siberia and Central Asia, most notably in the June 1941 deportations and the March 1949 Operation Priboi tied to agricultural collectivization. Tens of thousands more fled west as refugees in 1944 ahead of the returning Red Army. The Baltic states regained independence in 1991.
contested: The Baltic states and most Western governments treat the 1940 annexation as an illegal occupation that was never legally valid, consistent with the US 'Welles Declaration' non-recognition policy; the Soviet Union, and Russia since, characterized it as a lawful incorporation, a position rejected by Baltic governments and most international bodies.

Russia has never recognised the deportations as a crime and disputes these framings.

title: Soviet Annexation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina
actors: The Soviet Union annexed Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina from Romania in 1940 under the secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, lost the territory to Romanian and German forces in 1941, and reoccupied and permanently annexed it in 1944, forming the Moldavian SSR.
peopleRange: roughly 400,000 combined: about 82,000 Bessarabian and 40,000–45,000 Bukovinian Germans resettled to Germany in 1940, plus tens of thousands deported to Siberia and Central Asia in 1941 and again in 1949 (about 35,000 in the single July 1949 operation), alongside separate wartime deportations of Jews to Transnistria under Romanian administration
territoryDesc: Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina, formerly part of Romania

flows.label: Bessarabia/Bukovina → Siberia (Soviet deportations)
Bessarabian/Bukovinian Germans → Germany

summary: In June 1940, acting on the secret protocol of the 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the Soviet Union issued an ultimatum forcing Romania to cede Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina, which were incorporated into a new Moldavian SSR and parts of the Ukrainian SSR. Most of the region's ethnic German minority was resettled to Germany under a parallel agreement, while Soviet security services deported tens of thousands of others considered politically unreliable to Siberia and Central Asia. Romanian and German forces retook the territory in 1941, during which Romanian authorities deported tens of thousands of Jews to Transnistria, and the Red Army reoccupied and permanently annexed it in 1944, with further mass deportations following in 1949 and 1951 tied to collectivization. The territory forms the core of modern Moldova.
contested: The legality of the 1940 and 1944 annexations is disputed by Moldova and most Western governments, since they derived from the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact's secret protocols, whose existence the Soviet Union denied until 1989; this contrasts with territorial changes achieved through openly negotiated international treaties.

sources.title: Soviet occupation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina - Wikipedia
Bessarabia - Britannica

deathsNote: The range is R.J. Rummel's estimate of 18,000-57,000 deaths among the 200,000-300,000 people persecuted in Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina in 1940-41; it was made before the Soviet archives opened and has not been confirmed by them. Archive-based work by the Moldovan historian Igor Cașu documents the deportation operations precisely — 29,839 people in June 1941, 35,050 in July 1949, 2,617 in April 1951 — but not the mortality among deportees in Kazakhstan, Komi and Siberia, which is where most of the deaths occurred. title: Soviet Deportations from Occupied Eastern Poland
actors: The Soviet NKVD deported Polish citizens from the territories annexed in 1939 to special settlements, camps and exile in Siberia, Kazakhstan and the far north
peopleRange: NKVD transport records account for about 320,000 to 330,000 Polish citizens deported in four waves between February 1940 and June 1941: military settlers and foresters with their families in February 1940, families of arrested officers and officials in April 1940, refugees from German-occupied Poland, many of them Jews, in June 1940, and inhabitants of the border districts in May-June 1941. Polish emigre and later Polish official estimates have ranged from 700,000 to 1.5 million, counting also those arrested, conscripted or sentenced. The lower figures come from NKVD convoy and settlement registers published after 1991 and used by Pavel Polian; the higher ones from wartime Polish government records and survivor registration.

Western Belorussia -> Kazakhstan (Karaganda region)

summary: After the Soviet Union annexed eastern Poland under the secret protocol of the German-Soviet pact, the NKVD removed categories of the population considered hostile: settlers granted land after the Polish-Soviet war, forest workers, families of officers and officials already arrested, refugees who had fled the German zone and refused Soviet passports, and border-district residents. Deportees travelled in unheated freight cars to special settlements, labour camps and forced residence in Siberia, Kazakhstan, Komi and Arkhangelsk, where they worked in logging, mining and agriculture. Conditions in the first winter were severe and mortality among children and the elderly was high. Most survivors were amnestied after the German invasion of the USSR in 1941 under the Sikorski-Mayski agreement, and tens of thousands left the Soviet Union with the Anders Army through Iran, though many others remained until after the war.
contested: The number deported is disputed by roughly a factor of four between NKVD registers and the wartime Polish estimates, and the two counts use different categories.

violenceNote: The seizure of property, compulsory labour in the settlements and the imposition of Soviet citizenship on Polish citizens are documented in NKVD deportation orders and settlement records used by Polian and by the Polish Institute of National Remembrance.

NKVD transport records opened in the 1990s document about 320,000-330,000 deported in the four waves of February, April and June 1940 and June 1941; Polish government-in-exile estimates ran to 1-1.5 million, and the archival figure is now the scholarly consensus.

title: Displacement by Strategic Bombing in Germany and Japan
actors: Allied air forces destroyed German and Japanese cities, and both governments evacuated urban populations under compulsion
peopleRange: The United States Strategic Bombing Survey found that 3.6 million German dwelling units, about a fifth of the national stock, were destroyed or heavily damaged and that 7.5 million Germans were made homeless; in the roughly fifty main target cities about 40 per cent of dwellings were destroyed. For Japan the Survey found that about 40 per cent of the built-up area of the 66 cities attacked was destroyed and that roughly 30 per cent of the entire urban population lost their homes, some 8.5 million people, on top of the compulsory evacuation of schoolchildren and non-essential residents from the cities. German war-emergency evacuation programmes moved several million women, children and schoolchildren to rural areas and to occupied and allied territories. The figures come from the Survey's own field investigation of city records, published in 1945-46.

flows.label: Bombed Rhine-Ruhr cities -> reception districts in southern Germany
Tokyo -> rural evacuation districts

summary: Area bombing of cities by the Royal Air Force and the United States Army Air Forces, and the firebombing of Japanese cities from late 1944, destroyed housing on a scale that emptied urban populations into the countryside. In Germany raids such as those on Hamburg in July 1943 and Dresden in February 1945 rendered whole cities uninhabitable within days; the United States Strategic Bombing Survey counted 3.6 million dwellings destroyed or heavily damaged and 7.5 million people made homeless, alongside state-organised evacuation schemes that moved children and non-essential civilians out of the cities. In Japan the incendiary raid on Tokyo of 9-10 March 1945 burned out fifteen square miles of the city in a night, and by the surrender about 30 per cent of the urban population had lost their homes; the government had already ordered the evacuation of schoolchildren and of large numbers of urban residents. The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 destroyed those cities outright. Much of this displacement was temporary, but it overlapped with the flight of civilians before advancing armies and, in Germany, with the expulsions of 1945 onward.
contested: Whether area bombing of cities was lawful or proportionate has been debated since the war; no tribunal has ruled on it, and the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals did not charge aerial bombardment of cities.

sources.title: United States Strategic Bombing Survey, Summary Report (European War), 1945

For Japan the Survey estimated about 806,000 civilian casualties including roughly 330,000 deaths, a figure that includes the atomic bombings; Japanese estimates for Hiroshima and Nagasaki alone, counting deaths from radiation injury by the end of 1945, are higher.

The bombing acted on the urban share of these - roughly 45 million in German towns and cities and about 27 million in Japanese ones - so measured against urban populations alone the displacement share would be far higher.

title: The Farhud and the Denaturalisation of Iraq's Jews
actors: Rioters and elements of the Iraqi security forces attacked Baghdad's Jews in 1941; the Iraqi state later stripped Jews who emigrated of citizenship and froze their property
peopleRange: The Iraqi government's own commission of inquiry into the Farhud recorded 179 Jews killed and about 240 wounded, with some later estimates as high as 600 dead; roughly 900 houses and 500 businesses were looted. Emigration under Law 1 of March 1950 was recorded by the Iraqi authorities and by the Jewish Agency airlift: between 120,000 and 130,000 Jews left in 1950-51, out of a community of about 135,000, leaving roughly 6,000 behind.

flows.label: Iraqi Jews airlifted to Israel, Operations Ezra and Nehemiah

summary: On 1-2 June 1941, in the days between the collapse of Rashid Ali al-Gaylani's government and the entry of British-backed forces into Baghdad, crowds joined by police and soldiers attacked Jewish quarters of the city in the pogrom known as the Farhud; an Iraqi commission of inquiry counted 179 dead, and other estimates run higher. After 1948 Zionism was made a criminal offence, Jews were dismissed from public employment and some were tried and executed, and in March 1950 Law 1 allowed Jews to emigrate on condition of renouncing Iraqi nationality; Law 5 of March 1951 froze the property of those who had left. Between 1950 and 1952 some 120,000-130,000 Iraqi Jews were flown to Israel in Operations Ezra and Nehemiah, ending a community of more than two millennia. A series of bombings of Jewish targets in Baghdad in 1950-51 accelerated departures; responsibility remains disputed, with Iraqi courts convicting Zionist activists and other accounts attributing them to Iraqi nationalists, and the question has never been settled. This entry sits alongside the atlas's regional entry on the exodus of Jews from Arab and Muslim countries and treats the specifically Iraqi legal machinery.
contested: Responsibility for the 1950-51 Baghdad bombings, and whether British and Iraqi authorities could have stopped the Farhud sooner, are both disputed; the Iraqi state has never made a formal determination beyond the 1941 inquiry.

violenceNote: The Iraqi commission of inquiry of 1941, survivor testimony collected by the USHMM and the texts of Laws 1 of 1950 and 5 of 1951 document the killings, rapes, looting and the stripping of nationality.

title: German Anti-Partisan Warfare and Village Destruction in Belarus
actors: German security forces, SS units and auxiliary police burned villages and killed or deported their inhabitants during operations against partisans in occupied Belarus
peopleRange: The Belarusian state archives record that 209 towns and 9,200 villages were destroyed or burned, that 630 villages were annihilated together with their inhabitants, and that about 400,000 people were taken from Belarus to forced labour in Germany, of whom almost half did not return. Some 140 punitive expeditions were carried out. The figures come from the Soviet Extraordinary State Commission and postwar Belarusian archival compilations.

flows.label: Belarus -> forced labour in Germany
Cleared villages -> Trostenets and other camps near Minsk

summary: Belarus was the centre of Soviet partisan warfare and of the German response to it. Under directives that treated whole districts as bandit areas, SS and police units, Wehrmacht security divisions and locally recruited auxiliaries carried out large sweeps in which villages were burned, inhabitants shot or driven into camps, and livestock and grain removed; 'dead zones' were created from which the population was cleared entirely. Khatyn, whose 149 inhabitants were burned alive in a barn on 22 March 1943, became the emblem of these operations and the site of the national memorial. Belarusian archives count 630 villages destroyed with their people, 9,200 villages burned in whole or part, and about 400,000 people deported to labour in Germany. Trostenets outside Minsk, where about 206,500 people were killed according to the same archives, was among the largest killing sites in the occupied Soviet territories. Estimates of total wartime deaths in Belarus range from the Extraordinary State Commission's 2.2 million to about three million, roughly a quarter to a third of the prewar population, including some 800,000 Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
contested: The Soviet-era total of 2.2 million dead is now regarded by Belarusian archivists as an undercount, while some Western historians caution that Extraordinary State Commission figures were compiled to political specifications; the share of deaths attributable to anti-partisan operations as distinct from the Holocaust and from combat is not precisely separable.

sources.title: National Archives of the Republic of Belarus: The history of the war - a survey of events

deathsNote: Estimates of civilians killed specifically in anti-partisan operations in Belarus run from about 345,000, the figure derived by German historians from operational reports of the security forces, to 500,000-700,000 in Belarusian accounting that includes deaths in the associated camps and deportations. These are a subset of total Belarusian war deaths of 2.2 to 3 million, which also include the Holocaust, prisoner-of-war deaths and combat.

title: German Captivity and Mass Death of Soviet Prisoners of War
actors: The German army and the SS held Soviet prisoners of war in open enclosures without adequate food or shelter and shot those in designated categories
peopleRange: About 5.7 million Soviet service personnel fell into German hands between June 1941 and the end of the war, according to German army records; roughly 3.3 million of them, some 57 per cent, were dead by the war's end, and only about 930,000 remained in German custody in January 1945. The figures come from Wehrmacht prisoner-of-war administration returns compiled by German historians and summarised by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.

flows.label: Captured on the eastern front -> transit camps in occupied Poland
Soviet prisoners -> forced labour in the Reich from 1942

summary: German planning for the invasion of the Soviet Union assumed that captured Soviet soldiers would not be fed at the expense of the Reich. Prisoners were herded into open enclosures without shelter, sanitation or adequate rations, and hundreds of thousands died of starvation, exposure and typhus in the winter of 1941-42 alone. The Commissar Order of 6 June 1941 and the associated commando guidelines directed that political officers, Communist Party functionaries and Jews among the prisoners be identified and shot; SS selection teams operated inside the camps, and several thousand Soviet prisoners were among the first people killed with Zyklon B at Auschwitz in September 1941. From spring 1942, as German labour shortages grew, surviving prisoners were put to work in mines, agriculture and armaments. Of roughly 5.7 million captured, about 3.3 million died. Survivors who returned to the Soviet Union were frequently filtered through NKVD screening camps and some were sentenced to the Gulag.
contested: German army records are incomplete for the first months of the invasion, so estimates of deaths in the winter of 1941-42 rest partly on reconstruction; the Soviet Union's own accounting of returning prisoners was also politically shaped.
