title: The Great Famine in Axis-Occupied Greece
actors: German, Italian and Bulgarian occupation authorities requisitioned food and split Greece into zones while an Allied blockade sealed imports
peopleRange: Roughly 100,000 Greeks were expelled or fled from the Bulgarian occupation zone in eastern Macedonia and Thrace, and several hundred thousand more moved internally in search of food, chiefly out of Athens and Piraeus and the islands towards the grain-producing mainland; the figures come from Greek wartime relief agencies, the Red Cross and post-war Greek government reckonings, and internal food-driven movement was never systematically counted.
territoryDesc: Greece divided into German, Italian and Bulgarian occupation zones; Bulgaria annexed eastern Macedonia and Western Thrace in 1941

flows.label: Greeks expelled from the Bulgarian zone to Thessaloniki and the German zone

summary: After the Axis invasion of April 1941 Greece was divided into German, Italian and Bulgarian zones, its merchant fleet and transport were destroyed or seized, occupation forces requisitioned food and imposed occupation costs, and the Allied naval blockade cut off the grain imports on which Greece had depended. Mass starvation set in during the winter of 1941-42, worst in Athens, Piraeus and the islands, and estimates of excess deaths across the occupation range from about 100,000 to 450,000, with roughly 300,000 the figure most often cited; Violetta Hionidou's demographic study puts famine deaths at around 100,000-200,000 for the acute period. The Bulgarian administration in annexed eastern Macedonia and Thrace expelled or drove out roughly 100,000 Greeks, and the Drama uprising of September 1941 was suppressed with mass reprisal killings. From 1942 the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Swedish-Swiss Joint Relief Commission ran a negotiated relief operation through the blockade that substantially reduced mortality. The famine is generally attributed to a combination of occupation requisitioning, the collapse of internal transport and administration, hyperinflation and black markets, and the blockade, with historians disagreeing on the weight of each.
contested: The share of responsibility between Axis requisitioning, the Allied blockade and the collapse of Greek administration is debated, and the total death toll ranges from about 100,000 to 450,000.

baselineNote: The Greek census of 1940 counted 7,344,860 inhabitants. title: Italian Fascist Internment of Slovenes and Croats: Rab, Gonars and the Annexed Territories
actors: The Italian army interned civilians from the annexed Province of Ljubljana and the Croatian coast in camps on Rab and in Italy
peopleRange: Estimates of Slovene and Croat civilians interned by Italian forces range from around 25,000-30,000 from the Province of Ljubljana alone to figures above 100,000 for all Yugoslav civilians passing through Italian camps, the higher totals associated with the Italian historian Alessandra Kersevan. The Rab camp held up to about 15,000 internees at its peak in 1942-43; the first transport to Gonars in February 1942 carried 5,343 people, 1,643 of them children. Counts rest on Italian army and camp records and on the postwar Yugoslav commission's investigation.

flows.label: Civilians from the Province of Ljubljana to the Rab camp
Transfers from Rab to Gonars and other camps in Italy

summary: After Italy annexed the Province of Ljubljana and parts of the Croatian coast in 1941, the Italian Second Army responded to partisan activity with reprisals, house burnings and the mass internment of civilians. Camps were opened at Gonars and Monigo in Italy in early 1942 and on the island of Rab in July 1942, the latter holding whole families, including women, infants and the elderly, in tents behind wire; conditions there were severe enough that the historians Carlo Spartaco Capogreco and James Walston calculated an annual mortality rate of about 18 per cent, which they compared with 15 per cent at Buchenwald. Circulars issued by General Mario Roatta directed commanders to act without 'false compassion' and envisaged clearing and replacing populations, and are the principal documentary basis for characterising the policy as more than security internment. The camps were closed after Italy's armistice in September 1943; Yugoslav partisans evacuated some 2,500 Jewish internees from Rab, while some who remained were deported by German forces to Auschwitz. Yugoslavia, Greece and Ethiopia sought the extradition of about 1,200 Italians accused of war crimes, but no Italian was tried, and the episode was largely absent from Italian public memory for decades.
contested: Death figures for Rab range from Yugoslav commission findings of 4,641 dead, including 800 who died in transfers to Gonars and Padua, and a 1943 report by the Bishop of Krk of at least 3,500, down to around 2,000 in other estimates; more broadly, Italian and Slovene-Croatian historiography differ over whether the internment amounted to ethnic cleansing, and the failure to prosecute remains a live grievance.

Several hundred more died at Gonars, where 453 identified victims were reinterred in 1973.

title: The Japanese Occupation of Guam and the Manenggon Marches
actors: Japanese forces occupied Guam, conscripted CHamoru labour and in July 1944 marched nearly the whole civilian population into inland camps
peopleRange: Guampedia, drawing on survivor testimony and postwar US records, states that nearly the entire civilian population was ordered inland in July 1944 and that about 18,000 people were camped along the Manenggon river, with further camps in the south. No records were kept of how many died on the marches or in the camps.

flows.label: CHamoru marched from Hagatna and the villages to Manenggon

summary: Japan captured Guam within days of Pearl Harbor and administered it for two and a half years, requiring CHamoru civilians to work on airfields and fortifications and punishing those suspected of loyalty to the United States, including those who sheltered the American radioman George Tweed. As US forces approached in July 1944 the occupation authorities ordered the population out of the coastal villages and into the interior; nearly the whole civilian population walked, in many cases for days, to camps at Manenggon and other sites, where about 18,000 people lived without shelter, latrines, food or medicine until American troops reached them at the end of July. In the same weeks Japanese troops killed groups of CHamoru at Fena, Chagui'an, Tinta and Faha. Estimates of CHamoru deaths under the occupation are usually put between 1,000 and 2,000, though no systematic count was made. The United States compensated Guam's war survivors only partially and belatedly: a congressionally mandated Guam War Claims Review Commission reported in 2004, and legislation providing payments to survivors and their heirs followed in 2016.
contested: No records exist of deaths on the marches or in the camps, and the adequacy and timing of US war claims compensation for Guam has been a long-running political dispute.

title: The Siege of Leningrad
actors: German Army Group North, with Finnish forces to the north, encircled and starved the population of Leningrad
peopleRange: About 2.5 million people, including some 400,000 children, were inside the blockade ring when it closed on 8 September 1941. Roughly 1.4 million were evacuated across Lake Ladoga and by rail during the siege, about a million of them in 1942 alone. The figures come from Leningrad city administration and evacuation-commission records used by Richard Bidlack and Nikita Lomagin in their edition of the Soviet archival documents.

flows.label: Leningrad -> evacuation across Lake Ladoga (the Road of Life)

summary: German forces cut the last land route into Leningrad on 8 September 1941 and held the city under blockade for 872 days, until 27 January 1944. German planning documents envisaged that the city would be starved rather than stormed, and its population fed at no cost to the Reich. Rations fell in November 1941 to 125 grams of adulterated bread a day for dependants, and in the winter of 1941-42 the city lost people at a rate of thousands a day to starvation, cold and disease, compounded by artillery and air bombardment. A supply and evacuation route was improvised across the ice and water of Lake Ladoga, carrying about 1.4 million people out of the city over the course of the siege. Soviet-era figures put civilian deaths at about 632,000; postwar and post-Soviet scholarship generally places the toll between 800,000 and 1.1 million, including deaths among evacuees.
contested: Death tolls differ widely: the figure of 632,000 presented at Nuremberg was a wartime administrative count, while later reconstructions add unregistered deaths, deaths of refugees who had entered the city and deaths of evacuees after departure.

sources.title: Britannica: Siege of Leningrad
Richard Bidlack and Nikita Lomagin, The Leningrad Blockade, 1941-1944: A New Documentary History from the Soviet Archives (Yale University Press)

deathsNote: The lower figure is the Soviet count of civilian deaths presented to the Nuremberg tribunal; Britannica notes 650,000 deaths in 1942 alone. Bidlack and Lomagin and most current scholarship place total civilian deaths from starvation, cold, disease and bombardment at roughly 800,000 to 1.1 million, the higher end including those who died during or shortly after evacuation. Military deaths on the Leningrad fronts are counted separately and were far higher.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: German operational orders that the city was to be sealed and starved rather than accepted in surrender, and the effects of the blockade and bombardment, are documented in the German army records cited at Nuremberg and in the Soviet archival documents published by Bidlack and Lomagin.

The figures include refugees who had fled into the city from the Baltic and the surrounding oblast.

title: The Ustasha Regime and the Jasenovac Camps
actors: The Ustasha regime of the Axis-created Independent State of Croatia killed, expelled and forcibly converted Serbs and killed Jews and Roma
peopleRange: Roughly 300,000 to 400,000 Serbs fled or were expelled from the Independent State of Croatia to German-occupied Serbia and Italian-controlled zones between 1941 and 1945, and comparable numbers of Croats and Muslims were displaced by the ensuing civil war. Tens of thousands were held in the Jasenovac camp complex and its subcamps, including Stara Gradiska and the children's camps at Sisak and Jastrebarsko. Displacement figures come from German and Italian occupation reports and from refugee registration in Serbia; camp figures from the surviving Ustasha records and the postwar victim lists.

flows.label: Serbs expelled from the Independent State of Croatia -> German-occupied Serbia
Arrested Serbs, Jews and Roma -> Jasenovac camp complex

summary: The Independent State of Croatia, established under German and Italian sponsorship in April 1941 and run by Ante Pavelic's Ustasha movement, adopted racial laws within weeks and set out to remove the roughly two million Serbs in its territory by killing, expulsion and forced conversion to Catholicism, while destroying its Jewish and Roma populations. Massacres in the Kordun, Lika, Herzegovina and Bosnian Krajina in the summer of 1941 drove hundreds of thousands into flight and fed the Chetnik and Partisan insurgencies. The Jasenovac complex, operating from August 1941 to April 1945, was the regime's principal camp; the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum notes that estimates of those killed there range widely, and the Jasenovac Memorial Site maintains a list of 83,145 named victims, of whom about 47,600 were Serbs, 16,200 Roma, 13,100 Jews and 4,300 Croats, including more than 20,000 children. Yugoslav-era figures of 500,000 to 700,000 killed at Jasenovac, and later Croatian revisionist figures of only a few thousand, are both rejected by most current scholarship. The dispute over the numbers remains politically charged in Croatia and Serbia.
contested: The number killed at Jasenovac is bitterly disputed: Serbian nationalist accounts give figures of several hundred thousand, Croatian revisionist accounts give figures in the low tens of thousands or fewer, and the memorial site's name-by-name list stands at 83,145.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Jasenovac

deathsNote: Estimates of Serbs killed by the Ustasha regime across the Independent State of Croatia range from about 300,000 to 500,000, with roughly 30,000 Jews and 25,000 to 30,000 Roma killed. For the Jasenovac complex specifically, the memorial site's individually verified list stands at 83,145 names; the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum notes that scholarly estimates for Jasenovac range from around 77,000 to 100,000, against far higher Yugoslav-era claims and far lower revisionist ones. The disagreement is driven by the destruction of camp records in 1945 and by the political uses of the figures since.

baselineNote: The NDH's roughly 6.3 million inhabitants included about 1.9 million Serbs, some 39,000 Jews and between 25,000 and 40,000 Roma, figures derived from the 1931 Yugoslav census applied to the puppet state's 1941 borders. Victim totals remain disputed: the Jasenovac Memorial Site lists about 83,000 named victims while historians' estimates for the camp system run from roughly 80,000 to over 100,000, and for the regime as a whole substantially higher.

title: The United States Navy on Vieques, Puerto Rico
actors: The United States Navy expropriated most of the island of Vieques, evicted its residents into a central strip, and used the eastern end as a bombing and gunnery range for six decades
peopleRange: Roughly 3,000 people were displaced by the Navy's expropriations of 1941-1948, which took about 26,000 of the island's 33,000 acres — around two thirds of Vieques — and confined the civilian population to a central band; some families were resettled to St Croix in the US Virgin Islands. The figures come from Navy expropriation records, Puerto Rican government reporting and later congressional documentation. The island's population fell from about 10,000 before the war to roughly 7,000 by the 1950s and around 9,300 at the 2000 census.
territoryDesc: About 26,000 acres, roughly 105 km2 of the island's 135 km2, held by the Navy for a munitions depot in the west and a live-fire range in the east; most was transferred to the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the municipality after 2003 and remains under environmental clean-up.

flows.label: Displaced Viequenses resettled to St Croix

summary: From 1941 the United States Navy expropriated about two thirds of Vieques, a municipality of Puerto Rico, evicting families from sugar-growing land into a central civilian strip between a munitions depot in the west and a live-fire training range in the east. The range was used for naval gunnery, aerial bombing and amphibious exercises by the US and allied navies for six decades. Long-running local opposition became a mass movement after a civilian security guard, David Sanes, was killed by an errant bomb in April 1999; sustained civil disobedience and encampments on the range, and a referendum in 2001 in which islanders voted for the Navy to leave, led to the end of training in May 2003. The Navy lands passed largely to the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and the eastern range was placed on the Superfund national priorities list in 2005; contamination and elevated rates of illness on Vieques remain the subject of dispute and litigation. The atlas contained Guantanamo but no entry for military land-taking in Puerto Rico.
contested: Whether military contamination caused the elevated cancer and other illness rates reported on Vieques — asserted by island health advocates and the Puerto Rican government, and treated as unproven by the US federal Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, whose earlier findings were later reopened for review.

violenceNote: Navy expropriation files and Puerto Rican government reporting document the taking of homes and farmland and the eviction of residents in the 1940s.
baselineWhat: The population of the island municipality of Vieques, Puerto Rico, at the 1940 United States census, immediately before the Navy expropriations
baselineNote: The 1940 decennial census counted 10,362 residents on Vieques; the Navy took about two-thirds of the island in 1941-1948 and compressed the civilian population into a central strip, and by the 1960 census the municipality had fallen to about 7,200.

title: Deportation of the Volga Germans and Soviet Germans
actors: Soviet authorities deported the ethnic German population of the Volga German ASSR and other regions of the western USSR to Kazakhstan and Siberia shortly after the German invasion, citing suspected disloyalty; the Volga German ASSR was abolished.
peopleRange: at least 846,000 in the initial 1941 wave (about 480,000 from the Volga region alone), rising to over 900,000 including later waves and repatriations from other regions

flows.label: Volga German ASSR → Kazakh SSR
Volga German ASSR → Siberia

summary: Days after Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, Soviet authorities ordered the mass deportation of ethnic Germans, most prominently the roughly 480,000 residents of the Volga German Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, which was abolished. Deportations extended to Germans in Crimea, the North Caucasus, Ukraine, Moscow and elsewhere, bringing the total in the initial wave to at least 846,000, with further waves later exceeding 900,000. Deportees were sent to Kazakhstan and Siberia and typically conscripted into forced-labor battalions ('labor army'); historian estimates of deaths from the deportation and forced-labor system range up to roughly a quarter million. Most Volga Germans were not permitted to return, and many later emigrated to Germany after the Soviet collapse.
contested: Death toll estimates vary by source, generally ranging from roughly 45,000 (transit deaths alone) up to about 228,000–250,000 when forced-labor-related mortality is included; some historians and Russian-German advocacy groups characterize the deportation as ethnic persecution amounting to a war crime, though it is not generally classified as genocide in mainstream scholarship.

sources.title: Deportation of Soviet Germans (1941–1942) - Wikipedia
Volga German ASSR - Wikipedia

deathsNote: J. Otto Pohl estimates that about 50,000 people, some 6 per cent of the at least 846,340 Soviet Germans deported in 1941-42, died in transit, and that nearly a quarter of a million died overall as a result of the 1941-42 deportations and the smaller 1945-46 operations, including 60,000-70,000 who died in the labour battalions (Trudarmiya) and further deaths in the Kazakh and Siberian special settlements, where official figures showed about 8 per cent mortality in Kazakhstan for 1944-49 alone. The low end counts transit deaths only; the high end is Pohl's cumulative figure extending well past the 1941-42 deportation window. Soviet-era records systematically under-recorded special-settler mortality, so both ends rest on archival reconstructions rather than a contemporaneous count.

Autonomy for the Volga German ASSR, abolished in 1941, has never been restored

violenceNote: Forced labour in the Trudarmiya labour battalions and confinement under the special-settlement regime are documented by historians J. Otto Pohl and Irina Mukhina and in Human Rights Watch's 1991 study of the USSR's 'punished peoples'.

baselineNote: The 1939 Soviet census recorded 1,427,222 Germans, of whom about 366,000 lived in the Volga German ASSR abolished by the decree of 28 August 1941. Roughly 900,000 were deported east in 1941-42; those in territory overrun by the Wehrmacht were deported later or repatriated by force after 1945.

title: Internment of Japanese Americans and Japanese Canadians
actors: The United States and Canadian governments removed and confined their residents of Japanese ancestry, most of them citizens, from the Pacific coast
peopleRange: About 120,000 people held in ten War Relocation Authority camps in the United States (Britannica) and about 23,000 uprooted in Canada, of whom roughly 12,000 went to internment camps in the British Columbia interior, 4,000 to sugar-beet labour in Alberta and Manitoba and 700 to prisoner-of-war camps in Ontario (Canadian Museum for Human Rights).

flows.label: San Francisco Bay Area → Manzanar, California
Seattle and Puget Sound → Minidoka, Idaho
Vancouver and coastal British Columbia → Slocan Valley camps

summary: After Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor, the United States under Executive Order 9066 excluded people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast and held approximately 120,000 of them, about two-thirds US citizens, in ten guarded camps at Manzanar, Tule Lake, Poston, Gila River, Minidoka, Heart Mountain, Topaz, Granada, Rohwer and Jerome between 1942 and 1945. Canada acted in parallel, clearing a 100-mile coastal 'protected zone' that contained about 90 per cent of its Japanese Canadian population and uprooting some 23,000 people to interior camps, road gangs and prairie sugar-beet farms. Canadian internees' homes, farms, boats and businesses were confiscated and sold by the Custodian of Enemy Property to finance their own detention, and about 4,000 people were deported to Japan after the war; Japanese Canadians were not permitted to move freely again until 1949. Both states later acknowledged the policy as unjust: the United States passed the Civil Liberties Act in 1988 and Canada reached a redress agreement the same year, including a formal apology, individual payments and restoration of citizenship. The camps were not death camps and no mass killing occurred, but detention lasted years and dispossession was permanent for most families.
contested: The Canadian total is variously given as 21,000, 22,000 or 23,000 depending on whether Japanese nationals, naturalised citizens and Canadian-born are counted together, and historians dispute whether the post-war deportations to Japan should be described as voluntary 'repatriation' or as expulsion, since many of those sent were Canadian-born.

sources.title: Japanese American internment — Britannica
Japanese Canadian internment and the struggle for redress — Canadian Museum for Human Rights
Homicide in camp — Densho Encyclopedia

deathsNote: There was no mass death toll. The Densho Encyclopedia documents seven unarmed Japanese Americans shot dead by guards in US internment and War Relocation Authority camps between 1942 and 1944, including two men killed when troops fired on a protest at Manzanar and James Wakasa, shot near the fence at Topaz; sentries were acquitted in every case that went to trial. Roughly 1,800 more people died in the camps over four years from illness and old age, a figure broadly consistent with the mortality of a population of that size and not treated as excess mortality by the US camp records.
violenceNote: Detention without individual charge is documented by Britannica and the Canadian Museum for Human Rights; the CMHR also documents coerced labour on Alberta and Manitoba sugar-beet farms and the wartime stripping and post-war restoration of Japanese Canadian citizenship rights.
baselineWhat: The population of Japanese ancestry living in the mainland United States and in Canada in 1941
baselineNote: The 1940 US census counted 126,947 people of Japanese ancestry in the continental United States, about 112,000 of them in the three Pacific coast states; the 1941 Canadian census counted 23,149 in British Columbia and adjacent areas. Roughly two thirds in each country were citizens by birth.
shareCaveat: The denominator excludes the roughly 158,000 people of Japanese ancestry in Hawaii, who were not subject to mass removal; because removal on the mainland was near-total the ratio approaches 100 per cent and measures the completeness of the policy rather than its selectivity.

title: The Japanese Occupation of Southeast Asia: Internment, Romusha and Famine
actors: Japan interned Allied civilians and prisoners of war and conscripted millions of Asian labourers across its occupied territories
peopleRange: About 100,000 Dutch and other European civilians were interned in camps in the Dutch East Indies, and roughly 140,000 Allied prisoners of war were held across the Japanese-occupied territories, of whom about 60,000 were used with some 200,000 Asian labourers on the Burma-Siam railway. Estimates of Indonesian romusha mobilised on Java range from 4.1 million to 10 million, of whom about 300,000 were sent overseas. Figures come from Japanese and Allied camp records, the postwar Dutch government inquiries summarised by the NIOD Institute, and Allied war graves registration.

flows.label: Java -> romusha labour on the Burma-Siam railway and other projects
Allied prisoners of war from Singapore -> Burma-Siam railway

summary: Japanese occupation of the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Burma, the Dutch East Indies and Indochina brought mass internment and mass labour conscription. European civilians in the Indies, about 100,000 people, were held in camps where roughly one in six died. Allied prisoners of war were used as labour in violation of the conventions Japan had undertaken to apply: on the Burma-Siam railway some 12,000 of about 60,000 Allied prisoners died, alongside far higher mortality among the estimated 200,000 Asian labourers, of whom up to 90,000 are thought to have died. In Java the occupation authorities mobilised millions of romusha for construction and agriculture, sending about 300,000 abroad, from whom deaths are estimated at anywhere between 77,000 and 225,000 with total Indonesian romusha deaths put at considerably more than 300,000. Rice requisitioning, the collapse of shipping and forced crop substitution produced famine: about 2.4 million people are estimated to have died in Java in 1944-45, and in northern Vietnam the famine of 1944-45 killed between 400,000 and two million people, the higher figure being the Vietnamese official estimate. The Tokyo tribunal found that the ill-treatment of prisoners of war and civilian internees was a matter of policy, condoned and concealed at the highest levels.
contested: Death tolls for the Java and Vietnamese famines and for Asian labourers on Japanese projects vary widely, since neither the Japanese authorities nor the returning colonial administrations counted the Asian victims systematically.

sources.title: NIOD Institute for War, Holocaust and Genocide Studies: the Japanese occupation and the Pacific War in numbers

deathsNote: The range aggregates the principal counted and estimated components: about 13,000 to 16,800 deaths among European civilian internees in the Indies, some 12,000 Allied prisoners on the Burma-Siam railway and up to 90,000 Asian labourers there, more than 300,000 Indonesian romusha deaths, roughly 2.4 million famine deaths in Java in 1944-45, and 400,000 to 2 million in the northern Vietnamese famine. The Indonesian government's own postwar estimate of total deaths under the occupation was 4 million. Famine mortality figures are demographic reconstructions and carry the widest uncertainty.

atrocityFindings.finding: Found that the ill-treatment of prisoners of war and civilian internees, including their use as forced labour on the Burma-Siam railway, was a policy condoned and concealed by the Japanese government and high command

baselineNote: Contemporary colonial estimates give roughly 70 million in the Netherlands East Indies, 24 million in French Indochina, 17 million in Burma, 16 million in the Philippines and about 5 million in British Malaya and Singapore, totalling around 130 million in 1942.

title: The Pacific War in New Guinea: Conscripted Labour and Civilian Displacement
actors: Australian military administration and Japanese forces conscripted Papuans and New Guineans as carriers and labourers and drove villagers from their land
peopleRange: Australian New Guinea Administrative Unit records show tens of thousands of Papuans and New Guineans under compulsory labour agreements at any one time, with cumulative totals commonly given between 37,000 and 55,000 men for Australian service alone; Japanese forces conscripted labour in the areas they held. No count was made of villagers displaced by fighting, bombing and the destruction of gardens, which affected communities along the Kokoda track, the Huon peninsula, Rabaul and the north coast.

flows.label: Villagers displaced from Rabaul and the New Guinea islands

summary: When Japanese forces landed in New Guinea in 1942, the Australian territories were placed under the Australian New Guinea Administrative Unit, which used wartime regulations to conscript indigenous men as carriers, labourers and medical orderlies at fixed low rates of pay, with penalties for desertion; the carriers of the Kokoda campaign, later celebrated in Australia as the 'Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels', were largely conscripted, a point the Australian War Memorial itself now makes in setting the myth against the record. Japanese forces likewise requisitioned labour, food and land in the areas they controlled, and researchers working on the New Guinea campaign have documented sexual violence against local women by both armies. Villages were bombed, gardens destroyed and populations moved by the fighting along the north coast, in the Markham and Ramu valleys and around Rabaul, where the Tolai were displaced for the duration. Civilian deaths from fighting, disease and famine in the territories ran into the tens of thousands and were never systematically counted. Australian postwar compensation for war damage in the territories was limited.
contested: The Australian popular memory of willing indigenous helpers is contested by scholarship emphasising conscription and coercion; civilian death and displacement figures were never compiled by any authority.

sources.title: Australian War Memorial: The 'Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels' - looking beyond the myth
National WWII Museum: Angels and victims - the people of New Guinea in World War II

deathsNote: No authority counted indigenous civilian deaths in the New Guinea campaign. The range reflects estimates in the literature covering deaths of conscripted carriers from disease and exhaustion, civilians killed in fighting and bombing, and famine deaths where gardens were destroyed or populations moved; all are approximations.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Australian War Memorial and ANGAU records, and research published in the Journal of Pacific History on the New Guinea campaign, document compulsory labour, village destruction and sexual violence by both armies.

Any share calculated on this base carries an uncertainty of several hundred thousand.

title: Turkey's Wealth Tax and the Askale Labour Camp
actors: The Turkish state levied a discriminatory capital tax on non-Muslim citizens and sent defaulters to labour camps in eastern Anatolia
peopleRange: Around 1,400 men, by the most commonly used figure, were deported to labour camps at Askale and Sivrihisar for non-payment, all of them non-Muslims; some accounts give figures up to about 5,000 for those sent to labour service overall. Assessment records show tens of thousands of non-Muslim households taxed at rates several times those applied to Muslims, with property auctioned to meet the demands. Figures come from Turkish finance ministry records and from studies of the tax by Turkish and foreign historians.

flows.label: Defaulting non-Muslim taxpayers deported from Istanbul to the Askale camp
Emigration of Jews from Turkey after the tax, mainly to Israel from 1948

summary: The Varlik Vergisi, a one-off capital tax approved by the Turkish parliament on 11 November 1942, was presented as a wartime defence measure but was assessed through separate lists that taxed non-Muslim citizens, chiefly Greeks, Armenians, Jews and Levantines, at rates several times higher than Muslims, in some cases exceeding a taxpayer's entire wealth. There was no appeal, payment was demanded within fifteen days, and property including that of close relatives was seized and auctioned, in many cases to Muslim buyers at low prices. Those who could not pay were sent to labour camps in eastern Anatolia, principally Askale near Erzurum, where they worked on roads and in quarries with half their wages deducted against the debt; the law's exemption for men over fifty-five was frequently ignored, and twenty-one detainees died. The tax was repealed in March 1944 and outstanding debts cancelled after criticism from Turkey's wartime partners, but the confiscations were not reversed. The episode, together with the 1934 Thrace events and the 1955 Istanbul pogrom already in this atlas, is treated by historians as a major driver of the departure of Turkey's non-Muslim communities; Turkish governments have generally treated it as a fiscal measure of its time rather than as a discriminatory act requiring redress.
contested: Turkish official accounts have long presented the tax as a wartime revenue measure applied unevenly through administrative failure, while most historians describe its non-Muslim lists as deliberate discrimination intended to transfer minority-held wealth; the number sent to labour camps and the value of confiscated property are both disputed.

sources.title: Varlik Vergisi (Wikipedia)

deathsNote: Twenty-one deaths among those held in the eastern Anatolian labour camps are recorded in the standard accounts, mostly among elderly men unable to withstand the work and the climate. There was no killing beyond this; the tax's principal effects were dispossession and emigration rather than death.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Compulsory labour for defaulters, the separate classification of citizens by religion for tax purposes and the confiscation and auction of homes and businesses are documented in Turkish finance ministry records and in historical studies of the tax.
baselineWhat: The non-Muslim minority population of Turkey — Greeks, Armenians and Jews — at the time of the Wealth Tax
baselineNote: The Turkish census of 1935 recorded about 78,700 Jews and some 240,000 Christians (mainly Armenians and Greeks), giving a non-Muslim total of roughly 320,000 out of 16.2 million. The tax was assessed on about 87,000 taxpayers, a majority of them non-Muslim, and non-Muslims were assessed at several times the rate applied to Muslims.
shareCaveat: The affected figure counts only those defaulters actually deported to the Aşkale and Sivrihisar labour camps; the tax itself ruined a far larger number of families through forced sales of businesses and property.

title: The Wartime Internment of the Unangax (Aleut) of Alaska
actors: United States authorities evacuated Unangax villages in the Aleutians and held the people in camps in Southeast Alaska; Japanese forces deported the villagers of Attu to Japan
peopleRange: 881 Unangax from nine villages were removed by United States authorities in 1942, according to the National Park Service, and held for about two years in abandoned canneries, a herring saltery and a gold-mine camp in Southeast Alaska; 42 villagers of Attu were taken by Japanese forces to Hokkaido. Death figures in the American camps are recorded by site: 32 at Funter Bay, 20 at Ward Lake, 17 at Killisnoo and 5 at Burnett Inlet, a total of 74.

flows.label: Pribilof Islanders removed to Funter Bay, Southeast Alaska
Atka villagers removed to Ward Lake near Ketchikan
Attu villagers deported by Japanese forces to Hokkaido

summary: After Japanese forces bombed Dutch Harbor and occupied Attu and Kiska in June 1942, United States authorities evacuated Unangax residents of the Aleutian and Pribilof Islands, in most cases at a few hours' notice, and held them for roughly two years in disused industrial buildings in Southeast Alaska. Conditions were severe: at Funter Bay several hundred people shared a single toilet and drank contaminated water, and 74 people died across the camps, a death rate far above normal for the population. Villages left behind were looted and burned by American and Japanese forces, and four were never resettled; the Pribilof men were meanwhile taken back seasonally to harvest fur seals for the federal government. The 42 Attu villagers captured by Japanese forces were deported to Otaru on Hokkaido, where about half died. In 1982 the Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians reported to Congress on the treatment of both Japanese Americans and the Aleuts, and Congress provided restitution under the Aleutian and Pribilof Islands Restitution Act of 1988, paying surviving evacuees 12,000 dollars each and funding community and church compensation.
contested: Whether the evacuation was a protective measure or an act of racial discrimination is debated: the federal government presented it as removal from a war zone, while the 1982 commission and Unangax representatives emphasised that white residents of the same islands were not treated the same way and that conditions in the camps were unjustifiable.

The Wartime Internment of Native Alaskans (National WWII Museum)
Personal Justice Denied: Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians (US National Archives)

deathsNote: 74 deaths are documented by camp in the United States facilities, from tuberculosis, influenza, pneumonia and the conditions of confinement; roughly half of the 42 Attu villagers deported to Japan died there, which brings the combined toll to about 95-100. The figures come from federal records and from the 1982 commission's investigation.

atrocityFindings.finding: Reported to Congress in Personal Justice Denied on the evacuation and detention of the Aleuts as well as of Japanese Americans, finding the conditions of their detention indefensible and recommending restitution, which Congress enacted in 1988

violenceNote: Detention in unfit camps, the burning and looting of the evacuated villages and the seasonal return of Pribilof men to work the federal fur-seal harvest are documented by the National Park Service and by the Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians.
baselineWhat: The Unangax (Aleut) population of the Aleutian and Pribilof Islands on the eve of the 1942 evacuation
baselineNote: The National Park Service records 881 Unangax evacuated from nine villages by United States authorities, with a further 42 taken from Attu to Japan; contemporary Alaska Native rolls put the total island population at roughly 1,000-1,200, so the evacuation covered nearly the whole community. The number is small enough that the range chiefly reflects who was counted as resident.

title: The Bengal Famine of 1943
actors: Wartime requisitioning, boat and rice denial policies and market failure under British rule in India produced famine in Bengal
peopleRange: Hundreds of thousands of destitute villagers moved into Calcutta and other towns in search of food during 1943, and the Famine Inquiry Commission recorded large-scale distress migration across eastern Bengal; contemporary relief and municipal records suggest on the order of a million people were displaced within the province, though no register was kept. The evidentiary basis is the 1945 Famine Inquiry Commission report, provincial relief records and later demographic reconstruction.

flows.label: Rural eastern Bengal -> Calcutta

summary: Famine struck Bengal in 1943 after a cyclone and crop disease damaged the winter rice crop, the fall of Burma cut off imports, and prices rose sharply amid hoarding and speculation. Government measures compounded the crisis: a denial policy in coastal districts removed some 45,000 boats and stocks of rice to deny them to a possible Japanese invasion, provincial governments blocked inter-provincial grain movement, and priority was given to feeding Calcutta's war industries and the armed forces. Requests from the government of India for grain imports were repeatedly refused or reduced in London on shipping grounds. Death estimates range from about 1.5 million in the Famine Inquiry Commission's 1945 report to 3 million in later work, with Amartya Sen's study putting the toll at about 3 million and demographic reconstructions by Arup Maharatna and others at roughly 2.1 million. Causation remains argued: Sen emphasised entitlement failure amid adequate aggregate supply, Madhusree Mukerjee and others hold Churchill's war cabinet responsible for refusing relief shipments, and other historians stress crop shortfall, the loss of Burmese rice and provincial mismanagement. No British government has formally apologised.
contested: Both the death toll, ranging from about 1.5 million to 3 million, and the causation are disputed, with arguments dividing between entitlement failure and market breakdown, crop shortfall, and the deliberate policy choices of the British war cabinet.

sources.title: Britannica: Bengal famine of 1943
Conclusions of the 1943-44 Bengal Famine Commission (Hillsdale College Churchill Project)

deathsNote: The Famine Inquiry Commission of 1945 estimated about 1.5 million deaths from starvation and epidemic disease. Amartya Sen and Britannica give about 3 million; Arup Maharatna's demographic reconstruction gives roughly 2.1 million, and later work has proposed figures in between. The disagreement turns on how far excess deaths from cholera, malaria and smallpox in 1943-44 are attributed to the famine and on the reliability of Bengal's vital registration.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The boat denial and rice denial policies, the blocking of inter-provincial grain trade and the priority given to army and industrial rations are documented in the Famine Inquiry Commission report and in the India Office and war cabinet records examined by later historians.
baselineWhat: The population of the Bengal Presidency at the 1941 census of India
baselineNote: The 1941 census counted 60,306,525 people in Bengal. Excess mortality in 1943-44 is usually put at 2.1-3 million; the figure recorded here counts the destitute who left the countryside for Calcutta and the district towns, enumerated only partially by the Famine Inquiry Commission and relief agencies.
shareCaveat: The affected figure counts distress migration, not deaths, and rests on relief-agency estimates rather than an enumeration.

title: Istrian–Dalmatian Exodus of Italians
actors: Following Yugoslav Partisan and then communist control of Istria, Rijeka/Fiume, and Dalmatia—territory transferred from Italy chiefly under the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty—most of the local ethnic Italian population, along with some Slovenes and Croats, emigrated to Italy.
peopleRange: estimates range from about 200,000 to 350,000, depending on the source (191,421 per Croatian historian Vladimir Žerjavić; roughly 250,000 per Italian historian Raoul Pupo; up to 350,000 per some Italian estimates)
territoryDesc: Istria, the city of Rijeka/Fiume, and parts of Dalmatia, transferred from Italy to Yugoslavia

flows.label: Istria → Trieste/Italy
Dalmatia → Ancona/Italy

summary: As Yugoslav Partisan and subsequently Yugoslav communist authorities took control of Istria, the city of Rijeka (Fiume), and parts of Dalmatia—territory ceded by Italy chiefly under the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty—the great majority of the region's ethnic Italian population, along with some Slovenes and Croats opposed to the new communist government, departed for Italy over the following years. Estimates of the total number who left range from about 200,000 to 350,000. The exodus is closely linked in public memory to the 'foibe' killings, in which Yugoslav Partisans executed thousands of Italians (and some Slovenes/Croats accused of collaboration) and disposed of bodies in karst pits, though the exodus itself unfolded over a longer period through both violence and political pressure. A joint Italian-Slovenian historical commission later found the evidence did not establish a deliberate, centrally organized expulsion policy.
contested: The scale, causes, and characterization of the exodus are actively disputed: Italian historiography and diaspora organizations have often described it as a forced expulsion linked to ethnic persecution, while Croatian and Slovenian historiography has emphasized voluntary emigration amid the broader upheavals of regime change and war-related violence; a joint Italian-Slovenian commission found no evidence of a deliberate, organized expulsion policy, though it acknowledged intimidation and violence occurred.

sources.title: Istrian–Dalmatian exodus - Wikipedia
Foibe massacres - Wikipedia

deathsNote: Italian historian Raoul Pupo estimates 3,000–4,000 victims of the foibe killings and related deaths, revising his own earlier higher figure; Guido Rumici estimates 6,000–11,000 executed or dead in Yugoslav camps; Mario Pacor counts only 400–500 thrown into the foibe with about 4,000 deported. Claims of up to 20,000 circulate in Italian exile and nationalist accounts. The joint Italian–Slovene historical commission acknowledged 'hundreds of summary executions' without endorsing a total. Italian and Slovene/Croatian historians disagree over whether the victims were principally fascist officials and collaborators or largely civilians, and over whether the killings were spontaneous revenge or deliberate Titoist policy.

atrocityFindings.body: Slovene–Italian Historical and Cultural Commission (joint government-appointed commission)
atrocityFindings.finding: Concluded that the violence included 'hundreds of summary executions — victims were mostly thrown into the Karst chasms (foibe) — and the deportation of a great number of soldiers and civilians, who either wasted away or were killed during the deportation'

violenceNote: The joint Slovene–Italian historical commission recorded hundreds of summary executions with bodies disposed of in karst chasms and the deportation of large numbers of soldiers and civilians who died in Yugoslav captivity.
baselineWhat: The population of the territories transferred from Italy to Yugoslavia - Istria, Fiume/Rijeka, Zara and parts of the Julian March
baselineNote: The ceded areas held on the order of half a million people, of whom the Italian census of 1936 counted roughly 230,000-250,000 as Italian, against a Slovene and Croat majority; the ethnic composition of both the territory and the departing population is contested between Italian and Croatian/Slovene historiography. Estimates of the exodus range from about 200,000 to 350,000, with the Italian-Slovene-Croatian historians' commission settling on roughly 250,000.
shareCaveat: Both the size of the exodus and how many of those who left were Italian rather than Slavic-speaking are politically contested, and the departures ran over seventeen years, so the ratio carries a wide margin at both ends.

title: Deportation of the North Caucasus Peoples, Kalmyks, and Meskhetian Turks
actors: Soviet NKVD forces deported entire nationalities collectively accused of wartime disloyalty or unreliability — Kalmyks (December 1943), Chechens and Ingush (February 1944, Operation Lentil), Karachays and Balkars, and Meskhetian Turks, Kurds and Hemshils from southern Georgia (November 1944) — to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Siberia.
peopleRange: roughly 800,000 combined across the 1943–44 operations (about 496,000 Chechens and Ingush, 93,000 Kalmyks, 115,000 Meskhetian Turks and others, plus roughly 70,000 Karachays and 37,000 Balkars)

flows.label: Chechens & Ingush → Kazakh/Kyrgyz SSR
Kalmyks → Siberia
Meskhetian Turks → Uzbek SSR

summary: In late 1943 and 1944, Stalin's government carried out a series of forced deportations of entire ethnic groups from the North Caucasus and southern Georgia, on the grounds of alleged mass collaboration with German occupying forces (for the Kalmyks, Chechens, Ingush, Karachays and Balkars) or, in the case of Meskhetian Turks and neighboring groups, proximity to the Turkish border. In total roughly 800,000 people were transported, mostly in sealed freight cars, to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Siberia, and the affected peoples' autonomous republics were abolished. Mortality during transit and the following years from hunger, cold and disease was severe, with death-rate estimates for individual groups ranging from about 13% to over 20% in the first years alone. Survivors were confined to 'special settlements' under close surveillance until restrictions began easing after Stalin's death in 1953, with the Chechens and Ingush permitted to return to the Caucasus from 1957.
contested: Death toll estimates vary considerably by group and by the period counted, generally ranging from roughly 100,000 to over 200,000 across all groups; the governments of Chechnya, Ingushetia, Georgia and Kalmykia, along with many scholars, have characterized these deportations as genocide or ethnic cleansing, a term the Soviet Union never used and that Russian federal authorities have not formally adopted, while nonetheless recognizing the deportations as illegal Stalin-era repression under a 1991 Russian law.

Otto Pohl calculates about 123,000 Chechen and Ingush deaths to 1949 and the demographer Dalkhat Ediev about 145,800, and adding Kalmyk and Meskhetian Turk mortality brings archival-based totals to roughly 150,000-200,000. title: The Massacres of Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia
actors: The Ukrainian Insurgent Army and allied local units killed and expelled the Polish population of Volhynia and Eastern Galicia; Polish underground units carried out reprisals against Ukrainian villages
peopleRange: Between 300,000 and 400,000 Poles fled Volhynia and Eastern Galicia in 1943-1944, a figure reconstructed from Polish underground reports, wartime German administrative records and postwar repatriation registers. Killings are estimated by Poland's Institute of National Remembrance at around 100,000 Poles, with Ukrainian and some Western scholars giving 50,000-60,000 for Volhynia and a further 20,000-30,000 for Galicia; Polish reprisals killed an estimated 10,000-15,000 Ukrainians. Estimates rest on village-by-village testimony collections compiled decades later, which Polish and Ukrainian historians weigh differently.

flows.label: Polish survivors fleeing Volhynia, later resettled in western Poland

summary: From the spring of 1943 the Ukrainian Insurgent Army and allied village self-defence units conducted a campaign against the Polish rural population of Volhynia, spreading to Eastern Galicia in 1944, with the aim of removing Poles from territory claimed for a future Ukrainian state. Whole villages were destroyed in coordinated attacks, the largest on 11 July 1943 when scores of settlements were struck simultaneously. Polish underground formations and, later, Soviet-backed units carried out reprisal killings in Ukrainian villages. The killings drove the flight of several hundred thousand Poles westwards, feeding the population transfers and Operation Vistula already covered in the atlas. The events remain politically live: Poland's Sejm declared them a genocide in July 2016, a characterisation Ukraine's parliament rejected in a formal statement, and successive Ukrainian governments have declined to adopt it while acknowledging the killings.
contested: Whether the killings constitute genocide — affirmed by Poland's Sejm and Institute of National Remembrance, rejected by Ukraine's Verkhovna Rada and by parts of Ukrainian historiography, which emphasise the reciprocal character of the violence and the wartime context.

title: Bulgaria's Communist Labour Camps: Belene, Lovech and the Camp Network
actors: The Bulgarian communist state interned political opponents and people classed as socially undesirable in labour camps by administrative order
peopleRange: A commission of inquiry set up in 1990 found that some 12,000 men and women passed through the camps between 1944 and 1953 and a further 5,000 between 1956 and 1962; another estimate cited alongside it puts the total as high as 186,000, a figure that appears to count all forms of administrative punishment rather than camp internment. A witness account gives 7,000 held at Belene in 1952, against a documented 2,323 inmates there at the height of the repression under Valko Chervenkov. Roughly 100 camps operated over the period.

flows.label: Internees sent from Sofia and across Bulgaria to Belene island
Transfers to the Lovech quarry camp

summary: From 1944 the Bulgarian communist authorities operated camps to which people could be sent without trial by administrative decision. The largest was on Belene island in the Danube, opened in 1949, where inmates drained marshland and farmed; those sent there included opposition politicians, Protestant pastors convicted in the 1949 'Pastors' Trial', peasants who resisted collectivisation and, in the 1980s, ethnic Turks who refused the compulsory name changes of the 'Revival Process' recorded separately in this atlas. After a partial closure, the system's last and harshest camp opened at Lovech in 1959, where inmates broke stone in a quarry; 149 people are recorded as having died from abuse at Lovech and the adjacent women's camp at Skravena before both were closed in 1962. Detainees also included people held for 'social parasitism' or 'loose morals' rather than any political offence. A Bulgarian parliamentary and party inquiry examined the camps in 1990, and Belene continues to operate as a prison, which has complicated commemoration; former inmates have campaigned for recognition and access to files.
contested: The total number interned is unsettled, with the 1990 inquiry's figure of about 17,000 set against estimates an order of magnitude higher that use a broader definition of repression; responsibility has been little tested in court and the camps remain contested in Bulgarian politics.

sources.title: Forced labour camps in Communist Bulgaria (Wikipedia)

Totals for the whole camp network are not established; survivor accounts and later journalism suggest several hundred more died at Belene and elsewhere from beatings, malaria, hunger and shootings of those said to be escaping, but no register has been published.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

title: Deportation of the Crimean Tatars
actors: Soviet NKVD forces, on Stalin's order, deported the entire Crimean Tatar population from Crimea to Central Asia and the Urals as collective punishment for alleged wartime collaboration with Nazi Germany.
peopleRange: about 191,000–228,000 Crimean Tatars deported in May 1944 (some figures include related deportations of Crimean Greeks, Armenians, and Bulgarians later that year)

flows.label: Crimea → Uzbek SSR
Crimea → Russian SFSR/Siberia

summary: On 18–20 May 1944, NKVD troops rounded up and deported virtually the entire Crimean Tatar population—at least 191,000 and by some counts over 228,000 people—from Crimea to Uzbekistan and other parts of Central Asia and the Urals, packed into sealed freight cars. The Soviet government cited collective accusations of wartime collaboration with German occupation forces as justification, though this applied to only a portion of the population. Roughly 8,000 died during the journey itself, and thousands more died of hunger, disease, and harsh conditions in the following months and years in exile; scholarly death toll estimates through the following years range widely, from roughly 20,000 to over 40,000. Crimean Tatars were only permitted to return to Crimea beginning in the late 1980s.
contested: Ukraine's parliament (2015) and several other countries and legislatures have formally recognized the deportation as an act of genocide, a characterization endorsed by many scholars and by the Crimean Tatar Mejlis; Russia does not use the term genocide for the event, and precise mortality figures remain disputed due to incomplete Soviet-era records.

The dispute turns on whether Soviet registers undercounted and over what period deaths are attributed.

title: Expulsion of Ethnic Germans from Hungary and Yugoslavia
actors: Hungarian and Yugoslav communist-led authorities expelled or forced the flight of ethnic German (Danube Swabian) communities after the collapse of Axis control; in Yugoslavia many were first interned in camps.
peopleRange: roughly 500,000–720,000 combined: about 210,000–280,000 from Hungary and 300,000–445,000 from Yugoslavia
territoryDesc: German-settled communities in Hungary (Swabian Turkey and other regions) and Yugoslavia (Vojvodina, Slavonia)

flows.label: Hungarian Swabian communities → Austria/Germany
Vojvodina Germans → Austria/Germany

summary: As Axis forces retreated in 1944–45, ethnic German communities that had lived in Hungary and Yugoslavia for generations came under collective suspicion of collaboration. Hungary expelled roughly a quarter-million ethnic Germans in 1946–48 under Allied-sanctioned population transfer, while Yugoslavia's new communist government interned tens of thousands of Vojvodina Germans in camps where many died of hunger, disease and mistreatment before survivors were expelled or fled westward. Total displacement for the two countries combined is estimated at 500,000–720,000. The events largely ended a centuries-old German presence in the Danube basin outside Austria and Germany.
contested: The Yugoslav case is particularly disputed: some historians and Vojvodina German descendant organizations describe the camp internments (1945–48) as an act of state-organized collective punishment with a significant, disputed death toll, while other accounts emphasize the wartime context of Volksdeutsche collaboration with occupying forces; precise mortality figures for the Yugoslav camps are not firmly established.

sources.title: Flight and expulsion of Germans (1944-1950) - Wikipedia
Danube Swabians - Wikipedia

deathsNote: Almost all the deaths are Yugoslav: the West German Schieder Commission (1954-61) counted 69,000 civilian deaths there, of which 48,027 in Yugoslav internment camps such as Rudolfsgnad and Gakovo, and the German Federal Archives (1974) put the figure at 'at least 80,000'. A 1990s enumeration by Danube Swabian expellee organisations, working from named-victim lists, produced a lower total of about 58,000 confirmed dead — well below the West German government's 1958 estimate of 135,800 — and Rüdiger Overmans has criticised the population-balance method behind the higher official figures. For Hungary the Schieder Commission gives about 6,000 deaths, chiefly among the 30,000-35,000 civilians deported to the USSR for forced labour, alongside roughly 180,000-215,000 expelled westward. The gap between figures is methodological: confirmed named deaths versus demographic residuals, with Cold War politics pushing the official West German numbers upward.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: The West German Schieder Commission's own categories for Yugoslavia are 5,777 executed by Soviet and Yugoslav forces, 5,683 deportation deaths including 4,500-5,000 in Soviet forced labour, and 48,027 deaths in Yugoslav internment camps, with the 6,000 Hungarian-German deaths attributed to forced labour in the USSR; the German Federal Archives' 1974 report found about 8,000 of some 67,000 deaths in 49 large camps were due to violence and the rest to starvation, disease and maltreatment.
baselineWhat: The ethnic German population of Hungary and Yugoslavia before the expulsions
baselineNote: Hungary's 1941 census recorded 477,000 people with German as mother tongue but about 720,000 declaring German nationality, a gap that later shaped who was expelled. The Danube Swabians of Yugoslavia, mostly in the Vojvodina and Slavonia, numbered roughly 500,000-540,000 on the eve of the war.
shareCaveat: A large share of these communities was evacuated by German authorities or fled with the retreating Wehrmacht before the expulsion decrees, and is variously counted as evacuees or expellees.

title: Expulsion of Germans from Poland (Former Eastern Germany)
actors: Polish authorities and Soviet occupation forces expelled the ethnic German population of the former eastern German provinces transferred to Poland; many others had already fled ahead of the advancing Red Army in 1944–45.
peopleRange: roughly 6.9–8.5 million depending on source and methodology, of whom about 2.0 million remained in the territories as of early 1946 before final expulsion
territoryDesc: Former eastern German provinces of Silesia, Pomerania, eastern Brandenburg, and southern East Prussia, transferred to Poland under the Potsdam Agreement

flows.label: Breslau/Silesia → occupied Germany
Stettin/Pomerania → occupied Germany

summary: Following the Potsdam Agreement's transfer of former German territory to Poland, the resident ethnic German population was expelled westward into occupied Germany, in a process that combined organized 'transfers' with earlier chaotic wartime flight and postwar expulsions and internments. Estimates of the total affected range from about 6.9 to over 8 million people, making it the largest single component of the broader flight and expulsion of Germans from Central and Eastern Europe. Deaths during flight, expulsion, and in Polish-run camps are separately estimated at anywhere from roughly 500,000 to over 2 million, a range that remains one of the most disputed statistics of the postwar period. By 1950 only a small remnant German population remained in the territories, which were resettled with Poles from central Poland and from the annexed eastern territories.
contested: Death toll figures are sharply disputed, ranging from about 500,000–600,000 (based on documented individual cases) to 2.0–2.25 million (based on population-balance estimates originally produced by West German statistical offices); scholars also disagree on how much of the expulsion process should be characterized as organized policy versus wartime flight or local violence.

deathsNote: This is one of the most politically contested death tolls in post-war Europe. The West German Statistisches Bundesamt's 1958 population-balance study produced 2,225,000 deaths across all of Central and Eastern Europe, of which the Schieder Commission attributed roughly 2 million to the Oder-Neisse territories; the German Red Cross Search Service confirmed 473,013 civilian deaths by 1965 with about 1.9 million cases unresolved. The German Federal Archives' 1974 study found roughly 400,000-600,000 deaths from violent acts, and Rüdiger Overmans, Ingo Haar and the German Historical Institute argue for 500,000-600,000 documented deaths, holding that the higher figures are an artefact of Cold War-era population-balance methodology. German expellee organisations and successive West German governments favoured the high end; Polish historians and most recent German scholarship favour the low end. The parallel German-Czech commission revised the Czechoslovak figure down from 220,000 to 15,000-30,000, which is often cited as a precedent for the downward revision.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Internment in camps such as Łambinowice/Lamsdorf and Zgoda and the retention of Germans for labour before transfer are documented in the German Federal Archives' 1974 study of the expulsions and in the work of Rüdiger Overmans and Ingo Haar.

baselineNote: The German census of 1939 recorded about 9.6 million people in the provinces east of the Oder-Neisse line later assigned to Poland; pre-war Poland's own German minority added roughly 700,000-1 million. German and Polish official statistics differ on how many left as wartime evacuees rather than post-war expellees.

title: Finnish Karelia Cession and Evacuation
actors: Under the 1944 Moscow Armistice (confirmed by the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty), Finland ceded Karelia and other border areas to the Soviet Union; virtually the entire Finnish population evacuated westward rather than remain under Soviet rule.
peopleRange: about 410,000–430,000 Finns evacuated, roughly 11–12% of Finland's population
territoryDesc: Finnish Karelia (the Karelian Isthmus and Ladoga Karelia, including Vyborg), plus Petsamo and other smaller border areas

flows.label: Finnish Karelia → interior Finland

summary: Finland's defeat in the 1941–44 Continuation War against the Soviet Union led to the 1944 Moscow Armistice, under which Finland ceded Karelia, Petsamo, and other territories, later confirmed by the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty. Rather than live under Soviet rule, essentially the entire Finnish-speaking population of the ceded areas—about 410,000–430,000 people, over a tenth of Finland's population—evacuated to what remained of Finland, in an outcome Finland had also experienced on a smaller scale after the 1939–40 Winter War. Finland absorbed and resettled the evacuees under a dedicated land-redistribution program, avoiding the refugee camps seen elsewhere in postwar Europe. Vyborg, Finland's second-largest prewar city, and its surrounding region became part of the Soviet Union (later Russia).

No source provides a death range for the evacuation.

baselineNote: The ceded territory, about 11 per cent of Finland's area, held roughly 410,000-430,000 people, some 11-12 per cent of a national population of 3.7 million. Virtually the entire population was evacuated to the rest of Finland, first in 1940, then partly returning during the Continuation War, and finally in 1944; the Land Acquisition Act of 1945 resettled them across the country.

title: The German Scorched-Earth Evacuation of Finnmark and North Troms
actors: German forces retreating from the Murmansk front forcibly evacuated northern Norway's civilian population and burned its settlements
peopleRange: Norwegian accounts put the civilian population of the evacuation zone at close to 60,000 and record that around 25,000 people evaded the order by hiding in the mountains, in turf huts and in caves, including some 3,000 sheltering in the Bjornevatn mine tunnels near Kirkenes; the number actually moved south by sea and road is therefore usually given as roughly 45,000-50,000. The figures come from Norwegian wartime and reconstruction-era administrative records.

flows.label: Evacuees shipped from Finnmark to Trondelag and southern Norway
Coastal communities moved to Troms and the Lyngen line

summary: After Finland left the war in September 1944 and Soviet forces advanced into Sor-Varanger, the German 20th Mountain Army withdrew across northern Norway to a defensive line at Lyngen. On Hitler's order, carried out by Generaloberst Lothar Rendulic and pressed by Reichskommissar Josef Terboven after a voluntary evacuation organised by the Quisling administration failed, the population of Finnmark and North Troms was moved south by force and the region was systematically destroyed: about 12,000 dwellings, 180 lighthouses, 118 power stations and 10,000 km of telegraph line were burned or demolished, amounting on Norwegian estimates to some 30 per cent of all material war damage in Norway. Roughly 25,000 people evaded the order by hiding through the arctic winter, some in caves and mine tunnels; the sick and elderly shipped south were placed in institutions and many never returned. Sea Sami and Kven communities were among the hardest hit, and the postwar reconstruction that followed rebuilt the region in a standardised form that Sami organisations later argued accelerated assimilation, an issue examined by Norway's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which reported to the Storting in June 2023. At Nuremberg in 1948 the United States Military Tribunal in the Hostages Case acquitted Rendulic of the charge of wanton destruction in Norway, accepting that he could reasonably have believed the devastation militarily necessary, a holding since known as the Rendulic rule.
contested: Whether the destruction was a lawful military necessity or a war crime remains the central dispute: the Nuremberg tribunal accepted Rendulic's necessity defence, while Norwegian accounts treat the burning as a punitive devastation of a civilian region.

title: The US Missile Range at Kwajalein and the Concentration of Marshallese on Ebeye
actors: The United States took Kwajalein Atoll as a military base and missile range and moved its Marshallese population onto the small island of Ebeye
peopleRange: US trust territory and later Marshallese records show the landowners and residents of Kwajalein island removed to Ebeye from the late 1940s, further mid-atoll communities evacuated for missile testing from the early 1960s, and Ebeye's population rising from about 3,000 in 1968 to some 12,000 in the 2000s, on an island of roughly 80 acres, making it one of the most densely populated places on earth; the 2021 census recorded 8,416. No consolidated total of those displaced has been published.
territoryDesc: Kwajalein, the world's largest coral atoll lagoon, is used as the Ronald Reagan Ballistic Missile Defense Test Site; access to most of its islands is restricted

flows.label: Kwajalein islanders relocated to Ebeye
Mid-corridor islanders evacuated for missile testing

summary: US forces took Kwajalein from Japan in early 1944 and retained the atoll as a base, later converting it into the principal target and tracking range for American ballistic missile testing. Marshallese residents of Kwajalein island were moved to Ebeye, a small island in the same atoll, where housing was built for a fraction of their number; from the early 1960s residents of the mid-corridor islands were also evacuated as impact zones were established. Ebeye became overcrowded, with chronic problems of water, sanitation and disease, while its residents supplied much of the workforce for the base a short ferry ride away. Landowners protested by sailing back to and occupying their islands in the 'Operation Homecoming' actions of the early 1980s, securing improved land-use payments. Land use is now governed by the Compact of Free Association, first agreed in 1986 and extended in 2003 and again in 2023, under which the United States leases the atoll to 2066; displaced mid-corridor communities have not returned. The nuclear test relocations at Bikini and Enewetak are covered separately in the atlas.
contested: The adequacy of compensation and the terms of the land-use agreements are contested between Kwajalein landowners, the Marshallese government and the United States.

title: Soviet Deportation of Central European Civilians for Reparations Labour (malenkij robot)
actors: Soviet forces and the NKVD rounded up civilians in Hungary, Romania, Yugoslavia and the occupied German lands and deported them to labour camps in the USSR
peopleRange: Hungarian research since 1990 estimates up to 600,000 Hungarians deported, of whom about 200,000 were civilians rather than prisoners of war; some 100,000 civilians were seized in Budapest and its suburbs alone in the first wave to make up shortfalls in prisoner counts. Under State Defence Committee Order 7161 of December 1944 ethnic Germans of working age were deported from the occupied territories, including roughly 70,000-80,000 from Romania and tens of thousands from Yugoslavia and Hungary. Totals are reconstructions from GUPVI camp records and national survivor registers and remain approximate.

flows.label: Civilians seized in Budapest deported to Donbas mines
Ethnic Germans from Transylvania and the Banat to the Donbas and Urals
Deportees from Transcarpathia to camps in the Urals and Siberia

summary: As the Red Army moved into Central Europe in 1944-45, Soviet commands seized civilians for labour in the USSR, a practice remembered in Hungary and Transcarpathia by the phrase malenkij robot, a garbling of the Russian for 'a little work' used when men were rounded up ostensibly to clear rubble. Deportees were held by the NKVD's directorate for prisoners of war and internees, GUPVI, in a camp network parallel to the Gulag, and worked in mines, quarries and reconstruction across the Donbas, the Urals, Siberia and the Caucasus. A second, more organised wave in January 1945 followed State Defence Committee Order 7161, which directed the deportation of working-age ethnic Germans from the occupied territories; where regional quotas for Germans could not be met, ethnic Hungarians were taken instead. Hungarian sources estimate that 330,000-380,000 forced labourers returned, most between 1946 and 1948, with a final group of about 3,000 released only in 1953-1955, leaving an estimated 200,000 dead in transit or captivity. The episode was not researched or publicly commemorated until the fall of communism, and remains distinct from the westward expulsions of ethnic Germans recorded separately in this atlas.
contested: Numbers are estimates rather than counts: Soviet records conflate prisoners of war with seized civilians, national totals rest partly on survivor associations' registers, and Hungarian, Romanian and German figures for the same movements differ.

The round-ups took ethnic Germans (the Danube Swabians and Transylvanian Saxons, some 1.5-2 million across the three states), Hungarians seized in street sweeps in Budapest and the countryside, and civilians in the Soviet occupation zone, under different criteria in each country and with no common register. Soviet NKVD records indicate several hundred thousand deported, with mortality in the camps often put near a fifth.
