title: Poland's Postwar Border Shift (Curzon Line and Oder–Neisse)
actors: The Soviet Union annexed eastern prewar Poland (the Kresy), while Poland received compensatory former German territory east of the Oder and Neisse rivers, with both changes ratified at the Yalta and Potsdam conferences.
peopleRange: roughly 1.5–2.1 million ethnic Poles resettled from the Kresy into postwar Poland, alongside a reciprocal westward flow of Ukrainians and Belarusians
territoryDesc: USSR permanently annexed about 179,740 km² of prewar eastern Poland; Poland received about 103,000 km² of former German territory (Silesia, Pomerania, southern East Prussia) in compensation

flows.label: Lwów/Kresy → Wrocław, new western Poland
Ukrainians/Belarusians → Soviet Ukraine/Belarus

summary: At the 1943–45 Allied conferences, the Soviet Union secured the annexation of the eastern third of prewar Poland (the 'Kresy'), roughly along the Curzon Line, incorporating it into the Ukrainian, Belarusian and Lithuanian Soviet republics. As compensation, Poland's borders shifted west onto former German territory up to the Oder and Neisse rivers. Millions of ethnic Poles were resettled from the annexed east into the new Polish state, while Ukrainians and Belarusians in prewar Polish territory largely moved east. The border became Poland's internationally recognized eastern frontier and was confirmed in a 1990 treaty with reunified Germany on the west.
contested: Whether the 1945 border changes constituted a legitimate great-power settlement or an imposed loss of Polish sovereignty over the east is debated; some historians and Polish nationalist accounts describe the Soviet annexation of the Kresy as a continuation of the 1939 partition rather than a negotiated outcome.

sources.title: Territories of Poland annexed by the Soviet Union - Wikipedia
Recovered Territories - Wikipedia
Potsdam Conference - Britannica
Oder–Neisse Line - Britannica

deathsNote: The upper figure derives from the West German government's postwar demographic balance, which produced roughly 2 million dead expellees and long dominated official German literature; the German Federal Archives' 1974 review and later work by Rüdiger Overmans and Ingo Haar cut this sharply, to figures at or below 500,000-600,000, on the ground that the original method counted large numbers of 'unresolved cases' as deaths. The same methodological correction was applied by the 1995 joint German-Czech commission, which reduced Czechoslovak expulsion deaths from 220,000-270,000 to 15,000-30,000. About 3.5 million Germans were removed from the territories east of the Oder-Neisse line and 2.1 million Poles from the Soviet-annexed Kresy.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The West German Schieder documentation project, later joint German-Polish and German-Czech historical commissions, and Polish Institute of National Remembrance investigations into internment camps such as Łambinowice and Zgoda record internment, compulsory labour and wholesale confiscation of expellees' property.
baselineWhat: The Polish population of the prewar eastern territories (the Kresy) annexed by the Soviet Union
baselineNote: Poland's 1931 census recorded about 13.2 million inhabitants in the territories east of what became the Curzon Line, of whom roughly 5.3 million declared Polish as their mother tongue. The 1944-47 'repatriation' agreements moved about 1.5-1.8 million of them west into Poland's new borders; the shift also involved the expulsion of some 7 million Germans from the territories Poland gained, and the transfer of about 480,000 Ukrainians in the opposite direction.
shareCaveat: The Kresy Polish population had already been reduced by Soviet deportations in 1940-41, by German occupation and by the ethnic cleansing in Volhynia, so the 1931 denominator is much larger than the population actually present when the transfers began.

title: Polish–Ukrainian Population Transfers and Operation Vistula
actors: Poland and the Soviet Union carried out a bilateral population exchange of Poles and Ukrainians in 1944–46; in 1947 Poland's own communist authorities then forcibly dispersed the remaining Ukrainian, Lemko and Boyko minority under Operation Vistula.
peopleRange: roughly 1.4 million combined: about 787,000 Poles resettled from Soviet Ukraine into Poland, 482,000 Ukrainians resettled to the Ukrainian SSR (1944–46), and 140,000–150,000 Ukrainians, Lemkos and Boykos forcibly dispersed within Poland under Operation Vistula (1947)
territoryDesc: Southeastern Poland (Bieszczady and Low Beskid regions) and western Soviet Ukraine

flows.label: Poles from Soviet Ukraine → new western Poland
Ukrainians from Poland → Soviet Ukraine
Operation Vistula dispersal → northern/western Poland

summary: As Poland's borders shifted west, Polish and Soviet authorities agreed in September 1944 to a bilateral exchange in which ethnic Poles in the newly Soviet-annexed territories relocated to Poland and ethnic Ukrainians in Poland relocated to the Ukrainian SSR; roughly 787,000 Poles and 482,000 Ukrainians moved under this program by 1946. A substantial Ukrainian, Lemko and Boyko minority nonetheless remained in southeastern Poland, and in April–July 1947 the Polish communist government carried out Operation Vistula, forcibly dispersing roughly 140,000–150,000 of them across the newly acquired northern and western territories, partly as a security measure against the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and partly to enforce ethnic homogenization. The dispersal deliberately broke up communities to accelerate assimilation.
contested: Operation Vistula is characterized by many Ukrainian and some Polish historians as an act of ethnic cleansing and collective punishment, while it has also been presented by Polish authorities of the era as a security and pacification measure in response to UPA violence, including the killing of a senior Polish general; the Polish Senate issued a formal apology in 1990, but debate over framing and proportionality continues.

sources.title: Operation Vistula - Wikipedia
Polish population transfers in 1944-1946 - Wikipedia

deathsNote: No comprehensive toll exists. Poland's Institute of National Remembrance records 173 death sentences passed by military tribunals during Operation Vistula in 1947, deaths from torture, typhus and suicide among the nearly 4,000 Ukrainians (including 823 women and children) interned at the Jaworzno camp, and further deaths in transit in cattle wagons during the 1944-46 Polish-Soviet exchange, which moved roughly 480,000 Ukrainians east and 780,000 Poles west. The far larger Polish-Ukrainian massacres of 1943-47 in Volhynia and Galicia are counted separately and are themselves fiercely contested between Warsaw and Kyiv.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.body: Senate of the Republic of Poland
atrocityFindings.finding: Resolution of 3 August 1990 condemning Operation Vistula; President Kwaśniewski expressed regret in 2002 and Presidents Kaczyński and Yushchenko jointly condemned the operation as a violation of human rights in 2007

violenceNote: Poland's Institute of National Remembrance and the 1990 Senate resolution document internment without trial and mistreatment at the Jaworzno camp, the deliberate scattering of deportees to prevent community reconstitution, and the accompanying liquidation of the Greek Catholic Church's structures in Poland.
baselineWhat: The Poles living in the territories ceded to the Soviet Union and the Ukrainians and Lemkos living within postwar Poland's new borders
baselineNote: About 1.5 million Poles were moved west from the Kresy under the 1944 republican agreements, out of a Polish population there of roughly 1.5-2 million after wartime losses. Ukrainians and Lemkos in Poland's new southeastern borderlands numbered perhaps 650,000-700,000, of whom some 480,000 were transferred east by 1946 and about 140,000 dispersed to the northern and western territories under Operation Vistula in 1947.
shareCaveat: Two separate transfers in opposite directions are summed in the numerator, so the ratio measures total movement rather than the fate of any one community.

title: Soviet Annexation of Carpathian Ruthenia
actors: The Soviet Union pressured restored Czechoslovakia to cede Carpathian Ruthenia (Subcarpathian Rus'), which was annexed and incorporated into the Ukrainian SSR as Zakarpattia Oblast.
territoryDesc: Subcarpathian Rus', the easternmost region of interwar Czechoslovakia
summary: Carpathian Ruthenia (Subcarpathian Rus'), the easternmost province of prewar Czechoslovakia, was occupied by the Red Army in late 1944. A Soviet-organized local assembly requested union with the Ukrainian SSR, and Czechoslovakia formally ceded the territory in a June 1945 treaty, ratified by the Czechoslovak parliament in 1946. The region, home to Rusyn, Ukrainian, Hungarian, and other populations, became Zakarpattia (Transcarpathian) Oblast of the Ukrainian SSR and remains part of independent Ukraine today.
contested: Historians debate whether Czechoslovakia's cession was a genuinely free bilateral decision or was made under direct Soviet political and military pressure, given the Red Army's occupation of the territory at the time of the 'request' for annexation.

sources.title: Soviet annexation of Transcarpathia - Wikipedia
Carpathian Ruthenia during World War II - Wikipedia

deathsNote: The annexation itself — Czechoslovakia's cession of 12,777 km2 and about 450,000 inhabitants, formalised on 29 June 1945 and in force from 30 January 1946 — caused no mass killing, and roughly 120,000 people left the territory. Deaths did occur in the November 1944 round-up of Hungarian and German men for Soviet forced labour ('malenkij robot'), concentrated in the Szolyva/Svaliava transit camp; Soviet lists cited by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Mukachevo record more than 27,000 Transcarpathians held in POW and labour camps by summer 1945, and contemporary accounts describe heavy mortality from starvation, typhus and cold, but no reliable enumeration of the dead exists, so no range is given here.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: The Roman Catholic Diocese of Mukachevo, drawing on Soviet lists, records more than 27,000 Transcarpathians held in POW and labour camps by the summer of 1945 after the November 1944 'malenkij robot' round-up, with heavy mortality at the Szolyva/Svaliava camp from starvation, epidemic and cold.
baselineWhat: The population of Subcarpathian Rus' (Carpathian Ruthenia) at the Czechoslovak census of 1930
baselineNote: The 1930 Czechoslovak census counted 725,357 inhabitants of Subcarpathian Rus', including large Rusyn, Hungarian and Jewish populations; by the time of the Soviet annexation in 1945 the territory held roughly 800,000, its Jewish community of about 100,000 having been deported and largely murdered in 1944. Thousands of Hungarian and German men were deported to Soviet labour camps in 1944-45.

title: Soviet Annexation of Tuva
actors: The Soviet Union formally annexed the nominally independent Tuvan People's Republic, a Soviet client state since the 1920s, following a request from a Soviet-aligned Tuvan assembly, incorporating it as the Tuvan Autonomous Oblast.
territoryDesc: Tuvan People's Republic, in southern Siberia on the border with Mongolia
summary: Tuva, a sparsely populated region in southern Siberia, had functioned since 1921 as the nominally independent Tuvan People's Republic while remaining under close Soviet political and military control. In October 1944, its small assembly formally petitioned for incorporation into the USSR, and the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet accepted, making Tuva the Tuvan Autonomous Oblast (later Tuvan ASSR) within the Russian SFSR. Unlike most other annexations covered here, the transfer involved no mass displacement, but it eliminated the last vestige of Tuvan statehood and subjected the region's largely nomadic, Turkic-speaking population to Soviet administrative and collectivization policies.
contested: Some historians describe the 1944 'request' for annexation, approved by a small, Soviet-installed assembly without any popular referendum, as effectively a unilateral Soviet takeover of a state it already fully controlled rather than a genuine voluntary union.

sources.title: Tuvan People's Republic - Wikipedia
Tuva Republic - Refworld/World Directory of Minorities

deathsNote: The October-November 1944 accession was accomplished through votes of the Tuvan People's Revolutionary Party central committee and the Little Khural and a declaration presented to the USSR Presidium; no source records violent resistance or bloodshed attending the annexation itself. The lethal repression of Tuvans — the 1929 Soviet-backed coup and execution of Donduk Kuular, forced collectivisation, the purge of a third to a half of party members, and the destruction of Buddhist monasteries (from 25 lamaseries to one, and from about 4,000 lamas to fifteen, between 1929 and 1931) — occurred in the fifteen years before the annexation and is not enumerated in casualty terms.
baselineWhat: The population of the Tuvan People's Republic at its annexation
baselineNote: Tuva's own statistics are thin; the republic's population is usually given as roughly 95,000-100,000 in the mid-1940s, overwhelmingly Tuvan with a Russian settler minority of some 10,000-12,000. The Soviet census of 1959, the first full enumeration of the territory as the Tuvan Autonomous Oblast and then ASSR, counted 171,900.

title: Forced Repatriation of Soviet Citizens and the Filtration System
actors: The Soviet state, with the agreement of Britain and the United States at Yalta, repatriated Soviet prisoners of war, forced labourers and refugees from Western zones and screened them through NKVD filtration camps
peopleRange: About 5.2 million Soviet citizens were repatriated between 1944 and 1947, of whom roughly 2.3 million were handed over by the Western Allies; the figures come from the records of the Soviet Repatriation Administration under General Golikov, published after 1990, and are broadly accepted. Of those screened, Soviet archival tabulations analysed by Viktor Zemskov indicate around 58 per cent were released home, about 19 per cent conscripted, some 14 per cent sent to labour battalions and roughly 6-7 per cent — several hundred thousand people — transferred to the Gulag or to exile settlements. Around 45,000-50,000 Cossacks and their families were handed to Soviet forces at Lienz and Judenburg in mid-1945.

flows.label: Soviet prisoners of war and Ostarbeiter repatriated from the Western occupation zones
Cossacks and their families handed over by British forces at Lienz

summary: At Yalta in February 1945 the Allies agreed to repatriate each other's liberated nationals, and the Western powers applied this to Soviet citizens irrespective of whether they wished to return, using force at Lienz, Dachau, Plattling and elsewhere. Some 5.2 million people were moved east — former prisoners of war, Ostarbeiter conscripted into German industry, and refugees — and passed through NKVD filtration and verification points where their conduct under occupation was investigated. Most were released or conscripted, but several hundred thousand were sentenced to the Gulag or to exile settlement, and returning prisoners of war carried a durable stigma. Handovers of Cossacks and of Russians who had never held Soviet citizenship, including White emigres, produced suicides and killings during the transfers and became the subject of long controversy in Britain. The system connects the atlas's German forced-labour and Soviet prisoner-of-war entries to the postwar Gulag.
contested: Western responsibility for the handovers — particularly of Cossacks and of emigres who were not Soviet citizens — and the proportion of returnees actually imprisoned, which Cold War-era estimates put far higher than the Soviet archival tabulations released in the 1990s.

Some 1.5 million were passed to NKVD filtration or penal battalions and several hundred thousand successfully avoided return.

title: The Warsaw Uprising and the Expulsion of the City's Population
actors: German forces suppressed the Polish Home Army rising, killed civilians en masse, expelled the surviving population of Warsaw and demolished the city
peopleRange: About 550,000 inhabitants of Warsaw and some 100,000 people from surrounding districts were expelled after the capitulation of 2 October 1944, passing mainly through the Dulag 121 transit camp at Pruszkow, from which roughly 150,000 were sent to forced labour in the Reich and about 60,000 to concentration camps. The figures come from German transit camp records, the Polish Red Cross and the Warsaw Rising Museum.

flows.label: Warsaw -> Dulag 121 transit camp, Pruszkow
Pruszkow -> forced labour in Germany
Pruszkow -> concentration camps including Auschwitz and Ravensbrueck

summary: The Polish Home Army rose against the German occupation of Warsaw on 1 August 1944 as Soviet forces approached the Vistula. Over sixty-three days German units, including the Dirlewanger and Kaminski formations, retook the city district by district; in the Wola massacre of 5-7 August alone tens of thousands of civilians were shot in a matter of days. Soviet forces halted on the east bank and Allied airdrops were limited. After the capitulation on 2 October the entire remaining civilian population, about 550,000 people, was expelled through the transit camp at Pruszkow; some were sent to labour in Germany, some to concentration camps, and the rest dispersed across the General Government. German demolition squads then systematically destroyed what remained of the city until January 1945, so that roughly 85 per cent of the left-bank city lay in ruins at liberation. Warsaw's prewar population of about 1.3 million had already been reduced by the destruction of the ghetto and its inhabitants in 1942-43.
contested: The number of civilians killed during the rising is estimated rather than counted, and the responsibility of the Soviet command for halting on the Vistula while the rising was crushed remains politically disputed between Poland and Russia.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: The Warsaw Polish Uprising
Warsaw Rising Museum
Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum: On the sixtieth anniversary of the Warsaw Uprising

deathsNote: Estimates of civilians killed during the sixty-three days run from about 150,000 to 200,000, including some 40,000 to 65,000 shot in the Wola and Ochota massacres of early August; about 16,000 insurgents were also killed. The figures come from Polish postwar exhumation and registration work and are approximations, since many bodies were burned by German clearance units.
violenceNote: The mass shooting of civilians in Wola and Ochota, the expulsion of the population through Pruszkow and the planned demolition of the city are documented in German operational orders, Polish Red Cross records and the collections of the Warsaw Rising Museum.
baselineWhat: The population of Warsaw at the outbreak of the uprising in August 1944
baselineNote: Warsaw held about 1.3 million people before the war; after the murder of the ghetto's population and wartime deportations roughly 900,000-1,000,000 remained in the city in mid-1944. Some 150,000-200,000 civilians were killed during the 63-day rising, about 550,000 were expelled from the city through the Pruszków transit camp with a further 100,000 from the suburbs, and the Germans then demolished what was left.

title: Albania under Hoxha: Internal Exile, Internment Villages and the Political Prison System
actors: The Albanian communist state interned, deported and imprisoned people classed as class enemies, together with their families
peopleRange: The Institute for the Study of Communist Crimes and Consequences (ISKK), whose figures are used in a UNDP-supported framework study, counts 59,009 people subjected to internment or deportation between 1944 and 1990, with 12,500 formal deportation decisions recorded (a count that excludes juveniles and prisoners' children moved with their families). The same sources give about 25,000 people convicted as political prisoners in the archives, which researchers raise to 30,000-34,000 once the poorly documented years 1945-1946 are allowed for. Numbers rest on Interior Ministry and court archives opened after 1991.

flows.label: Deportation of families to internment villages in the Myzeqe plain (Lushnje, Fier)
Northern families deported to the Tepelena camp

summary: From 1945 the Albanian Party of Labour under Enver Hoxha combined a political prison and labour-camp system with a distinct regime of internim-debim, internment and deportation, under which whole families were moved by administrative decision to designated villages, mostly in the marshy Myzeqe plain around Lushnje and Fier, and required to live and work there under police supervision, often for decades and across generations. Barbed-wire camps operated between 1945 and 1954, the largest at Tepelena holding several thousand people including women and children; forced-labour prisons such as Spac and Burrel worked prisoners in copper and pyrite mines. ISKK figures record 7,022 deaths attributed to internment conditions, 984 political prisoners dead in prison and 5,577 men and 450 women executed under sentence. Restrictions were lifted with the collapse of the regime in 1990-1991. Albania has legislated on compensation and file access and has opened memorial sites at Spac and elsewhere, but the accounting has been slower and less complete than in most other former communist states, and campaigners describe the subject as under-addressed.
contested: Totals depend on which archival series are counted and how family members interned alongside a convicted relative are classified; researchers argue the official prisoner count understates the years 1945-1946, and there is continuing debate in Albania over compensation, prosecution and how the period should be taught.

sources.title: Framework Study on the prison system, internment and deportation in communist Albania (UNDP-hosted)

deathsNote: The lower bound is the ISKK count of deaths caused by conditions in internment (7,022) plus deaths of political prisoners in custody (984); the upper bound adds the 6,027 men and women recorded as executed under court sentence. The difference is a matter of what is being counted rather than of contested evidence.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: These forms are documented in the ISKK archival studies, in the UNDP-supported framework study on the prison and internment system and in survivor testimony collected by Albanian remembrance organisations.
baselineWhat: The population of Albania in 1945, when the communist state took power
baselineNote: Albania's 1945 census recorded 1,122,044 inhabitants. The figure of 59,009 comes from the post-communist Institute for the Study of Communist Crimes and Consequences and the Albanian state archives, covering those interned, internally exiled or imprisoned for political reasons, together with family members subjected to the same measures.

title: Australia's Stolen Generations
actors: Australian governments, churches and welfare bodies removed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families under protection and assimilation laws
peopleRange: No total count exists. The Bringing Them Home inquiry found that between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children were forcibly removed between 1910 and 1970. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare estimated 27,200 surviving members of the Stolen Generations aged 50 and over in 2018-19, about 21 per cent of Indigenous Australians in that age group, a figure roughly double its 2018 estimate of 13,800 as disclosure improved.
summary: From the early twentieth century until about 1970, Australian state, territory and Commonwealth authorities, working with churches and welfare agencies, removed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families under protection and assimilation legislation and placed them in institutions, foster homes or adoptive families, commonly with contact and language use forbidden. The 1997 national inquiry Bringing Them Home, conducted by the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, took evidence from more than 500 affected people and found that between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children had been forcibly removed between 1910 and 1970, that the removals constituted a gross violation of human rights, and that forcible removal was an act of genocide. It made recommendations for apology, reparations, records access and national standards, and the Commonwealth apology was delivered by Prime Minister Kevin Rudd on 13 February 2008. The Healing Foundation assessed in 2025 that only about 6 per cent of the inquiry's recommendations had been fully implemented. This entry covers the post-1945 portion of a policy running from roughly 1910; removals continued in some jurisdictions past 1970.
contested: The scale and the genocide finding are both disputed: the inquiry itself could not produce a total because records were incomplete or destroyed, and its conclusion that removal amounted to genocide, together with the one-in-three upper estimate, was contested by some historians and politicians in the public argument that followed the report, while survivor organisations maintain both.

sources.title: Bringing Them Home: report, findings and legacy — The Healing Foundation
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Stolen Generations — Australian Institute of Health and Welfare
Bringing Them Home report (1997) — Australian Human Rights Commission
The Stolen Generations — AIATSIS

deathsNote: No inquiry has attributed a death toll to the removals. Bringing Them Home documented lasting harm through severed family, cultural and language ties and elevated rates of ill health, incarceration and suicide among survivors, and the AIHW records substantially worse health, disability and economic outcomes for survivors than for other Indigenous Australians of the same age, but neither body quantified deaths caused by removal.

atrocityFindings.body: Australia's Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission (Bringing Them Home national inquiry)
atrocityFindings.finding: Between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children were forcibly removed from their families between 1910 and 1970; the forcible removal was an act of genocide and a gross violation of human rights.

violenceNote: Both forms were documented by the Bringing Them Home national inquiry, which recorded the compulsory removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and the deliberate severing of their language, kinship and cultural ties.
baselineWhat: The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population of Australia in the mid-1950s
baselineNote: Aboriginal people were excluded from official population counts until the 1967 referendum, so all earlier figures are undercounts: the 1954 census recorded about 75,000, while the 1971 census, the first full enumeration, counted 115,953. An Indigenous population of roughly 100,000 in the middle of the removal period is the best available reconstruction. The 1997 Bringing Them Home report concluded that between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children were removed from their families between 1910 and 1970.
shareCaveat: The removals ran for twenty-five years and fell on children, so dividing them by the whole Indigenous population of one year badly understates the reach of the policy; the Bringing Them Home report's own framing — between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children removed — is the meaningful ratio.

title: Removal of the Banabans to Rabi Island
actors: The British colonial administration and the British Phosphate Commissioners moved the Banaban people to Rabi Island in Fiji and continued mining their island
peopleRange: About 1,000 Banabans were resettled on Rabi from December 1945, with further movement in waves into the 1980s; the Rabi community grew from roughly 1,000 in 1945 to about 5,000 by 1995 and around 4,000 by the early 2000s. Banaba itself had only about 300 residents by 2005.
territoryDesc: Banaba (Ocean Island), about 6 km², annexed by Britain in 1900 and leased to phosphate interests; roughly 90 per cent of its surface, some 22 million tonnes of rock, was stripped and exported between 1900 and 1979, leaving most of the island uninhabitable.

flows.label: Banaba (Ocean Island) → Rabi Island, Fiji

summary: Banaba, a small raised-coral island in the western Pacific, was annexed by Britain in 1900 after high-grade phosphate was found there, and the British Phosphate Commissioners obtained exclusive rights to occupy and mine it. Japanese forces occupied the island from 1942 to 1945, deporting most inhabitants and massacring the remaining Gilbertese labourers in August 1945. Rather than returning the Banabans after the war, the colonial authorities declared Banaba uninhabitable and moved them to Rabi Island in Fiji, some 2,000 km away, which had been bought with royalties from the Banabans' own phosphate; about 1,000 people landed there from December 1945 to find an undeveloped island without housing or services. Mining continued on Banaba until the deposits were exhausted in 1979, by which time roughly 90 per cent of the island's surface had been removed. The Banabans sued Britain and the phosphate commissioners in the English courts from 1965; the litigation ended in 1979 without the damages sought, and in 1981 they accepted an ex gratia settlement of A$10 million. The Rabi community, now Fijian citizens with a distinct legal status, continues to press claims over the destruction of their homeland.
contested: Whether the move was consensual is disputed: British records describe agreement by Banaban leaders and the purchase of Rabi on their behalf, while Banaban accounts and later legal claims characterise the relocation as coerced, conducted without informed consent and on the false premise that the island was uninhabitable, and the amount of phosphate revenue actually paid to Banabans remains contested.

sources.title: Banaba — Britannica
Banabans in the Fiji Islands — Minority Rights Group
The Displacement and Dispossession of Banaba: an Overview — ICAAD

deathsNote: The 1945 relocation itself caused no significant death toll; hardship on arrival at an undeveloped Rabi was severe but no count of deaths exists. Separately, Britannica records that Japanese occupying forces massacred the Gilbertese labourers remaining on Banaba in August 1945, an act by a different actor in the immediately preceding period and not part of the British relocation.
violenceNote: Minority Rights Group and ICAAD document that phosphate mining stripped roughly 90 per cent of Banaba's surface between 1900 and 1979, destroying the village lands and cultivable ground of the removed population.
baselineWhat: The Banaban population of Ocean Island at the time of the removal
baselineNote: About 1,000 Banabans were landed on Rabi in December 1945, together with some 300 Gilbertese. The prewar community numbered roughly 1,000-1,300; it had been dispersed by the Japanese occupation to Nauru, Tarawa and Kosrae, and the survivors were gathered and shipped to Fiji rather than returned home.
shareCaveat: Effectively the whole community was moved, so the ratio is 100% by construction rather than by measurement.

title: Canada's Indian Residential School System
actors: The Canadian government and church bodies removed First Nations, Inuit and Métis children from their families and held them in residential institutions
peopleRange: At least 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children passed through 139 recognised residential schools across the system's full life (Truth and Reconciliation Commission, via CBC and Parks Canada). The commission did not publish a separate post-1945 total; roughly 80,000 former students were still living when the TRC reported in 2015, indicating that a large share of attendance fell in the period covered here.
summary: Canada operated a national system of church-run residential schools for Indigenous children under federal funding and authority; 139 institutions are formally recognised and at least 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children attended between 1883 and the closure of the last school in 1996. Attendance was compelled by law and administrative pressure, children were separated from parents for most of the year, punished for speaking their languages, and set to work under a half-day labour system, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission recorded extensive physical and sexual abuse. The TRC concluded in 2015 that the schools were 'an integral part of a conscious policy of cultural genocide'. Mortality was severe: the commission identified thousands of student deaths, largely from tuberculosis and influenza, and found the burial places of many children unmarked or unknown, a finding that gained wider attention after ground-penetrating radar surveys at former school sites from 2021. The Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement of 2007 produced $2.8 billion in compensation for 31,970 resolved abuse claims, a 2008 prime ministerial apology and the TRC's 94 Calls to Action. This entry covers the post-1945 portion of a system that began in the 1880s.
contested: The death toll is disputed in both directions: the TRC's named and unnamed registers document a few thousand deaths but the commission itself said records were destroyed or never kept, while claims about unmarked graves identified by radar since 2021 have been challenged by some commentators as unconfirmed pending excavation.

sources.title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission: By the numbers — CBC News
The Residential School System National Historic Event — Parks Canada

deathsNote: The low figure is the number of student deaths the Truth and Reconciliation Commission was able to document in its named and unnamed registers from surviving records; the high figure is the estimate given by commission chair Murray Sinclair, who judged the documented count a floor because attendance and death records were incomplete or destroyed. The gap is driven by record loss rather than by disagreement over what happened. CBC reports the TRC calculated a student mortality rate of roughly one in twenty-five across the system's life, with mortality far higher in the pre-1940 decades than in the period covered by this entry.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada
atrocityFindings.finding: Residential schooling was 'an integral part of a conscious policy of cultural genocide' directed at some 150,000 Indigenous children and their families.

violenceNote: All four forms were documented by Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which recorded compulsory removal of children, suppression of Indigenous languages and ceremony, sexual and physical abuse resulting in 31,970 resolved compensation claims, and the half-day labour system operated in the schools.
baselineWhat: The First Nations, Inuit and Métis population of Canada around the middle of the twentieth century
baselineNote: The 1951 census of Canada counted roughly 165,000 Indigenous people — about 156,000 registered Indians and about 10,000 Inuit — with Métis largely uncounted; by the 2021 census 1.8 million people identified as Indigenous. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's figure of about 150,000 children covers the whole life of the residential school system from the 1880s to 1996, not the 1945-96 window alone.

baselineSources.title: Canadian Indian residential school system — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The 150,000 children attended across more than a century and many generations, while the denominator is a single-year population snapshot, so the ratio is not the share of any one Indigenous population that was confined.

title: Expulsion of Sudeten Germans from Czechoslovakia
actors: The restored Czechoslovak state expelled its ethnic German minority under the Beneš decrees, following an initial wave of chaotic 'wild expulsions' and violence in the summer of 1945.
peopleRange: about 2.9–3.2 million, drawn largely from the Sudetenland and other German-populated border regions
territoryDesc: Sudetenland and other predominantly German-populated border districts of Czechoslovakia

flows.label: Sudetenland → occupied Bavaria/Germany

summary: After Czechoslovakia's restoration in 1945, its government moved to expel the roughly 3-million-strong ethnic German minority concentrated in the Sudetenland, first through unregulated 'wild' expulsions accompanied by violence and internment, and then through an organized transfer authorized by the Potsdam Agreement and carried out under presidential decrees issued by Edvard Beneš. The decrees also stripped expelled Germans (and, initially, ethnic Hungarians) of citizenship and property. Death toll estimates from a joint Czech-German historical commission range from roughly 15,000 to 30,000, far below earlier German estimates that ran into the hundreds of thousands. The expulsion permanently ended the centuries-old German presence in Bohemia and Moravia.
contested: Death toll estimates vary greatly, from the low tens of thousands (joint Czech-German commission) to earlier claims of 200,000 or more; the legality and moral legacy of the Beneš decrees, which remain in force in the Czech Republic, continue to be debated between Czech and German/Austrian perspectives.

sources.title: Expulsion of Germans from Czechoslovakia - Wikipedia
Demographic estimates of the flight and expulsion of Germans - Wikipedia

deathsNote: The German–Czech Joint Commission of Historians (1995–96) concluded that between 15,000 and 30,000 Germans died in connection with the expulsion from Czechoslovakia, finding the earlier West German figure to rest on faulty data. That earlier figure — roughly 270,000–273,000 — came from the West German government's 1958 demographic study Die deutschen Vertreibungsverluste and was a residual derived from population balances rather than a count of bodies; Czech historians argue the German baseline wrongly counted around 300,000 ethnic Czechs as Sudeten Germans. German expellee organisations favour the higher figure; Czech scholarship and the binational commission the lower one.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.body: German–Czech Joint Commission of Historians (established by the two governments)
atrocityFindings.finding: Revised the death toll of the expulsion from Czechoslovakia to 15,000–30,000, finding the 1958 West German government estimate of c. 270,000 to be based on faulty demographic data

violenceNote: The German–Czech Joint Commission of Historians and Czech scholarship on the 1945 'wild expulsions' document summary killings at Ústí nad Labem, Postoloprty and on the Brno death march, internment and compulsory labour in camps, and the blanket stripping of citizenship and confiscation of property under the Beneš decrees.
baselineWhat: The German population of the Czech lands
baselineNote: The Czechoslovak census of 1930 counted 3,231,688 Germans in Bohemia, Moravia and Czech Silesia, about 22% of the state's population. By the 1950 census fewer than 160,000 remained.

title: Repatriation of Japanese Settlers from Manchuria, Korea, Taiwan and Sakhalin
actors: Allied Occupation authorities and Japan repatriated Japanese civilians and soldiers from former colonies/occupied territories; Soviet, Chinese and Korean authorities controlled departures
peopleRange: approximately 6.6 million Japanese civilians and military personnel were repatriated (Manchuria ~1.5–1.7M, Korea ~700K–900K, Taiwan ~480K, Sakhalin/Kurils ~400K+, plus Southeast Asia/Pacific and Siberian POWs); tens of thousands died awaiting repatriation or in Soviet internment

flows.label: Manchuria (Changchun) → Maizuru, Japan
Korea (Seoul) → Hakata/Sasebo, Japan
Taiwan (Taipei) → Kagoshima, Japan
South Sakhalin → Hokkaido, Japan

summary: After Japan's August 1945 surrender, roughly 6.6 million Japanese civilians and demobilized soldiers stranded across its former empire were repatriated to the home islands over the following decade, mostly by 1949 but continuing into the late 1950s. The largest flows came from Manchuria, colonial Korea, Taiwan, and southern Sakhalin, with additional large groups of soldiers held in Soviet internment in Siberia. Tens of thousands died from disease, violence, or in Soviet labor camps before they could return, and an unknown number of Japanese children were left behind or separated from parents amid the chaos, particularly in Manchuria. The process was organized primarily by the US-led Allied occupation of Japan in cooperation with local Chinese, Korean, and Soviet authorities.
contested: Death tolls during the repatriation and Soviet internment, and the fate of Japanese who remained behind (including orphaned children in China), are debated; the historical framing of these settlers as colonizers versus displaced civilians also differs between Japanese and other regional historiography.

sources.title: Postwar Repatriation: Bringing Home the Millions of Japanese Stranded Overseas After the War
Japanese repatriation from Huludao
Homeward Bound: The Postwar Repatriation of Japanese Civilians in Shanghai, 1945-1948

deathsNote: Japanese government and Maizuru Repatriation Memorial Museum figures, summarised by Nippon.com, record that about 55,000 of roughly 575,000 Japanese held in Soviet 'Siberian internment' died in captivity, that some 245,000 died in Manchuria including in the fighting with Soviet forces and during flight, disease and mass suicide, and that about 400 died of cholera aboard quarantined repatriation ships in 1946. The low end counts internment deaths alone; the high end adds Manchurian civilian deaths during the collapse and flight, which some accounts attribute to the end of the war rather than to the repatriation itself.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Japanese government repatriation records and the Maizuru and Siberian internment memorial museums document the use of interned Japanese soldiers as forced labour in the Soviet Union, and historians of the Soviet occupation of Manchuria have documented widespread sexual violence against Japanese settlers during the 1945 collapse.
baselineWhat: Japanese nationals — soldiers, colonists and civilians — outside the home islands at the surrender in August 1945
baselineNote: Japanese and Allied Occupation figures put roughly 6.9 million Japanese abroad in August 1945, about 3.5 million of them military personnel and 3.3 million civilians, in Manchuria, Korea, Taiwan, Sakhalin, the Kurils, China proper and the Pacific. The repatriation programme returned about 6.6 million of them by 1950, with smaller returns continuing from Soviet custody to 1958.

title: The Battle of Okinawa, the Civilian Camps and the US Seizure of Okinawan Land
actors: US forces fought the 1945 battle among the civilian population, interned survivors in camps, and then expropriated Okinawan land for permanent bases under military administration
peopleRange: Okinawa Prefecture's records and US military reports indicate that some 250,000-300,000 civilians passed through US-run internment camps in the northern part of the main island in 1945, held for months and in some cases years while their home districts were built over. Land expropriation in the 1950s displaced the residents of villages including Isahama and communities on Iejima; an island-wide protest movement in 1956 drew a reported 250,000 participants. Bases still occupy roughly a fifth of Okinawa's main island.
territoryDesc: US bases came to cover about 20 per cent of Okinawa Island; Okinawa remained under US military administration until reversion to Japan in 1972

flows.label: Civilians moved into US camps in northern Okinawa, 1945
Okinawan emigration to Bolivia after land loss

summary: The battle fought on Okinawa between April and June 1945 killed an estimated 94,000-150,000 Okinawan civilians, a quarter to a third of the prefecture's population, including deaths in mass suicides in which Japanese troops distributed grenades and, in documented cases, ordered or pressed civilians to kill themselves and each other. Survivors were collected into US internment camps in the north while their villages, land and cemeteries were absorbed into military installations. Under US administration in the 1950s the military expropriated further land: when about 98 per cent of landowners refused to sign leases, forced seizures followed, remembered in Okinawa as 'bayonets and bulldozers', with the communities of Isahama, Iejima and others resisting, and a reported 250,000 people joining island-wide protests in 1956. Some displaced families accepted assisted emigration to Bolivia and elsewhere. Okinawa reverted to Japan in 1972 with the bases in place. Japan's textbook treatment of the compulsory mass suicides has been repeatedly contested: the Education Ministry ordered references to army orders removed in 2007, prompting mass protest in Okinawa, and an Osaka court in 2008 rejected a libel suit brought against the writer Kenzaburo Oe over the same question.
contested: Whether Japanese troops ordered the civilian mass suicides is disputed in Japanese politics and textbook policy; Okinawan testimony and the 2008 Osaka court judgment support the claim of military involvement, which some Japanese conservative groups and former officers deny.

sources.title: Battle of Okinawa
Steve Rabson, 'Henoko and the U.S. Military: A History of Dependence and Resistance', Asia-Pacific Journal

deathsNote: Both figures are for Okinawan civilians killed in the 1945 battle. The lower is the conventional estimate used in most military histories; the higher reflects Okinawa Prefecture's own tallies, which record more than 149,000 Okinawan names on the Cornerstone of Peace, including those who died of starvation and in mass suicides. The postwar land seizures caused injuries and arrests but not mass death.
violenceNote: Okinawa Prefecture's records, US military documents and survivor testimony collected in Japanese and Okinawan archives document the civilian deaths, the internment camps and the forced land seizures.
baselineWhat: The population of Okinawa Prefecture at the last pre-war census
baselineNote: The 1940 census counted 574,579 residents of Okinawa Prefecture. Between 94,000 and 150,000 Okinawan civilians, a quarter to a third of the prefecture's people, died in the 1945 battle; almost all survivors on the main island passed through US civilian camps, and the base land seizures of 1953-56 under 'bayonets and bulldozers' displaced further thousands of households.

baselineSources.title: United States Civil Administration of the Ryukyu Islands — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The affected figure combines wartime camp internment, which covered most surviving civilians in 1945, with the later land expropriations, which touched a different and much smaller group, so it should not be read as one population confined once.

title: Roma Persecution, Coerced Assimilation and Expulsion in Postwar Europe
actors: Communist and later democratic European states banned nomadism, dispersed and sterilised Roma, evicted them from settlements and expelled Roma migrants across EU borders
peopleRange: No single aggregate exists, and the entry covers a set of connected measures rather than one event. Components that can be counted include: Czechoslovakia's 1958 law prohibiting nomadic life, under which some 27,000 people were registered and immobilised, and its 1965 dispersal programme; the coercive sterilisation of Romani women in Czechoslovakia and its successor states, for which the Czech Republic legislated compensation in 2021 after a 2005 ombudsman's finding; the flight of an estimated 80,000-100,000 Roma and Ashkali from Kosovo in and after 1999; and France's 2010 camp clearances, under which several thousand Roma a year were returned to Romania and Bulgaria. Estimates of Europe's Roma population range from 10 to 12 million.

flows.label: Roma and Ashkali displaced from Kosovo after 1999
Roma returned from France to Romania and Bulgaria, 2010

summary: Roma across postwar Europe were subject to a sequence of coercive measures that the atlas's Porajmos entry, ending in 1945, does not reach. Communist states banned nomadism and dispersed Romani settlements — Czechoslovakia's law of 1958 and dispersal programme of 1965 are the best documented — and pursued assimilation through segregated schooling and, in Czechoslovakia and its successor states, the sterilisation of Romani women without valid consent, first exposed by Charter 77 in 1978, found unlawful by the Czech public defender of rights in 2005 and compensated by Czech legislation in 2021. After 1989, Roma were displaced by pogrom-style attacks in several countries, and some 80,000-100,000 Roma and Ashkali fled Kosovo in and after 1999. In western Europe, Italy's 2008 'nomad emergency' decrees, later annulled by the Italian courts, and France's 2010 clearance of Roma camps and organised returns to Romania and Bulgaria drew censure from the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner and the European Commission. The measures are unified less by a single perpetrator than by a continent-wide pattern documented by the Council of Europe and the European Roma Rights Centre.
contested: Whether the western European camp clearances and returns of 2008-2012 amounted to collective expulsion on ethnic grounds, as the European Roma Rights Centre and the Council of Europe's commissioner argued, or to lawful enforcement of residence rules, as the French and Italian governments maintained.

sources.title: Romani people in Czechoslovakia — Wikipedia
Parallel Report by the European Roma Rights Centre concerning France — OHCHR Universal Periodic Review
2010 French Roma repatriation — Wikipedia
Antiziganism — Wikipedia
Romani people in France — Wikipedia

deathsNote: There was no mass killing in this period. Deaths arose from individual racist attacks and from pogrom-style incidents in Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary and the Czech lands in the 1990s and 2000s, numbering in the dozens; these are documented case by case by the European Roma Rights Centre rather than aggregated.

atrocityFindings.body: Public Defender of Rights (Ombudsman), Czech Republic
atrocityFindings.finding: 2005 final statement concluding that Romani women had been sterilised without informed consent in breach of the law, prompting a government expression of regret in 2009 and a compensation act in 2021

violenceNote: The European Roma Rights Centre and the Council of Europe's Commissioner for Human Rights documented the camp clearances, forced evictions and statelessness affecting Roma in France, Italy and the former Yugoslavia.
baselineWhat: The Roma population of Europe, on the Council of Europe's working estimate
baselineNote: The Council of Europe's average estimate is roughly 10-12 million Roma in Europe, about 6 million of them in European Union states; national censuses record far fewer because many Roma do not declare their ethnicity, so official counts are typically a third to a half of the estimate. There is no reliable pan-European Roma population figure for 1945.
shareCaveat: The baseline is a present-day estimate while the events span 1945 to 2012, a period in which the Roma population of Europe roughly doubled, so any ratio against it understates the share of the community affected in the earlier decades.

title: Soviet Annexation of Königsberg (Kaliningrad)
actors: The Soviet Union annexed the northern third of East Prussia around Königsberg under the Potsdam Agreement, later formally expelling the remaining German population and resettling the area with Soviet citizens.
peopleRange: an estimated 100,000–193,000 Germans remained by 1945–46 (out of a prewar northern East Prussian population of roughly 1.2 million, most of whom had already fled, died, or been killed during the 1944–45 Soviet offensive) and were expelled by 1948
territoryDesc: Northern East Prussia surrounding Königsberg, reorganized as Kaliningrad Oblast of the Russian SFSR

flows.label: Königsberg region → occupied Germany

summary: The Potsdam Agreement awarded the northern portion of East Prussia, including the city of Königsberg, to the Soviet Union pending a final peace settlement that never occurred; the remainder went to Poland. Most of the prewar German population had already died or fled during the brutal Soviet advance of early 1945; the remnant, reduced by famine and disease under Soviet occupation, was formally expelled to Germany by 1947–48. The territory was renamed Kaliningrad in 1946 and resettled with Soviet citizens, becoming a militarized Russian exclave separated from the rest of the USSR/Russia by Lithuania and Poland.
contested: The permanence of the annexation, never confirmed by a final peace treaty, has periodically been questioned by some Western commentators, though it is broadly accepted in international practice as part of the postwar settlement; Germany does not press territorial claims.

sources.title: Kaliningrad Oblast - Wikipedia
History of Kaliningrad - Wikipedia
Potsdam Conference - Britannica

deathsNote: Andreas Kossert puts 100,000-126,000 German civilians in Königsberg at the Soviet capture in April 1945 and finds only around 24,000 still present to be deported in 1947, with hunger accounting for about 75% of deaths, epidemics (chiefly typhus) 2.6% and violence 15%. The wide range reflects that an unknown share left rather than died; Soviet records show 102,407 Germans deported from the oblast to the Soviet zone of Germany between 1947 and 1951.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Kossert's study of Königsberg under Soviet administration and the wider East Prussian literature document mass starvation and typhus among the trapped civilian population, mass rape by Soviet troops during and after the storming of the city, and the destruction or requisition of German property before the 1947-48 deportations.
baselineWhat: The pre-war population of the northern third of East Prussia that became the Kaliningrad Oblast
baselineNote: The 1939 German census gives roughly 1.1-1.2 million inhabitants for the districts later assigned to the Soviet Union, with Konigsberg itself at 372,000. Most fled or were evacuated ahead of the Red Army in the winter of 1944-45 or died in that flight; between about 100,000 and 140,000 Germans were still present when Soviet administration was established, and these were deported to the Soviet occupation zone of Germany in 1947-48.

baselineSources.title: Flight and expulsion of Germans (1944–1950) — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The 100,000 counts only the formal expulsions of 1947-48; the far larger flight and evacuation of 1944-45, and the deaths during it, are not in the numerator.

title: Soviet Seizure of South Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands
actors: Soviet Union invaded and annexed Japanese-administered South Sakhalin (Karafuto) and the Kuril Islands, expelling most Japanese and Ainu residents
peopleRange: roughly 400,000 Japanese residents of South Sakhalin and about 17,000–19,000 from the Kuril Islands were expelled/repatriated by 1949; a small Ainu population (~1,000+) was also displaced, while ethnic Koreans brought as forced labor were largely left stateless
territoryDesc: South Sakhalin (Karafuto, ~36,000 km2) and the Kuril Island chain (~10,500 km2), seized from Japan and incorporated into the USSR

flows.label: South Sakhalin → Hokkaido, Japan
Kuril Islands (Kunashir) → Nemuro, Japan

summary: In the final days of WWII and immediately after, Soviet forces invaded and occupied the Japanese-held southern half of Sakhalin Island and the Kuril Island chain, formally annexing them in 1945–46. Almost the entire Japanese civilian population, along with the small indigenous Ainu community, was expelled or repatriated to Japan by 1949, while ethnic Koreans who had been brought to the islands as forced laborers were largely denied Soviet or Japanese citizenship for years afterward. The USSR (and later Russia) has administered the territory since, while Japan has never recognized the loss of the four southernmost Kuril islands. No peace treaty formally ending the state of war between Japan and Russia has been signed, and the sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.
contested: Sovereignty over the Southern Kuril Islands (Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, the Habomai group) is disputed between Japan and Russia; Japan considers the 1945 seizure illegal and unresolved by treaty, while Russia regards its control as a legitimate outcome of WWII.

sources.title: Japanese evacuation of Karafuto and the Kuril Islands
Kuril Islands | Map, Population, History, & Dispute
The Southern Kuril Islands Dispute

deathsNote: Japanese-derived accounts of the August 1945 campaign put civilian casualties in Karafuto at 3,500-3,700, of which roughly 1,000 died under naval and machine-gun fire at Maoka and more than 2,400 drowned when Soviet submarines sank the evacuation ships Ogasawara Maru and Taito Maru in Aniva Gulf. The figure excludes Japanese and Soviet military dead and excludes later mortality among Japanese POWs interned in the USSR, for which no agreed Sakhalin-specific figure exists.
violenceNote: Japanese repatriate testimony and postwar Japanese accounts, summarised in the standard histories of the Maoka landing, record Soviet forces firing on civilians in European-style dress and on refugee shipping.
baselineWhat: The Japanese-administered population of Karafuto (South Sakhalin) and the Kuril Islands in August 1945
baselineNote: The Japanese census of 1941 counted about 406,000 people in Karafuto, with roughly 17,000 in the Kurils; wartime movement leaves the August 1945 figure near 400,000-420,000. It included Ainu and Nivkh communities and some 23,000-43,000 Koreans brought as wartime labour, most of whom were not included in the repatriation to Japan and remained stateless on Sakhalin.

title: Soviet "Special Settlement" Regime for Deported Nationalities
actors: The Soviet NKVD/MVD holding deported national and social groups as spetsposelentsy in designated settlements under administrative supervision and a ban on leaving the assigned perimeter
peopleRange: 2,753,356 deportees and special settlers registered by the MVD on 1 January 1953, up from 2,572,829 on 1 January 1950; Kazakhstan alone held 988,373 special settlers in January 1953, including 444,005 Germans, 244,674 Chechens, 95,241 Koreans and 80,844 Ingush
territoryDesc: Designated settlements across Kazakhstan, Central Asia, Siberia and the Urals, in which registered settlers had to report periodically to a commandant and were prohibited from leaving the perimeter of their assigned area
summary: Whole nationalities deported during and immediately after the Second World War - among them Volga Germans, Chechens, Ingush, Crimean Tatars, Balkars, Karachays, Kalmyks, Meskhetian Turks, Koreans, Greeks and large numbers from the annexed Baltic states, western Ukraine and Poland - were not imprisoned in camps but registered as "special settlers" in fixed places of residence. The regime was one of confinement rather than incarceration: settlers lived and worked in ordinary settlements but were legally second-class residents, obliged to register with an MVD commandant, forbidden to move without permission, and liable to criminal penalties, including long terms of hard labour, for leaving their assigned area. Archival counts opened after 1991 show 2.57 million registered in January 1950 and 2.75 million in January 1953, the peak of the system. After Stalin's death the regime was dismantled piecemeal by decrees through 1954-1956 removing groups from the register and from administrative supervision: Poles deported in 1936 in January 1956, Kalmyks in March, Greeks, Bulgarians and Armenians in March, Crimean Tatars, Balkars, Meskhetian Turks, Kurds and Hemshins in April, and Chechens and Ingush in July 1956 - the last expressly without the right to return to their homeland. In 1957-1958 the national autonomies of the Kalmyks, Chechens, Ingush, Karachays and Balkars were restored and those peoples were permitted to return, while the Crimean Tatars, Volga Germans and Meskhetian Turks were not, their return bans lasting into the late Soviet period; the Supreme Soviet declared the deportations criminal in November 1989.
contested: Soviet authorities justified the deportations as wartime security measures against collaboration and only conceded their unlawfulness in 1989; the numbers held and the mortality among special settlers were state secrets until the archives opened, and totals still vary between sources according to whether wartime labour-army conscripts, gulag prisoners and later Baltic and western Ukrainian deportees are counted within the same category.

sources.title: Special settlements in the Soviet Union - archival population figures and affected nationalities
Population transfer in the Soviet Union - the 1956 de-registration decrees and restoration of autonomies

deathsNote: NKVD/MVD registers analysed by Viktor Zemskov record on the order of 400,000 deaths among nationalities deported to special settlements in the 1940s, with recorded mortality of about 14.6 per cent among Meskhetian Turks, 17.4 per cent among Kalmyks, 19.6 per cent among Crimean deportees and 23.7 per cent among North Caucasus deportees; most of that mortality fell in 1944-47, so estimates for the post-1945 regime alone are lower and uncertain. Nicolas Werth puts total Soviet deportation-related mortality at 1-1.5 million across the whole Stalin period, and scholars dispute how far the archival registers undercount.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.finding: 2004 resolution recognising the 1944 deportation of the Chechen and Ingush peoples as genocide; Russia rejects the characterisation

title: Bikini Atoll and Marshall Islands Nuclear Test Relocations
actors: The United States relocated Marshallese communities from Bikini, Enewetak, Rongelap and Utirik atolls to conduct 67 nuclear weapons tests
peopleRange: the US relocated 167 Bikinians in 1946, about 145 Enewetak residents in 1947, and emergency-evacuated roughly 236 residents of Rongelap and Utirik in 1954 after fallout from the Castle Bravo test; several hundred more Rongelap residents left permanently in 1985 due to continuing contamination, and thousands more islanders across the Marshalls were exposed to fallout without formal relocation

flows.label: Bikini Atoll → Rongerik, then Kili Island
Enewetak Atoll → Ujelang Atoll
Rongelap Atoll → Mejatto, Kwajalein Atoll

summary: Between 1946 and 1958, the United States conducted 67 nuclear weapons tests in the Marshall Islands, then a US-administered UN trust territory, requiring the relocation of the indigenous populations of Bikini and Enewetak atolls before testing began. The March 1954 Castle Bravo thermonuclear test, far more powerful than expected, spread heavy fallout over inhabited Rongelap and Utirik atolls, prompting emergency evacuations and causing severe radiation sickness; many Rongelap residents left permanently in 1985 due to lingering contamination. Bikinians who were resettled to Rongerik and later Kili Island found the new locations unable to sustain them, and despite a 1968-69 attempt to resettle Bikini itself, elevated radiation levels forced a second evacuation in 1978, leaving the atoll uninhabited to this day. Compensation and cleanup disputes between affected communities and the US government continue.
contested: The adequacy of US compensation, cleanup, and health monitoring, and whether Bikini and other atolls are safe for permanent habitation, remain disputed between the US government, the Marshall Islands government, and affected communities.

sources.title: The Marshall Islands, once a U.S. nuclear test site, face oblivion again
Marshall Islands – Nuclear Museum
Bikini Atoll Nuclear Test Site (UNESCO World Heritage listing)

deathsNote: No source produces a death toll for the relocations themselves: the Bikinians moved to Rongerik in 1946 suffered near-starvation before being evacuated again in 1948, but no starvation deaths are documented. Radiation harm is expressed by the US National Cancer Institute and the US Department of Energy as several hundred projected excess cancers among exposed Marshallese rather than as a count of deaths, and the Nuclear Claims Tribunal awarded personal-injury compensation for radiogenic illness (a sum Congress never funded) rather than adjudicating fatalities.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: None of the listed forms is documented for this event by a named source; the harms recorded by the Nuclear Claims Tribunal and US agencies are displacement, contamination of homelands, radiation illness and the failure to evacuate Rongelap and Utirik before Castle Bravo fallout arrived.
baselineWhat: The combined population of the four atoll communities removed or evacuated for the United States nuclear test programme — Bikini, Enewetak, Rongelap and Utirik
baselineNote: The 167 residents of Bikini were removed in March 1946 and about 145 people of Enewetak in December 1947; 82 people from Rongelap and 157 from Utirik were evacuated after the Castle Bravo fallout of March 1954. The Marshall Islands as a whole held roughly 11,000-14,000 people at the time.
shareCaveat: The affected figure of about 1,000 includes people evacuated at different dates and descendants born in exile, so it exceeds the roughly 550 people living on the four atolls when the removals began and the resulting share passes 100 per cent.

title: Greek Civil War Displacement and Child Evacuations
actors: Fighting between the Greek government and the Communist-led Democratic Army of Greece produced large-scale internal displacement and cross-border refugee flows, including the removal of tens of thousands of children from conflict areas and government-directed mass evacuation of villages.
peopleRange: roughly 700,000–1,000,000 displaced inside Greece by counterinsurgency village clearances (Laiou's estimate is ~850,000), plus 100,000 or more who fled abroad and 28,000–32,000 children evacuated to Eastern Bloc countries

flows.label: Grammos/Vitsi region → Yugoslavia
Northern Greece → USSR (Tashkent)

summary: The 1946–49 Greek Civil War between the government and the Communist-led Democratic Army of Greece caused extensive displacement in the country's northern regions. As the Democratic Army was defeated in 1949, an estimated 100,000 or more fighters and civilians fled across the border into Yugoslavia and onward to other Eastern Bloc countries, including the Soviet Union. Separately, Communist forces evacuated roughly 28,000–32,000 children from combat zones to Eastern Bloc countries in 1948–49 for their safety, a program the Greek government and many Western accounts described at the time as forced abduction ('paidomazoma'). The Greek government simultaneously evacuated and relocated large numbers of villagers from contested areas as a counterinsurgency measure. Many refugees, particularly those identifying as ethnic Macedonians, were barred from returning to Greece for decades.
contested: The child evacuations remain sharply disputed: Greek government sources and much Western reporting characterized them as coercive abduction, while the Communist side and some scholars describe them as a wartime evacuation of children from danger, often with parental involvement; total refugee figures, especially for those identifying as ethnic Macedonians, also differ significantly between Greek and North Macedonian sources.

sources.title: Refugees of the Greek Civil War - Wikipedia
The Greek Civil War, 1946–1949 - Origins (Ohio State University)

deathsNote: Britannica gives 'more than 50,000 combatants' killed and more than 500,000 Greeks temporarily displaced; the standard higher figure of at least 80,000 dead includes civilians executed by both sides and deaths from reprisals and hunger. The Democratic Army of Greece's own claimed losses were 38,839 killed and 20,128 captured. Displacement estimates run to about 1,000,000 temporarily relocated. The child evacuations are separately contested: the Greek Communist Party says 28,000-32,000 children were evacuated to Eastern Bloc states, while Greek government and royalist accounts described the same operation as an abduction (paidomazoma) of about 30,000, and Queen Frederica's 'child towns' held more than 25,000 children, most with parents in the DSE. Neither child programme produced a documented mass death toll.
violenceNote: The removal of roughly 28,000-32,000 children by the Democratic Army of Greece to Eastern Bloc states and the placing of more than 25,000 children in Queen Frederica's 'child towns' are both documented, with distribution figures recorded by the receiving states; the Greek Communist Party describes its programme as evacuation and Greek government accounts as abduction (paidomazoma), and historians remain divided.
baselineWhat: The population of Greece at the start of the civil war
baselineNote: The 1940 census counted 7,344,860 and the 1951 census 7,632,801, implying roughly 7.4 million in 1946 after occupation losses and population exchange. Government and UN relief records put internal refugees at about 700,000 by 1949, mostly villagers moved out of mountain areas by the army; some 25,000-28,000 children were evacuated to Communist-bloc countries in the paidomazoma and a comparable number to government-run 'child towns'.
