baselineNote: Papua New Guinea's 1980 census counted about 128,000 on Bougainville and the 2000 census 175,160; no census could be taken during the conflict, so the 1990 population is interpolated at roughly 155,000-160,000. Estimates that the blockade contributed to as many as 15,000-20,000 deaths, mostly from lack of medicine, are contested and cannot be verified against any registration system.

title: First Nagorno-Karabakh War
actors: Armenian and ethnic Armenian Karabakh forces, backed by Armenia, fought Azerbaijani forces over the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast and seven adjacent Azerbaijani districts as the Soviet Union collapsed
peopleRange: roughly 1 million total: an estimated 600,000-800,000 Azerbaijanis displaced from Nagorno-Karabakh and surrounding districts, and roughly 300,000-400,000 Armenians who fled Azerbaijan proper, including after pogroms in Sumgait (1988) and Baku (1990)
territoryDesc: Nagorno-Karabakh (about 4,400 km²) plus seven surrounding Azerbaijani districts (about 7,500-9,200 km²), placed under Armenian/Karabakh Armenian control after the war

flows.label: Nagorno-Karabakh/adjacent districts → Baku (Azerbaijanis)
Azerbaijan proper → Armenia (Armenians)

summary: As the Soviet Union weakened, the predominantly ethnic Armenian Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast sought to join Armenia, triggering pogroms against Armenians in Azerbaijani cities and full-scale war after both republics gained independence in 1991. Armenian and Karabakh Armenian forces, with Armenian state backing, took control of Nagorno-Karabakh and seven surrounding Azerbaijani districts by the 1994 Bishkek ceasefire, displacing roughly 600,000-800,000 Azerbaijanis, while some 300,000-400,000 Armenians fled or were expelled from Azerbaijan proper. The unrecognized 'Republic of Artsakh' was established in the captured territory, and the conflict remained frozen for over two decades.
contested: Armenia and Karabakh Armenians framed the war as an exercise of self-determination; Azerbaijan and four UN Security Council resolutions (822, 853, 874, 884) characterized Armenian control of the seven surrounding districts as occupation of internationally recognized Azerbaijani territory; no state recognized Nagorno-Karabakh's independence.

sources.title: UN Security Council Resolution 822 (1993) - UN Digital Library
HRW: Azerbaijan - Seven Years of Conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh (1994)
Nagorno-Karabakh - Britannica

deathsNote: The International Crisis Group's field study put total deaths 'in the neighbourhood of 18,500', explicitly revising downward earlier claims of 18,000–20,000 Azerbaijani and at least 25,000 Armenian dead; figures of 20,000–30,000 remain in wide circulation in Armenian and Azerbaijani official and journalistic accounts, and both governments have incentives to emphasise their own losses. Crisis Group counts roughly 413,000 Armenians and 724,000 Azerbaijanis and Kurds displaced.

atrocityFindings.body: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)
atrocityFindings.finding: Chiragov and Others v. Armenia and Sargsyan v. Azerbaijan (both 16 June 2015): continuing violations of property and home rights of displaced Azerbaijanis and Armenians; Armenia found to exercise effective control over Nagorno-Karabakh and the adjacent districts

violenceNote: A CEPS study of the conflict records the February 1988 Sumgait pogrom against Armenians and the February 1992 Khojaly massacre of at least 485 Azerbaijani civilians fleeing the town, and the European Court of Human Rights in Chiragov and Sargsyan (2015) found continuing denial of access to abandoned homes and property on both sides.
baselineWhat: The combined population of Soviet Azerbaijan and Soviet Armenia at the 1989 census, the two republics between which the population was exchanged
baselineNote: The 1989 all-Union census counted 7,021,178 in the Azerbaijan SSR and 3,304,776 in the Armenian SSR, with 189,000 people in the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast, about three quarters of them Armenian. Displacement ran both ways: roughly 600,000 Azerbaijani internally displaced from Karabakh and the occupied districts, about 185,000-200,000 Azerbaijanis expelled from Armenia and about 300,000-350,000 Armenians from Azerbaijan proper.
shareCaveat: The numerator sums displacement in both directions across two states, so no single national population is the right denominator; against Azerbaijan alone the Azerbaijani share of displaced was about 11 per cent, and against Armenia the Armenian share was proportionally higher.

title: The Aceh Insurgency, Military Operations Zone and Martial Law Displacement
actors: Indonesian security forces fought the Free Aceh Movement (GAM), emptying villages and confining the province under military rule
peopleRange: Human Rights Watch recorded more than 100,000 people displaced in the first seven months of the martial law operation declared in May 2003, and Indonesian and UN agencies reported comparable numbers displaced in 1999-2001 during earlier operations, with tens of thousands moved into government-designated camps. A cumulative figure of roughly 300,000 across the conflict is an aggregate of these episodic counts, not a single register; many people were displaced more than once and returns were rapid, so totals are not additive with confidence.

flows.label: Villagers moved into camps in North Aceh and Bireuen

summary: The Free Aceh Movement launched an armed separatist campaign in 1976, and from 1989 to 1998 Aceh was designated a Military Operations Area (Daerah Operasi Militer), a period in which Indonesian human rights bodies later documented extrajudicial killings, disappearances, torture and sexual violence. After the fall of Suharto the conflict escalated again, and in May 2003 the Indonesian government declared martial law and launched its largest domestic military operation since East Timor; Human Rights Watch documented more than 100,000 people displaced within seven months, forced relocations into camps, restrictions on movement and journalist access, and summary executions. Estimates of total conflict deaths across 1976-2005 range from about 10,000 to 33,000, most of them civilians. The December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, which killed some 130,000 people in Aceh, transformed the political situation and was followed by the Helsinki Memorandum of Understanding of August 2005, which ended the war and granted Aceh special autonomy. An Aceh Truth and Reconciliation Commission was established in 2016 and has taken statements from thousands of victims, and in January 2023 President Joko Widodo acknowledged twelve past gross human rights violations by the Indonesian state, including cases in Aceh.
contested: Death and displacement totals for the conflict vary widely between Indonesian official figures, GAM claims and human rights organisations, and responsibility for particular killings is often disputed.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch, Aceh Under Martial Law: Inside the Secret War (2003)
Insurgency in Aceh
Antara News: Indonesia acknowledges 12 past major human rights violations (2023)

deathsNote: The lower figure is the conservative count of documented conflict deaths used by several conflict datasets; the higher figure comes from Acehnese civil society and truth-commission submissions that include disappearances and unrecovered victims from the 1989-98 Military Operations Area period. The gap reflects the absence of any independent count during military rule.

atrocityFindings.body: Government of Indonesia (President Joko Widodo)
atrocityFindings.finding: Publicly acknowledged twelve past cases of gross human rights violations by the state, including the Aceh Military Operations Area period, the Rumoh Geudong and Simpang KKA cases, and expressed regret on behalf of the state.

violenceNote: Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Indonesia's own national human rights commission Komnas HAM documented these forms in the Military Operations Area period and under martial law.

baselineNote: The 1990 census counted 3,416,156 people in Aceh, rising to about 4.0 million by 2000. Displacement was concentrated in North Aceh, East Aceh and Pidie during the 1989-98 Military Operations Zone and again under the 2003-04 martial law emergency.
shareCaveat: The affected figure is cumulative across sixteen years and two distinct emergencies; peak simultaneous displacement was far lower, and many were displaced more than once.

title: Crimean Tatar Return to Crimea and Its Obstruction
actors: Crimean Tatars deported in 1944 returned from Central Asia to Crimea as Soviet restrictions lapsed, and faced Soviet and then Ukrainian obstacles to citizenship, land and housing
peopleRange: About 260,000 of an estimated 400,000-550,000 Crimean Tatars had returned to Crimea by the time of the Council of Europe's report, with roughly 30,000 remaining in Uzbekistan and others in Kazakhstan and Russia (Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe).

flows.label: Uzbekistan and Central Asia → Crimea

summary: Deported wholesale to Central Asia in 1944 and barred from return for decades, Crimean Tatars began returning to Crimea in numbers from 1989 as Soviet restrictions collapsed. The Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly recorded some 260,000 returnees out of a diaspora of 400,000-550,000, with about 30,000 still in Uzbekistan. Return was not accompanied by restitution: returnees found their former homes occupied, were allocated land on poor peripheral sites where many built unauthorised settlements, and faced infrastructure gaps in which 70 per cent of settlements had electricity, 27 per cent running water and none any sewerage. Many arrived stateless or without Ukrainian citizenship, a problem addressed by a 1997 law under which some 25,000 stateless Crimean Tatars had received Ukrainian passports by mid-1999 and by a UNHCR statelessness programme that reported over 90 per cent holding Ukrainian citizenship by 2001; unemployment among returnees was put at around 60 per cent. Ukraine spent some 300 million dollars on the resettlement between 1991 and the report's date, which the Assembly judged insufficient against needs.
contested: Estimates of the total Crimean Tatar population eligible to return vary widely (400,000 to 550,000, excluding a much larger Turkish diaspora of older origin), and responsibility for the failure to restore property and land was disputed between Ukrainian national authorities, the Crimean administration and the successor states of the USSR.

sources.title: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe: Repatriation and integration of the Tatars of Crimea
UNHCR: Helping Crimean Tatars feel at home again

deathsNote: There was no significant death toll associated with the return itself; the lethal phase of this history was the 1944 deportation and the first years of special settlement in Central Asia, which are counted separately.
violenceNote: The Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly documented that large numbers of returning Crimean Tatars were left stateless or without citizenship of the state they had returned to, requiring a special 1997 naturalisation procedure.
baselineWhat: The Crimean Tatar population of the Soviet Union recorded at the 1989 census, overwhelmingly in Uzbekistan and the other Central Asian republics
baselineNote: The 1989 Soviet census counted 271,715 Crimean Tatars, of whom fewer than 40,000 had managed to return to Crimea; by the 2001 Ukrainian census 248,193 Crimean Tatars were living in Crimea. The return was self-organised and its scale is measured by these two censuses rather than by any resettlement programme.

title: The Kashmir Insurgency, Counter-Insurgency Displacement and the 2019 Reorganisation
actors: Indian security forces, Pakistan-backed and indigenous militant groups, and civilians displaced across and within the Line of Control
peopleRange: Beyond the separately recorded exodus of Kashmiri Pandits, official Indian figures record roughly 35,000-46,000 families - on the order of 150,000-250,000 people - displaced from villages along the Line of Control in Jammu division by shelling and infiltration between 1990 and 2003, of whom many have never returned; Pakistan-administered Kashmir hosts tens of thousands of people displaced from the Indian side. Figures come from Jammu and Kashmir state relief and rehabilitation department registers and from the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, and exclude unregistered movement.
territoryDesc: In August 2019 India revoked the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 and split the state into two federally administered union territories

flows.label: Villagers from the Line of Control belt to camps in Jammu

summary: An armed insurgency against Indian rule began in the Kashmir valley in 1989-90 and continues at lower intensity; Indian official figures put conflict deaths at roughly 41,000-45,000 since 1990, while Kashmiri civil-society organisations and the Jammu and Kashmir Coalition of Civil Society put the toll at 70,000 or more and document mass graves and thousands of enforced disappearances, which the Indian government disputes. Alongside the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits from the valley in 1990, recorded separately, tens of thousands of families were displaced from villages along the Line of Control by cross-border shelling and militant infiltration and housed in long-term camps in Jammu. Indian security legislation, principally the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act and the Public Safety Act, has been criticised by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, which published reports on the human rights situation in 2018 and 2019 covering both Indian- and Pakistan-administered Kashmir; India rejected both reports as fallacious and motivated. In August 2019 India revoked Article 370, splitting the state into two union territories, and imposed a months-long communications blackout and mass preventive detention in which thousands were held, including three former chief ministers; Pakistan and China objected to the reorganisation, and the Indian Supreme Court upheld the revocation in December 2023.
contested: Conflict death tolls, the existence and scale of enforced disappearances and mass graves, and the legality and consequences of the 2019 reorganisation are all disputed between the Indian government, Kashmiri civil society, and Pakistan.

sources.title: OHCHR statement: first-ever UN human rights report on Kashmir (2018)
Insurgency in Jammu and Kashmir
Revocation of the special status of Jammu and Kashmir (2019)
Human rights abuses in Jammu and Kashmir

deathsNote: The low figure is the Indian government's cumulative count of militants, security personnel and civilians killed since 1990, compiled by the Ministry of Home Affairs. The high figure comes from Kashmiri separatist and civil-society organisations, which include disappearances and unrecorded custodial deaths. Neither has been independently audited and access for independent investigators has been restricted.
violenceNote: The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, Amnesty International and the Jammu and Kashmir Coalition of Civil Society documented these forms, attributing them to Indian security forces and to armed groups respectively; India disputes the OHCHR findings.
baselineWhat: The population of the state of Jammu and Kashmir at the outbreak of the insurgency
baselineNote: The 1981 census counted 5,987,389 in Jammu and Kashmir; no census was held there in 1991 because of the insurgency, and projections put the population at roughly 7.7 million in 1990. The 2011 census counted 12,541,302. The displacement figure refers overwhelmingly to the Kashmiri Pandit exodus from the Valley beginning in January 1990, with estimates ranging from about 100,000 to 200,000 or more; Indian government relief registrations covered around 60,000 families.
shareCaveat: The displaced are almost entirely Kashmiri Pandits, a community of roughly 140,000-160,000 in the Valley, so measured against the whole state population the share of about 2 per cent conceals the near-total removal of that community; the 2019 reorganisation and communications blackout, by contrast, applied to all 12.5 million residents.

title: Liberian and Sierra Leonean Civil Wars
actors: Charles Taylor's NPFL and rival Liberian factions fought two civil wars; the conflict spilled into Sierra Leone, where the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), backed by Taylor, fought the government in a war marked by mass amputations and child soldier recruitment
peopleRange: combined, the wars killed an estimated 320,000 people (about 250,000 in Liberia, 70,000 in Sierra Leone) and displaced roughly 2-3 million people across both countries, including large refugee flows into Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire

flows.label: Liberia → Guinea (Conakry region)
Sierra Leone → Guinea
Liberia → Côte d'Ivoire

summary: Charles Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia (NPFL) launched an insurgency against President Samuel Doe in December 1989, beginning a first civil war (1989-1997) followed by a second (1999-2003) after Taylor himself became president; the fighting was marked by warlordism, ethnic massacres, and widespread recruitment of child soldiers. Taylor also backed the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) in neighboring Sierra Leone from 1991, whose decade-long war against the Sierra Leonean government became notorious for the mass amputation of civilians' limbs and 'blood diamond' financing. Combined, the two interlinked conflicts killed an estimated 320,000 people and displaced 2-3 million, sending large refugee populations into Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire; UN peacekeeping interventions and, in Sierra Leone, British military intervention helped end the fighting by 2002-2003, and both Taylor and RUF leader Foday Sankoh were later prosecuted for war crimes.

sources.title: Britannica: Sierra Leone - Civil War
BlackPast: The Sierra Leone Civil War (1991-2002)
Human Rights Watch: Sierra Leone

deathsNote: The conventional figures are about 200,000 dead in Liberia's first civil war (1989-97), about 50,000 in the second (1999-2003), and 'at least 50,000' in Sierra Leone with some 2,000,000 displaced (Britannica); higher Sierra Leone figures of 70,000-75,000 circulate without a distinct primary source. All of these are estimates rather than counts. The Sierra Leone Truth and Reconciliation Commission's statistical appendix documented 40,242 violations including 4,514 killings and explicitly cautioned that its database 'represents neither a complete census of human rights violations nor a random sample' and cannot be extrapolated to the population — a warning routinely ignored when the 50,000-75,000 range is quoted. The Liberian totals in particular are repeated across the literature without attribution to any original demographic study.

atrocityFindings.body: Special Court for Sierra Leone
atrocityFindings.finding: Convicted Charles Taylor on all eleven counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity — including terrorism, murder, rape, sexual slavery, conscription of child soldiers and enslavement — for planning and for aiding and abetting crimes by RUF/AFRC forces in Sierra Leone, sentencing him on 30 May 2012 to 50 years; the Appeals Chamber upheld conviction and sentence in September 2013

atrocityFindings.body: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Sierra Leone
atrocityFindings.finding: Found the leadership of the RUF, AFRC, Sierra Leone Army and Civil Defence Forces responsible for authorising, instigating or failing to prevent violations, with the RUF responsible for the largest number, and found that the country was systematically plundered by all factions; it also documented the role of Charles Taylor and the NPFL in intensifying the war

baselineNote: UN Population Division estimates give Liberia about 2.2-2.3 million and Sierra Leone about 4.0-4.1 million in 1989. At the peak, roughly half of Liberia's population and more than half of Sierra Leone's were displaced: UNHCR counted about 780,000 Liberian refugees and 500,000 Sierra Leonean refugees, with internal displacement of 1 million or more in each country at different points.
shareCaveat: The figure aggregates two countries and fourteen years across three wars, and counts people displaced repeatedly as fronts moved, while the combined population itself grew to about 8.5 million by 2003.

title: The 1989 United States Invasion of Panama and the Destruction of El Chorrillo
actors: United States forces invaded Panama to remove General Manuel Noriega; fighting and fire destroyed the El Chorrillo neighbourhood of Panama City
peopleRange: About 20,000 people lost their homes as a result of the urban fighting, chiefly in El Chorrillo, which adjoined the Panamanian Defence Forces headquarters; some 2,700 displaced families were later given 6,500 dollars each by the United States to rebuild or rehouse, a figure that provides the firmest basis for the total. Displaced residents were housed for months in shelters including Balboa High School. The figures come from United States and Panamanian reconstruction programmes and contemporary reporting rather than a formal census.

flows.label: El Chorrillo residents to emergency shelters in the former Canal Zone
Resettlement in new housing west of Panama City

summary: United States forces invaded Panama on 20 December 1989 to depose General Manuel Noriega, who had annulled the 1989 election results and been indicted in the United States on drug charges. The assault on the Panamanian Defence Forces headquarters, La Comandancia, set fires that destroyed much of the adjoining El Chorrillo, a densely populated neighbourhood of wooden tenements; United States accounts attribute part of the burning to Noriega's paramilitary Dignity Battalions, Panamanian residents and human rights groups to the American bombardment. The Pentagon put Panamanian deaths at 516, including 202 civilians; Americas Watch estimated about 300 civilian deaths, Panama's Institute of Legal Medicine reported 342-346 total dead by 1991, and Panamanian human rights organisations have claimed figures in the thousands. Around 20,000 people lost their homes, many living in shelters for more than a year before replacement housing was built, with recurrent complaints about its quality. The United Nations General Assembly, the Organization of American States and the European Parliament condemned the invasion as a violation of international law; the United States cited protection of its nationals, the canal treaties and the restoration of the elected government. Panama later created a commission to investigate the deaths, and 20 December is a national day of mourning.
contested: Civilian death figures are disputed by an order of magnitude, from roughly 200-300 in United States and Panamanian forensic accounts to 3,000 or more claimed by Panamanian human rights groups, with exhumations conducted in ways that destroyed evidence; responsibility for the fires in El Chorrillo, and the legality of the invasion, remain contested between the United States government and Panamanian and international bodies.

sources.title: United States invasion of Panama (Wikipedia)
Human Rights Watch, Human Rights in Post-Invasion Panama (1991)
UN General Assembly resolution 44/240 on the situation in Panama (UN Digital Library)

deathsNote: The Pentagon counted 202 civilians and 314 Panamanian soldiers killed; Americas Watch put civilian deaths at about 300, and Panama's Institute of Legal Medicine reported 342-346 dead in total by February 1991, of whom at least 280-305 were civilians. Panamanian human rights groups have long claimed 3,000 or more, a figure that has not been substantiated by exhumations, though Human Rights Watch noted that the exhumations were carried out with bulldozers and in disregard of the need to preserve evidence, so all figures are soft. Twenty-three United States soldiers and three United States civilians were killed.

title: Bhutanese Lhotshampa in the Eastern Nepal Camps
actors: Nepal hosting Lhotshampa expelled from Bhutan in UNHCR-administered camps without local integration, while Bhutan declined to accept their return
peopleRange: Over 100,000 Lhotshampa left or were expelled from Bhutan between 1988 and 1993; the seven camps in Jhapa and Morang districts peaked at over 107,000 residents in the mid-1990s and still held about 85,500 in January 2010; roughly 112,800 had been resettled to third countries by January 2019, about 85 per cent of them to the United States, leaving around 6,500-11,800 in two remaining camps
territoryDesc: Seven camps in Jhapa and Morang districts of eastern Nepal, including Beldangi I and II and Sanischare, consolidated into two camps as resettlement proceeded
summary: Following Bhutan's "one nation, one people" policies and the 1985 Citizenship Act, which required documentary proof of residence in 1958, more than 100,000 Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa from southern Bhutan lost their citizenship or left the country between 1988 and 1993, most travelling through India to eastern Nepal. Nepal admitted them into seven camps administered by UNHCR but did not permit local integration: residents faced restricted or controlled movement, restricted ability to work and limited access to the local justice system, and remained without any nationality for close to two decades while more than fifteen rounds of bilateral talks between Nepal and Bhutan produced no agreed repatriation. Bhutan classified many of those who left as voluntary emigrants and treated the associated political parties as anti-national, and declined to guarantee full citizenship and rights to returnees; property left behind was in many cases reallocated. From 2007 a group of resettlement countries led by the United States, with Canada, Australia, Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and New Zealand, began large-scale third-country resettlement, and by 2019 about 112,800 people had left. Those remaining, consolidated into two camps, are disproportionately elderly and separated from resettled relatives, and no repatriation to Bhutan has taken place.
contested: Bhutan maintains that most departures were voluntary emigration by people who could not prove lawful residence, and that some in the camps were never Bhutanese nationals, while the refugees, Nepal and human rights organisations describe a campaign of denationalisation and expulsion; the verification exercise agreed in the 2000s categorised only a small fraction as eligible to return and its methodology was rejected by refugee representatives.

sources.title: Bhutanese refugees - camp populations, restrictions in Nepal and third-country resettlement figures

deathsNote: Both fields are null because the confinement in UNHCR-administered camps in eastern Nepal has not produced a death toll; the camps held over 107,000 people at peak, about 112,800 were resettled to third countries from 2007 (roughly 85% to the United States) and around 10,000 remain, mostly elderly, with reported rising rates of depression and suicide that no body has quantified. Some sources report more than 300 people killed during the Bhutanese crackdown of the early 1990s, but that occurred in Bhutan rather than in the camps.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and UNHCR documented that Bhutan's 1985 Citizenship Act and 1988 census reclassified Lhotshampa as non-nationals — splitting members of the same family into different categories where pre-1958 residence could not be proved — leaving over 100,000 people stateless and unable to return.
baselineWhat: The Lhotshampa (ethnic Nepali) population of southern Bhutan around 1990
baselineNote: The figure is contested. Bhutan's 1988 census, whose reclassification of residents triggered the expulsions, is not published in a form that settles it; refugee organisations and outside observers put the Lhotshampa at roughly a third to 45 per cent of a Bhutanese population of about 600,000, that is 150,000-250,000, while the Bhutanese government maintains that many of those expelled were recent illegal immigrants rather than citizens. About 107,000 people were registered in the UNHCR camps in eastern Nepal in the 1990s.
shareCaveat: The 107,000 is the cumulative number registered in the camps over three decades, including children born there, not a snapshot of people expelled from Bhutan.
asOfNote: More than 113,000 refugees were resettled to third countries, above all the United States, between 2007 and 2016; UNHCR now counts a small remaining caseload in the Beldangi and Sanischare camps within a total Nepali refugee population of about 20,000, and neither return to Bhutan nor Nepali citizenship has been offered.

title: Exodus of Kashmiri Pandits
actors: Amid the outbreak of an armed insurgency and targeted killings and threats by militants in the Kashmir Valley, the Hindu Kashmiri Pandit minority fled in large numbers, mostly to Jammu and Delhi
peopleRange: estimates range widely, from roughly 100,000 to over 350,000, depending on source and the period counted

flows.label: Kashmir Valley → Jammu, India
Kashmir Valley → Delhi, India

summary: Beginning in late 1989 and escalating through 1990, an armed insurgency against Indian rule broke out in the Kashmir Valley, accompanied by targeted killings, threats, and intimidation directed at the region's Hindu Kashmiri Pandit minority by militant groups. Facing this violence, a large majority of the Valley's Pandit population, along with some Kashmiri Muslims, fled to Jammu, Delhi, and other parts of India, where many lived for years in refugee camps or migrant settlements. The precise number displaced is disputed, with estimates ranging from about 100,000 to over 350,000. The episode remains a highly sensitive and politically charged chapter of the broader Kashmir conflict, with most displaced Pandits still unable or unwilling to return.
contested: The scale of displacement and killings, and whether the episode should be characterized as ethnic cleansing or genocide, are disputed; some Kashmiri Pandit organizations use those terms, while other accounts, including some Kashmiri Muslim organizations, dispute aspects of the scale, causation, or characterization.

sources.title: Forced Migration Review: Frozen displacement - Kashmiri Pandits in India
Exodus of Kashmiri Hindus - overview via The Quint

deathsNote: Jammu and Kashmir state government records list 219 Kashmiri Pandits killed between 1989 and 2004, and India's Home Ministry recorded 217 Hindu civilian deaths for 1988-1991; the Kashmiri Pandit Sangharsh Samiti's own community surveys give 357 killed in 1990 alone and 399 over 1990-2011, while some Pandit organisations cite about 650 over two decades. Much higher figures circulating in Indian political debate are not supported by any of these tallies. Between 90,000 and 150,000 Pandits left the Valley, mostly in early 1990.
violenceNote: Indian Home Ministry and Jammu and Kashmir state records, surveys by the Kashmiri Pandit Sangharsh Samiti, and accounts compiled by human rights researchers document targeted assassinations of prominent Pandits, abductions of Pandit women followed by rape and murder, threats broadcast from mosques and posted in newspapers, and the burning of Pandit homes, shops and temples.
baselineWhat: The Kashmiri Pandit population of the Kashmir Valley immediately before the 1990 exodus
baselineNote: There is no direct count: projections from the 1981 census using decennial growth rates imply about 161,000 Hindus, most of them Kashmiri Pandits, in the Valley by 1991, and estimates in circulation range from about 120,000 to 300,000. Figures for those who left are drawn from relief-camp registration in Jammu and Delhi and from the 90,430 domicile certificates issued to displaced Pandits by June 2021.
shareCaveat: Both the resident population and the number who left are estimates derived from the same census projections and from relief registration, and figures on each side are contested politically, so the ratio can approach or exceed 100 per cent depending on the pairing chosen.

title: Iraqi Invasion and Annexation of Kuwait
actors: Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded and formally annexed Kuwait as its '19th province' in August 1990, citing historical and economic claims; a US-led multinational coalition expelled Iraqi forces in the Gulf War of January–February 1991.
peopleRange: An estimated 400,000-plus foreign workers fled Kuwait during the seven-month occupation, alongside several hundred thousand Kuwaitis who fled or were expelled; after liberation, an estimated 200,000–400,000 Palestinians were expelled from Kuwait in 1991 over the PLO's support for Iraq
territoryDesc: Kuwait (~17,818 km2) was formally annexed by Iraq for roughly seven months before the 1991 coalition military campaign restored its sovereignty and independence.

flows.label: Palestinians and foreign workers → Jordan
Kuwaitis fled → Saudi Arabia

summary: On 2 August 1990, Iraq invaded and occupied Kuwait, formally annexing it days later as Iraq's '19th province,' citing disputed historical claims, oil pricing disputes, and Kuwaiti debt from the Iran-Iraq war. The UN Security Council declared the annexation null and void and, after sanctions and a diplomatic ultimatum failed, authorized a US-led coalition that liberated Kuwait in a six-week campaign (Operation Desert Storm) in early 1991. During the seven-month occupation, several hundred thousand Kuwaitis and over 400,000 foreign workers fled the country, and Iraqi forces looted and set fire to hundreds of Kuwaiti oil wells during their retreat. After liberation, the Kuwaiti government and vigilante groups expelled roughly 200,000–400,000 Palestinian residents in reprisal for PLO leader Yasser Arafat's support for Iraq, devastating a community that had lived in Kuwait for decades.
contested: Iraq claimed historical territorial rights over Kuwait dating to Ottoman-era provincial boundaries, a claim rejected by Kuwait, the Arab League, and the international community; the post-liberation expulsion of Palestinians is itself sometimes treated as a distinct displacement event, and the proportion attributable to government policy versus community reprisal is debated.

sources.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
Human Rights Watch World Report 1991: Iraq and occupied Kuwait
Palestinian exodus from Kuwait (1990–91)

deathsNote: The range covers deaths in Kuwait during the invasion and seven-month occupation: roughly 1,000 Kuwaiti civilians died, about 295 Kuwaiti and 420 Iraqi military personnel were killed in the August 1990 fighting, and 605 Kuwaitis went missing, of whom only 236 sets of remains had been identified by 2009. It deliberately excludes Iraqi military deaths in the 1991 coalition campaign, for which published estimates span more than an order of magnitude — early US Defense Intelligence Agency figures around 100,000 were later revised sharply downward by analysts using aerial and unit-strength data.
violenceNote: Amnesty International's 1990 investigation and the ICRC's still-open missing-persons file document the arrest of over 2,000 Kuwaitis, torture including beating, electric shock and removal of fingernails, executions, the disappearance of 605 people, and systematic looting and destruction of property during the occupation.
baselineWhat: The population of Kuwait on the eve of the Iraqi invasion
baselineNote: Kuwaiti official estimates put the population at about 2.1 million in mid-1990, of whom roughly 600,000 were Kuwaiti citizens and the remainder expatriates, including some 400,000 Palestinians and large Egyptian, Indian and Bangladeshi communities. By the 1995 census the total had fallen to 1.58 million.
shareCaveat: Most of those who left were expatriate workers returning to their own countries; the mass expulsion of Kuwait's Palestinians came after liberation in 1991, as reprisal, rather than during the Iraqi occupation.

title: Departure and Expulsion of Palestinians from Kuwait
actors: Palestinians left Kuwait during the Iraqi occupation, and after liberation the Kuwaiti authorities dismissed, detained and deported those who remained and refused re-entry to those who had gone
peopleRange: Human Rights Watch recorded a Palestinian community of more than 350,000 in Kuwait before the Iraqi invasion of August 1990, about 180,000 of whom left during the occupation, and a residual population of roughly 80,000 by early November 1991 — a net reduction of some 270,000. Departures continued afterwards and the community fell to a few tens of thousands. The figures are HRW's estimates based on Kuwaiti government data, embassy reporting and community sources; no registration exercise covered the movement, and the boundary between flight, expulsion and refusal of re-entry is not sharp.

flows.label: Kuwait → Jordan
Kuwait → Iraq (deportations across the northern border)

summary: Kuwait's Palestinian community, more than 350,000 strong before August 1990 and central to the country's professional and administrative workforce, was largely dispersed by the Gulf crisis. Around 180,000 left during the Iraqi occupation, abandoning homes and property accumulated over decades. After liberation in February 1991 the Kuwaiti government, citing the PLO leadership's alignment with Iraq and alleged collaboration, refused with very few exceptions to allow those who had left to return, dismissed Palestinians from public employment, declined to renew residence permits, and subjected many to security detention and, in the immediate post-liberation weeks, to torture and extrajudicial killing. Human Rights Watch documented that about 2,000 Palestinians were taken by the authorities to the Iraqi border and deported, that stateless Palestinians holding Egyptian travel documents were given two weeks' notice to leave, and that families of detainees were pressured to depart. The Crown Prince publicly denied that Kuwait had expelled or would expel Palestinians. By November 1991 around 80,000 remained, including some 23,000 Gazans whose Egyptian travel documents entitled them to settle nowhere. Most of those who left went to Jordan.
contested: Kuwait denied that it expelled Palestinians, characterizing departures as voluntary and residual measures as security and immigration enforcement; human rights organizations characterized the same measures as collective punishment and forced expulsion.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch news release on the expulsion of Palestinians from Kuwait, 23 October 1991
Kuwait: Human Rights Developments Since Liberation — Middle East Watch / Human Rights Watch World Report 1992

deathsNote: There was no mass killing on a scale comparable to the displacement. Human Rights Watch and other organizations documented extrajudicial killings, deaths in custody under torture and disappearances of Palestinians and other residents in the weeks after liberation, numbering in the dozens to low hundreds; no comprehensive count was produced and Kuwaiti courts tried only a small number of cases.
violenceNote: Documented by Middle East Watch / Human Rights Watch in its 1991 reporting and 1992 World Report chapter on Kuwait.
baselineWhat: The Palestinian community resident in Kuwait before the Iraqi invasion of August 1990
baselineNote: Kuwait's pre-invasion Palestinian population is generally put at 350,000-400,000, the largest expatriate community in the emirate, out of a total population of about 2.1 million of whom roughly 60 per cent were non-citizens. Fewer than 30,000 remained by 1992.

baselineSources.title: Expulsion of Palestinians from Kuwait (1990–91) — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The figure combines those who left during the Iraqi occupation with those expelled or forced out after liberation; the two phases had different causes and are often reported together.

title: Expulsion of the Lhotshampa from Bhutan
actors: Bhutan's government, implementing 'One Nation, One People' citizenship and cultural policies, forced out or pressured the departure of a large share of its ethnic Nepali-speaking (Lhotshampa) population, many of whom were rendered stateless
peopleRange: over 100,000 fled or were expelled by the mid-1990s, roughly one-sixth of Bhutan's population at the time; refugee camp population in Nepal peaked at about 107,000

flows.label: Southern Bhutan → UNHCR refugee camps, eastern Nepal
Nepal refugee camps → third-country resettlement (mainly USA)

summary: During the late 1980s and 1990s, Bhutan's government implemented citizenship and cultural assimilation policies widely seen as targeting the Lhotshampa, an ethnic Nepali-speaking, largely Hindu minority concentrated in southern Bhutan. Following unrest and a 1990 crackdown, tens of thousands of Lhotshampa were expelled or fled, with departures peaking in the early-to-mid 1990s; by 1996 over 100,000 had left, and a network of UNHCR-run refugee camps in eastern Nepal reached a peak population of roughly 107,000. Bilateral talks between Bhutan and Nepal over repatriation failed to produce returns, and beginning in 2007 most camp residents were instead resettled to third countries, chiefly the United States. Many Lhotshampa describe the episode as a state-orchestrated campaign of ethnic cleansing.
contested: Bhutan's government has maintained that many who left did so voluntarily, signed 'voluntary migration' forms, or were not genuine Bhutanese citizens; Lhotshampa refugee organizations and international human rights groups describe the policies and expulsions as a deliberate campaign of ethnic cleansing.

sources.title: US Department of State, Bhutanese Refugees in Nepal
Minority Rights Group, Lhotshampas in Bhutan
The Diplomat, Bhutan's Dark Secret: The Lhotshampa Expulsion

deathsNote: No significant direct death toll; the harm is expulsion and statelessness. More than 100,000 Lhotshampa left or were forced out between the late 1980s and mid-1990s — roughly a sixth of Bhutan's population and about 40% of its ethnic Nepali community — and 85,544 were still in UNHCR camps in eastern Nepal in January 2010. Human Rights Watch's 2007 report on the case is titled 'Last Hope' and its 2008 work describes the policy as ethnic cleansing; Bhutan maintains the departures were voluntary emigration by illegal residents. Deaths from disease in the early Nepali camps were reported but never systematically enumerated.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Bhutan's 1985 Citizenship Act, requiring both parents to be Bhutanese and proof of domicile on or before 31 December 1958, excluded many long-resident Lhotshampa from citizenship, and Human Rights Watch — which titled its 2008 work on the case 'Bhutan's Ethnic Cleansing' — reported the detention of Lhotshampa political activists, educators and other civilians.
baselineWhat: The Lhotshampa (Nepali-speaking southern Bhutanese) population of Bhutan around 1990
baselineNote: Both the numerator and the denominator are contested. Bhutan claimed a national population of about 600,000 in 1990 but revised its own figure sharply at the 2005 census, which counted 672,425; estimates of the Lhotshampa share before the expulsions range from about a quarter to more than a third, implying roughly 150,000-250,000 people. The government characterises most of those who left as illegal immigrants who departed voluntarily, while refugee and human rights organisations record coerced 'voluntary migration' forms and citizenship stripping under the 1985 Citizenship Act and the 1988 census in the south.

baselineSources.title: Lhotshampas in Bhutan — Minority Rights Group

shareCaveat: Because Bhutan disputes both how many Lhotshampa lived in the country and whether those who left were citizens at all, the ratio rests on figures neither side accepts; a share of roughly half the community is the range most independent accounts support.

title: LTTE Expulsion of Muslims from Sri Lanka's Northern Province
actors: The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam ordered the entire Muslim population out of the five northern districts at gunpoint and confiscated their property
peopleRange: About 75,000 of the roughly 81,000 Muslims then living in the Northern Province were expelled within two weeks in October 1990, 67,000 of them registering immediately at displacement camps (Citizens' Commission on the Expulsion of the Muslims from the Northern Province).

flows.label: Jaffna and the northern districts → Puttalam

summary: In October 1990 the LTTE ordered the removal of the entire Muslim population from the northern districts of Jaffna, Kilinochchi, Mullaitivu, Mannar and parts of Vavuniya. The expulsions began at Chavakachcheri on 15 October and culminated in Jaffna town on 30 October, where residents were given two hours to leave; deadlines elsewhere ranged from two hours to a week. Departing families were permitted to keep only about 150 rupees in cash and a single set of clothes, with money, jewellery and property taken by LTTE cadres, and at least 35 businessmen were abducted for ransom. Around 75,000 people, almost the entire community, were displaced, most of them to Puttalam district outside the province, where many remained in welfare camps for two decades. A Sri Lankan Citizens' Commission documented the expulsion in 2011; the LTTE offered a qualified apology in 2002, and return has been partial and contested over land.
contested: The LTTE justified the expulsion as a security measure against Muslim home guards and army informants, a characterisation rejected by the Citizens' Commission and by the expelled community; the extent of restitution and land recovery since 2009 remains disputed.

sources.title: Groundviews: The Citizens' Commission on the Expulsion of the Muslims from the Northern Province by the LTTE in October 1990
Daily FT: LTTE's mass expulsion of Muslims from the north 30 years ago

deathsNote: The expulsion was carried out largely without mass killing: the Citizens' Commission records threats at gunpoint, abductions for ransom and comprehensive dispossession rather than a significant death toll. Deaths from the hardship of two decades of camp life in Puttalam have not been quantified.
violenceNote: The Citizens' Commission documented the confiscation of cash, jewellery and houses and the looting and destruction of shops belonging to expelled Muslims.
baselineWhat: The Muslim population of Sri Lanka's five northern districts
baselineNote: The 1981 census counted about 62,000 Muslims in the Northern Province, concentrated in Mannar and Jaffna; projected forward at national growth rates this gives roughly 72,000-80,000 by October 1990. No census was possible in the north during the war, so the figure is an estimate.

baselineSources.title: Expulsion of Muslims from the Northern Province by LTTE

shareCaveat: The expulsion order covered the entire community and was carried out within days, so the ratio is 100% by construction rather than by measurement.

title: The Expulsion of Yemeni Workers from Saudi Arabia
actors: Saudi Arabia revoked the privileged residence status of Yemeni workers after Yemen's position in the Gulf crisis, forcing a mass return
peopleRange: Estimates of Yemenis forced to leave Saudi Arabia in late 1990 and 1991 range from 800,000 to one million, roughly 8 per cent of newly unified Yemen's population; the figures come from Yemeni government returns, World Bank and IMF assessments of the remittance shock, and contemporary reporting including MERIP's 1993 survey. There was no registration of departures on the Saudi side, so the range reflects Yemeni receiving-side counts and estimates of the pre-crisis Yemeni workforce in the kingdom.

flows.label: Yemeni workers and families expelled from Saudi Arabia to Hudayda and the north

summary: For decades Yemenis had held a privileged position in Saudi Arabia, able to work and trade without the sponsorship required of other foreigners. After Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990, newly unified Yemen took a position on the Security Council and in the Arab League that Riyadh treated as support for Iraq, and in September 1990 Saudi Arabia withdrew the exemption, requiring Yemenis to obtain Saudi sponsors within a month. Between 800,000 and one million Yemenis left or were expelled within months, together with their families, in one of the largest sudden labour expulsions of the period and a close parallel to the simultaneous expulsion of Palestinians from Kuwait. The effect on Yemen was severe: remittances and Gulf assistance worth roughly 1.7 billion dollars a year were lost, poverty rose from about 15 to 35 per cent of the population and unemployment from about 4 to 25 per cent on the figures reported by MERIP and by international financial institutions, tent settlements grew around Hudayda and other towns, and returnee grievances fed the riots of December 1992 and the tensions that produced the 1994 civil war. Saudi Arabia has repeated smaller mass deportations of Yemenis since, notably in 2013.
contested: The total is a range rather than a count because no departure registration existed; how far the measure was a deliberate political sanction rather than a general tightening of labour rules is disputed between Saudi and Yemeni accounts.

sources.title: MERIP, 'Yemeni Workers Come Home' (1993)
Yemeni unification and the 1990-91 Gulf crisis
Saudi Arabia-Yemen relations

deathsNote: There was no significant death toll from the expulsion itself, which was an administrative removal of residence rights rather than a violent operation; the consequences were economic, and the sharp rise in poverty is likely to have raised mortality in ways never measured.
violenceNote: Contemporary reporting documented the sudden withdrawal of the legal status under which Yemenis had resided and worked, forcing departure; no other form is documented.
baselineWhat: The Yemeni worker population resident in Saudi Arabia before the 1990 Gulf crisis
baselineNote: Yemenis had held a privileged status exempting them from the Saudi sponsorship (kafala) system, and estimates of the community on the eve of the crisis range from about 800,000 to 1.5 million including dependants. When the exemption was revoked in September 1990 after Yemen's position on the Kuwait crisis, roughly 730,000-850,000 returned to Yemen within months, a shock equal to about 7 per cent of Yemen's own population of some 11.9 million and costing it an estimated $1.7 billion a year in remittances.
shareCaveat: Estimates of the resident community and of the number expelled overlap, so the ratio approaches 100 per cent by construction; measured against Yemen's population the return was about 7 per cent of the country.

title: Transnistria War
actors: Transnistrian separatists, backed by Russia's 14th Guards Army, fought Moldovan government forces over the mainly Russian/Ukrainian-speaking left bank of the Dniester
peopleRange: an estimated 100,000-130,000 people displaced, most temporarily, during the 1992 fighting
territoryDesc: Transnistria, a strip of land on the left bank of the Dniester River, about 4,100 km², de facto independent of Moldova since 1992 and unrecognized by any UN member state

flows.label: Transnistria → Chișinău-controlled Moldova

summary: As Moldova moved toward independence and closer ties with Romania, the mainly Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking population on the left bank of the Dniester declared the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic. Fighting escalated in 1992, with Russia's locally stationed 14th Guards Army intervening on the separatist side; a ceasefire that July left Russian troops stationed in the territory. An estimated 100,000-130,000 people were displaced, and Transnistria has remained a Russian-backed, internationally unrecognized breakaway territory ever since, despite a 1999 OSCE commitment by Russia to withdraw its forces.
contested: Transnistria's authorities and Russia describe the conflict as a defense of the region's population and identity; Moldova and most international bodies regard the territory as occupied Moldovan land, and Russia's continued military presence remains a point of ongoing dispute at the OSCE and in Moldova-Russia relations.

sources.title: OSCE Mission to Moldova
Crisis Group: Moldova - Regional Tensions over Transdniestria
Britannica: Transdniestria

deathsNote: Standard compilations put the toll at 'nearly one thousand' killed with about 3,000 wounded; the component military figures are 279-324 Moldovan and 364-913 Transnistrian dead, the Transnistrian span being wide because separatist force strength and losses were never independently audited. Moldovan and Transnistrian authorities each present the other side as responsible for civilian deaths in Bender.
violenceNote: The Russian Human Rights Center 'Memorial' documented Moldovan forces firing heavy machine guns at houses, courtyards and cars in Bender and Transnistrian forces beating and torturing captured Moldovan prisoners.
baselineWhat: The population of the left bank of the Dniester and Bender, the territory claimed by the separatist authorities, at the 1989 Soviet census
baselineNote: The last Soviet census recorded roughly 679,000 people in the districts that became the self-declared Transnistrian republic, in a Moldovan SSR of 4.34 million; the population was mixed, with Moldovans the largest single group ahead of Ukrainians and Russians.
shareCaveat: Many of those displaced fled from Bender and right-bank villages on the Moldovan side of the line rather than from the baseline territory, and most returned within months.

title: Village Evacuations and Displacement in South-East Turkey
actors: Turkish security forces emptied and burned Kurdish villages and hamlets in south-eastern Anatolia during the conflict with the PKK
peopleRange: 378,335 people from 820 villages and 2,345 hamlets on the Turkish state's own count; 953,680-1,201,200 in the survey the Turkish government itself commissioned from Hacettepe University in 2006; up to 3 million in estimates by the Turkish migrants' association Goc-Der and Kurdish organisations. The state figure counts only officially recorded evacuations; the Hacettepe range is a nationally representative household survey covering 1986-2005; the highest figures include secondary and economic movement and are not independently audited.

flows.label: Sirnak and Hakkari villages to Diyarbakir
Eastern provinces to Izmir and western Turkey

summary: During the armed conflict between the Turkish state and the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), and most intensively between 1991 and 1995, Turkish security forces cleared rural settlements across the mainly Kurdish south-east under emergency rule. Human Rights Watch documented troops and gendarmes surrounding villages, burning houses, stored grain, orchards and livestock, often after residents refused to join the state-armed 'village guard' militia, which numbered roughly 45,000 men by the mid-1990s; the government said evacuations were required to deny the PKK logistical support and that some villages were burned by the PKK itself. Turkish state figures record 378,335 people displaced from 820 villages and 2,345 hamlets, while a 2006 survey commissioned by the Turkish government from Hacettepe University put the total at 953,680 to 1,201,200 and Kurdish organisations claim up to three million; roughly 3,000 settlements were depopulated. Most of the displaced moved into Diyarbakir, Van, Batman and other regional cities and into Istanbul, Mersin and Izmir, where they formed large impoverished peripheries. The European Court of Human Rights repeatedly found Turkey responsible for the destruction of homes and property in these operations, and a 2004 compensation law and a village return programme produced limited returns; Human Rights Watch reported in 2002 that returns were being obstructed by village guards and unmet claims.
contested: The number displaced ranges from the state's 378,335 to over a million in the government's own commissioned survey and up to three million in Kurdish estimates, and responsibility for individual village burnings is disputed between the Turkish state and the PKK.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch, Displaced and Disregarded: Turkey's Failing Village Return Program (2002)
Human Rights Watch, Turkey: Forced Displacement of Ethnic Kurds from Southeastern Turkey (1994)
MERIP, 'Villages of No Return' (2005)
Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre - Turkey

deathsNote: No defensible death toll attaches to the evacuations themselves, which were principally expulsions rather than killings; they took place inside a wider conflict whose total dead the Turkish General Staff and independent tallies put at roughly 30,000-40,000 including combatants between 1984 and 1999. Human Rights Watch separately documented 'disappearances' and extrajudicial killings during and around the evacuations, in the hundreds rather than thousands.

atrocityFindings.finding: In Akdivar and Others v. Turkey the Court found Turkey responsible for the destruction of the applicants' homes and property in Kelekci village, violating Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; further judgments including Mentes and Selcuk and Asker reached the same conclusion in other villages.

baselineWhat: The population of the emergency-rule (OHAL) provinces of south-eastern and eastern Anatolia at the 1990 census
baselineNote: The emergency-rule region covered Diyarbakır, Hakkari, Mardin, Siirt, Şırnak, Batman, Bingöl, Tunceli, Van and Elazığ with Adıyaman, Bitlis and Muş as neighbouring provinces; their 1990 census totals sum to roughly six million. Displacement estimates diverge sharply: the Turkish government has cited about 380,000 evacuated from some 3,000 settlements, while parliamentary and human rights inquiries and Human Rights Watch put the total between one and three million.

title: Croatian War of Independence (Vukovar, Krajina, Operation Storm)
actors: Croatian government forces fought Croatian Serb rebels (Republic of Serbian Krajina) backed by the Yugoslav National Army; Croatia's August 1995 Operation Storm recaptured the Krajina
peopleRange: roughly 450,000 total: about 250,000 Croats and other non-Serbs expelled from Serb-held Krajina and Eastern Slavonia in 1991-92, and about 200,000 Croatian Serbs who fled during and after Operation Storm in August 1995
territoryDesc: The self-proclaimed Republic of Serbian Krajina, roughly a quarter to a third of Croatian territory, retaken by Croatia in 1995

flows.label: Vukovar/E. Slavonia → Croatian-held territory (1991-92)
Krajina → Serbia (Operation Storm, 1995)

summary: As Yugoslavia broke apart, Croatian Serbs backed by the Yugoslav army declared the Republic of Serbian Krajina and, alongside the 87-day siege and fall of Vukovar in 1991, expelled Croats and other non-Serbs from areas they controlled. In August 1995 Croatia's Operation Storm recaptured nearly all Krajina territory in days, triggering the flight of some 200,000 Croatian Serbs, accompanied by killings and destruction of property documented by the ICTY and human rights groups. The operation effectively ended large-scale ethnic Serb presence in the region and paved the way for the Dayton settlement later that year.
contested: Croatia treats Operation Storm as a legitimate liberation of occupied territory; the ICTY convicted then, on appeal in 2012, acquitted Croatian generals Gotovina and Markač of orchestrating a joint criminal enterprise, while still documenting widespread crimes against Serb civilians during the operation.

sources.title: ICTY - The Conflicts
HRW: Impunity for Abuses Committed During Operation Storm
UNHCR: Home again, 10 years after Croatia's Operation Storm

deathsNote: Croatian official and Croatian Memorial-Documentation Centre figures give roughly 15,000 Croatian dead or missing (about 8,700 soldiers and 6,300 civilians), while Serbian sources including the Veritas documentation centre count roughly 7,100-8,400 Serb dead or missing, producing an accepted total of over 20,000; the two sides disagree mainly over the classification of civilians versus combatants and over the number of Serb civilians killed during and after Operation Storm in August 1995.

Serbia (3 February 2015) — both Croatia's genocide claim and Serbia's counter-claim over Operation Storm dismissed for want of genocidal intent; the Court found the aim of crimes against ethnic Croats appeared to have been forced displacement rather than physical destruction

atrocityFindings.finding: Gotovina and Markač (IT-06-90) — convicted at trial in April 2011 over Operation Storm, then acquitted and released by the Appeals Chamber on 16 November 2012; the acquittal is celebrated in Croatia and rejected in Serbia

title: Georgia's Abkhaz and South Ossetian Wars
actors: Abkhaz and South Ossetian separatist forces, with volunteer and covert Russian support, fought Georgian government forces for control of the two regions as Georgia gained independence
peopleRange: an estimated 250,000-260,000 mostly ethnic Georgians displaced from Abkhazia, and roughly 40,000-100,000 displaced (Georgians and Ossetians) from the South Ossetia conflict
territoryDesc: Abkhazia (about 8,600 km²) and South Ossetia (about 3,900 km²), both remaining outside effective Georgian government control since these wars

flows.label: Abkhazia → Tbilisi-controlled Georgia (Georgians)
South Ossetia → Tbilisi-controlled Georgia

summary: As Georgia became independent from the Soviet Union, separatist movements in South Ossetia (1991-92) and Abkhazia (1992-93), aided by volunteers and covert support from Russia, fought and defeated Georgian government forces. An estimated 250,000-260,000 ethnic Georgians were expelled from Abkhazia amid documented atrocities, and tens of thousands more were displaced from South Ossetia. Both regions became de facto independent, unrecognized by the UN, with the conflicts remaining formally unresolved for decades and displaced Georgians largely unable to return.
contested: Georgia and UN General Assembly resolutions (adopted repeatedly since 2008) describe the expulsion of Georgians from Abkhazia as ethnic cleansing and affirm displaced persons' right of return; Abkhaz and South Ossetian authorities, along with Russia, frame the wars as legitimate struggles for self-determination against Georgian aggression.

HRW: Georgia/Abkhazia - Violations of the Laws of War and Russia's Role in the Conflict (1995)
UNHCR: Georgia country operation (IDPs from Abkhazia and South Ossetia)

deathsNote: For Abkhazia (1992-93), roughly 5,000 ethnic Georgians and about 4,000 Abkhaz are reported killed or missing, with around 250,000 Georgians displaced; for South Ossetia (1991-92) the International Crisis Group gives approximately 1,000 dead, with about 40,000 Ossetians and 23,000 Georgians displaced (figures compiled by Human Rights Watch). The wider range reflects Georgian government counts that put civilian deaths in Abkhazia alone at about 5,000 with 400 missing, against lower Abkhaz and Russian tallies; there was never an independent forensic count, and each side's figure serves its account of who was cleansed.

atrocityFindings.body: OSCE (Budapest 1994 and Lisbon 1996 Summit documents), as recorded by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe
atrocityFindings.finding: Condemned the forcible expulsion of the predominantly Georgian population of Abkhazia — roughly 250,000 people — as ethnic cleansing, and condemned the perpetrators of war crimes committed during the conflict; Abkhaz authorities and Russia reject the characterisation

violenceNote: The OSCE's Budapest (1994) and Lisbon (1996) summit documents, as recorded by the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly, condemned the mass destruction and forcible expulsion of Abkhazia's Georgian population as ethnic cleansing; Georgian government data cited alongside Human Rights Watch and 1994 US State Department reporting record about 5,000 civilians killed, and HRW separately documented the shelling of Georgian and Ossetian villages, blockades and hostage-taking in South Ossetia.
baselineWhat: The combined population of Abkhazia and South Ossetia at the last Soviet census
baselineNote: The 1989 Soviet census counted 525,061 in the Abkhaz ASSR - of whom about 46% Georgians and 18% Abkhaz - and 98,527 in the South Ossetian Autonomous Oblast. Abkhazia's recorded population had fallen below 250,000 by the 2003 count.
shareCaveat: Displaced Georgians from Abkhazia make up most of the numerator; measured against Abkhazia's Georgian population alone the expulsion was close to total.

title: Kenya's Encampment Policy: Dadaab and Kakuma
actors: The Kenyan government requiring refugees to reside in designated camps and to obtain movement passes to travel elsewhere, under the Refugees Act and its predecessor framework
peopleRange: 715,775 refugees and asylum seekers in the designated camps as of 28 February 2026 - 406,702 in Dadaab, 226,353 in Kakuma and 82,720 in Kalobeyei - out of 836,466 registered in Kenya overall, the remainder living in Nairobi, Mombasa, Nakuru and Eldoret
territoryDesc: The Dadaab complex in Garissa county near the Somali border and the Kakuma camp with the adjacent Kalobeyei integrated settlement in Turkana county, both in arid and remote regions far from major economic centres
summary: Kenya has required refugees to live in designated camps since the early 1990s, when Dadaab was opened for Somalis and Kakuma for Sudanese; refugees who leave the camps without a movement pass are liable to arrest, and access to formal employment, business licences and freedom of residence has been limited. Some of the camps have now operated for more than thirty years, with second and third generations born inside them, and the government has periodically announced closure - most prominently in 2016 and again in 2021 - on security grounds linked to the conflict in Somalia, plans that were suspended after litigation and international objection. The Refugees Act 2021 introduced a more inclusive framework, including provision for identity documents and easier access to work, and in March 2025 Kenya launched the Shirika Plan, which proposes to transform the camps into integrated settlements open to host communities and to move away from encampment toward inclusion and self-reliance. Implementation has been slow and contested locally, and a review one year on found the plan only partially realised, with most of the camp population still dependent on rations and without effective freedom of movement. The camp population continued to grow modestly through early 2026, with almost no voluntary repatriation recorded.
contested: Disputed are whether encampment is a legitimate exercise of sovereign control over a large refugee population with genuine security concerns, as successive Kenyan governments have argued, or an unlawful restriction of the freedom of movement guaranteed by the Refugee Convention and the Kenyan constitution, as Kenyan courts have partly found; also contested is how far the Shirika Plan changes the legal position rather than the rhetoric.

sources.title: UNHCR Kenya Statistics Package, 28 February 2026
USCRI: One Year On - Advancing the Promise of Kenya's Shirika Plan

deathsNote: Encampment is an administrative restriction on residence and movement and no source attributes a death toll to it. Kenya hosts more than 750,000 refugees, the majority in Dadaab and Kakuma, with over 100,000 in urban areas. Mortality and malnutrition inside the camps are monitored by UNHCR and MSF — with sharp spikes during the 2011 Somali famine influx — but are reported as rates against emergency thresholds, not as deaths attributable to the encampment policy.
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch's 2010 report 'Welcome to Kenya: Police Abuse of Somali Refugees' documented arbitrary detention, beatings amounting to ill-treatment and torture, and rape of Somali refugees by Kenyan police, with further mass arrests documented during Operation Usalama Watch in 2014.
baselineWhat: The registered refugee and asylum-seeker population of Kenya subject to the encampment policy
baselineNote: UNHCR's Kenya operational data records 857,065 refugees and asylum-seekers as of 30 June 2026 - 630,946 refugees and 226,119 asylum-seekers - of whom about 420,000 are in the Dadaab complex in Garissa, 319,000 in Kakuma and Kalobeyei in Turkana, and 118,000 in Nairobi. Camp residence and movement passes are required under the Refugees Act, with the urban caseload the principal exception.
asOfNote: UNHCR's Kenya figures are as of 30 June 2026 and are revised monthly; the camp population has grown with continued arrivals from Somalia, South Sudan and the Horn.

title: 1991 Kurdish Uprising and Refugee Crisis
actors: Following Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War, Kurds in northern Iraq rose up against Saddam Hussein's government; Iraqi forces crushed the uprising, prompting a mass refugee flight toward the Turkish and Iranian borders that led to a US/UK/France-enforced 'safe haven' and no-fly zone.
peopleRange: An estimated 1.5–2 million Kurds fled toward the Turkish and Iranian borders in March–April 1991

flows.label: Iraqi Kurdistan → Turkey border
Iraqi Kurdistan → Iran border

summary: After Iraq's defeat in the Gulf War in February 1991, Kurds in the north and Shia Arabs in the south rose up against Saddam Hussein's government, briefly seizing control of most Kurdish cities. Iraqi forces, using helicopter gunships not covered by the ceasefire terms, crushed the uprising within weeks, prompting an estimated 1.5–2 million Kurds to flee toward the mountainous Turkish and Iranian borders, where thousands died of exposure, hunger, and disease. The humanitarian crisis prompted the US, UK, and France to launch Operation Provide Comfort and impose a northern no-fly zone, enabling refugees to return and creating the conditions for the de facto autonomous Kurdistan Region that has persisted since. A separate, less internationally publicized crackdown followed the failed Shia uprising in southern Iraq.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch: Endless Torment - The 1991 Uprising in Iraq and Its Aftermath
UN Security Council Resolution 688 (1991) on repression of Iraqi civilians including Kurds - UN Digital Library

deathsNote: Human Rights Watch / Middle East Watch's 'Endless Torment' (1992) documented thousands killed in the suppression of the uprising by indiscriminate fire and summary execution but declined to give a total, citing lack of access; it reported a Greenpeace estimate that mortality among Kurdish and Shi'a refugees and displaced people averaged about 1,000 a day through April, May and June 1991, which underpins the top of this range, while roughly two million people fled — 1.4 million to Iran and 450,000 to Turkey. Iraq's government disputed all such figures, and most of the toll is death in flight from exposure, disease and lack of food rather than direct killing.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch / Middle East Watch and Amnesty International documented indiscriminate fire into residential areas, summary executions in streets, homes and hospitals, house-to-house mass arrests, helicopter attacks on fleeing civilian columns, torture, and thousands who remained unaccounted for a year later.
baselineWhat: The Kurdish population of northern Iraq at the time of the March 1991 uprising
baselineNote: Iraq's 1987 census and subsequent estimates put Kurds at roughly 20-23 per cent of an Iraqi population of about 18 million in 1991, that is some 3.6-4.1 million, concentrated in Dohuk, Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Kirkuk and Nineveh. Iraqi census categories and the status of Kirkuk are politically contested, so the figure is approximate.

title: Draining of the Mesopotamian Marshes and Marsh Arab Displacement
actors: In reprisal for the 1991 uprising, Saddam Hussein's government accelerated large-scale drainage of southern Iraq's marshes via canals and dikes, displacing and punishing the indigenous Marsh Arabs (Ma'dan) and destroying their traditional way of life.
peopleRange: More than 200,000 Marsh Arabs were displaced; the Ma'dan population fell from roughly 250,000–500,000 in the 1950s to as few as 20,000 remaining in the marshes by 2003, with an additional 80,000–120,000 fleeing to refugee camps in Iran
territoryDesc: Roughly 15,000–20,000 km2 of wetlands in southern Iraq were drained via engineered canals and dikes, eliminating up to 90% of the marshland by 2000; some re-flooding has occurred since 2003.

flows.label: Central/Amara marshes → Iran refugee camps
Southern marshes → Basra and other Iraqi cities

summary: The Mesopotamian Marshes of southern Iraq, home to the Marsh Arabs (Ma'dan) for millennia, were subjected to accelerated draining after the failed 1991 uprising, when Saddam Hussein's government built canals and dikes explicitly intended to punish the marshes' inhabitants, who had sheltered rebels and army deserters, and to deny insurgents refuge. By 2000, roughly 90% of the wetlands had been eliminated, and the Ma'dan population fell from an estimated 250,000–500,000 in the 1950s to as few as 20,000 living in the marshes by 2003. More than 200,000 people were displaced in total, with tens of thousands fleeing to refugee camps across the border in Iran and others moving to Iraqi towns and cities. Following the 2003 US-led invasion, dikes were breached and roughly half the marshland has since been re-flooded, though restoration remains partial and the Ma'dan community has not fully recovered.
contested: While environmental and engineering factors (upstream damming in Turkey and Syria, irrigation projects) also contributed to marsh decline, human rights organizations and many scholars regard the post-1991 drainage as a deliberate act of political and ethnic collective punishment; the Iraqi government at the time framed the works as land reclamation and agricultural development.

sources.title: Draining of the Mesopotamian Marshes
PBS Frontline: The Crimes of Saddam Hussein — The Marsh Arabs
What Happened to the Iraqi Marsh Arabs and their Land?

deathsNote: No comprehensive death toll has been produced, and it would be wrong to infer one from the population collapse: Human Rights Watch records that the Marsh Arab population of the marshlands fell from about 250,000 in 1991 to fewer than 40,000 by 2003, but attributes this overwhelmingly to displacement — roughly 40,000 refugees to Iran and 100,000-190,000 internally displaced — rather than to deaths. HRW documents specific killings, including some 2,500 villagers executed in August 1992 and about 150 in al-'Amara in 1998, but no aggregate. HRW characterises the campaign as crimes against humanity rather than genocide; the Iraqi High Tribunal's planned Marsh Arabs case was never completed after Saddam Hussein's execution.
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch's January 2003 backgrounder on the Iraqi government's assault on the Marsh Arabs documents murder, arbitrary imprisonment, torture, enforced disappearances and persecution alongside forced population transfer, including some 2,500 villagers executed in August 1992.
baselineWhat: The Marsh Arab population of the southern Iraqi marshes before the drainage campaign
baselineNote: The Marsh Arabs numbered about half a million in the 1950s and roughly 250,000 by the early 1990s, after decades of out-migration and the Iran-Iraq war. UNEP satellite analysis showed the marshes reduced to about a tenth of their former extent by 2000; UN estimates put those remaining in the marshes at as few as 20,000 by 2003, with 80,000-120,000 in refugee camps in Iran and the rest displaced within Iraq.
