title: Afghan Civil War and Taliban-Era Displacement
actors: Rival mujahidin factions destroyed much of Kabul in factional fighting, and Taliban forces later expelled and burned out civilian populations in the Shomali plain and massacred civilians in Hazara and Tajik areas
peopleRange: At least 700,000 internally displaced and 3.6 million Afghans still refugees by October 2001 (Forced Migration Review); over 100,000 displaced into the Panjshir valley and about 40,000 into Kabul within two weeks during the Taliban's Shomali offensive in August 1999, and over 172,000 crossing into Pakistan in 2000 (UN figures cited by Human Rights Watch).

flows.label: Shomali plain → Kabul, August 1999
Shomali plain → Panjshir valley
Afghanistan → Peshawar, Pakistan (2000)

summary: The mujahidin capture of Kabul in April 1992 prompted the return of some 900,000 refugees, the largest and fastest repatriation UNHCR had then assisted, but factional fighting for control of the capital destroyed a third of the city by 1995 and killed an estimated 50,000 people, about 25,000 of them in 1994 alone. The Taliban's advance, taking Kabul in 1996 and Mazar-i-Sharif in 1998, produced fresh exoduses of professionals and of ethnic minorities, particularly Hazaras. During the August 1999 Shomali offensive the Taliban forced civilians from their homes and then burned houses, crops, wells and irrigation canals to prevent return; the UN estimated some 40,000 people reached Kabul in two weeks and over 100,000 were displaced into the Panjshir valley, while about a thousand Tajik men were separated from their families and detained. Human Rights Watch recorded the killing of at least 2,000 people, mostly Hazara civilians, at Mazar-i-Sharif in 1998 and at least 178 civilians at Yakaolang in January 2001, after which Taliban forces burned the town and surrounding villages. By October 2001 at least 700,000 Afghans were internally displaced and 3.6 million remained refugees.
contested: Responsibility for the destruction of Kabul in 1992-96 is disputed among the mujahidin factions involved, and no agreed nationwide death or displacement total for the period exists; drought from 1999 onwards compounded conflict displacement in ways sources separate differently.

sources.title: Hiram Ruiz, Afghanistan: conflict and displacement 1978 to 2001 (Forced Migration Review)
Human Rights Watch World Report 2000 - Afghanistan (Refworld)

deathsNote: Both figures relate to Kabul only: Human Rights Watch estimated about 25,000 killed in Kabul in 1994 alone, mostly civilians hit by rocket and artillery fire, while Forced Migration Review gives roughly 50,000 deaths in the fight for the capital between 1992 and 1996. Countrywide deaths for the decade, including the Mazar-i-Sharif and Yakaolang massacres and the drought years, have never been credibly aggregated.
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch documented the massacres at Mazar-i-Sharif and Yakaolang, the shooting and arrest of men during the Shomali expulsions, the burning of homes, crops and wells, and the detention of about a thousand Tajik men.
baselineWhat: The population of Afghanistan at the start of the factional civil war in 1992
baselineNote: UN estimates put Afghanistan's resident population at roughly 14-16 million in 1992; no census had been completed since the partial count of 1979, and the figure excludes the several million Afghans already living as refugees in Pakistan and Iran after the Soviet war.

baselineSources.title: World Population Prospects — UN Population Division

shareCaveat: Displacement in this period layered on top of the Soviet-war exodus that had already sent some 6 million Afghans abroad, and large numbers moved back and forth across the Pakistani border more than once, so the figure is not a clean count of newly uprooted individuals.

title: The Algerian Civil War: Village Massacres and Mass Displacement
actors: Armed Islamist groups and Algerian security forces and militias fought a decade-long war marked by village massacres and the emptying of the countryside
peopleRange: Algerian government and UN agency estimates put internal displacement at 1-1.5 million people during the 1990s, most of them moving from rural areas of the Mitidja, Chlef and the interior into towns and the coastal cities; the figure was never established by registration and is an administrative estimate. Several hundred thousand Algerians also left the country, mainly for France.

flows.label: Flight from the Mitidja plain into Algiers

summary: After the army cancelled the second round of legislative elections in January 1992, which the Islamic Salvation Front was poised to win, an insurgency developed that by 1994-95 had become a war of massacres. Armed groups, principally the Armed Islamic Group, killed civilians in villages of the Mitidja and the western interior, with individual massacres at Rais, Bentalha and Relizane in 1997 killing hundreds each; security forces and state-armed village militias conducted sweeps, and Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented thousands of enforced disappearances by state agents. Villagers abandoned the countryside in large numbers for the towns. The Algerian government has put the death toll at 150,000-200,000; independent estimates range from about 60,000 to 200,000. Responsibility for some of the largest massacres is contested: the state attributes them to the armed groups, while former officers and some researchers have alleged army complicity or infiltration, allegations Algiers rejects and which no independent inquiry has been permitted to test. The 2005 Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation granted amnesties and criminalised public questioning of the security forces' conduct.
contested: Responsibility for the 1997-98 village massacres, and the true death toll, remain disputed; Algeria has refused international inquiry and criminalised some forms of public debate about the period.

sources.title: Algerian Civil War
Human Rights Watch, Algeria: reports on the conflict
Human Rights Watch, Algeria 1998 report

deathsNote: The low end reflects independent estimates based on documented incidents; the high end is the Algerian government's own figure of 150,000-200,000, later used by President Bouteflika. Deaths include civilians killed in massacres, insurgents, security forces and the disappeared.
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented the village massacres, torture in detention and thousands of enforced disappearances attributed to state agents.
baselineWhat: The population of Algeria in 1992, at the start of the civil war
baselineNote: Algeria's Office National des Statistiques recorded a population of about 26.3 million in 1992, between the censuses of 1987 (23.0 million) and 1998 (29.1 million).
shareCaveat: The 1.5 million is largely rural flight to the towns and to Algiers rather than registered displacement, and it was compiled from government and humanitarian estimates during a period when independent access to the countryside was extremely limited.

title: Bosnian War and Ethnic Cleansing
actors: Bosnian Serb forces (VRS), backed by Serbia, waged a campaign of ethnic cleansing against Bosniaks and Croats; Bosniak and Croat forces also displaced civilians in areas under their control, including during the 1992-94 Croat-Bosniak war
peopleRange: about 2.2 million people, more than half of Bosnia and Herzegovina's prewar population of roughly 4.4 million
territoryDesc: Bosnia and Herzegovina's entire territory, partitioned by the 1995 Dayton Agreement into the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (about 51%) and Republika Srpska (about 49%), largely following wartime front lines

flows.label: Prijedor area (Bosniaks/Croats expelled) → Federation territory / abroad
Podrinje enclaves → Tuzla (Bosniaks)
Sarajevo suburbs → Republika Srpska (Serbs, post-Dayton 1996)

summary: The breakup of Yugoslavia triggered a three-sided war in Bosnia and Herzegovina among Bosniaks, Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats, marked by sieges (notably Sarajevo, besieged for nearly four years), concentration camps and systematic campaigns of ethnic cleansing. The ICTY convicted numerous Bosnian Serb, Croat and, to a lesser extent, Bosniak commanders and political leaders of war crimes and crimes against humanity, with the largest share of documented atrocities attributed to Bosnian Serb forces. The 1995 Dayton Agreement ended the fighting and froze the resulting demographic partition into two entities. An estimated 100,000 people were killed and about 2.2 million displaced, one of the largest displacement crises in Europe since 1945.
contested: The overall scale and attribution of atrocities differ by source; Bosnian Serb political leaders and Republika Srpska institutions have historically minimized or disputed ICTY findings, while ICTY and ICJ (Bosnia v. Serbia) judgments stand as the formal legal record for specific crimes, including genocide at Srebrenica.

sources.title: ICTY - The Conflicts
Britannica: Bosnian War
USHMM: Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1992-1995

deathsNote: Two independent counts converge: the Research and Documentation Centre in Sarajevo (Mirsad Tokača, 'Bosnian Book of the Dead') named 95,940 dead, and the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor's Demographic Unit reached a census-based estimate of 104,732 killed in a January 2010 report after twelve years of data collection. Both figures displaced the wartime Bosnian government estimate of 200,000-250,000, which is still favoured by some Bosniak political actors and victims' associations who regard the lower counts as minimising the war; some Bosnian Serb actors in turn dispute the ethnic distribution within these totals. The counts include soldiers as well as civilians.

atrocityFindings.finding: Prosecutor v. Radislav Krstić: confirmed that Bosnian Serb forces committed genocide against the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica in July 1995; Krstić convicted of aiding and abetting genocide

atrocityFindings.body: International Court of Justice
atrocityFindings.finding: Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro: genocide was committed at Srebrenica in July 1995, but Serbia was not responsible for committing it; Serbia did violate its obligations to prevent the genocide and to punish it by failing to transfer Ratko Mladić to the ICTY

atrocityFindings.body: ICTY (Trial Chamber)
atrocityFindings.finding: Prosecutor v. Kunarac, Kovač and Vuković ('Foča'): first convictions for rape, torture and enslavement of Muslim women and girls as crimes against humanity

violenceNote: Documented by the ICTY in Krstić (genocide and mass execution at Srebrenica), Kunarac (rape, torture and sexual enslavement at Foča), and the Prijedor and Sarajevo-siege cases (detention camps, torture, terrorising a civilian population by siege and sniping, and destruction of homes and religious property), and by the ICJ's 2007 judgment.
baselineWhat: The population of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the census of 1991, the last before the war
baselineNote: The 1991 Yugoslav census counted 4,377,033 people in Bosnia and Herzegovina: about 43.5 per cent Bosniak, 31.2 per cent Serb and 17.4 per cent Croat. It is the standard baseline used by the ICTY and by post-war demographic studies.

baselineSources.title: Demographics of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The affected figure combines internally displaced people and refugees abroad at the war's peak; a significant number were displaced more than once, so it overstates the number of distinct individuals somewhat.

title: Ossetian-Ingush Conflict and Expulsion from the Prigorodny District
actors: North Ossetian interior ministry troops and paramilitaries, with Russian forces implicated, expelled the Ingush population of the disputed Prigorodny district of North Ossetia
peopleRange: Between 34,500 and 64,000 Ingush forcibly displaced from the Prigorodny district and North Ossetia; about 9,000 Ossetians also fled, most of whom had returned by mid-1994 (Human Rights Watch).
territoryDesc: The Prigorodny district, transferred from Ingushetia to North Ossetia after the 1944 deportation of the Ingush and claimed by Ingushetia since

flows.label: Prigorodny district → Ingushetia (Nazran)

summary: Fighting broke out on 31 October 1992 over the Prigorodny district, an area east of Vladikavkaz that had been transferred to North Ossetia after the wartime deportation of the Ingush and to which Ingushetia laid claim after the 1991 Russian rehabilitation law. Six days of fighting left about 583 people dead according to the Russian Procuracy, 350 of them Ingush and 192 Ossetians, with 939 wounded and 261 reported missing. Human Rights Watch found that most of the estimated 34,500 to 64,000 Ingush displaced had been forcibly expelled by Ossetian forces, often with the support of, or in the presence of, Russian interior ministry and army units, and that thousands of homes were destroyed. Violations were committed by North and South Ossetian formations, Ingush militias and Russian units. Return was slow and obstructed despite federal decrees permitting it; Minority Rights Group estimates that about 30,000 Ingush returned to the Prigorodny region and the outskirts of Vladikavkaz over the following decade, and the district remains a source of dispute.
contested: Russian federal responsibility is disputed: Human Rights Watch found Russian forces implicated in the expulsions either by standing aside or by direct support, which Moscow denied; the displacement figure is itself uncertain within a range of 34,500 to 64,000, and the underlying territorial claim to Prigorodny remains unresolved.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch: Russian Federation - The Ingush-Ossetian Conflict in the Prigorodnyi Region (Refworld)
Minority Rights Group: Ingush in the Russian Federation

deathsNote: The figure of 583 dead between 31 October and 5 November 1992, comprising 350 Ingush and 192 Ossetians, comes from the Russian Federation Procuracy and is the only official count; a further 261 people were reported missing and are not included in it, so the true toll is likely somewhat higher.
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch documented the destruction of thousands of Ingush homes, killings of civilians by Ossetian and Ingush formations, and hundreds of people reported missing.
baselineWhat: The Ingush population of the Prigorodny district and the rest of North Ossetia before the October 1992 conflict
baselineNote: The baseline is contested because many Ingush who returned after the 1957 rehabilitation lived in North Ossetia without residence permits and were undercounted. The 1989 Soviet census recorded 32,783 Ingush in the North Ossetian ASSR; the republic's own passport service gave about 34,500 by 1992; the Russian Federal Migration Service and Ingush authorities gave 46,000-64,000. Human Rights Watch concluded that between 34,500 and 64,000 Ingush were forcibly displaced in the week from 31 October 1992.

baselineSources.title: Russian Federation: The Ingush-Ossetian Conflict in the Prigorodnyi Region — Human Rights Watch (Refworld)

shareCaveat: Numerator and denominator are drawn from the same disputed estimates of an undercounted community, so the ratio necessarily approaches 100 per cent; what it records is that virtually the entire Ingush population of the district was expelled, not a measured proportion.

title: Prijedor Camps and the Expulsion of Non-Serbs
actors: Bosnian Serb forces seized Prijedor municipality in north-west Bosnia, detained non-Serb civilians in the Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje camps and expelled the rest
peopleRange: About 47,000 non-Serbs displaced from Prijedor municipality through attacks, mass arrests and camp internment, with roughly 3,334 people passing through Omarska alone and 2,000-3,000 held there at any one time, plus further thousands in Keraterm and Trnopolje (ICTY, Kvocka et al. trial judgement).
summary: Bosnian Serb forces took over the Prijedor municipality on 30 April 1992 in a planned operation involving more than 1,500 armed men, then dismissed non-Serbs from employment, imposed movement restrictions and attacked the Muslim villages of Hambarine and Kozarac in May. About 800 civilians were killed in the assault on Kozarac. Detainees were held at the Omarska mine, the Keraterm ceramics factory and the Trnopolje camp; the ICTY found in Kvocka and others that Omarska held roughly 3,334 people in conditions of extreme overcrowding, starvation rations, beatings on arrival and at interrogation, and rape of the small number of women detained, with prisoners losing 25-35 kilograms. In August 1992, 188 of 200 men separated from a convoy were executed at Korićanske Stijene on Mount Vlašić. Roughly 47,000 non-Serbs were displaced from the municipality. The ICTY charged 27 people over crimes in Prijedor; Milomir Stakić received 40 years, Biljana Plavšić pleaded guilty to the ethnic cleansing campaign, and camp personnel including Miroslav Kvočka, Zoran Žigić and Duško Tadić were convicted.
contested: Bosnian Serb political accounts have described Trnopolje as an open reception centre rather than a detention camp and disputed the characterisation of the 1992 takeover as ethnic cleansing; the ICTY rejected these characterisations, but no comprehensive death total for Prijedor has been judicially established.

sources.title: ICTY Outreach: Ethnic Cleansing in Prijedor
ICTY, Prosecutor v. Kvocka et al., Trial Judgement (2001)
ICTY case: Milomir Stakic (IT-97-24)

deathsNote: The tribunal materials cited here establish specific figures rather than a total: about 800 civilians killed in the attack on Kozarac and 188 men executed at Korićanske Stijene, alongside numerous killings in the camps. No comprehensive death toll for Prijedor municipality is given in these sources, and estimates by survivor associations are higher than anything judicially confirmed.

atrocityFindings.finding: Convicted camp personnel in Kvocka et al. of persecution, murder and torture as crimes against humanity for the operation of the Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje camps

atrocityFindings.body: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia
atrocityFindings.finding: Sentenced Milomir Stakic, the civilian leader of Prijedor, to 40 years for crimes including extermination and persecution of the municipality's non-Serb population

violenceNote: All of these forms were established in ICTY judgements arising from Prijedor, principally Kvocka et al. and Stakic.

baselineNote: The 1991 census recorded 112,470 people in Prijedor: about 49,500 Muslims (Bosniaks), 47,800 Serbs, 6,300 Croats and 6,400 who declared themselves Yugoslav. Bosniaks and Croats together, roughly 55,800 people, are the population the takeover acted on; counting those who declared as Yugoslav would raise the figure to about 62,000.

title: Tajik Civil War
actors: A civil war between the secular post-Soviet government of Tajikistan, backed by Russia and Uzbekistan, and a coalition of Islamist, democratic, and regionally based opposition forces caused widespread internal displacement and refugee flight into Afghanistan
peopleRange: estimates range from roughly 600,000 to 1.2 million internally displaced or made refugees, out of a population of about 5.5 million; an estimated 50,000–100,000 people were killed

flows.label: Rural districts of Tajikistan → Dushanbe (internally displaced)
Southern Tajikistan (Kulob region) → northern Afghanistan (refugees)

summary: Following the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union, Tajikistan descended into civil war in 1992 between the government, dominated by figures from the Kulob and Leninabad regions and backed by Russia and Uzbekistan, and an opposition coalition of Islamist, democratic, and regionally based (mainly Garmi and Pamiri) groups. The war, fought largely along regional and clan lines, killed an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands within the country, while roughly 60,000–100,000 fled as refugees into northern Afghanistan. A 1997 peace agreement, brokered with UN and Russian involvement, ended the fighting and incorporated opposition elements into a power-sharing government. Most displaced Tajiks eventually returned home in the years following the peace accord.
contested: Death toll estimates vary widely by source, and the war's characterization (a regional/clan conflict, an ideological conflict between secularists and Islamists, or a proxy conflict involving Russia and neighboring states) remains debated among scholars.

sources.title: Conciliation Resources, The Tajik civil war: Causes and dynamics
UNHCR: Review of UNHCR Activities in Tajikistan
Tajikistan - Britannica

deathsNote: Conciliation Resources' Accord series records between 20,000 and 60,000 people killed in the first year of fighting alone, with about 50,000 lives lost between May and December 1992; totals of up to 100,000 for the whole 1992-97 war circulate widely in the secondary literature and in Tajik government statements, while event-based conflict datasets record substantially fewer. Roughly 600,000 people — a tenth of the population — were internally displaced and at least 80,000 fled abroad, mostly to Afghanistan. No independent post-war count was ever conducted, and the Rahmon government has had little incentive to revisit the figures.
violenceNote: Conciliation Resources' Accord study of the war records that many unarmed civilians were murdered in the rural south, apparently in order to force them to flee their homes.
baselineWhat: The population of Tajikistan at the outbreak of the civil war
baselineNote: The 1989 Soviet census counted 5,092,603 and the population was about 5.5 million in 1992. UNHCR reported roughly 600,000 internally displaced and some 60,000-80,000 who fled to Afghanistan, with several hundred thousand more, mainly Russians and other Europeans, leaving for other post-Soviet states; the war killed an estimated 50,000-100,000 people.

title: Burundi's 1993 Crisis and Civil War
actors: After soldiers assassinated President Melchior Ndadaye, Hutu killings of Tutsi civilians and army reprisals against Hutu drove mass flight; the army later confined rural civilians in 'regroupment' camps
peopleRange: UNHCR's Great Lakes chronology records that some 700,000 people fled into Rwanda, Tanzania and Zaire in the weeks after the 21 October 1993 assassination. This is the best-documented single figure. Internal displacement ran alongside it throughout the war: the International Crisis Group reported roughly 350,000 people confined in army-supervised 'regroupment' camps by early 1997, and a second forced regroupment around Bujumbura in 1999–2000 affected several hundred thousand more. Cumulative displacement over 1993–2005 therefore substantially exceeds the 700,000 headline figure, but no reconciled total exists.

flows.label: Northern Burundi → Rwanda
Burundi → Tanzania (Kigoma camps)

summary: Melchior Ndadaye, Burundi's first Hutu president, was assassinated by soldiers on 21 October 1993, three months after taking office. Killings of Tutsi civilians by Hutu supporters of the ruling FRODEBU party followed in much of the countryside, and the Tutsi-dominated army conducted reprisals against Hutu. UNHCR recorded some 700,000 people fleeing to Rwanda, Tanzania and Zaire. The violence became a civil war that lasted until the 2003–05 transition, killing an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 people. From February 1996 the army forcibly concentrated rural populations in guarded 'regroupment' camps, holding around 350,000 people by early 1997 according to the International Crisis Group, a policy repeated around Bujumbura in 1999–2000 and criticized by humanitarian agencies. A UN International Commission of Inquiry reported in 1996 that acts of genocide had been committed against the Tutsi minority after 21 October 1993, and also documented indiscriminate killings of Hutu by the army, gendarmerie and Tutsi civilians.
contested: Responsibility for the assassination and the legal characterization of the ensuing killings remain disputed, with the 1996 UN commission finding acts of genocide against Tutsi while also documenting large-scale army and militia killings of Hutu.

sources.title: Commission of Inquiry: Burundi — United States Institute of Peace, Truth Commission Digital Collection
Refugees Magazine Issue 110 — Great Lakes Chronology, UNHCR
Burundi Under Siege — International Crisis Group (via Refworld)

deathsNote: The International Crisis Group put the toll at over 200,000 by 1998; figures of around 300,000 are commonly cited for the whole 1993–2005 war. The range reflects the absence of any systematic mortality survey, the mixing of massacre deaths with combat deaths and with war-related disease and hunger, and the difficulty of counting deaths in the regroupment camps.

atrocityFindings.body: International Commission of Inquiry for Burundi (established by UN Security Council resolution 1012)
atrocityFindings.finding: Concluded that acts of genocide against the Tutsi minority were committed in Burundi after 21 October 1993, implicating members and local officials of the FRODEBU party, and also documented indiscriminate killings of Hutu by the army, gendarmerie and Tutsi civilians

violenceNote: Documented by the UN International Commission of Inquiry for Burundi and by the International Crisis Group, which described the destruction of dwellings and forced relocation into army-controlled camps.
baselineWhat: The population of Burundi at the time of the 1993 assassination and the crisis that followed
baselineNote: The 1990 census counted 5.29 million and UN estimates give about 5.9 million for 1993. In the months after President Ndadaye's assassination in October 1993 some 700,000 people fled to Tanzania, Rwanda and Zaire and several hundred thousand more were displaced internally, many into army-supervised regroupment camps that at their height in 1999-2000 held around 350,000 people; the war's death toll is usually put at about 300,000.

title: West Bank Closure, Permit and Barrier Regime
actors: Israeli military and civil administration restricting Palestinian movement in the occupied West Bank through checkpoints, gates, permits, the separation barrier and Area C planning controls
peopleRange: About 3.4 million Palestinians whose movement is permanently or intermittently restricted by 925 documented obstacles as of December 2025 (OCHA, April 2026 fact sheet), including more than 14,000 people living between the barrier and the Green Line who need permits or coordination to reach the rest of the West Bank
territoryDesc: The West Bank including East Jerusalem, about 5,655 km², of which roughly 60 per cent is Area C under full Israeli control; the separation barrier runs about 700 km, mostly inside the West Bank
summary: Since the general closure policy introduced in the early 1990s, Palestinian movement in the West Bank has been governed by a system of physical obstacles and individual permits: OCHA documented 925 movement obstacles as of December 2025, a 43 per cent increase on the twenty-year average, comprising 89 staffed checkpoints, 218 partial checkpoints, 232 road gates, 167 earthmounds, 114 linear closures and 105 roadblocks, with more than 120 new road gates installed during 2025 alone. About half of these obstacles block or hinder access between Palestinian towns and villages and main roads, and around a fifth block access to farmland, producing enclaves in which communities depend on gates opened at the discretion of the military. Construction of the separation barrier from 2002, about 85 per cent of it inside the West Bank, placed communities and land on the Israeli side and created a "seam zone" whose residents require permits to live in their own homes. Access to East Jerusalem, including its hospitals, is permit-based: of 87,427 patient permit applications in 2025, 36 per cent were denied or unresolved by the appointment date. The International Court of Justice held in its advisory opinion of 9 July 2004 that the barrier's route in occupied territory and its associated regime were contrary to international law and impeded freedom of movement, and in its advisory opinion of 19 July 2024 it held Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful and found that Israeli legislation and measures breach the prohibition of racial segregation and apartheid in Article 3 of the Racial Discrimination Convention. Israel rejects both opinions, maintaining that the barrier and closures are temporary security measures that have reduced attacks and that the territory's status is a matter for negotiation.
contested: Disputed are the legal status of the territory and of the barrier, the characterisation of the restrictions as security measures versus a permanent regime of segregation and de facto annexation, and the authority of the ICJ's 2004 and 2024 advisory opinions, which are non-binding in form and which Israel and some states reject as one-sided while the General Assembly, most states and UN human rights bodies treat them as authoritative statements of the applicable law.

sources.title: OCHA oPt: Movement and Access in the West Bank, April 2026
ICJ, Legal Consequences of the Construction of a Wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Advisory Opinion of 9 July 2004 (case file)
OHCHR: Experts on the ICJ advisory opinion of 19 July 2024 on the occupied Palestinian territory

deathsNote: No source attributes a quantified death toll to the closure, permit and barrier regime itself. OCHA and B'Tselem record Palestinian and Israeli fatalities in the West Bank from armed clashes, Israeli military operations and settler violence, and OCHA documents deaths following delays at checkpoints for patients and women in labour, but these are counted under conflict violence and access-to-health indicators rather than as a toll of the movement regime. What the regime is measured in is obstruction: OCHA recorded 925 movement obstacles as of December 2025, 43 per cent above the twenty-year average of 647, restricting 3.4 million people.

atrocityFindings.body: International Court of Justice
atrocityFindings.finding: Advisory opinion on the legal consequences of Israeli policies in the Occupied Palestinian Territory: Israel's continued presence in the territory is unlawful; settlements and the associated régime violate international law; Israel's restrictions on Palestinian movement amount to prohibited discrimination under the ICCPR and ICESCR, and its practices include forcible transfer. The Court reaffirmed its 2004 finding that the separation wall's route in the West Bank is contrary to international law. Israel rejects the opinion

violenceNote: OCHA documents the closure regime and the demolition of Palestinian homes and structures in the West Bank, and the ICJ's 2024 advisory opinion found that Israeli practices in the occupied territory include land confiscation and forcible transfer of the Palestinian population.
baselineWhat: The Palestinian population of the occupied West Bank including East Jerusalem
baselineNote: Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimates put the West Bank at roughly 3.3-3.4 million in the mid-2020s, projected from the 2017 census. Israeli demographers have disputed PCBS projections as overstated by up to a few hundred thousand; the order of magnitude is not in dispute.

baselineSources.title: PCBS, Conditions of the Palestinian Population, World Population Day 2026

shareCaveat: The closure and permit regime applies to the whole population, so numerator and denominator are the same figure and the ratio is 100% by construction rather than by measurement.
asOfNote: Checkpoint, gate and permit restrictions were sharply tightened after October 2023 and remained in force through 2026; OCHA's counts of movement obstacles are updated periodically and have risen.

title: First and Second Chechen Wars
actors: Russian federal forces fought Chechen separatists in two wars (1994-96 and 1999-2000), the second including the destructive siege and recapture of Grozny
peopleRange: an estimated 500,000-800,000 people displaced across the two wars, many repeatedly, with Grozny left largely in ruins
territoryDesc: Chechnya, which held de facto independence from 1996 to 1999 after the first war before being reconquered by Russian forces and reincorporated into the Russian Federation

flows.label: Grozny/Chechnya → Ingushetia
Grozny/Chechnya → Dagestan

summary: Russia fought two wars in Chechnya after the republic declared independence following the Soviet collapse: the First Chechen War (1994-96), which ended in a humiliating Russian withdrawal and de facto Chechen independence, and the Second Chechen War (1999-2000), launched after apartment bombings blamed on Chechen militants, which culminated in the destruction and recapture of Grozny. Both wars caused massive civilian displacement, mostly into neighboring Russian republics, and were marked by widely documented abuses on both sides, including indiscriminate shelling, disappearances and reprisal killings. Chechnya was reincorporated into the Russian Federation under a Moscow-backed government following the second war.
contested: Russia has characterized the second war as a counter-terrorism operation; the European Court of Human Rights issued numerous judgments finding Russia responsible for extrajudicial killings, torture and enforced disappearances in Chechnya, findings Russia has disputed or only partially complied with.

sources.title: ECtHR: Factsheet on armed conflicts (Chechnya case law)
HRW: Russia's Implementation of European Court of Human Rights Judgments on Chechnya
Chechnya - Britannica

deathsNote: Memorial's Aleksandr Cherkasov estimated roughly 75,000 civilian deaths across both wars (30,000–40,000 in 1994–96 and about 25,000 thereafter); the Russian Human Rights Commissioner's office cited about 90,000 combined civilian and military dead; Chechen official Taus Dzhabrailov claimed 160,000, a figure the Jamestown Foundation and analysts treated as politically motivated and unverified. Russia's own presidential human rights commission under Sergei Kovalev reported nearly 25,000 civilian deaths in Grozny alone in early 1995. The low end is a civilian count and the high end purports to include combatants, so the two ends are not strictly like for like.

atrocityFindings.body: European Court of Human Rights
atrocityFindings.finding: Isayeva v. Russia (2005): violation of Article 2 (right to life) for the bombing of Katyr-Yurt; massive use of indiscriminate free-fall FAB-250 and FAB-500 bombs in a populated area held incompatible with the caution required of a law-enforcement body, and evacuation and warning measures found inadequate

violenceNote: The European Court of Human Rights in Isayeva v. Russia (2005) found unlawful civilian deaths from indiscriminate aerial bombardment, and Memorial and Human Rights Watch documented enforced disappearances after 'mopping-up' operations, torture in filtration and detention facilities, and the near-total destruction of Grozny.
baselineWhat: The population of Chechnya on the eve of the first Russian campaign
baselineNote: The 1989 Soviet census counted 1,270,429 people in the Checheno-Ingush ASSR, of whom about 1.1 million lived in the territory that became the Chechen Republic; emigration between 1991 and 1994, particularly of Russians, had reduced this somewhat by the time federal forces entered in December 1994.
shareCaveat: The displacement total spans two wars five years apart and counts movements rather than distinct people — many families fled Grozny in 1994-96, returned, and fled again in 1999 — so it approaches the size of the entire resident population without meaning that almost everyone was displaced once.

title: Rwandan Genocide and Refugee Flight to Zaire
actors: Hutu-extremist government forces and Interahamwe militias killed Tutsi and moderate Hutu civilians; the Tutsi-led RPF's military victory triggered a mass flight of Hutu civilians and former perpetrators into Zaire
peopleRange: roughly 2 million Hutu refugees fled to Zaire, plus several hundred thousand more to Tanzania and Burundi; the genocide itself killed an estimated 800,000 to 1,000,000 people, mostly ethnic Tutsi

flows.label: Rwanda → Goma, Zaire
Southern Rwanda → Bukavu, Zaire
Rwanda → Ngara, Tanzania

summary: Between April and July 1994, extremist Hutu political and military leaders in Rwanda organized the systematic killing of an estimated 800,000 to 1,000,000 people, overwhelmingly ethnic Tutsi and moderate Hutu, in a genocide recognized as such by the United Nations. As the Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front advanced and took power, roughly 2 million Hutu civilians, including many genocide perpetrators, fled into neighboring Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), creating one of the largest and fastest refugee flows of the late 20th century, concentrated around Goma and Bukavu. Conditions in the refugee camps were dire, with a cholera epidemic killing tens of thousands within weeks. In 1996–97, a Rwandan-backed rebellion (the First Congo War) forcibly dispersed and drove home much of the refugee population, while armed remnants of the Rwandan genocidal forces remained in eastern Zaire, fueling subsequent regional conflict.
contested: The Rwandan genocide is formally and near-universally recognized as genocide; the subsequent conduct of RPF forces toward Hutu refugees in Zaire, including allegations of large-scale killings during the 1996-97 forced repatriation, remains a disputed and unresolved subject of a leaked 2010 UN mapping report.

sources.title: UN: Outreach Programme on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda
UNHCR: The Rwandan Genocide (State of the World's Refugees)
UNHCR: A decade on the run - Rwandan refugees

deathsNote: Alison Des Forges's Human Rights Watch study estimated at least 500,000 Tutsi killed; Britannica and most UN accounts put the toll at more than 800,000; the Rwandan government's own census of victims returned 1,074,017, a figure some demographers regard as high relative to the pre-genocide Tutsi population. Not included in this range are the tens of thousands of Hutu refugees who died of cholera in the Goma camps in mid-1994 and the deaths of 'probably tens of thousands' of Hutu in the 1996–97 attacks in Zaire recorded by the UN Mapping Report — separate events with separate and contested counts.

atrocityFindings.body: International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda
atrocityFindings.finding: Prosecutor v. Jean-Paul Akayesu, judgment of 2 September 1998: the first conviction for genocide by an international tribunal, finding an intention 'to wipe out the Tutsi group in its entirety' and holding that systematic rape of Tutsi women constituted an act of genocide

atrocityFindings.body: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (DRC Mapping Report)
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that attacks on Hutu refugees in Zaire/DRC in 1996–97 killed 'probably tens of thousands' and constituted crimes against humanity, and that the systematic character of the killings 'could be characterised as crimes of genocide' if the requisite intent were proven — a question the report said only a court could settle; Rwanda rejects the genocide framing

violenceNote: The ICTR in Akayesu (1998) found systematic killing of Tutsi civilians and systematic rape of Tutsi women amounting to genocide, and the 2010 UN Mapping Report documented massacres and summary killings of Hutu refugees including women and children in eastern Zaire in 1996–97.
baselineWhat: The population of Rwanda at the 1991 census, the last before the genocide
baselineNote: The August 1991 census recorded 7,157,551 people. Its ethnic categories — 91 per cent Hutu, 8.4 per cent Tutsi — were themselves a product of the identity-card system that made the genocide administratively possible, and the Tutsi share is widely regarded as understated. Between April and July 1994 roughly 800,000 people, overwhelmingly Tutsi, were killed; the exodus to Zaire and Tanzania in July 1994 moved about 2 million, overwhelmingly Hutu.
shareCaveat: The two million refers to the refugee exodus that followed the RPF victory and was overwhelmingly Hutu; it is a different population from the roughly 800,000, mostly Tutsi, killed in the genocide, and the two must not be added or conflated.

title: Eritrea's Indefinite National Service and the Exodus
actors: The Eritrean government conscripts its population into open-ended national service, and hundreds of thousands have fled the country
peopleRange: UNHCR recorded about 580,000 Eritrean refugees and asylum seekers worldwide by the early 2020s, from a population of roughly 3.5 million, one of the highest per-capita refugee outflows in the world; the UN Commission of Inquiry estimated that around 5,000 people were leaving each month at the peak in 2014-15. Estimates of the number held in national service at a given time run into the hundreds of thousands. Figures come from UNHCR registration in Ethiopia, Sudan, Israel and Europe and from the UN Commission of Inquiry; Eritrea publishes no statistics and disputes the characterisation.

flows.label: Eritreans fleeing to eastern Sudan and to Tigray camps
Onward movement through Sinai to Israel and to Europe

summary: Eritrea's National Service Proclamation of 1995 established eighteen months of compulsory service, but after the 1998-2000 border war with Ethiopia the government extended service indefinitely under the Warsai-Yikealo Development Campaign of 2002, assigning conscripts to the army, to ministries and to state and party-owned construction and mining enterprises for pay well below subsistence and for periods that in many cases have lasted decades. The United Nations Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea concluded in 2015 and 2016 that Eritrean officials had committed crimes against humanity, including enslavement through indefinite conscription, imprisonment, enforced disappearance, torture, persecution, rape and murder, and estimated that thousands were fleeing every month. Eritrea rejected the Commission's findings as politically motivated and denies that service is indefinite in practice. Large numbers of the resulting refugees moved through Sudan and Libya to Europe, and thousands were kidnapped and tortured for ransom in the Sinai in the early 2010s. Eritrean refugee camps in Tigray were attacked and largely destroyed during the 2020-22 Tigray war.
contested: Eritrea rejects the UN Commission of Inquiry's findings and disputes that national service amounts to enslavement or that it is indefinite in practice; no independent access to the country has been permitted.

sources.title: UN Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea
Human Rights Watch: Eritrea country page
Conscription in Eritrea

deathsNote: No defensible range. Deaths in detention, in the Sinai kidnapping networks and in Mediterranean crossings by Eritreans have been documented in the hundreds to low thousands by IOM and by researchers, but no total attributable to the national service system exists and no independent monitoring inside Eritrea is possible.

atrocityFindings.body: United Nations Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea
atrocityFindings.finding: Found reasonable grounds to believe that Eritrean officials have committed crimes against humanity, namely enslavement, imprisonment, enforced disappearance, torture, other inhumane acts, persecution, rape and murder, since 1991, in the context of indefinite national service and the detention system.

violenceNote: The UN Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea documented all of these forms in national service and the associated detention system.
baselineWhat: The population of Eritrea when indefinite national service began
baselineNote: Eritrea has never held a census. UN estimates give roughly 3.2 million in the mid-1990s and about 3.5 million today; the government has at times claimed figures above 5 million, and some demographers argue the true total is lower still given the scale of emigration.
shareCaveat: The 600,000 is a cumulative outflow accumulated over three decades, set against a single-year denominator; and since conscription falls on those of service age, the share of that cohort who have left is much higher than the national ratio suggests.
asOfNote: UNHCR has counted roughly half a million or more Eritrean refugees and asylum seekers in recent years; the count is complicated by onward movement to Europe and by the collapse of the Tigray camps in 2020-21.

title: Srebrenica Genocide
actors: Bosnian Serb Army (VRS) under General Ratko Mladić overran the UN-declared 'safe area' of Srebrenica, separating and killing Bosniak men and boys while expelling the remaining population
peopleRange: about 25,000-30,000 women, children and elderly forcibly bussed out of the enclave, in addition to roughly 8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed
territoryDesc: The UN-designated 'safe area' enclave of Srebrenica in eastern Bosnia, under-defended by a small Dutch UN peacekeeping battalion

flows.label: Srebrenica enclave → Tuzla (women, children, elderly)

summary: In July 1995, VRS forces under General Ratko Mladić captured the UN 'safe area' of Srebrenica, overwhelming the lightly armed Dutch peacekeeping contingent stationed there. Over the following days, VRS forces separated an estimated 8,000 Bosniak men and boys from their families and killed them, while forcibly transporting roughly 25,000-30,000 women, children and elderly to Bosniak-held territory near Tuzla. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice both formally found that genocide occurred at Srebrenica.
contested: The ICTY (Krstić, Karadžić, Mladić judgments) and the ICJ's 2007 judgment in Bosnia v. Serbia both found genocide occurred, though the ICJ found Serbia itself not directly responsible for committing genocide, only for failing to prevent and punish it; Republika Srpska institutions have at times disputed or minimized the genocide characterization, generating recurring diplomatic controversy.

sources.title: IRMCT/ICTY: Srebrenica genocide cases
ICJ: Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (2007 Judgment)
UN: International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica

deathsNote: The ICTY Appeals Chamber in Krstić (2004) found that between 7,000 and 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were killed, and the UN uses 'up to 8,000 killed or went missing'; the higher end reflects the 8,372 names recorded by the Srebrenica-Potočari Memorial with identifications by the International Commission on Missing Persons. Republika Srpska bodies have at various times published far lower figures, positions Bosniak organisations and the tribunals reject.

atrocityFindings.body: ICTY
atrocityFindings.finding: Prosecutor v. Radislav Krstić, Appeals Chamber: the mass killing of Bosnian Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica was genocide; forcible transfer of some 30,000 women, children and elderly complemented the genocidal scheme

atrocityFindings.body: ICJ
atrocityFindings.finding: Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro: the July 1995 Srebrenica killings were genocide; Serbia was not found to have committed or been complicit in it but breached its obligations to prevent the genocide and to cooperate with the ICTY

atrocityFindings.body: United Nations
atrocityFindings.finding: UN commemoration materials record judicial findings of genocide and 16 individual convictions for crimes at Srebrenica

violenceNote: The ICTY's Krstić and subsequent Srebrenica judgments established the organised executions, the concealment of bodies in secondary mass graves, sexual assaults at the Potočari compound and the destruction of Bosniak property in the enclave.
baselineWhat: The population of the Srebrenica UN 'safe area' in July 1995
baselineNote: UN and ICTY estimates put the enclave's population at roughly 36,000-42,000 in July 1995, overwhelmingly Bosniak. This was far above the prewar Srebrenica municipality (37,211 at the 1991 census, of whom about 27,000 were Bosniaks), because the enclave had absorbed tens of thousands displaced from eastern Bosnia while many original residents had left.
shareCaveat: The 30,000 counts those expelled from the enclave; the roughly 8,000 men and boys killed are a subset, so the percentage measures the emptying of the safe area rather than the killing.

title: Nepal's Maoist Conflict and Rural Displacement
actors: The Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) and Nepalese state security forces drove rural populations from the mid-western hills
peopleRange: Estimates of people internally displaced by the conflict range from around 100,000 to 200,000 in Nepali government and Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre reporting, and up to 400,000-600,000 in NGO estimates that include conflict-driven movement to India and to Kathmandu, which is hard to separate from Nepal's long-standing labour migration. The lower figures come from district-level registration and humanitarian assessments; the higher ones from survey extrapolation by Nepali NGOs.

flows.label: Displacement from the mid-western hills to Kathmandu and the Terai

summary: The Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) launched an armed insurgency in February 1996 that spread across most of Nepal's districts before ending with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of November 2006. Roughly 13,000-17,000 people were killed, the majority by state security forces according to the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights' Nepal Conflict Report of 2012, which documented unlawful killings, torture and enforced disappearances by both sides and identified more than 9,000 individual incidents. Rural populations left the mid-western hill districts under Maoist taxation, forced recruitment including of children, abductions and executions of alleged informers, and under army and armed-police operations, cordon-and-search and detention; teachers, local officials and landowners were particularly targeted. Estimates of internal displacement range from about 100,000 to 200,000 in official and IDMC reporting to several hundred thousand in NGO figures that include movement to India, which is difficult to distinguish from Nepal's established seasonal labour migration. Nepal established a Truth and Reconciliation Commission and a Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappeared Persons in 2015; both have received tens of thousands of complaints and have been criticised by the Supreme Court of Nepal, OHCHR and victims' groups for failing to deliver prosecutions, and the enabling law was amended in 2024.
contested: Displacement figures vary by a factor of several depending on whether conflict-driven movement to India is counted; responsibility for particular killings and disappearances remains largely unadjudicated.

sources.title: OHCHR, The Nepal Conflict Report (2012)
Nepalese Civil War
Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre - Nepal

deathsNote: The lower figure is the count of documented conflict deaths used by the Nepali government and the International Committee of the Red Cross; the higher figure comes from the Informal Sector Service Centre (INSEC), which maintained the most complete Nepali casualty database and includes cases the state did not record. OHCHR's 2012 report attributes the majority of documented killings to state forces.
violenceNote: The OHCHR Nepal Conflict Report of 2012 documented all of these forms and attributed them to both the security forces and the Maoist party.
baselineWhat: The population of Nepal at the start of the Maoist insurgency in 1996
baselineNote: UN Population Division estimates put Nepal at about 21.9 million in 1996; the 2001 census counted 23,151,423. Displacement was concentrated in the mid-western and far-western hills - Rolpa, Rukum, Jajarkot, Salyan - where both the Maoists and the security forces drove people from villages.
shareCaveat: Displacement estimates for the conflict range from about 100,000 to 200,000 in government and IDMC figures and to 600,000 or more in accounts that include economic migration to India, which is hard to separate from conflict flight.

title: Northern Uganda's 'Protected Villages' and the Lord's Resistance Army War
actors: The Ugandan army moved the rural Acholi population into guarded camps during the war against the Lord's Resistance Army, which abducted tens of thousands of civilians
peopleRange: UN and Ugandan government figures put the camp population at roughly 1.8-2 million at its peak in 2005, in over 200 camps, comprising more than 90 per cent of the Acholi population of Gulu, Kitgum and Pader districts and large parts of Lango and Teso. The Lord's Resistance Army is estimated by the Survey of War Affected Youth and by UNICEF to have abducted between 24,000 and 66,000 children and young people over the war. Figures come from UN OCHA and government camp registration and from population-based surveys.

flows.label: Rural Acholi moved into protected villages around Gulu and Kitgum

summary: From 1996 the Ugandan army ordered the rural population of Acholiland into 'protected villages', giving families days to move and firing on those who remained; by 2005 some 1.8 to 2 million people were living in more than 200 camps, which were overcrowded, dependent on food aid, and only partly protected, being attacked repeatedly by the Lord's Resistance Army. A 2005 mortality survey by the Ugandan Ministry of Health with WHO and UN agencies found roughly 1,000 excess deaths a week in the camps, overwhelmingly from malaria, AIDS and other preventable causes rather than violence, a rate the survey described as far above emergency thresholds. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted an estimated 24,000-66,000 children and young people to serve as fighters, porters and wives, and committed massacres including at Barlonyo in 2004. Uganda referred the situation to the International Criminal Court in 2003; the Court issued arrest warrants for Joseph Kony and four commanders in 2005 and in 2021 convicted Dominic Ongwen of 61 counts of crimes against humanity and war crimes, including attacks on the Pajule, Odek, Lukodi and Abok camps. Camps were dismantled from 2006 after the Juba talks and most residents had returned by 2011; the Ugandan government maintained the camps were necessary protection, while human rights organisations and Acholi leaders characterised them as forced encampment.
contested: Whether the encampment was protective or amounted to forced displacement is disputed between the Ugandan government and Acholi civil society and human rights organisations; the abduction figure ranges from 24,000 to 66,000 depending on survey method.

sources.title: UNHCR, A Time Between: Moving on from internal displacement in northern Uganda (2010)
International Criminal Court: The Prosecutor v. Dominic Ongwen
Lord's Resistance Army insurgency

deathsNote: The lower figure is a conservative reading of the 2005 Ministry of Health/WHO mortality survey, which found around 1,000 excess deaths a week in the camps at that time, extended over the peak camp years. The higher figure is the extrapolation used by some Ugandan and international advocacy organisations across the whole encampment period. Violent deaths from LRA attacks and army operations are a small fraction of the total; most excess deaths were from disease and malnutrition in the camps.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.body: International Criminal Court, Trial Chamber IX
atrocityFindings.finding: Convicted Dominic Ongwen, a Lord's Resistance Army commander, of 61 counts of crimes against humanity and war crimes, including attacks on the Pajule, Odek, Lukodi and Abok camps for internally displaced persons, murder, enslavement, forced marriage, rape and the conscription of child soldiers.

violenceNote: The International Criminal Court, Human Rights Watch and the 2005 Ministry of Health/WHO survey documented abductions of children, forced marriage and rape, massacres at camps, and mortality from hunger and disease inside them.
baselineWhat: The population of the Acholi sub-region of northern Uganda — Gulu, Kitgum and Pader districts — at the 2002 census
baselineNote: Uganda's 2002 census counted about 1.15 million people in the three Acholi districts, of whom aid agencies estimated more than 90 per cent were living in 'protected villages' at the peak in 2003-2005. The wider camp population of roughly 1.8 million also included displaced people from the Lango and Teso sub-regions further south.
shareCaveat: The affected figure covers a wider area than the baseline: it includes displaced people from Lango and Teso as well as Acholiland, so the ratio against the Acholi population alone overstates the share of that sub-region.

title: United States Immigration Detention and Family Separation
actors: The United States government detained non-citizens in a nationwide network of federal, county and privately operated facilities pending removal, and in 2018 separated children from parents prosecuted at the border
peopleRange: The detained population grew from an average daily figure of roughly 8,500 in the mid-1990s, after the mandatory-detention provisions of the 1996 Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, to about 50,000 in 2019 and to a recorded single-day peak of 73,400 in mid-January 2026 according to the Vera Institute's analysis of ICE data. Vera reports that some 444,900 people were booked into detention between January 2025 and March 2026 and that 152 new facilities were opened. Under the 2018 'zero tolerance' policy at least 2,800 children were separated from parents in the period covered by court order, and the Department of Health and Human Services Inspector General reported in January 2019 that thousands more had been separated before that period than had previously been disclosed.
territoryDesc: A network of more than 200 detention facilities across the United States, mostly county jails and privately operated centres under contract to Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
summary: Legislation of 1996 made detention mandatory for broad categories of non-citizens facing removal, and the detained population grew steadily thereafter through a network of federal, county and privately run facilities. In 2018 the 'zero tolerance' prosecution policy at the south-west border produced the systematic separation of children from parents; a federal court in Ms L. v. ICE ordered reunification in June 2018, and the Department of Health and Human Services Inspector General reported that the number separated was substantially larger than the government had acknowledged and that no adequate tracking system existed. Detention numbers rose sharply again from 2025: the Vera Institute of Justice, analysing ICE data, recorded a single-day population of 73,400 in January 2026, exceeding all previous peaks, with 152 new facilities opened and roughly 444,900 people booked into detention since January 2025. Conditions, medical care and deaths in custody have been the subject of DHS Office of Inspector General reports and litigation. The atlas already contains Guantanamo and El Salvador's mass incarceration; the largest immigration detention system in the world was absent.
contested: Whether the system constitutes civil confinement incidental to immigration enforcement, as successive US administrations maintain, or arbitrary detention, as UN human rights bodies and litigants have argued; and the true number of children separated in 2017-2018, which the HHS Inspector General found the government could not establish.

sources.title: Immigration detention in the United States — Wikipedia
Separated Children Placed in Office of Refugee Resettlement Care — HHS Office of Inspector General (2019)

deathsNote: There is no mass death toll. ICE reports deaths in custody individually, typically in the range of a handful to a few dozen a year, with higher counts in some years; advocacy organisations argue the official figures undercount deaths shortly after release. The harm documented by inspectors general and courts is detention itself, medical neglect and the separation of children rather than lethal violence.

atrocityFindings.body: Office of Inspector General, US Department of Health and Human Services
atrocityFindings.finding: January 2019 report finding that thousands more children were separated from their parents than the government had reported, and that agencies lacked an adequate system to identify and track separated children

violenceNote: The HHS Inspector General and the federal court in Ms L. v. ICE documented the separation of children from parents; DHS Inspector General reports document detention conditions.
baselineWhat: The non-citizen population resident in the United States
baselineNote: Migration Policy Institute tabulations of Census Bureau data put the foreign-born population at 50.2 million in 2024, of whom about 25.8 million were naturalised citizens, leaving roughly 24.4 million non-citizens; MPI estimates about 13.7 million of these were unauthorised as of mid-2023. The detention system's own scale is measured differently: the Vera Institute records a record single-day population of more than 73,400 in mid-January 2026, against an average daily population of about 19,000 in the mid-1990s.

baselineSources.title: Frequently Requested Statistics on Immigrants and Immigration in the United States — Migration Policy Institute

shareCaveat: The affected figure is a single-day detention count, not the number of people detained over the thirty years covered: annual book-ins have run into the hundreds of thousands, so the cumulative total is in the millions and the ratio understates the system's reach by more than an order of magnitude.
asOfNote: The 73,400 figure is the record single-day detention population recorded in mid-January 2026 and continues to move; Vera and TRAC update it from ICE's own releases.

title: Congo-Brazzaville's Civil Wars and the Emptying of the Capital
actors: Militias loyal to Denis Sassou-Nguesso, Pascal Lissouba and Bernard Kolélas, with Angolan military backing for Sassou-Nguesso, fought for Brazzaville and the southern provinces, driving civilians into the forests of the Pool
peopleRange: The Global IDP Project's country profile records approximately 500,000 people displaced from Brazzaville alone during the June–October 1997 war, out of a city of 858,000, and an estimated 810,000 displaced from December 1998 onward — about 30 per cent of the national population of 2.7 million. Whole towns emptied, including Dolisie (80,000) and Nkayi (60,000). The figures come from UN humanitarian agency and NGO estimates made during the fighting, not from registration; the two waves overlap, so cumulative displacement cannot simply be added. Most of those displaced returned during 2000.

flows.label: Brazzaville → forests of the Pool
Dolisie and southern towns → Pool and interior

summary: Fighting between militias attached to Congo-Brazzaville's rival political leaders destroyed much of Brazzaville in the June–October 1997 war, which ended with Denis Sassou-Nguesso's return to power with Angolan military support. A second round from December 1998 centred on the southern Pool, Bouenza, Niari and Lékoumou regions. According to the Global IDP Project profile, roughly 500,000 people fled Brazzaville in 1997 and an estimated 810,000 — about 30 per cent of the population — were displaced from December 1998, with the towns of Dolisie and Nkayi emptied entirely. Médecins Sans Frontières reported that more than 250,000 people fled the capital into the forests of the Pool in December 1998, where they were beyond the reach of aid for months; when about 200,000 returned from May 1999, MSF recorded 14,700 cases of severe and 31,000 of moderate malnutrition, describing an unprecedented nutritional and medical emergency. Most of the displaced went home during 2000, though the Pool remained unstable.
contested: No agreed death toll exists for either war, and responsibility for specific massacres — including the disappearance of returnees at the Brazzaville river port in 1999 — remains disputed between the government and human rights organizations.

sources.title: Profile of Internal Displacement: Republic of Congo (Brazzaville) — Global IDP Project / Norwegian Refugee Council
Congo-Brazzaville: Chronicle of a Forgotten War — Médecins Sans Frontières

deathsNote: No systematic count of the dead was made in either war. Estimates for the 1997 battle for Brazzaville range from several thousand to over ten thousand, and further thousands died in 1998–99, but these figures come from press and diplomatic reporting rather than from surveys. MSF's data on returnees — 14,700 severely and 31,000 moderately malnourished by October 1999 — indicate substantial mortality in the Pool forests from hunger and disease that was never quantified.
violenceNote: Large-scale destruction and looting of homes in Brazzaville and the southern towns is documented in the Global IDP Project country profile.
baselineWhat: The population of the Republic of the Congo at the outbreak of the 1997 war
baselineNote: UN Population Division estimates put the country at about 2.8-2.9 million in 1997, of whom roughly 950,000 lived in Brazzaville. The June-October 1997 war emptied much of the capital, and the 1998-99 fighting in the Pool region displaced most of its population into the forest; UN agencies estimated some 810,000 people displaced in total, about a third of whom were still displaced at the end of 1999.

baselineSources.title: Republic of the Congo Civil War (1997–1999) — Wikipedia
Demographics of the Republic of the Congo — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: Displacement was heavily concentrated in Brazzaville and the Pool region rather than spread across the country, so the national ratio understates the near-total emptying of the capital's southern districts.

title: Ethiopia–Eritrea Border War
actors: Ethiopia and Eritrea fought over the disputed border town of Badme and adjacent territory; both governments expelled or deported each other's nationals
peopleRange: an estimated 1 million people were displaced on both sides of the border; tens of thousands of Eritreans in Ethiopia and Ethiopians in Eritrea were deported or expelled by the opposing government
territoryDesc: the core dispute centered on Badme and adjacent border areas (roughly 400 km2 immediately contested); a 2002 international Boundary Commission ruling awarded Badme to Eritrea but was not implemented by Ethiopia until a 2018 peace agreement

flows.label: Badme border area → Shire, Tigray (Ethiopia)
Deportation of Ethiopians from Eritrea

summary: Seven years after Eritrean independence, a border dispute over the town of Badme escalated into full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea from May 1998 to June 2000, involving trench warfare reminiscent of World War I and killing an estimated 70,000-100,000 soldiers on both sides. The war displaced roughly 1 million civilians from border areas, and both governments expelled or deported tens of thousands of each other's nationals and dual-heritage residents on grounds of national security. A 2000 peace agreement created a UN-monitored buffer zone, and an independent Boundary Commission ruled in 2002 that Badme belonged to Eritrea, but Ethiopia refused to withdraw for nearly two decades, leaving the two countries in a state of 'no war, no peace' until a 2018 rapprochement formally ended the conflict.
contested: Ethiopia disputed and refused to implement the 2002 Boundary Commission's award of Badme to Eritrea for sixteen years, a delay both sides characterized differently as either a security necessity or an illegal occupation.

sources.title: ACCORD: The Ethiopia-Eritrea Border Conflict and the Role of the International Community
GlobalSecurity.org: Eritrea Border war with Ethiopia (1998-2000)

deathsNote: Most international reporting settled on about 70,000 dead on both sides; the Encyclopedia of Conflicts Since World War II (2015) gives roughly 19,000 Eritrean and 120,000 Ethiopian soldiers killed, near 140,000. Each government's own claims serve its case — Eritrea acknowledged 19,000 of its soldiers killed while Ethiopia claimed 34,000-60,000 of its own and up to 67,000 Eritrean dead — and some regional analysts have suggested figures as high as 300,000. Press access restrictions meant none of these were independently verified.

atrocityFindings.body: Eritrea-Ethiopia Claims Commission (PCA)
atrocityFindings.finding: Partial Awards on Civilians' Claims of 28 April 2004 (Eritrea's Claims 15, 16, 23 & 27-32 and Ethiopia's Claim 5), binding arbitration under the 2000 Algiers Agreement adjudicating each state's liability for its treatment and expulsion of the other's nationals during the war

violenceNote: Human Rights Watch documented detainees subjected in some cases to torture, rape and other degrading treatment, and recorded the deportation of 77,000 Eritreans and Ethiopians of Eritrean origin from Ethiopia with their belongings confiscated and citizenship stripped, alongside an estimated 70,000 Ethiopians expelled from Eritrea — matters also litigated before the Claims Commission.
baselineWhat: The combined populations of Ethiopia and Eritrea at the outbreak of the border war
baselineNote: World Bank and UN Population Division series give Ethiopia about 63.9 million and Eritrea about 3.2 million in 1998. The burden fell very unevenly: displacement and expulsions in Eritrea alone are usually put at 750,000 or more, close to a quarter of its population, while Ethiopian displacement was concentrated in Tigray and Afar.
shareCaveat: The share against both national populations is dominated by Ethiopia's size and badly understates the effect on Eritrea, where roughly one person in four was displaced or expelled.

title: Kosovo War, NATO Intervention, and Reverse Exodus
actors: Yugoslav/Serb security forces fought the Kosovo Liberation Army and expelled Kosovo Albanian civilians; NATO conducted a 78-day bombing campaign in 1999 without UN Security Council authorization; after the Serb withdrawal, Kosovo Serbs and Roma faced revenge attacks and fled
peopleRange: an estimated 848,000 Kosovo Albanians fled or were expelled abroad and up to 590,000 more were displaced internally during the 1998-99 war (UNHCR); roughly 200,000 Serbs and Roma subsequently fled Kosovo after the withdrawal of Yugoslav forces in mid-1999
territoryDesc: Kosovo, then an autonomous province of Serbia within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, placed under UN administration (UNMIK) per Security Council Resolution 1244 after the war

flows.label: Kosovo → Albania (Albanian refugees, 1998-99)
Kosovo → North Macedonia (Albanian refugees, 1998-99)
Kosovo → Serbia proper (Serb/Roma exodus, 1999-2000)

summary: Fighting between Yugoslav/Serb forces and the Kosovo Liberation Army escalated through 1998 into a campaign that expelled hundreds of thousands of ethnic Albanians and included massacres such as at Račak. In March 1999, NATO launched a 78-day air campaign against Yugoslavia without UN Security Council authorization, citing humanitarian necessity; Belgrade withdrew its forces in June 1999 and Kosovo came under UN administration. In the aftermath, an estimated 200,000 Kosovo Serbs and Roma fled or were driven out amid revenge violence, with further unrest, including riots in March 2004, entrenching their displacement.
contested: NATO's intervention's legality remains disputed absent Security Council authorization; NATO and most Western governments frame it as necessary humanitarian intervention, while Serbia and Russia characterize it as an illegal act of aggression; casualty and displacement figures also vary somewhat between Serbian, Kosovo Albanian and international sources.

sources.title: UNHCR: The Kosovo Refugee Crisis - independent evaluation of UNHCR's emergency response
OSCE/ODIHR: Human Rights in Kosovo - As Seen, As Told (Volume I)
Britannica: Kosovo conflict

deathsNote: The Humanitarian Law Center's Kosovo Memory Book, compiled name by name, documents just over 13,500 people killed or missing between 1998 and 2000 across all communities; wartime allegations by NATO governments of up to 100,000 Kosovo Albanians killed were not borne out by ICTY exhumations, while Serbian sources emphasise the roughly 500 Yugoslav civilians Human Rights Watch found were killed by NATO bombing and the Serbs and Roma killed after June 1999.

atrocityFindings.body: ICTY
atrocityFindings.finding: Milutinović et al. (IT-05-87) — five senior Serbian and Yugoslav officials convicted on 26 February 2009 of crimes against humanity for the campaign of deportation and forcible transfer of Kosovo Albanians, with four convictions upheld on appeal in January 2014; Serbia's authorities have disputed the characterisation of a state campaign

violenceNote: ICTY judgements, Human Rights Watch's 'Under Orders: War Crimes in Kosovo' and the OSCE's 'Kosovo/Kosova: As Seen, As Told' documented massacres and summary executions of Albanian civilians, rape, mass expulsion and house burning, and — after June 1999 — killings of Serbs and Roma and the destruction of Serbian Orthodox churches.
baselineWhat: The population of Kosovo on the eve of the war
baselineNote: The 1991 Yugoslav census was boycotted by Kosovo Albanians, so all figures for the 1990s are estimates; these run from about 1.9 to 2.2 million, of which roughly 82-90% Albanian and 8-10% Serb. The first postwar census was not held until 2011.
shareCaveat: The 1.5 million counts almost everyone displaced at some point, including repeat displacement, refugees who returned within months of June 1999, and the roughly 200,000 Serbs and Roma who fled afterwards - so it approaches the whole population without meaning that the whole population was permanently displaced.

title: Second Congo War ("Africa's World War")
actors: Nine African states and numerous rebel and militia groups fought in the Democratic Republic of the Congo following the fall of Mobutu, in what became the deadliest conflict since World War II by some estimates
peopleRange: an estimated 2.2–3.4 million people were internally displaced at the war's height, plus regional refugee flows; the International Rescue Committee estimated 3.3–5.4 million excess deaths from 1998–2008, mostly from disease and hunger, a figure disputed by some demographers as too high

flows.label: Goma region → Kisangani
Bukavu → Burundi border areas
Eastern DRC → Kinshasa (internal flight)

summary: The Second Congo War began in 1998 when Rwanda and Uganda backed rebels against the government of Laurent Kabila (whom they had earlier helped install), drawing in Angola, Zimbabwe, Namibia, and other states along with dozens of local militias in a conflict over territory, resources, and regional security. Fighting and its humanitarian consequences, especially disease and malnutrition among displaced populations, produced what the International Rescue Committee called the world's deadliest conflict since World War II, with a widely cited but contested estimate of 3.3–5.4 million excess deaths between 1998 and 2008. At its peak roughly 2.2–3.4 million people were internally displaced within the DRC, concentrated in the eastern provinces. A 2002-03 peace process formally ended the war, though armed conflict and displacement in eastern DRC have continued intermittently ever since.
contested: The IRC's mortality estimate of 5.4 million excess deaths has been challenged by some public health researchers and demographers as methodologically overstated; lower estimates in the range of 1-3 million are also cited.

sources.title: IRC: Mortality in the Democratic Republic of Congo: An ongoing crisis
ReliefWeb: Conflict in DR Congo deadliest since World War II, says the IRC
EBSCO Research Starters: Second Congo War 1998-2003

deathsNote: The International Rescue Committee's mortality surveys produced 5.4 million excess deaths for 1998-2007, of which it attributed only around 350,000 to direct violence and the remainder to disease and malnutrition — a figure very frequently misquoted as a count of people killed. The Human Security Report Project at Simon Fraser University argued the pre-war baseline mortality rate had been set too low for a country with the DRC's development indicators and recalculated the toll to roughly 2.8 million, and under 900,000 using a different baseline; IRC co-author Richard Brennan conceded that insecurity forced assumptions and extrapolations but maintained the findings stand.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: ICC
atrocityFindings.finding: Prosecutor v. Bosco Ntaganda — trial for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ituri, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, pillage and the conscription of children under 15, opened 2 September 2015 (conviction 2019, upheld on appeal 2021); companion cases against Thomas Lubanga and Germain Katanga arose from the same conflict

violenceNote: The UN Mapping Report on the DRC (2010), ICC judgements against Lubanga, Katanga and Ntaganda, and Human Rights Watch documented massacres including the 'Effacer le tableau' campaign against Mbuti communities, mass rape and sexual slavery, forced labour in mining areas, pillage and village burning, and the abduction and conscription of children into armed groups.
baselineWhat: The population of the Democratic Republic of the Congo at the outbreak of the second war
baselineNote: The DRC's last full census was in 1984, when it counted 30.7 million; UN Population Division estimates put the country at roughly 46-47 million in 1998, so the figure is a projection rather than an enumeration. The International Rescue Committee's mortality surveys estimated 3.9 million excess deaths by 2004 and 5.4 million by 2008, figures later criticised by the Human Security Report Project for their baseline assumptions; displacement peaked at over three million people in 2003.
