title: The Solomon Islands Tensions and the Expulsion of Malaitans from Guadalcanal
actors: Guadalcanal militants drove Malaitan settlers from rural Guadalcanal; a Malaitan militia seized Honiara and the police armoury and forced the prime minister's resignation
peopleRange: Estimates of those displaced range from about 20,000 to 35,000, most of them Malaitan settlers driven from rural Guadalcanal into Honiara or back to Malaita between late 1998 and 2000; the figures come from the Solomon Islands Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which reported in 2012, and from contemporary UN and Australian assessments. The country's total population at the 1999 census was about 409,000, so the displacement affected on the order of 5-8 per cent of the population.

flows.label: Malaitan settlers driven from rural Guadalcanal into Honiara
Displaced Malaitans returning to Malaita

summary: From late 1998 militants on Guadalcanal, organised as the Guadalcanal Revolutionary Army and later the Isatabu Freedom Movement, attacked and drove out Malaitan settlers who had migrated to the island over previous decades, in a conflict over land, employment and the distribution of state resources. Malaitans formed the Malaita Eagle Force, which in June 2000 seized the Honiara police armoury, took the prime minister hostage and forced his resignation. Between 20,000 and 35,000 people were displaced, most of them Malaitans; the state effectively ceased to function, and a 2000 peace agreement at Townsville did not hold. Australia led the Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands from July 2003, which disarmed the militias and restored basic administration. The Solomon Islands Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Sir Peter Kenilorea, delivered its report in 2012, documenting around 200 killings together with widespread destruction of property, torture and sexual violence, and criticised the government for delaying publication. The Pacific island states outside Fiji, Bougainville and Nauru were thinly covered in the atlas.
contested: Responsibility and reparation: the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's report was withheld from official publication for a period after its 2012 completion, and its findings on the conduct of particular militia and state actors remain politically disputed in Solomon Islands.

sources.title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Solomon Islands) — Wikipedia
Solomon Islands Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Final Report, Volume 1
Solomon Islands Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Final Report, Volume 2 — Government of Solomon Islands
Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands — Wikipedia

deathsNote: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented approximately 200 killings during the Tensions, based on statements taken from victims and witnesses; the Commission itself cautioned that its figure is a floor, since not all deaths were reported to it, and slightly higher counts circulate in contemporary reporting.

atrocityFindings.body: Solomon Islands Truth and Reconciliation Commission
atrocityFindings.finding: 2012 final report documenting some 200 killings, torture, sexual violence, forced displacement and destruction of property during the Tensions of 1998-2003, and making recommendations on reparations and reconciliation

violenceNote: The Solomon Islands Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented killings, torture, rape and the burning of homes by militia on both sides.
baselineWhat: The population of Guadalcanal province and Honiara
baselineNote: The 1999 Solomon Islands census counted about 60,000 in Guadalcanal province and about 49,000 in Honiara, out of a national population of roughly 409,000. Malaitan settlers on Guadalcanal, the main target of the expulsions, are usually put at 20,000-35,000.

title: The 1999 Invasion of Dagestan and the Displacement of its Border Villages
actors: Armed groups from Chechnya seized villages in western Dagestan; Russian federal forces and Dagestani militias drove them out with air and artillery attacks
peopleRange: About 32,000 Dagestani civilians were displaced by the fighting, a figure drawn from Russian and Dagestani authorities' registrations of people evacuated from the Botlikh, Tsumada and Novolak districts and from the Kadar-zone villages; many returned within months to destroyed or damaged houses. Civilian casualties were never systematically compiled.

flows.label: Villagers from Botlikh and Tsumada districts to Makhachkala and lowland Dagestan
Displacement from Novolakskoye and the Kadar zone

summary: In August 1999 armed formations led by Shamil Basayev and the commander known as Ibn al-Khattab crossed from Chechnya into the Botlikh and Tsumada districts of western Dagestan and proclaimed an Islamic state; a second incursion followed in September into the Novolak district, alongside fighting for the Kadar-zone villages of Karamakhi and Chabanmakhi, which had asserted autonomy from the republican authorities. Russian federal forces, Dagestani police and locally raised volunteer militias expelled the fighters by mid-September, using heavy air and artillery bombardment that destroyed much of several highland villages. Federal authorities announced 275 servicemen killed, 15 missing and about 937 wounded; insurgent losses were put by Russian sources in the high hundreds to low thousands, and the number of civilians killed was never compiled. Roughly 32,000 civilians were displaced. The invasion, together with the apartment bombings in Russian cities that month, was the immediate trigger for the second Russian campaign in Chechnya recorded separately in this atlas; the displaced population of Novolakskoye, itself a district resettled by Laks after the 1944 deportation of the Chechen-Akkins, was caught in a longer-running dispute over land and return.
contested: Russian official accounts, the accounts of the insurgent commanders and later journalistic investigations differ over how the incursion was planned and whether elements of the Russian security services had foreknowledge; civilian casualties and the proportionality of the federal bombardment were never independently established.

sources.title: War of Dagestan (Wikipedia)

deathsNote: The range combines announced federal losses of 275 dead with Russian estimates of several hundred to about two thousand insurgents killed; it is uncertain chiefly because insurgent losses were claimed by the side that inflicted them and because civilian deaths, which both sides largely ignored, were never counted.
violenceNote: The destruction of houses in Botlikh, Karamakhi, Chabanmakhi and Novolakskoye by air and artillery attack was reported by Russian and international media and by Dagestani local authorities compensating residents.
baselineWhat: The population of the Republic of Dagestan in 1999, of which the fighting affected the Botlikh, Tsumada, Novolak and Kadar-valley districts
baselineNote: Russian official estimates put Dagestan's population at about 2.12 million in 1999 (2002 census: 2,576,531). The districts directly emptied — Botlikhsky, Tsumadinsky, Novolaksky and the Buinaksk highland villages — held on the order of 100,000 people between them, so the displacement affected roughly a third of the immediate war zone.
shareCaveat: The displacement was concentrated in a handful of border districts, so a share of the whole republic understates its local intensity, where entire villages were emptied and several were destroyed.

title: Zimbabwe's Land Seizures and Operation Murambatsvina
actors: The Mugabe government's fast-track land reform seized thousands of white-owned commercial farms from 2000; in 2005 the government's Operation Murambatsvina demolished urban informal settlements and vending sites, disproportionately affecting opposition supporters
peopleRange: Operation Murambatsvina directly affected an estimated 700,000 people who lost their homes, livelihoods or both, according to a 2005 UN Special Envoy report; the preceding land reform program displaced several hundred thousand farm workers and roughly 4,000 white commercial farm-owning families

flows.label: Harare urban settlements → peri-urban/rural areas

summary: Beginning in 2000, Zimbabwe's government under Robert Mugabe launched a 'fast-track' land reform program that saw war veterans and government supporters forcibly occupy and seize most of the country's roughly 4,000 white-owned commercial farms, displacing farm owners and, more numerously, hundreds of thousands of Black farm workers and their families, while agricultural production collapsed. In May-July 2005, the government carried out Operation Murambatsvina ('drive out the rubbish'), a mass demolition campaign against urban informal housing, market stalls and small businesses, officially described as urban cleanup but widely seen as retaliation against urban populations that had voted for the opposition. A UN Special Envoy report by Anna Tibaijuka found that Murambatsvina directly affected an estimated 700,000 people through loss of homes, livelihoods, or both, and criticized the operation as carried out with indifference to human suffering and in violation of international law.
contested: The Zimbabwean government described Murambatsvina as a legitimate urban clean-up and anti-crime operation; the UN Special Envoy's 2005 report and human rights organizations characterized it as a mass forced eviction conducted in violation of international law.

sources.title: UN Special Envoy Report on Operation Murambatsvina (Tibaijuka Report)
International Crisis Group: Zimbabwe's Operation Murambatsvina - The Tipping Point?
UN Press: Tibaijuka press conference

deathsNote: Neither the land seizures nor Operation Murambatsvina produced a mass death toll; the harm is dispossession and demolition. The UN Special Envoy Anna Tibaijuka's 2005 report found that approximately 700,000 people lost their homes, livelihoods or both, and characterised the evictions as indiscriminate, unjustified and in breach of national and international law, but records no deaths. On the farm invasions, an audit by FactCheckZW of the available counts gives seven white farmers killed by end-2000 (Human Rights Watch), 28 for 2000-2014 (Eddie Cross) and 29 for 2000-2016 (Commercial Farmers Union, a figure that includes deaths in unrelated crimes), alongside 34 black farm workers and managers killed by May 2000 and an uncorroborated claim of 78 by 2017; FactCheckZW rejects the characterisation of the programme as genocide. The Gukurahundi massacres of 1983-87, with far higher tolls, are a separate event.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Special Envoy on Human Settlements Issues in Zimbabwe (Anna Tibaijuka)
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that Operation Murambatsvina was carried out 'with indifference to human suffering', was indiscriminate and unjustified, breached national and international human rights law governing evictions and precipitated a humanitarian crisis affecting some 700,000 people directly

atrocityFindings.body: SADC Tribunal, Mike Campbell (Pvt) Ltd and Others v Republic of Zimbabwe
atrocityFindings.finding: Held by majority that the fast-track land programme under Constitutional Amendment 17 amounted to de facto racial discrimination contrary to Article 6(2) of the SADC Treaty, unanimously that it denied applicants access to courts contrary to Article 4(c), and unanimously that fair compensation was due; Zimbabwe refused to comply and SADC suspended the Tribunal in 2010

violenceNote: The UN Special Envoy Anna Tibaijuka's 2005 report found that the demolition campaign left approximately 700,000 people without homes, livelihoods or both, and breached national and international law governing evictions.
baselineWhat: The population of Zimbabwe at the 2002 census
baselineNote: The 2002 census counted 11,631,657 people, of whom roughly 4 million lived in urban areas. The UN Special Envoy's report of July 2005 (the Tibaijuka report) estimated that Operation Murambatsvina directly destroyed the homes or livelihoods of about 700,000 people and affected some 2.4 million indirectly. Separately, fast-track land reform from 2000 transferred several thousand commercial farms and displaced an estimated 150,000-200,000 farm worker households.
shareCaveat: The 700,000 is the Murambatsvina urban demolition figure alone and counts people who lost homes or livelihoods, not only those physically displaced; the farm seizures affected a further large number of farm workers and dependants who are not in this count.

title: Australian Offshore Detention on Nauru and Manus Island
actors: Australia transferring asylum seekers who arrived by boat to processing centres in Nauru and Papua New Guinea under bilateral agreements, with the host states holding formal legal responsibility
peopleRange: About 1,500 people were sent to Nauru in the first phase (a 2006 Australian Human Rights Commission report counted 1,509), and roughly 3,000-4,000 more were transferred in the phase beginning in 2012; the centres peaked at 1,233 detainees on Nauru in August 2014 and 1,353 on Manus in January 2014, and by 2021-2022 only about 100-150 people remained in each country
territoryDesc: The Regional Processing Centre on Nauru, an island state of 21 km², and the centre at Lombrum on Manus Island, Papua New Guinea, with later accommodation sites at Lorengau

flows.label: Christmas Island → Nauru and Manus

summary: Under the "Pacific Solution" from 2001 and again from August 2012, Australia transferred asylum seekers intercepted at sea to processing centres on Nauru and on Manus Island in Papua New Guinea, where they were held while claims were assessed, with successive Australian governments stating that anyone arriving by boat would never be resettled in Australia. Detention was prolonged and indefinite, with people held for years while resettlement options were negotiated with third countries including the United States, New Zealand and Cambodia. The Supreme Court of Papua New Guinea ruled on 26 April 2016 that detention at the Manus centre breached the constitutional right to personal liberty and was therefore illegal, and ordered both governments to end it; the centre formally closed on 31 October 2017, when about 690 men remained and several hundred refused to leave, and they were moved to alternative accommodation on the island. The Nauru centre wound down to zero residents in March 2019 and was reactivated under a new agreement in September 2021 as a standing capability. At least eight people died in connection with the Manus operation between 2013 and 2019, from suicide, violence and delayed medical treatment, and leaked incident reports and repeated UN and medical assessments documented severe mental health deterioration among detainees. Australia maintains that the policy ended deaths at sea by deterring boat voyages and that its operation is lawful; UN human rights bodies, the UNHCR and Australian medical and legal organisations have found the arrangements to constitute arbitrary and indefinite detention with serious health consequences.
contested: The main disputes are whether the transfers constitute detention attributable to Australia at all - Australia argues the centres were operated under host-state law and that participants were not in Australian custody - whether the deterrence rationale justifies indefinite confinement of people later recognised as refugees, and whether the regime breaches the Refugee Convention's non-penalisation provisions and the prohibition of arbitrary detention.

sources.title: Nauru Regional Processing Centre - dates of operation, peak population and current status
Manus Regional Processing Centre - peak population, PNG Supreme Court ruling of 26 April 2016, closure and deaths
Pacific Solution - the 2001-2008 phase and transfer figures

deathsNote: At least eight men died in connection with the Manus Island centre between 2014 and 2019 — including the murder of Reza Barati during the February 2014 disturbances, Hamid Kehazaei's death from sepsis after delayed medical evacuation, a drowning and several suicides — and refugee advocacy organisations including the Refugee Council of Australia count at least fourteen deaths across Manus and Nauru combined. The Australian government has never published a consolidated figure, which is the main source of the range.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.body: Supreme Court of Papua New Guinea
atrocityFindings.finding: Ruling of 26 April 2016 that detention at the Manus Regional Processing Centre breached the constitutional right to personal liberty and was illegal, ordering both governments to cease it; Australia's government rejected the ruling's implications for its own responsibility

violenceNote: The PNG Supreme Court found the Manus detention unlawful, the Australian government's 2015 Moss Review and the leaked 'Nauru Files' documented sexual assault, self-harm and abuse of children in the Nauru centre, and Amnesty International's 2016 report 'Island of Despair' characterised the deliberate infliction of these conditions on Nauru as amounting to torture — a characterisation the Australian government rejects.
baselineWhat: The people who reached Australia by boat as asylum seekers between 2008 and 2013, the group from which offshore transfers were selected
baselineNote: Australian Parliamentary Library figures record roughly 51,000 irregular maritime arrivals between 2008 and the end of 2013. Of these, about 4,180 were transferred to Nauru and Manus Island after offshore processing resumed on 13 August 2012; a handful of further transfers have occurred since 2022 under the 'enduring' Nauru arrangement.

baselineSources.title: Offshore processing statistics — Refugee Council of Australia

asOfNote: The Refugee Council of Australia's statistics run to 30 September 2025 and record 163 people transferred to Nauru since May 2022; a small population remains in Nauru under the continuing arrangement, while the Manus Island centre closed in 2017.

title: Côte d'Ivoire's Division and Post-Election Crisis
actors: Forces Nouvelles rebels held the north from 2002 while government forces and allied militias held the south; in 2010–11 forces loyal to Laurent Gbagbo and to Alassane Ouattara fought for control, with mass killings of civilians on both sides
peopleRange: The ICC Prosecutor's account of the 2010–11 post-electoral crisis cites approximately one million people displaced, the great majority within Côte d'Ivoire and concentrated in Abidjan and the west. Human Rights Watch recorded nearly 40,000 refugees crossing into Liberia between the second round of the election and 24 February 2011, a figure that rose sharply during the March–April fighting. Several hundred thousand were also displaced during the 2002–03 war and its aftermath. The figures are UN and NGO operational estimates rather than registrations, and the waves overlap.
territoryDesc: From September 2002 until 2011 the Forces Nouvelles administered roughly the northern half of Côte d'Ivoire, separated from the government-held south by a UN- and French-patrolled buffer zone (the 'zone of confidence').

flows.label: Western Côte d'Ivoire → Liberia (by February 2011)
Abidjan → interior towns

summary: A failed coup in September 2002 split Côte d'Ivoire between a rebel-held north and a government-held south, divided by a buffer zone patrolled by French and UN troops, a division that lasted until 2011. Laurent Gbagbo's refusal to concede the November 2010 presidential election to Alassane Ouattara triggered six months of violence. Human Rights Watch documented at least 3,000 civilians killed and more than 150 women raped between November 2010 and May 2011, naming pro-Gbagbo units including the Republican Guard, CECOS and the Young Patriots militia, and pro-Ouattara Republican Forces and Invisible Commandos; the largest single massacre took place at Duékoué in March 2011. The ICC Prosecutor cited widespread and systematic attacks on civilians, roughly one million people displaced, mass graves in Abidjan, and widespread arbitrary arrests, disappearances and rape. Laurent Gbagbo and Charles Blé Goudé were tried at the ICC for crimes against humanity and acquitted in January 2019, an acquittal upheld on appeal in March 2021. No senior pro-Ouattara commander has been convicted for crimes committed by his forces.
contested: Accountability is strongly disputed: the ICC's only defendants were from the losing side and were acquitted, and Ivorian and international human rights organizations argue that crimes by pro-Ouattara forces, including at Duékoué, have gone unprosecuted.

sources.title: 'They Killed Them Like It Was Nothing': The Need for Justice for Côte d'Ivoire's Post-Election Crimes — Human Rights Watch
Situation in Côte d'Ivoire — International Criminal Court

deathsNote: Human Rights Watch documented at least 3,000 civilians killed during the six months of the post-electoral crisis, an explicit minimum based on investigated cases rather than an estimate of the total. No comprehensive toll has been produced for the 2010–11 crisis or for the 2002–04 war and the years of division, so the upper bound is not established.

atrocityFindings.body: International Criminal Court
atrocityFindings.finding: Charged Laurent Gbagbo and Charles Blé Goudé with crimes against humanity (murder, rape, other inhumane acts, attempted murder and persecution) for the 2010–11 post-electoral violence; the Trial Chamber acquitted both on 15 January 2019 and the Appeals Chamber upheld the acquittals on 31 March 2021

violenceNote: Documented by Human Rights Watch's 2011 investigation and by the ICC Prosecutor's filings in the Côte d'Ivoire situation.
baselineWhat: The population of Cote d'Ivoire when the country divided
baselineNote: The 1998 census counted 15.4 million and estimates for 2002 give about 17-18 million. Roughly a quarter were immigrants or of recent immigrant descent, mostly from Burkina Faso and Mali - the fact at the centre of the ivoirite dispute over nationality and land that drove the conflict.
shareCaveat: The 1 million spans two distinct crises nine years apart - the 2002 partition and the 2010-11 post-election war - and includes both internal displacement and flight into Liberia and Ghana.

title: Extraterritorial Detention at Guantanamo Bay
actors: The United States holding foreign nationals captured in counter-terrorism operations at a naval base on leased Cuban territory, outside the ordinary reach of United States immigration and criminal courts
peopleRange: 779-780 men from 48 countries have been held since January 2002; the population peaked at more than 680 in May 2003 and had fallen to 15 by January 2025, of whom nine were charged or convicted before military commissions, three were approved for transfer and three were held in "law of war" detention without charge
territoryDesc: The detention facilities at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, a base held by the United States under a 1903 lease over which the United States exercises complete jurisdiction and control while Cuba retains ultimate sovereignty
summary: From January 2002 the United States transferred men captured in Afghanistan, Pakistan and elsewhere to a detention facility at its naval base in Guantanamo Bay, chosen in part because the government argued that its location outside United States sovereign territory placed detainees beyond the reach of the federal courts. The administration classified them as unlawful enemy combatants rather than prisoners of war and asserted that they could be held under the law of war until the end of hostilities without criminal charge; a small number were prosecuted before military commissions, and the case against those accused of the September 11 attacks has not reached trial after more than a decade of pre-trial litigation. The Supreme Court progressively rejected the jurisdictional argument, holding in Rasul v. Bush (2004) that federal habeas statutes reached the base, in Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (2006) that the original commissions were unlawful, and in Boumediene v. Bush (2008) that detainees have a constitutional right to habeas corpus and that the Military Commissions Act's suspension of it was invalid. Most detainees were released or transferred without charge to third countries; by January 2025 fifteen remained, several of them held for more than twenty years, including men cleared for transfer years earlier who could not be resettled. UN special procedures and human rights organisations have found the detention arbitrary, criticised the conditions of confinement and the effects of earlier torture in CIA custody, and called for closure, while successive United States administrations have differed on closure but maintained that law-of-war detention is lawful.
contested: At issue are whether indefinite detention without criminal charge is lawful under the law of armed conflict in a conflict with no defined end, as the United States asserts, or arbitrary detention prohibited by the ICCPR, as UN special procedures and human rights bodies have found; whether the ICCPR applies extraterritorially at the base, which the United States has long disputed; and whether the military commission system provides a fair trial.

sources.title: Guantanamo Bay detention camp - total and current detainee numbers, legal status and UN criticism
Boumediene v. Bush (2008) - habeas corpus rights of Guantanamo detainees

deathsNote: US Department of Defense records nine detainee deaths at Guantanamo since 2002, six of them classified as suicides; there is no dispute about the magnitude, only about causes — Seton Hall Law's Center for Policy and Research and reporting in Harper's Magazine have challenged the official finding that the three men who died on 10 June 2006 killed themselves, a challenge the Pentagon rejects.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.body: UN Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights while countering terrorism (Fionnuala Ní Aoláin)
atrocityFindings.finding: Technical Visit to the United States and Guantánamo Detention Facility (report of 26 June 2023), finding that detainees remain subject to ongoing cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment and that the legacy of torture and rendition is unremedied; the United States disagreed with a number of the report's factual and legal conclusions

violenceNote: The International Committee of the Red Cross (2004 assessment reported in the press) described an intentional system of cruel and degrading treatment amounting to torture, and the UN Special Rapporteur on counter-terrorism concluded in 2023 that indefinite detention without trial and continuing cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment persist.
baselineWhat: No defined population was subject to the policy; detainees were seized in some 40 countries and no group of which they form a share can be specified
baselineNote: About 780 men have been held at Guantanamo since January 2002. They were captured across Afghanistan, Pakistan and many other states, often by bounty, and belonged to no bounded community or territory, so any denominator - a national population, a religious group - would be arbitrary and misleading. The meaningful figures are the cumulative total held and the number remaining.

baselineSources.title: List of current detainees at Guantanamo Bay

asOfNote: The 780 figure is cumulative since 2002; fifteen men remained in detention as of August 2025 after eleven Yemenis were transferred to Oman in January 2025, and the number changes with each transfer.

title: Darfur Conflict
actors: Sudanese government forces and allied Janjaweed militias (later reorganized as the Rapid Support Forces) fought Darfuri rebel groups; the campaign against Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa communities was formally declared genocide by the United States
peopleRange: about 2.7 million were displaced in the first phase from 2003; after the 2023 resumption Darfur holds roughly 64% of Sudan's 8.8 million internally displaced, on the order of 5.5 million as of mid-2026

flows.label: El Fasher, Darfur → Chad refugee camps
El Geneina, West Darfur → Chad

summary: Beginning in 2003, non-Arab Darfuri rebel groups took up arms against Sudan's central government over marginalization; Khartoum responded with a scorched-earth counterinsurgency campaign using regular forces and allied Arab militias known as the Janjaweed, targeting the Fur, Masalit, and Zaghawa ethnic groups. The United States government formally declared the campaign genocide in 2004, while a 2005 UN Commission of Inquiry found evidence of war crimes and crimes against humanity but did not conclude genocide had occurred; the International Criminal Court later indicted Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir on genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity charges. The initial 2003-2005 phase displaced an estimated 2.7 million people and killed roughly 200,000-400,000, with death toll estimates varying considerably by source. Violence in Darfur, including large-scale killings in El Geneina and the 2024-25 siege of El Fasher, resurged dramatically after the outbreak of Sudan's broader civil war in April 2023.
contested: The U.S. government and some scholars have formally characterized the 2003-2005 campaign as genocide; the UN Commission of Inquiry stopped short of that designation while finding war crimes and crimes against humanity; death toll estimates range from roughly 200,000 to 400,000 or higher.

sources.title: US Holocaust Memorial Museum: Darfur
US Congress H.Con.Res.467: Declaring genocide in Darfur, Sudan (2004)
GAO: Darfur Crisis - Death Estimates Demonstrate Severity of Crisis

deathsNote: The figure of about 200,000 was the working UN estimate from 2006 and remains the most frequently cited; the US GAO's 2007 review of six competing estimates for February 2003 to August 2005 found figures reported by the State Department and others reaching about 400,000, the highest associated with the analyst Eric Reeves. Degomme and Guha-Sapir's 2010 Lancet study for CRED estimated roughly 298,000 excess deaths through 2008 and found that around 80 per cent were from disease rather than violence — a distinction routinely lost when the number is quoted as a count of people killed. Sudan's government under Omar al-Bashir rejected all of these, putting the toll at about 10,000 and accusing the UN of exaggeration. The range given here is an excess-mortality range and is not comparable with a direct-killing count.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: International Criminal Court (Pre-Trial Chamber I)
atrocityFindings.finding: Second arrest warrant for Omar Hassan Ahmad al-Bashir adding three counts of genocide against the Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa groups — killing, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about physical destruction — supplementing the 2009 warrant for war crimes and crimes against humanity. Sudan has never surrendered al-Bashir and rejects the Court's jurisdiction

atrocityFindings.body: UN International Commission of Inquiry on Darfur
atrocityFindings.finding: Concluded that Sudanese government forces and militias committed widespread and systematic crimes against humanity and war crimes including mass killing, torture, rape and forced displacement, but that the Government of Sudan had not pursued a policy of genocide and that genocidal intent was not established; recommended referral to the ICC. This finding is in tension with the ICC's later genocide counts and with the US government's 2004 genocide determination

violenceNote: Documented by the UN International Commission of Inquiry on Darfur (2005) — mass killing, torture, rape and forced displacement by government forces and allied militias — and charged by the ICC Prosecutor against Omar al-Bashir as murder, extermination, rape, torture and pillage; Sudan rejects both.
baselineWhat: The population of the Darfur region of Sudan at the outbreak of the conflict in 2003
baselineNote: Sudan's 2008 census recorded roughly 7.5 million people in the Darfur states, implying about 6 million in 2003; the 2008 count was boycotted in parts of the region and is disputed by Darfuri groups, and no census has been held since. Estimates for Darfur's population today run from 9 to 11 million.

baselineSources.title: Explore Sudan's conflict, displacement and humanitarian needs — ACAPS

shareCaveat: The figure spans two distinct wars — the 2003-2005 campaign and the RSF offensives since 2023 — and many Darfuris displaced in the first were displaced again in the second, while the region's population grew by half over the period, so the share against a 2003 base overstates the proportion of individuals affected.
asOfNote: Displacement in Darfur has continued to grow through 2025-26 with the fall of El Fasher and the emptying of the Zamzam and Abu Shouk camps, and no verified region-wide total has been published since.

title: 2003 Iraq War and Sectarian Displacement
actors: A US-led coalition invaded Iraq and toppled Saddam Hussein's government in 2003; the ensuing insurgency and, especially, the 2006–2008 Sunni–Shia sectarian civil war displaced millions of Iraqis internally and to neighboring countries, mainly Syria and Jordan.
peopleRange: Approximately 4.7 million Iraqis were displaced by 2008: roughly 2.7 million internally and about 2 million as refugees, mainly in Syria and Jordan

flows.label: Baghdad → Syria
Baghdad → Jordan
Baghdad → Iraqi Kurdistan (internal displacement)

summary: The 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq toppled Saddam Hussein's government but was followed by a prolonged insurgency and, from 2006, an intense Sunni–Shia sectarian civil war marked by militia violence, bombings of mosques and markets, and ethnic cleansing of mixed neighborhoods, particularly in Baghdad. By 2007–2008, an estimated 4.7 million Iraqis had been displaced, roughly 2.7 million internally within Iraq and about 2 million as refugees, overwhelmingly in Syria and Jordan, which together hosted the bulk of the externally displaced population. Baghdad's demographic makeup shifted markedly as previously mixed neighborhoods became segregated along sectarian lines. Displacement eased somewhat after 2008 as violence declined, though it was later compounded by the rise of ISIS after 2014.
contested: Estimates of both displacement and civilian death tolls from this period vary substantially between coalition, Iraqi government, and independent sources (such as the disputed Lancet mortality surveys), and responsibility for the sectarian violence is debated among historians and the parties involved.

sources.title: Migration Policy Institute: The Iraqi Refugee Crisis
Brookings: Iraq's Displaced — Where to Turn?
ICRC Casebook: Iraq — Situation of Internally Displaced Persons

deathsNote: These ends measure different things and are not comparable. Iraq Body Count's incident-verified record of violent civilian deaths reached 114,212 for 2003–2011, with roughly 90% of them by 2009 — a documentary floor, not an estimate. The high end is the Burnham et al. Lancet survey of 2006, which estimated about 655,000 excess deaths through mid-2006 and was heavily contested on sampling grounds; the later University Collaborative Iraq Mortality Study in PLOS Medicine (2013) estimated about 461,000 excess deaths for 2003–2011 with a 95% uncertainty interval of 48,000–751,000, and the WHO-backed IFHS survey produced a death rate roughly between IBC and the Lancet. Excess-mortality estimates include deaths from collapsed health services and displacement, and are frequently misquoted as counts of people killed.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: UNAMI's bi-monthly Human Rights Reports (2006–2007), Human Rights Watch, and the US Army's own Taguba investigation into Abu Ghraib documented sectarian mass killings and bodies bearing signs of summary execution, torture in official and militia-run detention, enforced disappearance, and the seizure and destruction of homes during sectarian expulsions in Baghdad.
baselineWhat: The population of Iraq at the time of the 2003 invasion
baselineNote: UN estimates put Iraq's population at roughly 26 million in 2003; no full census had been taken since 1987 outside the Kurdish region, so all figures for the period are projections.

baselineSources.title: World Population Prospects — UN Population Division

shareCaveat: The affected figure adds internally displaced people (about 2.7 million at the 2008 peak) to refugees abroad (about 2 million, mostly in Syria and Jordan); large numbers later returned, and some were displaced again after 2014, so it is a peak rather than a permanent total.

title: Military Operations and Mass Displacement in Pakistan's Tribal Districts
actors: The Pakistani military conducted successive offensives against militant groups in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas and Malakand, evacuating whole districts
peopleRange: UNHCR and Pakistani authorities registered around 2-3 million people displaced in weeks by the Malakand and Swat operation of April-May 2009, described by UNHCR at the time as one of the largest and most rapid displacements in recent history; the North Waziristan operation Zarb-e-Azb of June 2014 displaced around 1 million registered people; and successive operations in Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Orakzai, Kurram and South Waziristan from 2008 displaced hundreds of thousands more. Cumulative registered displacement across 2008-2016 is generally put at about 5 million, from Pakistan's FATA Disaster Management Authority and UNHCR registration; people displaced repeatedly are counted more than once.
territoryDesc: The Federally Administered Tribal Areas were merged into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province by constitutional amendment in 2018, ending a separate colonial-era legal regime

flows.label: North Waziristan to Bannu during Operation Zarb-e-Azb
Swat and Malakand to Mardan, Peshawar and Nowshera, 2009

summary: From 2004 the Pakistani army fought a series of campaigns against the Pakistani Taliban and allied groups in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas and adjoining districts, each of which required or produced the evacuation of the civilian population. The largest single episode was the Malakand and Swat operation of spring 2009, when two to three million people left in a matter of weeks, most staying with host families rather than in camps; Operation Zarb-e-Azb in North Waziristan from June 2014 displaced about a million registered people to Bannu and beyond, with the district closed to civilians for years. Displacement was accompanied by curfews, the destruction of houses and bazaars in militant-held areas by both air strikes and militants, and by collective punishment provisions under the colonial-era Frontier Crimes Regulation. Returns were organised in phases from 2015 and mostly completed by 2018, when the tribal areas were merged into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the Frontier Crimes Regulation abolished; returnees found extensive destruction and, in some agencies, restrictions on movement. Independent access to the areas during operations was almost entirely closed, so casualty and damage assessments rest largely on official statements.
contested: Civilian casualty figures from military operations and from US drone strikes in the same areas are disputed; the Pakistani military's counts differ from those of local organisations and of the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

sources.title: Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre - Pakistan
Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (war in North-West Pakistan)
Operation Zarb-e-Azb

deathsNote: No defensible range for civilian deaths caused by the operations themselves. Total conflict deaths in Pakistan from militancy and counter-militancy across 2003-2018 are usually put at 60,000-80,000 in Pakistani official and South Asia Terrorism Portal tallies, but these cover the whole country and include militants and security forces, and cannot be attributed to the displacement operations specifically.
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch and Pakistani human rights organisations documented house demolitions in cleared areas and detention without charge under the Actions (in Aid of Civil Power) Regulation.
baselineWhat: The combined population of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas and Malakand Division at the census nearest the start of the operations
baselineNote: The 1998 census counted 3.18 million in FATA and 4,262,700 in Malakand Division, a combined 7.44 million; by the 2017 census the same areas held about 5.0 million and 7.51 million respectively, some 12.5 million in all. The 2009 Swat and Bajaur operations alone displaced over two million people in a matter of weeks, one of the fastest mass displacements on record, and successive operations through 2014-16 in North and South Waziristan and Khyber displaced hundreds of thousands more.

baselineSources.title: 2009 internal displacement crisis in Pakistan — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: Families were displaced repeatedly across successive operations between 2004 and 2018, so the five-million figure counts displacements rather than distinct people, and the denominator itself grew by two-thirds over the same period.

title: Closure and Blockade of the Gaza Strip
actors: Israel controlling Gaza's land, sea and air access, with Egypt controlling the Rafah crossing, following the Hamas takeover of the territory in June 2007
peopleRange: About 2.1 million people living in the Gaza Strip before October 2023 and roughly 2 million as of 2026, of whom about 1.7 million are UNRWA-registered refugees; before 2000 up to half a million exits a month were recorded, falling to roughly 4,000 a month in the first seven years of the closure
territoryDesc: The Gaza Strip, about 365 km²; as of 2026 Israeli forces hold positions covering roughly half the territory behind the ceasefire's "yellow line", restricting civilian access to that area
summary: After Hamas took control of Gaza in June 2007 Israel designated the territory a "hostile entity" and intensified pre-existing restrictions, closing most crossings to people and goods, imposing a naval blockade and a land buffer zone, and permitting exit through Erez only for defined categories such as medical patients, traders and staff of international organisations; Egypt has separately opened and closed the Rafah crossing according to its own policy. OCHA has recorded that the population grew by more than half during the closure while permitted exits fell by orders of magnitude, and has said the measures raise concerns of collective punishment under international humanitarian and human rights law, calling for the closure to be lifted in line with Security Council resolution 1860. Israel states that the restrictions are a lawful response to armed attacks and to arms smuggling by an organisation it and several states designate as terrorist, and that it permits humanitarian goods and medical exits. Following the October 2023 attacks and the war that followed, movement was almost entirely halted and both crossings were closed for extended periods. Under the ceasefire that began in October 2025 the Rafah crossing reopened on 2 February 2026 on a limited basis, supervised by an EU border assistance mission with Egyptian and Israeli vetting, initially at about 50 people a day in each direction for medical evacuation and return, against a WHO estimate of more than 20,000 patients needing treatment abroad; goods were not admitted through it and reconstruction materials remained restricted.
contested: The central disputes are whether the closure is a lawful blockade and security measure, as Israel maintains, or an unlawful collective punishment and, in the view of many UN bodies and human rights organisations, a form of confinement of the whole civilian population; whether Israel remains the occupying power in Gaza after its 2005 withdrawal, which the ICJ affirmed in 2024 and Israel rejects; and the extent to which Egypt's control of Rafah shares responsibility for the restriction on exit.

sources.title: OCHA oPt: The humanitarian impact of 15 years of the blockade on the Gaza Strip (June 2022)
NPR: Gaza's Rafah border crossing with Egypt reopens for limited traffic (2 February 2026)
Al Jazeera: 'Neither war nor peace' - what Gaza looks like six months into the ceasefire (10 April 2026)

deathsNote: Both fields are null because no body has produced an aggregate death toll attributable to the closure regime itself; its documented harm is deprivation rather than killing. Discrete enforcement deaths are counted separately — ten passengers were killed in the May 2010 Mavi Marmara flotilla raid — and WHO and Physicians for Human Rights-Israel have recorded deaths of patients who died awaiting exit permits, but these have never been aggregated into a toll. Deaths since October 2023 are counted under the Gaza war entry.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation
violenceNote: The ICRC and major human rights organisations have characterised the closure as collective punishment under the Fourth Geneva Convention, and the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification declared famine in Gaza Governorate from 22 August to 19 December 2025.
baselineWhat: The population of the Gaza Strip
baselineNote: The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated the Gaza Strip at about 2.1 million in mid-2023, roughly 1.6 million of them registered refugees; at the imposition of the closure in June 2007 the population was about 1.4 million. The closure regime applies to the entire population, which is why the confined figure and the population figure are the same number.

baselineSources.title: Blockade of the Gaza Strip — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The population grew by roughly half over the closure's span, from about 1.4 million in 2007 to 2.1 million in 2023, so a single-year denominator understates the number of people who have lived under it.
asOfNote: OCHA's reporting through 2026 continues to describe Gaza's population as about 2.1 million; the figure is uncertain after the war's mortality and departures and PCBS has not published a post-war enumeration.

title: Kenya's 2007–08 Post-Election Violence and Displacement
actors: Organized youth gangs and militias aligned with rival political camps attacked communities identified with the other side, and police shot demonstrators, driving mass ethnic separation in the Rift Valley and beyond
peopleRange: Kenya's Commission of Inquiry into Post-Election Violence (the Waki Commission) recorded at least 663,921 people internally displaced, the figure cited by Human Rights Watch. The ICC Prosecutor's filings used a lower figure of approximately 350,000. The Waki number derives from government and Kenya Red Cross registration of displaced people at camps and host sites; the ICC figure appears to count a narrower category. Many of those displaced were tenants and farm workers who never returned to the Rift Valley.

flows.label: Rift Valley → Nyanza and western Kenya
Uasin Gishu → Central Kenya

summary: The disputed announcement of Mwai Kibaki's re-election on 30 December 2007 set off two months of violence concentrated in the Rift Valley, Nyanza, western Kenya and the slums of Nairobi. Attacks were organized along ethnic and political lines, with the burning of homes, evictions of tenants and farm workers, killings at roadblocks and, in the most notorious case, the burning alive of dozens of people sheltering in a church at Kiambaa. Police shot large numbers of demonstrators. The Waki Commission documented 1,133 people killed between 27 December 2007 and the end of February 2008 and at least 663,921 internally displaced; the ICC Prosecutor cited over 1,000 killed, more than 900 documented acts of rape and sexual violence, over 3,500 seriously injured and around 350,000 displaced across six of Kenya's eight provinces. A power-sharing agreement in February 2008 ended the violence. The Waki Commission recommended a special tribunal; it was never created, the ICC cases against six suspects collapsed, and Human Rights Watch found that by 2011 only two murder convictions had resulted.
contested: Responsibility at the political level was never judicially established: the ICC cases against all six suspects, including two men who later became president and deputy president, were withdrawn or not confirmed, with the Prosecutor alleging witness interference and the defendants asserting the cases were baseless.

sources.title: 'Turning Pebbles': Evading Accountability for Post-Election Violence in Kenya — Human Rights Watch
Situation in the Republic of Kenya — International Criminal Court

deathsNote: The Waki Commission's figure of 1,133 dead between 27 December 2007 and the end of February 2008 is a documented count of individual deaths, and functions as a floor rather than an estimate; the ICC Prosecutor described 'over 1,000' killed. Some Kenyan civil society organizations consider the true number higher because deaths in remote areas and among displaced people were not captured, but no higher figure has been systematically established.

atrocityFindings.body: Commission of Inquiry into Post-Election Violence (Waki Commission), Kenya
atrocityFindings.finding: Documented 1,133 people killed and at least 663,921 internally displaced, found the violence to have been in part organized and financed, and recommended a special tribunal to try those most responsible — a recommendation the government did not implement

atrocityFindings.body: International Criminal Court, Pre-Trial Chamber II
atrocityFindings.finding: Authorized the Prosecutor's proprio motu investigation in March 2010 into crimes against humanity in Kenya; charges against all six named suspects were subsequently withdrawn or not confirmed, and the investigation was closed in November 2023

violenceNote: Documented by the Waki Commission, by the ICC Prosecutor's filings recording over 900 acts of rape and sexual violence, and by Human Rights Watch.
baselineWhat: The population of Kenya at the time of the December 2007 election
baselineNote: The 2009 census counted 38,610,097, implying roughly 37.7 million at the end of 2007. The Commission of Inquiry into Post-Election Violence (the Waki Commission) recorded 1,133 deaths and around 350,000 internally displaced in camps, with government and humanitarian figures for total displacement including those who moved in with host communities reaching about 664,000.
shareCaveat: Displacement was concentrated in the Rift Valley, Nyanza and the Nairobi and Naivasha settlements rather than spread nationally, so the national share understates the effect in the affected districts.

title: Internal Displacement from Criminal Violence in Mexico
actors: Cartels and armed criminal groups, and in places security forces, drove rural and small-town populations from their homes across northern, western and southern Mexico
peopleRange: More than 392,000 internally displaced by violence at the end of 2023 according to IDMC; Mexico's statistics agency INEGI separately estimated in its 2024 victimisation survey that about 1,006,800 people changed residence for personal safety because of criminal activity during 2023 alone. The gap reflects different definitions and methods, and Mexico produces no official IDP register.

flows.label: Sierra of Sinaloa → Culiacán (approximate)
Guerrero highlands → Acapulco and coastal towns (approximate)

summary: Since the militarised counter-narcotics campaign launched in December 2006, contests between criminal organisations and between those organisations and the state have emptied villages and urban districts in Guerrero, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Chihuahua, Tamaulipas, Zacatecas and Chiapas, through massacres, extortion, forced recruitment and the burning of homes. IDMC counted more than 392,000 people internally displaced by violence at the end of 2023, while INEGI's national victimisation survey put the number who moved for safety reasons during 2023 alone above one million; Mexico has no official register of the internally displaced and only adopted framework legislation on displacement at state level in a minority of states. The associated disappearances are on a scale of their own: UN experts noted in May 2022 that Mexico's official registry had passed 100,000 disappeared persons, up from about 5,000 reported missing in 2011, and warned of a chronic pattern of impunity, with enforced disappearances continuing daily. Displacement is typically short-distance and unrecorded, with families moving to municipal capitals or across state lines and rarely receiving assistance.
contested: The scale is disputed: IDMC's figure counts people it can verify as displaced by violence, INEGI's household survey produces a figure more than twice as large by asking about safety-driven moves, and the Mexican government has at times denied that internal displacement of this magnitude exists.

sources.title: UNHCR Mexico Internally Displaced People (IDPs) Fact Sheet, August 2024 — ReliefWeb
Mexico: Dark landmark of 100,000 disappearances reflects pattern of impunity, UN experts warn — OHCHR

deathsNote: No body has produced a death toll for displacement-related violence specifically. Mexico's homicide totals since 2007 run into the hundreds of thousands and its official registry of missing and disappeared persons passed 100,000 in May 2022, but neither figure isolates deaths caused by or accompanying displacement, so no range is given.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances and the UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances
atrocityFindings.finding: Mexico's official registry passed 100,000 disappeared persons in May 2022, reflecting a chronic pattern of impunity, with enforced disappearances continuing daily and registered figures likely undercounting the real scale.

violenceNote: Enforced disappearance in Mexico is documented by the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances and the UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances, which recorded the passing of 100,000 registered disappearances in 2022.
baselineWhat: The population of Mexico at the start of the militarised campaign against the cartels
baselineNote: INEGI's 2010 census counted 112.3 million people, implying about 110 million in 2007 when federal forces were deployed against the cartels; the displacement figure is the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre's cumulative stock of people internally displaced by criminal and other violence.

baselineSources.title: IDMC, Global Report on Internal Displacement 2025

shareCaveat: Displacement is concentrated in a handful of states — Guerrero, Chiapas, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Chihuahua and Zacatecas — so a share of the national population makes it look marginal while local shares are far higher.
asOfNote: The figure is IDMC's end-of-year stock of people internally displaced by criminal violence in Mexico and is revised each year as new displacements and returns are recorded.

title: Australia's Northern Territory Emergency Response
actors: The Australian government imposed emergency measures on prescribed Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory, taking compulsory leases over their townships and controlling residents' welfare income
peopleRange: The measures did not physically displace people; they applied to about 45,500 Aboriginal residents of 73 prescribed communities and associated outstations and town camps in the Northern Territory, a figure from the Australian government's own implementation reporting. Compulsory five-year leases were taken over 64-65 community townships, and income management initially quarantined half of welfare payments for all Aboriginal residents of prescribed areas, later extended on a non-racial basis. The permit system controlling access to Aboriginal land was partly removed, and the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 was suspended in relation to the measures until 2010.
territoryDesc: Compulsory five-year leases over 64-65 Aboriginal community townships in the Northern Territory, granting the Commonwealth control of land held under the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act; sources differ between 64 and 65.
summary: In June 2007, following the Little Children are Sacred report on child sexual abuse in Northern Territory Aboriginal communities, the Australian government announced an emergency response that went well beyond the report's recommendations. Legislation passed in August 2007 imposed alcohol and pornography bans, compulsory income management of welfare payments, compulsory five-year leases over 64-65 community townships, changes to the permit system and the deployment of additional police and, initially, army logistics to 73 prescribed communities of about 45,500 people. The measures were made possible by suspending the Racial Discrimination Act 1975, restored in 2010 when the scheme was redesigned in ostensibly non-discriminatory terms. In 2010 the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the rights of indigenous peoples, James Anaya, reported that the intervention was incompatible with Australia's human rights obligations, discriminated on racial grounds and undermined self-determination, while accepting the seriousness of the problems it addressed. The framework continued as Stronger Futures until 2022. The intervention divided Aboriginal opinion in the Territory and remains contested in Australia.
contested: Whether the response was a justified emergency child-protection measure, as the Australian government maintained, or a racially discriminatory imposition, as the UN Special Rapporteur and many Aboriginal organisations argued; the suspension of the Racial Discrimination Act is the central point of dispute, and Aboriginal opinion in affected communities was itself divided.

sources.title: Northern Territory National Emergency Response — Wikipedia
Observations on the Northern Territory Emergency Response in Australia — Report of the UN Special Rapporteur James Anaya (2010)
The Northern Territory Intervention — Castan Centre for Human Rights Law, Monash University

deathsNote: There was no death toll. The intervention operated through land leases, welfare quarantining, alcohol restrictions and increased policing; its documented harms are legal, economic and social rather than lethal.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights and fundamental freedoms of indigenous people (James Anaya)
atrocityFindings.finding: 2010 report finding that the Northern Territory Emergency Response, including the suspension of the Racial Discrimination Act, was incompatible with Australia's international obligations, discriminated on racial grounds and limited indigenous self-determination

violenceNote: The UN Special Rapporteur documented the suspension of racial discrimination protections and the removal of decision-making powers from Aboriginal communities and land-holding bodies.
baselineWhat: The Aboriginal population of the 73 prescribed communities in the Northern Territory when the intervention began
baselineNote: The intervention applied initially to 73 prescribed communities together with town camps and Aboriginal land, and the figure usually cited by the NTER Review Board and human rights bodies for the population directly covered is about 45,000-46,000 people. The Northern Territory's total Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population at the 2006 census was 66,582, and by 2011 measures such as compulsory income management had been extended beyond the original communities.

baselineSources.title: Social Justice Report 2007, Chapter 3: The Northern Territory 'Emergency Response' intervention — Australian Human Rights Commission
Northern Territory National Emergency Response — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The measures were extended and altered over fifteen years, including the 2012 Stronger Futures legislation, so the population subject to them was not fixed at the 2007 figure.

title: Russo-Georgian War (South Ossetia/Abkhazia)
actors: Georgian forces shelled Tskhinvali and moved into South Ossetia; Russia responded with a large-scale military intervention in both South Ossetia and Abkhazia, then recognized both as independent states
peopleRange: about 192,000 people displaced during the five-day war (EU-commissioned Tagliavini report), including ethnic Georgians from South Ossetia and the surrounding buffer zone, and Ossetians who fled to Russia; roughly 20,000-30,000 ethnic Georgians remain unable to return
territoryDesc: South Ossetia and Abkhazia, recognized by Russia as independent states after the war (also recognized by a small number of other states including Nicaragua, Venezuela, Nauru and Syria)

flows.label: South Ossetia buffer zone → Tbilisi-controlled Georgia (Georgians)
South Ossetia → North Ossetia, Russia (Ossetians)

summary: In August 2008, after rising tensions and cross-border shelling, Georgian forces attacked Tskhinvali, the South Ossetian capital; Russia responded with a five-day military intervention that pushed into undisputed Georgian territory before a French-brokered ceasefire. Russia subsequently recognized Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states, a move rejected by Georgia and most of the international community. An EU-commissioned inquiry (the Tagliavini Report, 2009) found Georgia had initiated the attack on Tskhinvali but that this followed a period of provocations, and that Russia's subsequent actions exceeded the bounds of proportionate self-defense in parts of undisputed Georgian territory; about 192,000 people were displaced.
contested: Responsibility for starting the war is formally disputed: the Tagliavini Report attributed the initial shelling to Georgia while criticizing disproportionate Russian actions afterward; the European Court of Human Rights ruled in Georgia v. Russia (II), 2021, that Russia exercised effective control over South Ossetia and Abkhazia and was responsible for human rights violations there after the ceasefire.

sources.title: Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Conflict in Georgia (Tagliavini Report, 2009)
ECtHR: Grand Chamber judgment in Georgia v. Russia (II), 21 January 2021 (press release)
UNHCR: Georgia country operation (displacement overview)

deathsNote: The EU-mandated Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Conflict in Georgia (the Tagliavini report, 2009) totalled approximately 850 deaths: Georgia reported 170 servicemen, 14 police and 228 civilians killed; Russia 67 servicemen; South Ossetian authorities 365 dead. Sources converge closely at this level. The main contested figure is Russia's initial claim of some 2,000 civilians killed in Tskhinvali, which Russian investigators themselves later revised down to about 162 — a discrepancy the Mission noted, since the higher figure had been used to justify the intervention.

atrocityFindings.body: Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Conflict in Georgia (EU/Tagliavini Commission)
atrocityFindings.finding: Concluded that 'several elements suggest the conclusion that ethnic cleansing was carried out against ethnic Georgians in South Ossetia both during and after the August 2008 conflict', while also finding that Georgia's artillery attack on Tskhinvali opened the hostilities

atrocityFindings.body: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), Georgia v. Russia (II)
atrocityFindings.finding: Found Russia responsible for an administrative practice of killings of civilians and burning and looting of houses in South Ossetia and the buffer zone, torture of Georgian prisoners of war, inhuman detention of about 160 civilians, and the inability of roughly 23,000 displaced Georgians to return; the Court held Russia had no jurisdiction during the active phase of hostilities (8-12 August 2008)

violenceNote: The European Court of Human Rights in Georgia v. Russia (II) (2021) found an administrative practice of summary killings of civilians and the burning and looting of Georgian houses in South Ossetia and the buffer zone, torture of Georgian prisoners of war, and the inhuman and degrading detention of about 160 civilians.
baselineWhat: The population of Georgia including Abkhazia and South Ossetia in 2008
baselineNote: Georgia's official estimate for 2008, on the basis later revised by the 2014 census, was about 4.38 million for territory under Tbilisi's control; South Ossetia held roughly 70,000 people and Abkhazia about 215,000-240,000. Peak displacement recorded by UNHCR and the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre was about 192,000, of whom some 127,000 were displaced within Georgia and about 30,000-38,000 South Ossetians crossed briefly into North Ossetia.
shareCaveat: The 192,000 is a peak count: most of those displaced returned within weeks, and about 26,000-35,000 remained displaced long term, so the ratio measures momentary flight rather than lasting expulsion.

title: Kosovo's Declaration of Independence
actors: Kosovo's assembly unilaterally declared independence from Serbia; recognized by the United States and most EU/NATO states, rejected by Serbia, Russia, China and several EU members
peopleRange: no new mass displacement directly resulted from the declaration itself
territoryDesc: The territory of Kosovo, approximately 10,887 km², formerly a province of Serbia administered by the UN since 1999
summary: On 17 February 2008, Kosovo's assembly declared independence from Serbia, ending nearly a decade of UN administration under Resolution 1244. Serbia rejected the declaration as illegal, and Kosovo's sovereignty remains contested: as of 2026 it is recognized by roughly 100 of 193 UN member states, including the United States and most EU and NATO countries, but not by Serbia, Russia, China, or five EU members (Spain, Greece, Cyprus, Romania and Slovakia). The 2010 International Court of Justice advisory opinion found the declaration itself did not violate international law, though it did not rule on Kosovo's statehood as such.
contested: Kosovo's sovereignty and UN membership remain blocked by Serbia and Russia; the legal status of the declaration versus the underlying question of statehood is itself a matter of ongoing dispute among states and scholars.

sources.title: ICJ: Advisory Opinion on Kosovo's Declaration of Independence (2010)
UN Security Council Resolution 1244 (1999) - UN Digital Library
Britannica: Kosovo

deathsNote: The declaration of independence itself was a legal and political act and caused no significant loss of life. It was followed by rioting in Belgrade and by unrest in northern Kosovo in February-March 2008 in which a small number of people died, but no source attributes a death toll to the declaration. The lethal events in Kosovo belong to the 1998-99 war and its aftermath, which are separate entries.

atrocityFindings.body: International Court of Justice
atrocityFindings.finding: Advisory opinion: the unilateral declaration of independence of 17 February 2008 did not violate general international law, Security Council resolution 1244 (1999) or the Constitutional Framework (10 votes to 4). Serbia rejects the political conclusions drawn from the opinion and continues to refuse recognition, as do Russia, China and several EU member states

baselineWhat: The population of Kosovo at the 2008 declaration of independence
baselineNote: No census had been held since 1981 when independence was declared; the 2011 census, boycotted by most Serbs in the north, counted 1,739,825 people, and Kosovo Agency of Statistics back-estimates for 2008 fall around 1.8 million. Serbian authorities dispute Kosovo's statistics and count the territory within Serbia.
shareCaveat: This is a change of sovereignty with no displaced or confined population attached to it; the affected count is zero and a percentage is not meaningful.

title: Boko Haram Insurgency and Lake Chad Basin Displacement
actors: The jihadist group Boko Haram, and its offshoot ISWAP, waged an insurgency based in northeastern Nigeria that spread into Cameroon, Chad and Niger; regional military operations also displaced civilians
peopleRange: roughly 2.6–3.3 million displaced across the Lake Chad Basin — north-east Nigeria, Cameroon's Far North, western Chad and south-east Niger — over the course of the insurgency

flows.label: Borno State, Nigeria → Minawao camp, Cameroon
Borno State → Diffa, Niger
Borno State → Baga Sola, Chad
Rural Borno → Maiduguri IDP camps (internal)

summary: The jihadist insurgency Boko Haram, founded in northeastern Nigeria in the early 2000s, launched an armed uprising in 2009 seeking to establish an Islamic state, and by the mid-2010s had seized territory across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states and expanded operations into neighboring Cameroon, Chad and Niger around Lake Chad. A 2016 split produced the rival Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP). Insurgent attacks, mass abductions (including the 2014 kidnapping of 276 schoolgirls in Chibok), and government counterinsurgency operations have together displaced roughly 2.6-3 million people across the four-country Lake Chad Basin region, with around 2 million displaced within Nigeria alone, and have directly killed an estimated 35,000-40,000 people since 2009, with the wider humanitarian toll, including famine-linked deaths, considered substantially higher. The crisis remains active, with periodic upsurges in violence and displacement as of the mid-2020s.

sources.title: IOM: Over 2.6 Million Displaced in Lake Chad Basin
IOM: Lake Chad Basin Displacement Affects Nearly Three Million People
IDMC: Looking beyond Boko Haram in the Lake Chad region

deathsNote: UNDP's 2021 study estimated some 350,000 deaths attributable to the conflict in north-east Nigeria by end-2020, but roughly 314,000 of these were indirect — mainly children under five dying from the collapse of food, water and health systems — leaving about 35,000 direct conflict deaths. The 350,000 headline is routinely quoted as a killing toll, which UNDP explicitly did not claim; the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect earlier cited around 17,000 killed in the fighting. Figures cover Nigeria only, not Cameroon, Chad or Niger.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: International Criminal Court, Office of the Prosecutor
atrocityFindings.finding: On concluding the Nigeria preliminary examination, found a reasonable basis to believe Boko Haram and its splinter groups committed murder, rape, sexual slavery including forced pregnancy and forced marriage, enslavement, torture, cruel treatment, child recruitment and persecution, and that Nigerian security forces committed murder, rape, torture, enforced disappearance, forcible transfer of population, illegal detention and child recruitment

violenceNote: The ICC Prosecutor's December 2020 statement concluding the Nigeria preliminary examination named murder, rape and sexual slavery, enslavement, torture and child recruitment by Boko Haram and ISWAP, and murder, rape, torture, enforced disappearance, forcible transfer and illegal detention by Nigerian security forces; UNICEF, OCHA and Human Rights Watch have documented the same abduction and mass-killing patterns across the Lake Chad Basin.
baselineWhat: The population of the conflict-affected areas of the Lake Chad basin - Borno, Yobe and Adamawa states in Nigeria, Far North Cameroon, Diffa in Niger and the Lac province of Chad - when the insurgency escalated
baselineNote: Nigeria's 2006 census gave Borno 4.17 million, Yobe 2.32 million and Adamawa 3.17 million; Far North Cameroon held roughly 3.5 million and Diffa and Lac about 1.2 million between them, giving some 14-15 million around 2009. OCHA now describes a considerably larger affected population in the same areas, reflecting rapid growth over the intervening years.
shareCaveat: The displacement total is cumulative across four countries and seventeen years and includes people displaced repeatedly and, in the Nigerian case, large numbers subsequently returned or relocated when camps were closed from 2021.
asOfNote: OCHA and IOM reporting through 2026 continues to record several million displaced across the basin; the figure moves with each round of military operations, camp closures and returns.

title: Closed IDP Camps at Menik Farm, Sri Lanka
actors: The Sri Lankan government and military holding Tamil civilians who left the final conflict zone in guarded camps in Vavuniya district pending screening for LTTE membership
peopleRange: About 280,000-300,000 civilians were moved into camps in Vavuniya district in the closing weeks of the civil war in 2009, of whom more than 200,000 were held at Menik Farm alone, making it briefly one of the largest settlements in the country; by September 2009 around 10,000 residents had been separated out as suspected LTTE members
territoryDesc: The Menik Farm complex of fenced zones near Cheddikulam in Vavuniya district, together with smaller camps and public buildings used as holding sites across the Vanni
summary: When the Sri Lankan civil war ended in May 2009, civilians who emerged from the last LTTE-held pocket were transported to closed camps in Vavuniya district, the largest of which, Menik Farm, held more than 200,000 people behind fencing and under military administration. Residents were initially not permitted to leave at all, humanitarian and media access was tightly controlled, and families were separated when individuals were removed for screening. The government said the restrictions were necessary to clear landmines in the north before return and to identify LTTE cadres hiding among the displaced, and it undertook to release the population within six months. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and human rights organisations described the sites as internment camps, and Tamil political representatives used stronger language still. From 1 December 2009 restrictions were partially eased so that residents could leave for up to fifteen days after registering with the authorities, and some were released permanently subject to police reporting; the military said it would trace those who failed to return. Resettlement proceeded unevenly over the following two years and Menik Farm was officially closed on 25 September 2012, though thousands of families remained without a permanent place of return years afterwards.
contested: Disputed are whether the confinement was a proportionate and temporary security and demining measure, as the government maintained, or unlawful mass internment of a civilian population on ethnic lines; the duration of detention, the adequacy of the screening process, and the scale of disappearances of people removed from the camps remain the subject of competing accounts.

sources.title: Menik Farm - camp population, movement restrictions, government justification and closure
Human rights in Sri Lanka - post-war detention and rehabilitation facilities

deathsNote: No source establishes a death toll for the closed camps themselves. Human Rights Watch's October 2009 reporting on Menik Farm documented severe overcrowding, water rationing well below UN minimums, flooding and deteriorating shelter, but provided no aggregate mortality figure; deaths from the final phase of the war that immediately preceded internment are counted under the civil war entry.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch documented that the Sri Lankan government was holding 255,551 displaced Tamils in camps and hospitals in late September 2009, 'unlawfully depriving them of their liberty and freedom of movement', and described the screening process as a pretext for prolonged detention.
baselineWhat: The Tamil civilian population trapped in the LTTE-held Vanni during the final phase of the war
baselineNote: The government's own pre-offensive estimates put the civilian population of the Vanni at 100,000-150,000, while UN agencies working from food distribution and local administrative records argued for 300,000-360,000; the roughly 290,000 people who actually emerged and were interned settled the dispute in favour of the higher figure, and it became central to the later argument over civilian casualties in the final months.
shareCaveat: The camps held very nearly everyone who left the conflict zone, so the ratio approaches 100 per cent by construction; it describes the completeness of the internment rather than a selection from a wider population.

title: June 2010 Ethnic Violence in Southern Kyrgyzstan
actors: Kyrgyz crowds and armed groups, with elements of the security forces implicated, attacked ethnic Uzbek neighbourhoods in Osh and Jalal-Abad following the collapse of central authority
peopleRange: More than 400,000 displaced according to the Kyrgyzstan Inquiry Commission, of whom roughly 75,000-100,000 crossed briefly into Uzbekistan before returning within weeks; over 1,800 houses destroyed according to official data cited by Human Rights Watch, with satellite imagery indicating several thousand buildings destroyed in total.

flows.label: Osh and Jalal-Abad → Andijan region, Uzbekistan

summary: In the political vacuum that followed the April 2010 overthrow of President Bakiyev, violence erupted in Osh on 11 June 2010 and spread to Jalal-Abad, lasting about four days. The independent Kyrgyzstan Inquiry Commission, chaired by Kimmo Kiljunen, recorded at least 470 deaths, around three-quarters of them ethnic Uzbeks, some 1,900 injured and more than 400,000 people displaced; Human Rights Watch cites official data of 426 deaths, 276 of them Uzbek. Whole Uzbek mahallas were burned. The Commission concluded that if proven in court, certain acts, including murder, rape and other sexual violence and persecution directed against the Uzbek minority, would amount to crimes against humanity, and found that the authorities had failed in their duty to prevent the violence and protect citizens. Human Rights Watch subsequently documented torture, arbitrary arrest and unfair trials in an investigation and prosecution process that fell disproportionately on ethnic Uzbeks. A Kyrgyz national commission reached a different conclusion in January 2011, attributing provocation to the Uzbek minority. Similar interethnic violence in Osh in 1990 forms the background to the events.
contested: Responsibility is directly disputed: the international Kyrgyzstan Inquiry Commission found the violence disproportionately targeted ethnic Uzbeks and may constitute crimes against humanity, while the Kyrgyz national commission attributed provocation to Uzbek leaders; the role of army and police units in the attacks is also contested.

sources.title: FIDH: Conclusions of the International Investigation Commission's report on the June 2010 events in Kyrgyzstan
Human Rights Watch: Distorted Justice - Kyrgyzstan's Flawed Investigations and Trials on the 2010 Violence

deathsNote: The lower figure is the official Kyrgyz death count cited by Human Rights Watch (276 Uzbeks, 105 Kyrgyz, 45 unidentified); the higher figure is the Kyrgyzstan Inquiry Commission's, which found about 74 per cent of the dead were ethnic Uzbeks. The gap reflects unidentified bodies and deaths not registered with the authorities.

atrocityFindings.body: Kyrgyzstan Inquiry Commission (independent international commission)
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that acts including murder, rape and other forms of sexual violence, physical violence and persecution directed at ethnic Uzbeks would, if proven in court, constitute crimes against humanity, and that the authorities failed to prevent the violence
