violenceNote: The Kyrgyzstan Inquiry Commission documented murder, rape and other sexual violence and destruction of Uzbek property, and Human Rights Watch documented torture and arbitrary detention in the investigations that followed.
baselineWhat: The population of Osh and Jalal-Abad provinces including Osh city
baselineNote: Kyrgyz national statistics for 2010 give roughly 1.35 million in Osh province and Osh city combined and about 1.0 million in Jalal-Abad. Ethnic Uzbeks, the principal victims, numbered around 700,000-750,000 across southern Kyrgyzstan.
shareCaveat: The 400,000 counts everyone displaced at the height of the violence, including short-distance and short-duration flight; about 75,000 crossed into Uzbekistan and most had returned within weeks.

title: Libya since 2011: Forced Displacement and Migrant Detention
actors: Armed groups expelled whole communities — most completely the town of Tawergha — during and after the 2011 uprising and the 2014–2020 civil wars, while successive authorities and militias have arbitrarily detained migrants and refugees in a network of centres
peopleRange: This is an order-of-magnitude estimate of cumulative conflict displacement since 2011 rather than a single measured figure. Verified reference points: Human Rights Watch records the entire population of Tawergha, about 48,000 people, displaced since August 2011 and still unable to return in 2019, and over 125,000 people internally displaced as of August 2024, including communities expelled from Benghazi and Derna since 2014. Displacement peaked far higher during the 2011 war and the 2014–2020 fighting, with several hundred thousand displaced at a time before large-scale returns. Separately, IOM recorded over 760,000 migrants in Libya in July 2024, tens of thousands of whom have passed through arbitrary detention; they are not counted in the displacement figure.

flows.label: Tawergha → camps in Tripoli, Benghazi and elsewhere
Benghazi and Derna → western Libya and abroad

summary: Libya's 2011 uprising and the civil wars that followed produced repeated waves of displacement and a system of detention for migrants and refugees. The clearest single case of forced displacement is Tawergha: its entire civilian population of roughly 48,000, accused collectively of siding with Gaddafi's forces against Misrata, fled in August 2011 and was prevented from returning for years; Human Rights Watch found the town systematically destroyed and looted, described the expulsion as collective punishment that may amount to crimes against humanity, and reported that as of December 2018 only about 100 families had attempted to resettle. Communities were also expelled from Benghazi and Derna by the Libyan Arab Armed Forces from 2014. Human Rights Watch recorded over 125,000 internally displaced people as of August 2024. In parallel, migrants and refugees intercepted at sea by the EU-supported Libyan Coast Guard — 16,466 by September 2024 — are held in facilities controlled by state bodies and armed groups. The UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Libya concluded in March 2023 that there were reasonable grounds to believe war crimes and crimes against humanity had been committed, including murder, enslavement, torture, rape and sexual slavery, and that migrants had been systematically targeted and tortured.
contested: Responsibility for the Tawergha expulsion is disputed between Misratan authorities, who cite crimes committed by Tawerghans in 2011, and human rights organizations, which describe collective punishment; the role of EU support for the Libyan Coast Guard in enabling detention abuses is contested between the EU and the UN Fact-Finding Mission.

sources.title: Libya: Displaced Population Can't Go Home — Human Rights Watch
Libya: Urgent action needed to remedy deteriorating human rights situation, UN Fact-Finding Mission warns in final report — OHCHR
World Report 2025: Libya — Human Rights Watch

deathsNote: No cumulative death toll for Libya since 2011 has been established, and the available counts are partial and cover different things: Human Rights Watch cites 1,536 people found dead or missing in the central Mediterranean after departing Libya in 2024 alone, while deaths in detention, in the 2011 war and in the 2014–2020 civil wars have never been systematically counted. The UN Fact-Finding Mission documented murder, extrajudicial killing and enforced disappearance without producing totals.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Libya (Human Rights Council)
atrocityFindings.finding: Concluded in its final report that there are reasonable grounds to believe a wide array of war crimes and crimes against humanity have been committed by state security forces and armed groups, including arbitrary detention, murder, rape, enslavement, extrajudicial killing and enforced disappearance, and that migrants in particular have been systematically tortured and subjected to sexual slavery

violenceNote: Documented by the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Libya in its March 2023 final report and by Human Rights Watch, which recorded the systematic destruction and looting of Tawergha.
baselineWhat: The population of Libya at the start of the 2011 uprising
baselineNote: World Bank and UN Population Division estimates put Libya at about 6.2 million in 2011. The displacement counted here includes the complete emptying of Tawergha - some 40,000 people expelled in 2011 and unable to return until 2018 - alongside the displacement waves of the 2014-2020 civil wars.
shareCaveat: The figure is cumulative displacement since 2011, not a current stock: IOM has recorded most Libyan IDPs as returned, with roughly 125,000 still displaced in recent rounds, while the separately detained migrant population is not drawn from the Libyan baseline at all.
asOfNote: IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix rounds through 2025 record several hundred thousand migrants present in Libya alongside a much reduced IDP caseload; both figures are revised at each round.

title: South Sudan Independence and Civil War
actors: South Sudan seceded from Sudan in 2011 after a referendum; a 2013 power struggle between President Salva Kiir and former Vice President Riek Machar's forces triggered a civil war fought largely along ethnic lines
peopleRange: the 2013-2020 civil war displaced about 4 million people, including roughly 2.2 million refugees in neighboring countries and 1.8 million internally displaced; an estimated 190,000-380,000 people died
territoryDesc: South Sudan (about 644,000 km2) became Africa's newest state after seceding from Sudan in July 2011; the oil-rich Abyei area straddling the border remains disputed, administered under interim arrangements pending an unresolved final status referendum

flows.label: South Sudan → Bidi Bidi, Uganda
South Sudan → Kakuma, Kenya
South Sudan → Gambela, Ethiopia
Abyei/border area → Sudan

summary: South Sudan became independent from Sudan in July 2011 following a 2005 peace agreement and a near-unanimous 2011 referendum, but the disputed, oil-producing Abyei border area was left unresolved, with a promised referendum there never held. In December 2013, a political and military split between President Salva Kiir (Dinka) and former Vice President Riek Machar (Nuer) escalated into a civil war marked by ethnically targeted violence; a 2018 peace deal and unity government only partially stemmed the fighting. The war displaced roughly 4 million people, including about 2.2 million refugees in Uganda, Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya and elsewhere and 1.8 million internally displaced, with death toll estimates ranging from about 190,000 to 380,000. A UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan documented widespread atrocities, including ethnically targeted killings and sexual violence, by multiple armed actors.
contested: Death toll estimates for the 2013-2020 civil war vary considerably, from roughly 190,000 (battle-related) to a widely cited 380,000 including indirect deaths; the legal status of Abyei remains unresolved between Sudan and South Sudan.

sources.title: Congressional Research Service: South Sudan's Civil War
CFR Global Conflict Tracker: Instability in South Sudan
Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect: South Sudan

deathsNote: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine's 2018 statistical study estimated roughly 383,000 excess deaths between December 2013 and April 2018 — widely reported as about 400,000 — of which around half, some 190,000, were violent deaths, the remainder attributable to disease and hunger caused by the conflict. The headline figure is frequently misquoted as the number of people 'killed', which the study's own decomposition does not support. More than 4 million people were displaced, about 2.5 million of them across borders.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan
atrocityFindings.finding: Standing Human Rights Council commission established in 2016 that has repeatedly documented violations amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity, with a particular focus on conflict-related sexual violence, and has named individuals it holds responsible

violenceNote: The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan and UNMISS documented ethnically targeted massacres such as the December 2013 killings of Nuer civilians in Juba and the 2014 Bentiu massacre of more than 400 people, conflict-related sexual violence used systematically, and the obstruction of aid and destruction of villages that drove the LSHTM-measured excess mortality.
baselineWhat: The population of South Sudan at independence
baselineNote: The 2008 Sudanese census counted 8.26 million people in the southern states, a figure the Juba authorities rejected as a substantial undercount; UN estimates put South Sudan at about 10.3-10.5 million at independence in 2011. At the peak of the civil war some 2.3 million people were refugees, chiefly in Uganda, Sudan and Ethiopia, and about 1.9 million were displaced internally, with roughly 200,000 sheltering in UN protection-of-civilians sites.

baselineSources.title: UNHCR Operational Data Portal: South Sudan situation

shareCaveat: The total combines refugees and internally displaced people over seven years and includes repeated displacements of the same families, so it is not a count of distinct individuals.

title: Syrian Civil War: Refugees and Internal Displacement
actors: A popular uprising against the government of Bashar al-Assad escalated into a multi-sided civil war involving Syrian government forces, an array of opposition and jihadist groups, Kurdish-led forces, and foreign militaries (Russia, Iran, Turkey, the US, and Israel), driving the largest displacement crisis in the world until Assad's government fell in December 2024.
peopleRange: about 13 million at the peak — roughly 6.8 million refugees and 6.5 million internally displaced; since the fall of the Assad government UNHCR has recorded some 1.67 million refugee returns and 1.9 million IDP returns, with about 5.5 million still internally displaced as of mid-2026

flows.label: Aleppo → Turkey
Homs/Damascus area → Lebanon
Deraa/southern Syria → Jordan (Zaatari camp)
Idlib → IDP camps, northwest Syria

summary: What began as peaceful protests against Bashar al-Assad's government in March 2011 escalated into a full-scale civil war involving the Syrian government (backed by Russia and Iran), a fragmented array of opposition and jihadist factions, Kurdish-led forces in the northeast, Turkey, and periodic Israeli and US strikes. Over more than a decade, the war displaced over 13 million people at its peak: roughly 6.8 million refugees, hosted mainly by Turkey, Lebanon, and Jordan, and 6.7–7.2 million internally displaced within Syria, alongside hundreds of thousands of deaths. Chemical weapons attacks, sieges of cities such as Aleppo and Ghouta, and the rise and fall of ISIS's self-declared caliphate compounded the humanitarian crisis. Assad's government collapsed in a rapid opposition offensive in December 2024, after which over a million Syrians began returning from abroad and from internal displacement, though the country's political transition and the fate of millions of remaining refugees and IDPs remained unresolved as of 2026.
contested: Casualty and displacement estimates vary among UN agencies, the former Syrian government, and opposition-aligned monitoring groups (such as the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights); characterizations of the conflict's origins and the roles of foreign state and non-state actors remain politically disputed.

sources.title: UNHCR: Syria Regional Refugee Response operational data
UNHCR: Historic return of displaced Syrians presents opportunity and urgent challenges
Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre: Syria

deathsNote: The UN Human Rights Office's statistically modelled estimate of 306,887 civilian deaths (95 per cent credible interval 281,443-337,971) covers 1 March 2011 to 31 March 2021 and counts civilians only, combining 143,350 individually documented deaths with 163,537 imputed via multiple systems estimation; the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights' nearly 618,000 covers all deaths including 343,344 combatants through 2024 and excludes over 55,000 it believes died under torture in government detention but could not document. The former Syrian government rejected both, and neither total captures the March 2025 coastal killings or later violence.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic
atrocityFindings.finding: Established by Human Rights Council resolution S-17/1 on 22 August 2011; successive reports found war crimes and crimes against humanity including systematic torture and deaths in detention ('Web of Agony'), sieges and starvation, chemical weapons use, enforced disappearance and forced displacement, and in 2025 found the March coastal violence widespread and systematic

atrocityFindings.body: UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR)
atrocityFindings.finding: Report of 28 June 2022 estimating 306,887 civilian deaths over the conflict's first decade

violenceNote: The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria, OHCHR, the Syrian Network for Human Rights and Human Rights Watch documented sieges and deliberate starvation of civilian areas, chemical attacks, systematic torture and deaths in government detention, tens of thousands of enforced disappearances, sexual violence, and the destruction of homes and neighbourhoods.
baselineWhat: The population of Syria at the start of the uprising
baselineNote: World Bank and UN series put Syria's population at about 21 million in 2011; the Syrian Central Bureau of Statistics projected 22.5 million from the 2004 census. At the peak of the displacement roughly 6.8 million Syrians were registered as refugees, chiefly in Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan, and about 7 million were displaced inside the country — together more than half the pre-war population.

baselineSources.title: UNHCR Operational Data Portal: Syrian Arab Republic

shareCaveat: The total counts refugees and internally displaced people together and includes people displaced repeatedly over fourteen years, so it is not a count of distinct individuals; substantial returns since the change of government have reduced the standing figure.
asOfNote: Displacement figures have been falling since the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, with over a million refugee returns recorded and the UN projecting up to a million more during 2026, so the headline figure describes the war's peak rather than the current position.

title: Northern Mali's Seizure and the Malian Conflict
actors: The Tuareg MNLA and then the Islamist groups Ansar Dine, MUJAO and AQIM seized northern Mali in 2012; French and Malian forces retook the towns in 2013, after which jihadist groups, ethnic militias, the Malian army and Russian Wagner personnel have fought across the centre and north
peopleRange: Human Rights Watch recorded roughly 400,000 people displaced from northern Mali in 2012, split between internal displacement and refugees in Mauritania, Burkina Faso and Niger. ACAPS reported about 355,000 internally displaced as of April 2024, down from over 440,000 in October 2022, alongside 288,123 Malian refugees in asylum countries. A central estimate of around half a million displaced at a given point is defensible; the figures are UNHCR, IOM-DTM and government estimates and different waves involve the same populations.
territoryDesc: The regions of Timbuktu, Gao and Kidal — roughly two-thirds of Mali's land area — were held by the MNLA and then by Ansar Dine, MUJAO and AQIM from April 2012 until the French-led intervention of January 2013.

flows.label: Timbuktu region → Mbera camp, Mauritania
Gao region → Niger (Tillabéri)
Mopti and central Mali → Bamako

summary: In early 2012 Tuareg fighters of the MNLA, many returning armed from Libya, seized northern Mali, and were rapidly displaced by the Islamist groups Ansar Dine, MUJAO and AQIM, which governed Timbuktu, Gao and Kidal until French forces intervened in January 2013. Human Rights Watch documented summary executions, rape, amputations, recruitment of children as young as eleven and the destruction of religious and cultural sites, together with executions and disappearances by the Malian army, and recorded some 400,000 people displaced. The conflict subsequently spread south into central Mali and across the borders into Burkina Faso and western Niger, drawing in the jihadist coalitions JNIM and Islamic State in the Greater Sahara and communal militias. In May 2023 the UN human rights office reported that Malian troops and foreign military personnel had killed over 500 people at Moura in March 2022, the great majority summarily executed, with at least 58 women and girls raped, and stated that these acts amount to war crimes and could amount to crimes against humanity. Around 355,000 people remained internally displaced in Mali in April 2024, with a further 288,000 Malian refugees abroad.
contested: Mali's authorities reject the UN's findings on Moura, maintaining that the operation killed combatants, and denied investigators access to the site; the presence and conduct of Russian Wagner personnel is disputed between Bamako and Western governments.

sources.title: World Report 2013: Mali — Human Rights Watch
Malian troops, foreign military personnel killed over 500 people during military operation in Moura in March 2022 — UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR)
Mali: Situation of internal displacement — ACAPS briefing note, June 2024

deathsNote: No authoritative cumulative death toll exists for the Malian conflict since 2012. Individual episodes have been documented in detail — most notably the UN human rights office's finding that over 500 people were killed at Moura in March 2022 — but there has been no country-wide mortality study, and event-based conflict monitoring datasets covering the Sahel are not reconciled with one another.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR) / UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in Mali
atrocityFindings.finding: Reported that Malian armed forces and foreign military personnel killed more than 500 people during the operation at Moura in March 2022, the vast majority summarily executed, with at least 58 women and girls raped or subjected to sexual violence, and that these acts amount to war crimes and could amount to crimes against humanity

violenceNote: Documented by Human Rights Watch for the 2012–13 occupation of the north, including the destruction of shrines and manuscripts in Timbuktu, and by the UN Human Rights Office for the 2022 Moura operation.
baselineWhat: The population of Mali's three northern regions — Timbuktu, Gao and Kidal — seized in 2012
baselineNote: Mali's 2009 census recorded 681,691 in Tombouctou region, 544,120 in Gao and 67,739 in Kidal, about 1.29 million in total across a territory larger than France. UNHCR and OCHA recorded roughly 500,000 displaced from the north in 2012-13, split between internally displaced Malians and refugees in Mauritania, Niger and Burkina Faso.
shareCaveat: The 500,000 covers the 2012-13 displacement from the north; the conflict has since spread to central Mali and the Liptako-Gourma borderlands, where the displaced population is drawn from a much larger denominator not included here.
asOfNote: The conflict continues and current displacement figures, published by OCHA and UNHCR, reflect a different and largely central-Malian geography from the 2012 northern seizure this figure describes.

title: Rohingya Confined in Closed Camps and Villages in Rakhine State, Myanmar
actors: Myanmar state and Rakhine State authorities, and since 2024 the Arakan Army, confining Rohingya and Kaman Muslims to camps and villages under movement restrictions and statelessness imposed by the 1982 Citizenship Law
peopleRange: About 130,000-146,000 Rohingya and Kaman Muslims held in some 24 camps in central Rakhine since 2012 (Human Rights Watch counted 131,900 in 2020; Australian government reporting cited by the UK Home Office in 2025 gives around 145,000 in displacement camps), within a wider Rohingya population in Rakhine of roughly 500,000-600,000 subject to township-level movement restrictions
territoryDesc: Around 24 camps and camp-like settlements in Sittwe, Pauktaw, Myebon, Kyaukpyu and other townships of central Rakhine, together with segregated villages and the Aung Mingalar quarter of Sittwe
summary: After communal violence in 2012 displaced more than 140,000 people in Rakhine State, Myanmar authorities moved Rohingya and Kaman Muslims into camps in central Rakhine and did not allow them to return home, maintaining the camps with barbed-wire fencing, checkpoints, curfews and a permission system that in practice prevents residents from leaving. A 2019 survey found that 99.6 per cent of Rohingya respondents reported being prevented from travelling outside their township, and residents have described paying bribes and passing through multiple checkpoints to reach hospitals or markets. The confinement rests on a wider legal architecture: the 1982 Citizenship Law, which ties citizenship to membership of recognised national races and requires proof of pre-1948 residence, has been applied to exclude the Rohingya and render them stateless across generations. From 2017 the government announced a camp-closure programme, but it has largely built permanent structures on or near existing camp sites without restoring freedom of movement or land, an approach that UN assessments have said contributes to permanent segregation. Human Rights Watch characterises the regime as apartheid and persecution amounting to crimes against humanity; Myanmar's governments have rejected this, describing the arrangements as temporary humanitarian shelter and security management. Since the Arakan Army took control of most of Rakhine State in 2024 the camps have changed hands but restrictions on movement, arbitrary arrest and denial of citizenship have continued, and the state is largely cut off from humanitarian access.
contested: At issue is whether the camps are humanitarian shelter that residents are free in principle to leave, as successive Myanmar governments have maintained, or indefinite detention on ethnic and religious grounds amounting to the crimes against humanity of apartheid and persecution, as Human Rights Watch, the UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar's mandate and several UN bodies have argued; the exclusion of the Rohingya from the 1982 Citizenship Law's list of national races is likewise defended in Myanmar as a factual determination about historical residence and described externally as discriminatory denationalisation.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch, "An Open Prison without End": Myanmar's Mass Detention of Rohingya in Rakhine State (October 2020)
UK Home Office, Country Policy and Information Note: Rohingya, Burma (January 2026)

deathsNote: No source quantifies mortality attributable to the confinement regime as such. The 2012 violence that produced the camps killed a number Myanmar's government put in the low hundreds, with Human Rights Watch documenting at least 70 Rohingya killed in a single day at Yan Thei and bodies dumped in mass graves; deaths in the camps from denied healthcare, and deaths at sea among those who fled by boat between 2012 and 2015, are documented qualitatively by UNHCR, MSF and the UN Fact-Finding Mission but have never been enumerated. The mass killings of the 2016-17 clearance operations are a separate event.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar
atrocityFindings.finding: Found decades of institutionalised persecution of the Rohingya — denial of legal status and citizenship, segregation in camps and confined areas, and severe restrictions on movement, food, education, healthcare, marriage and birth registration — amounting to crimes against humanity, and recommended investigation of Myanmar's senior generals for genocide

atrocityFindings.body: International Court of Justice
atrocityFindings.finding: The Gambia v. Myanmar, provisional measures: the Rohingya 'appear to constitute a protected group' under the Genocide Convention and face a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice; Myanmar unanimously ordered to prevent genocidal acts, control its armed forces, preserve evidence and report to the Court. Myanmar contests the allegations

violenceNote: Documented by Human Rights Watch in 'All You Can Do is Pray' (2013) — at least 70 killed at Yan Thei, mass graves, mass round-ups of Rohingya, at least 4,862 structures and nine Sittwe mosques destroyed, and the denial of citizenship under the 1982 Citizenship Law — and by the UN Fact-Finding Mission (2018) on segregation, confinement and denial of legal status.
baselineWhat: The Rohingya population of Rakhine State, Myanmar, before the 2012 violence
baselineNote: Rohingya were excluded from Myanmar's 2014 census, so all figures are estimates: about 1.0-1.4 million lived in Rakhine State before 2017, concentrated in the northern townships where they were 80-98 per cent of the population. Around 140,000 were confined to camps in central Rakhine after the 2012 violence, more than 740,000 fled to Bangladesh in 2017, and roughly 300,000-600,000 remain in Rakhine.

baselineSources.title: Human Rights Watch, Myanmar: Mass Detention of Rohingya in Squalid Camps

shareCaveat: The confined population is a share of those who remained in Rakhine, not of the pre-2012 Rohingya population, most of which has since been expelled to Bangladesh.
asOfNote: Camp populations and movement restrictions have shifted since the Arakan Army took control of most of Rakhine State in 2024-25, and current numbers are not independently verifiable.

title: Central African Republic Conflict and the Flight of the Muslim Population
actors: The Séléka coalition seized power in Bangui in March 2013; anti-balaka militias then attacked Muslim civilians across the west, and ex-Séléka groups attacked Christian communities, emptying much of the country's Muslim population into Chad and Cameroon
peopleRange: UNHCR reported over 935,000 people displaced inside CAR in January 2014, the peak of the crisis, of whom more than half were in Bangui. IDMC recorded 426,200 IDPs and 457,480 CAR refugees in neighbouring countries as of May 2015, with most having fled since December 2012. Displacement has remained between roughly 600,000 and 750,000 IDPs plus a similar number of refugees in the years since. A figure of about one million displaced at any given time is the reasonable central estimate; these are UNHCR and IDMC operational estimates, and the same people appear in successive waves.

flows.label: Western CAR → Cameroon (Garoua-Boulaï and the eastern border)
Northern CAR → Chad (Sido)

summary: The mainly Muslim Séléka coalition took Bangui in March 2013 and its fighters committed widespread killings and looting against non-Muslim communities. From late 2013 the anti-balaka, self-defence militias drawn largely from Christian and animist communities, attacked Muslim civilians across the west of the country; Human Rights Watch documented massacres in Bossangoa, Zéré and elsewhere and recorded 450,000 people displaced and over 70,000 refugees by December 2013. The UN International Commission of Inquiry, reporting on 22 December 2014, found that all parties — FACA, Séléka and anti-balaka — had committed war crimes, that the anti-balaka campaign against Muslims amounted to ethnic cleansing constituting a crime against humanity, and that the threshold for genocidal intent had not been established. It estimated 3,000 to 6,000 people killed while calling this a probable radical under-estimate. Most of the Muslim population of the west left for Chad and Cameroon or was evacuated; displacement inside the country peaked above 935,000 in January 2014 and has remained high, with continued fighting in the east and centre through the 2020s.
contested: Whether the violence against CAR's Muslims amounted to genocide was contested: the UN Commission of Inquiry found ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity but concluded that genocidal intent was not established, a conclusion some advocacy organizations disputed.

sources.title: 'They Came To Kill': Escalating Atrocities in the Central African Republic — Human Rights Watch
Final report of the International Commission of Inquiry on the Central African Republic (S/2014/928)
Central African Republic: IDPs face significant challenges as instability and political transition continue — IDMC

deathsNote: The range is the UN International Commission of Inquiry's own estimate for the period it examined, which it described as likely a radical under-estimate because insecurity and lack of access prevented systematic investigation across most of the country. Deaths in the years since 2015 are not included in the range and have never been comprehensively counted.

atrocityFindings.body: International Commission of Inquiry on the Central African Republic (UN Security Council resolution 2127)
atrocityFindings.finding: Found that all parties committed war crimes, that the anti-balaka campaign of ethnic cleansing against the Muslim population constituted a crime against humanity, and that the evidentiary threshold for genocidal intent had not been met; estimated 3,000–6,000 killed while calling this a likely radical under-estimate

violenceNote: Documented by Human Rights Watch's field investigations in 2013 and by the UN International Commission of Inquiry, which recorded the deliberate denial of access to food, water and medical care to besieged Muslim communities.
baselineWhat: The population of the Central African Republic when the Seleka took Bangui
baselineNote: UN estimates give about 4.6-4.7 million for 2013; the last census was in 2003. The Muslim population, the main target of the anti-balaka campaign of 2013-14, was roughly 10-15% of the total and was almost entirely driven out of the west of the country.
shareCaveat: The 1 million combines internally displaced people with refugees in Cameroon, Chad and the DRC, and counts repeat displacement over more than a decade; measured against the Muslim population of the west, the displacement was close to total.
asOfNote: UNHCR figures for CAR displacement have hovered around a million through the mid-2020s, roughly half internally displaced and half refugees, with periodic spikes around elections.

title: Russia's Annexation of Crimea
actors: Unmarked Russian troops ('little green men') seized control of Crimea following Ukraine's Euromaidan revolution; Russia staged a referendum and formally annexed the peninsula in March 2014
peopleRange: an estimated 30,000-40,000 people, disproportionately Crimean Tatars and pro-Ukrainian residents, fled to mainland Ukraine in the initial period, with further displacement and repression of Crimean Tatars since
territoryDesc: The Crimean peninsula, approximately 27,000 km², annexed by Russia and administered as Russian federal territory, not recognized as such by Ukraine or most UN member states

flows.label: Crimea → Kyiv-controlled Ukraine

summary: In late February 2014, unmarked Russian soldiers seized key sites across Crimea following the ouster of Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych. Russia organized a referendum on 16 March 2014, held under military occupation and not observed by credible international monitors, and formally annexed Crimea two days later. The UN General Assembly (Resolution 68/262) declared the referendum invalid and affirmed Ukraine's territorial integrity; tens of thousands fled to mainland Ukraine, and Crimean Tatars in particular have faced ongoing repression, including prosecutions and disappearances documented by UN and Council of Europe monitors.
contested: Russia asserts Crimea is historically Russian territory and that the referendum reflected the will of its population; Ukraine and most states regard the annexation as an illegal use of force and violation of the 1994 Budapest Memorandum's security assurances, and do not recognize Russian sovereignty over the peninsula.

sources.title: UN General Assembly Resolution 68/262, Territorial integrity of Ukraine (2014) - UN Digital Library
OHCHR: Situation of human rights in the temporarily occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea and Sevastopol (A/HRC/53/64)
HRW: Rights in Retreat - Abuses in Crimea

deathsNote: The seizure of Crimea was accomplished with very little loss of life and no source establishes a meaningful death range. Human Rights Watch's 2014 report documented at least 14 abductions or enforced disappearances of Crimean Tatars and pro-Ukrainian activists, of whom at least two were later found dead — including the activist Reshat Ametov — and a small number of Ukrainian servicemen were killed in isolated incidents; HRW characterised the pattern as intimidation and harassment rather than large-scale killing.

atrocityFindings.body: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)
atrocityFindings.finding: Ukraine v. Russia (re Crimea), judgment of 25 June 2024: Russia held responsible for an administrative practice of violations of most substantive Convention provisions in occupied Crimea, including that courts applying Russian law there were not 'established by law' under Article 6

violenceNote: Human Rights Watch's 'Rights in Retreat: Abuses in Crimea' (2014) documented at least 14 abductions and enforced disappearances, torture including electric shocks and beatings by 'self-defence' units, unlawful detention, and the coercive imposition of Russian citizenship on residents; the ECtHR's 2024 Grand Chamber judgment found an administrative practice of such violations, which Russia rejects.
baselineWhat: The population of Crimea, including Sevastopol, at the time of the 2014 annexation
baselineNote: Ukrainian statistics for early 2014 gave about 1.97 million in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and about 385,000 in Sevastopol; the Russian-conducted census of October 2014 counted 2,284,769 in the peninsula as a whole. Ethnic Russians were about 65 per cent, Ukrainians about 16 per cent and Crimean Tatars about 12 per cent at the 2001 Ukrainian census.

baselineSources.title: Annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The affected figure counts those who left for mainland Ukraine and registered as displaced, chiefly Crimean Tatars and Ukrainians; the whole population came under changed sovereignty, so the percentage measures flight, not the reach of the annexation.

title: War in Donbas
actors: Russian-backed separatists proclaiming the 'Donetsk' and 'Luhansk People's Republics', supported by Russian personnel and materiel, fought Ukrainian government forces in eastern Ukraine
peopleRange: roughly 1.5-2 million people displaced within Ukraine by the mid-2010s, plus contested Russian claims of hosting over 1 million refugees from the region
territoryDesc: Parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts held by Russian-backed separatists from 2014, prior to Russia's full recognition and further seizure of territory in 2022

flows.label: Donetsk/Luhansk → government-controlled Ukraine
Donetsk/Luhansk → Russia

summary: Following Russia's annexation of Crimea, Russian-backed armed groups seized government buildings and territory in Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts in spring 2014, proclaiming separatist 'people's republics.' Ukrainian forces fought to contain the separatists in a war that, despite the 2014 and 2015 Minsk agreements, settled into a low-intensity but continuous conflict along a roughly 400-kilometer front until Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The war displaced an estimated 1.5-2 million people, including over a million registered by Russian authorities as arrivals, a figure Ukrainian and Western analysts say reflects coerced relocation in part by Russian authorities, a figure Ukraine and Western analysts view partly as involving coerced relocation.
contested: Russia denied direct military involvement in Donbas throughout the period despite extensive documentation, including from the Joint Investigation Team into the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17, which found Russian military involvement; Ukraine and Western governments describe the war as a Russian-directed proxy conflict, and figures for refugee flows to Russia are disputed given allegations of coercion.

sources.title: OSCE Special Monitoring Mission to Ukraine (closed) - reports archive
Joint Investigation Team: MH17 investigation (Dutch Police)
UNHCR: Ukraine emergency

deathsNote: OHCHR's estimate for the pre-February-2022 conflict is 14,200-14,400 killed in total, comprising at least 3,404 civilians (including the 298 killed aboard flight MH17), around 4,400 Ukrainian forces and around 6,500 members of armed groups. This total is frequently misquoted — notably in Russian official statements — as 14,000 civilian deaths, which OHCHR's own breakdown contradicts.
violenceNote: The OHCHR Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine documented arbitrary and incommunicado detention, credible torture allegations including electrocution, and cases meeting the definition of enforced disappearance in territory held by the self-proclaimed republics.
baselineWhat: The combined population of Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts at the start of 2014
baselineNote: The State Statistics Service of Ukraine recorded 4,343,900 residents of Donetsk oblast and 2,239,500 of Luhansk oblast on 1 January 2014. Both figures were themselves estimates rolled forward from the 2001 census, Ukraine's last.
shareCaveat: The two million combines people registered as internally displaced inside Ukraine with those who left for Russia, and registration was tied to benefits, so double-counting and lapsed registrations make the total uncertain.

title: ISIS Territorial Seizure and the Yazidi Genocide in Sinjar
actors: The Islamic State (ISIS) seized large swaths of Iraq and Syria in 2014, declaring a self-styled 'caliphate'; its August 2014 assault on Sinjar targeted the Yazidi religious minority with mass killings, abductions, and sexual enslavement, subsequently recognized as genocide by the UN and several national governments and courts.
peopleRange: About 200,000 people, mostly Yazidis, fled the Sinjar area in early August 2014; an estimated 5,000 Yazidis (some studies put the range at 2,100–4,400) were killed and 5,000–10,800 women and girls were abducted, many enslaved; ISIS's broader 2014 advance displaced several million Iraqis and Syrians
territoryDesc: At its territorial peak in 2014–2015, ISIS controlled an estimated 100,000 km2 across Iraq and Syria, home to some 8 million people, before losing all held territory by March 2019.

flows.label: Sinjar → Sinjar Mountain (initial flight)
Sinjar → Duhok/Zakho, Iraqi Kurdistan
Sinjar → northeast Syria (Hasakah area)

summary: In summer 2014, ISIS swept across northern and western Iraq, capturing Mosul and large parts of Syria to declare a self-proclaimed 'caliphate' that at its peak controlled roughly 100,000 km2 and around 8 million people. On 3 August 2014, ISIS fighters attacked the Yazidi-majority Sinjar region, killing an estimated 5,000 Yazidi men, abducting thousands of women and girls into sexual slavery, and forcing roughly 200,000 people to flee, tens of thousands to the barren Sinjar Mountains where many died of thirst and exposure before a US-backed air campaign and Kurdish ground forces opened a corridor to safety. The UN, the US, and other governments and courts have formally recognized these acts as genocide against the Yazidi people. ISIS was militarily defeated as a territorial entity by 2017 in Iraq and 2019 in Syria, though displaced Yazidi and other communities have only partially returned to Sinjar, and an insurgency has continued at lower intensity.
contested: Death and enslavement figures rely on survivor testimony and demographic extrapolation, producing a wide estimated range; while genocide recognition of the Sinjar atrocities is now widespread, accountability for perpetrators and the fate of thousands still missing remain unresolved.

sources.title: Yazidi genocide
Yazda: The Yazidi Genocide
PBS Frontline: Where Are the Yazidis Almost a Decade After ISIS's Genocidal Campaign?

deathsNote: The only survey-based estimate is Cetorelli et al. (PLOS Medicine, 2017), a retrospective household survey which put Yazidi deaths in August 2014 at 3,100 (95% CI 2,100-4,400) — about 1,400 executed by shooting, beheading or burning and about 1,700 dying on Mount Sinjar from starvation, dehydration or injury during the siege — alongside 6,800 kidnapped (95% CI 4,200-10,800). The authors note the survey undercounts families with no survivors. Kurdistan Regional Government and Yazidi organisations, and figures repeated by UN officials, give totals around 5,000 killed, which is the basis for the upper bound; mass-grave exhumations by UNITAD and Iraqi authorities remain incomplete.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic
atrocityFindings.finding: In 'They came to destroy: ISIS Crimes Against the Yazidis' (A/HRC/32/CRP.2), determined that ISIS is committing genocide against the Yazidis, as well as crimes against humanity and war crimes: 'Genocide has occurred and is ongoing'

atrocityFindings.body: UNITAD (UN Investigative Team to Promote Accountability for Crimes Committed by Da'esh/ISIL)
atrocityFindings.finding: Told the Security Council on 10 May 2021 that there is 'clear and convincing evidence' that ISIL's crimes against the Yazidis in Sinjar constitute genocide

atrocityFindings.body: Higher Regional Court of Frankfurt, upheld by the German Federal Court of Justice
atrocityFindings.finding: Convicted the ISIS member Taha Al-J. of genocide against the Yazidis and sentenced him to life imprisonment — the world's first genocide conviction for the Yazidi case; confirmed on appeal in a decision published in January 2023

violenceNote: The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria's 2016 report documents killings, sexual slavery, enslavement, forced conversion, separation of families and the transfer of Yazidi children to ISIS fighters; UNITAD reached the same conclusions in 2021, and Cetorelli et al. (PLOS Medicine, 2017) estimated that about 1,700 of the roughly 3,100 dead died of starvation, dehydration or injury during the siege of Mount Sinjar.
baselineWhat: The Yazidi population of Iraq in 2014, concentrated in the Sinjar district and the Shekhan area
baselineNote: Iraq's last full census was in 1987, so the Yazidi population is estimated from ration-card registers, KRG administrative data and community organisations; figures for 2014 generally run between 400,000 and 550,000, with the great majority in Sinjar district. UN investigators recorded roughly 6,400 Yazidis abducted in August 2014 and some 3,100 killed.

baselineSources.title: Genocide of Yazidis by the Islamic State — Wikipedia

shareCaveat: The 350,000 counts the displacement of the Sinjar population as a whole, which included Yazidis, Sunni and Shia Arabs, Turkmen and Christians, while the genocide charge concerns the Yazidis specifically; the two should not be read as the same population.

title: Yemen War and Mass Displacement
actors: Houthi (Ansar Allah) forces seized the capital Sanaa in 2014–2015, prompting a Saudi- and UAE-led coalition military intervention on behalf of the internationally recognized Yemeni government; the resulting war has produced one of the world's largest humanitarian crises.
peopleRange: An estimated 4.5 million people remain internally displaced as of the mid-2020s, out of more than 6 million displaced at some point since 2015
territoryDesc: Houthi forces control much of northern and western Yemen (roughly a third of the country's land area but the majority of its population), including the capital Sanaa, while the internationally recognized government and allied forces hold the south and east.

flows.label: Sanaa area → Marib (IDP influx)
Hodeidah → Taiz
Taiz → Aden

summary: Houthi forces, drawn from Yemen's Zaidi Shia minority, captured Sanaa in 2014 and forced out the government of President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, who fled to Saudi Arabia. In March 2015, a Saudi- and UAE-led coalition began a military intervention, including a prolonged air campaign and naval blockade, to restore the government, precipitating years of grinding conflict, famine conditions, and a cholera epidemic. Over 4.5 million Yemenis remain internally displaced as of the mid-2020s, out of more than 6 million displaced at some point during the war, with front-line cities such as Hodeidah, Taiz, and Marib absorbing large IDP populations. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 substantially reduced large-scale fighting, but the country remains split between Houthi-controlled northern territories and government/coalition-aligned areas in the south, and a comprehensive political settlement had not been reached as of 2026.
contested: Responsibility for civilian harm — including coalition airstrikes, the blockade's effect on famine, and Houthi conduct such as landmine use and blocking aid — is disputed among the warring parties, and total displacement and death tolls (including indirect famine- and disease-related deaths) vary substantially between UN agencies and parties to the conflict.

sources.title: UNHCR Yemen Protection Brief (December 2024)
UNHCR: Yemen Crisis Explained
IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix: Yemen

deathsNote: UNDP's 2021 'Assessing the Impact of War in Yemen' estimated 377,000 deaths attributable to the conflict by the end of 2021, of which 154,000 were direct deaths from combat and violence and 223,000 indirect deaths from hunger, disease and the collapse of health services — nearly 60 per cent indirect, and about 259,000 of the total among children under five. The low end of the range is the direct-death figure, close to the event-based tallies compiled by ACLED; the high end is the modelled total including indirect deaths, and the two are not interchangeable. Both figures stop at end-2021 and the war has continued; parties to the conflict dispute the apportionment of responsibility rather than the aggregate.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: UN Group of Eminent International and Regional Experts on Yemen (Human Rights Council)
atrocityFindings.finding: Third report, 'A Pandemic of Impunity in a Tortured Land': violations amounting to war crimes committed by all parties — the Government of Yemen, the Houthis, the Southern Transitional Council and the Saudi- and UAE-led coalition — including indiscriminate attacks, arbitrary deprivation of life, enforced disappearance, torture, sexual violence and child recruitment; the Group urged UN Security Council referral of the situation to the ICC. The Group's mandate was not renewed by the Human Rights Council in October 2021 after lobbying by Saudi Arabia and its allies

violenceNote: Documented by the UN Group of Eminent International and Regional Experts on Yemen in its September 2020 report, which attributed arbitrary deprivation of life and murder of civilians, enforced disappearance, arbitrary detention, torture and gender-based including sexual violence to all parties to the conflict.
baselineWhat: The population of Yemen when the war began
baselineNote: UN estimates put Yemen at about 26.5 million in 2014; the last census was in 2004, which counted 19.7 million. The population is now estimated above 34 million.
shareCaveat: The figure is a stock of people currently displaced, not a cumulative count; many Yemenis have been displaced repeatedly, and the population has grown by roughly a third since the baseline year.
asOfNote: IOM and UNHCR have put Yemen's internally displaced at roughly 4.5 million since 2022-23 and the figure has moved little; access constraints in Houthi-controlled areas make it approximate.

title: Burkina Faso's Displacement Crisis
actors: Jihadist groups affiliated to JNIM and Islamic State in the Sahel, the Burkinabè army and the pro-government Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland have attacked and besieged civilian communities, producing one of the world's largest internal displacement crises
peopleRange: Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 states that by August 2024 the conflict had forced over 2.3 million people from their homes, of whom 2.1 million were displaced inside Burkina Faso and over 200,000 had fled abroad. UNHCR cites over 2 million internally displaced at the end of 2024 on government figures, with over one million recorded returns. The Burkinabè authorities stopped publishing official displacement data in 2023, so more recent figures are humanitarian estimates. In 2023 the Norwegian Refugee Council counted almost 2 million IDPs and 800,000 people living under armed-group blockade, half of them in the town of Djibo.

flows.label: Sahel and Centre-Nord regions → Ouagadougou and southern towns
Eastern Burkina Faso → Niger (Tillabéri)
Southern Burkina Faso → northern Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire

summary: Jihadist violence spreading from Mali reached Burkina Faso from 2015 and escalated sharply after 2018, producing what became, in proportion to population, one of the largest internal displacement crises in the world. Human Rights Watch reported that by August 2024 more than 2.3 million people had been forced from their homes, 2.1 million of them inside the country. Both sides have attacked civilians: HRW recorded Islamist armed groups killing 1,004 civilians in 259 attacks between January and August 2024, and the army and the pro-government Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland killing at least 1,000 civilians between January and July 2024, including the summary execution of at least 223 civilians, among them 56 children, at Nondin and Soro in February 2024, and up to 400 civilians during operations in April and May. Islamist groups have besieged dozens of towns, cutting inhabitants off from food and aid; the Norwegian Refugee Council reported 800,000 people under blockade in 2023, half in Djibo. Two military coups in 2022 did not reverse the trend, and the government has restricted humanitarian access and expelled journalists and aid organizations. The same conflict system has displaced hundreds of thousands in western Niger's Tillabéri region.
contested: The military governments that took power in 2022 dispute international reporting on army and militia massacres and have suspended media outlets that carried it; official displacement statistics ceased to be published in 2023, so current totals rely on humanitarian estimates that the authorities have not endorsed.

sources.title: World Report 2025: Burkina Faso — Human Rights Watch
Burkina Faso — UNHCR
Burkina Faso is the world's most neglected crisis — Norwegian Refugee Council

deathsNote: No cumulative death toll has been established. Human Rights Watch's documented figures for a single eight-month period in 2024 — 1,004 civilians killed by Islamist armed groups and at least 1,000 by the army and pro-government militias — indicate a scale of several thousand civilian deaths per year, but there has been no mortality survey and access restrictions prevent systematic counting.
violenceNote: Documented by Human Rights Watch, which recorded summary executions by the army and the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland and mass attacks by Islamist groups, and by the Norwegian Refugee Council, which documented the blockade of towns cutting inhabitants off from food and aid.
baselineWhat: The population of Burkina Faso at the national census of 2019
baselineNote: Burkina Faso's fifth general census, held in 2019, counted 20,505,155 residents; the country's population has since grown to roughly 23-24 million.

baselineSources.title: Burkina Faso — Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre

asOfNote: The junta stopped publishing CONASUR's registration data after March 2023, when 2,062,534 internally displaced people were recorded; later totals of about 2.1 million are estimates by humanitarian agencies and the real figure is widely believed to be higher.

title: Europe's External Border: Hotspot Detention, Containment and Pushbacks
actors: European Union member states and Frontex confined arriving asylum seekers in island hotspots and closed centres, contained them in transit countries under bilateral deals, and conducted summary returns at land and sea borders
peopleRange: About 1.01 million people reached Europe by sea in 2015 and roughly 1.3 million asylum applications were lodged in the EU that year — UNHCR arrival tracking and Eurostat application data respectively, both direct counts. Arrivals fell after the March 2016 EU-Turkey statement and the closing of the Balkan route but have continued at 100,000-300,000 a year. Containment figures are separately documented: the Moria centre on Lesbos, built for about 3,000 people, held roughly 20,000 in early 2020 before it burned in September of that year.
territoryDesc: Reception and identification centres on the Greek Aegean islands and in southern Italy, closed controlled-access centres from 2021, and fenced land borders at Evros, Melilla and Ceuta and along the Poland-Belarus frontier.

flows.label: Aegean crossings from Turkey to the Greek islands
Central Mediterranean crossings from Libya to Lampedusa

summary: After more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean in 2015, the European Union adopted a containment approach built on island hotspots in Greece and Italy, the March 2016 statement with Turkey, and cooperation with Libyan and other authorities to intercept departures. Asylum seekers were held for extended periods in facilities far beyond their capacity — Moria on Lesbos held roughly 20,000 people in a site designed for 3,000 before it burned in 2020 — and from 2021 in new closed controlled-access centres with restricted entry and exit. Human rights bodies including the Council of Europe's Commissioner for Human Rights, UNHCR and the EU's own anti-fraud office have documented summary returns without asylum assessment at the Greek-Turkish, Croatian, Spanish and Polish borders, which the states concerned deny or defend as border protection. IOM's Missing Migrants Project has recorded more than 30,000 deaths and disappearances in the Mediterranean since 2014. The system is Europe's largest contemporary confinement regime and was absent from the atlas.
contested: Whether interceptions and summary returns at the EU's borders constitute unlawful refoulement and collective expulsion, as UNHCR, the Council of Europe's Commissioner for Human Rights and numerous NGOs argue, or lawful border enforcement, as Greece, Croatia, Poland and Spain maintain; and the extent of Frontex's involvement, examined in a 2022 OLAF investigation.

sources.title: Mediterranean Situation — UNHCR Operational Data Portal
European migrant crisis — Wikipedia
Moria refugee camp — Wikipedia

deathsNote: IOM's Missing Migrants Project has recorded upwards of 25,000 deaths and disappearances in the Mediterranean since 2014 from confirmed reports; the higher end reflects IOM's own caution that many shipwrecks leave no survivors to report them, so the recorded total is a minimum. Deaths inside reception facilities are counted separately by national authorities and are far smaller.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: UNHCR, the Council of Europe's Commissioner for Human Rights and the Greek and Italian ombudsman institutions have documented prolonged detention of asylum seekers in the hotspot and closed-centre system.
baselineWhat: The people who arrived irregularly at the European Union's external borders from 2015 onward
baselineNote: UNHCR's operational data record about 1.03 million Mediterranean sea arrivals in 2015 alone and a cumulative total of roughly 2.5-3 million sea and land arrivals to Europe between 2015 and the mid-2020s; Frontex detection figures for the same period are higher because they count crossings rather than people. There is no resident population that this event acts on, so arrivals are the only meaningful denominator.

baselineSources.title: UNHCR Operational Data Portal: Mediterranean situation

shareCaveat: Both numerator and denominator are cumulative flows over a decade rather than population stocks, so the percentage is a share of arrivals held or pushed back, not a share of any resident population.
asOfNote: Detention, containment and pushback figures are compiled from national and NGO monitoring and continue to change with each year's arrivals and with EU policy, including the pact on migration and asylum now entering force.

title: Venezuelan Refugee and Migrant Crisis
actors: Economic collapse, hyperinflation, and political repression under the Chávez and Maduro governments drove sustained mass emigration from Venezuela, accelerating sharply after 2017
peopleRange: over 7.9 million Venezuelans have left the country as of 2025-26 (UNHCR/R4V), one of the largest displacement crises in the world, with some estimates exceeding 8 million

flows.label: Venezuela → Colombia
Venezuela → Peru
Venezuela → United States

summary: Since roughly 2015, and accelerating sharply from 2017 onward, an economic collapse marked by hyperinflation, shortages, and political repression under President Nicolás Maduro has driven one of the largest displacement crises in recent history. As of 2025-26, over 7.9 million Venezuelans, close to a quarter of the country's population, have left the country, with Colombia, Peru, Brazil, Ecuador, Chile and the United States hosting the largest numbers. The crisis has strained host-country services across Latin America and produced one of the world's largest cross-border displacement flows outside a formal war zone.
contested: The Maduro government attributes the crisis primarily to US and international sanctions; most independent economists, the opposition and many international observers attribute it chiefly to government economic mismanagement and corruption, with sanctions viewed as a contributing but secondary factor.

sources.title: R4V: Refugees and Migrants from Venezuela
UNHCR: Venezuela situation
USA for UNHCR: Venezuela Crisis

deathsNote: No significant death toll is attributable to the emigration itself; the harm is displacement and destitution, with UNHCR and the R4V inter-agency platform counting roughly 7.7-7.9 million refugees and migrants who have left Venezuela. Two adjacent tolls are sometimes conflated with it and should be kept separate: the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela recorded 5,094 killings by security forces in 2,552 incidents (2014-2019, not all necessarily unlawful) as part of the repression that drove emigration, and IOM's Missing Migrants Project documents deaths on the Darién Gap route, which are not disaggregated by nationality. The Maduro government rejects the Fact-Finding Mission's findings and disputes the migration figures as inflated by sanctions-focused advocacy.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela
atrocityFindings.finding: Found reasonable grounds to believe crimes against humanity were committed — extrajudicial executions, enforced disappearances, arbitrary detention and torture — pursuant to State policies with the knowledge of senior officials

violenceNote: These forms were documented by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela (2020) in the state repression that drove the emigration — extrajudicial executions, enforced disappearances, arbitrary detention and torture including sexual violence — not in the movement of people itself.
baselineWhat: The population of Venezuela in 2015, at the start of the mass exodus
baselineNote: UN Population Division and World Bank estimates put Venezuela's population at roughly 30.1 million in 2015. Venezuela has held no census since 2011, and the emigration itself has since reduced the resident population, with estimates for the mid-2020s ranging from about 28 to 30 million depending on how emigrants are treated.

baselineSources.title: Refugees and Migrants from Venezuela — R4V (UNHCR/IOM Inter-Agency Platform)

shareCaveat: The R4V total is a stock of Venezuelans currently outside the country, not a cumulative count of departures, and it includes returnees and onward movers; because emigration has itself shrunk the resident population, the share of Venezuelans abroad relative to those remaining is higher than the ratio to the 2015 baseline.
asOfNote: The headline figure is the R4V inter-agency population estimate as of its February 2026 update and is revised every few months.

title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency and Displacement, Mozambique
actors: An Islamist insurgency known locally as al-Shabaab and claimed by the Islamic State has attacked towns and villages in northern Mozambique, and government forces and Rwandan and SADC troops have fought it, emptying much of Cabo Delgado province
peopleRange: UNHCR states that displacement exceeded one million people at the peak of the conflict in 2021–22 and that over 582,000 were still displaced in northern Mozambique as of January 2024, with about 632,400 having returned since the military intervention of July 2021. ACAPS counted approximately 834,300 internally displaced and 420,200 returnees across the three affected provinces as of April 2023. The figures come from IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix and UNHCR operational monitoring; ACAPS notes that reported numbers fluctuate between sources and that data is limited by restricted access and press freedom.

flows.label: Northern Cabo Delgado → Pemba and southern districts
Cabo Delgado → Nampula province

summary: Attacks by an Islamist insurgency began in Mocímboa da Praia in October 2017 and escalated into a war across northern Cabo Delgado, a province where major offshore gas projects were under development. Insurgents seized towns, burned villages and beheaded civilians; government forces and, from 2021, Rwandan and SADC contingents pushed them back from the main towns without ending the insurgency. ACAPS recorded more than 2,000 fatalities, mostly civilians, and over one million people displaced as of April 2023, counting both those still displaced and those who had returned. UNHCR reports displacement exceeding one million at the 2021–22 peak, with more than 582,000 still displaced in January 2024 and around 632,400 returns since July 2021. Renewed attacks in 2024 and 2025 displaced further waves. Access restrictions, limited press freedom and government reluctance to acknowledge the conflict's severity have left the data incomplete.
contested: The insurgency's relationship to the Islamic State and the weight of local grievances over land, exclusion and the gas industry as against transnational jihadism are debated among analysts; the Mozambican government has been criticized for understating the conflict's scale.

sources.title: Displaced people in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado plead for peace — UNHCR
Mozambique: impact of the five-year conflict in Cabo Delgado — ACAPS thematic report, July 2023
Mozambique — Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC)

deathsNote: ACAPS records more than 2,000 fatalities, mostly civilians, from violence since 2017; this is a floor drawn from event monitoring. Event datasets that include combatant deaths give substantially higher totals. ACAPS itself notes limited and fluctuating data because of restricted access and constrained reporting from the province, so no upper bound is established.
violenceNote: Attacks on civilians and the burning of villages and towns are documented by ACAPS and UNHCR.
baselineWhat: The population of Cabo Delgado province at the 2017 Mozambican census, taken as the insurgency began
baselineNote: Mozambique's National Statistics Institute counted 2,333,278 in Cabo Delgado in the census of August 2017, the month before the first attack at Mocimboa da Praia. Displacement recorded by IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix rose to about 946,000 in northern Mozambique by early 2022, the peak, then fell with large-scale returns before renewed attacks in Chiure, Ancuabe and Macomia drove fresh waves from 2024 onwards; the cumulative figure of about a million counts people displaced at least once.
shareCaveat: Displacement in Cabo Delgado is highly cyclical: large numbers have returned home and been displaced again, so a cumulative total counts the same people more than once and a point-in-time total is much lower than a million.
asOfNote: IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix and OCHA continue to revise northern Mozambique displacement figures through 2026 as returns and new attacks alternate.

title: Cameroon's Anglophone Crisis
actors: Cameroonian security forces and armed Anglophone separatist groups have fought in the North-West and South-West regions, both attacking civilians and driving them into the bush, into other regions and into Nigeria
peopleRange: Figures have varied widely with access and methodology. The Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect cites at least 334,098 internally displaced in the two Anglophone regions and more than 76,493 refugees in Nigeria; OCHA and UNHCR assessments in 2019–2021 put IDPs from the crisis at over 700,000 at peak, and UNHCR counted 969,000 IDPs nationwide as of 30 June 2025 across all of Cameroon's crises, including the Lake Chad and CAR-related displacement counted elsewhere in this atlas. A central estimate of roughly half a million displaced by the Anglophone conflict specifically is defensible; all figures are humanitarian operational estimates, not registrations.

flows.label: North-West and South-West Cameroon → Cross River State, Nigeria
South-West → Douala and the Littoral

summary: Protests by Anglophone lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's North-West and South-West regions in late 2016 against the use of French in courts and schools were met with force; by 2017 armed separatist groups had declared an independent 'Ambazonia' and a full insurgency was under way. The Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect records more than 6,500 people killed since 2016 and states the real figure is believed to be higher, with at least 334,098 internally displaced and more than 76,493 refugees in Nigeria. Security forces have been documented committing extrajudicial killings, sexual violence, arbitrary detention, torture and the burning of villages; separatists have killed, kidnapped and extorted civilians, imposed an education boycott and attacked schools, students, teachers, health facilities and aid workers. UNHCR counted 969,000 internally displaced people in Cameroon as of mid-2025 across all of the country's crises. The conflict has attracted little international attention and no international judicial process.
contested: The Cameroonian government rejects characterizations of the conflict as a war and disputes casualty and displacement figures produced by UN agencies and human rights organizations; responsibility for specific massacres, such as Ngarbuh in February 2020, was initially denied by the government before a partial official admission.

sources.title: Cameroon — Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect
Cameroon — UNHCR

deathsNote: The Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect cites over 6,500 killed since 2016 and states that the actual number is believed to be higher; the figure aggregates event-based conflict monitoring rather than a systematic count, and no upper bound has been established because much of the affected countryside is inaccessible to monitors.
violenceNote: These forms are attributed to state security forces and, apart from the burning of villages, to separatist groups by the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect, drawing on UN and human rights organization reporting.
baselineWhat: The population of Cameroon's North-West and South-West regions at the start of the crisis
baselineNote: Cameroonian statistical projections from the 2005 census put the North-West at roughly 2 million and the South-West at about 1.5 million in the mid-2010s - some 3.5 million people, close to a fifth of the national population. No census has been held since 2005, so regional figures are projections.
shareCaveat: The affected figure is cumulative displacement since 2017 and exceeds the number displaced at any one time; many have moved repeatedly between bush, towns and other regions.
asOfNote: ACAPS recorded over 334,000 people internally displaced within the North-West and South-West and more than 76,000 refugees in Nigeria as of February 2025, well below cumulative totals because of repeated returns and re-displacement.

title: Displacement in Eastern DR Congo
actors: Fighting between the Congolese army, the M23 movement backed by Rwanda according to UN experts, and scores of other armed groups has repeatedly uprooted civilians across North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri
peopleRange: about 5 million internally displaced and roughly 8.2 million forcibly displaced in total as of 2026, among the largest displacement crises in the world; figures move sharply with each offensive

flows.label: North Kivu → Rwanda
South Kivu → Burundi
Ituri → Uganda

summary: Eastern DR Congo has been in near-continuous conflict since the Second Congo War formally ended, with more than a hundred armed groups active across North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri. The resurgence of the M23 movement from 2021, which UN groups of experts have reported receiving Rwandan military support, drove repeated mass flight around Goma, culminating in the group's capture of Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. Roughly 5 million people are internally displaced and about 8.2 million forcibly displaced in total, making this one of the largest and least-reported displacement crises in the world. Displacement here is highly repetitive: many families have fled multiple times, and camps around Goma have been overrun and emptied more than once.
contested: Rwanda denies the UN experts' findings that it arms and directs M23, and displacement counts fluctuate sharply between agencies and with each offensive.

sources.title: UNHCR Global Appeal 2026 – Democratic Republic of the Congo situation
IDMC – Democratic Republic of the Congo country profile
UN OCHA – Democratic Republic of the Congo

deathsNote: No consolidated count exists for this phase. The Kivu Security Tracker (Human Rights Watch and the Congo Research Group) recorded about 1,900 civilians killed and more than 3,300 abducted by over 130 armed groups in the Kivus in its first two years alone (June 2017-June 2019); the UN Human Rights Office documented hundreds of civilian killings in single months of 2025, including 319 by M23 and Rwandan forces in Rutshuru in July 2025 and 70 by the ADF in Ituri in one attack. DRC's prime minister said more than 7,000 people were killed in the east in the first weeks of 2025, a figure well above UN verified counts for the fall of Goma, and Rwanda denies the UN experts' finding that it backs M23. Compilations of ACLED event data across all armed actors since 2017 run to the tens of thousands.

atrocityFindings.body: UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR)
atrocityFindings.finding: Statement of the High Commissioner, August 2025, documenting the killing of 319 civilians by M23 and Rwanda Defence Force members in Rutshuru in July 2025, mass killings of worshippers and farmers by the ADF in Ituri, and rape by armed groups in South Kivu; Rwanda and M23 reject the attributions

violenceNote: The UN Human Rights Office, the Kivu Security Tracker (Human Rights Watch and the Congo Research Group) and Human Rights Watch documented summary executions of civilians by M23 in Goma, mass killings by the ADF and CODECO, rape, mass abductions including of children recruited by armed groups, and the burning and looting of homes, shops and villages.
baselineWhat: The population of the eastern provinces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo — North and South Kivu, Ituri and Tanganyika
baselineNote: The DRC has had no census since 1984, so provincial figures are projections: the four eastern provinces most affected by the fighting are estimated to hold roughly 25 million people out of a national total of about 100 million. Displacement in the east has run between five and seven million people in recent years, the largest internal displacement crisis in Africa, and rose sharply after the M23 offensives that took Goma and Bukavu in early 2025.

baselineSources.title: UNHCR Operational Data Portal: Democratic Republic of the Congo

shareCaveat: Displacement here is highly repetitive — hundreds of thousands of people are displaced several times a year and many return between episodes — so the headline figure counts displacements as much as distinct people.
asOfNote: The displacement figure is drawn from OCHA and UNHCR monitoring during the M23 offensive and its aftermath and changes month to month as front lines shift and populations return.

title: Ethiopia's Mass Internal Displacement of 2017-2019
actors: Communal and regional conflict along the Oromia-Somali and Gedeo-West Guji boundaries drove the largest new internal displacement in the world in 2018
peopleRange: The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre recorded about 2.9 million new internal displacements in Ethiopia in 2018, the highest figure of any country that year; the Norwegian Refugee Council reported 1.4 million in the first half of 2018 alone, of which around one million were in Gedeo and West Guji and about 200,000 along the Oromia-Somali boundary, while IOM's displacement tracking identified 970,000 displaced in Gedeo and West Guji by September 2018. Figures come from IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix rounds, NRC field reporting and IDMC's annual compilation, and are movement counts rather than distinct individuals.

flows.label: Gedeo displacement from West Guji into Gedeo zone
Oromo and Somali displaced across the Oromia-Somali regional boundary

summary: Between 2017 and 2019 Ethiopia experienced the largest new internal displacement of any country in the world, driven by conflict along the boundary between the Oromia and Somali regions, in which regional special police forces were implicated and hundreds of thousands of Oromo and Somali residents were expelled in both directions, and by the outbreak of violence between Gedeo and Guji Oromo communities in April 2018, which displaced up to 970,000 people into Gedeo zone in a matter of weeks. Further displacement followed in Benishangul-Gumuz, in the Amhara-Tigray boundary areas and around Addis Ababa. The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre recorded around 2.9 million new displacements in 2018 alone, and the Norwegian Refugee Council reported in September 2018 that Ethiopia had more newly displaced people in the first half of that year - 1.4 million - than any other country. From 2019 the federal government pursued a rapid returns programme; the Norwegian Refugee Council, Human Rights Watch and humanitarian agencies reported that returns were in places pressured or premature and that assistance was withdrawn from people who had not returned voluntarily, which the government denied. The displacement crisis preceded and partly shaped the later Tigray war, which is recorded separately.
contested: Whether the 2019 returns were voluntary is disputed between the Ethiopian federal government and humanitarian organisations; displacement counts are movement figures and overstate distinct individuals.

sources.title: Norwegian Refugee Council: Ethiopia tops global list of highest internal displacement in 2018
IOM identifies 970,000 displaced people in Ethiopia's Gedeo and West Guji
Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre: Ethiopia

deathsNote: No reliable death toll exists for the 2017-19 communal violence. Reported killings in the Oromia-Somali and Gedeo-West Guji conflicts run into the hundreds to low thousands in media and human rights reporting, but no systematic count was made and the displacement, not the killing, was the defining feature.
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch and the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission documented the burning of homes and killings of civilians during the Oromia-Somali and Gedeo-West Guji violence.
baselineWhat: The combined population of Ethiopia's Oromia, Somali and Southern Nations (SNNP) regions, where the displacement occurred
baselineNote: Central Statistical Agency projections from the 2007 census put Oromia at about 35.5 million, SNNPR at 19.2 million and the Somali region at 5.7 million for 2017-18, roughly 60.4 million of Ethiopia's then 105-109 million. Ethiopia has not held a census since 2007, so all regional figures are projections and the Somali region's in particular is contested.
shareCaveat: IDMC counts new displacements rather than displaced people, so anyone displaced more than once during 2017-19 is counted more than once; a large share of those displaced from Gedeo and West Guji were also returned under government pressure within months, in returns the UN did not consider voluntary.

title: Rohingya Confined in the Cox's Bazar Camps, Bangladesh
actors: Bangladeshi authorities holding Rohingya refugees from Myanmar in fenced camps under an encampment policy that grants no formal refugee status and no right to work
peopleRange: Close to one million Rohingya across 33 camps in Cox's Bazar district plus Bhasan Char, on joint Government of Bangladesh-UNHCR registration data as of mid-2026; around 750,000 arrived in the August 2017 exodus, joining roughly 200,000-300,000 already present from earlier waves, and an estimated 150,000 further arrivals were recorded in 2024-2025 as fighting spread in Rakhine State
territoryDesc: 33 camps in Ukhiya and Teknaf sub-districts, Cox's Bazar, including the contiguous Kutupalong-Balukhali expansion site, one of the largest refugee settlements in the world, plus the silt island of Bhasan Char in the Bay of Bengal

flows.label: Cox's Bazar → Bhasan Char

summary: Bangladesh is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention and treats the Rohingya as "forcibly displaced Myanmar nationals" rather than refugees, confining them to camps in Cox's Bazar under a policy that bars formal employment, restricts access to Bangla-language and accredited education, and requires permission to leave the camp area.
