From 2019 the authorities erected barbed-wire perimeter fencing around the camps and installed watchtowers and checkpoints, which the government described as a security and anti-trafficking measure and which humanitarian organisations said impeded movement and cost lives during fires and floods. From December 2020 the government relocated refugees to Bhasan Char, a low-lying island roughly 60 km offshore developed to decongest the camps; some 34,500 people were living there as of December 2025, and movement between the island and the mainland requires official permission through a process that Fortify Rights in January 2026 described as opaque and arbitrary. Bangladesh states that all relocations were voluntary and that the island offers better living conditions than the congested mainland camps; Fortify Rights and other groups documented misleading inducements and threats and characterise the arrangement as de facto arbitrary detention. As of 2026 there has been no verified voluntary repatriation to Myanmar, funding shortfalls have cut rations and services, and the population continues to grow through new arrivals and births.
contested: Disputed points include whether the relocations to Bhasan Char were genuinely voluntary, whether the island regime amounts to arbitrary detention or to a legitimate decongestion and development programme, whether the camp fencing is a protection measure or a confinement measure, and whether Bangladesh's refusal to grant refugee status and work rights is a lawful sovereign policy given its non-party status to the Refugee Convention or a breach of customary international law.

sources.title: UNHCR Operational Data Portal - Bangladesh (Rohingya refugee response)
Fortify Rights: Bangladesh - Close Bhasan Char, End Rohingya Island Detention Policy (21 January 2026)
UK Home Office, Country Policy and Information Note: Rohingya, Burma (January 2026)

deathsNote: Both fields are null because the encampment policy itself has no aggregate death toll. Deaths occur from camp fires, landslides — Human Rights Watch reported fatal landslides in July 2026 — armed-group violence inside the camps, and sea crossings by those attempting to leave, but no body aggregates these as a toll of confinement, and the mass killing that produced this refugee population is counted under Myanmar's 2016-17 clearance operations.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps
violenceNote: Human Rights Watch documents that over a million Rohingya are held in camps under unsafe conditions with violence by armed groups and security forces, behind barbed-wire fencing and movement restrictions, with some relocated to the isolated island of Bhasan Char under conditions refugees describe as confinement.
baselineWhat: The Rohingya population of northern Rakhine State, Myanmar, before the expulsion of August 2017, from which the camp population is drawn
baselineNote: Myanmar's 2014 census excluded people identifying as Rohingya and the government published an estimate of about 1,090,000 non-enumerated residents in Rakhine State. Bangladesh had already been hosting some 200,000-300,000 Rohingya from earlier expulsions before the 2017 influx of roughly 750,000.
shareCaveat: The camp population includes people who arrived before 2017 and children born in the camps since, so it is not simply a subset of the 2017 Rakhine baseline.
asOfNote: UNHCR's Bangladesh operation reports close to one million Rohingya refugees as of 30 June 2026, a figure that has risen with new arrivals since 2024 as fighting in Rakhine State intensified.

title: Xinjiang Internment and Re-education System
actors: Chinese state and Xinjiang regional authorities holding Uyghurs, Kazakhs and other Turkic Muslims in extrajudicial "vocational education and training centres" and, later, in the formal prison system
peopleRange: Most external estimates of those held in the VETC system at its 2017-2019 peak cluster around "at least one million", with an upper bound of roughly 1.5-1.8 million; these rest on leaked Chinese police and government files, budget and construction tenders, satellite imagery of 380-plus suspected facilities identified by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, and extrapolation from county-level data in Kashgar and Hotan. OHCHR stated in August 2022 that it was "not in a position to confirm estimates of total numbers of individuals affected". China stated in 2020 that an average of 1.3 million people a year had received "vocational training" between 2014 and 2019 and that all trainees had "graduated".
summary: From 2017 Chinese authorities in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region built a network of facilities in which large numbers of Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities were held without criminal charge, trial or judicial review, initially denied and from October 2018 described by the government as lawful "vocational education and training centres" for counter-terrorism and de-extremification. Detention was triggered by conduct such as praying, travelling abroad, contacting relatives overseas or possessing religious material, flagged in part through a regional data-aggregation platform. The OHCHR assessment of 31 August 2022 concluded that "a pattern of large-scale arbitrary detention occurred in VETC facilities, at least during 2017 to 2019, affecting a significant proportion of the Uyghur and other predominantly Muslim ethnic minority community", and that the underlying legal framework remained intact and "could be re-engaged at any point". From about 2019 the system shifted toward formal imprisonment through the criminal courts and toward state-organised labour-transfer schemes moving workers within Xinjiang and to factories in other provinces; ASPI documented over 80,000 such transfers in 2017-2019 and later reporting has documented further movements. China maintains that the centres have closed, that all trainees graduated into employment, that participation in labour programmes is voluntary poverty alleviation, and that external accounts are fabrications by hostile states; it rejects the OHCHR assessment as unlawful and politically driven. As of 2026 there is no independent access to the region, no accountability mechanism has been created, and OHCHR has said that aspects of the labour-transfer programmes may amount to forcible transfer and/or enslavement as crimes against humanity.
contested: Nearly every element is disputed: the number detained (from China's account of voluntary trainees to external estimates above a million), whether the facilities were schools or places of detention, whether labour transfers are voluntary employment or coercion, and the correct legal label - OHCHR said the violations "may constitute international crimes, in particular crimes against humanity" while declining to use the word genocide, the United States and several parliaments have adopted genocide determinations, other governments including many members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation have publicly endorsed China's counter-terrorism framing, and a 2022 Human Rights Council vote declined even to debate the OHCHR findings.

atrocityFindings.finding: OHCHR Assessment of human rights concerns in Xinjiang: the extent of arbitrary and discriminatory detention of Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities 'may constitute international crimes, in particular crimes against humanity'; credible allegations of torture, forced medical treatment and sexual and gender-based violence

atrocityFindings.finding: Resolution of 20 January 2022 recognising China's treatment of Uyghurs as crimes against humanity and genocide; the United States and several other parliaments have adopted comparable determinations, while China denies the allegations and has refused independent UN access

violenceNote: The OHCHR's 2022 Xinjiang assessment found credible allegations of large-scale arbitrary detention, patterns of torture and ill-treatment including forced medical treatment, and incidents of sexual and gender-based violence, recommended investigation of forced-labour allegations, and documented far-reaching restrictions on religious practice; Amnesty International has documented the same categories and China rejects the findings.

baselineNote: China's 2010 census recorded 10.0 million Uyghurs, 1.42 million Kazakhs and about 190,000 Kyrgyz in Xinjiang; projecting forward gives roughly 12-13 million Turkic Muslims at the start of the internment campaign. Chinese official statistics after 2017 are disputed, with researchers including Adrian Zenz arguing that birth-suppression policies have depressed subsequent counts.

title: Al-Hol and Roj Camps, North-East Syria
actors: Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces and their civil administration holding families associated with the Islamic State group, mostly women and children, without charge or judicial review; the Syrian government took over al-Hol in January 2026
peopleRange: Al-Hol peaked at about 73,000 residents in 2019 after the fall of Baghouz; it held around 24,000-28,000 at the start of 2026, comprising roughly 14,500 Syrians, 4,000 Iraqis and about 6,200-12,500 third-country nationals depending on the count used, of whom more than 95 per cent of the foreigners were women and children; Roj held about 2,300 foreign women and children in February 2026, and around 8,500 people were unaccounted for after the al-Hol departures
territoryDesc: Two fenced camps in Hasakah governorate, north-east Syria: al-Hol near the Iraqi border and the smaller Roj camp near Derik/al-Malikiyah, both with guarded perimeters and annexes for foreign nationals
summary: After the territorial defeat of the Islamic State group in 2019, tens of thousands of people who had left the group's last enclaves were held in fenced camps in north-east Syria run by the Kurdish-led authorities, principally al-Hol and the smaller Roj, which housed foreign nationals from more than sixty countries. Residents, the overwhelming majority of them women and children and almost none of them charged with any offence, could not leave; conditions were life-threatening, with killings inside al-Hol, inadequate water and medical care, and children making up around two-thirds of the population. The Kurdish-led administration described the camps as a security necessity and repeatedly asked states to repatriate their nationals, which many did slowly or not at all, citing security and evidentiary difficulties; Iraq began organised returns of its citizens to a transit facility from 2021. Following a military offensive in the north-east that forced the Syrian Democratic Forces to withdraw, Syrian government security forces took control of al-Hol on 20-21 January 2026 and announced its full evacuation by 22 February; departures were largely unplanned, with residents leaving by bus, on foot and with smugglers, and by mid-February the population had fallen to the low thousands. Human Rights Watch, which had described the detention as arbitrary and unlawful, warned that the chaotic manner of the closure exposed people to trafficking, exploitation and armed-group recruitment, and that thousands were unaccounted for. Roj remained under SDF control in early 2026 and was expected to close.
contested: Disputed are whether holding uncharged family members constituted arbitrary detention or a necessary security measure in the absence of any functioning judicial process, whose responsibility the foreign nationals were - the Kurdish-led administration, the states of nationality, or the coalition members supporting the SDF - and whether the 2026 evacuation amounted to a release from unlawful detention or a security failure that dispersed a population without screening or protection.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch: Northeast Syria - Camp Closures Leave Thousands Stranded (23 February 2026)
Al Jazeera: Exodus of ISIL-linked detainees from Syria camp sparks security concerns (17 February 2026)

deathsNote: There is no comprehensive cumulative death toll for the camps. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria reported in September 2019 that at least 390 children had died at al-Hol from malnutrition and untreated wounds amid 'hundreds of preventable deaths', and the Kurdish Red Crescent, cited by Human Rights Watch, documented at least 371 child deaths in al-Hol in 2019 alone; the UN separately recorded 90 murders inside al-Hol in 2021 and 42 between January and mid-November 2022. The upper figure reflects the accumulation of these documented categories rather than a single source's total.
deathsBasis: deaths in transit or in camps

atrocityFindings.finding: Reported that up to 70,000 people, the vast majority women and children under 12, were interned at al-Hol in 'deplorable and inhumane conditions' with a 'woefully inadequate' humanitarian response, and identified a shared responsibility of Member States that refuse repatriation, with thousands of children unregistered and at risk of statelessness

The affected figure is the camps' own peak population, about 73,000 in al-Hol in 2019, of whom roughly half were Iraqis and about a fifth third-country nationals.

asOfNote: Al-Hol was emptied and formally closed on 22 February 2026 after the Syrian government took control of the site in January; about 8,500 people remained in the camp system at that point, including some 2,300 foreign women and children still held at Roj.

title: Belarus since 2020: Mass Detention and the Post-Election Exodus
actors: Belarusian security forces detained, prosecuted and imprisoned protesters and critics, prompting large-scale emigration
peopleRange: OHCHR recorded at least 37,000 people detained between May 2020 and May 2021, about 13,500 of them in the six days from 9 August 2020; the human rights centre Viasna and other monitors counted between 1,000 and roughly 1,500 recognised political prisoners at different points from 2021 onward. On emigration, a 2026 study using EU residence-permit and social-security data estimates 400,000-418,000 Belarusian citizens living and working abroad by the end of 2024, including 265,000-282,000 permanently resident in the EU, most having arrived in 2020-2024; Poland and Lithuania account for over 90 per cent of the EU total. Not all of this movement is political, and the estimates are modelled rather than counted.

flows.label: Belarusians to Poland
Belarusians to Lithuania
Belarusians to Georgia

summary: After the disputed presidential election of 9 August 2020, mass protests in Belarus were met with a sustained police and security response. The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights reported that at least 37,000 people were detained between May 2020 and May 2021, and found that torture and ill-treatment of detainees were widespread and systematic, recommending that the pattern be assessed under international criminal law; independent monitors including Viasna, whose own leaders were imprisoned, have listed over a thousand people held on politically motivated charges at any given time since. Independent media, trade unions and non-governmental organisations were liquidated, and opposition figures were prosecuted in absentia. A large emigration followed, concentrated in Poland, Lithuania and Georgia, with recent estimates putting the number of Belarusians living abroad at around 400,000 by the end of 2024, more than four per cent of the population, at an estimated cost of over three per cent of GDP. The Belarusian government denies that it holds political prisoners, describing those convicted as having committed criminal offences including extremism, and has periodically pardoned or released groups of prisoners.
contested: The Belarusian authorities reject the characterisation of the detentions as arbitrary or politically motivated and dispute the findings of UN and non-governmental monitors; estimates of emigration are modelled from residence and employment data and mix political and economic movement.

atrocityFindings.finding: Examination of the human rights situation in Belarus found torture and ill-treatment of detainees to be widespread and systematic and concluded that the scale and patterns of violations required further assessment under international criminal law

baselineNote: Belstat, the national statistical committee, recorded 9,349,645 residents on 1 January 2020. asOfNote: Emigration and political imprisonment both continue; the emigration estimate is compiled from destination-country residence permits and is revised as those series are updated.

title: Second Nagorno-Karabakh War
actors: Azerbaijan, using Turkish-made drones and reportedly Syrian mercenaries, launched a 44-day offensive against Armenian/Karabakh Armenian forces; Russia brokered a ceasefire and deployed peacekeepers
peopleRange: roughly 90,000-100,000 ethnic Armenians displaced from Nagorno-Karabakh during and after the fighting
territoryDesc: Azerbaijan recaptured most of the seven districts surrounding Nagorno-Karabakh and part of Nagorno-Karabakh itself, including the town of Shusha/Shushi

flows.label: Nagorno-Karabakh → Armenia (wartime displacement)

summary: In September-November 2020, Azerbaijan launched a large-scale offensive to reclaim territory lost in the 1990s, using Turkish drones and, according to multiple observers, Syrian mercenaries. The 44-day war ended with a Russian-brokered ceasefire on 10 November 2020 under which Azerbaijan regained most of the seven surrounding districts and part of Nagorno-Karabakh itself, and Russian peacekeepers were deployed to the remaining Armenian-held core. Roughly 90,000-100,000 ethnic Armenians were displaced, some temporarily and some permanently, and both sides faced documented allegations of abuses, including videos of mistreatment of prisoners of war.
contested: Armenia and international monitors criticized Azerbaijan's and Armenia's respective use of cluster munitions and mistreatment of POWs; Azerbaijan frames the war as the liberation of its internationally recognized territory, while Armenia and Karabakh Armenians describe territorial losses and continued insecurity for the remaining Armenian population.

sources.title: International Crisis Group: The Nagorno-Karabakh Conflict - A Visual Explainer
HRW: Azerbaijan - Unlawful Strikes in Nagorno-Karabakh
HRW: Armenia - Unlawful Rocket, Missile Strikes on Azerbaijan

deathsNote: Armenia's defence ministry ultimately acknowledged 3,825 servicemen killed and 187 missing and Azerbaijan 2,906 killed, with roughly 185 civilians killed on the two sides combined; the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights separately documented at least 541 Syrian fighters recruited by Turkey killed, which Azerbaijan and Turkey deny were present at all, accounting for most of the gap between the low and high ends.

baselineNote: The Artsakh census of 2015 counted about 145,000 people, 99.7% of them Armenian. The territory's population was reported at roughly 120,000 by 2021 and was almost entirely emptied after Azerbaijan's September 2023 offensive.
shareCaveat: The 90,000 counts people displaced during the 44-day war, most of whom returned within months; the near-total depopulation of Karabakh came with the 2023 offensive, a separate event.

title: Tigray War
actors: The Ethiopian federal government, with allied Eritrean and Amhara regional forces, fought the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) for control of Ethiopia's Tigray region
peopleRange: an estimated 2.5-2.7 million people were internally displaced within Tigray, with hundreds of thousands more affected in neighboring Amhara and Afar regions; death toll estimates vary enormously and are heavily disputed, ranging from roughly 162,000 up to an African Union mediator's estimate of about 600,000

flows.label: Tigray → Hamdayet, Sudan
Tigray → Shire (internal displacement camps)

summary: War broke out in November 2020 between Ethiopia's federal government under Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the regional ruling party, after months of rising tension; Eritrean forces and Amhara regional militia fought alongside the federal army. The conflict was marked by widespread reports of massacres, sexual violence used as a weapon of war, and a de facto blockade of Tigray that contributed to famine-like conditions; a UN-mandated International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia found reasonable grounds to believe multiple parties, including Eritrean forces, committed war crimes, crimes against humanity, and acts amounting to ethnic cleansing. An estimated 2.5-2.7 million people were internally displaced within Tigray at the conflict's height. A November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement ended major hostilities, though Eritrean forces and disputed territorial control in western Tigray have complicated implementation, and death toll estimates remain unusually wide-ranging and contested.
contested: Death toll estimates are strongly disputed, ranging from roughly 162,000 in some studies to an African Union mediator's estimate near 600,000; a UN-mandated commission found evidence of ethnic cleansing and other atrocities by multiple parties, a characterization contested by the Ethiopian and Eritrean governments.

sources.title: OCHA: Ethiopia - Internal Displacement Overview (June 2024)
Wikipedia: Casualties of the Tigray war
Africa Center for Strategic Studies: Rising Tensions in Tigray Risk Regional Conflict

deathsNote: There has been no census-based mortality study. Researchers at Ghent University, combining violence, famine and collapse of medical access, estimated 162,000-378,000 deaths; the African Union's chief mediator Olusegun Obasanjo publicly cited about 600,000, the figure most often quoted at the upper end. A peer-reviewed diaspora survey published in Population Health Metrics (2025) estimated more than 102,000 excess deaths among those aged 15 and over (95% CI 17,455-159,382), of which 72% were from intentional injury and 28% from starvation or disease, while cautioning that its urban, higher-wealth sample probably understates the toll; Uppsala's battle-related fatality series records over 100,000 for 2022 alone. The Ethiopian federal government disputes the higher figures and has published no count of its own, while Tigrayan authorities and diaspora organisations favour the 500,000-600,000 range.
deathsBasis: excess mortality incl. disease and starvation

atrocityFindings.body: International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (ICHREE), UN Human Rights Council
atrocityFindings.finding: Found war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by parties to the conflict, including systematic rape and sexual violence, and warned of an acute risk of further atrocity crimes (A/HRC/51/46, 2022; A/HRC/54/55 and the comprehensive findings and legal determination A/HRC/54/CRP.3, 2023); Ethiopia rejected the Commission's mandate and successfully lobbied against its renewal

atrocityFindings.body: United States Department of State (Secretary Antony Blinken)
atrocityFindings.finding: Stated on 10 March 2021 that 'acts of ethnic cleansing' had been committed in western Tigray and called for full accountability; the Ethiopian government publicly rejected the characterisation

violenceNote: The UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia documented 'mass killings, rape, starvation, destruction of schools and medical facilities, forced displacement and arbitrary detention', singling out systematic rape and sexual violence by Eritrean troops and Amhara militia and recording the arrest, detention and torture of civilians.
baselineWhat: The population of Ethiopia's Tigray region on the eve of the war
baselineNote: The 2007 Ethiopian census counted 4,316,988 in Tigray and the Ethiopian Statistical Service's projection for 2022 is 5,738,996. Figures of 6-7 million are also cited, and no census has been held since 2007; the region's wartime population is further complicated by the expulsion of Tigrayans from Western Tigray.
shareCaveat: Displacement also affected neighbouring Amhara and Afar, whose populations are not in this denominator, so the numerator draws on a wider base than the baseline covers.

title: Gang Control and Mass Displacement in Haiti
actors: Armed gangs seized control of most of Port-au-Prince and stretches of the Artibonite and Centre departments, driving residents out amid state collapse
peopleRange: About 1.4 million internally displaced by September 2025, roughly double the previous year, according to OCHA's 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan; displacement passed 1 million in January 2025, up from about 520,500 in September 2024 (IOM/DG ECHO).

flows.label: Port-au-Prince → Centre department (Hinche and surrounds)
Port-au-Prince → Grand'Anse and the southern peninsula

summary: After the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, armed gangs consolidated control over most of the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and expanded into the Artibonite and Centre departments, using killings, arson and sexual violence to clear neighbourhoods. Internal displacement rose from about 520,500 people in September 2024 to more than 1 million in January 2025 and roughly 1.4 million by September 2025, close to one in eight Haitians, with about 69 per cent of recorded movements occurring outside the capital. The UN Human Rights Office recorded 5,601 people killed, 2,212 injured and 1,494 kidnapped in gang violence in 2024, including a massacre in Cité Soleil in early December in which at least 207 people, mostly elderly, were killed; it also documented 315 lynchings and 281 summary executions by specialised police units over the same year. Three-quarters of the displaced shelter with host families in the provinces, and the rest largely in formal sites in the capital. OCHA projected 6.4 million people needing emergency assistance in 2026 with only about 10 per cent of inpatient health facilities nationally still fully operational.
contested: Responsibility is contested in that the UN documents both gang atrocities and unlawful killings by police units and by vigilante 'bwa kale' mobs, and the displacement figures rest on IOM site and household tracking in areas that are frequently inaccessible, so totals are revised substantially between rounds.

The UN treats its own figures as a floor, since insecurity prevents verification in gang-held areas.

violenceNote: Both forms are documented in the UN Human Rights Office's 2024 figures for Haiti, which record gang massacres including the Cité Soleil killings and 281 summary executions attributed to specialised police units.

baselineNote: UN estimates and IHSI projections put Haiti at roughly 11.7-11.9 million in the mid-2020s; the last full census was in 2003. Displacement is concentrated in the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area (about 2.8 million) and the Artibonite and Centre departments, but IOM reports the displaced total nationally.

title: Myanmar Civil War Displacement Since the 2021 Coup
actors: Myanmar's military (Tatmadaw), which seized power in a February 2021 coup, has fought an expanding array of resistance forces and ethnic armed organizations, driving mass internal displacement and refugee flight
peopleRange: close to 4 million internally displaced as of early 2026, the large majority displaced after the February 2021 coup, plus roughly 1.5 million who have fled to Thailand, India, Bangladesh and elsewhere

flows.label: Sagaing Region → Thailand border (Mae Sot)
Kayin (Karen) State → Mae Sot, Thailand
Chin State → Mizoram, India

summary: Myanmar's military seized power from the elected civilian government in February 2021, triggering nationwide protests that the military suppressed with lethal force, followed by an expanding armed conflict as newly formed "People's Defense Forces" allied with long-standing ethnic armed organizations across the country. Fighting, airstrikes, and village burnings have driven mass displacement, with the UN recording roughly 3.48 million internally displaced people as of late 2024, about 3.21 million of them displaced since the coup, concentrated in Sagaing, Kayin, Kayah, Chin, and Rakhine regions. Hundreds of thousands more have crossed into Thailand, India, and Bangladesh as refugees. The conflict, combined with a collapsing economy, has produced Myanmar's largest displacement crisis in decades, compounding earlier internal displacement including the Rohingya crisis in Rakhine State.
contested: Myanmar's military government disputes casualty and displacement figures reported by the UN, opposition National Unity Government, and independent trackers, and characterizes much of the fighting as a response to "terrorism" by resistance forces, a framing rejected by opposition and rights groups.

Myanmar Emergency Update (as of end November 2024)
Myanmar

ACLED and the reporting around it stress there is no official toll and that event-based monitoring undercounts; the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners maintains a much smaller separate count restricted to individually verified civilians killed by the junta. Because no upper-bound survey or excess-mortality study has been published, the figure is presented as a documented floor rather than a range.

baselineNote: The 2014 census counted 51.5 million, with parts of Rakhine State excluded from enumeration; UN estimates give about 54 million for 2021. The junta's 2024 census was only partially conducted and its results are not treated as reliable.

title: 2021 Taliban Takeover and Afghan Displacement
actors: The Taliban seized control of Afghanistan as US and NATO forces withdrew in August 2021, triggering internal displacement and refugee flight, later compounded by large-scale expulsions of Afghans from Pakistan and Iran
peopleRange: roughly 700,000 newly displaced inside Afghanistan in 2021 alone, on top of a pre-existing displaced population of several million; since late 2023 Pakistan and Iran have returned or expelled some 5.4 million Afghans, including about 2.9 million during 2025

flows.label: Afghanistan → Pakistan (post-2021 refugee flight)
Pakistan → Afghanistan (forced returns/expulsions, 2023–2025)
Afghanistan → Iran

summary: As US and NATO forces completed their withdrawal in August 2021, the Taliban rapidly seized control of Afghanistan, prompting a new wave of displacement, including an estimated 700,000 people newly displaced within the country that year alone amid the collapse of the Afghan government and subsequent economic crisis. Hundreds of thousands of Afghans, including former government employees, security personnel, and members of at-risk groups, fled or sought evacuation abroad, mainly to Pakistan and Iran. From 2023 onward, Pakistan and, separately, Iran launched large-scale campaigns to expel undocumented Afghan migrants and refugees, together returning well over 2 million people to Afghanistan under often difficult conditions, even as the country continued to face a humanitarian and economic crisis under Taliban rule.
contested: Total displacement and return figures are disputed and fluctuate as reporting continues; Pakistan and Iran describe their expulsion campaigns as enforcement against undocumented or unregistered migrants, while UN agencies and Afghan advocacy groups describe many of the returns as forced and occurring amid unsafe or precarious conditions in Afghanistan.

sources.title: UNHCR, Afghanistan Refugee Crisis Explained
UN News, Afghanistan: 270,000 newly displaced this year, warns UNHCR (2021)
House of Commons Library, Afghanistan: Refugees and displaced people

deathsNote: No comprehensive count exists for the period after 15 August 2021. The ISKP suicide bombing at Kabul airport on 26 August 2021 killed over 180 people (169 Afghans and 13 US service members); UNAMA has documented several hundred extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrests, cases of torture and enforced disappearances of former government officials and security force personnel, and Human Rights Watch documented the same pattern in its 2021-22 investigations; ISKP attacks on Hazara Shia mosques, schools and neighbourhoods have killed hundreds more. Far larger mortality attributed to the post-2021 economic collapse, banking sanctions and aid cuts is not counted here, and the Taliban authorities dispute UNAMA's findings.
violenceNote: UNAMA's human rights reporting and Human Rights Watch documented extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, arbitrary detention and torture of former Afghan National Defence and Security Forces members and former government officials after August 2021, despite the Taliban's declared amnesty.
baselineWhat: The population of Afghanistan when the Taliban took power
baselineNote: UN Population Division estimates put Afghanistan at about 40.1 million in 2021. IOM and UNHCR recorded roughly 700,000 newly internally displaced in 2021 alone on top of an existing 3.5 million IDP caseload, and several hundred thousand left the country; since late 2023, mass expulsions have run the other way, with UNHCR reporting 5.4 million Afghans returned from Iran and Pakistan.

baselineSources.title: UNHCR seeks support for solutions as 5.4 million Afghans return since late 2023 — UNHCR

shareCaveat: The numerator counts displacement caused by the takeover, while the dominant movement since 2023 has been forced return: more Afghans have been pushed back into the country by Iran and Pakistan than left it after August 2021, so the net direction of displacement has reversed.
asOfNote: UNHCR's briefing note of 13 February 2026 reports 5.4 million Afghans returned from Iran and Pakistan since October 2023, including 2.9 million during 2025; displacement and returnee figures are revised continuously.

title: El Salvador's State of Exception and Mass Incarceration
actors: The Salvadoran government suspended constitutional guarantees and detained tens of thousands of people without individualised charge in an anti-gang campaign
peopleRange: About 85,000 people detained since the state of exception was declared in March 2022, equal to roughly 1.4 per cent of the national population; Human Rights Watch estimates around 109,000 people held in a prison system built for about 70,000, and WOLA reports over 110,000 currently imprisoned. Over 3,300 of those detained have been children.
summary: El Salvador declared a state of exception in March 2022 after a weekend in which gangs killed dozens of people, suspending constitutional guarantees including the right to be informed of the reason for arrest and access to a lawyer. Security forces have since detained roughly 85,000 people, about 1.4 per cent of the population, largely on the basis of appearance, neighbourhood and anonymous tips rather than individualised evidence, and mass hearings have been conducted online with hundreds of defendants at a time. Human Rights Watch documented torture and severe beatings during arrest and detention, extreme overcrowding requiring detainees to sleep standing or on floors, immersion in ice water for up to two hours, denial of medication, and 66 cases of children subjected to torture and abusive conditions. Salvadoran human rights organisations record more than 350 deaths in state custody since March 2022, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights has documented torture and other cruel and inhuman treatment in detention centres. The government credits the policy with an over-80 per cent fall in homicides and it retains broad domestic support; the CECOT mega-prison at Tecoluca, designed for 20,000 and later expanded toward 40,000, has become the emblem of the policy and in 2025 received men deported from the United States. The measure has been renewed by the legislature every month since it began.
contested: What is disputed is not the number of arrests but their lawfulness and effect: the government presents the campaign as a lawful emergency that dismantled the gangs and cut homicides by over 80 per cent, while the Inter-American Commission, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Salvadoran organisations describe systematic arbitrary detention, torture and deaths in custody, with Amnesty arguing in 2026 that the pattern could amount to crimes against humanity.

title: Russia's Full-Scale Invasion of Ukraine
actors: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, occupying large areas of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts and purporting to annex them in September 2022

summary: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, the largest conventional war in Europe since 1945, and has occupied significant portions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts in addition to Crimea. In September 2022, Russia declared the annexation of four partially occupied oblasts, a move the UN General Assembly (Resolution ES-11/4) declared to have no validity under international law. As of early 2026, an estimated 5.9 million Ukrainians remain refugees abroad and about 3.7 million are internally displaced; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for President Vladimir Putin and Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia, with Ukraine estimating thousands of children affected.
contested: Russia denies wrongdoing regarding child transfers, describing them as evacuations for children's safety and welfare; Ukraine, the ICC and many governments characterize them as unlawful deportations amounting to a war crime; the ICJ has separate pending proceedings on genocide allegations Ukraine brought against Russia, and the scale of both battlefield casualties and total displacement is estimated variously by different sources.

deathsNote: No agreed total exists and both governments treat their own losses as classified. The low end is a documented floor: Mediazona and the BBC Russian Service had confirmed 236,000 named Russian military dead by 31 July 2026 (an acknowledged undercount), Ukraine's President Zelensky has publicly given a figure of about 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers killed, and OHCHR had verified 15,578 Ukrainian civilians killed as of the figure cited by Russia Matters in mid-2026. The high end reflects Western intelligence and CSIS estimates of Russian military casualties around 1,000,000 killed and wounded and Ukrainian casualties of 250,000-600,000, which imply combined deaths in the high hundreds of thousands. Russia disputes OHCHR's civilian figures and counters with its own claim of 8,012 civilians killed by Ukrainian action; Ukraine's official military-loss figures are widely regarded by Western analysts as understated.

title: The Mass Expulsion of Afghans from Pakistan and Iran
actors: Pakistan and Iran deported or pressured out millions of Afghan refugees and migrants after 2023
peopleRange: UNHCR reported in mid-2026 that more than six million Afghans had returned from Pakistan and Iran since late 2023, having earlier reported 5.4 million; Pakistan launched its Illegal Foreigners Repatriation Plan on 3 October 2023 with a 1 November deadline, and Iran ran parallel mass deportations that accelerated sharply in 2025. Figures come from UNHCR and IOM border monitoring at Torkham, Spin Boldak, Islam Qala and Milak, which count crossings rather than individuals, so repeat crossings and voluntary returns are included in the totals.

flows.label: Afghans expelled from Pakistan via Torkham and Spin Boldak
Afghans deported from Iran via Islam Qala and Milak

summary: Pakistan announced its Illegal Foreigners Repatriation Plan in October 2023, requiring undocumented foreigners - overwhelmingly Afghans, many born in Pakistan - to leave by 1 November or face deportation, and subsequently extended the policy in phases to holders of Afghan Citizen Cards and then to Proof of Registration cardholders. Iran, which hosted a larger Afghan population, ran parallel deportations that increased sharply in 2025. UNHCR reported more than six million returns and deportations from the two countries between late 2023 and mid-2026, the largest movement of Afghans since the 1980s, into a country under Taliban rule with a collapsed economy, restricted aid and severe restrictions on women and girls. UNHCR, IOM and human rights organisations including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have described elements of the campaigns as refoulement and documented arbitrary detention, property loss, extortion at checkpoints and family separation; Pakistan and Iran maintain that they are enforcing immigration law after decades of hosting refugees with limited international support. Returnees have concentrated in Kabul, Nangarhar, Kandahar and Herat, where humanitarian agencies report severe shortages of shelter, water and work.
contested: Whether the returns are voluntary or amount to refoulement is disputed between Pakistan and Iran on one side and UNHCR and human rights organisations on the other; border-crossing counts also overstate distinct individuals.

title: Gaza War: Mass Displacement since October 2023

peopleRange: UN OCHA estimated about 1.9 million people, roughly 90% of Gaza's 2.1 million population, were displaced at least once since October 2023, many repeatedly, some more than ten times

summary: After the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, which killed about 1,200 people and saw around 251 taken hostage into Gaza, Israel launched an extensive air and ground campaign against Hamas across the Gaza Strip. Israeli forces issued repeated evacuation orders, pushing the population south and then into ever-shrinking designated 'humanitarian' or 'safe' zones such as Al-Mawasi, while establishing military corridors, including the Netzarim and Philadelphi corridors, that fragmented the territory; UN OCHA estimated some 1.9 million people, about 90% of Gaza's population, were displaced at least once, many repeatedly. The offensive caused tens of thousands of deaths according to the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry (figures cited by the UN as broadly reliable) and widespread destruction of housing, hospitals, and infrastructure, alongside a severe hunger crisis. A ceasefire-and-hostage framework was reached in January 2025 followed by renewed fighting, and by 2026 the situation remained volatile, with large-scale displacement, destruction, and humanitarian access constraints continuing amid a partial and contested ceasefire process.
contested: Israel states its evacuation orders and buffer zones are necessary military measures to protect civilians and defeat Hamas, while the UN, HRW, Amnesty International, and other bodies have characterized the scale, repetition, and conditions of displacement as amounting to unlawful forced displacement; a genocide case brought by South Africa is pending before the ICJ, a characterization Israel rejects, and casualty/displacement figures from Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry and UN agencies are disputed by the Israeli government, which cites different combatant/civilian breakdowns.

deathsNote: The Gaza Ministry of Health recorded 73,770 Palestinians killed as of 3 May 2026; a January 2025 Lancet capture-recapture study found the ministry had undercounted trauma deaths by about 41%, and a November 2025 Max Planck Institute study estimated 100,000-126,000 violent deaths, 27% children under 15 and 24% women. All of these measure violent death; the separate July 2024 Lancet correspondence figure of 'up to 186,000' is an indirect-and-direct excess-mortality projection and is not comparable to a killed count, though it is frequently quoted as one. Israeli officials have disputed the ministry's figures, while an IDF official accepted a total above 71,000 in January 2026; 1,139 people were killed in Israel on 7 October 2023 and Israeli military fatalities passed 1,100 by late 2025.

title: 2023 Azerbaijani Offensive and Exodus of Karabakh Armenians
actors: Azerbaijan launched a rapid military offensive on 19-20 September 2023 after a nine-month blockade of the Lachin corridor, leading to the surrender and dissolution of the unrecognized Republic of Artsakh and the flight of nearly its entire population
peopleRange: over 100,600 ethnic Armenians (an estimated 99% or more of Nagorno-Karabakh's population) fled to Armenia between 24 September and 3 October 2023
territoryDesc: The remaining Armenian-held core of Nagorno-Karabakh, brought under full Azerbaijani control; the Republic of Artsakh formally dissolved on 1 January 2024

flows.label: Nagorno-Karabakh → Armenia (exodus, Sept-Oct 2023)

summary: After a roughly nine-month blockade of the Lachin corridor (the sole route between Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh) that the International Court of Justice ordered Azerbaijan to lift in February 2023, Azerbaijan launched a rapid military offensive on 19-20 September 2023 that led to the surrender of Karabakh Armenian forces. Within about ten days, over 100,600 ethnic Armenians, well over 99% of the enclave's population, fled to Armenia, and the unrecognized Republic of Artsakh dissolved itself on 1 January 2024. A fuel depot explosion during the exodus killed over 200 people, and dozens more died during the journey.
contested: The European Parliament, Council of Europe and several governments have characterized the exodus as ethnic cleansing, and some individuals and organizations (including a former ICC prosecutor) have alleged genocide; Azerbaijan denies these characterizations, states the departure was voluntary, and points to its offer of reintegration guarantees that Armenians did not trust given prior conduct.

sources.title: ICJ: Armenia v. Azerbaijan (CERD) - provisional measures on the Lachin Corridor
International Crisis Group: Armenia Struggles to Cope with Exodus from Nagorno-Karabakh

deathsNote: A Karabakh emergency-services official, Hunan Tadevosian, told RFE/RL that more than 200 Karabakh soldiers and about two dozen civilians were killed in the 19-20 September 2023 offensive, and that at least 220 died in the 25 September Berkadzor fuel-depot explosion during the exodus, with about 150 bodies burned beyond recognition and 50 people missing; Azerbaijan reported 192 of its own servicemen killed. The low end counts only Armenian military and civilian deaths in the offensive itself; the high end adds the fuel-depot disaster (a non-combat explosion at a distribution point during the flight) and Azerbaijani military losses. Armenian sources fold the depot deaths into the toll of the operation; Azerbaijan treats them as an accident unconnected to its 'anti-terror measures'.

Azerbaijan maintains the departure was voluntary and rejects the characterisation of the exodus as ethnic cleansing

title: Sudan War (SAF–RSF Conflict)
actors: The Sudanese Armed Forces under Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces under Gen. Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo fought for control of the state
peopleRange: more than 12 million people had been displaced by 2025, including over 8 million internally displaced and roughly 4 million refugees in Chad, Egypt, South Sudan and other neighboring countries, making it the world's largest displacement crisis; some figures began to decline slightly in 2025-26 as limited returns occurred

flows.label: Khartoum/Darfur → Adré, Chad
Khartoum → Egypt (Aswan/Cairo)

summary: Fighting erupted in April 2023 between Sudan's regular armed forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), former allies who had jointly staged a 2021 coup, after a dispute over the RSF's integration into the military. The war has devastated Khartoum and spread across the country, with especially severe atrocities in Darfur, including mass killings in El Geneina in 2023 and a prolonged RSF siege of El Fasher. By 2025 the conflict had displaced more than 12 million people, more than any other active crisis in the world, including over 8 million people displaced within Sudan and roughly 4 million refugees in Chad, Egypt, South Sudan and other neighboring states, alongside famine conditions confirmed in parts of Darfur. In January 2025, the United States government determined that the RSF had committed genocide against the Masalit and other non-Arab communities in Darfur.
contested: The U.S. State Department's January 2025 genocide determination against the RSF is disputed by the RSF and by Sudan's rival government; casualty figures for the war are considered a significant undercount given restricted humanitarian access, and estimates of the total death toll vary widely, from tens of thousands to potentially over 150,000.

sources.title: IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix: Two Years of Conflict in Sudan
UNHCR: Sudan Emergency
Migration Policy Institute: War-Torn Sudan Has Become the World's Leading Displacement Crisis

deathsNote: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine's capture-recapture study estimated more than 61,000 all-cause deaths in Khartoum State alone between April 2023 and June 2024, of which more than 26,000 were violent — the violent deaths in that one state exceeding ACLED's 20,178 recorded for the whole country at the time — and found that over 90 per cent of deaths went unrecorded. The same research group's national estimate for the first eighteen months was about 62,000 (roughly 18,900 direct and 43,500 indirect), rising to about 130,000 under a different indirect-to-direct multiplier, and the authors describe their own figure as very conservative. The US special envoy Tom Perriello told a Senate committee in 2024 that existing estimates of 15,000-30,000 could be an undercount by a factor of ten to fifteen and that 'some think it's 150,000'. All sources agree the true toll is higher and rising; ACLED's event-based tally is lower by design and should not be read as a total.

atrocityFindings.finding: Found war crimes and crimes against humanity by both the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces, including indiscriminate airstrikes and shelling of civilians and civilian infrastructure, rape and sexual slavery, arbitrary detention and torture, pillage, and the RSF's assaults on non-Arab communities, in particular the Masalit in and around El Geneina
